title: מבנה הסוגיות – Sanhedrin
note: חלוקה לסוגיות ולשלבי הדיון שנוצרה בבינה מלאכותית באתר talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).
note_de: KI-erzeugte Einteilung in Sugjot und Argumentationsschritte von talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum); englisch, hebräisch wo dort vorhanden.
note_en: AI-generated sugya sections and argument steps from talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Monetary cases require three judges
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Monetary cases require three judges
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins by listing cases that require three judges: monetary cases, thefts, injuries, and various fines.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that monetary cases require three judges.

items.text: Dispute on the number for מוציא שם רע
items.text_en: Dispute on the number for מוציא שם רע
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir holds that the case of the defamer of a bride requires three judges, but the Sages argue it requires twenty-three because it involves capital matters.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that cases of rape, seduction, and defamation of a bride require three judges, according to Rabbi Meir.
The Sages object that the defamer of a bride requires twenty-three judges because it involves capital matters.

items.text: Lashes require three, but Rabbi Yishmael says twenty-three
items.text_en: Lashes require three, but Rabbi Yishmael says twenty-three
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that lashes require three judges, but in the name of Rabbi Yishmael it is said they require twenty-three.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that lashes require three judges.

sub.text: Mishnah (in the name of Rabbi Yishmael)
sub.text_en: Mishnah (in the name of Rabbi Yishmael)
sub.desc_en: In the name of Rabbi Yishmael, it is said that lashes require twenty-three judges.

items.text: Intercalation of month and year
items.text_en: Intercalation of month and year
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses the number of judges needed for intercalating the month (three) and the year (three according to Rabbi Meir, but Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel prescribes a process starting with three, deliberating with five, and concluding with seven).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that intercalation of the month requires three judges, and intercalation of the year requires three judges according to Rabbi Meir.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel prescribes a process for intercalating the year: starting with three, deliberating with five, and concluding with seven, but if they finish with three, the year is intercalated.

items.text: Various cases requiring three judges
items.text_en: Various cases requiring three judges
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists additional cases requiring three judges: semikhah, eglah arufah, chalitzah, mi'un, neta revai, ma'aser sheni, hekdeshot, and movable valuations. Rabbi Yehudah adds that one of the three must be a kohen.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that semikhah (ordination) and eglah arufah (the broken-necked heifer) require three judges, according to Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Yehudah argues that these cases require five judges, not three.
The Mishnah adds that chalitzah (the release from levirate marriage) and mi'un (a minor's refusal of marriage) require three judges.

sub.text: Mishnah's list (neta revai, ma'aser sheni, hekdeshot, valuations)
sub.text_en: Mishnah's list (neta revai, ma'aser sheni, hekdeshot, valuations)
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists neta revai (fourth-year vineyard fruit), ma'aser sheni (second tithe) of unknown value, hekdeshot (consecrated items), and movable valuations as requiring three judges.
Rabbi Yehudah adds that one of the three judges for these cases must be a kohen (priest).

items.text: Land and human valuations require nine and a kohen
items.text_en: Land and human valuations require nine and a kohen
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that land valuations require nine judges and a kohen, and human valuations are similar.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that land valuations require nine judges and a kohen, and human valuations are similar.

items.text: Capital cases require twenty-three
items.text_en: Capital cases require twenty-three
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists capital cases requiring twenty-three judges: bestiality, a gored ox, and dangerous animals. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva offer differing views on dangerous animals.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that capital cases require twenty-three judges, listing bestiality and a gored ox with scriptural support.
Rabbi Eliezer states that for dangerous animals, anyone who kills them first acquires merit, implying no court trial is needed.
Rabbi Akiva disagrees and rules that dangerous animals also require a court of twenty-three judges for their execution.

items.text: Cases requiring the Great Sanhedrin of seventy-one
items.text_en: Cases requiring the Great Sanhedrin of seventy-one
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists matters that require the Great Sanhedrin of seventy-one: judging a tribe, a false prophet, the High Priest, declaring a discretionary war, expanding Jerusalem or the Temple courtyards, appointing Sanhedrins for tribes, and declaring an apostate city.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases requiring the Great Sanhedrin of seventy-one: judging a tribe, a false prophet, and the High Priest.
The Mishnah adds that declaring a discretionary war requires the Great Sanhedrin.
The Mishnah states that expanding Jerusalem or the Temple courtyards requires the Great Sanhedrin.
The Mishnah rules that appointing Sanhedrins for tribes requires the Great Sanhedrin.
The Mishnah concludes that declaring an apostate city requires the Great Sanhedrin, with restrictions on location and number.

items.text: Derivation of the sizes of the Great and Small Sanhedrin
items.text_en: Derivation of the sizes of the Great and Small Sanhedrin
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the size of the Great Sanhedrin (seventy-one) from the verse about Moses and the seventy elders, and the Small Sanhedrin (twenty-three) from the verses about the congregation judging and saving, with additional verses providing the numbers ten and three.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the sizes of the Great Sanhedrin (seventy-one) and the Small Sanhedrin (twenty-three).
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source for the Great Sanhedrin's size of seventy-one.
The Gemara cites the verse 'אספה לי שבעים איש' (Numbers 11:16) and adds Moses to reach seventy-one.
Rabbi Yehudah objects that the Great Sanhedrin is only seventy, excluding Moses.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source for the Small Sanhedrin's size of twenty-three.
The Gemara derives twenty judges from the verses 'ושפטו העדה' and 'והצילו העדה' (Numbers 35:24-25), each 'עדה' being ten.
The Gemara proves that 'עדה' means ten from the verse 'עד מתי לעדה הרעה הזאת' (Numbers 14:27), excluding Joshua and Caleb.
The Gemara asks for the source of the additional three judges to reach twenty-three.

The Gemara derives the three additional judges from the verses 'לא תהיה אחרי רבים לרעת' and 'אחרי רבים להטות' (Exodus 23:2), requiring a majority of at least two for a guilty verdict, thus needing a court of twenty-three.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Size of Sanhedrin and city population
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Size of Sanhedrin and city population
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a court must not be even-numbered, so they add one, totaling twenty-three. It then discusses the minimum city population for a Sanhedrin: one hundred twenty, or according to Rabbi Nechemya, two hundred thirty, corresponding to leaders of tens.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a court must not be even-numbered, so they add one, totaling twenty-three judges.
The Mishnah states the minimum city population for a Sanhedrin is one hundred twenty, according to the Tanna Kamma.
Rabbi Nechemya gives an alternative opinion: two hundred thirty, corresponding to leaders of tens.

items.text: Gemara's question: What are 'monetary laws'?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: What are 'monetary laws'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Are theft and damages not monetary laws? Rabbi Avahu explains that the Mishnah specifies theft and damages as examples, but admissions and loans are excluded. The Gemara clarifies that this distinction is necessary because the biblical source for three judges is specifically about theft and damages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Are theft and damages not monetary laws, so why does the Mishnah list them separately?
Rabbi Avahu explains that the Mishnah is specifying: 'What are monetary laws? Theft and damages,' but admissions and loans are excluded.

The Gemara explains why both terms are necessary: if only 'monetary laws' were taught, one might include admissions and loans; if only 'theft and damages,' one might think the same applies to admissions and loans, but the biblical source for three judges is specifically theft and damages.
The Gemara cites the biblical verse for theft and argues by analogy that damages are included, concluding that admissions and loans are excluded.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why distinguish?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why distinguish?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference this distinction makes. If it means that admissions and loans do not require three judges, that contradicts Rabbi Avahu's statement that two judges are invalid for monetary cases. Rather, it means that they do not require expert judges (מומחין).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference the mishna's distinction makes, suggesting that if it means admissions and loans do not require three judges, that contradicts Rabbi Avahu's ruling that two judges are invalid for monetary cases.
The Gemara answers that the distinction is that admissions and loans do not require expert judges (מומחין), unlike robbery and personal injury.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: The logic of requiring experts
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: The logic of requiring experts
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the underlying assumption: if one holds that the Torah sections are combined (עירוב פרשיות), then expert judges should be required even for admissions and loans. If not, why require three judges at all? It concludes that one holds they are combined, but expert judges are not required due to Rabbi Chanina's teaching that both monetary and capital cases require inquiry and examination by Torah law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Tanna of the Mishnah assumes: if he holds that the Torah sections are combined (עירוב פרשיות), then expert judges should be required even for admissions and loans; if not, why require three judges at all?

The Gemara resolves that the Tanna holds the sections are combined, but expert judges are not required because of Rabbi Chanina's teaching that both monetary and capital cases require inquiry and examination by Torah law.

items.text: Gemara's question on the rationale for not requiring interrogation
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the rationale for not requiring interrogation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why monetary cases do not require interrogation, and answers that it is to prevent locking the door before borrowers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why monetary cases do not require interrogation (דרישה וחקירה).
The Gemara answers that the reason is to prevent locking the door before borrowers (דלת בפני לוין).

items.text: Objection: If judges err, should they not pay?
items.text_en: Objection: If judges err, should they not pay?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if judges are not required to interrogate, they might err and not have to pay, which would also lock the door before borrowers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if judges are not required to interrogate witnesses, they might err and not have to pay, which would also lock the door before borrowers.

items.text: Resolution: The Mishnah teaches two categories
items.text_en: Resolution: The Mishnah teaches two categories
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah actually teaches two separate categories: monetary cases with three laymen, and thefts and injuries with three experts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah actually teaches two separate categories: monetary cases with three laymen, and thefts and injuries with three experts.

items.text: Further question: Why three for each?
items.text_en: Further question: Why three for each?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why three judges are needed for each category, implying a redundancy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists three judges for each category, implying redundancy.

items.text: Rava and Rav Acha's explanations
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Acha's explanations
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah teaches two categories due to Rabbi Chanina's teaching. Rav Acha bar Rav Ika says that from the Torah even one judge is valid, but the requirement for three is due to 'yoshvei kranot' (unqualified judges). The Gemara objects that even with three there could be unqualified judges, and that if they err they should not pay, which would increase the problem.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah teaches two categories (דיני ממונות and גזילות וחבלות) because of Rabbi Chanina's teaching.
Rav Acha bar Rav Ika states that from the Torah even one judge is valid, but the requirement for three is due to יושבי קרנות (unqualified judges).
The Gemara objects that even with three judges there could be unqualified judges, though it concedes that at least one is learned.
The Gemara further objects that if unqualified judges err they should not pay, which would increase the problem of יושבי קרנות.

items.text: Difference between Rava and Rav Acha
items.text_en: Difference between Rava and Rav Acha
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the practical difference between Rava and Rav Acha: whether they accept Shmuel's ruling that two judges' verdict is valid but they are called a 'brazen court'. Rava rejects Shmuel's ruling, while Rav Acha accepts it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between Rava and Rav Acha bar Rav Ika regarding the number of judges required for monetary cases.
The Gemara explains that the difference lies in their stance on Shmuel's ruling: Rava rejects Shmuel's view that two judges' verdict is valid but called a 'brazen court', while Rav Acha accepts it.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah's listing of damages
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah's listing of damages
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists 'nezek' (damage) and 'chazi nezek' (half-damage) separately, as they seem to overlap with 'chavalot' (injuries). It explains that 'nezek' is included because of 'chazi nezek', and 'chazi nezek' is a penalty. The Gemara then notes a dispute about whether 'chazi nezek' is a penalty or monetary, and concludes that the Mishnah lists it because of other penalties like double payment and four/five-fold payment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah lists 'nezek' (damage) and 'chazi nezek' (half-damage) separately, since they seem to overlap with 'chavalot' (injuries).
The Gemara answers that 'nezek' is included because the Mishnah wants to list 'chazi nezek' (half-damage), so it also lists full damage.
The Gemara objects that 'chazi nezek' (half-damage) also overlaps with 'chavalot' (injuries).
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah lists monetary cases (ממונא) and penalties (קנסא) separately.
The Gemara notes that this works for those who say 'chazi nezeka is a penalty' (פלגא ניזקא קנסא).
The Gemara asks what can be said for those who hold 'chazi nezeka is monetary' (פלגא ניזקא ממונא).

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah lists 'chazi nezek' because it wants to include other penalties like double payment (תשלומי כפל) and four/five-fold payment (תשלומי ארבעה וחמשה), which are monetary.

items.text: Transition from previous daf: half-damages as fixed payment
items.text_en: Transition from previous daf: half-damages as fixed payment
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that half-damages (חצי נזק) are a fixed payment not dependent on the offender's person, and the Tanna included 'damages' (נזק) alongside 'half-damages' for completeness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that half-damages (חצי נזק) are a fixed payment not dependent on the offender's person, and the Tanna included 'damages' (נזק) alongside 'half-damages' for completeness.

items.text: Derivation of three judges from verses
items.text_en: Derivation of three judges from verses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yoshiyah derives three judges from three occurrences of 'Elohim' in Exodus 22:7-8. Rabbi Yonatan rejects the first occurrence as a mere introductory phrase and derives two judges from the remaining two, then adds one to avoid an even-numbered court, totaling three.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source requiring three judges for monetary cases.
Rabbi Yoshiyah derives three judges from three occurrences of 'אֱלֹהִים' (Elohim) in Exodus 22:7-8.
Rabbi Yonatan rejects the first occurrence as a mere introductory phrase, derives two judges from the remaining two, and adds one to avoid an even-numbered court, totaling three.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: Do they dispute interpreting initial phrases?
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: Do they dispute interpreting initial phrases?
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the dispute is about whether to interpret initial phrases (תחילות). It concludes that both agree not to interpret them; Rabbi Yoshiyah argues the first 'Elohim' is extra and teaches a count, while Rabbi Yonatan says it is just common language.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Yoshiyah and Rabbi Yonatan is about whether one derives tallies from the first mention of a term in the Torah.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion, stating that everyone agrees one does not derive tallies from the first mention.
Rabbi Yoshiyah argues that the verse's use of 'אל האלהים' (to the court) instead of 'אל השופט' (to the judge) shows it is extra and intended to count toward the tally.
Rabbi Yonatan responds that the verse uses common language, as people say 'one who has a case should approach the judge,' so no unique halakha is derived from the first usage.

items.text: Challenge: Does Rabbi Yoshiyah reject a 'leaning court'?
items.text_en: Challenge: Does Rabbi Yoshiyah reject a 'leaning court'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Rabbi Yoshiyah seems to reject the concept of a 'leaning court' (בית דין נוטה) from a verse. It resolves that Rabbi Yoshiyah follows Rabbi Yehudah, who limits the leaning court to the Great Sanhedrin. Rabbi Yoshiyah applies the verse only to capital cases, not monetary ones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Rabbi Yoshiyah seems to reject the concept of a 'leaning court' (בית דין נוטה), citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives it from a verse.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yoshiyah follows Rabbi Yehudah, who limits the 'leaning court' to the Great Sanhedrin of seventy (not seventy-one).
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehudah's position about the 'leaning court' is only known regarding the Great Sanhedrin, not other courts.

The Gemara cites a baraita about semichat zekeinim (סמיכת זקנים) and עגלה ערופה (the broken-necked heifer), where Rabbi Yehudah requires five judges, showing he does apply the 'leaning court' principle to other courts.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yoshiyah is more stringent than Rabbi Yehudah: Rabbi Yehudah rejects the 'leaning court' only for the Great Sanhedrin, but Rabbi Yoshiyah rejects it for all courts, applying the verse only to capital cases (דיני נפשות).

items.text: Objection from Mishnah: majority rule in monetary cases
items.text_en: Objection from Mishnah: majority rule in monetary cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a Mishnah (Sanhedrin 3:2) rules by majority in monetary cases, implying three judges suffice. It answers that even Rabbi Yoshiyah agrees, deriving majority rule in monetary cases via a kal vachomer from capital cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a Mishnah ruling by majority in monetary cases contradicts Rabbi Yoshiyah's view that majority applies only in capital cases.
The Gemara answers that even Rabbi Yoshiyah agrees, deriving majority rule in monetary cases via a kal vachomer (קל וחומר) from capital cases.

items.text: Rabbi's view: five judges for monetary cases
items.text_en: Rabbi's view: five judges for monetary cases
items.desc_en: A baraisa states Rabbi requires five judges so that the verdict can be reached by three. Rabbi Avahu objects that this logic would absurdly require 141 for the Great Sanhedrin. The Gemara explains that the verse 'approach to Elohim' means three from the start. Rabbi derives five from a gezerah shavah on 'Elohim'.

sub.desc_en: The baraisa states that monetary cases require three judges, but Rabbi requires five so that the verdict can be reached by three.
Rabbi Avahu objects that Rabbi's logic would absurdly require 141 judges for the Great Sanhedrin and 45 for the Small Sanhedrin.
The Gemara explains that for the Sanhedrin, the verse specifies the number from the start, and similarly the verse 'approach to Elohim' means three from the beginning.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi derives five judges from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'Elohim', yielding two judges, and adds one to avoid an evenly split court, totaling five.

items.text: Opening statement: Rabbanan's reading of 'yarshien'
items.text_en: Opening statement: Rabbanan's reading of 'yarshien'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Rabbanan read the word as 'yarshien' (defective spelling), implying they follow the masoretic tradition rather than the written text.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Rabbanan read the word as 'יַרְשִׁיעֻן' (defective spelling), showing their reliance on the masoretic tradition.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's list of five authorities who hold 'yesh em la-mikra'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's list of five authorities who hold 'yesh em la-mikra'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quotes Rabbi Yochanan listing five authorities: Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi), Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz, Beit Shammai, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Akiva, all of whom hold the principle that the written text is authoritative.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan a list of five authorities who all hold the principle of 'yesh em la-mikra' (the written text is authoritative).

items.text: Proof for Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) and Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz
items.text_en: Proof for Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) and Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi's view was already mentioned. For Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz, a baraita recounts that students asked about a woman giving birth to a female being impure for seventy days; he initially answered based on analogy, but later retracted, saying the word is read as 'shvu'ayim' (double), following the written text.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi's view (that there is an 'אם למקרא' — a parent text) was already mentioned earlier.
A baraita recounts that students asked Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz: if I read the word as 'שבעים' (seventy), could a woman giving birth to a female be impure for seventy days?

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz's initial answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz's initial answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz initially answered by analogy: just as the purification period for a female is double that for a male, so too the impurity period for a female is double.

After the students left, Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz retracted his answer, saying they need not rely on analogy because the word is read as 'שבועיים' (double), following the written text — applying the principle of 'יש אם למקרא' (the written text is authoritative).

items.text: Proof for Beit Shammai
items.text_en: Proof for Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Beit Shammai require two placements for a sin-offering, while Beit Hillel accept one. Rav Huna explains Beit Shammai's reasoning: the word 'karnot' appears six times in the Torah, four for the mitzvah and two to invalidate. Beit Hillel read 'karnot' as 'karnat' (defective), yielding only four occurrences. The Gemara questions whether all could be for the mitzvah, but concludes that atonement cannot be found without some being essential.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Beit Shammai require two placements for a sin-offering, while Beit Hillel accept one.
Rav Huna explains Beit Shammai's reasoning: the word 'קרנות' appears six times in the Torah, four for the mitzvah and two to invalidate.
Beit Hillel read 'קרנות' as 'קרנת' (defective), yielding only four occurrences: three for the mitzvah and one to invalidate.
The Gemara questions whether all occurrences could be for the mitzvah, but concludes that atonement cannot be found without some being essential.

items.text: Proof for Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Proof for Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses the minimum size of a sukkah: the Sages require two walls of proper size and a third even a handbreadth, while Rabbi Shimon requires three proper walls and a fourth even a handbreadth. The Gemara explains that the Sages hold 'yesh em la-masoret' (the tradition is authoritative), reading 'basukkot' as 'basukkat' (defective) yielding four occurrences, leaving three after deducting one for the verse itself, and the tradition removes the third. Rabbi Shimon holds 'yesh em la-mikra', reading 'basukkot' plene six times, leaving four, and the tradition removes the fourth.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Shimon regarding the minimum number of sukkah walls: the Sages require two proper walls and a third even a handbreadth, while Rabbi Shimon requires three proper walls and a fourth even a handbreadth.
The Gemara asks: On what principle do they disagree?
The Gemara explains the dispute: the Sages hold 'yesh em la-masoret' (the tradition is authoritative), while Rabbi Shimon holds 'yesh em la-mikra' (the written text is authoritative).

The Gemara elaborates: the Sages read 'בסכת' (defective) three times, yielding four total occurrences; after deducting one for the verse itself, three remain, and the tradition removes the third, leaving the third wall as a handbreadth.

The Gemara elaborates: Rabbi Shimon reads 'בסכות' (plene) three times, yielding six total occurrences; after deducting one for the verse itself, four remain, and the tradition removes the fourth, leaving the fourth wall as a handbreadth.

items.text: Proof for Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Proof for Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Akiva derives from the verse 'al kol nafshot met' (with a plene spelling) that a quarter-log of blood from two corpses imparts tent impurity, as 'nafshot' implies two souls with one measure. The Sages, however, read 'nafshot' defectively, rejecting this derivation.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Akiva's derivation that a quarter-log of blood from two corpses imparts tent impurity, based on the plene spelling 'נפשת' (two souls with one measure).
The Sages reject Rabbi Akiva's derivation, noting that the verse actually reads 'נפשת' (defectively), implying only one soul.

items.text: Challenge by Rav Acha bar Yaakov
items.text_en: Challenge by Rav Acha bar Yaakov
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov challenges the premise: is there anyone who does not hold 'yesh em la-mikra'? He cites a baraita that interprets 'bachalev imo' (with a plene spelling) to exclude something, implying that even those who follow the masoretic tradition still rely on the written text.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov challenges the premise: is there anyone who does NOT hold 'יש אם למקרא'? He cites a baraita showing that even the Sages who seem to follow the Masoretic tradition actually rely on it.

items.text: Clarifying the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Clarifying the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both Rabbi and the Rabbis agree on the principle of יש אם למקרא, but they disagree about the interpretation of the verse 'ירשעון אלהים'—Rabbi reads it as referring to others, while the Rabbis read it as referring to both parties.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by asserting that the principle of יש אם למקרא (the written text is authoritative) is agreed upon.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi and the Rabbis both accept the principle but disagree on the interpretation of 'ירשעון אלהים'—Rabbi reads it as referring to others, the Rabbis as referring to both parties.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz is not disputed
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz is not disputed
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Rabbis do not dispute Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz's position, implying agreement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Rabbis do not dispute Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz's position, implying their agreement.

items.text: Beit Hillel's derivation from 'וכפר'
items.text_en: Beit Hillel's derivation from 'וכפר'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Beit Hillel uses the repetition of 'וכפר' to teach that a single application of blood atones, despite a logical argument suggesting otherwise. The Gemara presents the logical arguments and concludes with the scriptural derivation that even one, two, or three applications are effective.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita where Beit Hillel derives from the repetition of 'וכפר' that a single application of blood atones, despite a logical argument suggesting otherwise.

The baraita presents a logical argument: just as blood applied below (on the outer altar) atones with one application, so too blood applied above (on the inner altar) should atone with one application.
The baraita raises an objection: just as blood applied inside (the Holy of Holies) requires all applications, so too blood applied outside should require all applications.
The baraita resolves the objection by preferring an analogy between external (חוּץ) and external, rather than external and internal.

The baraita raises another objection: the sin-offering with four horns (the outer altar) should be compared to the sin-offering with four horns (the inner altar), and the current case lacks that feature.
The baraita concludes with a scriptural derivation: the repetition of 'וכפר' teaches that even one, two, or three applications are effective.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis about סככא
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis about סככא
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis disagree about whether the covering (סככא) requires a scriptural verse—Rabbi Shimon holds it does not, while the Rabbis hold it does.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis disagree about whether the covering (סככא) requires a scriptural verse—Rabbi Shimon holds it does not, while the Rabbis hold it does.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis about 'נפשות'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis about 'נפשות'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis disagree about the meaning of 'נפשות'—Rabbi Akiva holds it implies two, while the Rabbis hold it implies many.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis regarding the meaning of 'נפשות'.
Rabbi Akiva holds that the plural form 'נפשות' implies specifically two (witnesses).
The Rabbis hold that 'נפשות' means any plurality (at least two, but not limited to two).

items.text: Challenge to the principle of יש אם למקרא from tefillin and other cases
items.text_en: Challenge to the principle of יש אם למקרא from tefillin and other cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that all agree on יש אם למקרא, citing a baraita about tefillin where Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva derive four compartments differently. It then distinguishes cases where the written and oral forms differ, but notes that even when they are identical (like 'חלב'/'חלב' and 'יראה'/'יראה'), disputes still occur, as with Yochanan ben Dahavai's ruling about a blind person.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether all authorities agree on the principle of יש אם למקרא (the written text is authoritative), citing a baraita about tefillin.
The baraita cites Rabbi Yishmael's view that the three written forms of 'totafot' yield four compartments, and Rabbi Akiva's alternative derivation from the words 'tat' and 'pat'.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute applies only where the written and oral forms differ, but when they are identical (like 'חלב'/'חלב'), all agree on יש אם למקרא.
The Gemara objects that the words 'יראה' and 'יראה' are identical in spelling yet a dispute exists, citing Yochanan ben Dahavai's ruling about a blind person.

The baraita cites Yochanan ben Dahavai in the name of Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima that a blind person is exempt from the pilgrimage appearance (ראייה), deriving from the identical forms 'יראה'/'יראה' that just as one comes to see with both eyes, so one appears with both eyes.

items.text: Rav Acha's resolution regarding cooking a kid
items.text_en: Rav Acha's resolution regarding cooking a kid
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika explains that the verse 'לא תבשל גדי' prohibits the manner of cooking, not just the act, resolving a potential contradiction.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika resolves the contradiction by asserting that the verse 'לֹא תְבַשֵּׁל גְּדִי' prohibits the manner of cooking (דֶּרֶךְ בִּישּׁוּל), not merely the act of cooking a kid.

items.text: Introduction to monetary laws requiring three judges
items.text_en: Introduction to monetary laws requiring three judges
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new topic: monetary laws are adjudicated by three judges, as taught by the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis teach that monetary laws are adjudicated by three judges.

items.text: Opening statement: expert judge adjudicates alone
items.text_en: Opening statement: expert judge adjudicates alone
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a judge is an expert for the public (מומחה לרבים), he may judge even alone. Rav Nachman and Rabbi Chiyya each declare themselves as such experts who judge monetary cases alone.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a judge is an expert for the public (מומחה לרבים), he may judge even alone.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution: authority without formal permission
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution: authority without formal permission
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a judge who is learned and competent but lacks formal authorization (רשותא) from the Exilarch can render valid judgments. It brings a proof from Mar Zutra, who judged and erred; Rav Yosef ruled that if the litigants accepted him, he does not pay, implying his judgment is valid even without authorization.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a judge who is learned and competent but lacks formal authorization (רשותא) from the Exilarch can render valid judgments.
The Gemara brings a proof from Mar Zutra, who judged and erred; Rav Yosef ruled that if the litigants accepted him, he does not pay, implying his judgment is valid even without authorization.
The Gemara concludes that even without authorization, the judge's ruling is valid (דִּינֵיהּ דִּינָא).

items.text: Rav and Shmuel: need for authorization from Exilarch
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel: need for authorization from Exilarch
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel both state that one who wishes to judge and be exempt from paying if he errs should receive authorization from the Exilarch's court.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: For one who is learned, expert, and holds authority but does not actually hold the formal appointment, is his judgment valid or not?
Shmuel similarly states that one should receive authorization from the Exilarch's court.

items.text: Authority transfer within and between jurisdictions
items.text_en: Authority transfer within and between jurisdictions
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that authorization from the Exilarch in Babylonia (שבט) and from the Nasi in the Land of Israel (מחוקק) is valid within its own jurisdiction and also from one to the other, citing a baraita that identifies the 'scepter' with the Exilarchs and the 'lawgiver' with Hillel's descendants.

sub.desc_en: A digression: authority transfer within and between jurisdictions is effective, as the scepter (Exilarch) here and the lawgiver (Nasi) there both hold authority.

items.text: Question: does authority from Israel to Babylonia work?
items.text_en: Question: does authority from Israel to Babylonia work?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether authorization from the Nasi in Israel is valid in Babylonia. It brings a case of Rabbah bar Chanah, who had authorization from Rabbi Chiyya (in Israel) but erred; Rabbi Chiyya told him to pay if not accepted, implying the authorization did not transfer to Babylonia.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: But does it not work? Rabba bar Rav Huna, when arguing with the Exilarch's house, said: I hold authority not from you but from Abba Mari, who from Rav, who from Rabbi Chiyya, who from Rabbi. So transfer does work.

items.text: Challenge and resolution: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's claim
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's claim
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the conclusion by citing Rabbah bar Rav Huna, who claimed authorization from Rabbi through a chain, implying it should work. It resolves that his claim was only for general matters (במילתא דעלמא), not for judging. It then explains that Rabbah bar Chanah's authorization was for border towns (לעיירות העומדים על הגבולין).

sub.desc_en: An objection: but Rabbah bar Rav Huna, when arguing with the Exilarch's house, said: I hold authority not from you but from my father, who got it from Rav, who got it from Rabbi Chiyya, who got it from Rabbi! This is a worldly matter that establishes them.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbah bar Rav Huna's claim was only for general matters (במילתא דעלמא), not for judging; and explains that Rabbah bar Chanah's authorization was specifically for border towns.

items.text: Definition of authorization: Rabbi Chiyya's request for Rabbah bar Chanah and Rav
items.text_en: Definition of authorization: Rabbi Chiyya's request for Rabbah bar Chanah and Rav
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains what authorization (רשותא) entailed: Rabbi Chiyya asked Rabbi to grant Rabbah bar Chanah permission to teach, judge, and permit firstborns, but for Rav (his nephew) he asked to permit teaching and judging but not permitting firstborns. It then clarifies the familial relationship: Rav was Rabbi Chiyya's sister's son, while Rabbah bar Chanah was his brother's son.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the authorization (רשותא) actually consisted of, introducing the story of Rabbah bar Chanah descending to Babylonia.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Chiyya's request for Rabbah bar Chanah
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chiyya's request for Rabbah bar Chanah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya asked Rabbi to grant Rabbah bar Chanah permission to teach, judge, and permit firstborns, and Rabbi granted all three.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Chiyya's request for Rav
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chiyya's request for Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya asked Rabbi to grant Rav permission to teach and judge, but not to permit firstborns, and Rabbi granted accordingly.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Chiyya called Rabbah bar Chanah 'my brother's son' and Rav 'my sister's son'.
The Gemara objects that if one thought the difference was merely factual, it cites a tradition that all these sages were siblings, so the relationship should be the same.

The Gemara resolves that Rav was Rabbi Chiyya's sister's son (making him a nephew through a sister), while Rabbah bar Chanah was his brother's son (not through a sister), explaining the different terminology.

items.text: Alternative explanation
items.text_en: Alternative explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation (ואיבעית אימא) for the distinction between Rav and Rabbah bar Chanah, but the text breaks off without elaboration.

sub.desc_en: Answer: Rav and Rabbah bar Chanah were two sons of a brother. Rabbi Chiyya was the brother of Abba bar Achah Karsala. Rabbah bar Chanah was the son of Rabbi Chiyya's brother, Rav was the son of Rabbi Chiyya's sister. That's why Rabbi Chiyya told Rabbi: 'My sister's son goes down' (for Rav), and 'My nephew goes down' (for Rabbah bar Chanah).

items.text: Why Rav did not permit firstborns for Rabbah bar Chanah
items.text_en: Why Rav did not permit firstborns for Rabbah bar Chanah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rav did not permit firstborn animals for Rabbah bar Chanah, given his wisdom. It suggests it was because Rav was more expert in blemishes, and permitting might lead to error.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rav did not permit firstborn animals for Rabbah bar Chanah, given his wisdom, and suggests it was because Rav was not expert in blemishes.
The Gemara objects that Rav himself claimed to have spent eighteen months with a shepherd to distinguish between a permanent and a temporary blemish.
The Gemara answers that Rav refrained from permitting to honor Rabbah bar Chanah.
The Gemara offers an alternative answer: Rav was more expert in blemishes and permitted rare ones, leading people to mistakenly permit temporary blemishes.

items.text: The incident that led to requiring permission
items.text_en: The incident that led to requiring permission
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why a student needs permission to rule, citing an incident where Rabbi's student misled people about disqualifying liquids, leading to a decree that a student may not rule without permission from his teacher.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if a student is already learned (גמיר), why does he need to take permission from his teacher to rule?
The Gemara answers: it is because of an incident that occurred (which demonstrated the danger of a student ruling without permission).

A baraita recounts: Rabbi visited a place and saw people kneading dough in טומאה (ritual impurity); they explained that a student had ruled that מי בצעים (marsh water) does not make food susceptible to impurity, but the student had actually taught about מי ביצים (egg water), and they misunderstood.

The Gemara adds that the people also mistakenly thought that water disqualified for the red heifer (חטאת) cannot make food susceptible, but the Gemara clarifies that for הכשר (susceptibility to impurity), any water qualifies.
The baraita concludes: at that time, they decreed that a student may not rule unless he takes permission from his teacher.

items.text: Tanchum's ruling in the presence of his teacher
items.text_en: Tanchum's ruling in the presence of his teacher
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Tanchum ruled about soaking wheat on Passover, and was challenged because his teacher was nearby, violating the rule against ruling in one's teacher's vicinity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Tanchum, son of Rabbi Ami, arrived at Cheter and ruled that it is permitted to soak wheat on Passover.
The people object that Rabbi Mani from Tzur is nearby, citing the baraita that a student may not rule in his teacher's vicinity unless he is three parasangs away.
Tanchum responds that he was not aware of his teacher's presence, explaining his ruling.

items.text: Rabbi Chiya's encounter with a priest in a cemetery
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiya's encounter with a priest in a cemetery
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Rabbi Chiya identified a man standing in a cemetery as a priest, and deduced that his father had profaned him by marrying a divorcee.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara narrates that Rabbi Chiya saw a man standing in a cemetery.
Rabbi Chiya asks the man if he is not the son of a certain priest.
The man confirms that he is indeed the son of that priest.
The Gemara concludes that the man's father had high eyes (lustful), set his eyes on a divorcee, and thereby profaned his son from the priesthood.

items.text: The scope of permission: conditional permission
items.text_en: The scope of permission: conditional permission
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether permission to rule can be conditional, and cites Rabbi Yochanan's statement to Rav Shemen that he is permitted until he comes to them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether permission to rule can be granted conditionally, given that the basic permission is already effective.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's statement to Rav Shemen as evidence that permission can be conditional, since Rabbi Yochanan said 'you are permitted until you come to us'.

items.text: The validity of a court of two judges
items.text_en: The validity of a court of two judges
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that two judges who judged, their judgment is valid but they are called a brazen court. Rava objects from a mishna requiring adding judges when two acquit and one is unsure, but the Gemara distinguishes because there they initially sat as three.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that two judges who judged, their judgment is valid but they are called a brazen court.
Rav Nachman sits and teaches this halacha (הלכה) of Shmuel.
Rava objects from a mishna requiring adding judges when two acquit and two convict and one is unsure, arguing that if two judges' verdict is valid, this case should also be valid.
The Gemara distinguishes: there they initially sat as three, so the case is different; here they did not sit with the intention of a three-judge court.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on two judges for compromise
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on two judges for compromise
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says judgment requires three but compromise can be done by two, and the parties cannot retract from a compromise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that judgment requires three judges but compromise can be done by two, and the parties cannot retract from a compromise.

items.text: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Avahu's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Avahu's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Rabbis disagree with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, citing Rabbi Avahu's statement that according to all opinions, a court of two is invalid. It then challenges this by asking if Rabbi Avahu is contradicting himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if you say the Rabbis disagree with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, then Rabbi Avahu's statement that two judges are universally invalid contradicts that, so you are pitting one authority against another.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's statement and the objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's statement and the objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu states that two judges for monetary cases are invalid according to all opinions. Rabbi Abba objects with a baraita that says a judge who errs in judgment must pay from his own pocket, implying the judgment is valid. The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a case where the litigants accepted the judge.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu states that two judges who adjudicate monetary cases are invalid according to all opinions.
Rabbi Abba objects with a baraita that says a judge who errs in judgment must pay from his own pocket, implying the judgment is valid.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a case where the litigants accepted the judge, and he pays because they said 'you judged us according to Torah law'.

items.text: Clarifying the type of error in judgment
items.text_en: Clarifying the type of error in judgment
items.desc_en: Rav Safra asks Rabbi Abba what type of error the judge made. If it was an error in a Mishnah, the judgment should be reversed. The Gemara concludes it was an error in weighing opinions (shikul hada'at). Rav Pappa defines this as a case where two Tannaim or Amoraim disagree without a settled halakha, and the judge followed the minority view.

sub.text: Rav Safra's question to Rabbi Abba
sub.text_en: Rav Safra's question to Rabbi Abba
sub.desc_en: Rav Safra asks Rabbi Abba what type of error the judge made.
The Gemara rejects the possibility that the error was in a Mishnah, citing Rav Sheishet's ruling that such an error is reversed.
The Gemara concludes that the error was in weighing opinions (שיקול הדעת).
The Gemara asks what constitutes an error in weighing opinions.
Rav Pappa defines it as a case where two Tannaim or Amoraim disagree without a settled halakha, and the judge followed the minority view.

items.text: Debate on the number of judges for compromise (bittzua)
items.text_en: Debate on the number of judges for compromise (bittzua)
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Meir says compromise requires three judges, while the Sages say it can be done by one. The Gemara initially assumes they disagree about whether a court of two is valid for judgment, but then explains that all agree judgment requires three; the dispute is whether compromise is compared to judgment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to resolve the issue by citing a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Meir says compromise (ביצוע) requires three judges.
The baraita continues: the Sages say compromise can be done by a single judge.
The Gemara notes that initially it was assumed that all agree compromise is compared to judgment (דין).
The Gemara asks: is the dispute about whether judgment requires three or two judges?
The Gemara rejects this: all agree judgment requires three; the dispute is whether compromise is compared to judgment (דין) or not.

items.text: Three opinions on the number for compromise
items.text_en: Three opinions on the number for compromise
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests there are three Tannaitic opinions: compromise requires three, two, or one. Rav Acha bar Rav Ika explains that the one who says two actually means even one is sufficient, but two are needed to serve as witnesses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes: there are three Tannaitic positions on compromise — one requires three, one requires two, and one requires one.
Rav Acha (or Rabbi Yeymar) explains: the one who says two actually means even one suffices, but he said two so that there would be witnesses to the compromise.

items.text: Rav Ashi's inference about compromise requiring a kinyan
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's inference about compromise requiring a kinyan
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi infers from the dispute that compromise does not require a formal acquisition (kinyan), because if it did, even the one who requires three could suffice with two to perform the kinyan. The Gemara concludes that the halakha is that compromise does require a kinyan.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi infers from the dispute that compromise does not require a formal acquisition (קניין), because if it did, even the one requiring three could suffice with two and have them acquire from him.
The Gemara concludes: the halacha is that compromise does require a formal acquisition.

items.text: Baraita: Compromise requires three like judgment
items.text_en: Baraita: Compromise requires three like judgment
items.desc_en: A baraita states that just as judgment requires three, so too compromise requires three.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis taught in a baraita: just as judgment requires three, so too arbitration requires three.

items.text: Opening principle: after verdict, no compromise
items.text_en: Opening principle: after verdict, no compromise
items.desc_en: The Gemara states a general rule: once the verdict has been reached, the judge may not suggest compromise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a general rule: once the verdict has been reached, the judge may not suggest compromise.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGlili and others: compromise is forbidden
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGlili and others: compromise is forbidden
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGlili forbids compromise, calling it a sin. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Meir each interpret the verse "בֹּצֵעַ בֵּרֵךְ נִאֵץ ה׳" to condemn those who bless a compromiser or bless Judah for his suggestion to sell Joseph.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a mnemonic device alluding to the names of tanna'im in the coming discussion.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGlili
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGlili
sub.desc_en: רבי אליעזר בן רבי יוסי הגלילי (Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGlili) rules that compromise is forbidden, that the compromiser is a sinner, and that anyone who blesses him is cursing God, citing the verse 'בֹצֵעַ בֵּרֵךְ נִאֵץ ה׳' (Psalms 10:3).
The baraita contrasts Moses, who insisted that judgment pierce the mountain, with Aaron, who was a lover of peace and made peace between people, citing Malachi 2:6.
רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer) gives an example: one who steals wheat, bakes it, and separates חלה (the priestly portion) cannot bless but rather curses God, citing the same verse.
רבי מאיר (Rabbi Meir) interprets the term 'בּוֹצֵעַ' as referring to Judah, who spoke of profit (בֶּצַע) in selling Joseph, and says that anyone who blesses Judah is cursing God.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: compromise is a mitzvah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: compromise is a mitzvah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha argues that compromise is a mitzvah, citing verses that combine justice and peace ("אֱמֶת וּמִשְׁפַּט שָׁלוֹם") and justice and charity ("מִשְׁפָּט וּצְדָקָה"), concluding that such a combination is compromise.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha opens by stating that compromise is a mitzvah, citing the verse 'אֱמֶת וּמִשְׁפַּט שָׁלוֹם' (truth and peaceful judgment) and arguing that the only judgment containing peace is compromise.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha adds a second supporting proof from David, who performed 'מִשְׁפָּט וּצְדָקָה' (justice and charity), arguing that the only justice containing charity is compromise.

items.text: Tanna Kamma and Rabbi: compromise as justice and charity
items.text_en: Tanna Kamma and Rabbi: compromise as justice and charity
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma describes a case where a judge pays a poor litigant from his own pocket after ruling against him, calling this both justice and charity. Rabbi objects to the verse's wording and reinterprets it to mean that even without paying, returning stolen property is both justice and charity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the opinion of the first tanna (Tanna Kamma): a judge who rules against a poor litigant and pays him from his own pocket performs both justice and charity.

The Gemara explains the Tanna Kamma's position: justice for the plaintiff (restoring his money) and charity for the poor defendant (paying from the judge's own house), and cites the verse about David as support.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi objects to the Tanna Kamma's interpretation: the verse says 'to all his people,' not just to the poor, so the explanation is problematic.

Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi resolves the difficulty: even without paying from his own pocket, the judge performs justice (returning the money to the plaintiff) and charity (removing the stolen item from the defendant's possession).

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya and Reish Lakish: when compromise is permitted
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya and Reish Lakish: when compromise is permitted
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya rules that before knowing the direction of the verdict, the judge may tell litigants to compromise, but after knowing, he may not. Reish Lakish adds that if one litigant is powerful, the judge may refuse to hear the case entirely before knowing the verdict, to avoid danger.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya rules that before knowing the verdict's direction, the judge may tell litigants to compromise, but after knowing, he may not, citing a verse.
Reish Lakish adds that if one litigant is powerful, the judge may refuse to hear the case entirely before knowing the verdict, to avoid danger, but after knowing, he must judge, citing a verse.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and Rabbi Chanin: obligations of students and judges
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and Rabbi Chanin: obligations of students and judges
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha teaches that a student who sees a point in favor of a poor litigant must speak up. Rabbi Chanin warns against being intimidated. The Gemara then exhorts judges to remember before whom they judge, citing verses, and concludes that a judge has only what his eyes see.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha teaches that a student who sees a point in favor of a poor litigant must not remain silent, citing the verse 'לֹא תָגוּרוּ מִפְּנֵי אִישׁ' (do not be intimidated by anyone).
Rabbi Chanin adds that one should not withhold words out of fear of anyone, and witnesses must know before whom they testify, citing the verse 'וְעָמְדוּ שְׁנֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים... לִפְנֵי ה׳'.
The Gemara exhorts judges to know before whom they judge, citing the verse 'אֱלֹהִים נִצָּב בַּעֲדַת אֵל' (God stands in the divine assembly).
The Gemara further cites Jehoshaphat's admonition to judges: 'רְאוּ מָה אַתֶּם עֹשִׂים כִּי לֹא לְאָדָם תִּשְׁפְּטוּ כִּי אִם לַה׳' (see what you do, for you judge not for man but for the Lord).
The Gemara addresses a judge's potential reluctance by citing the verse 'עִמָּכֶם בִּדְבַר מִשְׁפָּט' (with you in the matter of judgment), concluding that a judge has only what his eyes see.

items.text: Definition of 'gemar din' and Rav's ruling
items.text_en: Definition of 'gemar din' and Rav's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav defines 'gemar din' as the judge saying 'You are liable' or 'You are exempt.' Rav rules the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, but Rav Huna's practice of offering litigants a choice between judgment and compromise raises a question about the meaning of 'mitzvah' in Rabbi Yehoshua's statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes 'gemar din' (final judgment), and Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers that it is when the judge declares 'You are liable' or 'You are exempt.'
Rav rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who holds that it is a mitzvah to seek compromise (ביצוע).
The Gemara objects: Rav Huna, Rav's student, would offer litigants a choice between judgment and compromise, which seems to contradict Rav's ruling that compromise is a mitzvah.
The Gemara questions what exactly Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha meant by 'mitzvah' (commandment) in his statement about compromise.

items.text: Dispute about whether offering compromise is a mitzvah or a reshus
items.text_en: Dispute about whether offering compromise is a mitzvah or a reshus
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the difference between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha: the Tanna Kamma holds that offering compromise is optional (reshus), while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha holds it is a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the judge says 'it is a mitzvah to tell them: do you want judgment or compromise?' that is identical to the Tanna Kamma's position, so what is the difference between them?
The Gemara answers: the difference between them is whether offering compromise is a mitzvah (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha) or merely a reshus (Tanna Kamma).

items.text: Distinction from Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya
items.text_en: Distinction from Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes this dispute from that of Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, who holds that once a judge knows the direction of the law, he may not suggest compromise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and the first Tanna is identical to the position of Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, who forbids suggesting compromise once the judge knows the direction of the law.

items.text: The Golden Calf narrative as a source for Aaron's compromise
items.text_en: The Golden Calf narrative as a source for Aaron's compromise
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai explains that Aaron's building of the altar for the Golden Calf was a calculated compromise to avoid immediate bloodshed, as he saw Chur killed before him. He reasoned that a sin with potential for repentance was preferable to irreversible destruction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that the dispute about the verse 'פוטר מים ראשית מדון' (the beginning of strife is like letting out water) is related to Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai's interpretation of the Golden Calf narrative.
Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai states that the verse 'וירא אהרן ויבן מזבח לפניו' (Aaron saw and built an altar before it) refers to Aaron's compromise during the Golden Calf incident.
The Gemara asks what Aaron saw that led him to build the altar.

sub.text: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet citing Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet citing Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet in the name of Rabbi Elazar answers that Aaron saw Chur (חור) slaughtered before him.

sub.text: Aaron's reasoning (as narrated by the Gemara)
sub.text_en: Aaron's reasoning (as narrated by the Gemara)
sub.desc_en: Aaron reasoned that if he refused the people now, they would kill him like Chur, fulfilling the verse 'if a priest and prophet is slain in the sanctuary', leaving them without remedy forever; therefore, it was better to let them build the calf, as they could later repent.

items.text: Interpretation of 'Poter mayim reishis madon'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'Poter mayim reishis madon'
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna interprets the verse 'Poter mayim reishis madon' to mean that a person is first judged for neglecting Torah study. Rav Huna and Abaye offer analogies to explain how beginning a case or study leads to its completion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how these Tannaim interpret the verse 'פוטר מים ראשית מדון' (letting out water is the beginning of strife).
Rav Hamnuna explains that a person is first judged for neglecting Torah study, citing the verse 'פוטר מים ראשית מדון' (letting out water is the beginning of strife).
Rav Huna compares this to a water channel in a cistern: once it is widened, it flows freely, illustrating how beginning Torah study leads to its completion.
Abaye compares this to a camel's load: once it is raised, it stays raised, illustrating how beginning a case or study leads to its completion.

items.text: Mnemonic for the following proverbs
items.text_en: Mnemonic for the following proverbs
items.desc_en: A mnemonic 'Shim'i and two seven songs' is provided to introduce a series of proverbs interpreted by Shmuel and Rav Huna.

sub.desc_en: A mnemonic 'Shim'i and two seven songs' is provided to introduce a series of proverbs interpreted by Shmuel and Rav Huna.

items.text: Shmuel's interpretations of folk proverbs
items.text_en: Shmuel's interpretations of folk proverbs
items.desc_en: Shmuel explains six folk proverbs by citing biblical verses, demonstrating that these proverbs allude to divine justice and the consequences of sin.

sub.desc_en: An anonymous folk proverb is recited: 'Fortunate is one who hears and is silent; one hundred evils pass him by.'

Shmuel interprets the proverb as alluding to the verse 'פוטר מים ראשית מדון' (one who avoids the beginning of strife), meaning the 'head of a hundred judgments' — one who stays silent avoids many disputes.
A second folk proverb is recited: 'A thief who steals two or three times is not killed.'

Shmuel interprets the proverb as alluding to the verse 'על שלשה פשעי ישראל ועל ארבעה לא אשיבנו' (for three transgressions of Israel and for four I will not turn it back), meaning God punishes only after repeated offenses.
A third folk proverb is recited: 'Seven pits for the peaceful one, and one for the evildoer.'
Shmuel interprets the proverb as alluding to the verse 'כי שבע יפול צדיק וקם ורשע יפול באחת' (for a righteous man falls seven times and rises, but the wicked falls in one).
A fourth folk proverb is recited: 'One who leaves the court having taken a cloak — let him sing a song and go on his way.'

Shmuel interprets the proverb as alluding to the verse 'וגם כל העם הזה על מקומו יבוא בשלום' (and all this people shall return to their place in peace), meaning one who loses in court but accepts the verdict will go in peace.
A fifth folk proverb is recited: 'She is sleeping, and the palm tree is low.'

Shmuel interprets the proverb as alluding to the verse 'בעצלתים ימך המקרה ובשפלות ידים ידלף הבית' (through slothfulness the roof sinks, and through idleness the house leaks), meaning laziness leads to ruin.
A sixth folk proverb is recited: 'The man I trusted — he raised his axe and stood against me.'
Shmuel interprets the proverb as alluding to the verse 'גם איש שלומי אשר בטחתי בו' (even my close friend whom I trusted), meaning betrayal by a trusted friend.

items.text: Rav Huna's interpretation of a proverb about love and distance
items.text_en: Rav Huna's interpretation of a proverb about love and distance
items.desc_en: Rav Huna interprets a proverb about the intensity of love and physical space, citing verses about the Ark and the Temple to show that when love was strong, a small space sufficed, but later even a large space was insufficient.

sub.desc_en: A proverb is recited: when love was strong, a narrow bed sufficed; now that love is weak, a sixty-cubit bed is not enough.
Rav Huna responds that the proverb is supported by verses: initially, God's presence rested in the ten-handbreadth space of the Ark and cover, showing that strong love needed little space.

Rav Huna contrasts the later verse describing Solomon's sixty-cubit Temple with the verse where God says 'what house can you build for Me,' showing that when love weakened, even a vast space was insufficient.

items.text: Proof that 'lo saguru' means gathering
items.text_en: Proof that 'lo saguru' means gathering
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman, Rav Acha bar Yaakov, and Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika each cite verses to prove that the root 'agur' means to gather or store, as used in the context of judges not gathering words.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where is it derived that the word 'לֹא תָגוּרוּ' (do not gather) is a term of gathering?
Rav Nachman cites the verse 'וְיַיִן לֹא תִשְׁתֶּה וְלֹא תֶאֱגֹר' (and wine you shall not drink nor store) to prove that 'אגר' means to gather.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov cites the verse 'תָּכִין בַּקַּיִץ לַחְמָהּ אָגְרָה בַקָּצִיר מַאֲכָלָהּ' (she prepares her bread in summer, she gathers her food in harvest) to prove the same.

sub.text: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika cites the verse 'אֹגֵר בַּקַּיִץ בֵּן מַשְׂכִּיל' (he who gathers in summer is a wise son) to prove the same.

items.text: Rewards and punishments for judges
items.text_en: Rewards and punishments for judges
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan teaches that a judge who judges truthfully causes the Shechinah to dwell in Israel, while one who perverts justice causes it to depart. He further warns that a judge who takes from one and gives to another unjustly will have his life taken by God, and that a judge should always imagine a sword between his thighs and Gehinnom open beneath him.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan teaches that a judge who judges a true judgment causes the Shechinah to dwell in Israel, citing the verse 'אֱלֹהִים נִצָּב בַּעֲדַת אֵל'.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: He adds that a judge who does not judge truthfully causes the Shechinah to depart from Israel, citing the verse 'מִשֹּׁד עֲנִיִּים מֵאַנְקַת אֶבְיוֹנִים'.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: He further warns that a judge who takes from one and gives to another unjustly will have his life taken by God, citing the verse 'כִּי ה׳ יָרִיב רִיבָם וְקָבַע אֶת קֹבְעֵיהֶם נָפֶשׁ'.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: He concludes that a judge should always imagine a sword between his thighs and Gehinnom open beneath him.

items.text: Opening: The fear of judgment and the need for clarity
items.text_en: Opening: The fear of judgment and the need for clarity
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a verse about Solomon's bed, interpreted as referring to the fear of Gehinnom. Then, Rabbi Yoshiya (or Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak) and Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yonatan derive from verses that a judge must only rule on a case that is as clear to him as morning or as a forbidden sister.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing a verse about Solomon's bed and interprets it as referring to the fear of Gehinnom (גיהנם), which is likened to night.

sub.text: Rabbi Yoshiya (or Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yoshiya (or Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yoshiya (or Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak) derives from the verse 'דִּינוּ לַבֹּקֶר מִשְׁפָּט' that a judge must only rule on a case that is as clear to him as morning (כַּבֹּקֶר).

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yonatan derives from the verse 'אֱמֹר לַחׇכְמָה אֲחֹתִי אָתְּ' that a judge must only rule on a case that is as clear to him as a forbidden sister (אֲחוֹתְךָ שֶׁהִיא אֲסוּרָה לְךָ).

items.text: Collective responsibility and gathering judges
items.text_en: Collective responsibility and gathering judges
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that ten judges sitting in judgment all bear a collective responsibility, even a student sitting before his teacher. Rav Huna and Rav Ashi would gather multiple scholars or experts when a difficult case came before them, so that the burden would be shared.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that ten judges sitting in judgment all bear a collective responsibility (a 'necklace' around their necks).
The Gemara objects that this principle is obvious.
The Gemara clarifies that the statement is necessary only for a student sitting before his teacher, who might think he bears no responsibility.
Rav Huna would gather ten rabbis from the study hall when a case came before him, so that the burden would be shared like a beam carried by many.
Rav Ashi would gather all the butchers of the town when a difficult case (טריפתא) came before him, so that the burden would be shared.

items.text: The judge as king vs. priest
items.text_en: The judge as king vs. priest
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Kohen expounds a verse: a judge who is like a king, needing nothing, will establish the land; but one who is like a priest seeking gifts will destroy it.

sub.text: Rav Dimi citing Rav Nachman bar Kohen
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi citing Rav Nachman bar Kohen
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rav Nachman bar Kohen expounded a verse: a judge who is like a king needing nothing will establish the land, but one who is like a priest seeking gifts will destroy it.

items.text: Appointing an unworthy judge is like planting an asherah
items.text_en: Appointing an unworthy judge is like planting an asherah
items.desc_en: The house of the Nasi appointed an unqualified judge. The interpreter of Reish Lakish was asked to rebuke him but was silent. He then opened with a verse condemning the appointment. Reish Lakish states that appointing an unworthy judge is like planting an asherah, and Rav Ashi adds that in a place with Torah scholars, it is like planting it next to the altar.

sub.desc_en: The house of the Nasi appointed an unqualified judge, and the interpreter of Reish Lakish was asked to rebuke him but remained silent.
He opened with a verse condemning the appointment, warning that God will punish those who appoint such judges.
Reish Lakish states that appointing an unworthy judge is like planting an asherah, and Rav Ashi adds that in a place with Torah scholars, it is like planting it next to the altar.

items.text: The prohibition of 'gods of silver and gold'
items.text_en: The prohibition of 'gods of silver and gold'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the verse prohibiting gods of silver and gold, implying wooden gods are permitted. Rav Ashi explains it refers to a judge who comes for money or gold.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the verse prohibiting gods of silver and gold, implying that wooden gods are permitted.
Rav Ashi explains that the verse refers to a judge who comes for money or gold, not to literal idols.

items.text: The judge's humility and the transient nature of honor
items.text_en: The judge's humility and the transient nature of honor
items.desc_en: Rav would recite a prayer when entering court, expressing his reluctance to judge and his hope to leave as he entered. He and Mar Zutra the Pious would recite verses about the fleeting nature of human greatness when seeing crowds following them.

sub.desc_en: Rav recites a prayer upon entering court, expressing his reluctance to judge and his hope to leave as he entered.
Rav recites a verse about the fleeting nature of human greatness when seeing crowds following him, and Mar Zutra the Pious does the same on festivals.

items.text: Deliberation in judgment and the judge's tools
items.text_en: Deliberation in judgment and the judge's tools
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara and Rabbi Eliezer derive from the verse 'Do not ascend by steps' that judges must be deliberate and not step over people's heads. Rabbi Yirmeya (or Rabbi Chiya bar Abba) explains that the verse 'which you shall place' refers to the judge's tools. Rav Huna would ask for his 'store tools': a staff, strap, shofar, and sandal.

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara asks for the scriptural source of the rabbinic directive to be deliberate in judgment, citing the juxtaposition of 'Do not ascend by steps' with 'And these are the judgments'.
Rabbi Eliezer derives from the same verse that a judge must not step over the heads of the holy people.
The Gemara questions why the verse says 'which you shall place' (תָּשִׂים) instead of 'which you shall teach' (תְּלַמְּדֵם).
Rabbi Yirmeya (or alternatively Rabbi Chiya bar Abba) explains that 'which you shall place' refers to the judge's tools.
Rav Huna would request his 'store tools'—a staff, strap, shofar, and sandal—when going to judge, illustrating the judge's implements.

items.text: Instructions for judges: impartiality and proper procedure
items.text_en: Instructions for judges: impartiality and proper procedure
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says a judge must be ready with staff and strap. Rabbi Chanina warns against hearing one litigant without the other. Rav Kahana derives from 'lo tisa' that a judge should not cause a litigant to speak improperly. Reish Lakish says to clarify the case before cutting it. Rav Yehuda explains that judgment applies even between a house and an attic, or between an oven and a stove. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar debate the meaning of 'do not recognize faces'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse 'וָאֲצַוֶּה אֶת שֹׁפְטֵיכֶם' to mean a judge must be ready with staff and strap (מקל ורצועה) for enforcement.
Rav Kahana derives from the verse 'לֹא תִשָּׂא' (do not bear) that a judge should not cause a litigant to speak improperly (לא תשיא).
Reish Lakish interprets 'וּשְׁפַטְתֶּם צֶדֶק' to mean clarify the case (צדק) before cutting it (חתכהו).
Rav Yehuda explains that judgment applies even between a house and an attic, as per 'בֵּין אִישׁ וּבֵין אָחִיו וּבֵין גֵּרוֹ'.
Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar debate the meaning of 'לֹא תַכִּירוּ פָנִים': Rabbi Yehuda says do not recognize him (favorably), Rabbi Elazar says do not make him unrecognizable (harshly).

items.text: A judge's impartiality with an acquaintance
items.text_en: A judge's impartiality with an acquaintance
items.desc_en: Rav's host came before him for judgment. Rav asked if he was his host, and the man confirmed. The host then stated he had a case. The Gemara implies Rav's impartiality despite their relationship.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara narrates that Rav's host came before him for judgment, and after Rav confirmed their relationship, the host stated he had a case.

items.text: Rav's instruction to judge and the principle of equal importance of small and large cases
items.text_en: Rav's instruction to judge and the principle of equal importance of small and large cases
items.desc_en: Rav tells Rav Kahana to judge a case, but when Rav Kahana shows arrogance, Rav warns him with the verse 'like the small, like the great you shall hear.' Resh Lakish explains this means a case of a perutah should be as precious as one of a hundred maneh, not for deliberation but for priority.

sub.desc_en: Rav tells Rav Kahana to go judge a case, but seeing his arrogance, Rav threatens to excommunicate him if he does not comply.
Resh Lakish explains the verse 'like the small, like the great you shall hear' to mean a case of a perutah should be as precious as one of a hundred maneh, not for deliberation but for priority.

items.text: Exegesis on 'Do not fear any man' and 'For the judgment is God's'
items.text_en: Exegesis on 'Do not fear any man' and 'For the judgment is God's'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanan interprets 'Do not fear any man' as not withholding your words out of fear. Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina explains that God says wicked judges not only take money unjustly but also burden Him to restore the money.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanan interprets the verse 'Do not fear any man' as a warning not to withhold one's words out of fear of a person.
Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina explains that God says wicked judges not only take money unjustly but also burden Him to restore the money to its owners.

items.text: Moses' punishment and the principle of bringing reward/punishment through worthy/unworthy
items.text_en: Moses' punishment and the principle of bringing reward/punishment through worthy/unworthy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina (or Rabbi Yoshiya) says Moses was punished for bringing a difficult case before God, as per the verse. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects, noting the verse says 'I will hear it,' not 'I will make you hear.' The Gemara then cites a baraita that the section of inheritances was fitting to be written by Moses but the daughters of Zelophehad merited it, and the wood-gatherer's section was written through him, teaching that punishment comes through the guilty and reward through the worthy.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina (or Rabbi Yoshiya) states that Moses was punished for bringing a difficult case before God, citing the verse 'וַיַּקְרֵב מֹשֶׁה אֶת מִשְׁפָּטָן לִפְנֵי ה׳' (Moses brought their judgment before God).

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects: the verse says 'וּשְׁמַעְתִּיו' (I will hear it), not 'וְאַשְׁמִיעֲכֶם' (I will make you hear), implying Moses was not punished for bringing the case but for his own lack of knowledge.
