The Gemara explains that the correct version is that initially both were disqualified, but when the anasiim (oppressors) increased—referring to the arnona tax, as Rabbi Yannai's proclamation shows—the Sages reverted to disqualifying only merchants.

items.text: Resh Lakish tests the intercalation court
items.text_en: Resh Lakish tests the intercalation court
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish accompanies Rabbi Chiyya bar Zarnoki and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak as they go to intercalate the year. He observes a priest plowing and another pruning vines, and questions their fitness. They offer excuses that the work is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish joins Rabbi Chiyya bar Zarnoki and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak as they go to intercalate the year in Asya, to observe their actions.
Resh Lakish sees a priest plowing and challenges the rabbis: a priest who plows during the Sabbatical year is suspect.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Zarnoki and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak's first excuse
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Zarnoki and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak's first excuse
sub.desc_en: They excuse the priest by saying he can claim he is an אגיסטוון (a sharecropper who receives a portion of the produce) and thus the plowing is permitted.
Resh Lakish sees another priest pruning vines and again challenges his fitness.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Zarnoki and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak's second excuse
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Zarnoki and Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak's second excuse
sub.desc_en: They excuse the second priest by saying he can claim he needs the branches for the עקל (the twisted rope used in the olive press), which is permitted.
Resh Lakish rejects their excuse, saying only the heart knows whether the pruning is truly for the עקל (the permitted purpose) or for the עקלקלות (the twisted vines, i.e., for forbidden cultivation).

items.text: Why priests are suspected regarding the Sabbatical year
items.text_en: Why priests are suspected regarding the Sabbatical year
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why priests are suspected of violating Sabbatical year laws, citing a mishnah about terumah falling into Sabbatical year produce. Rav Chiyya in the name of Ulla states that this shows priests are suspected regarding the Sabbatical year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which of the two incidents Resh Lakish mentioned first.

The Gemara answers that Resh Lakish first mentioned the second incident (the vine-dresser), because if he had mentioned the first incident first, the priests could have given the same excuse for both.
The Gemara asks why Resh Lakish specifically questioned the priest's actions, implying priests are suspect regarding the Sabbatical year.
The Gemara cites a mishnah about a se'ah of תרומה (priestly portion) falling into Sabbatical year produce, which must be left to rot if the mixture is less than 1:100.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya in the name of Ulla
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya in the name of Ulla
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya in the name of Ulla concludes that this mishnah proves priests are suspected of violating Sabbatical year laws.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on the intercalation court
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on the intercalation court
items.desc_en: The intercalation court, feeling pressured, removes the ladder and leaves. Rabbi Yochanan initially questions whether those suspected of violating the Sabbatical year are fit to intercalate. He then retracts, citing a precedent of three shepherds, but ultimately distinguishes the cases, calling this a 'band of wickedness' not counted in a minyan.

sub.desc_en: The intercalation court, feeling pressured, removes the ladder and leaves.
Rabbi Yochanan questions whether those suspected of violating the Sabbatical year are fit to intercalate the year.
Rabbi Yochanan retracts his question, citing a precedent of three shepherds whose calculations the rabbis relied upon.
Rabbi Yochanan distinguishes the cases: the shepherds repented and the rabbis later intercalated through them, but here it is a 'band of wickedness' (קֶשֶׁר רְשָׁעִים) not counted in a minyan.

items.text: The court's complaint and Rabbi Yochanan's response
items.text_en: The court's complaint and Rabbi Yochanan's response
items.desc_en: The intercalation court comes before Rabbi Yochanan and complains that he called them 'shepherds of cattle' and said nothing. Rabbi Yochanan responds that even if he called them 'shepherds of sheep', what could they say?

sub.text: Narrative: the intercalation court comes before Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Narrative: the intercalation court comes before Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The intercalation court comes before Rabbi Yochanan and complains that he called them 'shepherds of cattle' and said nothing.
Rabbi Yochanan responds that even if he called them 'shepherds of sheep', what could they say?

items.text: The story of Shevna and the 'band of wickedness'
items.text_en: The story of Shevna and the 'band of wickedness'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the concept of a 'band of wickedness' through the story of Shevna and Hezekiah. Shevna, who led a large following, conspired with Sennacherib, but the prophet assured Hezekiah that the wicked band is not counted in the majority. The story continues with Shevna's punishment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the 'band of wickedness' (קֶשֶׁר רְשָׁעִים) refers to.

The Gemara recounts that Shevna taught 130,000 people and Hezekiah 110,000, and when Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem, Shevna shot an arrow with a note declaring his faction's surrender, citing the verse about the wicked drawing the bow.
Hezekiah feared that God would follow the majority, but the prophet assured him that a band of wickedness is not counted in the majority.
Shevna went to hew a tomb in the Davidic burial grounds, but the prophet rebuked him, declaring that God would cast him far away.
Rav comments that the tossing of a man (טִלְטוּלָא דְּגַבְרָא) is more severe than that of a woman.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's interpretation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's interpretation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina derives from the verse 'וְעֹטְךָ עָטֹה' that Shevna was afflicted with צרעת (leprosy), via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) to the verse about covering the lip.
A Tanna (תנא) concludes that because Shevna sought disgrace for his master's house, his honor was turned to shame, and when he left, Gabriel locked the door of his camp against him.

items.text: Story of Shebna's punishment
items.text_en: Story of Shebna's punishment
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Shebna was punished by being dragged over thorns after mocking the Sages who asked about his caravan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Shebna was punished by being dragged over thorns after mocking the Sages who asked about his caravan.

items.text: Interpretation of Shebna's character and the verse 'כי השתות יהרסון'
items.text_en: Interpretation of Shebna's character and the verse 'כי השתות יהרסון'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that Shebna was a man of pleasure, and the Gemara brings three interpretations of the verse 'כי השתות יהרסון' by Rav Yehuda, Rav Eina, and Ulla, relating to Hezekiah, the Temple, or the wicked man's thoughts.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar introduces that Shebna was a man of pleasure, linking his description to the biblical term 'sochen' (steward).
The Gemara cites the verse 'For the foundations will be destroyed; what has the righteous done?' as a prooftext about Shebna.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda and Rav Eina's interpretations
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda and Rav Eina's interpretations
sub.desc_en: One of them (Rav Yehuda or Rav Eina) interprets the 'foundations' as referring to Hezekiah and his party, asking: if they are destroyed, what has the righteous done?

sub.text: Rav Yehuda and Rav Eina's second interpretation
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda and Rav Eina's second interpretation
sub.desc_en: The other of them interprets the 'foundations' as the Temple, asking: if the Temple is destroyed, what has the righteous done?
Ulla interprets the 'foundations' as the wicked man's thoughts (of Shebna), asking: if not destroyed, what has the righteous done?

items.text: Support for the interpretations of 'שתות'
items.text_en: Support for the interpretations of 'שתות'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the scriptural basis for each interpretation: for Ulla's view (wicked man's thoughts), for the Temple view (the Foundation Stone), and for Hezekiah's view (the righteous called 'שתות' from verses about foundations).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that for the view that 'שתות' refers to the wicked man's thoughts, the verse 'כי השתות יהרסון' fits directly.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation for the Temple view
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation for the Temple view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that for the view that 'שתות' refers to the Temple, the Foundation Stone (אבן שתייה) is called 'שתייה', supporting the connection.
The Gemara asks: for the view that 'שתות' refers to Hezekiah and his party, where do we find righteous people called 'שתות'?
The Gemara answers with two verses: 'כי לה׳ מצוקי ארץ וישת עליהם תבל' and 'הפלא עצה הגדיל תושיה', showing that righteous people are called 'שתות' (foundations).

items.text: Derivations from the word 'תושיה'
items.text_en: Derivations from the word 'תושיה'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanan gives three explanations for the name 'תושיה', and Ulla and Rabbah discuss whether thought (machshavah) is effective for Torah study, with a distinction if it is for its own sake.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanan gives three explanations for the name 'תושיה' (Torah): it weakens a person, it was given in secret because of the Satan, and it consists of words of 'תוהו' (chaos) on which the world is founded.

Ulla asserts that thought (מחשבה) is effective even for Torah study, citing the verse 'מפר מחשבות ערומים' (He frustrates the plans of the cunning) to show that thought can prevent Torah from being realized.
Rabbah qualifies Ulla's statement: if people are engaged in Torah for its own sake (לשמה), thought does not affect them, citing the verse 'ועצת ה' היא תקום' (the counsel of the Lord will stand).

items.text: Disqualification of a shepherd and the need for proclamation
items.text_en: Disqualification of a shepherd and the need for proclamation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Avahu rule that a shepherd requires a court proclamation to be disqualified, with a dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina, and a clarification of Rav Yehuda's statement about a 'stam ro'eh' being invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda introduces a conditional statement about disqualification.
Rabbi Avahu reports in the name of Rabbi Elazar that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Avahu adds in the name of Rabbi Elazar that all such disqualifications require a court proclamation (הכרזה).
The Gemara presents a dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina regarding whether a shepherd requires a court proclamation to be disqualified.
The Gemara resolves the dispute by explaining that Rav Yehuda's statement 'a stam shepherd is invalid' means that a proclamation is issued for him by default (בסתמא).

items.text: Dispute about a document signed by robbers
items.text_en: Dispute about a document signed by robbers
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel thought to validate a document signed by two robbers because no proclamation was made, but Rava objected, distinguishing between rabbinic and Torah-level robbers.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel considered validating a document signed by two robbers because no proclamation had been made against them.
Rava objected, distinguishing between a rabbinic-level robber (גזלן דרבנן) who requires a proclamation and a Torah-level robber (גזלן דאורייתא) who does not.

items.text: Laws of disqualification for various sinners: 'davar acher', 'arayot', 'ganav'
items.text_en: Laws of disqualification for various sinners: 'davar acher', 'arayot', 'ganav'
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that those who eat 'davar acher' publicly are disqualified, but not in private; he also rules that one suspected of 'arayot' is valid for testimony, with Rava and Ravina qualifying this for a woman's testimony; and Rav Nachman defines a 'ganav' as one who steals in Nisan or Tishrei only under certain conditions.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a mnemonic sign for the following three laws: 'davar acher', 'arayot', and 'ganav'.
Rav Nachman rules that those who eat 'davar acher' (a euphemism for forbidden food) are disqualified from giving testimony.

sub.text: Stam's qualification of Rav Nachman's ruling
sub.text_en: Stam's qualification of Rav Nachman's ruling
sub.desc_en: The gemara qualifies that this disqualification applies only when done publicly and when the person could have eaten privately; if done out of necessity for survival, it is permitted.
Rav Nachman rules that one suspected of forbidden sexual relations (עריות) is still valid for testimony.
Rav Sheshet objects: can one who carries forty lashes on his shoulder (i.e., is flogged for such a sin) be considered valid?
Rava states that Rav Nachman concedes that such a person is disqualified regarding a woman's testimony (e.g., to permit her remarriage).

sub.text: Ravina's or Rav Pappa's further qualification
sub.text_en: Ravina's or Rav Pappa's further qualification
sub.desc_en: Ravina (or Rav Pappa) clarifies that this disqualification applies only to removing her from her husband (i.e., testifying that she committed adultery), but not to bringing her into marriage (i.e., testifying that her husband died).

The gemara asks: this is obvious! Perhaps one might think that the adulterer prefers the forbidden woman because 'stolen waters are sweet' (Proverbs 9:17), so he would testify falsely to bring her to him.
The gemara resolves: the ruling teaches that as long as she remains with her husband, she is readily available to him, so he has no incentive to lie to bring her to him.
Rav Nachman rules that one who steals in Nisan or Tishrei is not called a thief (i.e., is not disqualified from testimony).

sub.text: Stam's qualification of Rav Nachman's ruling
sub.text_en: Stam's qualification of Rav Nachman's ruling
sub.desc_en: The gemara qualifies that this leniency applies only to a sharecropper (אריסא), for a small amount, and for an item whose processing is complete.

items.text: Cases of disqualification and the story of grave-diggers on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Cases of disqualification and the story of grave-diggers on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites cases of Rav Zevid disqualifying thieves, and a dispute between Rav Pappa and Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua regarding grave-diggers who worked on the first day of Shavuot, with the latter arguing they thought it was a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rav Zevid disqualified two of his tenant farmers as witnesses: one for stealing a kab of barley and another for stealing a bundle of myrtle.

The Gemara introduces a case of grave-diggers who buried a corpse on the first day of Shavuot, where Rav Pappa excommunicated and disqualified them, while Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua deemed them fit.
Rav Pappa objects that the grave-diggers are surely wicked for violating Yom Tov, and Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua replies that they thought it was a mitzvah to bury the dead.
Rav Pappa further objects that the rabbis excommunicated them, and Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua explains that the grave-diggers thought the excommunication was for their own atonement.
The Gemara ends the narrative with 'It was stated,' signaling a transition to a different discussion.

items.text: Abaye and Rava dispute the disqualification of a conspiring witness
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava dispute the disqualification of a conspiring witness
items.desc_en: Abaye holds that a conspiring witness is disqualified retroactively from the time he testified, because he was a wicked person then. Rava holds he is disqualified only from the time of the conspiracy onward, because the law of conspiring witnesses is a novelty and applies only from its enactment. Some say Rava agrees with Abaye in principle but rules from now onward due to loss to purchasers. The difference between them is in cases where two witnesses testified about one person, or where they are disqualified for robbery.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that a conspiring witness (עֵד זוֹמֵם) is disqualified retroactively (לְמַפְרֵעַ) from the time he testified, because he was a wicked person (רָשָׁע) then, and the Torah says 'do not place a wicked person as a witness'.

Rava argues that the witness is disqualified only from now onward (מִיכָּן וּלְהַבָּא), because the law of conspiring witnesses is a novelty (חִידּוּשׁ) and applies only from the time of its enactment.
An alternative version states that Rava actually agrees with Abaye in principle, but rules from now onward due to loss to purchasers (פְּסֵידָא דְלָקוֹחוֹת).

The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two positions, and answers: cases where two witnesses testified about one person, or where they are disqualified for robbery (גַּזְלָנוּתָא).

items.text: Practical ruling and mnemonic
items.text_en: Practical ruling and mnemonic
items.desc_en: Rav Pappi acted in accordance with Rava, but Mar bar Rav Ashi ruled the law follows Abaye. The Gemara states that the law follows Abaye in the mnemonic 'יַע״ל קַגַ״ם' (which includes this case).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappi acted in accordance with Rava's position.
Mar bar Rav Ashi ruled that the law follows Abaye.
The Gemara rules that the law follows Abaye in the mnemonic 'יַע״ל קַגַ״ם' (which includes this case).

items.text: Dispute about a defiant sinner (מוּמָר לְהַכְעִיס)
items.text_en: Dispute about a defiant sinner (מוּמָר לְהַכְעִיס)
items.desc_en: A gluttonous sinner (מוּמָר אוֹכֵל נְבֵילוֹת לְתֵיאָבוֹן) is universally disqualified. For a defiant sinner (לְהַכְעִיס), Abaye disqualifies him because he is wicked, while Rava deems him fit, requiring a sinner of violence (רָשָׁע דְּחָמָס).

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that a gluttonous sinner (מוּמָר אוֹכֵל נְבֵילוֹת לְתֵיאָבוֹן) is universally disqualified from testimony.
The gemara presents the dispute regarding a defiant sinner (מוּמָר לְהַכְעִיס): Abaye disqualifies him, while Rava deems him fit.
Abaye explains his position: the defiant sinner is wicked (רָשָׁע), and the Torah commands not to appoint a wicked person as a witness.
Rava explains his position: only a sinner of violence (רָשָׁע דְּחָמָס) is disqualified, not a defiant sinner who merely violates prohibitions.

items.text: Attempted refutation of Abaye from a baraita
items.text_en: Attempted refutation of Abaye from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita lists robbers and those who misuse oaths as examples of 'wicked' witnesses. The Gemara initially thinks this includes false oaths, which would refute Abaye, but deflects by limiting it to monetary oaths. Another baraita lists robbers and usurers, which is a conclusive refutation of Abaye.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists robbers and those who misuse oaths as 'wicked' witnesses, and asks whether this includes both false oaths (שבועת שוא) and monetary oaths (שבועת ממון), which would refute Abaye's position.
The Gemara deflects the objection by limiting the baraita to monetary oaths only, explaining that 'oaths' here refers to oaths in general (שבועות דעלמא), not false oaths.
The Gemara raises another baraita that lists robbers and usurers as 'wicked' witnesses, which is a conclusive refutation of Abaye's position.

items.text: Connecting the dispute to Tannaim: Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Connecting the dispute to Tannaim: Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Abaye follows Rabbi Meir (who disqualifies a conspiring witness for all Torah matters) and Rava follows Rabbi Yosei (who limits disqualification to capital cases). It then refines: all agree on Rabbi Yosei's view; the dispute is within Rabbi Meir's view, where Abaye applies it broadly, while Rava limits it to cases where the witness is harmful to both Heaven and people.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute between Abaye and Rava aligns with a Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Meir (who disqualifies a conspiring witness for all Torah matters) and Rabbi Yosei (who limits disqualification to capital cases).
The Gemara asks whether Abaye follows Rabbi Meir (applying leniency to stringency) and Rava follows Rabbi Yosei (not applying leniency to stringency).
The Gemara rejects the alignment, stating that all agree on Rabbi Yosei's view; the dispute is only within Rabbi Meir's view.

The Gemara resolves that Abaye applies Rabbi Meir's disqualification broadly, while Rava limits it to cases where the witness is harmful to both Heaven and people (as in monetary cases), not where he is harmful only to Heaven (as in eating neveilot to anger).

items.text: Final ruling and a supporting story
items.text_en: Final ruling and a supporting story
items.desc_en: The law follows Abaye despite the refutation, because the refutation was according to Rabbi Yosei, and the law follows Rabbi Yosei over Rabbi Meir, but here the Mishnah was anonymously taught like Rabbi Meir. The Gemara illustrates with a story: Bar Chama killed someone, and the Exilarch asked Rav Abba bar Yaakov to investigate; two witnesses testified, then the accused brought two witnesses who disqualified one of them by testifying he stole a kav of dates.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that the law follows Abaye's position that a conspiring witness is retroactively disqualified.
The Gemara objects: but Abaye's position was refuted earlier!
The Gemara answers that the refutation was according to Rabbi Yosei's opinion, not Rabbi Meir's.
The Gemara objects: even if it is Rabbi Yosei, the law follows Rabbi Yosei over Rabbi Meir, so why rule like Abaye?
The Gemara acknowledges the general rule that the law follows Rabbi Yosei over Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara resolves that the case is different because the Mishnah was anonymously taught according to Rabbi Meir, and an anonymous Mishnah is authoritative.
The Gemara asks: where was such an anonymous Mishnah taught?

The Gemara illustrates with a story: Bar Chama killed someone, the Exilarch asked Rav Abba bar Yaakov to investigate, two witnesses testified, then the accused brought two witnesses who disqualified one of them by testifying he stole a kav of dates.

items.text: Opening statement: קַתָּא דְבוּרְטְיָא
items.text_en: Opening statement: קַתָּא דְבוּרְטְיָא
items.desc_en: A brief opening phrase, possibly a name or title, setting the context for the following discussion.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with the phrase 'קַתָּא דְבוּרְטְיָא' (a small pitcher), likely a nickname or title, setting the context for the following discussion.

items.text: Rav Pappa's initial question and objection
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's initial question and objection
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks about the ruling regarding a witness who was a conspiring witness in monetary cases, citing the principle that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei disagree, and the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei, who says such a witness is valid for capital cases.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: 'What is your opinion? Do you hold like Rabbi Meir?'
The gemara answers that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yosei, who holds that a witness who was found to be a conspiring witness (עדים זוממים) in monetary cases is still fit for capital cases.

items.text: Rav Pappa's distinction: an anonymous mishnah follows Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's distinction: an anonymous mishnah follows Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa argues that the principle applies only when there is no anonymous mishnah (stam) following Rabbi Meir, but here there is an anonymous mishnah that follows Rabbi Meir, so the halakha is like Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappi objects that the rule applies only where the Tanna (תנא) did not establish an anonymous mishnah (סתם משנה) like Rabbi Meir, but here the Tanna did establish an anonymous mishnah like Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: identifying the anonymous mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: identifying the anonymous mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which mishnah is anonymous and follows Rabbi Meir. It considers a mishnah about who is fit to judge capital cases, and suggests it might be Rabbi Meir, but then raises a difficulty: perhaps it deals with disqualification due to lineage (yichusin), not with a conspiring witness. The Gemara resolves that the mishnah indeed deals with lineage, not with a conspiring witness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which mishnah is anonymous and follows Rabbi Meir, and suggests it might be the mishnah about who is fit to judge capital cases, attributing it to Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the mishnah deals with disqualification due to lineage (יוחסין), not with a conspiring witness.
The Gemara resolves that the mishnah indeed deals with disqualification due to lineage, not with a conspiring witness, by showing that the latter clause only makes sense in that context.

items.text: Gemara's conclusion: the anonymous mishnah is about disqualifications
items.text_en: Gemara's conclusion: the anonymous mishnah is about disqualifications
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies another anonymous mishnah listing those disqualified from testimony (e.g., gamblers, usurers). It argues that this mishnah must follow Rabbi Meir, because according to Rabbi Yosei, women are disqualified from capital cases, yet these individuals would be valid, which is not the case. Therefore, the mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, who disqualifies them from all cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an anonymous mishnah listing those disqualified from testimony (gamblers, usurers, etc.) and notes the rule that any testimony a woman is invalid for, these individuals are also invalid for.

The Gemara asks whose opinion this mishnah follows, and suggests that if it were Rabbi Yosei, there would be a contradiction: women are disqualified from capital testimony, yet these individuals would be valid for capital cases, which is not the case.
The Gemara concludes that the mishnah must follow Rabbi Meir, who disqualifies these individuals from all testimony, including capital cases.

items.text: Bar Hama's praise
items.text_en: Bar Hama's praise
items.desc_en: Bar Hama stands up, kisses Rav Pappa's feet, and accepts to pay his poll tax for the entire year, showing great respect for Rav Pappa's insight.

sub.desc_en: Bar Chama stood up, kissed Rav Pappi's foot, and accepted to pay his tax for the entire year as a reward for his successful argument.

items.text: Mishnah: listing of relatives disqualified from testimony
items.text_en: Mishnah: listing of relatives disqualified from testimony
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists relatives who are disqualified from testifying, including brothers, uncles, in-laws, and their children and sons-in-law. Rabbi Yosei notes that this is the mishnah of Rabbi Akiva, but the earlier mishnah included a broader category. Rabbi Yehuda adds that even if the relationship ends (e.g., daughter dies but leaves children), the relative remains disqualified. The mishnah also discusses a friend (shoshbin) and an enemy (one who hasn't spoken for three days due to enmity), but the Sages say Jews are not suspected of such partiality.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah lists the relatives who are disqualified from testifying, including brothers, uncles, in-laws, and their children and sons-in-law, with the exception of a חורג (stepson) alone.

Rabbi Yosei notes that this is the mishnah of Rabbi Akiva, but the earlier mishnah included a broader category: a paternal uncle, a cousin, and anyone eligible to inherit him, and anyone related to him at that time.

The mishnah states that if a relative became distant (e.g., through divorce), he is כשר (fit to testify), but Rabbi Yehuda adds that even if the daughter dies but leaves children, the father-in-law remains a relative and is disqualified.
The mishnah discusses a friend (שושבין, best man) and an enemy (one who hasn't spoken for three days due to enmity), but the Sages say that Jews are not suspected of such partiality.

items.text: Gemara: scriptural source for disqualification of relatives
items.text_en: Gemara: scriptural source for disqualification of relatives
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the disqualification of relatives from the verse 'Lo yumutu avot al banim' (Deut 24:16), interpreting it as 'fathers shall not be put to death on the testimony of sons, and sons not on the testimony of fathers.' It addresses a contradiction with the verse 'Poked avon avot al banim' (Exod 34:7), resolving that the latter applies when children continue their fathers' sins. The Gemara also addresses the concept of mutual responsibility (areivut) from Lev 26:37, explaining it applies when they could have protested but did not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source disqualifying relatives from testimony.
A baraita cites the verse 'לֹא יוּמְתוּ אָבוֹת עַל בָּנִים' (Deut 24:16) and notes it cannot mean simple vicarious punishment, since that is already stated in 'אִישׁ בְּחֶטְאוֹ יוּמָתוּ'.
The baraita interprets the verse as disqualifying fathers from testifying about sons and sons from testifying about fathers.
The Gemara objects that children are sometimes punished for fathers' sins, citing the verse 'פֹּקֵד עֲוֹן אָבוֹת עַל בָּנִים' (Exod 34:7).
The Gemara answers that the verse applies only when children continue their fathers' sinful practices.
A baraita supports this by citing the verse 'וְאַף בַּעֲוֹנֹת אֲבֹתָם אִתָּם יִמָּקּוּ' (Lev 26:39) and explaining it applies when they hold their fathers' deeds in their hands.
The Gemara objects further, citing the verse 'וְכָשְׁלוּ אִישׁ בְּאָחִיו' (Lev 26:37) which teaches mutual responsibility (עֲרֵבוּת) for each other's sins.
The Gemara answers that mutual responsibility applies only when they could have protested the sin but did not.

items.text: Deriving fathers and sons from the verse
items.text_en: Deriving fathers and sons from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verse explicitly disqualifies fathers for sons and sons for fathers, and all the more so fathers for each other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the verse explicitly disqualifies fathers for sons and sons for fathers, and all the more so fathers for each other.

items.text: Deriving sons for each other
items.text_en: Deriving sons for each other
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know sons are disqualified for each other, and answers that the verse uses 'banim' to include even sons for each other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we derive that sons are disqualified for each other (i.e., a son cannot testify about another son).
The Gemara answers that if the verse only intended fathers for sons, it would have written 'fathers for a son'; the plural 'בנים' (sons) teaches that even sons are disqualified for each other.

items.text: Deriving sons unrelated to each other
items.text_en: Deriving sons unrelated to each other
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama suggests a logical derivation that sons unrelated to each other are also disqualified, but Rava objects with a counterexample from the Mishnah about brothers testifying together. The Gemara resolves that the disqualification comes from the general law of hazamah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have derived that sons are disqualified from testifying with each other (brothers), but how do we derive that sons are disqualified from testifying with anyone else (unrelated witnesses)?
Rami bar Chama proposes a logical argument: if sons unrelated to each other were valid, then a conspiring witness (עד זומם) could be executed based on his brother's testimony, which is impossible.

Rava objects with a counterexample from the Mishnah: three brothers plus one other form three testimonies but one testimony for hazamah, yet a conspiring witness pays money based on his brother's testimony, showing the logic is flawed.
The Gemara resolves that the disqualification of sons unrelated to each other comes from the general law of hazamah (הזמה), not from Rami bar Chama's logic.

items.text: Confirming the derivation from the verse
items.text_en: Confirming the derivation from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the verse's wording 'ubanim' includes even sons unrelated to each other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the verse's wording 'וּבָנִים' (and sons) includes even sons unrelated to each other, as otherwise the verse could have said 'וּבֵן' (and a son).

items.text: Deriving maternal relatives
items.text_en: Deriving maternal relatives
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that maternal relatives are also disqualified from the double mention of 'avot' in the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have derived disqualification of paternal relatives; from where do we derive maternal relatives?
The Gemara answers: the verse uses 'אבות' twice; if the first mention is not needed for paternal relatives, apply it to maternal relatives.

items.text: Deriving disqualification for merit cases
items.text_en: Deriving disqualification for merit cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that relatives are disqualified even for testimony that benefits the accused, from the double mention of 'yumtu'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found that relatives are disqualified for testimony that harms (חובה), but from where do we derive disqualification for testimony that benefits (זכות)?
The Gemara answers: the verse uses the word 'יוּמְתוּ' (they shall be put to death) twice; if it is not needed for the case of liability (חובה), apply it to the case of merit (זכות).

items.text: Deriving disqualification for monetary cases
items.text_en: Deriving disqualification for monetary cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that relatives are disqualified in monetary cases as well, from the verse 'mishpat echad yihyeh lachem'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have derived disqualification of relatives in capital cases; from where do we derive it in monetary cases?
The Gemara answers: the verse 'מִשְׁפַּט אֶחָד יִהְיֶה לָכֶם' (one law shall be for you) teaches that the same disqualification applies in monetary cases.

items.text: Rav's statement and the discussion on third-degree relatives
items.text_en: Rav's statement and the discussion on third-degree relatives
items.desc_en: Rav states that his uncle and his uncle's son and son-in-law may not testify for him, and vice versa. The Gemara questions this, noting that the Mishnah only disqualifies second-degree relatives, not third-degree. It then discusses whether Rav's 'son-in-law' means his son's son-in-law or his actual son-in-law, and concludes that Rav follows Rabbi Elazar's opinion, but only partially.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that his uncle, his uncle's son, and his uncle's son-in-law may not testify for him, and likewise he and his son and son-in-law may not testify for his uncle.
The Gemara questions Rav's ruling, noting that the Mishnah only disqualifies second-degree relatives (שני בשני) and first-degree relatives (שני בראשון), but not third-degree relatives (שלישי בראשון).
The Gemara suggests that the 'son-in-law' in Rav's statement refers to his son's son-in-law, making it a third-degree relative.
The Gemara objects: if Rav meant his son's son-in-law, why didn't he simply say 'his son's son'?
The Gemara answers that Rav incidentally teaches that a husband is considered like his wife (for purposes of disqualification).

sub.text: Gemara's objection from Rabbi Chiyya's baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from Rabbi Chiyya's baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rabbi Chiyya's baraita lists eight primary relatives (אבות) totaling twenty-four disqualifications, but Rav's ruling would yield thirty-two, contradicting the baraita.
The Gemara revises: Rav's 'son-in-law' is his actual son-in-law, but since he comes from outside the family, he is considered like a different generation.
The Gemara objects: if so, Rav's son-in-law is a third-degree relative to a second-degree relative (שלישי בשני), yet Rav permits such a relative.
The Gemara answers that Rav follows Rabbi Elazar's opinion, who disqualifies a wider range of relatives.
The Gemara objects again: even according to Rabbi Elazar, Rav's son-in-law is still a third-degree relative to a second-degree relative, which Rav permits.

The Gemara resolves: Rav agrees with Rabbi Elazar on one point (disqualifying third-degree relatives in the first generation) but disagrees on another (permitting third-degree relatives in the second generation).
Rav derives his ruling from the verse 'לֹא יוּמְתוּ אָבוֹת עַל בָּנִים וּבָנִים', interpreting the extra 'וּבָנִים' to include a later generation.
Rabbi Elazar interprets the verse differently: the Torah says 'עַל בָּנִים' to cast the disqualifications of fathers onto sons (i.e., all descendants of a father are disqualified).

items.text: Rav Nachman's and Rav Ashi's additions
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's and Rav Ashi's additions
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman lists additional relatives who may not testify, and Rav Ashi asks about the brother of one's father-in-law, which is answered by a Tanna's statement.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman lists relatives through the mother-in-law who may not testify about him.
A baraita is cited that lists husbands of sisters and aunts, with their sons and sons-in-law, as disqualified witnesses.
Rav Ashi asks about the halakha regarding the brother of one's father-in-law and his descendants.
Ulla answers that the mishna already teaches these relationships from the perspective of the younger generation.

items.text: Question about testifying for one's wife's sister's husband
items.text_en: Question about testifying for one's wife's sister's husband
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a man may testify regarding his wife's sister's husband (חורגו). Two versions of the question are presented: in Sura they say the husband is like his wife, and in Pumbedita they say the wife is like her husband, citing a verse to prove that a woman is considered like her husband for familial relations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a man may testify regarding his wife's sister's husband (אשת חורגו).
In Sura they say the husband is like his wife (i.e., the husband is considered a relative through the wife).
In Pumbedita they say the wife is like her husband, citing a verse to prove that a woman is considered like her husband for familial relations.

items.text: Clarification of 'his son' and 'his brother' in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Clarification of 'his son' and 'his brother' in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's listing of 'his son' and 'his brother' as relatives, noting that 'his son' is already included as 'his brother'. Rabbi Yirmeya explains it refers to a brother's son (nephew). Rav Chisda validates testimony for a brother's son, but others object citing Rabbi Yirmeya's ruling. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah distinguishes between a brother from the father and a brother from the mother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists 'his son' separately from 'his brother', since a son is also a brother.
Rabbi Yirmeya explains that 'his son' refers to a brother's son (nephew), not a direct son.
Rav Chisda validates testimony for a brother's son (nephew), supporting Rabbi Yirmeya's interpretation.
Others object to Rav Chisda, citing Rabbi Yirmeya's ruling, but Rav Chisda rejects it.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah distinguishes between a brother from the father and a brother from the mother.

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling on fathers of the groom and bride
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling on fathers of the groom and bride
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the father of the groom and the father of the bride may testify for each other, as they are not related to each other except through marriage, which is like a thorn in the side.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that the father of the groom and the father of the bride may testify for each other, as their connection is only through marriage, which is like a thorn in the side.

items.text: Testimony for one's betrothed wife
items.text_en: Testimony for one's betrothed wife
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah says a man may testify for his betrothed wife. Ravina limits this to removing her from a situation (e.g., freeing her from captivity), but not for bringing her into one (e.g., establishing her status). The Gemara concludes that he is not believed in either case, citing Rabbi Chiya bar Ami's statement that a betrothed wife is not considered a close relative for mourning or inheritance, but the husband's closeness of mind to her is relevant for testimony.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah states that a man may testify for his betrothed wife.

Ravina limits Rabbah bar bar Chanah's ruling: the man is believed only to remove her from a situation (e.g., freeing her from captivity), but not to bring her into one (e.g., establishing her status).
The Gemara rejects Ravina's distinction and concludes that the man is not believed in either case.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Ami citing Ulla
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Ami citing Ulla
sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports its conclusion by citing Rabbi Chiya bar Ami in the name of Ulla, who states that a betrothed wife is not considered a close relative for mourning, impurity, or inheritance.

The Gemara distinguishes: regarding mourning and inheritance, the Torah requires actual blood relation (שארו), which she lacks; but regarding testimony, the concern is the husband's closeness of mind (איקרבי דעתא) to her, which does apply.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda regarding חורגו and גיסו
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda regarding חורגו and גיסו
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one's wife's sister's husband (חורגו) is a relative only by himself. A baraita adds that Rabbi Yosei says his brother-in-law (גיסו) is also a relative only by himself, while another baraita says Rabbi Yehuda says only חורגו. The Gemara analyzes the possible interpretations: whether each Tanna includes the other relative by extension, or whether they disagree on which relative is included. It concludes that Rabbi Yosei holds that גיסו is a relative only by himself, and all the more so חורגו, while the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda and the baraita follows Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one's wife's sister's husband (חורגו) is a relative only by himself.
A baraita cites the Tanna Kamma saying חורגו alone, and Rabbi Yosei adds that his brother-in-law (גיסו) is also a relative only by himself.
Another baraita states that גיסו is alone, and Rabbi Yehuda says only חורגו.
The Gemara asks what the baraitot mean.
The Gemara suggests that each Tanna includes the other relative by extension, but then objects that the Mishnah listing גיסו with his son and son-in-law would then match neither opinion.
The Gemara suggests that each Tanna excludes only his own relative, but then objects that Rabbi Chiyya's list of 24 relatives would then match neither.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from Rabbi Chiyya's list
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from Rabbi Chiyya's list
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Chiyya's list of 24 relatives would match neither Rabbi Yosei nor Rabbi Yehuda under this interpretation.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yosei holds גיסו alone and all the more so חורגו, while the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda and the baraita follows Rabbi Yosei.

items.text: Practical application and dispute about the halakha
items.text_en: Practical application and dispute about the halakha
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says Shmuel ruled the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei. A case arose where two brothers-in-law signed a document, and Rav Yosef sought to validate it based on Shmuel's ruling. Abaye objects, questioning whether Rabbi Yosei of the Mishnah (who validates a brother-in-law) or of the baraita (who disqualifies him) is meant. Shmuel's own statement about himself and Pinchas being brothers and brothers-in-law suggests he validates only such cases, but the Gemara questions this. Ultimately, Rav Yosef advises acquiring the document with a delivery of witnesses, following Rabbi Elazar, despite Rabbi Abba's objection about a forged document.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports that Shmuel ruled the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.
A case arose where two brothers-in-law signed a document, and Rav Yosef sought to validate it based on Shmuel's ruling.
Abaye objects, questioning whether Rabbi Yosei of the Mishnah (who validates a brother-in-law) or of the baraita (who disqualifies him) is meant.
The Gemara rejects the objection, noting that Shmuel's statement about himself and Pinchas being brothers and brothers-in-law suggests he validates only such cases.
The Gemara questions whether Shmuel's statement was specifically about brothers-in-law, not about the general rule.
Rav Yosef advises acquiring the document with a delivery of witnesses, following Rabbi Elazar's method.
Rabbi Abba objects that Rabbi Elazar himself admits a forged document is invalid.
Rav Yosef dismisses the objection, saying he will not allow the challenge to stand.

items.text: Final ruling on Rabbi Yehuda's opinion and a related teaching
items.text_en: Final ruling on Rabbi Yehuda's opinion and a related teaching
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum and others quote Rav that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, but Rava and Rabbah bar bar Chanah quote Rav Nachman and Rabbi Yochanan that it does not. Some teach Rabbah bar bar Chanah's statement in the context of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's teaching about a judge who was once a relative but became distant, and Rabbi Yochanan rules the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.

sub.text: Rav's ruling via chain of transmission
sub.text_en: Rav's ruling via chain of transmission
sub.desc_en: Rav, via a chain of tradents, rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda's opinion regarding the list of relatives.
Rava, citing Rav Nachman, contradicts Rav by ruling that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's supporting statement
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's supporting statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah, citing Rabbi Yochanan, independently confirms that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.
Some transmit Rabbah bar bar Chanah's statement in the context of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's teaching about a judge who was once a relative but became distant.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah, citing Rabbi Yochanan, rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's position on the judge who was once a relative.

items.text: Disqualification of a judge who was previously close to the litigants
items.text_en: Disqualification of a judge who was previously close to the litigants
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a case where relatives who had become distant came before a judge for a ruling. The judge disqualified himself, not because he was a relative, but because they had not accepted his authority. The litigants challenged him, citing a letter from the West that the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda (who disqualifies relatives).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a case where relatives who had become distant came before a judge, and the judge disqualified himself.
The litigants challenge the judge, suggesting he follows Rabbi Yehuda's disqualification of relatives, and cite a letter from the West that the law does not follow Rabbi Yehuda.
The judge clarifies that his disqualification is not due to being a relative, but because the litigants did not accept his authority.

items.text: Duration of disqualification for a friend or enemy
items.text_en: Duration of disqualification for a friend or enemy
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a friend (shoshvin) or enemy is disqualified from judging. The Gemara asks how long this disqualification lasts. Rabbi Abba in the name of Rav says it lasts for the seven days of the wedding feast, while others in the name of Rava say it applies even from the first day onward.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines a friend as a shoshvin (best man) and an enemy as someone who has not spoken for three days out of animosity.
The Gemara asks how long the disqualification of a friend lasts.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba in the name of Rav states that the disqualification lasts for all seven days of the wedding feast.

sub.text: Rabbanan in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rabbanan in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: The Rabbanan in the name of Rava say that the disqualification applies even from the first day onward.

items.text: Source for disqualifying a friend from judging
items.text_en: Source for disqualifying a friend from judging
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks a biblical source for disqualifying a friend, since the verse only mentions an enemy. It initially suggests a homiletic reading of the verse, but then rejects it because the verse does not actually say 'friend'. Instead, it concludes that the reason is logical: just as an enemy is disqualified because his mind is distant, so too a friend is disqualified because his mind is close.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'וְהוּא לֹא אוֹיֵב לוֹ' (and he was not his enemy) to teach that one may testify for him, and 'וְלֹא מְבַקֵּשׁ רָעָתוֹ' (and he did not seek his harm) to teach that one may judge him.
The Gemara asks: we have found a source for an enemy (שׂוֹנֵא), but from where do we derive the disqualification of a friend (אוֹהֵב)?
The Gemara initially suggests a homiletic reading of the verse as if it said 'וְלֹא אוֹהֵב לוֹ' (and not a friend to him), implying both enemy and friend are disqualified.
The Gemara objects: is the word 'אוֹהֵב' (friend) actually written in the verse? It is not.

The Gemara concludes that the disqualification of a friend is based on logic (סְבָרָא): just as an enemy is disqualified because his mind is distant (מְרַחֲקָא דַּעְתֵּיהּ), so too a friend is disqualified because his mind is close (מְקָרְבָא דַּעְתֵּיהּ).

items.text: Alternative interpretation of the verse for other disqualifications
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation of the verse for other disqualifications
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Sages derive from the verse 'He is not an enemy and does not seek his harm'. One interpretation applies it to a judge who is an enemy of a litigant. Another interpretation, from Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, teaches that two Torah scholars who hate each other may not sit together in judgment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Sages derive from the verse 'He is not an enemy and does not seek his harm'.
One interpretation applies the verse to a judge who is an enemy of a litigant.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda teaches that two Torah scholars who hate each other may not sit together in judgment.

items.text: Mishnah: Procedure for examining witnesses and rendering verdict
items.text_en: Mishnah: Procedure for examining witnesses and rendering verdict
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the process of examining witnesses: they are brought into a room, intimidated, and questioned individually. The witness must say 'In our presence he admitted to owing 200 zuz'. After both witnesses are examined, the judges deliberate. If they agree, the verdict is announced. A judge who disagrees is warned not to gossip about the deliberation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by describing the initial procedure for examining witnesses: they are brought into a room, intimidated, and all people are removed except the senior witness.
The Mishnah specifies the required testimony: the witness must say 'In our presence he admitted to owing 200 zuz', not merely hearsay.
The Mishnah states that after both witnesses are examined and their testimonies align, the judges deliberate.
The Mishnah rules on majority verdicts: two say innocent or guilty decides, and if there is a tie or a 'I don't know' vote, additional judges are added.
The Mishnah describes that after deliberation, the parties are brought back and the senior judge announces the verdict.
The Mishnah concludes by warning a dissenting judge not to gossip about the deliberation, citing verses against talebearing.

items.text: Gemara: How to intimidate witnesses
items.text_en: Gemara: How to intimidate witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses what verse is recited to intimidate witnesses. Rav Yehuda suggests a verse about false gifts. Rava objects that witnesses might dismiss it as a general proverb, and proposes a verse about a sharp arrow. Rav Ashi objects similarly and reports a tradition from Nathan bar Mar Zutra that the court says 'False witnesses, go to your wages', citing the story of Naboth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: How do we intimidate the witnesses?
Rav Yehuda proposes reciting the verse 'נשיאים ורוח וגשם אין איש מתהלל במתת שקר' (Clouds and wind without rain is a man who boasts of a false gift).
Rava objects that witnesses could dismiss the verse as a general proverb about a famine year.
Rava proposes reciting the verse 'מפיץ וחרב וחץ שנון איש עונה ברעהו עד שקר' (A club and sword and sharp arrow is a man who testifies falsely against his neighbor).
Rav Ashi objects that witnesses could dismiss the verse as a general proverb about a plague year.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's tradition from Nathan bar Mar Zutra
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's tradition from Nathan bar Mar Zutra
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports a tradition from Nathan bar Mar Zutra that the court says 'False witnesses, go to your wages', citing the story of Naboth.

items.text: Requirement that the witness say 'You are my witnesses'
items.text_en: Requirement that the witness say 'You are my witnesses'
items.desc_en: The Gemara supports Rav Yehuda's statement that the witness must say 'You are my witnesses' for the testimony to be valid. It cites a ruling of Rabbi Yochanan that if someone says 'I have a maneh in your hand' and the other admits, but later claims he was joking, he is exempt. A baraita adds that even if he hid witnesses behind a fence and the debtor refused to admit in their presence out of fear, he is still exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Yehuda's statement in the name of Rav that the witness must explicitly say 'You are my witnesses' for the testimony to be valid.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that if someone says 'I have a maneh in your hand' and the other admits, but later claims he was joking, he is exempt, supporting the need for formal witness designation.
A baraita repeats the same ruling that an admission followed by a claim of jest is exempt.
The baraita adds that even if the creditor hid witnesses behind a fence and the debtor refused to admit in their presence out of fear, the debtor is still exempt if he later claims he was joking.

items.text: The exception: No claims are raised for an inciter
items.text_en: The exception: No claims are raised for an inciter
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for an inciter (mesit), the court does not raise claims on his behalf. It explains that the Mishnah is incomplete: in capital cases, the court does raise claims, but not for an inciter. Rabbi Chama bar Chanina explains the distinction from the verse 'Do not pity or cover for him'. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani derives it from the primordial serpent, who had many claims but did not raise them. Chizkiya, Rav Mesharshiya, and Rav Ashi each derive the principle that adding to a command detracts from it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that no claims are raised on behalf of an inciter (mesit).
The Gemara asks why the inciter is mentioned here, and explains that the Mishnah is incomplete: in capital cases the court does raise claims, but not for an inciter.
The Gemara asks what is different about an inciter, and Rabbi Chama bar Chanina answers that the Torah says 'Do not pity or cover for him'.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani derives from the primordial serpent that the court does not raise claims for an inciter, because the serpent had many claims but did not raise them, and God did not raise them for him.
Chizkiya derives from the verse 'Do not eat from it and do not touch it' that adding to a command detracts from it.
Rav Mesharshiya derives the same principle from the dimensions of the ark: 'two and a half cubits its length'.
Rav Ashi derives the principle from the verse 'eleven curtains'.

items.text: Opening principle: denial marks a denier
items.text_en: Opening principle: denial marks a denier
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general rule: if someone says 'these things never happened,' he is considered a denier (כַפְרָן). This sets the stage for discussing admissions and denials.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a general rule: if someone says 'these things never happened,' he is considered a denier (כַפְרָן).

items.text: Rav Pappa's clarification: people forget trivial matters
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's clarification: people forget trivial matters
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa quotes Rava: the rule about being a denier applies only to matters that people would not normally forget. This introduces the idea that forgetfulness can excuse a denial.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa reports in Rava's name that the rule of being deemed a denier applies only to matters people would not normally forget, thereby qualifying the earlier statement.

items.text: Two cases of hidden witnesses and denial
items.text_en: Two cases of hidden witnesses and denial
items.desc_en: Two stories illustrate when a debtor denies a loan in front of hidden witnesses. In the first, Rav Kahana rules that since the debtor said 'no,' the witnesses are valid. In the second, Reish Lakish similarly rules that the debtor's explicit 'no' makes the witnesses effective.

sub.desc_en: A story: a man hides witnesses in a canopy, asks another about a debt, the other says 'yes,' then rejects the witnesses by saying 'no.'
Rav Kahana rules that since the debtor explicitly said 'no,' the witnesses are not effective.
A second story: a man hides witnesses in a grave, asks about a debt, the other says 'yes,' then rejects the witnesses by saying 'no.'
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish similarly rules that the debtor's explicit 'no' invalidates the witnesses.

items.text: Ravina/Rav Pappa: inference about 'you are my witnesses'
items.text_en: Ravina/Rav Pappa: inference about 'you are my witnesses'
items.desc_en: Ravina (or Rav Pappa) infers from the previous cases that the requirement for the debtor to say 'you are my witnesses' applies whether the debtor or the lender says it, as long as the debtor does not object. Silence is considered acceptance.

sub.desc_en: Ravina (or Rav Pappa) infers from the earlier cases that the rule of Rav Yehuda citing Rav — that one must say 'אתם עדיי (you are my witnesses)' — applies whether the debtor or the lender says it, as long as the debtor remains silent; silence is acceptance, and only explicit refusal ('no') exempts.

items.text: Case of 'Kab Rashu' and Rav Nachman's principle
items.text_en: Case of 'Kab Rashu' and Rav Nachman's principle
items.desc_en: A man called 'Kab Rashu' (a small measure of poverty) named his creditors before death. Rav Nachman rules that a person is unlikely to falsely incriminate himself (אדם עשוי שלא להשביע את עצמו), so his statement is believed.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case where a man called 'Kab Rashu' (a small measure of poverty) named his creditors before death.
Rav Nachman rules that a person is unlikely to falsely incriminate himself (אדם עשוי שלא להשביע את עצמו), so his statement is believed.

items.text: Case of 'Achbara d'Shacheiv a'Dinarei' and dispute about heirs
items.text_en: Case of 'Achbara d'Shacheiv a'Dinarei' and dispute about heirs
items.desc_en: A man called 'Achbara d'Shacheiv a'Dinarei' (a mouse lying on coins) named his creditors on his deathbed. Rabbi Yishmael limits the principle to the living, but Rabbi Chiya extends it to heirs. The heirs paid half and sought to retract, but Rabbi Chiya says the elder has already ruled.

sub.desc_en: Introduces the case of a man nicknamed 'Achbara d'Shacheiv a'Dinarei' who on his deathbed named his creditors, and after his death the creditors sued the heirs.
Rabbi Yishmael limits the principle of 'a person is not expected to satisfy himself' (i.e., the debtor's admission is credible only while alive) to the living, but not after death.

After the heirs paid half and sought to retract, Rabbi Chiya extends the principle to heirs, ruling that just as a person is not expected to satisfy himself, so too he is not expected to satisfy his children, and the elder has already ruled.

items.text: Admission before two or three: writing the document
items.text_en: Admission before two or three: writing the document
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one admits before two witnesses and they acquire from him, they write; otherwise not. Before three, there is a dispute: Rav Ammi says write, Rav Asi says not. Rav Ada bar Ahava distinguishes based on whether the witnesses gathered themselves or were gathered by the litigant. Rava requires saying 'you are my judges,' and Mar bar Rav Ashi requires setting a place and summoning to court.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: if one admits before two witnesses and they acquire from him, they write; otherwise they do not write.

The Gemara raises the case of admission before three without acquisition, and presents the dispute between Rav Ammi (who says write) and Rav Asi (who says not), with Rav deferring to Rav Asi's position.
Rav Ada bar Ahava distinguishes: if the witnesses gathered themselves, we do not write; if the litigant gathered them, we write.
Rava objects: even if the litigant gathered them, we do not write unless he explicitly said 'you are my judges.'

sub.text: Mar bar Rav Ashi's further requirement
sub.text_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi's further requirement
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi adds a further requirement: even if he said 'you are my judges,' we do not write until they set a place and send summons to court.

items.text: Admission for movables vs. land, and movables in hand
items.text_en: Admission for movables vs. land, and movables in hand
items.desc_en: For movables, if there was acquisition, they write; otherwise not. For land without acquisition, there is a dispute: Ameimar says no, Mar Zutra says yes, and the halakha follows Mar Zutra. Ravina and Rav Ashi debate whether movables that are still in hand are like land (Ravina) or require collection (Rav Ashi).

sub.desc_en: The stam states the rule: for admission of movables with acquisition they write, without acquisition they do not write.
The gemara asks: for land without acquisition, what is the law?
Ameimar rules that they do not write a document for land without acquisition.
Mar Zutra rules that they do write a document for land without acquisition.
The stam rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Mar Zutra: they write.
The gemara shifts to a narrative: Ravina visited Dimeharya, and Rav Dimi bar Rav Huna asked him a question.

sub.text: Rav Dimi bar Rav Huna's question
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi bar Rav Huna's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi bar Rav Huna asks Ravina: what is the law for movables that are still in hand (present and identifiable)?
Ravina answers that such movables are like land (and a document is written even without acquisition).
Rav Ashi disagrees: since they require collection (גוביינא), they are not like land and a document is not written.

items.text: Admission document lacking 'write and sign' formula
items.text_en: Admission document lacking 'write and sign' formula
items.desc_en: A document of admission that did not contain the phrase 'say to us, write and sign and give to him' is invalid according to Abaye and Rava, citing Reish Lakish's principle that witnesses do not sign unless the matter is significant. Rav Papi objects that the court scribes know the formula, and indeed they did.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case of an admission document that lacked the formula 'say to us, write and sign and give to him'.
Abaye and Rava both rule that this is the case of Reish Lakish's principle, implying the document is invalid.
Reish Lakish's principle is cited: witnesses do not sign a document unless the matter is significant.
Rav Papi (or Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua) objects: is there anything we do not know that the court scribes know?
The Gemara resolves the objection by noting that when they inquired of Abaye's and Rava's scribes, the scribes indeed knew the formula, confirming the document's invalidity.

items.text: Another admission document with 'duchran pitgamei'
items.text_en: Another admission document with 'duchran pitgamei'
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces another case of an admission document that contained the phrase 'duchran pitgamei' (record of matters), leaving the discussion open for further analysis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces another case of an admission document that contained the phrase 'דוכדן פיתגמי' (record of matters), leaving the discussion open for further analysis.

items.text: Concern about court documents lacking standard phrasing
items.text_en: Concern about court documents lacking standard phrasing
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a document that lacks the standard phrase 'we were in a session of three and one is not present.' Ravina thought it matched Resh Lakish's view, but Rav Nathan bar Ami said Rava taught that in such a case we suspect the court erred. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says if it says 'Be Dina' it is sufficient, but the Gemara raises concerns about a presumptuous court and whether the court followed Shmuel's view, and the document's additional phrases resolve these concerns.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions a document that lacks the standard phrase 'we were in a session of three and one is not present.'
Ravina thought the document matched Resh Lakish's view.
Rav Nathan bar Ami objects, citing Rava that in such a case we suspect the court erred.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says if the document says 'Be Dina' it is sufficient.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the court was a presumptuous court (בית דין חצוף) that followed Shmuel's view that two judges suffice.
The Gemara resolves that the document's additional phrases, mentioning the court of Rav Ashi and his rulings, show it was a proper court following Shmuel's view.

items.text: Baraita on testimony about hidden money and dreams
items.text_en: Baraita on testimony about hidden money and dreams
items.desc_en: A baraita presents cases where someone claims to have seen a father hide money and declare it for a specific person or as second tithe. The ruling depends on whether the money is accessible. Another case involves a dream telling someone about money left by his father, and the ruling is that dreams are irrelevant.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a case where a witness reports seeing a father hide money in a chest and declare it for a specific person or as second tithe, ruling that if the declaration was made in the house (where the money is accessible) it is invalid, but if in the field (inaccessible) it is valid.
The baraita generalizes the principle: if the money is accessible to the father (in his hand), his statement stands; if not, it is meaningless.

The baraita presents a second case where the children themselves saw the father hide money and declare it, ruling that if he spoke as one handing over (מסר) the statement stands, but if as one evading (מערים) it is void.
The baraita concludes with a case of a dream telling someone about money left by his father, ruling that dreams are irrelevant and have no legal effect.

items.text: Debate on how to write the verdict
items.text_en: Debate on how to write the verdict
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses how to record a verdict when two say 'innocent' and two say 'guilty.' Rabbi Yochanan says write 'innocent,' Resh Lakish says write 'so-and-so and so-and-so acquit, and so-and-so and so-and-so convict,' and Rabbi Eliezer says write 'from their words so-and-so is acquitted.' The Gemara explores the practical differences between these formulations, initially considering payment of the judge's share, then the prohibition of gossip (לא תלך רכיל), and finally the concern of falsehood. The conclusion is that they write 'from their words so-and-so is acquitted.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the verdict should be written when two judges say 'innocent' and two say 'guilty.'
Rabbi Yochanan says to write simply 'innocent.'
Resh Lakish says to write 'so-and-so and so-and-so acquit, and so-and-so and so-and-so convict.'
Rabbi Eliezer says to write 'from their words so-and-so is acquitted.'
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between these formulations.
The Gemara initially suggests the difference is whether the third judge must pay his share of the fee along with the others.
The Gemara objects: according to Rabbi Yochanan who writes 'innocent,' the third judge could argue that the others would not have been paid without him.
The Gemara revises: the difference is whether the other judges must pay the third judge's share.
The Gemara objects again: the other judges could argue that without the third judge, the case would not have been resolved at all.
The Gemara concludes the difference is the prohibition of gossip (לא תלך רכיל).
Resh Lakish explains his formulation avoids the appearance of falsehood.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Elazar holds both concerns, so they write 'from their words so-and-so is acquitted.'

items.text: Procedure after deliberation: who is brought in?
items.text_en: Procedure after deliberation: who is brought in?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says that after the judges finish deliberating, they bring them in. The Gemara asks: bring in whom? Not the litigants, as they are already there, but the witnesses. This follows the view of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, not Rabbi Nathan. Alternatively, it could mean the litigants, and it follows Rabbi Nechemya's practice. A contradiction is resolved by saying the baraita that brings in witnesses is not according to Rabbi Nathan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: after deliberation, who is brought in? Not the litigants, as they are already there, but the witnesses.
The Gemara answers that this follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, not Rabbi Nathan, who requires witnesses to testify together.
A baraita cites Rabbi Nathan's view that testimony is not valid until both testify together, contrasting with the Mishnah's procedure.
The Gemara offers an alternative: it refers to bringing in the litigants, following Rabbi Nechemya's practice of the refined Jerusalemites.
The Gemara resolves a contradiction between baraitot by stating that the baraita bringing in witnesses is not according to Rabbi Nathan.

items.text: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha on testimony
items.text_en: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha on testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between the first Tanna and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha regarding whether witnesses must see the event simultaneously. Two explanations are given: one based on reason (each witness testifies about a different coin) and one based on a verse (עד or אחד). The Tanna Kamma derives from 'one' that they must see together, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha derives from 'or he saw' that any seeing suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita stating the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha regarding whether witnesses must see the event simultaneously.
The Gemara asks what underlies the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha.
The Gemara gives a reason-based explanation: Tanna Kamma holds each witness testifies about a different coin, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha holds both testify about the same coin.
The Gemara gives a verse-based explanation: Tanna Kamma derives from 'עד' and 'אחד' that both must see together, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha derives from 'או ראה' that any seeing suffices.

items.text: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Nathan on testimony in court
items.text_en: Dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Nathan on testimony in court
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between the first Tanna and Rabbi Nathan regarding whether testimony must be given simultaneously in court. Two explanations: one based on reason (a single witness comes for an oath, not for monetary matters) and one based on a verse (אם לא יגיד). The Tanna Kamma holds that testimony must be given together, while Rabbi Nathan holds that we combine their testimonies even if given on different days.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that testimony is not established in court unless both witnesses testify together, while Rabbi Nathan holds that we hear each witness separately even on different days.
The Gemara asks: what is the basis of their dispute?

The Gemara offers a reason-based explanation: the first Tanna holds that a single witness comes only for an oath, not for monetary matters, while Rabbi Nathan argues that even when they come together they do not testify simultaneously, so we should combine their testimonies here as well.

The Gemara offers a verse-based explanation: the first Tanna derives from 'אם לא יגיד' (if he does not testify) that testimony must be given together, while Rabbi Nathan interprets the verse more broadly.

items.text: Resolving the dispute: analogy between testimony and sight
items.text_en: Resolving the dispute: analogy between testimony and sight
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the earlier dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha and the Rabbis is not about the law itself but about whether we analogize testimony (hagadah) to sight (re'iyah). One side holds we do analogize, the other does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the dispute by explaining that all agree with the Rabbis against Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, and the disagreement is only about whether we analogize testimony (הגדה) to sight (ראיה).

items.text: Story of Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim's ordination
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim's ordination
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim sought ordination from Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina but was unsuccessful. He then sat before Rabbi Yochanan, who asked if anyone knew the halakha like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha. Rabbi Shimon claimed to know, and after being ordained, he revealed that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha admitted to Rabbi Natan. Rabbi Yochanan was disappointed, but Rabbi Zeira concluded that once ordained, the ordination stands.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim persistently sought ordination from Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina but was unsuccessful.
Rabbi Yochanan asks if anyone knows the halakha like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim claims to know, requesting ordination first.
After being ordained, Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim reveals that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha admitted to Rabbi Natan.
Rabbi Yochanan objects that if Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha already disagreed on the main issue of visual evidence, the lesser point of testimony is obvious.
Rabbi Zeira concludes that since Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim was ordained, the ordination stands despite the disappointment.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Ulla on the halakha
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Ulla on the halakha
items.desc_en: Rav rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha for both land and movables. Ulla limits it to land only.

sub.text: Rav's ruling via Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin
sub.text_en: Rav's ruling via Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin
sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha for both land and movables.
Ulla limits the halakha to land only, excluding movables.

items.text: Abaye's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye questions whether there is a dispute at all, citing Rav Huna's statement that the Sages agree with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha regarding land testimony, and a baraita listing cases of agreement. The Gemara resolves that the dispute is only about whether the Sages disagree in other cases.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges the assumption that there is a dispute, citing Rav Huna's statement that the Sages agree with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha regarding land testimony.
A baraita taught by Rav Idi bar Avin lists cases where the Sages agree with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, including testimony about a firstborn, land, and presumptive ownership.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the dispute is between different Amoraim: one holds that the Sages disagree with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, and the other holds that they do not.

items.text: Clarifying the baraita: 'ken shebaben'
items.text_en: Clarifying the baraita: 'ken shebaben'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the phrase 'ken shebaben' in the baraita: it refers to a case where one witness says two spots on the back and another says two on the belly, which is valid testimony, not half-testimony.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the baraita's phrase 'ken shebaben' means, and rejects the possibility that it refers to one witness testifying about one spot on the back and another about one on the belly, because that would be half-testimony.
The Gemara answers that the phrase refers to one witness saying two spots on the back and another saying two on the belly, which constitutes valid testimony.

items.text: Conflicting traditions from Rav and Ulla
items.text_en: Conflicting traditions from Rav and Ulla
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports that Ulla ruled like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha for both land and movables, while others from Mehoza report that Rabbi Zeira said in Rav's name that it applies only to land.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports that Ulla ruled like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha for both land and movables.
Others from Mehoza report that Rabbi Zeira said in Rav's name that the ruling applies only to land, not movables.

items.text: Rav's principle of 'hoda'ah achar hoda'ah' and its challenge
items.text_en: Rav's principle of 'hoda'ah achar hoda'ah' and its challenge
items.desc_en: Rav's ruling is based on his principle that admission after admission combines, but admission after loan does not. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenges this, arguing that if the later witness does not see the earlier admission, it should not combine. The Gemara resolves with a scenario where the debtor tells the later witness about the earlier admission. Rav Nachman then questions whether this is just 'hoda'ah achar halva'ah', and the Gemara responds with a sharp retort.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav's ruling follows his own principle: הודאה אחר הודאה (admission after admission) and הודאה אחר הלואה (admission after loan) combine, but הלואה אחר הלואה (loan after loan) and הלואה אחר הודאה (loan after admission) do not combine.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenges Rav's principle: just as in הלואה אחר הלואה the later witness does not see the earlier loan, so too in הודאה אחר הודאה the later witness does not see the earlier admission, so why should they combine?

sub.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's response
sub.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's response
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna answers that the debtor tells the later witness: 'Regarding this sum that I admitted before you, I also admitted it before so-and-so,' thus linking the two admissions.
