Rav Nachman objects: the later witness knows, but the earlier witness does not know about the later admission, so the combination is still problematic.

sub.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna resolves that the debtor goes back and tells the earlier witness about the later admission, and the earlier witness expresses satisfaction that his mind is put at ease.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects: what satisfaction is there? Rava (or Rav Sheshet) already struck this down — this is merely הודאה אחר הלואה (admission after loan), which Rav himself said does not combine.

sub.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's sharp retort
sub.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's sharp retort
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna retorts sharply: this is what I have heard about you — that you uproot date palms and stand them upright (i.e., you make clever but destructive arguments).

items.text: Nehardeans' ruling: all combinations valid
items.text_en: Nehardeans' ruling: all combinations valid
items.desc_en: The Nehardeans rule that all combinations of admission and loan combine, following Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha.

sub.desc_en: The Nehardeans rule that all combinations of admission and loan combine, following Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha.

items.text: Contradictory testimony in monetary and capital cases
items.text_en: Contradictory testimony in monetary and capital cases
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that testimony contradicting in details (bedikot) is valid in monetary cases. Rava limits this to descriptions of the container, not the money itself. The Gemara questions whether this applies to capital cases, citing Rav Chisda's distinction: contradiction about the weapon invalidates, but about the color of clothes is valid.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that testimony contradicting each other in details (בדיקות) is valid in monetary cases.
Rava limits Rav Yehuda's ruling: contradiction about the container (ארנקי) is valid, but contradiction about the money itself (מנה) invalidates the testimony.
The Gemara questions whether the same distinction applies in capital cases, implying that contradiction about the container might be invalid there.
Rav Chisda distinguishes in capital cases: contradiction about the weapon invalidates, but contradiction about the color of clothes is valid, supporting the distinction.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on combining testimonies
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on combining testimonies
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Nehardeans' ruling that even contradictory testimonies (e.g., one says 'black maneh' and another 'white maneh') are combined, asking if this aligns with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's view, which only applies when they don't contradict each other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Nehardeans' ruling by asking whether they are conflating two separate cases of witnesses.

items.text: Nehardeans' ruling and challenge from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
items.text_en: Nehardeans' ruling and challenge from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
items.desc_en: The Nehardeans assert that even contradictory testimonies are combined. The Gemara challenges this by noting that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha only permits combining when testimonies do not contradict each other, not when they do.

sub.desc_en: The Nehardeans rule that even contradictory testimonies (one says 'black mane', the other 'white mane') are combined.
The Gemara questions whether the Nehardeans follow Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha, who only permits combining when testimonies do not contradict each other.

items.text: Attribution to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's baraita
items.text_en: Attribution to Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the issue by attributing the Nehardeans' view to a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that when one witness says '200' and another '100', the latter is included in the former; they only dispute when a single pair of witnesses gives contradictory amounts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the Nehardeans' view by attributing it to a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that when two sets of witnesses give different amounts, the larger includes the smaller.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: The baraita states that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree when two sets of witnesses give conflicting amounts, but dispute when a single set gives contradictory amounts.

items.text: Case of wine and oil barrels and Rabbi Ammi's ruling
items.text_en: Case of wine and oil barrels and Rabbi Ammi's ruling
items.desc_en: A case arises where one witness says 'barrel of wine' and another 'barrel of oil'. Rabbi Ammi rules the defendant must pay for a wine barrel, seemingly following Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. The Gemara questions this, as the items are not included in each other, and resolves that the payment is for the value (דְּמֵי) of the barrel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where one witness says 'barrel of wine' and another says 'barrel of oil'; Rabbi Ammi ruled that the defendant must pay for a wine barrel from the oil barrel.

The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Ammi follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, noting that Rabbi Shimon's principle of inclusion (יש בכלל) applies only when one amount includes the other, not to different items like wine and oil.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Ammi's ruling was not for the barrel itself but for its monetary value (דְּמֵי), so the witnesses agree on the value of a barrel.

items.text: Case of upper and lower rooms and Rabbi's ruling
items.text_en: Case of upper and lower rooms and Rabbi's ruling
items.desc_en: A case where one witness says 'upper room' and another 'lower room' is brought before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who combines their testimonies. This is cited by Rabbi Chanina.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina reports a case where one witness says 'the upper room' and another says 'the lower room', and Rabbi combined their testimonies.

items.text: Prohibition against revealing court deliberations
items.text_en: Prohibition against revealing court deliberations
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from verses that a judge who leaves court must not say 'I acquitted but my colleagues convicted' because it is gossip. A story is told of a student who revealed a matter from the study hall after 22 years and was expelled by Rav Ammi.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from verses that a judge who leaves court must not reveal his own acquittal and colleagues' conviction, as it constitutes gossip (רכילות).
A story is told of a student who revealed a matter from the study hall after 22 years and was expelled by Rav Ammi, who declared him a revealer of secrets.

items.text: Mishnah: Thirty-day limit for bringing evidence
items.text_en: Mishnah: Thirty-day limit for bringing evidence
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a litigant can overturn a verdict by bringing evidence within thirty days; after that, he cannot. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel questions what if he only found evidence after thirty days. The Mishnah details cases where a litigant initially claims no witnesses or evidence but later produces them, which is invalid, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's further questions.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that a litigant may overturn a verdict by bringing evidence within thirty days, but not after.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel questions what a litigant should do if he only found evidence after thirty days.
The Mishnah states that if a litigant initially claims no witnesses or evidence but later produces them, it is invalid.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel questions what a litigant should do if he did not know he had witnesses or evidence and later found them.
The Mishnah rules that if a litigant, seeing he is about to lose, suddenly calls witnesses or produces evidence, it is invalid.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute over halakha between Rabba bar Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute over halakha between Rabba bar Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna rules the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and not the Sages. The Gemara clarifies this teaches that even post-facto the verdict is reversed. Then Rabba bar Rav Huna cites Rabbi Yochanan that the halakha follows the Sages, not Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, specifically for this case of 'final evidence' (רְאָיָה אַחֲרוֹנָה), but elsewhere the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, except for the exceptions listed by Rabbi Yochanan (עֵרֶב, צַיְדָן, and this case).

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel) and not the חכמים (Sages).

The Gemara asks: Since Rabba bar Rav Huna already stated that the הלכה (binding law) follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel), it is obvious that the הלכה (binding law) does not follow the חכמים (Sages); why is the second statement necessary?
The Gemara answers: The second statement teaches that even if a court ruled לכתחילה (the ideal standard) according to the חכמים (Sages), the verdict is reversed post-facto.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Huna citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna cites Rabbi Yochanan that the הלכה (binding law) follows the חכמים (Sages) and not רבן שמעון בן גמליאל (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel) in the case of 'final evidence' (רְאָיָה אַחֲרוֹנָה).

The Gemara again asks: Since Rabbi Yochanan already said the הלכה (binding law) follows the חכמים (Sages), it is obvious that it does not follow רבן שמעון בן גמליאל (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel); why is the second statement needed?

The Gemara answers: The second statement teaches that specifically in this case of 'final evidence' (רְאָיָה אַחֲרוֹנָה) the הלכה (binding law) does not follow רבן שמעון בן גמליאל (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel), but in all other cases it does.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana cites Rabbi Yochanan's general rule that the הלכה (binding law) follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel) everywhere in the משנה (Mishna) except for three cases: עֵרֶב (guarantor), צַיְדָן (Tzaidan), and this case of רְאָיָה אַחֲרוֹנָה (final evidence).

items.text: Stories of Rav Nachman's rulings on evidence
items.text_en: Stories of Rav Nachman's rulings on evidence
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules against a minor who initially claims no witnesses or evidence, but later people offer to testify about his father's affairs; Rav Nachman says even the Sages would agree the minor is unaware. In another case, a woman produces a document and claims it was paid; Rav Nachman believes her, and Rava questions if this follows Rabbi's view that documents are acquired by delivery. Rav Nachman distinguishes because she could have destroyed it.

sub.desc_en: A minor is brought to Rav Nachman for judgment, claims no witnesses or evidence, and Rav Nachman rules against him.
The minor cries, people offer to testify about his father's affairs, and Rav Nachman rules that even the Sages would agree the minor is unaware of such matters.
A woman produces a document and claims it was already paid; Rav Nachman believes her.
Rava questions Rav Nachman, asking if his ruling follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view that documents are acquired by delivery.
Rav Nachman distinguishes the case because the woman could have destroyed the document, so her claim is credible.

items.text: Alternative version: Rav Nachman did not believe her
items.text_en: Alternative version: Rav Nachman did not believe her
items.desc_en: Some say Rav Nachman did not believe the woman. Rava questions this, noting she could have destroyed the document, implying she should be believed.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Nachman did not believe her, and Rava objects that she could have torn it up.
Rava questions Rav Nachman, noting that the woman could have destroyed the document, implying she should be believed.

items.text: Gemara's rejection of the possibility of retracting a confession after it is established in court
items.text_en: Gemara's rejection of the possibility of retracting a confession after it is established in court
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that once a confession is established in court, we do not say that the defendant can retract it. This is a brief ruling that closes the previous discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that once a confession is established in court (בית דין), we do not say the defendant can retract it.

items.text: Rava's objection to Rav Nachman from a baraita about a simpon
items.text_en: Rava's objection to Rav Nachman from a baraita about a simpon
items.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita about a simpon (a document of gift) that is valid when it emerges from a third party, implying the third party is believed. This refutes Rav Nachman's position, and the Gemara declares it a conclusive refutation.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita about a simpon (a document of gift) that is valid when it emerges from a third party, implying the third party is believed, which refutes Rav Nachman's position.
The Gemara declares that Rava's objection is a conclusive refutation of Rav Nachman's position.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's first version: a litigant may bring evidence until he says 'bring so-and-so to testify for me'
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's first version: a litigant may bring evidence until he says 'bring so-and-so to testify for me'
items.desc_en: When Rav Dimi came, he reported that Rabbi Yochanan said a litigant can always bring evidence and refute the verdict until his claims are sealed and he says 'approach so-and-so and testify for me.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled a litigant may bring evidence and refute the verdict until his claims are sealed and he says 'approach so-and-so and testify for me.'

items.text: Gemara's difficulty with Rabbi Yochanan's statement: it mixes two opinions
items.text_en: Gemara's difficulty with Rabbi Yochanan's statement: it mixes two opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes an internal contradiction: 'until his claims are sealed' follows the Rabbis, while 'until he says bring witnesses' follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. It then considers that the whole statement might be Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's, but cites a rule that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's rulings are generally accepted except in three cases, one of which is 'the final evidence' (ראיה אחרונה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in Rabbi Yochanan's statement: the first clause ('until his claims are sealed') follows the Rabbis, while the second clause ('until he says bring witnesses') follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

The Gemara considers that the entire statement might be Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's, but then objects by citing Rabba bar bar Chana's report that Rabbi Yochanan ruled that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's rulings are generally accepted except for three cases, one of which is 'the final evidence' (ראיה אחרונה).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's corrected version: until the court tells him to bring witnesses and he says he has none
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's corrected version: until the court tells him to bring witnesses and he says he has none
items.desc_en: When Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda came, he reported Rabbi Yochanan's corrected statement: a litigant can bring evidence until the court tells him 'bring witnesses' and he says 'I have no witnesses,' 'bring proof' and he says 'I have no proof.' But if witnesses come from overseas or a document was deposited with another, he can still bring evidence and refute.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan's corrected version: a litigant can bring evidence until the court tells him to bring witnesses and he says he has none, but witnesses from overseas or a deposited document can still be brought.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on venue: the defendant is forced to go to the central court
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on venue: the defendant is forced to go to the central court
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reported Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: if one litigant says 'let us be judged here' and the other says 'let us go to the central court,' we force him to go to the central court. Rabbi Elazar objects: should a creditor spend a maneh to collect a maneh? Rather, we force him to be judged in his own city.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: if one litigant says 'let us be judged here' and the other says 'let us go to the central court,' we force him to go to the central court.
Rabbi Elazar objects: should a creditor spend a maneh to collect a maneh? Rather, we force him to be judged in his own city.

items.text: Rav Safra's version: the defendant is judged in his city, and if needed, they write and send questions
items.text_en: Rav Safra's version: the defendant is judged in his city, and if needed, they write and send questions
items.desc_en: Rav Safra said Rabbi Yochanan ruled: if two litigants disagree about venue, we force the defendant to be judged in his city. If a question arises, they write and send it. And if a litigant demands a written explanation of the verdict, they write and give it to him.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: when two litigants disagree about venue, we force the defendant to be judged in his city, and if a question arises, they write and send it.
Rabbi Yochanan adds: if a litigant demands a written explanation of the verdict, they write and give it to him.

items.text: The yevamah follows the yavam; scriptural basis
items.text_en: The yevamah follows the yavam; scriptural basis
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a yevamah (levirate widow) must go after the yavam to be released. Rabbi Ami says even from Tiberias to Tzippori. Rav Kahana cites the verse: 'and the elders of his city shall call him'—not the elders of her city.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the rule that a yevamah (levirate widow) must go after the yavam to be released.
The Gemara asks how far the yevamah must go after the yavam.
Rabbi Ami answers that she must go even from Tiberias to Tzippori.
Rav Kahana cites the verse 'וְקָרְאוּ לוֹ זִקְנֵי עִירוֹ' (and the elders of his city shall call him) — not the elders of her city — as the scriptural basis for the rule.

items.text: Amemar's ruling: force to go to the central court, with distinction between borrower and lender
items.text_en: Amemar's ruling: force to go to the central court, with distinction between borrower and lender
items.desc_en: Amemar rules that we force the litigant to go to the central court. Rav Ashi objects citing Rabbi Elazar's opinion. Amemar explains: Rabbi Elazar's ruling applies when the borrower says it to the lender, but the lender can force the borrower because 'the borrower is a slave to the lender.'

sub.desc_en: Amemar rules that the halacha is that we force the litigant to go to the central court.
Rav Ashi objects to Amemar, citing Rabbi Elazar's opinion that we force the litigant to be judged in his own city.

Amemar resolves the contradiction by distinguishing: Rabbi Elazar's ruling applies when the borrower says it to the lender, but the lender can force the borrower because 'the borrower is a slave to the lender.'

items.text: The story of Mar Ukva and the dispute about venue
items.text_en: The story of Mar Ukva and the dispute about venue
items.desc_en: The court sent a message to Mar Ukva: 'To him who is honored like Batya, peace. Ukvan the Babylonian complained before us: Yirmeya my brother forced me to travel. Tell him: judge him yourselves; if he listens, good; if not, force him to appear before us in Tiberias.' The Gemara initially questions the apparent contradiction in the message, then resolves it.

sub.desc_en: The court sends a message to Mar Ukva regarding Ukvan the Babylonian's complaint against Yirmeya.
The Gemara questions the apparent contradiction in the message: first it says 'tell him' (implying they judge), then 'force him to appear before us in Tiberias' (implying he must come).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the message means 'tell him to judge him yourselves; if he listens, good; if not, force him to appear before us in Tiberias.'

items.text: Rav Ashi's explanation: the case involved fines, which are not adjudicated in Babylonia
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation: the case involved fines, which are not adjudicated in Babylonia
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the case involved fines (קנסות), which are not adjudicated in Babylonia. The court's message was merely to honor Mar Ukva, not to assert jurisdiction.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by explaining that the case involved fines (קנסות), which are not adjudicated in Babylonia, and the court's message was merely to honor Mar Ukva.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Differences between monetary and capital cases
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Differences between monetary and capital cases
items.desc_en: The Mishnah enumerates the distinctions between monetary and capital cases, including number of judges, opening arguments, verdict procedures, and qualifications of judges, all derived from the verse 'one judgment shall be for you'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that both monetary and capital cases require inquiry and examination, citing the verse 'one judgment shall be for you'.
The Mishnah lists the first difference: monetary cases require three judges, capital cases twenty-three; monetary cases open for both acquittal and conviction, capital cases only for acquittal.
The Mishnah lists the second difference: monetary cases are decided by a majority of one for either side, capital cases by a majority of one for acquittal but two for conviction.
The Mishnah lists the third difference: monetary cases allow reversal of verdict for either side, capital cases only for acquittal.
The Mishnah lists the fourth difference: in monetary cases all may argue for either side, in capital cases all may argue for acquittal but not for conviction.

The Mishnah lists the fifth difference: in monetary cases a judge who argued for conviction may later argue for acquittal and vice versa, but in capital cases one who argued for acquittal cannot later argue for conviction.
The Mishnah lists the sixth difference: monetary cases are tried by day and may be concluded at night, capital cases must be both tried and concluded by day.

The Mishnah lists the seventh difference: monetary cases are concluded the same day for either side, capital cases for acquittal the same day and for conviction the next day, so they are not tried on the eve of שבת (Sabbath) or a festival.
The Mishnah lists the eighth difference: in monetary and purity cases the eldest judge begins, in capital cases the judges begin from the side.
The Mishnah lists the ninth difference: all are fit to judge monetary cases, but only priests, Levites, and Israelites who marry into the priesthood are fit to judge capital cases.

items.text: Gemara's question: Do monetary cases require interrogation?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Do monetary cases require interrogation?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's implication that monetary cases require interrogation and cross-examination, citing a baraita where a loan document dated in the Sabbatical year is valid despite witnesses' apparent contradiction, suggesting no interrogation is needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether monetary cases require interrogation and cross-examination, citing a baraita where a loan document dated in the Sabbatical year is valid despite witnesses' apparent contradiction, suggesting no interrogation is needed.

items.text: Gemara's counter-challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's counter-challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a stronger challenge from the rule that post-dated loan documents are valid, and resolves that even in the extreme case of the Sabbatical year, the document is valid because the Sabbatical year ultimately cancels debts, so there is no concern about antedating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a stronger challenge: according to your reasoning, the Mishnah that post-dated loan documents are valid also contradicts the requirement of דרישה וחקירה (interrogation and investigation), since the witnesses could have been elsewhere.

The Gemara resolves that the challenge is not difficult, because the Mishnah's case of a post-dated document from the Sabbatical year is even stronger: since the Sabbatical year ultimately cancels debts, there is no concern about antedating, so the document is valid.

items.text: Gemara's conclusion: The contradiction remains
items.text_en: Gemara's conclusion: The contradiction remains
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that despite the attempted resolution, the contradiction between the Mishnah and the baraita remains unresolved, marking it with the mnemonic 'Chaf, Reish, Pei, Samekh'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that despite the attempted resolution, the contradiction between the Mishnah and the baraita remains unresolved, marking it with the mnemonic 'Chaf, Reish, Pei, Samekh'.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's resolution: Torah law vs. rabbinic enactment
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's resolution: Torah law vs. rabbinic enactment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina explains that by Torah law, both monetary and capital cases require interrogation, but the Sages waived it for monetary cases to avoid discouraging lenders from lending.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina resolves the contradiction by stating that by Torah law both monetary and capital cases require interrogation, but the Sages waived it for monetary cases to prevent discouraging lenders.

items.text: Opening challenge: the contradiction between the Mishnah and the concern for lenders
items.text_en: Opening challenge: the contradiction between the Mishnah and the concern for lenders
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: if judges who err do not pay, this would cause lenders to fear lending, contradicting the Mishnah's implication that they do not pay.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if judges who err do not pay, would that not close the door before borrowers?

items.text: Rava's and Rav Pappa's resolutions: distinction between penal and monetary cases, and between genuine and fraudulent claims
items.text_en: Rava's and Rav Pappa's resolutions: distinction between penal and monetary cases, and between genuine and fraudulent claims
items.desc_en: Rava distinguishes the Mishnah as dealing with penal cases, while the concern about lenders applies to admissions and loans. Rav Pappa argues both are about admissions and loans, but one is a fraudulent claim and the other is not, citing Resh Lakish's teaching on the two verses of 'justice'.

sub.desc_en: Rava distinguishes the Mishnah here as dealing with penal cases, while the other sources deal with admissions and loans.
Rav Pappa argues that both sources are about admissions and loans, but one is a fraudulent claim and the other is not.
Resh Lakish reconciles the two verses about justice, distinguishing between a fraudulent trial and a non-fraudulent one, supporting Rav Pappa's distinction.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution: one verse for judgment, one for compromise
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution: one verse for judgment, one for compromise
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the two verses of 'justice' refer to judgment and compromise. A baraita illustrates this with examples of ships and camels, and explains how to prioritize when one is laden and the other is not, or one is near and the other far, and when both are equal, compromise is used.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that the two verses of 'justice' refer to judgment and compromise, resolving the contradiction.
A baraita is cited to support Rav Ashi, explaining that one 'justice' is for judgment and one for compromise, illustrated by the examples of two ships and two camels.

The baraita resolves the practical application: when one is laden and the other not, the laden goes first; when one is near and the other far, the far goes first; when equal, compromise with compensation is imposed.

items.text: Baraitot on pursuing justice: following the best court and the locations of sages
items.text_en: Baraitot on pursuing justice: following the best court and the locations of sages
items.desc_en: Two baraitot expound 'צדק צדק תרדף' to mean following a good court, listing specific sages and their locations, and also to follow sages to their study sessions, listing many sages and their places.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita expounds 'צדק צדק תרדף' to mean follow a good court, listing Rabbi Eliezer in Lod and Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai in Berur Chayil.
A brief digression describes the sounds of a mill in Burni indicating a son's circumcision week, and a lamp in Berur Chayil indicating a wedding feast.
The second baraita expounds the same verse to mean follow sages to their study sessions, listing many sages and their locations, culminating in the Chamber of Hewn Stone.

items.text: Discussion on how to open monetary cases: various formulations for inviting defense
items.text_en: Discussion on how to open monetary cases: various formulations for inviting defense
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses how to invite the defendant to present a defense. Rav Yehuda suggests asking 'Who says as you do?' Ulla objects that this would intimidate them, and proposes asking about witnesses for discrediting. Rabba objects that this would be opening a defense that is also a liability for the other party. After analysis, Rabba suggests asking about witnesses to contradict. Rav Kahana, Abaye, Rava, and Rav Ashi offer alternative formulations, and a baraita supports Abaye and Rava's version.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to formulate the opening invitation for the defense in monetary cases.
Rav Yehuda proposes asking the defendant: 'Who says as you do?'
Ulla objects that this formulation would intimidate (literally 'seal') the defendant, citing a baraita about moving witnesses to unsettle them.
The Gemara rejects the comparison: there the witnesses are passively unsettled, here the court actively intimidates.
Ulla proposes asking the defendant: 'Do you have witnesses to discredit them (as conspiring witnesses)?'
Rabba objects that this opens a defense for one party that is also a liability for the other.
The Gemara questions whether it is truly a liability, citing a Mishnah that conspiring witnesses are not executed until the verdict is finalized.
Rabba clarifies: if the defendant remains silent until the verdict and then brings witnesses to discredit, it becomes a liability for the other party.
Rabba proposes asking the defendant: 'Do you have witnesses to contradict them?'
Rav Kahana proposes saying: 'From your words so-and-so is vindicated.'
Abaye and Rava both propose saying: 'If you did not kill, do not fear.'
Rav Ashi proposes saying: 'Whoever knows a merit for him should come and teach on his behalf.'
A baraita supports Abaye and Rava's version, citing Rabbi's formulation from the Sotah passage: 'If no man has lain with you and if you have not gone astray...'

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that in capital cases, one begins with arguments for acquittal. This sets the stage for the Gemara's discussion on monetary cases.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that in capital cases, one begins with arguments for acquittal.

items.text: Gemara's question from a baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's question from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says monetary verdicts are reversed, but a baraita states that if a judge errs, his ruling stands and he must pay from his own pocket.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that says a judge's erroneous ruling is upheld and he must pay from his own pocket.

items.text: First answer: Rav Yosef distinguishes expert vs. non-expert
items.text_en: First answer: Rav Yosef distinguishes expert vs. non-expert
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a non-expert judge (whose ruling is reversed) and an expert judge (whose ruling stands). However, the Gemara objects that an expert judge is exempt from payment, not that his ruling is irreversible.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a מומחה (expert judge) and a non-expert.
The Gemara objects that a baraita explicitly says a מומחה לבית דין (expert appointed by the court) is exempt from paying, implying his ruling is not reversed.

items.text: Second answer: Rav Nachman distinguishes presence of a greater scholar
items.text_en: Second answer: Rav Nachman distinguishes presence of a greater scholar
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that the Mishnah refers to a case where there is a greater scholar than the judge, so the verdict is reversed; the baraita refers to a case where there is no greater scholar, so the ruling stands.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman distinguishes between a case where there is a greater sage who can reverse the ruling and where there is not.

items.text: Third answer: Rav Sheshet distinguishes error in Mishnah vs. error in judgment
items.text_en: Third answer: Rav Sheshet distinguishes error in Mishnah vs. error in judgment
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet offers a different distinction: an error in a Mishnah (a clear textual mistake) is reversible, while an error in judgment (weighing conflicting opinions) is not reversible.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet distinguishes between an error in a explicit Mishnah ruling (טעה בדבר משנה) and an error in weighing opinions (טעה בשיקול הדעת), citing Rav Asi's principle.

items.text: Clarification of 'error in Mishnah' by Ravina and Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Clarification of 'error in Mishnah' by Ravina and Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether an error in the teachings of great sages like Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Oshaya, or even Rav and Shmuel, is considered an error in a Mishnah. Rav Ashi affirms, but when asked about their own opinions, he dismisses the question, implying they are not authoritative enough.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rav Ashi whether even an error regarding the teachings of Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Oshaya is considered a טעה בדבר משנה, and Rav Ashi affirms.
Ravina asks whether even an error regarding Rav and Shmuel is included, and Rav Ashi again affirms.
Ravina asks whether even an error regarding their own rulings is included, and Rav Ashi dismisses the question, implying they are not authoritative enough.

items.text: Definition of 'error in judgment' by Rav Pappa
items.text_en: Definition of 'error in judgment' by Rav Pappa
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa defines an error in judgment as a case where two Tannaim or Amoraim disagree, the halakha is not established, and the judge follows one opinion while the prevailing sugya supports the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for a definition of טעה בשיקול הדעת, and Rav Pappa provides an example of conflicting Tannaim or Amoraim with no settled halacha.

Rav Pappa defines an error in judgment as a case where two Tannaim or Amoraim disagree, the halakha is not established, and the judge follows one opinion while the prevailing sugya supports the other.

items.text: Challenge from the cow of Beit Menachem
items.text_en: Challenge from the cow of Beit Menachem
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna challenges Rav Sheshet's distinction using the story of Rabbi Tarfon's cow. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva told Rabbi Tarfon he was exempt because he was a court-recognized expert, but if an error in a Mishnah were reversible, Rabbi Akiva should have said the ruling is void. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Akiva gave two reasons: first, it was an error in a Mishnah (reversible), and second, even if it were an error in judgment, Rabbi Tarfon was exempt as a public expert.

sub.text: Rav Hamnuna's challenge to Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's challenge to Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna challenges Rav Sheshet by citing the case of the cow of Beit Menachem, which Rabbi Tarfon fed to dogs.
The case was brought before the sages in Yavneh, who permitted the cow based on the testimony of Todros the Doctor that such practice was standard in Alexandria.

sub.text: Rabbi Tarfon's lament and Rabbi Akiva's response
sub.text_en: Rabbi Tarfon's lament and Rabbi Akiva's response
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tarfon laments his loss, and Rabbi Akiva tells him he is exempt because he is a court-recognized expert (מומחה לרבים).

The Gemara objects: if Rav Sheshet's distinction were correct, Rabbi Akiva should have told Rabbi Tarfon that he erred in a Mishnah (טועה בדבר משנה) and the ruling is reversible, rather than citing the exemption of a מומחה.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Akiva gave two reasons: first, it was an error in a Mishnah (reversible), and second, even if it were an error in judgment (שיקול הדעת), Rabbi Tarfon was exempt as a public expert (מומחה לרבים).

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation of the challenge
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation of the challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains to Rava that the challenge was not about the cow itself (which was already fed to dogs), but about the logic: if an error in a Mishnah is reversible, then Rabbi Akiva should have told Rabbi Tarfon that his ruling was void, not just that he was exempt from payment.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asks Rava what challenge Rav Hamnuna could have raised from the cow incident, since the cow was already fed to dogs and cannot be returned.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation of the challenge
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation of the challenge
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the challenge was about the logic: if an error in a Mishnah is reversible, Rabbi Akiva should have told Rabbi Tarfon that his ruling was void, not just that he was exempt from payment.

items.text: Rav Chisda's distinction: taking and giving with hands
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's distinction: taking and giving with hands
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda offers another resolution: the Mishnah refers to a case where the judge physically handled the money (e.g., collected it), while the baraita refers to a case where he did not. The Gemara questions how a judge can be liable for acquitting a guilty party without handling money, and answers that saying 'you are exempt' is considered like taking and giving.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda distinguishes: the Mishnah refers to a case where the judge physically handled the money (e.g., collected it), while the baraita refers to a case where he did not.
The Gemara questions how a judge can be liable for acquitting a guilty party without physically handling money, since the judge merely says 'you are exempt'.
The Gemara answers that saying 'you are exempt' is considered like taking and giving with the hand, thus the judge is liable.

items.text: Final resolution of the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Final resolution of the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction in the Mishnah's phrase 'both for acquittal and for conviction' by explaining that it means only one thing: monetary cases are reversed for acquittal, which is itself a form of conviction (for the other party). The same applies to capital cases: they are reversed for acquittal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the Mishnah's wording by explaining that the phrase 'both for acquittal and for conviction' is actually a single statement: monetary cases are reversed for acquittal, which is itself a form of conviction for the other party, and the same applies to capital cases.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's phrase 'between'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's phrase 'between'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that we do not reverse to convict, asking whose liability is at stake. It suggests it refers to the blood redeemer, but then objects that we would not kill someone for the blood redeemer's sake, and questions the double use of 'between'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'we do not reverse to convict', interpreting it as a pure merit case versus a merit that is actually a liability.
The Gemara suggests the liability is for the blood redeemer, but objects that we would not kill the defendant for the blood redeemer's sake.
The Gemara raises a further difficulty about the double use of the word 'between' in the Mishnah.

items.text: Ravina's resolution: case of a pledge
items.text_en: Ravina's resolution: case of a pledge
items.desc_en: Ravina explains the Mishnah's case as one where the defendant had a pledge from the plaintiff and took it from him, and the court's error involved ritual purity matters like defiling the pure or purifying the impure.

sub.desc_en: Ravina resolves the Mishnah's case as one where the defendant held a pledge from the plaintiff and took it, and the court's error involved טומאה (ritual impurity) matters—defiling the pure or purifying the impure.

items.text: Baraita on returning a convicted defendant and exception for the enticer
items.text_en: Baraita on returning a convicted defendant and exception for the enticer
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from verses that a court may reverse a capital verdict to acquit but not to convict. Rav Shimi bar Ashi and Rav Kahana add that for an enticer (mesit), the opposite applies: we do reverse to convict, based on verses commanding no mercy.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites verses to establish that a court may reverse a capital verdict to acquit but not to convict.

sub.text: Rav Shimi bar Ashi and Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi and Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi and Rav Kahana add that for an enticer (mesit), the opposite rule applies: we reverse to convict, based on verses commanding no mercy.

items.text: Derivation for those liable to exile and lashes
items.text_en: Derivation for those liable to exile and lashes
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Sheshet about the source for returning a verdict for those liable to exile and lashes. The answer comes from a verbal analogy on 'murderer' and 'wicked'. A baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Sheshet for the scriptural source that a verdict of exile may be returned in favor of the defendant.
The Gemara answers that the source is a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'רוצח' (murderer) from the laws of exile.
The Gemara raises the parallel question: what is the source for returning a verdict for those liable to lashes?
The Gemara answers that the source is a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'רשע' (wicked) from the context of lashes.
A baraita is cited that explicitly supports both derivations: exile from 'רוצח' and lashes from 'רשע'.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction: error in matters Sadducees deny vs. admit
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction: error in matters Sadducees deny vs. admit
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a court reverses only if the error was in a matter the Sadducees do not admit, but if in a matter they admit, the verdict stands. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba asks about an error in adultery, and Rabbi Yochanan responds cryptically, but Rabbi Ami reports that for adultery the court does reverse. Rabbi Avahu clarifies that the case where they do not reverse is when the error was in an unnatural manner.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that a court reverses a verdict only if the error was in a matter the Sadducees do not admit, but if in a matter they admit, the verdict stands.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba asks Rabbi Yochanan about the case of an error in adultery, and Rabbi Yochanan responds cryptically.
Rabbi Ami reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled that for an error in adultery, the court does reverse the verdict.
Rabbi Avahu clarifies that the case where the court does not reverse is when the error was in an unnatural manner of intercourse.

items.text: Question on 'all' in monetary laws and resolution
items.text_en: Question on 'all' in monetary laws and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'all' in the Mishnah's phrase 'monetary laws, all...' includes even witnesses. It suggests the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, who says a witness may testify for acquittal but not conviction. Rav Pappa resolves that it refers to one of the students, and all agree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the word 'all' in the Mishnah's phrase 'monetary laws, all...' includes even witnesses.
The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, who permits a witness to testify for acquittal but not conviction, and not the Sages.
A baraita is cited: the verse 'one witness shall not testify against a person' is interpreted by Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda to allow testimony for acquittal but not for conviction.
Rav Pappa resolves that the Mishnah refers to one of the students, and all agree that a student may testify for acquittal but not conviction.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda and the Rabbis on a witness testifying for acquittal
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda and the Rabbis on a witness testifying for acquittal
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's reasoning from the verse 'עֵד אֶחָד לֹא יַעֲנֶה בְנֶפֶשׁ לָמוּת' that a witness may testify for acquittal but not for conviction. Resh Lakish explains the Rabbis' position that such testimony appears as if the witness is biased in his own testimony. The Gemara then clarifies how the Rabbis interpret the word 'לָמוּת' to refer to a student who wishes to argue for conviction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reasoning of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, who derives from the verse 'עֵד אֶחָד לֹא יַעֲנֶה בְנֶפֶשׁ לָמוּת' that a witness may testify for acquittal but not for conviction.
Resh Lakish explains the Rabbis' position: a witness testifying for acquittal appears biased (נוגע בעדותו) because he is involved in the case.
The Gemara asks how the Rabbis interpret the word 'לָמוּת' in the verse.
A baraita is cited: a witness who wishes to argue for acquittal is not heard, and a student who wishes to argue for conviction is also not heard, based on the verse.

items.text: Rav's ruling on a judge changing his vote after deliberation
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on a judge changing his vote after deliberation
items.desc_en: Rav states that the rule that one who argues for acquittal cannot later argue for conviction applies only during the deliberation stage, but at the final verdict stage, such a change is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the prohibition against a judge changing from acquittal to conviction applies only during the deliberation stage (שעת משא ומתן), but at the final verdict stage (שעת גמר דין) such a change is permitted.

items.text: Challenge to Rav from the Mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav from the Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav from the Mishnah which states that on the next day, one who argued for conviction may argue for acquittal, but not vice versa. The Gemara notes that the next day is the final verdict stage, but resolves that the Mishnah refers to the deliberation stage, as there is also deliberation on the next day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav by citing the Mishnah that on the next day, one who argued for conviction may argue for acquittal, but not vice versa.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to the deliberation stage (שעת משא ומתן), not the final verdict stage, since deliberation also occurs on the next day.

items.text: Support for Rav from the Mishnah's language
items.text_en: Support for Rav from the Mishnah's language
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a support from the Mishnah that only those who argue for conviction may see the arguments of those who acquit, implying that the reverse is not taught. The Gemara explains that the Tanna focuses on acquittal, not conviction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a support from the Mishnah that only those arguing for conviction may see the arguments of those who acquit.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah does not also teach the reverse, that those who acquit may see the arguments of those who convict.
The Gemara explains that the Tanna focuses on acquittal, not conviction, so the reverse is not taught.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav from Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's ruling that if a student who argued for acquittal dies, we consider him as if alive, implying he cannot change his vote. The Gemara answers that currently he did not retract. A message from the academy states that according to Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina, the ruling is 'אֵין מוּצָא' (he is not considered retracted).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav by citing Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's ruling that if a student who argued for acquittal dies, we consider him as if alive and standing in his place, implying he cannot change his vote.
The Gemara objects: Why treat him as if alive? Perhaps if he were alive, he would have retracted his position.
The Gemara answers: Currently, he did not retract, so we consider his original vote as final.
A message from the academy clarifies that according to Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina, the ruling is 'אֵין מוּצָא' (he is not considered retracted), resolving the challenge.

items.text: Challenge from the scribes' practice and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from the scribes' practice and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav from the practice that scribes write both the arguments for acquittal and conviction. The Gemara questions why they write arguments for acquittal, suggesting it is because if a judge later finds a reason for conviction, we do not consider it. The Gemara resolves that it is to prevent two judges from citing the same verse for different reasons, as per Rabbi Asi's question to Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that two scribes write both the arguments for acquittal and conviction.
The Gemara questions why the scribes write arguments for acquittal, suggesting it is because if a judge later finds a reason for conviction, we do not consider it.
The Gemara answers that the purpose is to prevent two judges from citing the same verse for different reasons, as per Rabbi Asi's question to Rabbi Yochanan.

items.text: Source for the principle that one verse can yield multiple interpretations
items.text_en: Source for the principle that one verse can yield multiple interpretations
items.desc_en: Abaye cites the verse 'אַחַת דִּבֶּר אֱלֹהִים שְׁתַּיִם זוּ שָׁמָעְתִּי' to show that one verse can yield multiple interpretations, but one interpretation cannot come from multiple verses. The school of Rabbi Yishmael adds a metaphor of a hammer splitting into many sparks.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the principle that one verse can yield multiple interpretations.
Abaye cites the verse 'אַחַת דִּבֶּר אֱלֹהִים שְׁתַּיִם זוּ שָׁמָעְתִּי' to prove that one verse yields multiple interpretations, but one interpretation does not come from multiple verses.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael adds a metaphor of a hammer splitting into many sparks to illustrate that one verse can yield multiple interpretations.

items.text: Examples of one reason from two verses and the dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabban Gamliel
items.text_en: Examples of one reason from two verses and the dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabban Gamliel
items.desc_en: Rav Zevid gives an example from the Mishnah about the altar sanctifying what is fit for it. Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabban Gamliel both derive the same law from different verses, but they disagree on the details regarding blood and libations. The Gemara then cites Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's alternative example.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for an example of one reason derived from two verses.
Rav Zevid cites the Mishnah about the altar sanctifying what is fit for it, and Rabbi Yehoshua's derivation from the verse 'העולה על מוקדה' (the burnt-offering on the fire-pile).
Rabban Gamliel derives the same law from the verse 'היא העולה על מוקדה על המזבח' (it is the burnt-offering on the fire-pile on the altar), expanding the rule to everything fit for the altar.
The Gemara explains that both sages are adding disqualifications (פסולין), each deriving from a different word in the verse.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's continuation shows they actually disagree about blood and libations, so this is not a case of one reason from two verses.
Rav Pappa offers a different example from a baraita where Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives a law from a verse, providing a genuine case of one reason from two verses.

items.text: Derivation that only fit animals are sanctified on the altar
items.text_en: Derivation that only fit animals are sanctified on the altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'All who touch the altar shall be sanctified' to exclude unfit animals. Rabbi Akiva and the first Tanna derive this from 'lambs' and 'burnt offering' respectively, with a dispute about bird offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by interpreting the verse 'All who touch the altar shall be sanctified' to exclude unfit animals, presenting the Tanna Kamma's derivation from 'lambs' and Rabbi Akiva's derivation from 'burnt offering'.
The Gemara asks what both Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Akiva exclude, and notes that one derives from 'lambs' and the other from 'burnt offering'.
Rav Adda bar Ahava objects that the practical difference between the two derivations is whether bird burnt offerings are included, since 'lambs' excludes birds but 'burnt offering' includes them.

items.text: Dispute about liability for slaughter and sprinkling
items.text_en: Dispute about liability for slaughter and sprinkling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva derive that one is liable for sprinkling blood outside the Temple. Rabbi Avahu notes a difference: according to Rabbi Yishmael, one is liable only for sprinkling, while Rabbi Akiva holds one liable for both slaughter and sprinkling. Abaye argues that even Rabbi Akiva holds only one liability because all acts are included in 'there you shall do'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yishmael derives from the verse 'דם יחשב לאיש ההוא דם שפך' (it shall be considered blood, he shed blood) that one who sprinkles blood outside is included in the liability.

Rabbi Akiva derives the inclusion of sprinkling from the word 'או זבח' (or slaughtered), and the gemara notes that both Tannaim agree they are including sprinkling, differing only in their scriptural derivation.

Rabbi Avahu objects that there is a practical difference between them: according to Rabbi Yishmael one is liable only for sprinkling, while according to Rabbi Akiva one is liable for both slaughter and sprinkling.

Abaye resolves the objection by arguing that even according to Rabbi Akiva one is liable only for one act, because the verse 'שם תעלה עולותיך ושם תעשה' (there you shall offer your burnt offerings and there you shall do) groups all sacrificial acts together as a single prohibition.

items.text: Source that monetary cases are judged by day
items.text_en: Source that monetary cases are judged by day
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Chiya bar Pappa that the verse 'and they shall judge the people at all times' implies day. Rava resolves a contradiction: the day is for beginning judgment, night for concluding.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the Mishnah's rule that monetary cases are judged by day.
Rabbi Chiya bar Pappa cites the verse 'וְשָׁפְטוּ אֶת הָעָם בְּכׇל עֵת' (and they shall judge the people at all times) as the source, implying day.
The Gemara objects that if the verse implies day, then even the beginning of judgment should be at night, which is not the case.
Rava resolves the contradiction between the two verses: day is for beginning judgment, night for concluding it.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's derivation from the juxtaposition of disputes and plagues
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's derivation from the juxtaposition of disputes and plagues
items.desc_en: The Mishnah is not like Rabbi Meir, who derives from the verse that disputes are like plagues: judged by day, not by blind judges, and plagues are like disputes: not by relatives. The Gemara rejects a possible inference that plagues require three judges, citing that even one priest suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah is not like Rabbi Meir, citing his baraita that questions the juxtaposition of disputes and plagues.
Rabbi Meir derives from the juxtaposition that disputes are judged by day and not by blind judges, and plagues are not judged by relatives.
The Gemara objects that one might infer plagues require three judges like disputes, but the verse shows even one priest suffices.

items.text: The blind judge and the resolution of conflicting Mishnayot
items.text_en: The blind judge and the resolution of conflicting Mishnayot
items.desc_en: A blind man in Rabbi Yochanan's neighborhood judged cases, and Rabbi Yochanan did not object. The Gemara questions this because Rabbi Yochanan ruled that a blind person in one eye is disqualified. The resolution is that Rabbi Yochanan found another Mishnah that says monetary cases are judged by day and concluded by night, which is more authoritative.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that a blind man in Rabbi Yochanan's neighborhood judged cases, and Rabbi Yochanan did not object.
The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yochanan could allow this, given his own ruling that a blind person in one eye is disqualified from judging.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yochanan found another Mishnah (דיני ממונות דנין ביום וגומרין בלילה) which he considered more authoritative.
The Gemara explains why the second Mishnah is stronger: either because it is a סתם משנה (anonymous Mishnah) of the majority, or because it is taught in the context of monetary law.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's interpretation of verses and the law of inheritance
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's interpretation of verses and the law of inheritance
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Meir uses the verse 'and they shall judge the people at all times' to include a cloudy day. The verse 'on the day he causes his sons to inherit' is used for inheritance by day, but the Gemara clarifies it refers to the law of inheritance as a judgment. Rav Yehuda's ruling about three visitors writing a will or judging by day is cited, and Rav Chisda adds that at night they may write but not judge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Meir interprets the verse 'וְשָׁפְטוּ אֶת הָעָם בְּכׇל עֵת' (and they shall judge the people at all times), since he does not use it for the law of daytime judgment.
Rava answers that Rabbi Meir uses the verse to include a cloudy day (יוֹם הַמְעוּנָּן) as a valid time for judging, citing the Mishnah about leprosy signs.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah that leprosy signs are not examined in the morning, evening, or on a cloudy day, to explain the relevance of a cloudy day for judgment.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Meir uses the verse 'בְּיוֹם הַנְחִילוֹ אֶת בָּנָיו' (on the day he causes his sons to inherit), since he does not use it for daytime inheritance.
Rabba bar Chanina teaches before Rav Nachman that the verse teaches that inheritance is allocated by day, not by night.
Rav Nachman objects that if the verse is taken literally, a person who dies at night would not be inherited by his sons, which is absurd.
The Gemara clarifies that the verse refers to the law of inheritance as a judgment (דִּין נַחֲלוֹת), citing a baraita that the entire passage is treated as a judgment.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav rules that three visitors may write a will or judge by day, but two may only write.
Rav Chisda adds that at night they may write but not judge, because they become witnesses and a witness cannot become a judge.

items.text: Source that capital cases are judged by day
items.text_en: Source that capital cases are judged by day
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Chiya cites the verse 'and hang them before the sun' to derive that capital cases are judged by day. Rav Chisda proves that 'hanging' means execution by hanging from another verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source that capital cases are judged by day.
Rav Shimi bar Chiya cites the verse 'וְהוֹקַע אוֹתָם לַה׳ נֶגֶד הַשָּׁמֶשׁ' (and hang them before the sun) to derive that capital cases are judged by day.

Rav Chisda proves that 'הוֹקָעָה' (hanging) refers to execution by hanging, citing the verse 'וְהוֹקַעֲנוּם לַה׳ בְּגִבְעַת שָׁאוּל בְּחִיר ה׳' (and we will hang them for the Lord in Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of the Lord).

items.text: Source for appointing courts after the sin of the golden calf
items.text_en: Source for appointing courts after the sin of the golden calf
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses about Ritzpah and the sin of the golden calf, then explains that God told Moses to appoint courts to turn away wrath, not because two cannot be judged in one day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses about Ritzpah and the sin of the golden calf, then questions why the leaders were punished if the people sinned.

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that God told Moses to appoint courts, and the Gemara rejects the possibility that this was because two cannot be judged in one day, citing Rav Chisda's distinction between two different death penalties and one.
The Gemara resolves that the courts were appointed to turn away the wrath of God from Israel.

items.text: Source for completing monetary cases on the same day
items.text_en: Source for completing monetary cases on the same day
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for completing monetary cases on the same day. Rabbi Chanina and Rava offer different verses, and the Gemara reconciles the alternative interpretation of one verse with Rabbi Elazar's teaching about delaying charity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source of the rule that monetary cases are concluded on the same day.
Rabbi Chanina cites the verse 'מְלֵאֲתִי מִשְׁפָּט צֶדֶק יָלִין בָּהּ וְעַתָּה מְרַצְּחִים' (Full of justice, righteousness lodges in her, but now murderers) as the source.
Rava cites the verse 'אַשְּׁרוּ חָמוֹץ' (Woe to those who leaven), interpreting it as a curse on a judge who delays his verdict.
The Gemara objects that the verse 'אַשְּׁרוּ חָמוֹץ' actually means 'leavened bread,' not 'delaying judgment,' so Rava's interpretation is forced.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Chanina's verse is used, given that it is also needed for another teaching.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Chanina's verse is used for Rabbi Elazar's teaching that delaying charity distribution is like shedding blood, but only for bread and dates, not for coins, wheat, or barley.

items.text: Reason capital cases cannot be concluded on Shabbat eve
items.text_en: Reason capital cases cannot be concluded on Shabbat eve
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that capital cases cannot be concluded on Shabbat eve because it is impossible to avoid delaying the verdict or violating Shabbat. Various options are considered and rejected due to the requirement of execution 'before the sun' and the need to avoid afflicting the defendant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why capital cases cannot be concluded on Shabbat eve (ערב שבת).
The Gemara answers that it is impossible to avoid either delaying the verdict or violating Shabbat.
The Gemara asks how one might attempt to conduct the trial on Shabbat eve.
The Gemara rejects the option of completing the trial on Shabbat eve itself, because the judges might find a reason to acquit and would need to delay the verdict.
The Gemara rejects the option of completing the trial on Shabbat and executing on Shabbat, because execution (רציחה) does not override Shabbat.
The Gemara rejects executing on Saturday night, because the verse requires execution 'before the sun' (נגד השמש), i.e., during daytime.
The Gemara rejects completing the trial on Shabbat and executing on Sunday, because that would afflict the defendant (עינוי הדין) by delaying the verdict.
The Gemara rejects trying on Shabbat eve and concluding on Sunday, because the judges might forget their reasoning over Shabbat, despite the scribes' notes.
The Gemara concludes that it is therefore impossible to conduct capital cases on Shabbat eve without violating halacha.

items.text: Kal vachomer for burying a met mitzvah on Shabbat
items.text_en: Kal vachomer for burying a met mitzvah on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish proposes a kal vachomer to Rabbi Yochanan: if Temple service, which overrides Shabbat, is overridden by burying a met mitzvah, then surely burying a met mitzvah overrides Shabbat. The Gemara cites a baraisa about a kohen going to slaughter his paschal lamb or circumcise his son.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) to Rabbi Yochanan: if Temple service, which overrides Shabbat, is overridden by burying a met mitzvah (an unattended corpse), then surely burying a met mitzvah overrides Shabbat.

The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'לְאָבִיו וּלְאִמּוֹ' (to his father and to his mother) that a kohen who is going to slaughter his paschal lamb or circumcise his son is permitted to become impure for a met mitzvah, showing that burial overrides Temple service.

items.text: Opening derivation: Kohen and met mitzvah
items.text_en: Opening derivation: Kohen and met mitzvah
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by considering whether a Kohen Gadol who hears of a death may become impure. It derives from the verse 'וּלְאַחֹתוֹ' that he may not become impure for his sister, but he may become impure for a met mitzvah (an unattended corpse).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a Kohen Gadol who hears of a death may become impure, and answers that the verse 'לֹא יִטַּמֵּא' (he shall not become impure) prohibits it.
The Gemara derives from the verse 'וּלְאַחֹתוֹ' that the Kohen Gadol may not become impure for his sister, but he may become impure for a met mitzvah (an unattended corpse).

items.text: First kal vachomer: burial of met mitzvah and Shabbat
items.text_en: First kal vachomer: burial of met mitzvah and Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer: if Shabbat is overridden for the Temple service, then burial of a met mitzvah should override Shabbat. An objection is raised: execution (רציחה) overrides the service but not Shabbat, disproving the kal vachomer. The Gemara then counters with another kal vachomer that execution should override Shabbat, based on the verse 'מֵעִם מִזְבְּחִי תִּקָּחֶנּוּ לָמוּת'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer: if Shabbat is overridden for the Temple service, then burial of a met mitzvah should override Shabbat.
An objection is raised: execution (רציחה) overrides the Temple service but does not override Shabbat, disproving the kal vachomer.
The Gemara counters with another kal vachomer: if execution overrides the Temple service (based on the verse 'מֵעִם מִזְבְּחִי תִּקָּחֶנּוּ לָמוּת'), then it should also override Shabbat.

items.text: Rava's initial answer: Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Rava's initial answer: Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: Rava cites the Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael who interprets the verse 'לֹא תְבַעֲרוּ אֵשׁ' as excluding execution from Shabbat. The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Yosei this verse comes for a negative commandment, and according to Rabbi Natan it comes to divide (to make each prohibited act separate).

sub.desc_en: Rava cites the Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael who interprets the verse 'לֹא תְבַעֲרוּ אֵשׁ' as excluding execution from Shabbat, and notes that according to Rabbi Yosei this verse comes for a negative commandment, and according to Rabbi Natan it comes to divide (to make each prohibited act separate).

items.text: Rava's revised answer: the word 'מוֹשָׁבוֹת'
items.text_en: Rava's revised answer: the word 'מוֹשָׁבוֹת'
items.desc_en: Rava reinterprets: the difficulty is with the word 'מוֹשָׁבוֹת'. Since Shabbat is a personal obligation that applies both in and outside the Land, why does the Torah write 'מוֹשָׁבוֹת'? A student of Rabbi Yishmael explains: it is a gezerah shavah linking 'מוֹשָׁבוֹת' here to 'מוֹשָׁבוֹת' in the context of courts, teaching that the prohibition of burning fire applies to court proceedings (execution) on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rava revises the difficulty: the Tanna's problem is with the word 'מוֹשָׁבוֹת' — since Shabbat is a personal obligation (חובת הגוף) applying everywhere, why does the Torah write 'מוֹשָׁבוֹת' at all?

A student of Rabbi Yishmael explains the need for 'מוֹשָׁבוֹת': without it, one might think that capital punishment (מיתת בית דין) is permitted on Shabbat, since the verse 'וְהוּמָת' could apply even on Shabbat; the word 'מוֹשָׁבוֹת' teaches otherwise.

The gemara resolves the difficulty by a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy): 'מוֹשָׁבוֹת' here is linked to 'מוֹשָׁבוֹת' in the context of courts (בית דין), teaching that the prohibition of burning fire on Shabbat applies to court-ordered execution, thus excluding capital punishment from the general Shabbat prohibition.

items.text: Abaye's kal vachomer and Rava's conclusion
items.text_en: Abaye's kal vachomer and Rava's conclusion
items.desc_en: Abaye argues: since execution does not override Shabbat, it certainly does not override the Temple service (a fortiori). The verse 'מֵעִם מִזְבְּחִי תִּקָּחֶנּוּ לָמוּת' is explained as referring to an individual sacrifice, which does not override Shabbat. Rava concludes that execution does not override an individual sacrifice either, by a kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: Abaye argues by קל וחומר (a fortiori): since execution does not override Shabbat, it certainly does not override the Temple service.
The gemara explains that the verse 'מֵעִם מִזְבְּחִי תִּקָּחֶנּוּ לָמוּת' refers to an individual sacrifice, which does not override Shabbat.
Rava concludes that execution does not override an individual sacrifice either, by a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument.

items.text: Derivation of the rule that execution does not override Yom Tov
items.text_en: Derivation of the rule that execution does not override Yom Tov
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially attempts to derive from a kal vachomer that execution does not push aside Yom Tov, but questions the premise based on differing views about offerings on Yom Tov. Rava resolves by citing the verse 'from My altar' referring to the daily offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if Yom Tov, which is pushed aside for a private offering, is not overridden by execution, then a private offering, which overrides Yom Tov, should certainly not be overridden by execution.

The Gemara objects that the kal vachomer only works according to the view that voluntary offerings (נדרים ונדבות) are not brought on Yom Tov, but according to the view that they are brought, the premise collapses.
Rava states that according to the view that voluntary offerings are brought on Yom Tov, the verse 'from My altar' (מעם מזבחי) is not fulfilled at all, so the kal vachomer is unnecessary.

Rava explains that even according to the view that voluntary offerings are not brought on Yom Tov, the verse 'from My altar' refers specifically to the daily offering (תמיד), which is the unique altar-offering, and the Torah says 'from My altar you shall take him to die'.

items.text: Rav's claim about his counting in Rabbi's court
items.text_en: Rav's claim about his counting in Rabbi's court
items.desc_en: Rav states that he was present in Rabbi's counting and they would begin with him, contradicting the Mishnah that one begins from the greatest. Rabbah bar Rava explains that in Rabbi's court they always began from the side.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that he was present in Rabbi's counting and they would begin with him, contradicting the Mishnah that one begins from the greatest.
Rabbah bar Rava explains that in Rabbi's court they always began from the side, so Rav's being first did not violate the rule.

items.text: Historical survey of Torah and greatness in one place
items.text_en: Historical survey of Torah and greatness in one place
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rava states that from Moses until Rabbi, Torah and greatness were never found together. The Gemara challenges with examples like Joshua, Saul, David, Solomon, Hezekiah, and Ezra, but each is answered by noting a contemporary who shared the greatness. Rav Adda bar Ahava extends the claim to the period from Rabbi to Rav Ashi.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rava states that from Moses until Rabbi, Torah and greatness were never found together in one person.
The Gemara challenges with Joshua and Phinehas, but answers that Eleazar and the elders shared their greatness.
The Gemara challenges with Saul, but answers that Samuel shared his greatness, and the claim refers to all their years.
The Gemara challenges with David, but answers that Ira the Jairite shared his greatness, and the claim refers to all their years.
The Gemara challenges with Solomon, but answers that Shimei ben Gera shared his greatness, and the claim refers to all his years.
The Gemara challenges with Hezekiah and Ezra, answering that Shebna and Nehemiah shared their greatness respectively.
Rav Adda bar Ahava extends the claim from Rabbi to Rav Ashi, and answers the challenge of Huna bar Natan by noting he was subordinate to Rav Ashi.

items.text: Scriptural sources for beginning from the side in capital cases
items.text_en: Scriptural sources for beginning from the side in capital cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the rule that capital cases begin from the side. Rav Acha bar Pappa derives it from the verse 'lo ta'aneh al rav', and Rabbah bar bar Chanah cites Rabbi Yochanan's proof from David's actions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the rule that capital cases begin from the side.
Rav Acha bar Pappa derives the rule from the verse 'לֹא תַעֲנֶה עַל רִב' (do not testify against a great one), interpreted as beginning from the side.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan's proof
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan's proof
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah cites Rabbi Yochanan's alternative proof from David's actions, where David first had his men gird their swords and only then girded his own, showing beginning from the side.

items.text: Rav's ruling on a teacher judging with his student in capital cases
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on a teacher judging with his student in capital cases
items.desc_en: Rav states that a person may teach his student and judge with him in capital cases. A baraisa challenges this, stating that in capital cases a father and son or teacher and student count as only one.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that a person may teach his student and then judge with him in capital cases.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraisa that in capital cases a father and son or teacher and student count as only one, contradicting Rav's ruling.

items.text: Rav's statement about his students
items.text_en: Rav's statement about his students
items.desc_en: Rav explains that his students Rav Kahana and Rav Asi needed his teaching but not his reasoning, establishing a principle about judicial qualifications.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that his students Rav Kahana and Rav Asi needed his teaching but not his reasoning, establishing a principle about judicial qualifications.

items.text: Ten differences between monetary and capital cases
items.text_en: Ten differences between monetary and capital cases
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu lists ten differences between monetary and capital cases, noting that all except the requirement of twenty-three judges apply to an ox that is stoned. Rav Acha bar Pappa derives this from a verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu lists ten differences between monetary and capital cases, noting that all except the requirement of twenty-three judges apply to an ox that is stoned.
Rav Acha bar Pappa derives from the verse 'לֹא תַטֶּה מִשְׁפַּט אֶבְיֹנְךָ בְּרִיבוֹ' that one may deviate from the standard capital procedure for an ox that is stoned.

items.text: Clarifying the count of ten
items.text_en: Clarifying the count of ten
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how there are ten differences when only nine are listed, and explains that the exclusion of certain judges and the requirement of twenty-three are considered one item.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Avahu's list of ten differences between monetary and capital cases contains only nine items.
The Gemara answers that the exclusion of certain judges and the requirement of twenty-three are counted as one item, making the total ten.

items.text: Additional disqualifications for capital cases
items.text_en: Additional disqualifications for capital cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes another difference: an old man, a eunuch, and one without children are disqualified from capital cases, and Rabbi Yehuda adds a cruel person. The opposite applies to a mesit (enticer).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes an additional disqualification for capital cases: an old man, a eunuch, and one without children are not seated on the Sanhedrin.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that a cruel person is also disqualified from capital cases.
The Gemara states that the opposite applies to a mesit (enticer), citing the verse 'לֹא תַחְמֹל וְלֹא תְכַסֶּה עָלָיו' (do not pity nor cover for him).

items.text: Who is qualified for monetary cases
items.text_en: Who is qualified for monetary cases
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all are qualified for monetary cases, and Rav Yehuda explains this includes a mamzer. The Gemara clarifies that this is needed alongside a separate teaching about a ger, and explains why both are necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what additional case the Mishnah's inclusive term 'all' comes to include in monetary cases.
Rav Yehuda answers that the Mishnah's inclusive language comes to include a mamzer (bastard) as qualified for monetary cases.
The Gemara objects that this same teaching about a mamzer was already stated elsewhere, so why is it repeated here?
The Gemara answers that one teaching comes to include a ger (convert) and the other to include a mamzer, so both are needed.
The Gemara explains why both teachings are necessary: each case has a unique factor that would otherwise exclude the other, so both must be stated explicitly.

items.text: Qualifications for capital cases: blemish-free judges
items.text_en: Qualifications for capital cases: blemish-free judges
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that not all are qualified for capital cases, as judges must be free from any blemish, derived from verses. It rejects the possibility of a physical blemish and establishes that judges must be similar to Moses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why not everyone is qualified to judge capital cases.
