Rav Yosef teaches that just as a court must be free of injustice, so too it must be free of any blemish, and Ameimar cites the verse 'כֻּלָּךְ יָפָה רַעְיָתִי וּמוּם אֵין בָּךְ' (Song of Songs 4:7) as support.
The Gemara objects that the verse might refer to a literal physical blemish.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov rejects the literal interpretation, citing the verse 'וְהִתְיַצְּבוּ שָׁם עִמָּךְ' (Exodus 34:2) to show that judges must be similar to Moses.
The Gemara objects that the requirement of similarity to Moses at Sinai was due to the Divine Presence, not a general rule for judges.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the objection by citing the verse 'וְנָשְׂאוּ אִתָּךְ' (Numbers 11:17), which applies to the seventy elders and establishes that judges must be similar to Moses in all contexts.

items.text: Mishnah: Layout of the Sanhedrin and scribes
items.text_en: Mishnah: Layout of the Sanhedrin and scribes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the Sanhedrin's semicircular arrangement and the two scribes who record votes, with Rabbi Yehuda adding a third scribe.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the Sanhedrin's semicircular arrangement so that the judges can see each other.
The Mishnah states that two scribes stand before the judges, one on the right and one on the left, recording the votes for conviction and acquittal.
Rabbi Yehuda adds a third scribe: one records acquittal votes, one records conviction votes, and the third records both.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Arrangement of the Sanhedrin
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Arrangement of the Sanhedrin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes three rows of disciples sitting before the Sanhedrin, each knowing his place. When a judge is needed, they promote from the first row, and fill vacancies from the congregation, placing the new member in the third row, not in the original seat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the arrangement of three rows of disciples before the Sanhedrin and the procedure for filling vacancies.

items.text: Gemara: Biblical source for the Sanhedrin's structure
items.text_en: Gemara: Biblical source for the Sanhedrin's structure
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina derives the Sanhedrin's arrangement from the verse 'Your navel is like a round goblet, let it not lack mixed wine.' The navel represents the Sanhedrin at the world's center; the goblet protects the world; the moon symbolizes its beauty; the mixed wine ensures a quorum of twenty-three for capital cases. The verse 'Your belly is a heap of wheat' teaches that all benefit from the Sanhedrin's reasoning, and 'hedged with lilies' that even a hedge of lilies cannot breach their integrity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters (the arrangement of the Sanhedrin) derived?
Rabbi Acha bar Chanina answers by citing the verse 'שָׁרְרֵךְ אַגַּן הַסַּהַר אַל יֶחְסַר הַמָּזֶג' (Song of Songs 7:3) as the source.
The Gemara expounds the verse: 'שָׁרְרֵךְ' refers to the Sanhedrin seated at the world's center, 'אַגַּן' protects the world, 'הַסַּהַר' resembles the moon.
The Gemara explains 'אַל יֶחְסַר הַמָּזֶג' as the rule that a judge may leave only if 23 remain, corresponding to a small Sanhedrin.

The Gemara expounds the continuation of the verse: 'בִּטְנֵךְ עֲרֵמַת חִטִּים' teaches that all benefit from the Sanhedrin's reasoning, and 'סוּגָה בַּשּׁוֹשַׁנִּים' teaches that even a hedge of roses is not breached.

items.text: A heretic's challenge to Rav Kahana
items.text_en: A heretic's challenge to Rav Kahana
items.desc_en: A heretic asks Rav Kahana: You permit being alone with a menstruant; can fire be near flax without igniting? Rav Kahana answers that the Torah testified about Israel, 'hedged with lilies' – even a hedge of lilies cannot breach their purity.

sub.desc_en: A heretic challenges Rav Kahana about the permissibility of seclusion with a menstruant, and Rav Kahana answers with the verse 'סוּגָה בַּשּׁוֹשַׁנִּים' to show that Israel's restraint is divinely guaranteed.
Rav Kahana answers that the Torah testified about Israel, 'hedged with lilies' – even a hedge of lilies cannot breach their purity.

items.text: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Zeira on Israel's merit
items.text_en: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Zeira on Israel's merit
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish derives from 'Your temple is like a pomegranate split' that even the empty ones among Israel are full of mitzvot like a pomegranate. Rabbi Zeira derives from 'He smelled the scent of his garments' that even the sinners (bogdav) are fragrant. A story follows about Rabbi Zeira's influence on local brigands, who repented after his death.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish derives from the verse 'כפלח הרמון רקתך' (Your temple is like a pomegranate split) that even the empty ones among Israel are full of mitzvot (commandments) like a pomegranate.
Rabbi Zeira derives from the verse 'וירח את ריח בגדיו' (He smelled the scent of his garments), reading 'בגדיו' as 'בוגדיו' (his traitors), that even the sinners among Israel are fragrant.
A story is told about brigands in Rabbi Zeira's neighborhood whom he drew close to encourage repentance; after his death, they repented.

items.text: Abaye on the promotion of disciples
items.text_en: Abaye on the promotion of disciples
items.desc_en: Abaye infers from the Mishnah that when they move, all move together. He explains that a promoted disciple cannot complain about losing his former seat, as they tell him: 'Be a tail to lions rather than a head to foxes.'

sub.desc_en: Abaye infers from the Mishnah that when the rows move up, all move together.
The Gemara objects: shouldn't the promoted disciple complain that he now sits at the end of the row?
Abaye answers that they tell him the proverb: 'Be a tail to lions rather than a head to foxes.'

items.text: Mishnah: Admonition of witnesses in capital cases
items.text_en: Mishnah: Admonition of witnesses in capital cases
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes how witnesses in capital cases are admonished: they are warned not to testify from conjecture or hearsay, and are told that capital cases differ from monetary ones – the blood of the accused and his descendants hang on them forever. It cites Cain's murder to show that one who destroys a single life is as if he destroyed a whole world, and one who saves a life is as if he saved a whole world. Man was created alone to promote peace and to declare God's greatness, as each person is unique.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by describing the admonition of witnesses in capital cases, warning them not to testify from conjecture, hearsay, or secondhand testimony, and reminding them of the court's scrutiny.
The Mishnah contrasts capital cases with monetary ones: in monetary cases, payment brings atonement, but in capital cases, the blood of the accused and his descendants hang on the witness forever.

The Mishnah cites Cain's murder of Abel, interpreting the plural 'דְּמֵי' (bloods) to include the blood of the victim and his potential descendants, and describing the blood scattered on trees and stones.
The Mishnah explains that man was created alone to teach that one who destroys a single life is as if he destroyed a whole world, and one who saves a single life is as if he saved a whole world.
The Mishnah states that man was created alone for the sake of peace, so that no one can claim superiority of lineage, and to refute heretics who claim multiple powers in heaven.

The Mishnah concludes that man was created alone to declare God's greatness: though a human mints many coins from one mold and they are identical, God stamps each person with the seal of Adam yet no one is alike, so each must say 'the world was created for me.'

items.text: Beginning of the continuation of the admonition
items.text_en: Beginning of the continuation of the admonition
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins a further warning to witnesses, suggesting they might say something, but the text is cut off here.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins a further warning to witnesses, suggesting they might say something, but the text is cut off here.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Admonition of witnesses
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Admonition of witnesses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah asks why we admonish witnesses in capital cases, given that the Torah already commands them to testify. It answers that we might think we have no stake in the matter, but Scripture says 'When the wicked perish, there is joy.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by asking why witnesses are admonished in capital cases, given the Torah already commands testimony, and answers that one might think we have no stake, but Scripture says 'When the wicked perish, there is joy.'

items.text: Gemara: How to admonish witnesses and the story of Shimon ben Shataḥ
items.text_en: Gemara: How to admonish witnesses and the story of Shimon ben Shataḥ
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita describing how to admonish witnesses, using a hypothetical scenario. Rabbi Shimon ben Shataḥ then recounts a personal incident where he saw a man with a sword and a dying victim, but could not execute him due to the requirement of two witnesses; the murderer was later killed by a snake.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the method of admonishing witnesses: the court suggests a hypothetical scenario of circumstantial evidence and declares that if that is all they saw, their testimony is invalid.

Rabbi Shimon ben Shataḥ recounts a personal incident where he saw a man with a sword and a dying victim, but could not execute him due to the requirement of two witnesses; the murderer was later killed by a snake.

items.text: Gemara: The snake as divine punishment and the four death penalties
items.text_en: Gemara: The snake as divine punishment and the four death penalties
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the snake was a punishment for murder, citing Rav Yosef's teaching that after the Temple's destruction, the four death penalties were not abolished but are carried out by divine means. It lists the corresponding natural deaths for each penalty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the snake that killed the murderer was a divine punishment for murder, given that Rav Yosef's teaching assigns snakebite to the penalty of burning.

sub.text: Rav Yosef / Tanna of the school of Hezekiah
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef / Tanna of the school of Hezekiah
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef teaches that after the Temple's destruction, the four death penalties were not abolished but are carried out by divine means.

sub.text: Stam / Tanna of the school of Hezekiah
sub.text_en: Stam / Tanna of the school of Hezekiah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists the corresponding natural deaths for each of the four death penalties: stoning, burning, decapitation, and strangulation.

items.text: Gemara: Alternative explanation for the snake
items.text_en: Gemara: Alternative explanation for the snake
items.desc_en: Some say the murderer had another sin, as the principle states that one liable for two court-imposed deaths is judged by the more severe one.

sub.desc_en: Some say the murderer had another sin, as the principle states: one liable for two court-imposed deaths is judged by the stricter one.

items.text: Gemara: Admonition in monetary vs. capital cases
items.text_en: Gemara: Admonition in monetary vs. capital cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that admonition is used in capital cases but not in monetary ones, aligning with Rabbi Acha's view. However, it challenges this by noting that even in monetary cases, testimony from a witness who heard from another is invalid, yet such testimony is accepted in capital cases. The Gemara concludes that admonition is also used in monetary cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that admonition (אומד) is not applied in capital cases but is applied in monetary cases.
The Gemara identifies this view as aligning with Rabbi Acha, who holds that circumstantial evidence is accepted in monetary cases.
The Gemara challenges the inference by noting that even in monetary cases, testimony from a witness who heard from another is invalid, yet such testimony is accepted in capital cases.

The Gemara concludes that just as testimony from a witness who heard from another is invalid in monetary cases but valid in capital ones, so too admonition (אומד) is applied in capital cases despite being invalid in monetary ones.

items.text: Gemara: Cain's killing of Abel and the expiatory power of exile
items.text_en: Gemara: Cain's killing of Abel and the expiatory power of exile
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Ḥiyya teaches that Cain inflicted many wounds on Abel, not knowing where the soul exits. He also states that the earth never again opened its mouth after receiving Abel's blood. The Gemara then discusses how exile atones for sin, with various opinions: Rabbi Yehuda says it atones for three things, Rabbi Yochanan says it atones for everything, citing the example of Jeconiah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Ḥiyya teaches that Cain inflicted many wounds on Abel, not knowing where the soul exits, until he reached the neck.
Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Ḥiyya states that after receiving Abel's blood, the earth never again opened its mouth for good, only for evil, as Hezekiah's objection and his response show.
Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Ḥiyya asserts that exile atones for half of sin, citing Cain's transition from wandering to settling.
Rav Yehuda says exile atones for three things (sword, famine, plague), citing a verse about leaving Jerusalem.
Rabbi Yochanan says exile atones for everything, citing Jeconiah's exile and his son Shealtiel's miraculous birth.

items.text: Interpretation of the names Shealtiel and Zerubbabel
items.text_en: Interpretation of the names Shealtiel and Zerubbabel
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation for the names Shealtiel (asked of God regarding his oath) and Zerubbabel (sown in Babylon), and identifies Nehemiah ben Hachaliah as his real name.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation for the names Shealtiel (asked of God regarding his oath) and Zerubbabel (sown in Babylon), and identifies Nehemiah ben Hachaliah as his real name.

items.text: The sons of Rabbi Chiyya and the secret of wine
items.text_en: The sons of Rabbi Chiyya and the secret of wine
items.desc_en: Judah and Hezekiah, sons of Rabbi Chiyya, were silent at Rabbi's table until he encouraged them to drink wine. After becoming intoxicated, they said that the son of David will not come until the two houses of Israel (the Exilarch in Babylon and the Nasi in the Land of Israel) cease. Rabbi objected, but Rabbi Chiyya defended them, noting that wine (יַיִן) and secret (סוֹד) have the same numerical value (70), so wine brings out secrets.

sub.desc_en: The narrative sets the scene: Judah and Hezekiah, sons of Rabbi Chiyya, were sitting silently at Rabbi's table until Rabbi encouraged them to drink wine so they would speak.
After becoming intoxicated, they declared that the son of David will not come until the two ruling houses of Israel (the Exilarch in Babylon and the Nasi in the Land of Israel) cease, citing a verse.
Rabbi objects, accusing them of casting thorns in his eyes by predicting the demise of the leadership.
Rabbi Chiyya defends his sons by noting that 'יַיִן' (wine) and 'סוֹד' (secret) both have the numerical value 70, so wine brings out secrets.

items.text: God's righteousness in advancing the exile
items.text_en: God's righteousness in advancing the exile
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda quotes Mar Ukva (or Rav Chisda himself) explaining why God brought evil upon Israel because He is righteous: God performed an act of charity by advancing the exile of Zedekiah while the exile of Jeconiah still existed. The Gemara elaborates on the scholars of Jeconiah's exile and Ulla adds that God advanced the exile by two years before the warning of 'and you will become corrupt' (Deut. 4:25). Rav Acha bar Yaakov calculates that 'quickly' (מְהֵרָה) in the verse equals 852 years.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda quotes Mar Ukva questioning the verse that God brought evil upon Israel because He is righteous.
He answers that God performed a charitable act by advancing the exile of Zedekiah while the exile of Jeconiah still existed.
The Gemara elaborates on the scholars of Jeconiah's exile, describing them as 'חָרָשׁ' (craftsman) and 'מַסְגֵּר' (locker) who were a thousand in number.
Ulla adds that God advanced the exile by two years before the warning of 'וְנוֹשַׁנְתֶּם' (and you will become corrupt).
Rav Acha bar Yaakov calculates that 'מְהֵרָה' (quickly) in the verse equals 852 years.

items.text: Reasons for creating Adam alone
items.text_en: Reasons for creating Adam alone
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma teaches that Adam was created alone to prevent heretics from claiming multiple powers in heaven, to prevent the righteous from boasting of their lineage and the wicked from excusing themselves, to prevent family feuds, and to prevent robbery and violence.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that Adam was created alone, and gives the first reason: to prevent heretics from claiming multiple powers in heaven.
The baraita gives a second reason: to prevent the righteous from boasting of their lineage and the wicked from excusing themselves.
The baraita gives a third reason: to prevent family feuds, arguing that if one ancestor already causes strife, two would cause even more.
The baraita gives a fourth reason: to prevent robbery and violence, arguing that if one ancestor already leads to theft, two would cause even more.

items.text: The greatness of God and the uniqueness of each person
items.text_en: The greatness of God and the uniqueness of each person
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma explains that Adam was created alone to proclaim God's greatness: while a human mints many coins from one mold, God stamps every person with the seal of Adam yet none are alike. The Gemara adds that faces differ to prevent people from claiming another's property. Rabbi Meir states that people differ in voice, appearance, and mind—voice and appearance for modesty, mind to prevent robbery.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the Tanna Kamma's statement that Adam was created alone to proclaim God's greatness: humans mint many coins from one mold, but God stamps every person with the seal of Adam yet none are alike, citing a verse.
The Gemara asks why people's faces are not alike, and answers that it prevents a person from seeing a nice house or woman and claiming it as his own, citing a verse.
Rabbi Meir adds that people differ in three things: voice, appearance, and mind—voice and appearance for modesty, mind to prevent robbery.

items.text: Why Adam was created on the eve of Shabbat
items.text_en: Why Adam was created on the eve of Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma teaches that Adam was created on the eve of Shabbat to prevent heretics from claiming God had a partner in creation, to humble him (a gnat preceded him), and so he could immediately enter into the mitzvah of Shabbat and the feast. A parable of a king who built a palace and prepared a feast before inviting guests is cited, with verses from Proverbs interpreted allegorically. The Gemara notes a contradiction in verses about God's throne, and explains that the serpent enticed Adam through the woman.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that Adam was created on the eve of Shabbat and gives three reasons: to prevent heretics from claiming a partner in creation, to humble him (a gnat preceded him), and so he could immediately enter into the mitzvah.
The baraita adds a fourth reason: so Adam could immediately enter the feast, illustrated by a parable of a king who built a palace and prepared a feast before inviting guests, citing Proverbs 9:1-3.

The Gemara interprets each phrase of the Proverbs verse allegorically: wisdom is God's attribute, the seven pillars are the seven days of creation, the feast is the world's resources, and the maidens are Adam and Eve.

Rabba bar bar Chana raises a contradiction: one verse says 'on the tops' (על גפי) and another says 'on a throne' (על כסא), resolving that initially God's presence was on the tops, but ultimately on the throne.
The Gemara explains that the verse 'Whoever is simple, let him turn in here; lacking of heart, she said to him' refers to the serpent enticing Adam through the woman, citing Proverbs 6:32.

items.text: Adam's dust gathered from the entire world
items.text_en: Adam's dust gathered from the entire world
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir states that Adam's dust was gathered from the entire world, citing verses about God's eyes roaming the earth. Rav Oshaya quotes Rav that Adam's dust was taken from the place of the altar.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Meir said Adam's dust was gathered from the entire world, citing verses; and Rav Oshaya said in the name of Rav that Adam the first man...
Rav Oshaya reports in Rav's name that Adam's dust was taken from the place of the altar.

items.text: Opening: Gathering of Adam's dust
items.text_en: Opening: Gathering of Adam's dust
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes how Adam's body was formed from dust gathered from various places, with his buttocks from Akra de-Agma.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes the gathering of Adam's dust from various lands, with Rav Acha specifying that his buttocks came from Akra de-Agma.

items.text: The twelve hours of Adam's creation
items.text_en: The twelve hours of Adam's creation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan bar Chanina details the twelve hours of the day of Adam's creation, from gathering dust to his expulsion, citing the verse 'Adam in his glory does not stay overnight.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan bar Chanina details the twelve hours of Adam's first day, from the gathering of his dust to his expulsion.

items.text: A wild beast only attacks when a person is like an animal
items.text_en: A wild beast only attacks when a person is like an animal
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama states that a wild beast only attacks a person if they have become like an animal, citing the verse 'He is compared to the beasts, they are like them.'

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama states that a wild animal does not attack a person unless the person has become like an animal, citing a verse.

items.text: Consultation with the ministering angels about creating man
items.text_en: Consultation with the ministering angels about creating man
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav recounts that God consulted three groups of ministering angels about creating man. The first two groups were burned for objecting, while the third group acquiesced. Later, when the generations of the Flood and the Dispersion sinned, the angels said 'Didn't the first ones speak well?' and God responded with the verse 'Even to old age I am He.'

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav recounts that God created a group of ministering angels and consulted them about creating man, describing his deeds.
The first group of angels objects with a verse, and God burns them; the same happens with the second group.
The third group of angels acquiesces, saying the world is God's and He may do as He wishes.

sub.text: Angels after the Flood and Dispersion
sub.text_en: Angels after the Flood and Dispersion
sub.desc_en: When the generations of the Flood and the Dispersion sin, the angels object that the first groups were right.
God responds with the verse 'Even to old age I am He, and to gray hairs I will bear,' indicating His enduring patience.

items.text: Adam's original size and its diminution
items.text_en: Adam's original size and its diminution
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says Adam originally spanned from one end of the world to the other, but after sinning God diminished him. Rabbi Elazar says Adam reached from earth to the firmament. The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between the verses by saying both describe the same measure.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that Adam originally spanned from one end of the world to the other, citing a verse, and that after sinning God diminished him, citing another verse.
Rabbi Elazar states that Adam reached from earth to the firmament, citing the same verses as Rav Yehuda.
The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction between the two descriptions by stating that both measure the same extent.

items.text: Adam spoke Aramaic and was shown future generations
items.text_en: Adam spoke Aramaic and was shown future generations
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says Adam spoke Aramaic, citing the verse 'How precious are Your friends to me, God.' Resh Lakish explains that God showed Adam all future generations and their scholars; when he reached Rabbi Akiva's generation, he rejoiced in his Torah but grieved at his death.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that Adam the First spoke Aramaic, citing a verse.

Resh Lakish explains that God showed Adam all future generations and their scholars; when Adam reached Rabbi Akiva's generation, he rejoiced in his Torah but grieved at his death, citing the same verse.

items.text: Adam's heresy: was he a min or a denier?
items.text_en: Adam's heresy: was he a min or a denier?
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says Adam was a min (heretic), interpreting 'Ayeka' as 'Where has your heart strayed?' Rabbi Yitzchak says he was a foreskin-puller. Rav Nachman says he was a denier of the principle, citing verses about breaking the covenant.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that Adam was a מין (heretic), interpreting the verse 'אַיֶּכָּה' (Where are you?) as 'אָן נָטָה לִבֶּךָ' (Where has your heart strayed?).

Rabbi Yitzchak offers a different interpretation: Adam was a foreskin-puller, citing the verse 'וְהֵמָּה כְּאָדָם עָבְרוּ בְרִית' (they like Adam have transgressed the covenant) and the verse 'אֶת בְּרִיתִי הֵפַר' (he has broken My covenant).
Rav Nachman says Adam was a denier of the principle (of God), citing the same verse 'עָבְרוּ בְרִית' and the verse 'עַל אֲשֶׁר עָזְבוּ אֶת בְּרִית ה׳' (because they forsook the covenant of the Lord).

items.text: Responding to a heretic: Jewish vs. non-Jewish
items.text_en: Responding to a heretic: Jewish vs. non-Jewish
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches to be diligent in Torah to answer a heretic. Rabbi Yochanan says this applies only to a non-Jewish heretic, but a Jewish heretic is even worse because he is more brazen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer says one should be diligent in Torah study to know how to answer a heretic (אפיקורוס).
Rabbi Yochanan clarifies that the Mishnah refers only to a gentile heretic, but a Jewish heretic is even more brazen.

items.text: Scriptural responses to heretical prooftexts
items.text_en: Scriptural responses to heretical prooftexts
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that wherever heretics have raised objections from plural language in Scripture, the refutation is nearby. He cites examples: 'Let us make man' followed by 'And God created man'; 'Let us go down' followed by 'And the Lord came down'; 'God was revealed to him' followed by 'God who answered me.' The Gemara explains that these plural forms show God consults with His heavenly court, as per the verse 'By the decree of the watchers is the matter.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that wherever heretics have raised objections, the refutation is nearby.
Rabbi Yochanan cites three scriptural examples where a plural form is immediately followed by a singular form, showing the refutation is adjacent.
The Gemara adds three more verses that use plural language for God, continuing the pattern of heretical prooftexts.
The Gemara explains that these plural forms show God consults with His heavenly court, citing Rabbi Yochanan's principle and the verse from Daniel.

items.text: The two thrones: for God and David, or for judgment and righteousness?
items.text_en: The two thrones: for God and David, or for judgment and righteousness?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the verse 'Thrones were set up.' One throne is for God and one for David, according to Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yosei rebukes him for profaning the Divine Presence. Alternatively, one is for judgment and one for righteousness. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya tells Rabbi Akiva to stick to halakha. The final view is one throne and one footstool.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: granted all the previous verses are answered, but what about the verse 'until thrones were set up' (Daniel 7:9) which uses the plural 'thrones'?
Rabbi Akiva answers: one throne is for God and one for King David, as taught in a baraita.
Rabbi Yosei rebukes Rabbi Akiva, saying: Akiva, how long will you profane the Divine Presence by suggesting a throne for David alongside God?
Rabbi Yosei offers an alternative: one throne is for judgment and one for righteousness.
The Gemara asks: did Rabbi Akiva accept Rabbi Yosei's correction or not?
The Gemara brings a baraita: one throne is for judgment and one for righteousness — the words of Rabbi Akiva, showing he accepted Rabbi Yosei's view.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya rebukes Rabbi Akiva: Akiva, what business do you have with aggadah? Go back to the laws of negaim and ohalot!

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's final view
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's final view
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya resolves: one throne is a seat and one is a footstool for God's feet.

items.text: Rav Idit's response to a heretic about Metatron
items.text_en: Rav Idit's response to a heretic about Metatron
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman says only one who can respond like Rav Idit should engage heretics. A heretic challenged Rav Idit about the verse 'Go up to the Lord,' which should say 'Go up to Me.' Rav Idit explained that this refers to Metatron, whose name is like his Master's, but he is not to be worshipped, as per 'Do not rebel against him' meaning 'Do not exchange Me for him.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that only one who can respond to heretics like Rav Idit should engage them.
A heretic challenges Rav Idit that the verse 'עֲלֵה אֶל ה (go up to the Lord)' should have said 'עֲלֵה אֵלַי (go up to Me).'
Rav Idit explains that the verse refers to Metatron (מטטרון), whose name is like his Master's, as it says 'כִּי שְׁמִי בְּקִרְבּוֹ (for My name is within him).'
The heretic objects that if Metatron has God's name, then people should worship him.
Rav Idit answers that the verse 'אַל תַּמֵּר בּוֹ (do not rebel against him)' means 'do not exchange Me for him.'
The heretic objects that if Metatron is not to be worshipped, why does the verse say 'לֹא יִשָּׂא לְפִשְׁעֲכֶם (he will not forgive your transgression)?'
Rav Idit resolves that we have a tradition (הֵימָנוּתָא בִּידַן) that we do not accept even a messenger (פַּרְוָונְקָא), as the verse says 'אִם אֵין פָּנֶיךָ הֹלְכִים (if Your presence does not go).'

items.text: A launderer's response to a heretic about 'from the Lord'
items.text_en: A launderer's response to a heretic about 'from the Lord'
items.desc_en: A heretic challenged Rabbi Yishmael about the verse 'The Lord rained... from the Lord,' which should say 'from Him.' A launderer responded by citing a similar construction in Lamech's words 'my wives' instead of 'my wife,' showing that Scripture sometimes speaks in a certain style. He learned this from Rabbi Meir's lessons, which included one-third halakha, one-third aggada, and one-third parables.

sub.desc_en: A heretic challenges Rabbi Yishmael about the verse 'The Lord rained... from the Lord' (מֵאֵת ה׳), arguing it should say 'from Him' (מֵאִתּוֹ).
A launderer intervenes, citing a parallel case in Lamech's words (נְשֵׁי לֶמֶךְ instead of נָשַׁיי) to show that Scripture sometimes uses a third-person style, thus answering the heretic.
The launderer explains that he learned this interpretive approach from Rabbi Meir's lessons.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's description of Rabbi Meir's teaching
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's description of Rabbi Meir's teaching
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan describes that Rabbi Meir's public lectures consisted of one-third halakha, one-third aggada, and one-third parables, and that he had three hundred fox parables, of which only three remain.

items.text: Caesar accuses God of theft; Rabban Gamliel's daughter refutes
items.text_en: Caesar accuses God of theft; Rabban Gamliel's daughter refutes
items.desc_en: Caesar cites the verse about God putting Adam to sleep to take a rib, calling God a thief. Rabban Gamliel's daughter intervenes, using a parable about a silver pitcher replaced with gold to argue that Adam gained a wife. She then demonstrates with raw meat that taking discreetly avoids disgust, justifying God's method.

sub.desc_en: Caesar accuses God of being a thief, citing the verse where God put Adam to sleep to take a rib.
Rabban Gamliel's daughter asks to respond, and uses a parable about a silver pitcher replaced with gold to argue that Adam gained a wife.
Caesar objects that God should have taken the rib openly rather than by stealth.
She demonstrates with raw meat that taking discreetly avoids disgust, justifying God's method of taking the rib while Adam slept.

items.text: Caesar questions God's knowledge of earthly matters
items.text_en: Caesar questions God's knowledge of earthly matters
items.desc_en: Caesar claims to know God's location and activity. Rabban Gamliel responds by sighing, and when asked why, explains he is distressed over a son overseas. He then rebukes Caesar: if you don't know where your son is on earth, how can you claim to know where God is in heaven?

sub.desc_en: Caesar asserts to Rabban Gamliel that he knows what God does and where He sits.
Rabban Gamliel sighs deeply, prompting Caesar to ask why.
Rabban Gamliel explains he is distressed over a son overseas, and Caesar admits he does not know where his own son is.
Rabban Gamliel rebukes Caesar: if you do not know where your son is on earth, how can you claim to know where God is in heaven?

items.text: Caesar boasts he can count stars; Rabban Gamliel refutes
items.text_en: Caesar boasts he can count stars; Rabban Gamliel refutes
items.desc_en: Caesar challenges the verse 'He counts the number of the stars,' claiming he can count them. He brings gourds and tosses them in a sieve. Rabban Gamliel tells him to count them, but Caesar cannot because they are spinning. Rabban Gamliel explains the sky similarly spins. An alternative version has Caesar counting his teeth and failing.

sub.desc_en: Caesar challenges Rabban Gamliel, claiming he can count the stars despite the verse that God counts them.
Rabban Gamliel brings gourds, tosses them in a sieve so they spin, and tells Caesar to count them, explaining that the sky similarly spins, making counting impossible.
An alternative version has Caesar counting his teeth and failing, with Rabban Gamliel drawing a parallel to counting the stars.

items.text: Caesar argues God created mountains but not wind; refuted by anatomy
items.text_en: Caesar argues God created mountains but not wind; refuted by anatomy
items.desc_en: Caesar cites a verse using different verbs for creating mountains and wind, suggesting different creators. Rabban Gamliel retorts that for humans, different verbs are also used for creating parts, yet they are from one God. He proves by analogy: a handbreadth in a person has two holes, yet one God created both, as per the verse about the ear and eye. Caesar concedes.

sub.desc_en: Caesar argues that the verse using different verbs for creating mountains and wind implies two creators, and challenges Rabban Gamliel with an analogy from human creation.
Rabban Gamliel refutes Caesar by citing the human body: a handbreadth has two holes, yet one God created both, as per the verse about the ear and eye, and Caesar concedes.

items.text: Magus claims dual deities; Amemar refutes
items.text_en: Magus claims dual deities; Amemar refutes
items.desc_en: A magus asserts that the upper half belongs to Hormiz and the lower to Ahormiz. Amemar retorts: if so, how does Ahormiz allow Hormiz to pass water through his territory? This implies the absurdity of dualism, as water from above passes through the lower realm.

sub.desc_en: A magus asserts to Amemar that the upper half of the world belongs to Hormiz and the lower half to Ahormiz, positing a dualistic division of divine authority.
Amemar objects: if the world is divided, how does Ahormiz allow Hormiz to pass water through his territory, implying the absurdity of dualism.

items.text: Caesar proposes unification; Rabbi Tanchum's clever response
items.text_en: Caesar proposes unification; Rabbi Tanchum's clever response
items.desc_en: Caesar suggests all nations become one. Rabbi Tanchum agrees on condition that the Romans circumcise themselves like Jews. Caesar admits the logic but throws Rabbi Tanchum to a lion, which does not eat him. A heretic claims the lion was not hungry, and when thrown himself, is eaten.

sub.desc_en: Caesar proposes that all nations become one, and Rabbi Tanchum cleverly responds that the Romans should circumcise themselves like Jews.
Caesar admits the logic but orders Rabbi Tanchum thrown to a lion, which does not eat him.
A heretic claims the lion was not hungry, and when thrown himself, is eaten.

items.text: Caesar questions how the Shechinah can be in ten places; Rabban Gamliel's analogy
items.text_en: Caesar questions how the Shechinah can be in ten places; Rabban Gamliel's analogy
items.desc_en: Caesar asks: if the Shechinah rests among every ten, how many Shechinahs are there? Rabban Gamliel has his servant strike Caesar with a strap. When Caesar asks why, Rabban Gamliel explains: if the sun, one of God's servants, can enter Caesar's house, how much more can the Shechinah be everywhere?

sub.desc_en: Caesar asks Rabban Gamliel: if the Shechinah rests among every ten, how many Shechinahs are there?
Rabban Gamliel calls his servant and strikes Caesar with a strap, then asks why the sun entered Caesar's house.
Caesar answers that the sun shines on the entire world, not just his house.
Rabban Gamliel argues by קל וחומר (a fortiori): if the sun, one of God's countless servants, enters everywhere, how much more so can the Shechinah be present everywhere.

items.text: Heretic mocks God's contradictory commands to Ezekiel; Rabbi Abahu explains
items.text_en: Heretic mocks God's contradictory commands to Ezekiel; Rabbi Abahu explains
items.desc_en: A heretic notes God told Ezekiel to lie on his left side and then on his right, implying inconsistency. A student asks about the reason for the Sabbatical year. Rabbi Abahu explains that God commanded Israel to work six years and rest the seventh, but they sinned and were exiled. He compares God's punishment to a merciful king who chastises the leaders, as God chastised Ezekiel to atone for Israel's sins.

sub.desc_en: A heretic mocks God as a trickster for commanding Ezekiel to lie first on his left side and then on his right side.
A student asks Rabbi Abahu about the reason for the Sabbatical year.
Rabbi Abahu announces that he will give an answer relevant to both the heretic and the student.

Rabbi Abahu explains that God commanded Israel to work six years and rest the seventh, but they sinned and were exiled; God punished Ezekiel as a merciful king chastises leaders, to atone for Israel's sins.

items.text: Heretic claims God is a priest; Rabbi Abahu defends immersion in fire
items.text_en: Heretic claims God is a priest; Rabbi Abahu defends immersion in fire
items.desc_en: A heretic argues that since God commanded 'take for Me a portion' (like a priest), He is a priest. He asks how God immersed after burying Moses, since water is measured by God. Rabbi Abahu answers that God immersed in fire, citing 'the Lord will come in fire.' The heretic objects that immersion is not in fire, but Rabbi Abahu retorts that primary immersion is in fire, as per the verse 'everything that cannot withstand fire, pass through water.'

sub.desc_en: A heretic argues to Rabbi Abahu that God is a priest because He commanded 'take for Me a portion' (תרומה), and asks how God immersed after burying Moses, since water is measured by God.
Rabbi Abahu answers that God immersed in fire, citing the verse 'the Lord will come in fire.'
The heretic objects that immersion is not performed in fire.
Rabbi Abahu retorts that primary immersion is in fire, citing the verse 'everything that cannot withstand fire, pass through water.'

items.text: Heretic questions Israel's uniqueness; Rabbi Avina cites their own verse
items.text_en: Heretic questions Israel's uniqueness; Rabbi Avina cites their own verse
items.desc_en: A heretic asks: what is the greatness of Israel being 'one nation on earth' when all nations are 'as nothing before Him'? Rabbi Avina retorts: your own verse testifies for us, as it is written... (the text cuts off).

sub.desc_en: A heretic asks Rabbi Avina: what is the greatness of Israel being 'one nation on earth' when all nations are 'as nothing before Him'?
Rabbi Avina retorts: your own verse testifies for us, as it is written (the text cuts off).

items.text: Opening contradiction: God's universal goodness vs. special favor
items.text_en: Opening contradiction: God's universal goodness vs. special favor
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar raises a contradiction between two verses: 'God is good to all' and 'God is good to those who wait for Him.' He resolves it with a parable: when watering a garden, one waters all; when weeding, one only weeds the best plants.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar raises a contradiction between two verses: one says God is good to all, another says God is good only to those who wait for Him.
Rabbi Elazar resolves the contradiction with a parable: when watering a garden, one waters all; when weeding, one only weeds the best plants.
Rabbi Acha bar Chanina cites the verse 'When the wicked perish, there is song' and applies it to the death of Ahab.

items.text: God does not rejoice at the downfall of the wicked
items.text_en: God does not rejoice at the downfall of the wicked
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse about rejoicing at the fall of the wicked, then questions whether God rejoices. Rabbi Yonatan explains that the phrase 'for He is good' is omitted from the Song of the Sea because God does not rejoice at the drowning of the Egyptians. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina adds that God does not rejoice, but others do, as indicated by the spelling 'יָשִׂישׂ'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Holy One, Blessed be He, rejoices at the downfall of the wicked.
Rabbi Yonatan explains that the phrase 'כי טוב' (for He is good) is omitted from the song of praise because God is not gladdened by the downfall of the wicked.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan cites the verse about the splitting of the Red Sea, where God rebukes the angels for wanting to sing while His handiwork (the Egyptians) drowns.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina resolves the contradiction: God Himself does not rejoice, but He causes others to rejoice.
The Gemara provides linguistic support: the verse uses 'יָשִׂישׂ' (causing joy) rather than 'יָשׂוּשׂ' (rejoicing), confirming that God causes joy but does not rejoice Himself.

items.text: Interpretation of 'the harlots washed'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'the harlots washed'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets the verse as referring to the fulfillment of two prophecies: one of Micaiah and one of Elijah. Rava disagrees, saying it refers to actual harlots that Jezebel placed in Ahab's chariot to warm him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets the verse 'the harlots washed' as referring to the fulfillment of two prophecies: one of Micaiah and one of Elijah.
Rava disagrees, saying the verse refers to actual harlots that Jezebel placed in Ahab's chariot to warm him.

items.text: Interpretation of 'a man drew a bow at random'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'a man drew a bow at random'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says the arrow hit 'according to its innocence' (by chance), while Rava says it was to fulfill two prophecies: one of Micaiah and one of Elijah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets 'letummo' as 'according to its innocence' (by chance), meaning the arrow hit without intention.
Rava interprets 'letummo' as 'to complete' two prophecies: one of Micaiah and one of Elijah.
The Gemara provides a mnemonic for forthcoming statements and introduces a question about the verse linking Ahab's call to Obadiah.

items.text: Obadiah's righteousness and prophecy
items.text_en: Obadiah's righteousness and prophecy
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why Obadiah's house was not blessed despite his fear of God, and why he merited prophecy. Rabbi Yitzchak says a heavenly voice declared that Obadiah feared God but Ahab's house was not destined for blessing. Rabbi Abba notes that Obadiah is praised more than Abraham. Rabbi Yitzchak explains Obadiah's prophecy was due to hiding prophets, and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Avahu debate why he hid them in groups of fifty.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains that Ahab questioned Obadiah's fear of God because his house was not blessed like those of Jacob and Joseph.
A Divine Voice declares that Obadiah indeed fears God greatly, but Ahab's house is not destined for blessing.
Rabbi Abba notes that Obadiah is praised more than Abraham because the term 'greatly' is used for Obadiah but not for Abraham.
Rabbi Yitzchak asks why Obadiah merited prophecy and answers that it was because he hid one hundred prophets in a cave.
The Gemara asks why Obadiah hid the prophets in groups of fifty rather than all together.
Rabbi Elazar says Obadiah learned from Jacob to divide the prophets to lessen danger.
Rabbi Avahu says the reason is that no cave can hold more than fifty people.
The Gemara asks why specifically Obadiah prophesied concerning Edom.

items.text: Why Obadiah prophesied against Edom
items.text_en: Why Obadiah prophesied against Edom
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains that Obadiah, who lived between two wicked people (Ahab and Jezebel) and did not learn from their ways, was chosen to prophesy against Esau, who lived between two righteous people (Isaac and Rebecca) and did not learn from them. Ephraim Miksha'ah adds that Obadiah was an Edomite convert.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains that Obadiah, who dwelled between two wicked people and did not learn from them, was chosen to prophesy against Esau, who dwelled between two righteous people and did not learn from them.

sub.text: Ephraim Miksha'ah in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Ephraim Miksha'ah in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Ephraim Miksha'ah adds that Obadiah was an Edomite convert, and cites the folk saying that the ax comes from the forest itself.

items.text: Interpretation of David's treatment of Moab and the king of Moab's sacrifice
items.text_en: Interpretation of David's treatment of Moab and the king of Moab's sacrifice
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains the proverb 'from within itself, a beam is taken to strike it' regarding David's measurement of Moab. Rav Dimi adds 'a thigh from within it rots.' The Gemara then debates whether the king of Moab's sacrifice of his son was for Heaven or idolatry, and resolves a contradiction about Israel following the practices of the nations.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai to explain the folk saying 'from within itself, a beam is taken to strike it' as applied to David's measurement of Moab.
Rav Dimi adds a parallel folk saying: 'a thigh from within it rots,' reinforcing the idea of self-destruction from within.
The Gemara presents a dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding whether the king of Moab's sacrifice of his son was for Heaven or for idolatry.
The Gemara raises an objection: according to the view that the sacrifice was for idolatry, why would the verse say 'there was great wrath upon Israel'?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi resolves the contradiction by explaining that Israel followed the corrupt practices of the nations, not the proper ones, thus incurring wrath.

items.text: The beauty of Esther and Sarah
items.text_en: The beauty of Esther and Sarah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa comments on the verse 'they departed from him and returned to the land' that Israel's enemies descended to the lowest level. He then notes that Esther's beauty, described as 'very beautiful,' had not reached half of Sarah's beauty, as Sarah is described with 'very' included.

sub.text: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's first statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's first statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa interprets the verse 'they departed from him and returned to the land' to mean that Israel's enemies descended to the lowest level.

sub.text: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's second statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's second statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa compares Esther's beauty, described as 'עַד מְאֹד' (very beautiful), to Sarah's beauty, concluding that Esther had not reached even half of Sarah's beauty because Sarah's description includes 'מְאֹד' (very) as part of the full phrase.

items.text: Mishnah: The seven cross-examinations and additional examinations
items.text_en: Mishnah: The seven cross-examinations and additional examinations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the seven חקירות (cross-examinations) regarding time and place, and the additional בדיקות (examinations) regarding recognition, warning, and idolatry. It notes that increasing examinations is praiseworthy, citing Ben Zakkai's examination about fig stalks.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the seven חקירות (cross-examinations) regarding time and place.
The Mishnah lists the additional בדיקות (examinations) regarding recognition, warning, and idolatry.
The Mishnah states that increasing examinations is praiseworthy, citing Ben Zakkai's examination about fig stalks.

items.text: Mishnah: Distinction between חקירות and בדיקות, and rules of contradictory testimony
items.text_en: Mishnah: Distinction between חקירות and בדיקות, and rules of contradictory testimony
items.desc_en: The Mishnah explains that if a witness says 'I don't know' regarding a חקירה, the testimony is void, but for a בדיקה it remains valid. It then discusses cases where witnesses contradict each other about the date or time, and when their testimony stands or is void, including Rabbi Yehuda's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah asks what distinguishes חקירות (investigations) from בדיקות (inquiries).
The Mishnah rules that for חקירות, if one witness says 'I don't know', the testimony is void; for בדיקות, even if both say 'we don't know', the testimony stands.
The Mishnah adds that for both types, if witnesses contradict each other, the testimony is void.
The Mishnah gives an example: one says the 2nd, another the 3rd — testimony stands, because one knows the month's intercalation and the other does not.
The Mishnah gives another example: one says the 3rd, another the 5th — testimony is void.
The Mishnah gives an example of time: one says 2 hours, another 3 — testimony stands; one says 3, another 5 — testimony is void.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that testimony stands even for a 3-hour gap, but for a 2-hour gap (5 vs. 7) it is void due to the sun's position.

items.text: Mishnah: Procedure after testimony, deliberation, and voting
items.text_en: Mishnah: Procedure after testimony, deliberation, and voting
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the process of bringing in the second witness, opening with defense, and the rules for students and the defendant speaking. It details the deliberation, voting, and addition of judges until a verdict is reached, including cases of tie and majority.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes bringing in the second witness, checking their testimony, opening with defense, and the rules for silencing a witness or student who speaks for the prosecution, while elevating a student who speaks for the defense.
The Mishnah rules that if there is substance to the words of the defendant or a student, the court listens, even if the defendant speaks in his own defense.
The Mishnah describes the procedure if no defense is found: adjourning to the next day, pairing judges, restricting food and wine, and deliberating overnight.

The Mishnah details the voting procedure: each judge states their position, a pro-conviction judge can switch to defense but not vice versa, scribes record errors, and a majority of 12 acquitting vs. 11 convicting results in acquittal.
The Mishnah rules that if 12 convict and 11 acquit, or if there is a tie or an 'I don't know' vote, additional judges are added in pairs up to 71.

The Mishnah concludes that if 36 acquit and 35 convict, the defendant is acquitted; if 36 convict and 35 acquit, they debate until one of the convicting judges sees the reasoning of the acquitting judges.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural source for the seven חקירות
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural source for the seven חקירות
items.desc_en: The Gemara, citing Rav Yehuda, derives the requirement for seven חקירות from three biblical verses that each use the word 'הֵיטֵב' (well), totaling seven instances.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (the seven חקירות) derived?
Rav Yehuda answers by citing three biblical verses, each containing the word 'הֵיטֵב' (well), totaling seven instances, which serve as the scriptural source for the seven חקירות.

items.text: Gemara's objection: why not write all cases separately?
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: why not write all cases separately?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the cases were not similar, the Torah could have written them separately. Since they are all written together, they learn from each other, and thus are considered as if written in one verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the cases were not similar, the Torah could have written them separately; since they are all written together, they learn from each other and are considered as if written in one verse.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: the cases are not similar
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: the cases are not similar
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the cases of an idolatrous city, idolatry, and conspiring witnesses are not similar to each other, listing their distinguishing features: the city's property is spared, idolatry is by the sword, and witnesses require warning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the three cases (idolatrous city, idolatry, conspiring witnesses) are not similar, listing each one's unique feature: the city's property is spared, idolatry is by the sword, and witnesses require warning.

items.text: Derivation via a גזירה שוה from
items.text_en: Derivation via a גזירה שוה from
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the common word

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the common word 'הֵיטֵב' (diligently) in the three verses establishes a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy), and since the term is superfluous (מופנה), the analogy cannot be refuted.
An objection is raised: the term is only free on one side, as in the case of an idolatrous city (עיר הנדחת) the word 'הֵיטֵב' is not superfluous, since all the words are needed.

The Gemara resolves that even in the idolatrous city verse, the term is free, because the Torah could have written 'דָּרוֹשׁ תִּדְרֹשׁ' (inquire you shall inquire) or 'חָקוֹר תַּחְקֹר' (investigate you shall investigate), but instead wrote 'הֵיטֵב' (diligently), showing it is superfluous for the verbal analogy.

items.text: Derivation of strangulation and burning via קל וחומר
items.text_en: Derivation of strangulation and burning via קל וחומר
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that those executed by strangulation are derived from stoning and decapitation via a קל וחומר, and burning from stoning. This works according to the Rabbis who hold stoning is more severe, but not according to Rabbi Shimon who holds burning is more severe.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests deriving those executed by strangulation and burning from stoning and decapitation via a קל וחומר (a fortiori inference).
The Gemara objects that this works for the Rabbis who hold stoning is more severe, but not for Rabbi Shimon who holds burning is more severe.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's answer: the extra
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's answer: the extra
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that the word

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda answers that the word 'וְהִנֵּה אֱמֶת נָכוֹן' (and behold, it is true and correct) appears twice, yielding eleven occurrences of 'הֵיטֵב' (well), which are allocated: seven for the seven inquiries, three for the גזירה שוה (verbal analogy), leaving one extra.

The Gemara explains that for Rabbi Shimon, the extra word brings in those executed by burning, while for the Rabbis, since burning is derived by קל וחומר (a fortiori argument), the Torah nonetheless wrote it explicitly.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's challenge and resolution: eight investigations
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's challenge and resolution: eight investigations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu suggests the extra word comes for an eighth investigation: 'at what hour'. The Gemara questions this based on the dispute about how precisely people remember time, and resolves that it comes for 'at what Jubilee cycle', distinguishing it from 'at what week'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu challenges that the extra word should introduce an eighth investigation, and the Gemara questions whether eight investigations exist.
The Gemara answers that an eighth investigation exists: 'at what hour'.
A baraita supports that they would examine the witness with eight investigations.

The Gemara objects that this works for Abaye according to Rabbi Meir or the second version, but not for Abaye according to Rabbi Yehuda or for Rava, who hold that people err significantly about the hour.
The Gemara resolves that the extra word comes for 'at what Jubilee cycle'.
The Gemara objects that this is the same as 'at what week'.
The Gemara resolves that it comes for 'at what Jubilee cycle' (distinct from week).
The Gemara explains that the other opinion does not require 'at what Jubilee cycle' because once you ask 'at what week', the Jubilee is implied.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's debate with the Sages about the need for detailed investigations
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's debate with the Sages about the need for detailed investigations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei argues that if someone says 'yesterday he killed', we ask about the week, year, month, and day. The Sages counter that if someone says 'now he killed', we ask about the day, hour, and place. The Gemara concludes that even if not strictly necessary, we impose these questions as a safeguard, following Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei opens by stating his position: if a witness says 'yesterday he killed', we ask about the week, year, month, and day of the month.
The Sages counter Rabbi Yosei: if a witness says 'now he killed', we ask about the day, hour, and place.
The Gemara resolves the debate: even though the detailed questions are not strictly necessary, we impose them as a safeguard, following Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's principle.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yosei's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yosei's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yosei's rationale: the phrase 'yesterday he killed' is common in most testimonies, whereas 'now he killed' is not common in most testimonies.

items.text: Baraita on the details of the investigation and the source for warning
items.text_en: Baraita on the details of the investigation and the source for warning
items.desc_en: A baraita lists the questions asked of witnesses: whether they recognize the defendant, whether he was a Jew, whether they warned him, etc. Ulla then derives the requirement for warning from the Torah, using a verse about incest, showing that the witnesses must explain the sin's severity.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists the initial questions asked of witnesses: whether they recognize the defendant, whether he was a Jew, whether they warned him, and whether he accepted the warning within the time frame of speech.
The baraita continues with questions specific to idolatry: which deity was worshipped and through which mode of worship (sacrifice, incense, libation, or prostration).

Ulla derives the requirement for warning (התראה) from the Torah, citing the verse about incest and explaining that the witnesses must show the defendant the severity of the sin, as the verse is otherwise superfluous for the punishment of כרת (excision).

items.text: Derivation of warning for lashes and capital punishment
items.text_en: Derivation of warning for lashes and capital punishment
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites three tannaitic sources that derive the requirement of warning from verses: the school of Hezekiah from 'כי יזיד', the school of Rabbi Yishmael from 'המוצאים אותו', and the school of Rabbi from 'על דבר אשר עינה'. It then explains why all three are necessary, and discusses why the Torah wrote two verses for stoning, concluding that for Rabbi Shimon it includes burning, and for the Rabbis it is a case where the Torah wrote something that could be derived by a fortiori reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Torah established a context for lashes (warning) from the verse about the betrothed maiden.
The school of Hezekiah teaches that the verse 'וְכִי יָזִיד אִישׁ' (when a man acts willfully) implies he was warned and still acted willfully.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the verse 'הַמֹּצְאִים אִתּוֹ מְקֹשֵׁשׁ עֵצִים' (those who found him gathering wood) implies he was warned and still gathered.
The school of Rabbi teaches that the verse 'עַל דְּבַר אֲשֶׁר עִנָּה' (over the matter which he afflicted) refers to the matter of speech (warning).

The Gemara explains that all three derivations are necessary: if only the verse about the sister were written, one might think warning applies only to lashes, not capital punishment, so the Torah wrote 'כי יזיד' (when he acts willfully).
The Gemara adds that if only 'כי יזיד' were written, one might think it applies only to decapitation (a lighter death), not stoning (a harsher death), so the additional verse is needed.
The Gemara asks why two verses about stoning are needed, and answers that for Rabbi Shimon they include burning.

For the Rabbis, the extra verse is a case where the Torah wrote something that could be derived by a fortiori reasoning (קל וחומר), and the Gemara concludes that this is the same principle for the other verses.

items.text: Derivation of 'permitting oneself to death'
items.text_en: Derivation of 'permitting oneself to death'
items.desc_en: Rava or Hezekiah derives from the verse 'יומת המת' that the accused must permit himself to death, meaning he must accept the death penalty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that the accused must permit himself to death (accept the death penalty)?
Rava (or alternatively Hezekiah) answers that the verse 'יוּמַת הַמֵּת' (the dead person shall be put to death) teaches that the accused must permit himself to death.

items.text: Testimony of witnesses to a betrothed young woman who are disqualified
items.text_en: Testimony of witnesses to a betrothed young woman who are disqualified
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan states that witnesses to a betrothed young woman who are found to be conspiring witnesses are not executed because they can claim they came only to forbid her to her husband. The Gemara clarifies that this applies when no warning was given)Skip, and the woman is a chaverah according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah, who holds that a chaver does not need warning. The Gemara then questions how the woman can be executed if the witnesses are not, and resolves that the testimony is one that cannot be rendered contradictory. It then discusses a case where the woman sinned twice, and explains why the case of a betrothed young woman is specifically mentioned.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan rules that conspiring witnesses who testified against a betrothed young woman are not executed, because they can claim they came only to forbid her to her husband.
The Gemara asks: But if they forewarned her, how can they claim they did not intend her death? And if they did not forewarn her, how could she be executed?

The Gemara answers: The case involves a woman who is a חֲבֵירָה (knowledgeable in Torah), according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah, who holds that a חָבֵר (knowledgeable person) does not require forewarning.
The Gemara asks: Since the witnesses are not killed, how can she be killed? Their testimony is one that cannot be rendered contradictory, and such testimony is invalid.
The Gemara resolves: Rav Chanan also means that since the witnesses are not killed, she is also not killed, because their testimony is one that cannot be rendered contradictory.

The Gemara asks: According to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehudah, how can you find a case where a חֲבֵירָה (knowledgeable woman) is executed? It answers: When she committed adultery and then committed adultery again.

The Gemara objects: The witnesses could still claim they came to forbid her to the second paramour. The answer: The case is where she sinned again with the first paramour or with a relative, to whom she was already forbidden.

The Gemara asks: Why specifically mention a betrothed young woman? Even a married woman would be the same. The answer: The novelty is that even for a betrothed woman who does not live with her husband, the witnesses can claim they came to forbid her to her husband.

items.text: Contradictory testimony regarding the method of killing
items.text_en: Contradictory testimony regarding the method of killing
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda distinguishes between contradictory testimony about the method of killing (e.g., sword vs. arrow), which is not 'correct' (valid), and about the color of his clothes, which is 'correct'. The Gemara challenges this with a baraita that says both are not 'correct', and Rav Chisda explains that the baraita refers to the garment used for strangulation. Further challenges about sandals and a story of Ben Zakkai examining fig stalks are resolved by specifying that the sandal was used to kick and kill, and that the fig stalks were used for a different crime or as a spit.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that contradictory testimony about the murder weapon (sword vs. arrow) is not valid, but about the color of garments (black vs. white) is valid.
The Gemara objects with a baraita that states both contradictions (weapon and garment color) render testimony invalid.
Rav Chisda resolves that the baraita refers to a scarf used for strangulation, so the contradiction about the weapon is indeed invalid, but garment color remains valid.
The Gemara objects with a baraita that a contradiction about sandal color also invalidates testimony.
The Gemara resolves that the case involves a sandal used to kick and kill, so the contradiction is about the murder weapon, not mere clothing.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from Ben Zakkai's examination
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from Ben Zakkai's examination
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects with a story where Ben Zakkai examined witnesses about fig stalks, implying even minor contradictions invalidate testimony.
Rami bar Chama answers that the case involves picking a fig on Shabbat, so the fig stalk details are directly relevant to the capital crime.
The Gemara objects that a baraita indicates the case was about murder under a fig tree, not Shabbat violation.
Rami bar Chama answers that the case involves stabbing with a fig branch, so the fig stalk details are about the murder weapon.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from Ben Zakkai's questions
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from Ben Zakkai's questions
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Ben Zakkai asked about the figs themselves (black or white), not just the branch, contradicting the weapon explanation.
Rav Yosef resolves that Ben Zakkai is exceptional, as he equates examinations with interrogations, so even minor contradictions invalidate testimony.

items.text: Identity of Ben Zakkai and his examination
items.text_en: Identity of Ben Zakkai and his examination
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Ben Zakkai is Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, noting that he was not in the Sanhedrin during its capital jurisdiction. It concludes that Ben Zakkai is a different person, a student sitting before his teacher, whose reasoning was accepted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who Ben Zakkai is, suggesting it might be Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, and questions whether he was in the Sanhedrin.
A baraita is cited stating that Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai lived 120 years, with the last 40 years spent teaching.
Another baraita states that 40 years before the Temple's destruction, the Sanhedrin was exiled and no longer judged capital cases, as clarified by Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avudimi.
A mishna is cited showing that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was active only after the Temple's destruction, when capital cases were no longer judged.
The Gemara concludes that Ben Zakkai is a different person, not Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, as Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would not call him by just 'Ben Zakkai' without a title.
The Gemara objects with a baraita that explicitly mentions Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai examining witnesses about fig stems.
The Gemara resolves that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was then a student sitting before his teacher, and his reasoning was accepted by the court.

items.text: Opening narrative about Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's titles
items.text_en: Opening narrative about Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's titles
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai studied, he was called 'ben Zakkai', and when he taught, he was called 'Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai', reflecting his status at different times.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai was called 'ben Zakkai' when studying and 'Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai' when teaching, reflecting his status at different times.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's phrase
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's phrase
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'even if two say', asking why it is necessary, since it is obvious that if one says 'I don't know', the testimony stands, and if two say so, it also stands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says 'even if two say' regarding bedikot, since it is obvious that if one says 'I don't know' the testimony stands, and if two say so it also stands.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's interpretation
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's interpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet explains that the Mishnah refers to חקירות, stating that even if two say 'we know' and one says 'I don't know', the testimony is void, aligning with Rabbi Akiva who equates three witnesses to two.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet answers that the Mishnah refers to the first clause about חקירות (cross-examinations): even if two say 'we know' and one says 'I don't know', their testimony is void, following Rabbi Akiva who equates three witnesses to two.

items.text: Rava's objection and alternative interpretation
items.text_en: Rava's objection and alternative interpretation
items.desc_en: Rava objects that the Mishnah says 'testimony stands', so he reinterprets: even in חקירות, if two say 'we know' and one says 'I don't know', the testimony stands, contrary to Rabbi Akiva.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that the Mishnah says 'their testimony stands', not 'void', and reinterprets: even in חקירות (cross-examinations), if two say 'we know' and one says 'I don't know', their testimony stands, contrary to Rabbi Akiva.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's question to Rav Kahana and Rav Safra
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question to Rav Kahana and Rav Safra
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks Rav Kahana and Rav Safra about a contradiction in the Mishnah: why are חקירות and בדיקות treated differently when both are from the Torah?

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces that Rav Kahana and Rav Safra were studying Sanhedrin in Rabbah's house, and Rami bar Chama met them and asked what they were saying about the tractate.
Rami bar Chama asks why חקירות (investigations) and בדיקות (inquiries) are treated differently when both are from the Torah.

items.text: Answer distinguishing between refutable and irrefutable testimony
items.text_en: Answer distinguishing between refutable and irrefutable testimony
items.desc_en: They answer that in חקירות, ignorance makes the testimony irrefutable (עדות שאי אתה יכול להזימה), while in בדיקות, it remains refutable, so the testimony stands. Rami bar Chama praises their answer.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Safra answer Rami bar Chama's question by distinguishing that in חקירות (cross-examinations), ignorance makes the testimony irrefutable (עדות שאי אתה יכול להזימה), while in בדיקות (investigations), it remains refutable, so the testimony stands.
Rami bar Chama praises their answer, and they respond with a compliment in return.

items.text: Limit for lunar testimony: until mid-month
items.text_en: Limit for lunar testimony: until mid-month
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the testimony about the new moon is accepted until the majority of the month (רובו של חודש).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: how much of a discrepancy in testimony about the new moon renders it void? Rabbi Yochanan answers: up to the majority of the month.
Rabbi Yochanan, transmitted via Rabbi Acha bar Chanina and Rabbi Asi, answers: testimony is accepted until the majority of the month (רובו של חודש).

items.text: Rava's proof and the Gemara's resolution
items.text_en: Rava's proof and the Gemara's resolution
items.desc_en: Rava brings a Mishnah where one says 'on the third' and another 'on the fifth', and their testimony is void, implying they know the majority of the month. The Gemara resolves that they know the exact day but might err by one day, not two.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a Mishnah where one witness says 'on the third' and another 'on the fifth' and their testimony is void, arguing this proves witnesses know the majority of the month.
The Gemara resolves that witnesses know the exact day but may err by one day, not two, so the Mishnah's case of a two-day discrepancy invalidates testimony.

items.text: Blessing on the new moon: until the moon is full
items.text_en: Blessing on the new moon: until the moon is full
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says the blessing on the new moon is recited until the moon's crescent is filled. Rav Yehuda says until seven days, while the Nehardeans say until sixteen days.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement on blessing the new moon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement on blessing the new moon
sub.desc_en: A digression: Rabbi Yochanan states that one may bless the new moon until its fullness; Rav Yehuda says until seven days, while the Nehardeans say until sixteen.

sub.text: Rav Yaakov bar Idi citing Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav Yaakov bar Idi citing Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda specifies that the blessing is recited until seven days of the month.
The Nehardeans say the blessing is recited until sixteen days of the month.

items.text: Gemara's observation on two opinions
items.text_en: Gemara's observation on two opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that both earlier opinions follow Rabbi Yochanan, but differ in their comparison: one compares to Yetra, the other to Nafya.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that both earlier opinions align with Rabbi Yochanan, differing only in their comparison: one likens to Yetra, the other to Nafya.

items.text: Question about blessing 'Hatov vehametiv'
items.text_en: Question about blessing 'Hatov vehametiv'
items.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti asks Ravina why one does not recite the blessing 'Hatov vehametiv' for the new moon. Ravina responds that since it is a regular occurrence, no blessing is recited.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti asks Ravina why one does not recite the blessing 'Hatov vehametiv' for the new moon.
Ravina responds that since the new moon is a regular occurrence, no blessing is recited, just as one does not recite 'Dayyan ha'emet' for a loss that is expected.

items.text: Blessing the new moon is like greeting the Shechinah
items.text_en: Blessing the new moon is like greeting the Shechinah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina quotes Rabbi Yochanan that one who blesses the new moon in its proper time is as if greeting the Shechinah. Abaye concludes that the blessing should be recited standing.

sub.text: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina quotes Rabbi Yochanan that one who blesses the new moon in its proper time is as if greeting the Shechinah.
The gemara provides a scriptural support for the comparison by linking the word 'זה' (this) in the moon blessing verse and the verse 'זה אלי' (this is my God).
Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael adds that if Israel had merited only to greet their Father in Heaven each month, it would be sufficient.
Abaye concludes that the blessing of the new moon should be recited standing (מעומד).

items.text: The text of the blessing for the new moon
items.text_en: The text of the blessing for the new moon
items.desc_en: Marimar and Mar Zutra support each other while blessing. Rav Acha tells Rav Ashi that in the West they bless 'Baruch mechadesh chodashim'. Rav Ashi notes that women also bless that way. The Gemara then cites Rav Yehuda's version of the full blessing.

sub.desc_en: Marimar and Mar Zutra support each other while reciting the blessing for the new moon.
Rav Acha tells Rav Ashi that in the West (Eretz Yisrael) they bless 'Baruch mechadesh chodashim' (Blessed is He who renews months).
Rav Ashi responds that even the women in his locale recite that same blessing.
The Gemara concludes that the proper blessing is the full version as taught by Rav Yehuda, which is then cited verbatim.

items.text: War of Torah requires bundles of Mishnah
items.text_en: War of Torah requires bundles of Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina quotes Rabbi Yochanan that one finds the war of Torah only in one who has bundles of Mishnah. Rav Yosef applies the verse to himself.

sub.text: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina citing Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina citing Rabbi Asi citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina quotes a chain of tradition that the war of Torah is found only in one who possesses bundles of Mishnah.

sub.text: Rav Yosef applying the verse to himself
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef applying the verse to himself
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef applies the verse 'ורב תבואות בכח שור' (abundant produce through the strength of an ox) to himself, indicating his mastery of Mishnah bundles.

items.text: Testimony about hours and sunrise
items.text_en: Testimony about hours and sunrise
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi rules that if one witness says before sunrise and another after, their testimony is void. The Gemara clarifies that even if one says 'before sunrise' and the other 'at sunrise', it is still void, lest one saw only a glimmer.
