sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi rules that if one witness says before sunrise and another after sunrise, their testimony is void.
The Gemara objects that both cases are obvious.
The Gemara explains that the ruling teaches that the case of 'at sunrise' is still void, lest the witness saw only a glimmer of light.

items.text: Duration of the judges' stay
items.text_en: Duration of the judges' stay
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the judges stay only that day, citing a baraita that if there is substance to his words, he never descends; if not, he stays all day. Abaye explains this applies to the case of no substance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the judges stay only that day and no longer, based on the Mishnah's phrase 'afterwards they bring them in'.
A baraita is cited: if there is substance to his words, he never descends; if not, he stays all day, so that his ascent is not a descent for him.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita's statement about staying all day applies only to the case where there is no substance to his words.

items.text: Why no wine for judges
items.text_en: Why no wine for judges
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why wine is not given to judges. Rabbi Acha bar Chanina cites a verse: 'And for rulers, no strong drink' – those engaged in the world's secrets should not become drunk.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why wine is not given to judges during the deliberation.
Rabbi Acha bar Chanina cites a verse (Proverbs 31:4) to explain that those engaged in the world's secrets (judging) should not become drunk.

items.text: If no merit found, they acquit him
items.text_en: If no merit found, they acquit him
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what if they find no merit. Rabbi Acha and Rabbi Yochanan say they acquit him. Rav Papa asks why not acquit from the start. Rabbi Yochanan answers: so the court does not leave confused. Another version: Rav Papa asks why add judges, and Rabbi Yosei agrees that one does not add to a court of 23.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what happens if the court finds no merit for the defendant.

sub.text: Rabbi Acha and Rabbi Yochanan's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Acha and Rabbi Yochanan's answer
sub.desc_en: Both Rabbi Acha and Rabbi Yochanan rule that they acquit him.
Rav Papa objects: why not acquit him from the start, without the added judges?
Abaye reports Rabbi Yochanan's reason: so the court does not leave confused.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Papa's objection
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Papa's objection
sub.desc_en: In an alternative version, Rav Papa asks Abaye: why add judges at all? Let the original court acquit him.

sub.text: Abaye's citation of Rabbi Yosei's baraita
sub.text_en: Abaye's citation of Rabbi Yosei's baraita
sub.desc_en: Abaye supports Rav Papa's view by citing Rabbi Yosei's baraita that one does not add to a court of 23, just as one does not add to the Great Sanhedrin of 71.

items.text: The phrase 'nizdakein hadin'
items.text_en: The phrase 'nizdakein hadin'
items.desc_en: The Tosefta states that in monetary cases one says 'nizdakein hadin', but not in capital cases. The Gemara debates whether it means the law is sharp or clarified. Rav Huna bar Manoach says reverse it; Rav Ashi says it means the law is wise. A challenge from a baraita supports Rav Ashi. Another version argues for 'sharp', but the Gemara concludes that the senior judge says it because the matter is incumbent on him.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta states that in monetary cases one says 'nizdakein hadin', but not in capital cases.
The Gemara asks what 'nizdakein hadin' means, and objects that if it meant 'the law is sharp', the wording should be reversed.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Manoach in the name of Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach in the name of Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Manoach says to reverse the phrase, so it means 'the law is sharp'.
Rav Ashi says not to reverse; 'nizdakein hadin' means 'the law is wise'.

The Gemara challenges with a baraita that the senior judge says 'nizdakein hadin', supporting Rav Ashi's interpretation that it means 'the law is wise', since the senior judge would not say it if it meant 'sharp' and embarrassed himself.
The Gemara rejects the challenge, arguing that being embarrassed by oneself is different from being embarrassed by others, so the senior judge could still say it even if it meant 'sharp'.
An alternative version objects that if 'nizdakein hadin' means 'the law is wise', the senior judge would be praising himself, which violates the verse 'Let another praise you, not your own mouth'.
The Gemara resolves that the matter of the court is different, because the responsibility is incumbent on the senior judge, as taught in a Mishnah that the senior judge announces the verdict.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Procedure for stoning
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Procedure for stoning
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that after the verdict, the condemned is taken out to the stoning place, which is outside the court. A signal system with a cloth and a horse is used to recall the court if someone has a merit to argue.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure after the verdict: the condemned is taken out to the stoning place outside the court, with a signal system using a cloth and a horse to recall the court if someone has a valid argument for merit.

items.text: Gemara's question on the location of the stoning place
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the location of the stoning place
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the stoning place is merely outside the court, citing a baraita that it is outside the three camps. It explains that the Mishnah's statement is relevant when the court sits outside the three camps, to avoid appearing as murderers and to allow for a possible rescue.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that the stoning place is merely outside the court, citing a baraita that it is outside the three camps.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's statement is relevant when the court sits outside the three camps, to avoid appearing as murderers and to allow for a possible rescue.

items.text: Derivation from the blasphemer: three camps
items.text_en: Derivation from the blasphemer: three camps
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the requirement for three camps. It cites a baraita that derives from the verse about the blasphemer, using a verbal analogy with the burnt offerings, that 'outside the camp' means outside all three camps.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the requirement that the place of stoning be outside three camps.
The baraita derives from the verse about the blasphemer, using a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) with the burnt offerings, that 'outside the camp' means outside all three camps.

items.text: Derivation for burnt offerings: three camps
items.text_en: Derivation for burnt offerings: three camps
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues to explain the source for the burnt offerings, citing a baraita that derives the three camps from the extra verses about the bull of the congregation and the ash.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: And from where do we derive the three camps for the burnt offerings?
The baraita cites the verse about the bull of the congregation and questions whether it means outside one camp or three.
The baraita resolves that the extra verse about the bull of the congregation teaches a second camp, and the extra verse about the ash teaches a third camp.

items.text: Rejection of alternative derivation from slaughter outside
items.text_en: Rejection of alternative derivation from slaughter outside
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers learning from the laws of slaughtering outside the Temple, which requires only one camp, but rejects it because the burnt offerings share the same phrase 'outside the camp' and have the characteristics of qualification and atonement, which are more similar to the blasphemer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes deriving the blasphemer's execution site from the laws of slaughtering outside the Temple (שחוטי חוץ), which require only one camp.

The Gemara argues that the burnt offerings (פרים הנשרפים) are a better source because they share the phrase 'הוצֵא אל מחוץ למחנה' and have the characteristics of qualification (מכשיר) and atonement (מכפר).
The Gemara counters that slaughtering outside is a better source because it involves a sinful person (אדם חוטא), a soul (נשמה), and the concept of piggul (פיגול).
The Gemara resolves that deriving from a source that also involves qualification (מכשיר) is preferable, so the burnt offerings are the better analogy.

items.text: Rav Pappa's alternative derivation from Moses' camp
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's alternative derivation from Moses' camp
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa offers a different derivation: Moses sat in the Levite camp, and the verse 'outside the camp' for the blasphemer means outside the Levite camp, while the execution verse means outside the Israelite camp, thus establishing three camps.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa opens with a question about where Moses sat, then derives that the verse 'הוֹצֵא אֶת הַמְקַלֵּל אֶל מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה' refers to outside the Levite camp, and 'וַיּוֹצִיאוּ אֶת הַמְקַלֵּל אֶל מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה' refers to outside the Israelite camp, establishing three camps.
The Gemara objects that the second verse is needed for the execution itself, not for establishing a third camp, since the execution is explicitly written.

items.text: The superfluous verses regarding the blasphemer's execution
items.text_en: The superfluous verses regarding the blasphemer's execution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the need for multiple verses describing the stoning of the blasphemer. It explains that each word teaches a specific law: 'אותו' excludes his clothing, 'אבן' indicates that if he dies from one stone it suffices, and 'אבנים' teaches that if not, additional stones are brought. The Tanna's statement is reinterpreted as 'if not for the verse, I would have said a gezerah shavah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the superfluous verse 'וַיִּרְגְּמוּ אֹתוֹ אָבֶן' (they stoned him with a stone) teaches.
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from 'אֹתוֹ' that the stoning is done without his clothing, and from 'אָבֶן' that if he dies from one stone it suffices.

The Gemara explains that both 'אָבֶן' (stone) and 'אֲבָנִים' (stones) are necessary: 'אָבֶן' teaches that one stone suffices if it kills, and 'אֲבָנִים' teaches that if not, additional stones are brought.

The Gemara resolves that the Tanna's statement 'נֶאֱמַר' (it is said) is actually 'אִילּוּ לֹא נֶאֱמַר' (if it were not said), meaning that without the verse a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) would have been needed, but now it is not.

items.text: Rav Ashi's interpretation of the verses and the Rabbis' objection
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's interpretation of the verses and the Rabbis' objection
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that Moses sat in the Levite camp, and each 'הוצא' in the verses refers to a different camp: first outside the Levite camp, then outside the Israelite camp, and finally 'וַיּוֹצִיאוּ' refers to the actual act. The Rabbis object, asking about the similar 'הוצא' verses in the context of the burnt bulls.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that Moses sat in the Levite camp, and each 'הוצא' in the verses refers to a different camp: first outside the Levite camp, then outside the Israelite camp, and finally 'וַיּוֹצִיאוּ' refers to the actual act.

The Gemara objects that the act of execution is explicitly written in the verse 'וּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל עָשׂוּ', and that verse is needed for other teachings (semikhah and rejection), not for the act itself.
The Rabbis ask Rav Ashi how he interprets the similar 'הוציא' verses in the context of the burnt bulls, leaving the question unresolved.

items.text: Rav Huna's inquiry about execution instruments and the wine for the condemned
items.text_en: Rav Huna's inquiry about execution instruments and the wine for the condemned
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that all execution instruments (stone, wood, sword, scarf) are from the community, not the condemned. He then questions whether the scarf used for waving and the horse used for running are from the community or the condemned. The Gemara adds that the wine and frankincense given to the condemned are from the community, as implied by the verse 'תנו שכר לאובד'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that all execution instruments (stone, wood, sword, scarf) are from the community, not the condemned, because we do not tell him to bring his own means of death.
Rav Huna inquires whether the scarf used for waving and the horse used for running are from the condemned (since they save his life) or from the court (since they are obligated to save him).

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Rav Ashi citing Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Rav Ashi citing Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda's teaching that the condemned is given wine and frankincense from the community, as implied by the verse 'תנו שכר לאובד', and the baraita about noblewomen donating them, supports that such items are from the community.

items.text: The case of a student who became mute after offering to argue for acquittal
items.text_en: The case of a student who became mute after offering to argue for acquittal
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Huna asks Rav Sheshet about a student who said 'I have a merit to argue' but then became mute. Rav Sheshet dismisses the question, but the Gemara clarifies that the case is where he spoke but then became mute. Rav Yosei bar Chanina rules that if a student argued for acquittal and died, he is considered alive and standing in his place; but if he only said he would argue, it is a question.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Huna's question to Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Huna's question to Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Huna asks Rav Sheshet about a student who said he has a merit to argue for acquittal but then became mute.
Rav Sheshet dismisses the question with a hand gesture, but the Gemara clarifies that the case is where he spoke and then became mute, leaving the question unresolved.
Rav Yosei bar Chanina rules that if a student argued for acquittal and died, he is considered alive and standing in his place; but if he only said he would argue, it remains a question.

items.text: The procedure for returning the condemned for further arguments
items.text_en: The procedure for returning the condemned for further arguments
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that even the condemned himself can argue for acquittal. The Gemara questions whether this applies after the first and second times, citing a baraita that for the first two times, the court returns him regardless of substance, but afterward only if there is substance. Rav Papa explains this means from the second time onward. Abaye explains that they appoint two rabbis to assess the substance, and they don't do so initially because the condemned is too frightened.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's rule that the condemned himself can argue for acquittal applies even after the first and second times.
The Gemara cites a baraita that for the first two times, the court returns the condemned regardless of substance, but afterward only if there is substance.
Rav Papa explains that the baraita's rule applies from the second time onward, reconciling it with the Mishnah.
The Gemara asks how the court knows whether the second time has passed.
Abaye explains that the court appoints two rabbis to assess the substance of the condemned's arguments.
The Gemara asks why the court does not appoint these rabbis from the very beginning.
The Gemara answers that initially the condemned is too frightened to articulate all his arguments, so the rabbis are not appointed until later.

items.text: The herald's announcement and the case of Jesus
items.text_en: The herald's announcement and the case of Jesus
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a herald goes out before the condemned. The Gemara adds that the herald must specify the day, hour, and place to allow potential alibi witnesses. It then questions why the herald only goes out before him and not earlier, citing the case of Jesus where the herald went out forty days beforehand. Ulla explains that Jesus was different because he was close to the government, and for a mesit, the Torah commands not to show mercy.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a merit is found the condemned is freed, otherwise he is stoned, and a herald precedes him announcing his name, crime, and witnesses, calling for anyone who knows a merit to come and testify.
Abaye adds that the herald must specify the day, hour, and place so that potential alibi witnesses can come and discredit the witnesses.
The Gemara questions why the herald goes out only before the condemned and not earlier, citing a baraita that for Jesus the herald went out forty days beforehand.

Ulla answers that Jesus was different because he was close to the government, and for a mesit (enticer) the Torah commands not to show mercy, so the herald was needed to find a merit to avoid executing a politically sensitive figure.

items.text: The execution of Jesus' five disciples
items.text_en: The execution of Jesus' five disciples
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Jesus had five disciples: Mattai, Nakkai, Netzer, Buni, and Todah. Each was brought before the court and argued for his life using a verse that seemed to support him, but the court countered with another verse that condemned him. All were executed.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces that Jesus had five disciples: Mattai, Nakkai, Netzer, Buni, and Todah.
Mattai is brought and argues that his name appears in a positive verse, 'מַתַּי אָבוֹא וְאֵרָאֶה פְּנֵי אֱלֹהִים' (When shall I come and appear before God?), implying he should not be executed.
The court counters Mattai's argument with a verse that uses his name in a negative context, 'מָתַי יָמוּת וְאָבַד שְׁמוֹ' (When will he die and his name perish?), condemning him.
Nakkai is brought and argues that his name appears in a positive verse, 'וְנָקִי וְצַדִּיק אַל תַּהֲרֹג' (Do not slay the innocent and righteous), implying he should not be executed.
The court counters Nakkai's argument with a verse that uses his name in a negative context, 'בַּמִּסְתָּרִים יַהֲרֹג נָקִי' (In secret places he murders the innocent), condemning him.
Netzer is brought and argues that his name appears in a positive verse, 'וְנֵצֶר מִשָּׁרָשָׁיו יִפְרֶה' (A branch from its roots will bear fruit), implying he should not be executed.

The court counters Netzer's argument with a verse that uses his name in a negative context, 'וְאַתָּה הָשְׁלַכְתָּ מִקִּבְרְךָ כְּנֵצֶר נִתְעָב' (You are cast out of your grave like an abhorrent branch), condemning him.
Buni is brought and argues that his name appears in a positive verse, 'בְּנִי בְכֹרִי יִשְׂרָאֵל' (My son, my firstborn, Israel), implying he should not be executed.

The court counters Buni's argument with a verse that uses his name in a negative context, 'הִנֵּה אָנֹכִי הוֹרֵג אֶת בִּנְךָ בְּכֹרֶךָ' (Behold, I am killing your son, your firstborn), condemning him.
Todah is brought and argues that his name appears in a positive verse, 'מִזְמוֹר לְתוֹדָה' (A psalm for thanksgiving), implying he should not be executed.

The court counters Todah's argument with a verse that uses his name in a negative context, 'זֹבֵחַ תּוֹדָה יְכַבְּדָנְנִי' (He who sacrifices a thanksgiving offering honors Me), implying that Todah will be sacrificed, condemning him.

items.text: Opening homilies of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.text_en: Opening homilies of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that one who subdues their evil inclination and confesses is credited as if they honored God in both worlds, citing Psalm 50:23. He further states that when the Temple stood, each sacrifice had its own reward, but a person of lowly spirit is considered as if they offered all sacrifices, and their prayer is not rejected, citing Psalm 51:19.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that one who subdues their evil inclination and confesses is credited as if they honored God in both worlds, citing Psalm 50:23.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that when the Temple stood, each sacrifice had its own reward, but a person of lowly spirit is considered as if they offered all sacrifices, and their prayer is not rejected, citing Psalm 51:19.

items.text: Mishnah: Confession before execution
items.text_en: Mishnah: Confession before execution
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that when a condemned person is ten cubits from the stoning place, they are told to confess, as all those executed confess, and one who confesses has a share in the World to Come, as seen with Achan. If the person does not know how to confess, they are told to say 'May my death be an atonement for all my sins.' Rabbi Yehuda adds that if the person knows they were framed by false witnesses, they say 'except for this sin,' but the Sages object that then everyone would say that to clear themselves.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that when a condemned person is ten cubits from the stoning place, they are told to confess, as all those executed confess, and one who confesses has a share in the World to Come, as demonstrated by Achan.
The Tanna Kamma rules that if the condemned person does not know how to confess, they are told to say 'May my death be an atonement for all my sins.'
Rabbi Yehuda adds that if the condemned person knows they were framed by false witnesses (מזומם), they say 'May my death be an atonement for all my sins except for this sin.'
The Sages object to Rabbi Yehuda's position, arguing that if this exception is allowed, everyone would say it to clear themselves.

items.text: Gemara: The meaning of 'na'
items.text_en: Gemara: The meaning of 'na'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita explaining that the word 'na' in Joshua's plea to Achan ('put now [na] honor') is a term of supplication.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines the word 'na' (נא) as a term of supplication, supporting the Mishnah's use of Joshua's plea to Achan.

items.text: Gemara: The story of Achan and the lottery
items.text_en: Gemara: The story of Achan and the lottery
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the dialogue between God, Joshua, and Achan. When God told Joshua that Israel had sinned, Joshua asked who sinned, and God replied that He is not an informer; Joshua should cast lots. The lot fell on Achan, who protested that Joshua and Eleazar were the great ones of the generation, and if he cast lots on them, it would fall on one of them. Joshua pleaded with Achan not to disparage the lots, as the Land of Israel would be divided by lot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the dialogue between God, Joshua, and Achan, where God tells Joshua that Israel has sinned, Joshua asks who sinned, God refuses to be an informer and instructs casting lots, the lot falls on Achan, Achan protests that the lot could fall on Joshua or Eleazar, and Joshua pleads with Achan not to disparage the lots because the Land of Israel will be divided by lot.

items.text: Gemara: 'Give thanks' – Ravina's explanation
items.text_en: Gemara: 'Give thanks' – Ravina's explanation
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that Joshua persuaded Achan with words, saying 'All we ask of you is a confession; give thanks and be acquitted.' Immediately, Achan responded with his confession.

sub.desc_en: Ravina explains that Joshua persuaded Achan with words, saying all they ask is a confession.
The gemara cites the verse showing Achan immediately responded with his confession.

items.text: Gemara: How many sacred items did Achan misappropriate?
items.text_en: Gemara: How many sacred items did Achan misappropriate?
items.desc_en: Rav Asi in the name of Rabbi Chanina teaches that Achan misappropriated three items from the ban (cherem): two from Moses' time and one from Joshua's, based on the phrase 'such and such I did.' Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon says five: four from Moses' time and one from Joshua's, based on the phrase 'I have sinned and such and such I did.' The Gemara asks why he was not punished earlier, and Rabbi Yochanan answers that God did not punish hidden sins until Israel crossed the Jordan.

sub.text: Rav Asi in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rav Asi in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rav Asi in the name of Rabbi Chanina teaches that Achan misappropriated three sacred items (חרמים): two from Moses' time and one from Joshua's, based on the phrase 'such and such I did.'

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon counters that Achan misappropriated five sacred items: four from Moses' time and one from Joshua's, based on the fuller confession 'I have sinned and such and such I did.'
The Gemara asks why Achan was not punished earlier for his hidden sins.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon answers that God did not punish hidden sins until Israel crossed the Jordan.

items.text: Gemara: Tannaitic dispute on hidden sins
items.text_en: Gemara: Tannaitic dispute on hidden sins
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a tannaitic dispute regarding the verse 'The hidden things belong to the Lord our God, but the revealed things are for us and our children forever.' Rabbi Yehuda explains the dots on certain words to teach that God did not punish hidden sins until Israel crossed the Jordan. Rabbi Nechemya objects, arguing that the verse says 'forever,' implying that God never punished hidden sins; rather, just as hidden sins were not punished, so too revealed sins were not punished until after crossing the Jordan.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda explains that the dots on the words 'לנו ולבנינו' and the 'ע' of 'עד' teach that God did not punish hidden sins until Israel crossed the Jordan.

Rabbi Nechemya objects that the verse says 'עד עולם' (forever), implying God never punished hidden sins; rather, just as hidden sins were not punished, so too revealed sins were not punished until after crossing the Jordan.

items.text: Opening question on Achan's family's knowledge
items.text_en: Opening question on Achan's family's knowledge
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Achan's family was punished, answering that his wife and children knew of his sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Achan's family was punished, and answers that it was because his wife and children knew of his sin.

items.text: Interpretation of 'חָטָא יִשְׂרָאֵל'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'חָטָא יִשְׂרָאֵל'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda explains that even though Israel sinned, they are still called Israel, using a proverb about an asa tree among reeds.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda explains that even though Achan sinned, he remains an Israelite, citing a folk saying about a myrtle among reeds.
Rabbi Abba supports the point with a proverb: an asa tree among reeds is still called asa.

items.text: Achan's five transgressions and his immoral act
items.text_en: Achan's five transgressions and his immoral act
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a in the name of Rabbi Yehuda bar Masparta derives from five instances of 'גַּם' that Achan violated all five books of the Torah, and also that he was one who drew back his foreskin, based on a verbal analogy. The Gemara clarifies that this teaches he was brazen even in the act itself.

sub.text: Rabbi Ila'a citing Rabbi Yehuda bar Masparta
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ila'a citing Rabbi Yehuda bar Masparta
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'a in the name of Rabbi Yehuda bar Masparta derives from five instances of 'גַּם' in the verse that Achan violated all five books of the Torah.

sub.text: Rabbi Ila'a citing Rabbi Yehuda bar Masparta
sub.text_en: Rabbi Ila'a citing Rabbi Yehuda bar Masparta
sub.desc_en: The same authority uses a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between 'בריתי' here and 'בריתי' in the context of circumcision to teach that Achan was one who drew back his foreskin (מושך בערלתו).
The Gemara asks: this is obvious — why was it necessary to derive that Achan was brazen in the matter of circumcision?
The Gemara resolves: the derivation teaches that Achan was brazen even in the act of circumcision itself, not merely in other matters.

items.text: Achan's sin with a betrothed maiden
items.text_en: Achan's sin with a betrothed maiden
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda derives from a verbal analogy that Achan had relations with a betrothed maiden. The Gemara questions whether this is obvious, and Ravina adds that his judgment was like that of a betrothed maiden, i.e., stoning.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda teaches that Achan committed a vile act by having relations with a betrothed maiden, derived from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) on the word 'נבלה'.
The Gemara objects that this is obvious, but then resolves that the teaching is necessary to counter the assumption that Achan did not go so far as to debase himself.
Ravina adds that Achan's punishment was like that of a betrothed maiden, i.e., stoning.

items.text: Why were Achan's children punished?
items.text_en: Why were Achan's children punished?
items.desc_en: The Exilarch asks Rav Huna why Achan's children were punished if they did not sin. Rav Huna responds by analogy: all Israel was punished with him, and it was to intimidate them.

sub.desc_en: The Exilarch asks Rav Huna why Achan's children were punished if they did not sin.
Rav Huna answers by analogy: just as all Israel were punished to intimidate them, so too Achan's children were punished to intimidate them.

items.text: Burning and stoning: two punishments?
items.text_en: Burning and stoning: two punishments?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Achan and his family were both burned and stoned. Ravina explains that those liable for burning were burned, and those liable for stoning were stoned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how they could be both burned and stoned.
Ravina answers that those deserving burning were burned, and those deserving stoning were stoned.

items.text: Interpretation of the spoils: the cloak
items.text_en: Interpretation of the spoils: the cloak
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate the meaning of 'אַדֶּרֶת שִׁנְעָר': Rav says it was a fine woolen cloak, Shmuel says it was a cloak of fine linen.

sub.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate the meaning of 'אדרת שנער' in the verse, with Rav saying it was a fine woolen cloak and Shmuel saying it was a cloak of fine linen.
Rav interprets 'אַדֶּרֶת שִׁנְעָר' as a fine woolen cloak (איצטלא דמילתא).
Shmuel interprets 'אַדֶּרֶת שִׁנְעָר' as a cloak of fine linen (סרבלא דצריפא).

items.text: Joshua's complaint and the thirty-six casualties
items.text_en: Joshua's complaint and the thirty-six casualties
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that Joshua cast the people's complaint before God, asking why the majority of the Sanhedrin should die for these sins. A dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya about the number of casualties is cited.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that Joshua castigated the Israelites before God, and a baraita records a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya about the number of casualties at Ai.

A baraita cites a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya about whether the thirty-six casualties were literal or included Yair ben Menashe who was equivalent to the majority of the Sanhedrin.

items.text: Moses the poor man, Joshua the rich man
items.text_en: Moses the poor man, Joshua the rich man
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rav interprets a verse: Moses, who spoke humbly, is the 'poor man', while Joshua, who spoke harshly, is the 'rich man'. The Gemara explores alternative proofs, ultimately settling on Joshua's complaint about crossing the Jordan.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman citing Rav interprets a verse about the poor man and the rich man as referring to Moses and Joshua, and then the Gemara questions this by comparing Joshua's conduct to that of Phinehas.
The Gemara rejects the initial proof, noting that Phinehas also argued with God, as shown by a verse about the plague.

The Gemara resolves that the true proof is from Joshua's complaint about crossing the Jordan, which Moses also made, but Joshua's additional statement about wishing to stay on the other side shows his arrogance.

items.text: God's rebuke to Joshua: 'קוּם לָךְ'
items.text_en: God's rebuke to Joshua: 'קוּם לָךְ'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Sheila teaches that God told Joshua his complaint was worse than the people's, because they distanced themselves sixty mil from the Jordan. After Joshua left, Rav expounded that Joshua did not deviate from Moses' commands, yet God said 'קוּם לָךְ' because Joshua caused the people to sin by not consulting the Urim and Thummim.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Sheila expounds that God told Joshua that his complaint was worse than the people's sin, because they distanced themselves sixty mil from the Jordan.
After Rabbi Sheila left, an amora was appointed to teach that Joshua did not deviate from Moses' commands.
The Gemara asks why God said 'קוּם לָךְ' (arise for yourself) to Joshua, and answers that it was because Joshua caused the people to sin by not following the command to set up stones.

items.text: Joshua and the angel: greeting at night
items.text_en: Joshua and the angel: greeting at night
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Joshua could bow to the angel at night, given Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one should not greet another at night due to fear of demons. It answers that the angel identified himself as the captain of God's host, and demons do not utter God's name in vain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Joshua could bow to the angel at night, given Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one should not greet another at night due to fear of demons.
The Gemara answers that the case is different because the angel identified himself as the captain of the Lord's host, and demons are known not to utter God's name in vain.

items.text: Torah study outweighs the daily offering
items.text_en: Torah study outweighs the daily offering
items.desc_en: The angel tells Joshua that the people neglected both the afternoon tamid and Torah study, and Joshua chooses to respond to the latter. Rabbi Yochanan and Samuel bar Inya deduce that Torah study is greater than offering the tamid.

sub.desc_en: The angel tells Joshua that the people neglected both the afternoon tamid and Torah study, and asks which one he came about.
Joshua answers that he came because of the neglect of Torah study.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that Joshua spent the night in the depth of halacha, indicating his focus on Torah study.
Samuel bar Inya in the name of Rav concludes that Torah study is greater than offering the daily tamid, based on the verse 'עתה באתי'.

items.text: The angel Pisqon and the verse about rebuke
items.text_en: The angel Pisqon and the verse about rebuke
items.desc_en: Abaye asks how the verse 'Do not go out hastily to quarrel' is interpreted in the West. The Gemara explains that when God told Ezekiel to rebuke Israel, the angel Pisqon intervened, arguing that God should not shame Abraham and Sarah. The angel's names and functions are then detailed.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Dimi how the verse 'Do not go out hastily to quarrel' is interpreted in the West.
The Gemara explains that when God told Ezekiel to rebuke Israel, the angel Pisqon intervened, arguing that God should not shame Abraham and Sarah.
The Gemara asks whether the angel has such extensive authority.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina answers that the angel has three names—Pisqon, Itmon, Sigron—each describing a different function.

items.text: Prayer before trouble and strengthening in prayer
items.text_en: Prayer before trouble and strengthening in prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that one should pray before trouble, citing Abraham's prayer between Bethel and Ai. Resh Lakish says that one who strengthens himself in prayer below will have no accusers above. Rabbi Yochanan says one should pray that all strengthen his power.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches from the verse that one should always pray before trouble, citing Abraham's prayer between Bethel and Ai as precedent.
Resh Lakish states that one who strengthens himself in prayer below will have no accusers above.
Rabbi Yochanan says one should pray that all strengthen his power, so that he has no accusers above.

items.text: Achan's confession and his name
items.text_en: Achan's confession and his name
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves that Achan's confession atoned for him, as Joshua said 'the Lord will trouble you this day' but not in the World to Come. It then debates whether his name was Zimri or Achan, with Rav and Shmuel offering different explanations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we know that Achan's confession atoned for him?
The baraita cites the verse 'הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה' (this day) to prove that Achan's trouble was limited to this world, implying atonement for the World to Come.

The baraita further cites the verse listing Zimri among the five sons of Zerah, interpreting 'כֻּלָּם חֲמִשָּׁה' (all five) to mean they all have a share in the World to Come, confirming Achan's atonement.

items.text: The confession of one being executed and the court's liability
items.text_en: The confession of one being executed and the court's liability
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses one who cannot confess properly; Rabbi Yehuda says to say 'May my death atone.' The Gemara relates a story of a man who, when led to execution, declared his innocence and placed the guilt on the witnesses. The Sages could not reverse the decree but said the blood is on the witnesses' necks. The Gemara questions whether this is obvious, and clarifies that it applies even if the witnesses retract, as long as they give a reason.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, presenting Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that the court says 'May my death atone' for one who cannot confess, and the Gemara objects that this seems to be for the court's own exoneration.
The Gemara explains that the court's statement is to prevent slander against the courts and witnesses, not for self-exoneration.
A baraita relates a story of a man led to execution who declared his innocence and placed guilt on the witnesses, and the Sages said he must be executed but the blood is on the witnesses' necks.
The Gemara asks: Is it obvious that the witnesses are blamed? Can the condemned simply accuse them at will?
The Gemara answers that the case is necessary where the witnesses retract their testimony.
The Gemara questions: Even if they retract, what does it matter? Once they have testified, they cannot retract.
The Gemara answers that the case is where the witnesses provide a reason for their retraction, as in the incident of Ba'ya Moksaa.

items.text: The Mishnah on stoning: covering the condemned
items.text_en: The Mishnah on stoning: covering the condemned
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when the condemned is four cubits from the stoning place, they strip him. Rabbi Yehuda says a man is covered in front, a woman both front and back. The Sages say a man is stoned naked, but a woman is not stoned naked.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that when the condemned is four cubits from the stoning place, they strip him of his garments.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that a man is covered in front, while a woman is covered both front and back.
The Sages counter that a man is stoned naked, but a woman is not stoned naked.

items.text: Opening Tosefta on covering the condemned
items.text_en: Opening Tosefta on covering the condemned
items.desc_en: The Tosefta states that a man is covered with one cloth in front, while a woman is covered with two cloths both front and back, because her entire body is considered nakedness. Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages disagree on whether a man is stoned naked and a woman clothed.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta opens with the rule that a man is covered with one cloth in front, while a woman is covered with two cloths both front and back, because her entire body is considered nakedness, as stated by Rabbi Yehuda.
The Sages disagree and state that a man is stoned naked, but a woman is not stoned naked.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Sages' reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Sages' reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the reason of the Sages, deriving from the verse 'and they shall stone him' that 'him' implies without his garment, but 'her' implies with her garment. Rabbi Yehuda argues that 'him' applies equally to both man and woman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of the Sages who require a man to be stoned naked but a woman clothed.
The Gemara explains that the verse 'וְרָגְמוּ אֹתוֹ' (and they shall stone him) implies 'him' without his garment, but 'her' with her garment.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that 'אותו' (him) without his garment applies equally to both man and woman.

items.text: Contradiction from the Sotah procedure
items.text_en: Contradiction from the Sotah procedure
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes an apparent contradiction: the Sages seem concerned about improper thoughts (hirhur) here, but in the Sotah ritual, Rabbi Yehuda is more concerned about modesty. Rabba resolves that in the Sotah case, the woman might leave the court innocent and young priests might be aroused, but here she is being killed, and the evil inclination only controls one whose eyes see.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Sages are concerned about improper thoughts (hirhur) here while Rabbi Yehuda is not, citing a contradictory baraita about the Sotah ritual.

Rabba resolves the contradiction: in the Sotah case, the woman might leave the court innocent and young priests might be aroused, but here she is being killed, and the evil inclination only controls one whose eyes see.

items.text: Rava's resolution and the principle of a beautiful death
items.text_en: Rava's resolution and the principle of a beautiful death
items.desc_en: Rava argues that Rabbi Yehuda's positions are not contradictory, as explained. The Sages' positions are also not contradictory, because the verse 'and all the women shall be admonished' provides a great lesson. Rav Nachman bar Rav Ada cites the verse 'Love your neighbor as yourself' to choose a beautiful death, and the Gemara clarifies that this principle is accepted by all, with the dispute being whether a person prefers dignity over physical comfort.

sub.desc_en: Rava questions why the apparent contradiction in Rabbi Yehuda's positions is considered problematic while the Sages' positions are not.

Rava resolves the contradiction in the Sages' positions by citing the verse 'וְנִוַּסְּרוּ כָּל הַנָּשִׁים' (and all the women shall be admonished), arguing that public stoning itself provides the greatest deterrent, so no additional humiliation is needed.
The Gemara objects: why not apply both the humiliation of stripping and the deterrent of public stoning?

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Ada's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Ada's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Ada cites the verse 'וְאָהַבְתָּ לְרֵעֲךָ כָּמוֹךָ' (Love your neighbor as yourself) to establish the principle of choosing a beautiful death, which precludes adding unnecessary humiliation.

The Gemara clarifies that the principle of choosing a beautiful death is universally accepted, and the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages is whether a person prefers dignity over physical comfort (נְיָחָא דְגוּפֵיהּ) or vice versa.

items.text: Mishnah: The stoning platform and procedure
items.text_en: Mishnah: The stoning platform and procedure
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the stoning platform as two stories high. One witness pushes the condemned onto his loins; if he dies, it suffices. Otherwise, the second witness drops a stone on his heart. If still alive, all Israel stones him, as per the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the stoning platform as two stories high, with the first witness pushing the condemned onto his loins and the second dropping a stone on his heart; if still alive, all Israel stones him.

items.text: Gemara: Height of the platform and the beautiful death principle
items.text_en: Gemara: Height of the platform and the beautiful death principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the platform's height plus the condemned's height totals three stories, questioning if such height is needed, citing a baraita that a pit for execution need only be ten handbreadths. Rav Nachman bar Rav Ada cites the principle of choosing a beautiful death, but the Gemara objects that a higher platform would be more beautiful, and answers that it would cause the body to become repulsive.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the condemned person's own height adds to the platform's two stories, totaling three stories.
The Gemara questions whether such a great height is necessary for execution.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that a pit for execution need only be ten handbreadths deep.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Rav Ada's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Ada's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Ada cites the principle of choosing a beautiful death (ברור לו מיתה יפה) from the verse 'ואהבת לרעך כמוך'.
The Gemara objects that if the principle is a beautiful death, a higher platform would be even more beautiful.
The Gemara resolves that a higher platform would cause the body to become repulsive (מנוול), thus the current height is optimal.

items.text: Derivation of stoning and pushing from Scripture
items.text_en: Derivation of stoning and pushing from Scripture
items.desc_en: The Tosefta derives that the execution involves both pushing (from 'yaro') and stoning (from 'sakol'), and that if the condemned dies from the push, it is sufficient. The Gemara asks whether this applies for all generations.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta cites a baraita that derives the requirement of pushing (דחייה) from the word 'יָרֹה' (he shall throw).
The Tosefta derives the requirement of stoning (סקילה) from the word 'סָקוֹל' (he shall stone).
The Tosefta derives that both stoning and pushing are required from the verse 'סָקוֹל יִסָּקֵל אוֹ יָרֹה יִיָּרֶה' (he shall be stoned or thrown).
The Tosefta derives that if the condemned dies from the push, it is sufficient, from the word 'אוֹ' (or) in the verse.
The Gemara asks whether this derivation applies for all generations (i.e., that the requirement of pushing and stoning is permanent).

items.text: The stone and the witnesses' role
items.text_en: The stone and the witnesses' role
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that if the first witness does not kill the condemned, the second witness takes the stone. It cites a baraita about a stone heavy enough for two men, and explains that the witnesses lift it together but one throws it, so that it comes with force.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'סקול יסקל' (he shall surely be stoned) as the source for the Mishnah's procedure.
The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that the second witness takes the stone, citing a baraita that the stone was a load for two men, implying one could not lift it alone.
The Gemara resolves that the witnesses lift the stone together, but one throws it alone, so that it comes with force.

items.text: The stone's reuse
items.text_en: The stone's reuse
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses a baraita that says no one ever reused the stone, clarifying that it does not mean it was done, but that if necessary it could be done.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the baraita's implication that the stone could be reused, citing a baraita that says no one ever reused it.
The Gemara clarifies that the baraita does not mean it was actually done, but that if necessary it could be done.

items.text: Burial of execution instruments
items.text_en: Burial of execution instruments
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a baraita that states the stone, tree, sword, and scarf used in executions are buried with the condemned. It resolves a contradiction with another baraita by explaining that 'with him' means in his possession, not literally buried with him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that all execution instruments (stone, tree, sword, scarf) are buried with the condemned.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from another baraita that says the instruments are not buried with the condemned.
Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by explaining that 'with him' means in his possession (buried in his grave area), not literally buried in the same grave.

items.text: Witnesses with severed hands
items.text_en: Witnesses with severed hands
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that if the witnesses' hands were cut off after testimony, the condemned is exempt because the verse requires 'the hand of the witnesses shall be upon him first.' The Gemara distinguishes this from witnesses who were originally amputees, who are disqualified because the verse refers to a hand that existed.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that if the witnesses' hands were severed after testimony, the condemned is exempt because the verse requires 'the hand of the witnesses shall be upon him first' and it is absent.
The Gemara asks whether witnesses who were originally amputees (גידמין) are also disqualified from participating in the execution.
The Gemara distinguishes that originally amputee witnesses are disqualified because the verse 'hand of the witnesses' refers to a hand that existed at the time of testimony.

items.text: The requirement for exact biblical wording
items.text_en: The requirement for exact biblical wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that allows execution based on testimony that the verdict was issued, even without the witnesses' hands. Shmuel limits this to when the witnesses are the same. The Gemara then questions whether we require the verse to be fulfilled exactly, citing a baraita about killing a murderer by any means if the prescribed death is impossible. It distinguishes because the verse says 'he shall be put to death' broadly, and notes that murderer and blood-avenger are two verses that come as one, which do not teach a general rule.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that allows execution based on testimony that the verdict was issued, even without the witnesses' hands.
Shmuel limits the baraita to when the witnesses are the same as those who testified at the trial.
The Gemara questions whether we require the verse to be fulfilled exactly, citing a baraita about killing a murderer by any means if the prescribed death is impossible.
The Gemara distinguishes because the verse says 'מוֹת יוּמַת' (he shall be put to death) broadly.
The Gemara rejects learning from this case because murderer and blood-avenger are two verses that come as one, which do not teach a general rule.

items.text: The blood-avenger verse
items.text_en: The blood-avenger verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the second verse: the blood-avenger may kill the murderer, and if there is no avenger, the court appoints one, as derived from 'when he meets him.'

sub.desc_en: The Tanna explains that the blood-avenger verse teaches that the avenger must kill the murderer, and if there is no avenger, the court appoints one, as derived from 'when he meets him.'

items.text: Objection from the wayward son
items.text_en: Objection from the wayward son
items.desc_en: Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda objects to Rav Ashi: do we not require the verse exactly? He cites a Mishnah that a wayward son is not judged if parents are amputees, etc., because the verse says 'they shall take hold of him' and not amputees, etc. The Gemara answers that there the entire verse is extra.

sub.text: Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda's objection
sub.text_en: Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda's objection
sub.desc_en: Mar Kashisha bar Rav Chisda objects to Rav Ashi that we do require the verse exactly, citing the Mishnah about the wayward son where each phrase excludes a specific disability.

The Gemara answers that the case of the wayward son is different because the entire verse is extra (יַתִּירָא), so the exclusions are derived from the extra wording, not from a general requirement that the verse be fulfilled exactly.

items.text: The condemned city's square
items.text_en: The condemned city's square
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah about a condemned city: if it has no square, Rabbi Yishmael says it is not a condemned city, while Rabbi Akiva says they make one. The Gemara explains they disagree about whether the square must be original, but both agree we require the verse exactly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a condemned city (עיר הנדחת) to challenge the principle that the verse must be followed exactly: Rabbi Yishmael says if it has no square it is not a condemned city, while Rabbi Akiva says they make one.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva only disagree about whether the square must be original (דמעיקרא) or can be made now, but both agree that the verse must be followed exactly (קרא כדכתיב).

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on exact wording
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on exact wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a leper missing a thumb, etc., where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon disagree about where to place the blood, showing that the requirement for exact wording is a tannaitic dispute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the tannaitic dispute by citing the Mishnah about a leper missing a thumb, etc., where the Tanna Kamma states that such a person never achieves purification.
Rabbi Eliezer states that the blood is placed on the missing limb's location and the leper is thereby purified.
Rabbi Shimon states that the blood is placed on the left thumb or big toe and the leper is thereby purified.

items.text: Mishnah: Who is hung?
items.text_en: Mishnah: Who is hung?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: All who are stoned are hung, according to Rabbi Eliezer; the Sages say only the blasphemer and idolater are hung. The man is hung facing the people, the woman facing the tree, according to Rabbi Eliezer; the Sages say a man is hung but not a woman. Rabbi Eliezer cites Shimon ben Shetach who hung women in Ashkelon, but they respond that he hung eighty women, and we do not judge two in one day.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that all who are stoned are hung.
The Sages counter that only the blasphemer and idolater are hung.

sub.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Eliezer on hanging orientation
sub.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Eliezer on hanging orientation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer rules that a man is hung facing the people and a woman facing the tree.
The Sages rule that a man is hung but a woman is not hung.
Rabbi Eliezer objects by citing Shimon ben Shetach who hung women in Ashkelon.
The Sages reject the precedent, noting that Shimon ben Shetach hung eighty women, and we do not judge two in one day.

items.text: Gemara: Exegetical basis for hanging
items.text_en: Gemara: Exegetical basis for hanging
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: from 'he is put to death and you hang him' one might think all executed are hung; the verse says 'for a hanged person is a curse of God,' comparing to the blasphemer who is stoned, so only those stoned are hung, according to Rabbi Eliezer. The Sages say: just as the blasphemer denied the foundation, so only those who denied the foundation. They disagree on exegetical methods: the Sages use general and specific principles, Rabbi Eliezer uses amplifications and restrictions. The Sages derive: 'he is put to death and you hang him' is a general, 'for a curse' is a specific; if they were adjacent, only the specific would apply, but here they are not, so the general includes all stoned, and the specific excludes others.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a general rule: from 'he is put to death and you hang him' one might think all executed are hung, but the verse 'for a hanged person is a curse of God' limits it to those stoned, according to Rabbi Eliezer.
The Sages respond: just as the blasphemer denied the foundation, so only those who denied the foundation are hung.
The Gemara asks: on what exegetical principle do they disagree?
The Gemara answers: the Sages use the principles of general and specific (כללי ופרטי), while Rabbi Eliezer uses amplifications and restrictions (ריבויי ומיעוטי).

The Gemara elaborates: the Sages apply the general-specific method: 'he is put to death and you hang him' is a general, 'for a curse' is a specific; since they are not adjacent, the general includes all stoned, and the specific excludes others.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the distance between the verses and its effect on Rabbi Eliezer's derivation
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the distance between the verses and its effect on Rabbi Eliezer's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that because the verses 'והומת ותלית' and 'כי קללת' are now distant from each other, Rabbi Eliezer's method of ריבויי ומיעוטי includes all those executed by stoning, not just idolaters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that because the verses 'והומת ותלית' and 'כי קללת' are now distant from each other, Rabbi Eliezer's method of ריבויי ומיעוטי includes all those executed by stoning, not just idolaters.

items.text: The Rabbis' derivation that women are not hanged
items.text_en: The Rabbis' derivation that women are not hanged
items.desc_en: The Rabbis derive from the verse 'אותו' that only the man is hanged, not the woman. They also cite the verse 'וכי יהיה באיש חטא' to exclude women entirely from the death penalty of hanging.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of the Rabbis who hold that women are not hanged.
The Rabbis derive from the verse 'וְתָלִיתָ אֹתוֹ' that the word 'אותו' (him) excludes a woman from hanging.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Eliezer interprets the same word 'אותו' to mean that the hanged person is hung without his clothing.
The Rabbis add a second derivation from the verse 'וְכִי יִהְיֶה בְאִישׁ חֵטְא', which specifies 'איש' (a man) and not a woman, excluding women entirely from the death penalty of hanging.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation of 'וכי יהיה באיש' and the inclusion of the rebellious son
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation of 'וכי יהיה באיש' and the inclusion of the rebellious son
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that Rabbi Eliezer uses the verse to exclude the rebellious son, but a contradiction arises from a baraita. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the verse actually includes the rebellious son through a מיעוט אחר מיעוט.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Eliezer derives from the verse 'וכי יהיה באיש' (and if there is in a man).
Reish Lakish answers that the verse excludes the rebellious son (בן סורר ומורה) from hanging.
The Gemara objects with a baraita that states Rabbi Eliezer holds the rebellious son is stoned and then hanged.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that the verse actually includes the rebellious son through a מיעוט אחר מיעוט (a restriction after a restriction, which serves to include).

items.text: The challenge from Shimon ben Shetach and Rav Chisda's resolution
items.text_en: The challenge from Shimon ben Shetach and Rav Chisda's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer challenges the Rabbis with the precedent of Shimon ben Shetach hanging women. Rav Chisda initially distinguishes between two deaths and one death, but the Gemara objects. He then clarifies that the distinction is between one death like two deaths (two offenses) and one death with one offense.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer challenges the Rabbis by citing the precedent of Shimon ben Shetach who hanged women, implying that women can be hanged.
Rav Chisda initially answers that the Mishnah's rule applies only to two different death penalties, but for a single death penalty, women are judged and hanged.
The Gemara objects that the incident with Shimon ben Shetach involved a single death penalty, yet the Rabbis told him that women are not judged.
Rav Chisda clarifies that the Mishnah's rule applies only to a single death penalty that resembles two deaths, i.e., two offenses, but for one death with one offense, women are judged and hanged.

items.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's objection and Rav Chisda's qualification
items.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's objection and Rav Chisda's qualification
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava objects with a baraita that states two people are not judged on the same day, even an adulterer and an adulteress. Rav Chisda limits this to a case of a priest's daughter and her paramour, or a priest's daughter and the conspiring witnesses against her.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava objects with a baraita that they do not judge two people on the same day, even an adulterer and an adulteress, and Rav Chisda limits this to a priest's daughter and her paramour, or a priest's daughter and her false witnesses.
Rav Chisda qualifies the baraita, limiting it to the case of a priest's daughter and her paramour, or a priest's daughter and the conspiring witnesses against her.

items.text: The principle of extra-legal punishment for the sake of a fence
items.text_en: The principle of extra-legal punishment for the sake of a fence
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov stating that a court may administer lashes and punishments not mandated by the Torah to make a fence for the Torah. Two stories illustrate this: one who rode a horse on Shabbat was stoned, and one who had relations with his wife under a fig tree was lashed, both due to the exigency of the hour.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's principle that a court may administer extra-legal punishments to make a fence for the Torah.
The baraita illustrates the principle with a story of a man who rode a horse on Shabbat and was stoned due to the exigency of the hour.
The baraita adds a second story of a man who had relations with his wife under a fig tree and was lashed due to the exigency of the hour.

items.text: The Mishnah on the procedure for hanging and the prohibition of leaving the body overnight
items.text_en: The Mishnah on the procedure for hanging and the prohibition of leaving the body overnight
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes how the condemned is hanged: a beam is sunk into the ground with a protruding piece, and the hands are bound. Rabbi Yosei says the beam leans against a wall. The body is taken down immediately; leaving it overnight violates the prohibition 'לא תלין נבלתו', because the hanged person is a curse against God, causing desecration of His name. Rabbi Meir adds that God grieves over the blood of the wicked, and certainly over the righteous.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah asks how the condemned is hanged and describes the procedure: a beam is sunk into the ground with a protruding piece, and the hands are bound together.
Rabbi Yosei says the beam leans against a wall, and the condemned is hanged like butchers do.

sub.text: Mishnah's ruling on taking down the body
sub.text_en: Mishnah's ruling on taking down the body
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that the body is taken down immediately; leaving it overnight violates the prohibition 'לֹא תָלִין נִבְלָתוֹ', because the hanged person is a curse against God, causing desecration of His name.
Rabbi Meir adds that God grieves over the blood of the wicked, and certainly over the righteous.

items.text: The general prohibition of leaving a dead body overnight and the burial arrangements
items.text_en: The general prohibition of leaving a dead body overnight and the burial arrangements
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that anyone who leaves their dead overnight violates a negative commandment, unless done for honor (e.g., to procure a coffin). The executed were not buried in ancestral tombs; two burial grounds were designated for different execution methods. After the flesh decomposed, the bones were gathered and buried in their place. Relatives would greet the judges and witnesses, indicating no hard feelings.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule that anyone who leaves their dead overnight violates a negative commandment (בל תלין).
The Gemara clarifies that if one delays burial to honor the deceased (e.g., to procure a coffin and shrouds), the prohibition does not apply.

The Mishnah describes the burial arrangements: executed individuals were not buried in ancestral tombs, but in two designated burial grounds; after the flesh decomposed, the bones were gathered and buried in their place, and relatives would greet the judges and witnesses to show no hard feelings.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that those executed were not mourned but were in a state of aninut, as aninut is only in the heart.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that relatives of an executed man do not observe mourning but may grieve in their hearts.

items.text: Gemara: Order of Hanging and Execution
items.text_en: Gemara: Order of Hanging and Execution
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse that execution precedes hanging, and describes the procedure: they delay until near sunset, execute, then hang, with one tying and one untying to fulfill the mitzvah of hanging.

sub.desc_en: The baraita derives from the verse that execution precedes hanging, and describes the procedure: delay until near sunset, execute, then hang, with one tying and one untying to fulfill the mitzvah of hanging.

items.text: Derivation: Hanging on a Tree Must Be Detached
items.text_en: Derivation: Hanging on a Tree Must Be Detached
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the tree for hanging must be detached, not attached, derived from 'ki kavur' (for burial). Rabbi Yosei argues it must also be uprooted, but the Sages say uprooting is nothing.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma teaches that the tree for hanging must be detached, not attached, derived from the verse 'כִּי קָבוֹר' (for burial), excluding a tree that requires both cutting and burial.
רבי יוסי (Rabbi Yosei) argues that the tree must be uprooted (detached from the ground), not just detached, excluding a tree that requires both uprooting and burial.
The Sages (רבנן) reject Rabbi Yosei's requirement, stating that uprooting (תְּלִישָׁה) is nothing (i.e., insignificant).

items.text: Reason for Hanging: The Blasphemer
items.text_en: Reason for Hanging: The Blasphemer
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the hanging is because the person blasphemed, and Rabbi Meir tells a parable of twin brothers—one king, one bandit—to show why the blasphemer is hanged.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the reason the blasphemer is hanged is because he blessed (cursed) God.
רבי מאיר (Rabbi Meir) tells a parable of twin brothers—one king, one bandit—to illustrate why the blasphemer must be taken down, to avoid desecrating God's name.

items.text: Derivation of 'Kilelat' for Blasphemy
items.text_en: Derivation of 'Kilelat' for Blasphemy
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava debate the meaning of 'kilelat' (lightness) in the context of blasphemy. The Gemara concludes that the word 'kilelat' teaches both the punishment of hanging and the prohibition of blasphemy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where does Rabbi Meir infer his interpretation of the word 'kilelat'?
Abaye explains that Rabbi Meir understands 'kilelat' as 'I am not light', meaning God is distressed.
Rava objects that if the meaning were 'heavy', the verse should have explicitly said 'my head is heavy for me' or 'my arm is heavy for me'.
Rava offers his own interpretation: 'kilelat' means 'the world is light for me', indicating God's distress.
The Gemara objects: The word 'kilelat' is needed for its own meaning (blasphemy); how can it also be interpreted as alluding to God's distress?
The Gemara responds: If the verse only meant 'one who curses', it should have said 'mekallel'; the unusual form 'kilelat' teaches an additional lesson.
The Gemara objects: Perhaps the entire verse comes only for this additional lesson (about God's distress), and not to teach the halakha of blasphemy.

The Gemara resolves: If the verse were only for the additional lesson, it should have said 'kalat' (lightness); the form 'kilelat' teaches both the punishment of hanging for blasphemy and God's distress.

items.text: Source for Burial from the Torah
items.text_en: Source for Burial from the Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai derives that one who delays burying his dead violates a negative commandment, and alternatively that there is a hint for burial from the Torah, from the verse 'ki kavur tikberenu'.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai derives from the doubled verb 'כי קבר תקברנו' (ki kavur tikberenu) that one who delays burying his dead violates a negative commandment.

sub.text: Alternative version of the same tradition
sub.text_en: Alternative version of the same tradition
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai derives from the same verse a hint (רמז) for the mitzva of burial from the Torah.

items.text: King Shapur's Question and Attempted Proofs for Burial
items.text_en: King Shapur's Question and Attempted Proofs for Burial
items.desc_en: King Shapur asks Rav Chama for the source of burial from the Torah; Rav Chama is silent. Rav Acha bar Yaakov criticizes him. The Gemara attempts to prove burial from the burial of the righteous, but each proof is rejected as mere custom.

sub.desc_en: King Shapur asks Rav Chama for the Torah source of burial; Rav Chama is silent and says nothing.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov criticizes Rav Chama, saying the world is handed over to fools, as he should have cited the verse 'כִּי קָבוֹר' (for you shall bury him).
The Gemara objects that King Shapur could have replied that the verse only requires making a coffin, not burial in the ground, and he does not accept the doubled verb as a source.
The Gemara suggests proving burial from the burial of the righteous patriarchs and from God burying Moses, but each is rejected as merely custom, not a mitzvah.
The Gemara cites the verse about Abijah being buried, but rejects it as merely following custom.
The Gemara cites Jeremiah's curse that the wicked shall not be buried, but rejects it as merely a deviation from custom, not a proof of a mitzvah.

items.text: Burial: For Disgrace or Atonement?
items.text_en: Burial: For Disgrace or Atonement?
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether burial is due to disgrace (of the body) or for atonement. The practical difference is if one says not to bury him. Proofs from the burial of the righteous and the wicked show it is for atonement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: is burial required because of the disgrace of leaving the body exposed, or because it provides atonement for the deceased?
The Gemara asks what practical difference this distinction makes, and explains: if one says he does not want to be buried, the reason determines whether his wish is honored.
The Gemara proposes a proof from the burial of the righteous patriarchs, and rejects the objection that the righteous do not need atonement by citing a verse that even the righteous sin.
The Gemara proposes another proof from the verse about Abijah, and answers that the righteous son achieves atonement through burial while the wicked sons do not.
The Gemara proposes a proof from Jeremiah's curse that the wicked should not be buried, indicating that burial is for atonement, since the curse withholds atonement.

items.text: Eulogy: For the Honor of the Living or the Dead?
items.text_en: Eulogy: For the Honor of the Living or the Dead?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether eulogy honors the living or the dead. The practical difference is if one says not to eulogize him, or regarding inheritance. Proofs from Abraham, the righteous, and the wicked show it honors the living.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: is a eulogy for the honor of the living or the dead, and notes the practical difference if one says not to eulogize him or regarding inheritance from heirs.

The Gemara brings a proof from Abraham eulogizing Sarah, suggesting that if eulogy were for the living, they would not delay burial for Abraham's honor, but answers that Sarah herself was satisfied with the delay for Abraham's honor.

The Gemara brings a proof from the eulogy of Abijah, son of Jeroboam, suggesting that if eulogy were for the living, the wicked family would not be honored, but answers that the righteous are satisfied when others are honored through them.

The Gemara brings a proof from Jeremiah's curse that the wicked should not be eulogized, suggesting that if eulogy were for the living, righteous survivors would deserve honor, but answers that the righteous are not satisfied when honored through the wicked.

The Gemara brings a proof from Jeremiah's words to Zedekiah, suggesting that if eulogy were for the living, it would not matter to the deceased, but answers that the eulogy honors the living, as Jeremiah tells Zedekiah that Israel will be honored through him.

items.text: Proof from Hezekiah's dragging his father's bones
items.text_en: Proof from Hezekiah's dragging his father's bones
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof that delaying burial for the living's honor is permitted, citing Hezekiah who dragged his father's bones on a rope bed. It explains this was for his father's atonement, and that Israel is willing to forego their honor for that purpose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a proof from the verse about Hezekiah dragging his father's bones, questioning why this was not considered disrespectful to the living.
The Gemara explains that Hezekiah delayed burial for his father's atonement, and Israel is willing to forego their honor for that purpose.

items.text: Proof from the request not to be eulogized in towns
items.text_en: Proof from the request not to be eulogized in towns
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another proof: one who says 'do not eulogize me in towns' shows concern for the living's honor, as he wants Israel to be honored through him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from a statement where someone said 'do not eulogize me in towns,' and questions how this relates to the honor of the living.
The Gemara answers that the speaker wanted Israel to be honored through him, showing concern for the living's honor.

items.text: Proof from delaying for honor: for the living
items.text_en: Proof from delaying for honor: for the living
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: one who delays a corpse overnight for its honor (to bring a coffin and shrouds) does not violate the prohibition. It initially assumes this is for the dead's honor, but concludes it is for the living's honor, as the Torah's prohibition only applies where there is disgrace.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: one who delays a corpse overnight for its honor, to bring a coffin and shrouds, does not violate the prohibition.
The Gemara asks: does this not mean for the honor of the dead?
The Gemara answers: no, it means for the honor of the living.
The Gemara objects: would one cause a corpse to be left overnight for the honor of the living?
The Gemara resolves: yes, because the Torah's prohibition applies only where there is disgrace, like a hanged person, but here there is no disgrace.

items.text: Clarification of the baraita
items.text_en: Clarification of the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the baraita: all actions done for the dead's honor are permitted, but the Gemara reinterprets it to mean that actions done for the living's honor involve no disgrace to the dead.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about delaying burial for the dead's honor and asks whether it proves the honor is for the dead.
The Gemara reinterprets the baraita: all actions are for the living's honor, and no disgrace to the dead is involved.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Nathan: honor of the dead
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Nathan: honor of the dead
items.desc_en: Rabbi Nathan says that a sign of atonement for the dead is if they are not eulogized or buried, or animals drag them. The Gemara concludes from this that the honor is for the dead, not the living.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nathan states that a sign of atonement for the dead is if they are not eulogized or buried, or animals drag them.
The Gemara concludes from Rabbi Nathan's statement that the honor is for the dead, not the living.

items.text: Reason for separate burial of the executed
items.text_en: Reason for separate burial of the executed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the executed were not buried with their ancestors. The Gemara explains this is because a wicked person is not buried next to a righteous one, citing the story of Elisha's bones reviving a dead man. It also discusses that a severe wicked person is not buried next to a lighter one, and that only two graves are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the executed were not buried with their ancestors, and answers that a wicked person is not buried next to a righteous one.
Rabbi Acha bar Chanina cites the verse about Elisha's bones reviving a dead man to prove that a wicked person is not buried next to a righteous one.
Rav Pappa objects that the revival might have been to fulfill Elisha's request for a double portion of his spirit, not to prove the rule about burial.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves that the double portion was fulfilled through healing Naaman's leprosy, which is considered like death, so the revival of the dead man remains a proof for the burial rule.
The Gemara extends the rule: a severely wicked person is not buried next to a lighter one, and explains that only two graves are needed because the tradition (גמרא) teaches this.

items.text: Principle: once rejected, remains rejected for sacrifices
items.text_en: Principle: once rejected, remains rejected for sacrifices
items.desc_en: Ulla and Rabbi Yochanan state that if someone ate forbidden fat and set aside a sacrifice, then apostatized and returned, the sacrifice is rejected. Similarly, if he became insane and recovered, it is rejected. The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that if someone ate forbidden fat, set aside a sacrifice, then apostatized and returned, the sacrifice is rejected because it was once rejected.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya citing Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya citing Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya transmits a parallel tradition from Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: if one ate forbidden fat, set aside a sacrifice, then became insane and recovered, the sacrifice is rejected.
The Gemara explains why both cases are needed: the first case (apostasy) involves active self-rejection, so the second case (insanity) might have been thought to be like sleep and not rejected.
