items.text: Anecdote about Nadav and Avihu
items.text_en: Anecdote about Nadav and Avihu
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a story about Moses and Aaron walking with Nadav and Avihu behind them, and Nadav expressing a desire for the elders to die so they could lead. God responded by showing who would bury whom. Rav Pappa comments on a folk saying. The section ends with Rabbi Eliezer beginning to speak.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a story of Moses and Aaron walking with Nadav and Avihu behind them, and all of Israel behind them.
Nadav asks Avihu when the two elders (Moses and Aaron) will die so that they can lead the generation.
God responds by saying it will be seen who buries whom, implying that Nadav and Avihu will die first.
Rav Pappa comments that this aligns with a folk saying about many old camels laden with hides of young camels.
Rabbi Eliezer begins to speak, marking a transition to a new topic.

items.text: Opening metaphor about a Torah scholar before an ignoramus
items.text_en: Opening metaphor about a Torah scholar before an ignoramus
items.desc_en: A metaphor comparing a Torah scholar's value in the eyes of an ignoramus to vessels of gold, silver, and clay, emphasizing that once broken, there is no repair.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a metaphor comparing a Torah scholar before an ignoramus to vessels of gold, silver, and clay, which once broken cannot be repaired.

items.text: The case of the daughter of a priest who committed adultery
items.text_en: The case of the daughter of a priest who committed adultery
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses an incident where Rav Chama bar Toviya burned a priest's daughter who committed adultery. Rav Yosef points out two errors: the law requires a priest for judgment, and the incident involved a Sadducean court. The Gemara then clarifies the sequence of testimony from Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts an incident where Rav Chama bar Toviya burned a priest's daughter who committed adultery.
Rav Yosef points out two errors in Rav Chama's action: the law requires a priest for judgment, and the incident involved a Sadducean court.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's testimony
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's testimony
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok testifies that the court in the incident was a Sadducean court.
The Gemara questions the sequence of Rabbi Elazar's testimonies and resolves that there were two separate incidents.
The Gemara asks which testimony Rabbi Elazar gave first and whether the court accepted it.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Elazar first testified as a child and was dismissed, then testified as an adult and was dismissed because the court was not expert.

items.text: Mishnah: The mitzvah of those executed by decapitation
items.text_en: Mishnah: The mitzvah of those executed by decapitation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that those sentenced to decapitation have their heads cut off with a sword, like the kingdom does. Rabbi Yehuda argues this is degrading and suggests placing the head on a block and cutting with an axe. The Sages respond that there is no more degrading death than that.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the mitzvah for those executed by decapitation: they strike off the head with a sword, as the kingdom does.
Rabbi Yehuda objects that the sword method is degrading and proposes placing the head on a block and cutting with an axe.
The Sages reject Rabbi Yehuda's proposal, stating that there is no more degrading death than that.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning and the Sages' response
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning and the Sages' response
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda knows his method is degrading but argues it avoids imitating gentile practices. The Sages counter that since the Torah prescribes a sword, it is not derived from gentile customs, as illustrated by the parallel case of burning for kings.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda admits to the Sages that his method is degrading but defends it as necessary to avoid imitating gentile practices, citing the prohibition against following their statutes.
The Sages counter that since the Torah prescribes a sword (סַיִיף) for execution, the practice is not derived from gentile customs.

The Gemara supports the Sages' position with a parallel: burning for kings is permitted because the Torah mentions burning, so it is not derived from gentile practices; similarly, the sword is Torah-based.

items.text: Source for execution by sword for murderers and the principle of a beautiful death
items.text_en: Source for execution by sword for murderers and the principle of a beautiful death
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for executing a murderer by sword, deriving it from the word 'nekama' (vengeance) which is associated with a sword. It then addresses alternative methods and establishes the principle of choosing a beautiful death based on 'v'ahavta l're'acha kamocha'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a murderer is executed by decapitation, noting that the idolatrous city is explicitly so punished but the murderer is not.
A baraita derives from the word 'nekama' (vengeance), linked to the sword of the covenant, that the murderer is executed by the sword.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the executioner should stab with the sword rather than decapitate, and answers that the verse says 'with the edge of the sword'.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the body should be cut in half, and Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha answers that the verse 'love your neighbor as yourself' requires selecting a compassionate death.
The Gemara asks: we have found the source for one who kills a Canaanite slave, but from where do we derive the execution of one who kills a freeman?
The Gemara proposes an a fortiori inference: if one who killed a slave is executed by sword, one who killed a freeman should certainly not be executed merely by strangulation.
The Gemara rejects the a fortiori inference, since according to the opinion that strangulation is more severe than decapitation, the murderer of a freeman could indeed be executed by strangulation.
A baraita derives from the comparison of all spillers of blood to the heifer whose neck is broken that murderers are executed by the sword and at the neck.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the heifer is decapitated with a cleaver at the nape, and Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha resolves that the verse 'love your neighbor as yourself' mandates selecting the most compassionate method.

items.text: Mishnah: The mitzvah of those executed by strangulation
items.text_en: Mishnah: The mitzvah of those executed by strangulation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for strangulation: the condemned is buried in dung up to his knees, a hard cloth is placed inside a soft one, wrapped around his neck, and two witnesses pull until he dies.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for strangulation: the condemned is buried in dung up to his knees, a hard cloth is placed inside a soft one, wrapped around his neck, and two witnesses pull until he dies.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation of strangulation for adulterers
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation of strangulation for adulterers
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the death penalty for adultery is by strangulation, based on the verse 'mot yumat' and the principle that a general death penalty is lenient (strangulation) unless specified otherwise. Rabbi Yonatan and Rabbi offer alternative derivations, and the Gemara rejects burning by comparing to the priest's daughter.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces exclusions from the adultery verse: 'איש' (a man) excludes a minor, 'אשר ינאף את אשת איש' excludes a minor's wife, and 'אשת רעהו' excludes the wife of others (non-Jews).
The baraita asks whether 'מות יומת' (he shall surely be put to death) means strangulation or any other death penalty mentioned in the Torah.
Rabbi Yoshiya answers that wherever the Torah states a death penalty without specification, one must apply the lenient option (strangulation), not the stringent one.
Rabbi Yonatan answers that the reason is not leniency but that any unspecified death penalty in the Torah is exclusively strangulation.
Rabbi answers by analogy: just as death by Heaven (מיתה בידי שמים) leaves no mark, so too death by human hands (מיתה בידי אדם) must be a death that leaves no mark, i.e., strangulation.

The Gemara objects: why not say burning (שרפה) is the death that leaves no mark? It answers that since the Torah specified burning for a priest's daughter who commits adultery, it implies that an ordinary adulteress is not subject to burning.

items.text: Question about Rabbi Yoshiyah's view on strangulation
items.text_en: Question about Rabbi Yoshiyah's view on strangulation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yoshiyah's position that strangulation is a death penalty, since it could be derived from the Torah's general command. It asks why not say the sword instead.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yoshiyah's view that strangulation is a death penalty, asking why not derive the sword instead.

items.text: Rava's answer: tradition of four death penalties
items.text_en: Rava's answer: tradition of four death penalties
items.desc_en: Rava answers that the four death penalties are a tradition received from Sinai, not derived from exegesis.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the four death penalties are a tradition received from Sinai, not derived from exegesis.

items.text: Clarifying the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Clarifying the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the earlier statement about one death penalty not being lighter refers to a dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the earlier statement about one death penalty not being lighter refers to, and answers that it is about the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis.

items.text: Derivation of stoning for other capital offenders
items.text_en: Derivation of stoning for other capital offenders
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Abaye whether other stoning penalties are derived from 'they shall surely be put to death' or 'their blood is upon them'. Abaye answers from 'their blood', and a baraita explains the need for both verses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Abaye whether other capital offenders who are stoned derive their penalty from 'מוֹת יוּמָתוּ' (they shall surely be put to death) or from 'דְּמֵיהֶם בָּם' (their blood is upon them).
Abaye answers that they derive from 'דְּמֵיהֶם בָּם' (their blood is upon them), arguing that if derived from 'מוֹת יוּמָתוּ', the extra phrase 'דְּמֵיהֶם' would be superfluous.
The Gemara objects: if the derivation is from 'דְּמֵיהֶם', then why is the verse 'מוֹת יוּמָתוּ' needed at all?
A baraita explains that 'מוֹת יוּמַת' teaches that if the prescribed death penalty cannot be carried out, the offender is executed by any possible death.

items.text: Discussion of the difficulty with deriving from 'they shall surely be put to death'
items.text_en: Discussion of the difficulty with deriving from 'they shall surely be put to death'
items.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti asks Ravina what difficulty would arise if derived from 'they shall surely be put to death'. They consider cases of an adulteress and one who strikes his father, concluding that the difficulty is about other stoning penalties themselves, which could be derived from the betrothed woman.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti asks Ravina what difficulty would arise if the halakha were derived from 'they shall surely be put to death'.

The Gemara suggests that the case of a married adulteress would pose a difficulty, but rejects this because the Torah's specification of stoning for a betrothed woman implies that a married woman is not stoned.

The Gemara suggests that the case of one who strikes his father or mother would pose a difficulty, but rejects this because one would derive the lenient punishment from the married adulteress rather than the stringent one from the necromancer.

Ravina resolves that the difficulty is about the other stoning penalties themselves, which could be derived from the betrothed woman's lenient punishment rather than from the necromancer's stringent one.

items.text: Mishnah: List of those stoned and details of incestuous relationships
items.text_en: Mishnah: List of those stoned and details of incestuous relationships
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists all those liable for stoning, then details the multiple prohibitions violated by one who sleeps with his mother, father's wife, or daughter-in-law, with Rabbi Yehuda's dissenting opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing all those liable for stoning.
The Mishnah states that one who sleeps with his mother is liable for two prohibitions, while Rabbi Yehuda says he is liable only for the mother.
The Mishnah details that one who sleeps with his father's wife is liable for two prohibitions, applying in all circumstances.
The Mishnah states that one who sleeps with his daughter-in-law is liable for two prohibitions, applying in all circumstances.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Yehuda's condition and the dispute with the Rabbis
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Yehuda's condition and the dispute with the Rabbis
items.desc_en: A baraita states Rabbi Yehuda's view that if the mother was not fit for the father, he is only liable for the mother. The Gemara clarifies this refers to those forbidden by a negative commandment, and Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Akiva that betrothal does not take effect for such women. Rav Oshaya raises an objection from a Mishnah about levirate marriage.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that if the mother was not suitable for the father, the son is liable only for the prohibition of the mother.

The Gemara asks what 'not suitable' means, and rejects the possibility that it refers to those liable for כרת (excision) or court-imposed death, since then even the Rabbis would agree she is not a wife.
The Gemara explains that it refers to those liable for a negative commandment, and Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Akiva that betrothal does not take effect for such women.

Rav Oshaya raises an objection from a Mishnah in Yevamot that a יבמה (levirate widow) forbidden by a prohibition of a מצוה (commandment) or sanctity performs חליצה (removal of the shoe) and does not enter יבום (levirate marriage), challenging the explanation.

items.text: Definition of Issur Mitzvah and Issur Kedushah
items.text_en: Definition of Issur Mitzvah and Issur Kedushah
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines 'issur mitzvah' as rabbinic prohibitions (secondary forbidden relations) and 'issur kedushah' as biblical prohibitions like a widow to a High Priest or a divorcee to a common priest, explaining the scriptural basis for the latter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara defines 'איסור מצוה (issur mitzvah)' as secondary forbidden relations (שניות) instituted by the Scribes, and explains the name: it is a מצוה (commandment) to heed the words of the Sages.

The Gemara defines 'איסור קדושה (issur kedushah)' as a widow to a High Priest or a divorcee or a חלוצה (halutzah, a woman who performed חליצה) to a common priest, and explains the name from the verse 'קדושים יהיו לאלהיהם' (they shall be holy to their God).

items.text: Rabbi Yehudah's Swap and the Challenge from Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehudah's Swap and the Challenge from Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Yehudah swaps the categories. The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehudah holds like Rabbi Akiva, who equates positive commandments with karet, and notes that those liable for karet are not subject to chalitzah or yibbum. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehudah speaks to the first Tanna but does not agree with him.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Yehudah swaps the categories of איסור מצוה (prohibition of a commandment) and איסור קדושה (prohibition of sanctity).

The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehudah holds like Rabbi Akiva, who equates those liable for negative commandments (לאוין) with those liable for karet (כרת), who are exempt from chalitzah (חליצה) and yibbum (ייבום).
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehudah speaks to the first Tanna (תנא קמא) but does not agree with him, so the swap is only for the sake of argument.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's Teaching and Abaye's Explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's Teaching and Abaye's Explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that Rabbi Yehudah says one is only liable for the mother alone. Abaye explains the scriptural basis: the verse 'your mother she is' implies liability only for the mother, not for the father's wife.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that Rabbi Yehudah holds one is liable only for the mother alone.
Abaye explains the scriptural basis: the verse 'אִמְּךָ הִיא' (she is your mother) implies liability only for the mother, not for the father's wife.

items.text: Objection from the Verse on Father's Wife
items.text_en: Objection from the Verse on Father's Wife
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: from the verse 'the nakedness of your father's wife' one might think liability is only for the father's wife, not the mother. This leads to a contradiction: if a woman is both mother and father's wife, one would be exempt entirely, which is absurd.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: from the verse about the father's wife, one might think liability is only for the father's wife, not the mother, leading to the absurd conclusion that a woman who is both mother and father's wife would be entirely exempt.

items.text: Refutation: The Verse Needed for Rav Shisha's Teaching
items.text_en: Refutation: The Verse Needed for Rav Shisha's Teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the verse 'your mother she is' is needed for Rav Shisha's teaching, both for the Rabbis and for Rabbi Yehudah, so it cannot be used for the previous derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse 'אִמְּךָ הִיא' (your mother she is) is needed for Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's teaching, both for the Rabbis and for Rabbi Yehudah, so it cannot be used for the previous derivation.

items.text: Rav Acha's Alternative: One Liability from 'Her Nakedness'
items.text_en: Rav Acha's Alternative: One Liability from 'Her Nakedness'
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika suggests that the verse 'her nakedness' implies liability for only one prohibition, not two. The Gemara objects from the case of a daughter-in-law, where one is liable for both daughter-in-law and married woman, and Rabbi Yehudah does not dispute. The Gemara resolves that since it is one body, even with two prohibitions, the verse 'her nakedness' applies.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika proposes that the verse 'עֶרְוָתָהּ' (her nakedness) implies liability for only one prohibition, not two.
The Gemara objects by applying the same logic to the case of a daughter-in-law, where the verse also says 'עֶרְוָתָהּ'.
The Gemara cites a baraita that one who has relations with his daughter-in-law is liable for both daughter-in-law and married woman, and Rabbi Yehudah does not dispute this.
The Gemara resolves that since it is one body, even with two prohibitions, the verse 'עֶרְוָתָהּ' applies, and the same logic applies to the mother case.

items.text: Rava's Conclusion: Gezeirah Shavah and the Two Verses
items.text_en: Rava's Conclusion: Gezeirah Shavah and the Two Verses
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Yehudah derives the prohibition of a father's wife from a gezeirah shavah on 'ervat avicha', including both when she is his mother and when she is not. The mother who is not the father's wife is derived from the verse 'your mother she is', limiting liability to the mother alone.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by asserting that Rabbi Yehudah interprets 'ערוות אביך' (the nakedness of your father) as referring to the father's wife, and derives the prohibition via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy).

Rava explains that the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) includes both the father's wife who is his mother and the father's wife who is not his mother, while the verse 'אמך היא' (your mother she is) limits liability for the mother who is not the father's wife to the mother alone, not the father's wife.

items.text: Derivation of punishment for one who sleeps with his father's wife
items.text_en: Derivation of punishment for one who sleeps with his father's wife
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rava's view, deriving from the verse "איש" that a minor is excluded. The verse "אשר ישכב את אשת אביו" includes both a father's wife who is his mother and one who is not. For a mother who is not a father's wife, a גזרה שוה is used. The punishment is stoning, derived from a גזרה שוה with אוב וידעוני. The warning is derived from "ערות אביך לא תגלה", which is interpreted to refer to a father's wife through a גזרה שוה.

sub.desc_en: The baraita supports Rava's view by deriving from the verse "איש" that a minor is excluded, and from "אשר ישכב את אשת אביו" that both a father's wife who is his mother and one who is not are included, and for a mother who is not a father's wife, a גזרה שוה (verbal analogy) is used.
The baraita derives that the punishment is stoning through a גזרה שוה (verbal analogy) with אוב וידעוני (necromancers and wizards), using the common phrase "דמיהם בם" (their blood is in them).

The baraita derives the warning (אזהרה) from the verse "ערות אביך לא תגלה", interpreting "ערות אביך" as referring to a father's wife through a גזרה שוה (verbal analogy) with the verse "ערות אביו גלה".

items.text: Derivation of warning and punishment for a mother who is not a father's wife
items.text_en: Derivation of warning and punishment for a mother who is not a father's wife
items.desc_en: The baraita continues, deriving the warning for a mother who is not a father's wife from "ערות אמך לא תגלה". For the punishment, a גזרה שוה is used to equate the warning and punishment. The verse "אמך היא" teaches that one is liable for her as a mother, not as a father's wife.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the warning verse implies both a mother who is the father's wife and one who is not, then asks for the source for a mother who is not the father's wife.
The baraita notes that the warning covers the mother who is not the father's wife, but asks for the source of the punishment.

sub.text: Baraita's answer via גזרה שוה (verbal analogy)
sub.text_en: Baraita's answer via גזרה שוה (verbal analogy)
sub.desc_en: The baraita uses a גזרה שוה (verbal analogy) between the warning and punishment verses to extend the punishment for a mother who is not the father's wife.
The baraita concludes that the verse 'אִמְּךָ הִיא' teaches that one is liable for her as a mother, not as a father's wife.

items.text: Dispute regarding Rabbi Yehuda's view on liability for sleeping with one's father
items.text_en: Dispute regarding Rabbi Yehuda's view on liability for sleeping with one's father
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Rabbis' interpretation of "ערות אביך" as literal. It then discusses Rav Yehuda's statement that a Noahide who sleeps with his father is liable for two, and with his uncle is liable for two. Rava clarifies that this refers to a Jewish person who sins unintentionally and brings a sacrifice. A baraita supports this, but there is a dispute about whether it aligns with Rabbi Yehuda. One opinion derives the liability for the father through a קל וחומר from the uncle, and the dispute is tied to the debate between Abaye and Rava about whether punishment can be derived through logical inference.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Rabbis derive the prohibition of sleeping with one's father from 'ערות אביך' (your father's nakedness) literally, and suggests it comes from the verse about male intercourse to impose two liabilities.
Rav Yehuda states that a Noahide who sleeps with his father is liable for two, and with his uncle is liable for two.

Rava clarifies that Rav Yehuda's statement refers to a Jewish person who sins unintentionally and brings a sacrifice, not a literal Noahide, because a Noahide would be executed and cannot be executed twice.
A baraita supports Rava's interpretation, stating that one who sleeps with his father is liable for two, and with his uncle is liable for two.
One opinion objects that the baraita does not align with Rabbi Yehuda's view.
Another opinion argues that the baraita can align with Rabbi Yehuda, deriving the liability for the father through a קל וחומר (a fortiori inference) from the uncle.
The Gemara resolves that the dispute between the two opinions hinges on the debate between Abaye and Rava: whether punishment can be derived through logical inference (עונשין מן הדין) or not.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis regarding the warning and punishment for a father's wife after death
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis regarding the warning and punishment for a father's wife after death
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Rabbis derive the warning for a father's wife from "ערות אשת אביך לא תגלה", while Rabbi Yehuda uses that verse for the warning after the father's death. The Rabbis derive the warning after death from the end of the verse. Rabbi Yehuda uses that end to teach that one is liable for the father's wife, not for another married woman. The Gemara questions a Mishna that seems to contradict Rabbi Yehuda, and Abaye explains that Rabbi Yehuda disputes it in a baraita. The Rabbis derive the punishment for a father's wife after death from the verse "ערות אביו גלה", which Rabbi Yehuda uses for a גזרה שוה. For a mother who is not a father's wife, the Rabbis derive the punishment from "אמך היא".

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the Rabbis derive the warning for a father's wife, and answers that it comes from the verse 'ערות אשת אביך לא תגלה'.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda uses that verse for the warning for a father's wife after the father's death.
The Gemara states that the Rabbis derive the warning after death from the end of the verse 'ערות אביך היא'.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda uses that end of the verse to teach that one is liable for the father's wife, not for another married woman.
The Gemara objects that a Mishna states one is liable for a father's wife both during the father's life and after his death, and asks whether Rabbi Yehuda disputes this.
Abaye answers that Rabbi Yehuda does dispute it in a baraita.
The Gemara asks where the Rabbis derive the punishment for a father's wife after death, noting that Rabbi Yehuda derives it via a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy).
The Gemara answers that the Rabbis use the verse 'ערות אביו גלה', which Rabbi Yehuda uses for a גזירה שוה, for the punishment after death.
The Gemara asks where the Rabbis derive the punishment for a mother who is not a father's wife, and Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi answers that the verse 'אמך היא' teaches it.

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi explains that the verse 'אמך היא' treats a mother who is not a father's wife like a mother who is a father's wife.

items.text: Clarification regarding one who sleeps with his daughter-in-law
items.text_en: Clarification regarding one who sleeps with his daughter-in-law
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one who sleeps with his daughter-in-law is not also liable for sleeping with his son's wife. Abaye answers that the verse begins with "כלתו" and ends with "אשת בנו", teaching that they are the same person.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one who sleeps with his daughter-in-law is not also liable for sleeping with his son's wife.
Abaye answers that the verse begins with "כלתו" and ends with "אשת בנו", teaching that they are the same person.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on one who sleeps with a male or an animal
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on one who sleeps with a male or an animal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who sleeps with a male or an animal, and a woman who brings an animal, are executed by stoning. It explains why the animal is killed. The Gemara derives the source for the male from a baraita, which includes both an adult and a minor male. Rabbi Yishmael comments on the verse. The punishment of stoning is derived from a גזרה שוה with אוב וידעוני.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those liable for stoning: one who sleeps with a male or an animal, and a woman who brings an animal, and explains the rationale for executing the animal.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the source for the male (the prohibition and punishment)?
A baraita is cited: the verse 'איש' excludes a minor, 'אשר ישכב את זכר' includes both adult and minor males, and 'משכבי אשה' teaches two modes of intercourse with a woman.
Rabbi Yishmael comments that this verse comes to teach and is itself learned from elsewhere.
The Gemara derives that the punishment is stoning through a גזרה שוה (verbal analogy) from the word 'דמיהם בם' used in the case of אוב וידעוני (necromancers).

items.text: Deriving the prohibition for the active and passive partner in male homosexual intercourse
items.text_en: Deriving the prohibition for the active and passive partner in male homosexual intercourse
items.desc_en: The Gemara first asks for the source of the prohibition (אזהרה) for the active partner, citing Leviticus 18:22. Then it seeks the source for the passive partner, which Rabbi Yishmael derives from Deuteronomy 23:18 and a supporting verse. Rabbi Akiva argues that the same verse (Leviticus 18:22) can be read as 'do not be lain' (לא תִשָּׁכֵב), thus covering both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the prohibition (אזהרה) for the active partner in male homosexual intercourse, and cites Leviticus 18:22 as the answer.
The Gemara asks for the source of the prohibition for the passive partner, and Rabbi Yishmael answers by citing Deuteronomy 23:18 and a supporting verse from I Kings 14:24.
Rabbi Akiva argues that no separate verse is needed; the same verse (Leviticus 18:22) can be read as 'do not be lain' (לא תִשָּׁכֵב), covering both the active and passive partner.

items.text: Deriving the punishment and prohibition for bestiality
items.text_en: Deriving the punishment and prohibition for bestiality
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the punishment for bestiality from a baraita, establishing that the death penalty is stoning. It then derives the punishment for the passive partner (the animal's receiver) from the verse 'כל שוכב עם בהמה מות יומת'. Finally, it derives the prohibition for the active partner from Leviticus 18:23, and for the passive partner from the same sources as before, with Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva repeating their respective positions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where the punishment for bestiality is derived, and cites a baraita that excludes a minor and includes any animal.
The Gemara derives that the death penalty for bestiality is stoning via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the inciter.
The Gemara asks from where the punishment for the passive partner in bestiality is derived, and answers that the verse 'כל שוכב עם בהמה מות יומת' applies to the passive partner.
The Gemara asks from where the prohibition for bestiality is derived, and cites Leviticus 18:23 for the active partner.
The Gemara asks from where the prohibition for the passive partner in bestiality is derived, and cites Rabbi Yishmael's position from the verse 'לא יהיה קדש'.
Rabbi Akiva states that the prohibition for the passive partner is derived from the verse itself by reading 'לא תתן שכבתך' as 'לא תתן שכיבתך'.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's ruling on the number of violations for the active partner
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's ruling on the number of violations for the active partner
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu states that according to Rabbi Yishmael, one who actively engages in male homosexual intercourse or bestiality is liable for two violations (one from the specific prohibition and one from 'לא יהיה קדש'), while according to Rabbi Akiva, only one violation applies since the two prohibitions are essentially the same.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of one who actively engages in male homosexual intercourse or brings a male upon himself.

Rabbi Avahu rules that according to Rabbi Yishmael the active partner is liable for two violations (one from 'לֹא תִשְׁכַּב' and one from 'לֹא יִהְיֶה קָדֵשׁ'), while according to Rabbi Akiva he is liable for only one.
Rabbi Avahu explains that according to Rabbi Akiva, the two prohibitions 'לֹא תִשְׁכַּב' and 'לֹא תִשָּׁכֵב' are considered the same prohibition, hence only one violation.

items.text: Abaye's challenge and alternative derivation for the passive partner's prohibition
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge and alternative derivation for the passive partner's prohibition
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that even according to Rabbi Yishmael, the passive partner is only liable for one violation because 'לא יהיה קדש' applies only to males (active partners). He then explains that Rabbi Yishmael actually derives the prohibition for the passive partner from the verse 'כל שוכב עם בהמה מות יומת', which is extended to the passive partner and includes both punishment and prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbi Avahu's ruling, arguing that even according to Rabbi Yishmael the passive partner is only liable for one violation because the verse 'לֹא יִהְיֶה קָדֵשׁ' applies only to males (active partners).
Abaye asks how Rabbi Yishmael derives the prohibition for the passive partner, and answers that it comes from the verse 'כׇּל שֹׁכֵב עִם בְּהֵמָה מוֹת יוּמָת'.

Abaye explains that the verse is applied to the passive partner by the principle that if it is not needed for the active partner, apply it to the passive partner, and the passive partner is expressed in the language of the active partner to teach that both receive punishment and prohibition.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu and Abaye on the passive partner's liability and the combined case
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu and Abaye on the passive partner's liability and the combined case
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu rules that according to Rabbi Akiva, the passive partner (with a male or animal) is liable for two violations (from the prohibitions against being lain with), while according to Rabbi Yishmael only one (from 'לא יהיה קדש'). Abaye counters that even according to Rabbi Yishmael, the passive partner is liable for two, because the verse 'כל שוכב' extends to the passive partner with both punishment and prohibition. The Gemara concludes that in the combined case of both active and passive acts, according to Rabbi Yishmael one is liable for three violations, and according to Rabbi Akiva for two.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu rules that for a passive partner with both a male and an animal, according to Rabbi Akiva he is liable for two violations (from 'לֹא תִשְׁכַּב' and 'לֹא תִתֵּן שְׁכׇבְתְּךָ'), but according to Rabbi Yishmael only one (from 'לֹא יִהְיֶה קָדֵשׁ').

Abaye objects that even according to Rabbi Yishmael, the passive partner is liable for two violations, because the verse 'כׇּל שֹׁכֵב עִם בְּהֵמָה מוֹת יוּמָת' extends to the passive partner with both punishment and prohibition.

The Gemara concludes that in the combined case of both active and passive acts with a male and an animal, according to Rabbi Yishmael one is liable for three violations, and according to Rabbi Akiva for two.

items.text: The age of majority for the passive partner in male intercourse
items.text_en: The age of majority for the passive partner in male intercourse
items.desc_en: A baraita states that for a male (passive partner), a minor is not treated like an adult, but for an animal, a young one is treated like an adult. Rav and Shmuel debate the age threshold: Rav says a boy under nine is not considered, while Shmuel says under three. Their dispute is based on whether the passive partner's liability depends on the active partner's capability (Rav) or on the verse 'משכבי אשה' (Shmuel). A supporting baraita for Rav is cited.

sub.desc_en: A baraita establishes that for male intercourse, a minor passive partner is not treated like an adult, but for bestiality, a young animal is treated like an adult.
The gemara asks what the baraita means by 'did not treat a minor like an adult'.
Rav explains that a boy under nine years old is not considered liable as a passive partner.
Shmuel explains that a boy under three years old is not considered liable as a passive partner.
The gemara asks what underlies the dispute between Rav and Shmuel.
Rav holds that the passive partner's liability mirrors the active partner's capability: only if the active partner is capable of intercourse (age nine) is the passive partner liable.
Shmuel derives the age from the verse 'משכבי אשה' (the two modes of lying with a woman), implying a minimum age of three, corresponding to the age at which a girl can engage in intercourse.
A baraita is cited in support of Rav, stating that a male of nine years and one day is the threshold.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who engages in bestiality, whether in the usual or unusual manner, and a woman who brings an animal upon herself, is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who engages in bestiality, whether in the usual or unusual manner, and a woman who brings an animal upon herself, is liable.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on the number of forbidden acts
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on the number of forbidden acts
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda teaches that for a woman there are two modes of intercourse (usual and unusual), but for an animal only one. Rav Pappa objects, arguing that for a woman, only the usual manner should be liable, while for an animal, every orifice should be liable.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda teaches that for a woman there are two modes of intercourse (usual and unusual), but for an animal only one.
Rav Pappa objects, arguing that for a woman only the usual manner should be liable, while for an animal every orifice should be liable.

items.text: Baraita supporting the Mishnah
items.text_en: Baraita supporting the Mishnah
items.desc_en: A Baraita is cited that contradicts both opinions, stating that a male nine years and one day old who engages in bestiality, and a woman who brings an animal upon herself, are liable in both usual and unusual manners.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that contradicts both Rav Nachman and Rav Pappa, stating that a nine-year-old boy or a woman with an animal is liable in both usual and unusual manners.

items.text: Discussion on העראה with a male and an animal
items.text_en: Discussion on העראה with a male and an animal
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rava about the liability for העראה (initial penetration) with a male. Rava responds that the verse already addresses it. Ravina then asks about העראה with an animal. Rava explains that the verse about העראה with a sister is superfluous and can be applied to an animal. The Gemara questions why the verse is placed among כרת punishments rather than court-imposed death penalties, and answers that since the entire verse is for exposition, it is written there.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rava about the liability for העראה (initial penetration) with a male.
Rava responds that the verse already addresses העראה with a male through the term 'משכבי אשה' (the two modes of lying with a woman).
Ravina then asks about the liability for העראה (initial penetration) with an animal.
Rava explains that the superfluous verse about העראה with a sister can be applied to an animal.
The Gemara questions why the verse about העראה with an animal is placed among כרת (divine excision) punishments rather than court-imposed death penalties.
The Gemara answers that since the entire verse is for exposition, it is written there.

items.text: Question about העראה with oneself
items.text_en: Question about העראה with oneself
items.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami asks Rav Sheshet about the liability for העראה with oneself. Rav Sheshet rebukes him. Rav Ashi explains that such a case is impossible in practice, but if one were to find it, it would involve a corpse. The liability depends on whether one holds that intercourse with a corpse is punishable.

sub.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami asks Rav Sheshet about the liability for העראה (intromission) performed with oneself.
Rav Sheshet rebukes Rav Achadvoi bar Ami, saying 'You have silenced me!' (implying the question is absurd or unanswerable).

Rav Ashi explains that the case is practically impossible, but if found, it would involve a corpse; liability depends on whether one holds that intercourse with a corpse is punishable, and if so, the person would be liable twice — once for the active and once for the passive role.

items.text: Question about a gentile engaging in bestiality
items.text_en: Question about a gentile engaging in bestiality
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a gentile who engages in bestiality is liable. The question is whether the requirement of both a stumbling block and disgrace is needed, or just a stumbling block. Rav Sheshet cites a verse about trees to argue that even without disgrace, liability exists. The Gemara objects that if so, a gentile who worships his animal should also be liable, but that is not the case. Abaye and Rava offer different explanations for why the animal is killed, and the Gemara addresses further objections.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rav Sheshet whether a gentile who engages in bestiality is liable, questioning if both a stumbling block (תקלה) and disgrace (קלון) are required or just a stumbling block.

Rav Sheshet cites a baraita about trees that are destroyed because they caused a stumbling block, arguing by קל וחומר (a fortiori) that a gentile who causes a stumbling block through bestiality is liable even without disgrace.
The Gemara objects that if the reasoning applies, a gentile who worships his animal should also be liable and the animal killed, but that is not the case for an Israelite who worships his animal.
Abaye explains that the animal killed for bestiality has great disgrace (קלונו מרובה), while the animal worshipped has little disgrace (קלונו מועט), so only the former is killed.
The Gemara objects that trees have no disgrace at all, yet the Torah commands their destruction, undermining Abaye's distinction.
The Gemara rejects the objection by noting that the discussion is about living creatures, regarding which the Torah is merciful, so the disgrace factor matters for them but not for trees.
Rava offers an alternative explanation: the animal is killed because it benefited from the transgression (נהנית מעבירה).
The Gemara objects that trees do not benefit from transgression, yet the Torah commands their destruction, undermining Rava's reasoning.
The Gemara again rejects the objection by noting the distinction between living creatures and trees regarding divine mercy.
The Gemara brings a supporting baraita that gives another reason for killing the animal: to prevent public shame, implying that disgrace is indeed a factor.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and two interpretations
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and two interpretations
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction between the first clause (תקלה without קלון) and the latter clause (תקלה and קלון). It first suggests the latter clause involves a gentile with a beast, then reinterprets that the first clause teaches liability even for קלון without תקלה, exemplified by an Israelite who unknowingly has intercourse with a beast.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction between the first clause (תקלה without קלון) and the latter clause (תקלה and קלון), and initially suggests the latter clause involves a gentile with a beast.
The Gemara reinterprets that the first clause teaches liability even for קלון without תקלה, exemplified by an Israelite who unknowingly has intercourse with a beast, as per Rav Hamnuna's query.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's dilemma
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's dilemma
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna raises a dilemma: for an Israelite who unknowingly has intercourse with a beast, do we require both תקלה and קלון (and here there is only קלון), or is קלון alone sufficient?

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna raises a dilemma: for an Israelite who unknowingly has intercourse with a beast, do we require both תקלה (stumbling) and קלון (disgrace), or is קלון alone sufficient?

items.text: Rav Yosef's attempted proof from a minor girl
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's attempted proof from a minor girl
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a Mishnah about a three-year-old girl: if one of the forbidden relations (including a beast) has intercourse with her, they are executed on her account, yet she is exempt. The Gemara notes that here there is קלון but no תקלה (since she is a minor), yet the Mishnah says they are executed, implying קלון alone suffices.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef introduces a Mishnah about a three-year-old girl who can be betrothed by intercourse, and various halachic consequences.

The Mishnah lists further effects: she renders her partner impure, and if married to a priest she eats תרומה (priestly portion), and if a disqualified person has intercourse with her she is disqualified from the priesthood.
The Mishnah states that if any of the forbidden relations (עריות) have intercourse with her, they are executed on her account, but she is exempt.

The Gemara notes that the Mishnah includes even a beast, and here there is קלון (disgrace) but no תקלה (sinful act) since she is a minor, yet the Mishnah says they are executed, implying קלון alone suffices.

items.text: Rejection: the minor is a willful sinner
items.text_en: Rejection: the minor is a willful sinner
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof: since the minor acted willfully (מזידה), there is also תקלה, but the Torah is merciful toward her; the beast, however, is not spared.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof from the minor girl: since she acted willfully (מזידה), there is also a stumbling block (תקלה), but the Torah is merciful toward her; the beast, however, is not spared.

items.text: Rava's attempted proof from a nine-year-old boy
items.text_en: Rava's attempted proof from a nine-year-old boy
items.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita about a nine-year-old boy: if he has intercourse with a forbidden relation, they are executed on his account, and the beast is stoned. Here there is קלון but no תקלה (since he is a minor), yet the beast is stoned. The Gemara again rejects: since he is willful, there is תקלה, but the Torah is merciful toward him, not the beast.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita about a nine-year-old boy who has intercourse with forbidden relations, including a beast that is stoned on his account, to argue that the beast is stoned even without תקלה (a halachic liability) since the boy is a minor.
The Gemara objects that in this case there is קלון (disgrace) but no תקלה (halachic liability), yet the baraita states the beast is stoned, seemingly supporting Rava's proof.
The Gemara rejects the proof: since the boy acts willfully (מזיד), there is indeed תקלה, but the Torah is merciful toward him (the minor) and not toward the beast, so the beast is stoned.

items.text: Final attempt: the 'דבר אחר' interpretation
items.text_en: Final attempt: the 'דבר אחר' interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a 'דבר אחר' (alternative explanation) that the beast is stoned to prevent gossip. It asks whether this implies the first clause refers to קלון without תקלה (an Israelite who errs). It concludes instead that the first clause refers to תקלה without קלון (a gentile with a beast), as per a query to Rav Sheshet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a 'דבר אחר' (alternative explanation) that the beast is stoned to prevent gossip.
The Gemara asks whether the first clause refers to קלון (disgrace) without תקלה (stumbling), i.e., an Israelite who errs with a beast.
The Gemara rejects this and concludes that the first clause refers to תקלה without קלון (a gentile with a beast), as per a query to Rav Sheshet.

items.text: Opening Mishnah of the next chapter
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah of the next chapter
items.desc_en: The Mishnah begins: 'The blasphemer is not liable until he pronounces the Name.' Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha adds a statement.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the blasphemer is not liable until he explicitly pronounces the Divine Name.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha adds a statement, though the text breaks off before his full words are given.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Procedure for blasphemy witnesses
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Procedure for blasphemy witnesses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes that during the trial witnesses testify using a substitute name (e.g., 'Yosei'), but after the verdict they are asked to state the exact blasphemy, upon which the judges stand and tear their garments without mending.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for blasphemy witnesses: they testify using a substitute name (e.g., 'Yosei'), and after the verdict, the chief witness states the exact blasphemy, the judges stand and tear their garments without mending, and the other witnesses say 'I am like him'.

items.text: Gemara's initial Tanna statement
items.text_en: Gemara's initial Tanna statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tanna who states that the blasphemer must 'bless the Name with the Name' – i.e., utter the Tetragrammaton while cursing.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the blasphemer is liable only when he pronounces the Tetragrammaton with the Tetragrammaton (i.e., curses the Name using the Name itself).

items.text: Derivation of 'נוקב' as cursing and requirement of 'שם בשם'
items.text_en: Derivation of 'נוקב' as cursing and requirement of 'שם בשם'
items.desc_en: Shmuel derives that 'נוקב' means cursing from the verse 'מה אקוב לא קבה אל'. The Gemara rejects alternative interpretations (boring, piercing, specifying) and concludes that the blasphemer must both utter the Name and curse, as implied by 'ויקב... ויקלל'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (that the blasphemer must curse the Name with the Name) derived?
Shmuel answers that the verse 'וְנוֹקֵב שֵׁם... בְּנׇקְבוֹ שֵׁם יוּמָת' implies the requirement of 'שם בשם' (uttering the Name while cursing).
The Gemara supports that 'נוקב' means cursing by citing the verse 'מָה אֶקֹּב לֹא קַבֹּה אֵל' and derives the warning from 'אֱלֹהִים לֹא תְּקַלֵּל'.
The Gemara objects: Perhaps 'נוקב' means boring/piercing, as in 'וַיִּקֹּב חֹר בְּדַלְתּוֹ', with the warning from 'וְאִבַּדְתֶּם אֶת שְׁמָם... לֹא תַעֲשׂוּן כֵּן לַה׳'.
The Gemara rejects the boring interpretation because it lacks the requirement of 'שם בשם' (uttering the Name with the Name).
The Gemara objects: Perhaps 'נוקב' means placing two Names together and cutting them, or pressing a Name against a knife and cutting; these are rejected as not being 'נוקב' in the required sense.
The Gemara objects: Perhaps 'נוקב' means specifying/designating a name, as in 'אֲשֶׁר נִקְּבוּ בְּשֵׁמוֹת', with the warning from 'אֵת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ תִּירָא'.
The Gemara rejects the specifying interpretation because it lacks 'שם בשם' and because the warning would be a positive commandment, which does not count as a warning for a capital offense.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: The verse 'וַיִּקֹּב... וַיְקַלֵּל' teaches that 'נוקב' means cursing.

The Gemara objects: Perhaps both 'נוקב' and 'מקלל' are required? The Gemara rejects this because the verse says 'הוֹצֵא אֶת הַמְקַלֵּל' and not 'הוֹצֵא אֶת הַנֹּקֵב וְהַמְקַלֵּל', proving they are one and the same.

items.text: Noahides and the inclusion of substitutes (כינויים)
items.text_en: Noahides and the inclusion of substitutes (כינויים)
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that 'איש איש' includes Noahides in the prohibition of blasphemy, and they are executed by the sword. Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha explains that the verse also includes substitutes (כינויים) according to Rabbi Meir. The Gemara then discusses the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding substitutes, and the position of Rabbi Meisha that a Noahide is liable even for a substitute.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that 'איש איש' includes Noahides in the prohibition of blasphemy, and they are executed by the sword.
The Gemara questions whether the inclusion of Noahides is derived from here or from another verse.
Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha explains that the baraisa is needed to include substitutes (כינויים) according to Rabbi Meir.
A baraisa cites Rabbi Meir's view that 'איש כי יקלל אלהיו' includes all substitutes (כינויים) for liability.
The Sages distinguish: the unique Name incurs the death penalty, while substitutes incur only a warning (אזהרה).
Rabbi Meisha states that a Noahide who blasphemes with a substitute (כינוי) is liable according to the Rabbis.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meisha's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meisha's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Meisha's reasoning: the verse 'כגר כאזרח' requires a unique Name for an Israelite or convert, but a Noahide is liable even with a substitute.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's use of the verse
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's use of the verse
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir uses 'כגר כאזרח' to teach that a convert and an Israelite are executed by stoning, while a Noahide is executed by the sword.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's use of the verse for the Sages
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha's use of the verse for the Sages
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha, the Sages use 'כגר כאזרח' to require a unique Name for a convert or Israelite, but not for a Noahide.
The Gemara resolves that the repetition 'איש איש' is merely the Torah speaking in human language, not adding a new halacha.

items.text: Baraisa listing the seven Noahide laws
items.text_en: Baraisa listing the seven Noahide laws
items.desc_en: A baraisa enumerates the seven commandments given to the descendants of Noah: courts, blasphemy, idolatry, forbidden relations, bloodshed, theft, and a limb from a living animal.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists the seven Noahide commandments: courts, blasphemy, idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, bloodshed, theft, and a limb from a living animal.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on additional Noahide prohibitions
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on additional Noahide prohibitions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists seven Noahide laws. Rabbi Chananya ben Gamla adds blood from a living animal, Rabbi Chidka adds castration, Rabbi Shimon adds sorcery, Rabbi Yosei derives all sorcery prohibitions from the Torah, and Rabbi Elazar adds kilayim, noting that Noahides are only forbidden in cross-breeding animals and grafting trees.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chananya ben Gamla adds the prohibition of blood from a living animal to the seven Noahide laws.
Rabbi Chidka adds the prohibition of castration.
Rabbi Shimon adds the prohibition of sorcery.
Rabbi Yosei derives all sorcery prohibitions from the Torah, citing the full list of forbidden practices and the principle that punishment follows warning.
Rabbi Elazar adds the prohibition of kilayim, specifying that Noahides are only forbidden in cross-breeding animals and grafting trees, not in wearing or sowing mixtures.

items.text: Derivation of the seven laws from Genesis 2:16
items.text_en: Derivation of the seven laws from Genesis 2:16
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives the seven Noahide laws from the verse 'And the Lord God commanded the man, saying: Of every tree of the garden you may freely eat.' Each word is expounded: 'commanded' refers to laws, 'Lord' to blasphemy, 'God' to idolatry, 'the man' to murder, 'saying' to forbidden sexual relations, 'of every tree of the garden' excludes theft, and 'you may freely eat' excludes a limb from a living animal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these seven Noahide laws derived?
Rabbi Yochanan cites the verse 'And the Lord God commanded the man, saying: Of every tree of the garden you may freely eat' and expounds each word to derive the seven Noahide laws.

items.text: Alternative derivation by Rabbi Yitzchak and prooftexts
items.text_en: Alternative derivation by Rabbi Yitzchak and prooftexts
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak teaches the opposite: 'commanded' refers to idolatry and 'God' to laws. The Gemara questions the source for 'commanded' as idolatry. Rav Chisda and Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi offer two verses: one from Exodus about the golden calf, and one from Hosea about Ephraim following a 'command' (idolatry).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak teaches the opposite interpretation: 'וַיְצַו' refers to idolatry and 'אֱלֹהִים' to laws.
The Gemara accepts the proof for 'אֱלֹהִים' as laws from the verse 'וְנִקְרַב בַּעַל הַבַּיִת אֶל הָאֱלֹהִים', but questions the source for 'וַיְצַו' as idolatry.

sub.text: Rav Chisda and Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi's answers
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi's answers
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi offer two prooftexts: one from Exodus about the golden calf ('סָרוּ מַהֵר... אֲשֶׁר צִוִּיתִם') and one from Hosea about Ephraim following a 'command' ('עָשׁוּק אֶפְרַיִם... כִּי הוֹאִיל הָלַךְ אַחֲרֵי צָו').

items.text: Dispute on whether a Noahide is liable for making an idol without bowing
items.text_en: Dispute on whether a Noahide is liable for making an idol without bowing
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the practical difference between the two prooftexts: according to the one who cites 'they made' (Exodus), a Noahide is liable from the moment of making an idol; according to the one who cites 'he went after' (Hosea), he is liable only after he goes after it and worships it. Rava objects, citing a baraita that a Noahide is only liable for acts for which a Jewish court would execute, excluding making without bowing. Rav Papa clarifies that the baraita excludes hugging and kissing, but only when done in an atypical manner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the two prooftexts for the prohibition of idolatry for Noahides.

The Gemara explains the difference: according to the one who cites 'עָשׂוּ' (they made), a Noahide is liable from the moment of making an idol; according to the one who cites 'כִּי הוֹאִיל הָלַךְ' (he went after), he is liable only after he goes after it and worships it.
Rava objects, citing a baraita that a Noahide is only liable for acts for which a Jewish court would execute, excluding making without bowing.
Rav Papa clarifies that the baraita excludes hugging and kissing, not making without bowing.
The Gemara objects that hugging and kissing in the typical manner of worship would be capital, and resolves that the baraita excludes only atypical forms of worship.

items.text: Were Noahides commanded about courts?
items.text_en: Were Noahides commanded about courts?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Noahides were commanded about laws (dinim), citing a baraita that at Marah, Israel received ten commandments: the seven Noahide laws plus laws, Shabbat, and honoring parents. Rav Nachman says the additional 'laws' refers to testimony, witnesses, and warning. Rava says it refers to fines. Rav Acha bar Yaakov says it refers to establishing courts in every district and city. The Gemara then cites a baraita that Noahides were indeed commanded to establish courts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Noahides were commanded about laws (dinim), citing a baraita that at Marah Israel received ten commandments including dinim.
The baraita explains that the additional commandments at Marah are derived from verses: dinim from 'חוק ומשפט', and Shabbat and honoring parents from 'כאשר צוך'.
Rav Nachman says the additional dinim at Marah were only needed for testimony, witnesses, and warning (התראה).
The Gemara objects: if so, why does the baraita say 'they added dinim' — these are procedural details, not new laws.
Rava says the additional dinim at Marah were needed for fines (קנסות).
The Gemara objects: still, the baraita should have said 'they added in dinim' (בדינין), not 'they added dinim' (דינין).
Rav Acha bar Yaakov says the additional dinim at Marah were for establishing courts in every district and city.
The Gemara questions: but weren't Noahides already commanded about courts?
A baraita states that just as Israel were commanded to establish courts in every district and city, so too were Noahides commanded.

items.text: The Tanna of the school of Menashe and the list of seven
items.text_en: The Tanna of the school of Menashe and the list of seven
items.desc_en: Rava concludes that the baraita follows the Tanna of the school of Menashe, who lists the seven Noahide laws differently: idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, murder, theft, limb from a living animal, castration, and kilayim. The Gemara then discusses Rabbi Yehuda's view that Adam was only commanded about idolatry, and the view of 'yesh omrim' that includes laws. It concludes by noting that the school of Menashe does not derive laws from 'vayetzav' but from separate verses.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by identifying the baraita as following the school of Menashe, which replaces judgment and blessing God's name with castration and diverse kinds.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Menashe
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Menashe
sub.desc_en: The school of Menashe lists the seven Noahide laws: idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, murder, theft, limb from a living animal, castration, and diverse kinds.
Rabbi Yehuda states that Adam was commanded only about idolatry, citing the verse 'וַיְצַו ה׳ אֱלֹהִים עַל הָאָדָם'.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira adds that Adam was also commanded concerning blessing the name of God.
Some say that Adam was also commanded concerning establishing courts of judgment.
The Gemara asks whose opinion is followed by Rav Yehuda citing Rav, who interprets the verse as including prohibitions against cursing, exchanging God, and fearing Him.
The Gemara answers that it follows the opinion of 'yesh omrim' (some say), who include all three matters.
The Gemara challenges the school of Menashe: if it interprets 'וַיְצַו' homiletically, it should include all laws; if not, from where does it derive its seven laws?

The Gemara answers that the school of Menashe does not interpret 'וַיְצַו' homiletically; each of its seven laws is derived from separate verses, beginning with idolatry and forbidden sexual relations.

items.text: Derivation of the seven Noahide laws from verses
items.text_en: Derivation of the seven Noahide laws from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives each of the seven Noahide laws (idolatry, sexual immorality, murder, robbery, limb from a living animal, castration, and kilayim) from specific biblical verses, with the opposing view explaining each verse differently.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael derives the prohibitions of sexual immorality and idolatry from the verse 'ותשחת הארץ' (the earth was corrupted), citing supporting verses for each.
The Gemara objects that the opposing view interprets the verse as merely describing their natural behavior, not as a prohibition.
The Gemara derives the prohibition of murder from the verse 'שופך דם האדם' (one who sheds human blood), and the opposing view says it merely describes their killing.
Rabbi Levi derives the prohibition of robbery from the verse 'כירק עשב' (as the green herb), distinguishing between wild and garden herbs, and the opposing view says it permits meat.

The Gemara derives the prohibition of eating a limb from a living animal from the verse 'אך בשר בנפשו דמו לא תאכלו' (but flesh with its lifeblood you shall not eat), and the opposing view says it permits creeping things.
The Gemara derives the prohibition of castration from the verse 'שרצו בארץ ורבו בה' (swarm in the earth and multiply), and the opposing view says it is merely a blessing.
The Gemara derives the prohibition of kilayim (mixed species) from the verse 'מהעוף למינהו' (from the bird according to its kind), and the opposing view says it is merely a command.

items.text: Rav Yosef's statement on three capital Noahide laws
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's statement on three capital Noahide laws
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports that the school of Rav holds that a Noahide is executed for only three of the seven laws: sexual immorality, murder, and blasphemy.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports that the school of Rav holds that a Noahide is executed for only three of the seven laws: sexual immorality, murder, and blasphemy.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's challenge to the three-law position
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's challenge to the three-law position
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet challenges Rav Yosef's statement, arguing that if the source for capital punishment is derived from murder, it should apply to all seven laws, and if from the verse 'ish ish', then idolatry should also be included.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet challenges Rav Yosef's statement: granted that capital punishment for murder is derived from the verse 'שופך דם האדם', but from where are the other two laws (גילוי עריות and ברכת השם) derived?

Rav Sheshet objects: if the source for capital punishment is derived from murder by analogy, it should apply to all seven Noahide laws; if it is derived from the verse 'איש איש', then idolatry should also be included, undermining the three-law position.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's revised statement and objection regarding idolatry
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's revised statement and objection regarding idolatry
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet revises the statement to four capital laws, but an objection is raised from a baraita that Noahides are only warned about idolatry, not executed. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that for Noahides, warning itself constitutes capital punishment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet revises the statement of Bei Rav to say that a Noahide is executed for four commandments.
The Gemara objects: is a Noahide executed for idolatry? A baraita states that for idolatry, a Noahide is only warned, not executed.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that for Noahides, the warning itself constitutes their capital punishment.

items.text: Rav Huna and Rav Yehudah's position: all seven are capital
items.text_en: Rav Huna and Rav Yehudah's position: all seven are capital
items.desc_en: Rav Huna, Rav Yehudah, and other students of Rav argue that a Noahide is executed for all seven laws, as the Torah revealed the death penalty for one and it applies to all.

sub.text: Rav Huna, Rav Yehudah, and other students of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Huna, Rav Yehudah, and other students of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Yehudah assert that a Noahide is executed for all seven commandments, since the Torah revealed the death penalty for one and it applies to all.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding robbery as a capital offense
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding robbery as a capital offense
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita that only prohibits robbery for Noahides without stating liability, but the Gemara resolves that the baraita's language of 'forbidden' is used for stylistic consistency, and various Amoraim explain the specific case of robbery that is not fully capital.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Is a Noahide executed for robbery? A baraita lists robbery as forbidden but not as a capital offense, using 'אסור' (forbidden) rather than 'חייב' (liable).
The Gemara answers that the baraita uses 'אסור' (forbidden) in the first clause for stylistic consistency with the second clause, which states 'מותר' (permitted) regarding a Jew robbing a gentile.
The Gemara objects further: In the same baraita, the section on bloodshed uses 'חייב' (liable) for a gentile killing a gentile or a Jew, so why not use 'חייב' for robbery as well?

The Gemara answers that in the bloodshed case, the baraita could not use 'אסור' (forbidden) because a gentile who kills a Jew is not merely forbidden but is subject to the rule of 'לא מעלין ולא מורידין' (do not save him, do not kill him), so 'חייב' was necessary.
The Gemara asks: What is the case of robbery that is analogous to the bloodshed case, where the robbery is not fully capital?
Rav Acha bar Yaakov suggests the case is a worker in a vineyard who eats grapes, but the Gemara rejects this because if it is during work it is permitted, and if not it is outright robbery.
Rav Pappa suggests the case is robbery of less than a פרוטה (small coin), but the Gemara objects that a gentile can forgive the debt, though the momentary distress is real.

sub.text: Rav Acha brei deRav Ika's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Acha brei deRav Ika's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha brei deRav Ika suggests the case is withholding a worker's wages, where a gentile doing so to another gentile or a Jew is forbidden, but a Jew doing so to a gentile is permitted.

items.text: Discussion of yefat to'ar and a case of murder
items.text_en: Discussion of yefat to'ar and a case of murder
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the case of yefat to'ar where a Noahide who designates a maidservant for his slave is executed, and notes that a similar case for murder is taught by Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul regarding a pursuer who could have been stopped by maiming.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the parallel case for יפת תואר (the beautiful captive woman) mentioned in the baraita.

sub.text: Rav Dimi citing Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi citing Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports in the name of Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Chanina that a Noahide who designates a maidservant for his slave and has relations with her is executed for it.
The Gemara notes that a parallel case for murder was not taught in the baraita.
Abaye says that if such a case is taught, it is the teaching of Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul
sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul's ruling that a pursuer who could have been stopped by maiming but was killed instead is liable.

items.text: Opening baraita on Noahide capital punishment
items.text_en: Opening baraita on Noahide capital punishment
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita found by Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha in the aggadic book of the school of Rav, stating that a Noahide is executed by a single judge, on the testimony of a single witness, without warning, based on testimony from a man and not a woman, and even from a relative. In the name of Rabbi Yishmael, they added that a Noahide is also executed for killing a fetus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita found by Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha in the aggadic book of the school of Rav, listing the lenient rules for Noahide capital punishment: single judge, single witness, no warning, testimony from a man not a woman, even a relative, and Rabbi Yishmael adds execution for killing a fetus.

items.text: Scriptural derivation for the leniencies
items.text_en: Scriptural derivation for the leniencies
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains the scriptural source for these leniencies: from the verse 'But your blood of your lives I will demand' (Genesis 9:5), the Gemara derives that a Noahide can be executed by a single judge, without warning, by a single witness, and even by a relative, and testimony from a woman is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the leniencies listed for Noahides.
Rav Yehuda derives from Genesis 9:5 that a Noahide is executed by a single judge, without warning, by a single witness, and even by a relative, and testimony from a woman is invalid.

items.text: Dispute regarding execution for killing a fetus
items.text_en: Dispute regarding execution for killing a fetus
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning for executing a Noahide who kills a fetus, based on the verse 'Whoever sheds the blood of man within man, his blood shall be shed' (Genesis 9:6). The first Tanna is identified as the school of Menashe, who holds that all Noahide executions are by strangulation, and he interprets the phrase 'within man' differently, applying it to the end of the verse to derive strangulation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning for executing a Noahide who kills a fetus.
The Gemara cites the verse 'Whoever sheds the blood of man within man, his blood shall be shed' (Genesis 9:6), interpreting 'man within man' as a fetus in its mother's womb.

The Gemara identifies the first Tanna as the school of Menashe, who holds that all Noahide executions are by strangulation, and explains that he interprets the phrase 'within man' at the end of the verse to derive strangulation.

items.text: Challenge regarding women's obligation in commandments
items.text_en: Challenge regarding women's obligation in commandments
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna challenges the exclusion of women's testimony, citing the verse about Abraham 'For I have known him, that he will command his children and his household after him' (Genesis 18:19), implying women are also commanded. He resolves it himself: 'his children' refers to the court system, and 'his household' to charity.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna challenges the exclusion of women from testimony by citing the verse 'For I have known him, that he will command his children and his household after him' (Genesis 18:19), implying women are also commanded.
Rav Hamnuna resolves his own challenge by interpreting 'his children' as referring to the court system and 'his household' to charity, thus not including women in the command to testify.

items.text: Questions about a female Noahide who kills or commits adultery
items.text_en: Questions about a female Noahide who kills or commits adultery
items.desc_en: Rav Avya Sava asks Rav Pappa: if a female Noahide kills, should she not be executed because the verse says 'from the hand of a man' and not 'from the hand of a woman'? Rav Pappa responds that Rav Yehuda said the verse 'Whoever sheds the blood of man' includes anyone. Similarly, regarding a female Noahide who commits adultery, the verse 'Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother' (Genesis 2:24) implies only a man, but Rav Yehuda explains that the verse 'and they shall become one flesh' (Genesis 2:24) reconnects them, including women.

sub.desc_en: Rav Avya Sava asks Rav Pappa whether a female Noahide who kills should not be executed, since the verse says 'from the hand of a man' and not 'from the hand of a woman'.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's answer citing Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's answer citing Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that Rav Yehuda explained the verse 'Whoever sheds the blood of man' includes anyone, regardless of gender.
Rav Avya Sava asks whether a female Noahide who commits adultery should not be executed, since the verse says 'Therefore a man shall leave' and not a woman.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's answer citing Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's answer citing Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that Rav Yehuda explained the verse 'and they shall become one flesh' reconnects them, including women in the prohibition.

items.text: Derivation that Noahides are warned against forbidden relations
items.text_en: Derivation that Noahides are warned against forbidden relations
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that the repetition of 'ish' (man) in Leviticus 18:6 ('Ish Ish') comes to include gentiles, who are warned against forbidden relations like Israelites. The Gemara questions whether this is derived from there or from the word 'lemor' in Genesis 18:19, which refers to forbidden relations. It answers: there it refers to their own forbidden relations, while here it refers to forbidden relations with Israelites, as the latter clause states: if a Noahide has relations with an Israelite's forbidden relation, he is judged by Israelite law. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says this is necessary to teach that such a case requires a court, witnesses, and warning.

sub.desc_en: The Sages taught a baraita that the repetition of 'איש' (man) in Leviticus 18:6 comes to include gentiles, who are warned against forbidden relations like Israelites.
The Gemara questions why this derivation is needed, since the word 'לאמר' (to say) in Genesis 18:19 already teaches about forbidden relations for Noahides.

The Gemara answers that the derivation there refers to their own forbidden relations, while here it refers to forbidden relations with Israelites, as the latter clause states that if a Noahide has relations with an Israelite's forbidden relation, he is judged by Israelite law.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that this derivation is necessary to teach that such a case requires a court, witnesses, and warning.

items.text: Refinement: the case of a betrothed maiden and a woman entered into marriage but not yet intimate
items.text_en: Refinement: the case of a betrothed maiden and a woman entered into marriage but not yet intimate
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that this would detract from the Noahide's leniencies. Rav Yochanan explains that the necessity is only for the case of a betrothed maiden (na'arah hame'orasah), which for Noahides does not exist, so we judge them by our law. The Gemara questions whether a married woman is judged by Noahide law, citing a baraita that a Noahide who has relations with a betrothed maiden is executed by stoning, but with a married woman by strangulation, whereas Noahide law would be decapitation. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that 'married woman' here refers to one who entered the wedding canopy but was not yet intimate, which for Noahides does not exist, so we judge them by our law. This is supported by a teaching of Rabbi Chanina.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the previous explanation would detract from the Noahide's leniencies.
Rav Yochanan explains that the necessity is only for the case of a betrothed maiden (נערה המאורסה), which for Noahides does not exist, so we judge them by our law.

The Gemara questions whether a married woman is judged by Noahide law, citing a baraita that a Noahide who has relations with a betrothed maiden is executed by stoning, but with a married woman by strangulation, whereas Noahide law would be decapitation.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that 'married woman' here refers to one who entered the wedding canopy but was not yet intimate, which for Noahides does not exist, so we judge them by our law.
This is supported by a teaching of Rabbi Chanina that a woman who has been intimate with her husband is subject to Noahide law, but one who entered the wedding canopy without intimacy is not.

items.text: Baraita on Rabbi Meir's and the Sages' dispute, and the limitation to betrothed maiden
items.text_en: Baraita on Rabbi Meir's and the Sages' dispute, and the limitation to betrothed maiden
