items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav Yochanan: Rabbi Meir says a Noahide is warned about any forbidden relation for which an Israelite court executes, but the Sages say there are many forbidden relations for which an Israelite court does not execute, yet a Noahide is warned. The baraita concludes: if a Noahide has relations with an Israelite's forbidden relation, he is judged by Israelite law; if with a Noahide's forbidden relation, by Noahide law; and we only have the case of a betrothed maiden. The Gemara questions why a woman who entered the canopy but was not intimate is not included, and answers that this Tanna is from the school of Menashe, who holds all Noahide executions are by strangulation, so both cases would be strangulation. The Gemara then questions Rabbi Meir's position, citing a baraita about a convert.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited supporting Rabbi Yochanan: Rabbi Meir says a Noahide is warned about any forbidden relation for which an Israelite court executes, while the Sages say there are many such relations for which the Israelite court does not execute yet the Noahide is warned.

The baraita continues: if a Noahide has relations with an Israelite's forbidden relation, he is judged by Israelite law; if with a Noahide's forbidden relation, by Noahide law; and we only have the case of a betrothed maiden.
The Gemara asks why a woman who entered the canopy but was not intimate is not included in the baraita's list.
The Gemara answers that this Tanna is from the school of Menashe, who holds all Noahide executions are by strangulation, so both cases would be strangulation and thus not distinct.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Meir's position, citing a baraita about a convert that appears to contradict it.

items.text: Laws of a convert's forbidden marriages
items.text_en: Laws of a convert's forbidden marriages
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a convert has maternal but not paternal lineage. It details which relatives he must divorce and which he may keep, with a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages. It also permits marriage to certain relatives and addresses marrying a woman and her daughter.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a convert has maternal lineage but not paternal lineage.
The Mishnah explains the rule: a convert must divorce a maternal sister but may keep a paternal sister.
The Mishnah continues: a convert must divorce a paternal aunt from the mother's side but may keep one from the father's side.
The Mishnah rules: a convert must divorce a maternal aunt from the mother's side, and records the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding a maternal aunt from the father's side.
Rabbi Meir's principle: any forbidden relation due to maternal lineage must be divorced, but due to paternal lineage may be kept.
The Mishnah lists relatives a convert is permitted to marry, including his brother's wife and father's brother's wife, and notes that this includes his father's wife.
The Mishnah rules: if a convert married a woman and her daughter, he must divorce one and may keep the other, but may not marry them לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
The Mishnah records a dispute: if his wife died, some say he is permitted to his mother-in-law, and some say he is forbidden.

items.text: Rav Yehuda resolves the contradiction
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda resolves the contradiction
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that the two conflicting opinions about a convert's marriage to his mother-in-law are both from Rabbi Meir, but one follows Rabbi Eliezer's view and the other follows Rabbi Akiva's view.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda resolves the apparent contradiction by attributing one opinion to Rabbi Meir following Rabbi Eliezer's view and the other to Rabbi Meir following Rabbi Akiva's view.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva interpret the verse
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva interpret the verse
items.desc_en: A baraita cites the verse 'Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother' and presents the interpretations of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Eliezer interprets 'father' as his father's sister and 'mother' as his mother's sister. Rabbi Akiva interprets 'father' as his father's wife and 'mother' as his actual mother. The verse also excludes homosexual relations, adultery, and bestiality.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'עַל כֵּן יַעֲזׇב אִישׁ אֶת אָבִיו וְאֶת אִמּוֹ' and presents Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation (father = father's sister, mother = mother's sister) and Rabbi Akiva's interpretation (father = father's wife, mother = actual mother).

The baraita continues to derive from the verse the exclusion of homosexual relations (וְדָבַק – not with a male), adultery (בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ – not with another's wife), and bestiality (וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד – excludes animals that do not become one flesh).

items.text: Gemara analyzes Rabbi Eliezer's and Rabbi Akiva's interpretations
items.text_en: Gemara analyzes Rabbi Eliezer's and Rabbi Akiva's interpretations
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Eliezer interprets 'father' as his father's sister rather than his actual father or his father's wife, and similarly for 'mother'. It explains that each interpretation is derived by excluding other possibilities based on the other parts of the verse. The same analysis is applied to Rabbi Akiva's interpretation, where 'father' refers to his father's wife after death, and 'mother' refers to his mother from rape.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Eliezer's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Eliezer's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation that 'his father' in the verse refers to his father's sister.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Eliezer does not interpret 'his father' as his actual father.
The Gemara answers that the verse already excludes a male relative through the phrase 'וְדָבַק' (and cleaves), which excludes a male.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Eliezer does not interpret 'his father' as his father's wife.
The Gemara answers that the verse already excludes another man's wife through the phrase 'בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ' (with his wife).
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Eliezer does not interpret 'his father' as his father's wife after the father's death.

The Gemara answers that 'his father' must be analogous to 'his mother': just as 'his mother' is not a marital relationship (but a blood relative), so too 'his father' must be a non-marital relationship, i.e., his father's sister.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Eliezer's position on mother
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Eliezer's position on mother
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Eliezer's interpretation that 'his mother' refers to his mother's sister.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Eliezer does not interpret 'his mother' as his actual mother.
The Gemara answers that the verse already excludes another man's wife through the phrase 'בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ'.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Eliezer does not interpret 'his mother' as his mother after her death.

The Gemara answers that 'his mother' must be analogous to 'his father': just as 'his father' is not a literal parent (but a relative), so too 'his mother' is not a literal parent, i.e., his mother's sister.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Akiva's interpretation that 'his father' refers to his father's wife.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Akiva does not interpret 'his father' as his actual father.
The Gemara answers that the verse already excludes a male relative through 'וְדָבַק'.
The Gemara objects that the same reasoning would exclude his father's wife, since she is another man's wife.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Akiva refers to his father's wife after the father's death, when she is no longer another man's wife.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Akiva's position on mother
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Akiva's position on mother
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Akiva's interpretation that 'his mother' refers to his actual mother.
The Gemara objects that his mother is also another man's wife, so the same exclusion should apply.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Akiva refers to his mother from rape, who was never married to his father, so she is not another man's wife.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to explain the fundamental disagreement between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva regarding the interpretation of the verse, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the fundamental point of dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva, but the text cuts off before the answer.

items.text: Clarifying the source for Rabbi Akiva's position
items.text_en: Clarifying the source for Rabbi Akiva's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva's view that a Noahide is forbidden to marry his father's sister is derived from the term 'ערוות אביו', which excludes a sister who is only 'שאר אביו'. The argument is that the term 'ערוות אביו' must refer to a relationship that mirrors the mother, which is only found with a sister.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the term 'ערוות אביו' must mirror the mother, which is only found with a sister.
Rabbi Akiva prefers to interpret 'ערוות אביו' as referring to the father's wife, excluding the father's sister who is called 'שאר אביו' and not 'ערוות אביו'.

items.text: Proof from Amram and Yocheved
items.text_en: Proof from Amram and Yocheved
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that a Noahide is permitted to marry his aunt from the father's side by citing the verse that Amram married Yocheved, his aunt. It suggests that 'דודתו' means from the mother, but the Gemara rejects this, saying it means from the father.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that a Noahide may marry his paternal aunt by citing the verse that Amram married Yocheved, his aunt, and asks whether 'דודתו' (his aunt) refers to the mother's side.
The Gemara rejects the proof, stating that 'דודתו' (his aunt) in the verse refers to the father's side, not the mother's.

items.text: Proof from Abraham and Sarah
items.text_en: Proof from Abraham and Sarah
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from Abraham's statement about Sarah, 'בת אבי היא אך לא בת אמי', implying that a daughter from the mother is forbidden. However, the Gemara clarifies that Sarah was actually Abraham's niece, not his sister, and the statement was about a familial connection from the father, not the mother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from Abraham's statement about Sarah, 'בת אבי היא אך לא בת אמי', implying that a daughter from the mother is forbidden.
The Gemara clarifies that Sarah was actually Abraham's niece, not his sister, and the statement was about a familial connection from the father, not the mother.

items.text: Proof from Adam not marrying his daughter
items.text_en: Proof from Adam not marrying his daughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a tradition that Adam did not marry his daughter so that Cain could marry his sister, implying that otherwise it would be forbidden. The Gemara responds that once permitted, it is entirely permitted, and the reason was for the sake of building the world.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a tradition that Adam did not marry his daughter, implying that if not for the reason of building the world, it would be forbidden for a gentile to marry his daughter.
The Gemara responds that once a relationship is permitted (as it was for Adam's children), it is entirely permitted, and the reason for Adam's restraint was only for the sake of building the world.

items.text: Rav Huna's dispute on a non-Jew marrying his daughter
items.text_en: Rav Huna's dispute on a non-Jew marrying his daughter
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that a non-Jew is permitted to marry his daughter, citing the reason Adam did not marry his daughter was for the sake of building the world. An alternative version says Rav Huna ruled it is forbidden, but the Gemara concludes the reason was still for the sake of building the world.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a non-Jew is permitted to marry his daughter, explaining that Adam did not marry his daughter only because Cain needed a wife, based on the verse 'עוֹלָם חֶסֶד יִבָּנֶה' (the world is built on kindness).

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Huna's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Huna's statement
sub.desc_en: An alternative version reports that Rav Huna ruled a non-Jew is forbidden to marry his daughter, but the Gemara concludes the reason was still for the sake of building the world through Cain's marriage.

items.text: Rav Chisda on a Canaanite slave
items.text_en: Rav Chisda on a Canaanite slave
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that a Canaanite slave is permitted to marry his mother and daughter because he has left the category of non-Jew but not entered the category of Jew.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that a Canaanite slave is permitted to marry his mother and daughter because he has left the category of non-Jew but not entered the category of Jew.

items.text: A Noahide who designates a maidservant for his slave
items.text_en: A Noahide who designates a maidservant for his slave
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Chanina rules that a Noahide who designates a maidservant for his slave and then has relations with her is executed. Rav Nachman defines when she becomes designated (when called 'רביתא דפלניא'), and Rav Huna defines when she becomes permitted (when she lets her hair down in public).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina rules that a Noahide who designates a maidservant for his slave and then has relations with her is executed.
The Gemara asks from when does the maidservant become designated as the slave's wife.
Rav Nachman answers that she is designated from the time people call her 'the maidservant of so-and-so'.
The Gemara asks from when is she permitted to others (i.e., when does the designation end).
Rav Huna answers that she becomes permitted when she lets her hair down in public, indicating she is no longer designated.

items.text: A Noahide who has unnatural relations with his wife
items.text_en: A Noahide who has unnatural relations with his wife
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Chanina rules that a Noahide who has unnatural relations with his wife is liable, based on the verse 'ודבק' excluding unnatural relations. Rava objects, questioning if a Noahide can be liable where a Jew is not. Rava then clarifies that a Noahide who has unnatural relations with another's wife is exempt, as the verse excludes both 'באשתו' and 'ודבק'.

sub.desc_en: רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) quoting רבי חנינא (Rabbi Chanina) rules that a בן נח (Noahide) who has unnatural relations with his wife is liable, based on the verse 'ודבק' (and shall cleave) which excludes unnatural relations.
רבא (Rava) objects: Is there any action for which a Jew is not liable but a gentile is liable?
רבא (Rava) clarifies: A בן נח (Noahide) who has unnatural relations with another's wife is exempt, as the verse excludes both 'באשתו' (with his wife) and 'ודבק' (and shall cleave).

items.text: A non-Jew who strikes a Jew
items.text_en: A non-Jew who strikes a Jew
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina rules that a non-Jew who strikes a Jew is liable to death, citing Moses killing the Egyptian. He further states that slapping a Jew is like slapping the Divine Presence, citing the verse 'מוקש אדם ילע קודש'.

sub.desc_en: רבי חנינא (Rabbi Chanina) rules that a non-Jew who strikes a Jew is liable to death, citing the verse about Moses striking the Egyptian.
רבי חנינא (Rabbi Chanina) adds that slapping a Jew is like slapping the Divine Presence, citing the verse 'מוקש אדם ילע קודש'.

items.text: One who raises a hand against another
items.text_en: One who raises a hand against another
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that one who raises a hand against another, even without striking, is called wicked, citing the verse 'למה תכה רעך'. Ze'iri quoting Rabbi Chanina says he is called a sinner. Rav Huna says his hand should be cut off, and he himself cut off a hand. Rabbi Elazar says he has no remedy but burial.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that one who raises a hand against another, even without striking, is called wicked, citing the verse 'למה תכה רעך'.
Ze'iri quoting Rabbi Chanina adds that such a person is called a sinner, citing the verse 'ואם לא לקחתי בחזקה' and the continuation 'ותהי חטאת הנערים גדולה מאד'.
Rav Huna says his hand should be cut off, citing the verse 'וזרוע רמה תשבר', and he himself cut off a hand.
Rabbi Elazar says such a person has no remedy but burial, citing the verse 'ואיש זרוע לו הארץ'.

items.text: Land given to the strong and working the land
items.text_en: Land given to the strong and working the land
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says land was only given to those with strong arms, citing the verse 'ואיש זרוע לו הארץ'. Reish Lakish interprets the verse 'עובד אדמתו ישבע לחם' to mean that if one makes himself a slave to the land, he will be satisfied with bread.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that land was only given to those with strong arms, citing the verse 'וְאִישׁ זְרוֹעַ לוֹ הָאָרֶץ' (a man of arm has the land).

Reish Lakish interprets the verse 'עֹבֵד אַדְמָתוֹ יִשְׂבַּע לָחֶם' (one who works his land will be satisfied with bread) to mean that if one makes himself a slave to the land, he will be satisfied with bread, and if not, he will not be satisfied.

items.text: A non-Jew who observes the Sabbath
items.text_en: A non-Jew who observes the Sabbath
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish rules that a non-Jew who observes the Sabbath is liable to death, citing the verse 'ויום ולילה לא ישבתו'. Ravina adds that this applies even to observing a weekday as the Sabbath. The Gemara asks why this is not counted among the seven Noahide laws, and answers that the list counts prohibitions, not positive commands.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish rules that a non-Jew who observes the Sabbath is liable to death, citing the verse 'ויום ולילה לא ישבתו' and the principle that their warning is their death sentence.
Ravina adds that the prohibition applies even to observing a weekday as the Sabbath.
The Gemara asks why Sabbath observance is not counted among the seven Noahide laws.
The Gemara answers that the list counts only prohibitions (שב ואל תעשה), not positive commands (קום עשה).

items.text: Gemara's question on including dinim among Noahide commands
items.text_en: Gemara's question on including dinim among Noahide commands
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah counts 'dinim' (courts) among the seven Noahide laws, since dinim is a positive command and would seem to violate the list containing only prohibitions or a mix. It notes that dinim is a positive command whose neglect involves sitting idle ('kum aseh ve-shev al ta'aseh').

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how 'dinim' (courts) is counted among the seven Noahide laws, since it is a positive command whose neglect involves sitting idle (קום עשה ושב אל תעשה).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's statement about gentile Torah study and its rebuttal
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's statement about gentile Torah study and its rebuttal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that a gentile who engages in Torah study is liable for death, citing 'Torah tzivah lanu Moshe morashah' – it is an inheritance for us, not them. The Gemara asks why this prohibition isn't counted among the seven Noahide laws, and explains that according to the version 'morashah' (inheritance), the gentile is stealing it; according to 'me'orasah' (betrothed), his punishment is stoning like a betrothed maiden.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that a gentile who engages in Torah study is liable for death, citing the verse 'תּוֹרָה צִוָּה לָנוּ מֹשֶׁה מוֹרָשָׁה' — it is an inheritance for us, not for them.

The Gemara asks why this prohibition is not counted among the seven Noahide laws, and provides two answers: according to the version 'מוֹרָשָׁה' (inheritance), the gentile is stealing it; according to 'מְאוֹרָסָה' (betrothed), his punishment is stoning like a betrothed maiden.

items.text: Objection from Rabbi Meir's baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from Rabbi Meir's baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Meir derives from 'asher ya'aseh otam ha'adam va-chai bahem' that even a gentile who engages in Torah is like a High Priest. The Gemara resolves that this applies only to their seven commandments, not to general Torah study.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Meir derives from 'asher ya'aseh otam ha'adam va-chai bahem' that even a gentile who engages in Torah is like a High Priest.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Meir's statement applies only to the seven Noahide commandments, not to general Torah study.

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel and the Sages on blood from a living animal
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel and the Sages on blood from a living animal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists 'blood from a living animal' as a Noahide prohibition according to Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel. The Gemara explains his reasoning by parsing the verse 'Ach basar be-nafsho damo lo tochelu' as including both a limb from a living animal and blood from a living animal. The Sages counter that the additional phrase 'damo be-nafsho lo tochel' is for permitting creeping things. A parallel verse is analyzed for 'ever min ha-chai' versus blood from a living animal.

sub.desc_en: The baraita reports that Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel adds blood from a living animal to the prohibitions for Noahides.
The gemara asks for the reasoning of Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel, explaining that he reads the verse as containing two prohibitions: meat with its soul and blood with its soul.
The Sages reject this interpretation, explaining that the extra phrase 'דמו' comes only to permit creeping things (which have a different status).

A parallel verse is cited showing that both a limb from a living animal and blood from a living animal are separately prohibited, with 'רקך' introducing the limb and 'כי הדם הוא הנפש' introducing the blood.
The Sages again reject, explaining that this verse refers specifically to blood from a wound through which the soul departs (blood that causes death), not general blood from a living animal.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's principle on commandments repeated at Sinai
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's principle on commandments repeated at Sinai
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why we need both the Noahide command and the restatement at Sinai. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina explains: any commandment stated to Noahides and repeated at Sinai applies to both; one stated to Noahides and not repeated applies only to Israel, not to Noahides. The only example is the sciatic nerve according to Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah needed both a commandment to the Noahides (בני נח) and its repetition at Sinai.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina answers: any mitzvah (מצוה) stated to Noahides and repeated at Sinai applies to both Israel and Noahides.
The Gemara completes the principle: a command given to Noahides but not repeated at Sinai applies only to Israel; the only case is the sciatic nerve (גיד הנשה) according to Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Challenges to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's principle and resolution
items.text_en: Challenges to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's principle and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if a commandment was repeated at Sinai, perhaps it is only for Israel, not Noahides? It proves from idolatry, which was repeated at Sinai and Noahides are punished for it, that it applies to both. The opposite challenge is raised for commandments not repeated: perhaps they apply only to Noahides? The Gemara answers that there is no case permitted to Israel and forbidden to Noahides.

sub.desc_en: Mar states Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's principle: any commandment given to Noahides and repeated at Sinai applies to both groups.
The Gemara objects: on the contrary, since it was repeated at Sinai, it should apply only to Israel, not to Noahides.
The Gemara proves from idolatry, which was repeated at Sinai and Noahides are punished for it, that the principle holds: it applies to both.
The Gemara raises the opposite challenge: for a commandment not repeated at Sinai, the principle says it applies only to Israel, but perhaps it should apply only to Noahides.
The Gemara resolves: there is no case permitted to Israel and forbidden to Noahides, so the principle stands.

items.text: Counterexamples and final restatement of the principle
items.text_en: Counterexamples and final restatement of the principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises two apparent counterexamples to the rule that nothing is permitted to Israel but forbidden to Noahides: the beautiful captive woman (yefat to'ar) and less than a perutah's worth (pachot mi-shaveh perutah). These are dismissed because Noahides are not subject to conquest or forgiveness. The principle is then restated fully by Mar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the beautiful captive woman (יְפַת תּוֹאַר) as a counterexample to the principle that nothing is permitted to Israel but forbidden to Noahides.
The Gemara dismisses the counterexample because Noahides are not subject to the laws of conquest (כיבוש) that permit the captive woman.
The Gemara raises a second counterexample: less than a perutah's worth (פחות משוה פרוטה), which is permitted to Israel but forbidden to Noahides.
The Gemara dismisses this counterexample because Noahides are not subject to the concept of forgiveness (מחילה) that permits less than a perutah's worth.
Mar restates the full principle: any commandment given to Noahides and repeated at Sinai applies to both Israel and Noahides.

items.text: קושיית מילה שנאמרה לבני נח ונשנית בסיני
items.text_en: Circumcision: reaffirmed at Sinai for Israel only
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: circumcision was commanded to Noahides (Abraham) and repeated at Sinai, yet it applies only to Israel, not Noahides. The answer is that the Sinai verse comes to permit circumcision on Shabbat.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מילה נאמרה לבני נח (לאברהם) ונשנית בסיני, ומכאן שהיא נאמרה לישראל ולא לבני נח. התשובה: הפסוק בסיני בא להתיר מילה בשבת, לא לחייב בני נח.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: circumcision was commanded to Noahides (Abraham) and repeated at Sinai, yet it applies only to Israel, not Noahides.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מילה נאמרה לבני נח ונשנית בסיני, ומכאן שהיא לישראל ולא לבני נח.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Sinai verse comes to permit circumcision on Shabbat, not to command Noahides.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: הפסוק בסיני בא להתיר מילה בשבת, לא לחייב בני נח.

items.text: קושיית פריה ורביה שנאמרה לבני נח ונשנית בסיני
items.text_en: Procreation: reaffirmed at Sinai for Israel only
items.desc_en: Another objection: procreation was commanded to Noahides and repeated at Sinai, yet it applies only to Israel. The answer is that the Sinai verse comes to teach that a matter requiring a count needs another count to permit it (i.e., the prohibition of marital relations during the giving of the Torah).
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: פריה ורביה נאמרה לבני נח ונשנית בסיני, ומכאן שהיא לישראל ולא לבני נח. התשובה: הפסוק בא להתיר דבר שנאסר במניין, שצריך מניין אחר להתירו.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects: procreation was commanded to Noahides and repeated at Sinai, yet it applies only to Israel, not to Noahides.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: פריה ורביה נאמרה לבני נח ונשנית בסיני, ומכאן שהיא לישראל ולא לבני נח.

sub.desc_en: The gemara answers: that verse comes to teach that a matter requiring a count (a prohibition) needs another count to permit it (i.e., the prohibition of marital relations during the giving of the Torah).
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: הפסוק בסיני בא ללמד שדבר שנאסר במניין צריך מניין אחר להתירו.

items.text: דחיית הקושיות: כל מצוה שנשנית באה לצורך אחר
items.text_en: Challenge: why not say every repetition is for a specific purpose?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if so, we could say every repeated commandment is for a specific purpose. The answer is that the question is about the warning (azhara) itself being repeated—why is that necessary? The conclusion is that only the prohibition of the sciatic nerve (gid hanasheh) was given to Noahides and not repeated, according to Rabbi Yehuda; the other commandments were repeated for a specific purpose, but otherwise they would not apply to Noahides at all.
items.desc: הגמרא דוחה: אם כל מצוה שנשנית באה לצורך אחר, אז כל מצוה שנאמרה לבני נח ונשנית בסיני אינה חוזרת לבני נח. אלא התשובה היא: האזהרה חוזרת ונשנית, ולמה לי? ומסיקים שאין לנו אלא גיד הנשה בלבד, ואילו האחרות לא נשנו אלא לצורך אחר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: if so, could we not say that every repeated commandment is for a specific purpose?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם כן, בכל מצווה שנשנית בסיני נאמר שהיא משום דבר מסוים?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: the question is about the warning (אזהרה) itself being repeated—why is that necessary?
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: האזהרה שנשנית בסיני מיותרת, ולכן יש צורך בטעם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes: only the prohibition of the sciatic nerve (גיד הנשה) was given to Noahides and not repeated, according to Rabbi Yehuda; the other commandments were repeated for a specific purpose, but otherwise they would not apply to Noahides at all.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסכמת: אין לנו אלא גיד הנשה בלבד, ורק לשיטת רבי יהודה.

items.text: בירור מצוות מילה: לאברהם בלבד ולבני קטורה
items.text_en: Circumcision originally commanded to Abraham and his descendants
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation: circumcision was originally commanded only to Abraham and his seed, not to all Noahides. The Gemara then discusses who is included: Ishmael is excluded by 'for in Isaac shall your seed be called', and Esau is excluded by 'in Isaac' but not all Isaac. Rabbi Oshaya objects: what about the children of Keturah? Rabbi Yosei bar Avin cites a verse to include them.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה איבעית אימא: מילה נאמרה לאברהם בלבד, לא לבני נח אחרים. דוחה: בני ישמעאל ובני עשו פטורים, אך בני קטורה חייבים, כרבי יוסי בר אבין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: circumcision was originally commanded only to Abraham and his seed, not to all Noahides.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציעה תירוץ חלופי: מצוות מילה נאמרה מלכתחילה לאברהם בלבד, ולא לבני נח.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if so, should the children of Ishmael be obligated in circumcision? It answers by citing the verse that Isaac is the designated seed.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם כן, בני ישמעאל היו צריכים להתחייב במילה, והתשובה: הפסוק 'כי ביצחק יקרא לך זרע' מוציא אותם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: should the children of Esau be obligated? It answers by interpreting 'in Isaac' to mean not all of Isaac's descendants.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: בני עשו היו צריכים להתחייב, והתשובה: 'ביצחק' – ולא כל יצחק.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya objects: if so, should the children of Keturah not be obligated? Rabbi Yosei bar Avin cites a verse to include them.
sub.desc: רב אושעיא מקשה: בני קטורה לא יתחייבו? ומביא את דברי רבי יוסי בר אבין ש'את בריתי הפר' מרבה בני קטורה.

items.text: היתר אכילת בשר לאדם הראשון ולבני נח
items.text_en: Permission to eat meat given to Noahides
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: Adam was not permitted to eat meat; only vegetation. When the Noahides came, meat was permitted, as it says 'like the green herb I have given you everything'. One might think that eating a limb from a living animal (eiver min hachai) is permitted, but the verse says 'but flesh with its life, its blood, you shall not eat'. Rav Huna explains that this applies only to animals whose blood is distinct from their flesh, excluding insects.
items.desc: רב יהודה אמר רב: אדם הראשון לא הותר לו בשר לאכילה, רק לבני נח הותר. ומכאן דין אבר מן החי, ויוצאים שרצים שאין דמם חלוק מבשרם.

sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states in the name of Rav that Adam was not permitted to eat meat, only vegetation, and that permission was granted to the Noahides, as the verse says 'like the green herb I have given you everything'.
sub.desc: רב יהודה בשם רב אומר: אדם הראשון לא הותר לו בשר לאכילה.

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises the possibility that one might think eating a limb from a living animal (אבר מן החי) is permitted, but the verse 'but flesh with its life, its blood, you shall not eat' prohibits it.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מוסיף: לבני נח הותר בשר, אך יש איסור אבר מן החי, ויצאו שרצים.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks whether the prohibition of eating a limb from a living animal might also apply to insects, and answers that the word 'אך' (but) excludes them.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מוסיף: לבני נח הותר בשר, אך יש איסור אבר מן החי, ויצאו שרצים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna explains that the verse's phrase 'דמו' (its blood) implies that the prohibition applies only to animals whose blood is distinct from their flesh, excluding insects whose blood is not distinct.
sub.desc: רב הונא מבאר: הפסוק 'דמו' ממעט שרצים שאין דמם חלוק מבשרם.

items.text: קושיות על היתר אכילת בשר: דגים, עופות ונחש
items.text_en: Objections from verses about dominion over fish, birds, and animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises objections from verses that say 'have dominion over the fish of the sea' and 'over the birds of the heavens'—perhaps these were for food? The answers are that they were for labor, not food. Fish and birds can be used for work, as illustrated by questions from Racha and Rabba bar Rav Huna. The verse about 'every creeping thing' comes to include the serpent, as per Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's teaching about the serpent's potential usefulness.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה מפסוקים על דגים ועופות: האם הותרו לאכילה? התשובה: למלאכה. ומביאה ברייתא על נחש ששימש כשליח טוב לפני הקללה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the verse 'וּרְדוּ בִּדְגַת הַיָּם' (have dominion over the fish of the sea), suggesting it might permit eating fish.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מפסוק 'ורדו בדגת הים' שמשמעו לאכילה, בניגוד לדברי רב יהודה שאמר אדם הראשון לא הותר לו בשר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the dominion was for labor, not for eating.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהכוונה ב'ורדו' היא למלאכה, לא לאכילה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether fish are suitable for labor.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם דגים ראויים למלאכה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Racha's question about driving a goat and a fish together to show that fish can be used for work.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם דגים ראויים למלאכה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection from the verse 'וּבְעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם' (and over the birds of the heavens), suggesting it permits eating birds.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהכוונה ב'ורדו' היא למלאכה, לא לאכילה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the dominion over birds was also for labor, not for eating.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מפסוק 'ורדו בדגת הים' שמשמעו לאכילה, בניגוד לדברי רב יהודה שאמר אדם הראשון לא הותר לו בשר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether birds are suitable for labor.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם עופות ראויים למלאכה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabba bar Rav Huna's question about threshing with geese and chickens to show that birds can be used for work.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם עופות ראויים למלאכה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the verse 'וּבְכׇל חַיָּה הָרֹמֶשֶׂת' (and over every creeping thing on the earth).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מפסוק 'ובכל חיה הרומשת על הארץ' שמשמעו לאכילה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that this verse comes to include the serpent, not to permit eating creeping things.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מפסוק 'ובכל חיה הרומשת על הארץ' שמשמעו לאכילה.

sub.text: ברייתא של רבי שמעון בן מנסיא
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya teaches that the serpent, if not cursed, could have been a great servant, bringing precious items and soil for gardening.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא המספרת על נחש ששימש כשליח טוב לפני הקללה, להסביר את הפסוק.

items.text: בשר היורד מן השמים: מחלוקת ודוגמאות
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima: Adam ate meat from heaven
items.desc_en: An objection from Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima: Adam reclined in the Garden of Eden and ministering angels roasted meat and strained wine for him. The Gemara answers that this was meat that descended from heaven. The Gemara then discusses whether impure meat can descend from heaven, citing a story about Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta and lions, and a question from Rabbi Zeira to Rabbi Avahu about a donkey-shaped object descending.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שאדם הראשון אכל בשר היורד מן השמים, ומקשה: האם יש בשר יורד מן השמים? ומביאה מעשה עם רבי שמעון בן חלפתא ואריות, ושאלה על דמות חמור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima, who says that Adam reclined in the Garden of Eden and ministering angels roasted meat and strained wine for him, implying that meat was permitted to Adam.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא המתארת שאדם הראשון אכל בשר ויין שהוגשו לו על ידי מלאכים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the meat in that story was meat that descended from heaven, not the meat of animals.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא המתארת שאדם הראשון אכל בשר ויין שהוגשו לו על ידי מלאכים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether there is such a thing as meat that descends from heaven.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה מעשה עם רבי שמעון בן חלפתא ואריות, המוכיח שיש בשר היורד מן השמים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers yes, citing a story about Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta, who was attacked by lions, and two thighs descended from heaven; the lions ate one, and he brought the other to the study hall, where the Sages ruled that no impure item descends from heaven.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה מעשה עם רבי שמעון בן חלפתא ואריות, המוכיח שיש בשר היורד מן השמים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Avahu what the halakha would be if a donkey-shaped object descended from heaven.
Rabbi Avahu dismisses the question, saying that the Sages already ruled that no impure item descends from heaven.

items.text: דברי רבי שמעון על כישוף
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon: even sorcery is prohibited to Noahides
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon says that sorcery is also prohibited to Noahides. The Gemara begins to explain his reasoning, citing a verse.
items.desc: רבי שמעון אומר: אף על הכישוף. ומבאר את טעמו, אך הקטע נקטע.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that Rabbi Shimon includes sorcery among the prohibitions for Noahides.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה מעשה ברבי שמעון בן חלפתא שאריות נתנו לו מן השמים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Shimon's opinion.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה מעשה ברבי שמעון בן חלפתא שאריות נתנו לו מן השמים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a verse as the basis for Rabbi Shimon's ruling.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה מעשה ברבי שמעון בן חלפתא שאריות נתנו לו מן השמים.

items.text: דין מכשפה וכלאיים
items.text_en: Derivation of death penalty for bestiality from sorcery
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that one who is liable for bestiality is also liable for sorcery, based on a verbal analogy between the verses 'You shall not permit a sorceress to live' and 'Whoever lies with an animal shall be put to death'.
items.desc: הגמרא דורשת את הפסוק 'מכשפה לא תחיה' ומקשרת אותו לפסוק 'כל שוכב עם בהמה מות יומת', כדי ללמוד שכל הנכלל באיסור שוכב עם בהמה נכלל גם באיסור מכשפה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from a verbal analogy that one liable for bestiality is also liable for sorcery.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשרת בין הפסוק 'מכשפה לא תחיה' לפסוק 'כל שוכב עם בהמה מות יומת' כדי ללמוד שכל הנכלל באיסור שוכב עם בהמה נכלל גם באיסור מכשפה.

items.text: דרשת רבי אלעזר על כלאיים
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's extension to kilayim and the derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar extends the death penalty to kilayim (forbidden mixtures). Samuel derives this from the verse 'You shall keep My statutes', interpreting it as statutes already legislated, referring to the prohibition of mixing species. The Gemara distinguishes this from a similar phrase that refers to future statutes.
items.desc: רבי אלעזר מוסיף שגם כלאיים בכלל. שמואל דורש מהפסוק 'את חוקותי תשמרו' חוקים שחקקתי כבר, ומקיש בהמתך בהרבעה לשדך בהרכבה, ומשווה דינם בארץ ובחו"ל. הגמרא דוחה דרשה אפשרית אחרת.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar extends the death penalty to kilayim (forbidden mixtures), and Shmuel derives it from the verse 'אֶת חֻקֹּתַי תִּשְׁמֹרוּ' (My statutes you shall keep), applying the same rules to animal crossbreeding and field sowing.
sub.desc: רבי אלעזר מוסיף שגם כלאיים בכלל דין מיתת בית דין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the same phrase 'חֻקֹּתַי' appears elsewhere, and the Gemara resolves that the verse here means 'keep the statutes from the beginning' (i.e., they were already given at Sinai).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם כן, גם בפסוק 'ושמרתם את חוקותי' נדרוש חוקים שחקקתי כבר?

sub.desc_en: Samuel derives the death penalty from the verse 'אֵת חֻקֹּתַי תִּשְׁמֹרוּ', interpreting it as statutes already legislated, referring to the prohibitions of mixing species.
sub.desc: רבי אלעזר מוסיף שגם כלאיים בכלל דין מיתת בית דין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates the analogy: just as the prohibition of animal crossbreeding applies both in the Land and outside, so too the prohibition of planting mixtures applies everywhere.

The Gemara objects: if the phrase 'keep My statutes' always refers to already-legislated statutes, then the similar phrase 'וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם אֶת חֻקֹּתַי' would also refer to past statutes, which is problematic.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם כן, גם בפסוק 'ושמרתם את חוקותי' נדרוש חוקים שחקקתי כבר?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: there the phrase refers to future statutes, but here 'אֶת חֻקֹּתַי תִּשְׁמֹרוּ' means 'keep the statutes from the beginning' (already legislated).
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: התם 'ושמרתם את חוקותי' משמע חוקים עתידיים, הכא 'את חוקותי תשמרו' משמע חוקים מעיקרא.

items.text: ברייתא של רבי יהושע בן קרחה
items.text_en: Mishnah citation regarding blasphemy
items.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, stating that the blasphemer is not liable until he pronounces the divine name explicitly.
items.desc: מובאת ברייתא של רבי יהושע בן קרחה, אך תוכנה לא מפורט כאן.

sub.text_en: Citation of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha's statement (abbreviated).
sub.desc: רבי יהושע בן קרחה מוסיף דין נוסף, אך דבריו נקטעו.

items.text: דין ברכת השם בארבע אותיות
items.text_en: Rabbi Acha bar Yaakov's statement on the divine name
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Yaakov states that one is only liable for blasphemy if he pronounces the four-letter name, excluding the two-letter name. The Gemara questions this as obvious from the Mishnah, but explains that it teaches that even a four-letter name is considered a name. An alternative version states that it teaches that a four-letter name is also a name, countering the notion that only a longer name is significant.
items.desc: רב אחא בר יעקב אומר שאינו חייב מיתה עד שיברך שם בן ארבע אותיות, להוציא שם בן שתי אותיות. הגמרא מקשה שזה פשוט מהמשנה, ומתרצת שזה בא להשמיענו שאין זה סתם מילה. יש גרסה אחרת ששם בן ארבע אותיות גם הוא שם.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov states that one is liable only for cursing the four-letter name, excluding the two-letter name.
sub.desc: רב אחא בר יעקב קובע שהמקלל אינו חייב מיתה עד שיברך שם בן ארבע אותיות, להוציא שם בן שתי אותיות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why this is not obvious from the Mishnah's use of 'Yosei smite Yosei', suggesting it might be a mere example.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שדין זה פשוט מהמשנה, שהרי שנינו 'יכה יוסי את יוסי'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Acha bar Yaakov teaches that the four-letter name is specifically required, not just an example.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Acha bar Yaakov
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Acha bar Yaakov
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Acha bar Yaakov concludes that the four-letter name is also a name for liability.
The Gemara again questions why this is not obvious, suggesting that only a grand name might be required.
The Gemara explains that Rav Acha bar Yaakov teaches that even the four-letter name is significant, countering the notion that only a longer name matters.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שדין זה פשוט מהמשנה, שהרי שנינו 'יכה יוסי את יוסי'.

items.text: Derivation of standing and tearing garments for blasphemy
items.text_en: Derivation of standing and tearing garments for blasphemy
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that judges must stand when hearing blasphemy from the story of Eglon, and that they must tear their garments from the story of Eliakim and Shebna. Rabbi Abahu derives that the tear is permanent from a verbal analogy with Elisha's tearing of his garments.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that when the judgment is concluded, the judges stand and tear their garments.
The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that the judges must stand?
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ami derives the obligation to stand from the story of Eglon, who stood when Ehud said he had a message from God, using a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument.
The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that the judges must tear their garments?
The Gemara cites the verse about Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah coming to Hezekiah with torn garments after hearing Rabshakeh's blasphemy.
The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that the tear is never fully stitched?

Rabbi Abahu derives the permanence of the tear via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between the tearing in the Rabshakeh story and Elisha's tearing of his garments, where the word 'קְרָעִים' teaches that they remain torn forever.

items.text: Tannaic source on who must tear garments
items.text_en: Tannaic source on who must tear garments
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that both the direct hearer and one who hears from a hearer must tear, but witnesses who already tore when they heard are exempt. The Gemara questions this, but resolves it from the verse that only King Hezekiah tore, not his officers.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that both the direct hearer and the one who hears from a hearer must tear, but witnesses are exempt because they already tore when they first heard, as shown by King Hezekiah's example.
The Gemara questions why witnesses are exempt, since they are hearing the blasphemy again now.
The Gemara resolves from the verse that only King Hezekiah tore his garments upon hearing Rabshakeh's blasphemy, not his officers, proving that those who already heard are exempt.

items.text: Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Chiyya on tearing for a gentile's blasphemy
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Chiyya on tearing for a gentile's blasphemy
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says one does not tear upon hearing blasphemy from a gentile, explaining that Rabshakeh was a Jewish apostate. He also says one only tears for the unique name, not a substitute. Rabbi Chiyya disagrees on both points, arguing that in the present era one does not tear at all, lest the garment become full of tears. The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Chiyya refers to hearing a substitute name from a gentile, implying that originally one would tear.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Samuel rules that one who hears a divine name (אזכרה) from a gentile is not obligated to tear, and explains that Rabshakeh, who caused King Hezekiah to tear, was a Jewish apostate.
Rav Yehuda further cites Samuel that tearing is only required for the unique name (שם המפורש), excluding a substitute name (כינוי).
Rabbi Chiyya disagrees on both points, ruling that in the present era one does not tear upon hearing a divine name, lest the garment become full of tears.
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Chiyya's statement refers to hearing a substitute name (כינוי) from a gentile, not from a Jew or the unique name.
The Gemara infers from Rabbi Chiyya's statement that originally (in Temple times) one would be obligated to tear for a substitute name from a gentile.

items.text: דין 'אף אני כמוהו' בעדות
items.text_en: The second and third witnesses saying 'I too'
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that the second witness saying 'I too' is valid in both monetary and capital cases, but the Sages instituted a higher standard. Here, since it is impossible, the Sages left the Torah law in place. The third witness saying 'I too' follows Rabbi Akiva, who equates three witnesses to two.
items.desc: השני אומר 'אף אני כמוהו'. ריש לקיש אומר שזה כשר בדיני ממונות ונפשות, ומעלה דרבנן היא. כאן שאי אפשר, העמידוהו על דין תורה. הגמרא דוחה שאם פסול, לא היינו הורגים. השלישי אומר 'אף אני כמוהו' וסתמא כרבי עקיבא שמקיש שלושה לשניים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the second witness says 'I too'.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציגה את הדין: השני בעדות אומר 'אף אני כמוהו'.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish infers that saying 'I too' is valid by Torah law in both monetary and capital cases, but the Sages instituted a higher standard; here, since it is impossible to avoid, the Sages left the Torah law in place.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציגה את הדין: השני בעדות אומר 'אף אני כמוהו'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if saying 'I too' were invalid by Torah law, how could we execute a person here just because it is impossible to do otherwise?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם היה פסול, לא היינו הורגים על פיו גם כשאי אפשר אחרת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's rule for the third witness saying 'I too' follows Rabbi Akiva, who equates three witnesses to two.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה שהשלישי האומר 'אף אני כמוהו' סתמא כרבי עקיבא, שמקיש שלושה לשניים.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: עבודות זרה וחיוביהן
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Acts of idolatry
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists acts of idolatry that incur the death penalty (worshiping, sacrificing, burning incense, libation, prostration, accepting as a god, saying 'You are my god') and acts that violate a negative commandment (hugging, kissing, honoring, spreading, washing, anointing, dressing, shoeing, vowing in its name, fulfilling a vow in its name). It also specifies the unique modes of worship for Peor and Merkulis.
items.desc: המשנה מפרטת את העבודות לעבודה זרה: העובד, המזבח, המקטר, המנסך, המשתחווה, המקבלו לאלוה והאומר 'אלי אתה' – חייבים מיתה. לעומת זאת, המגפף, המנשק, המכבד, המרבץ, המרחיץ, הסך, המלביש והמנעיל – עוברים בלא תעשה. הנודר בשמו והמקיים בשמו גם עוברים בלא תעשה. הפוער לבעל פעור והזורק אבן למרקוליס – זו עבודתם.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists acts of idolatry incurring the death penalty and those violating a negative commandment, including unique modes for Peor and Merkulis.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בפירוט העבודות לעבודה זרה המחייבות מיתה, לעומת אלו העוברות בלא תעשה, ומסיימת בדוגמאות לפעור ומרקוליס.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא: מהו 'אחד העובד'?
items.text_en: Gemara's question on 'one who worships'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'one who worships' since it already lists specific acts. Rabbi Yirmeya explains: the Mishnah means one who worships in its usual manner, and then lists specific acts (sacrificing, etc.) even if done not in their usual manner.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מה פירוש 'אחד העובד' במשנה? רבי ירמיה מסביר שהמשנה התכוונה: אחד העובד כדרכה, ואחד המזבח, המקטר, המנסך והמשתחווה – אפילו שלא כדרכה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'one who worships' includes, and Rabbi Yirmeya answers that it includes worshiping in its standard manner, while the listed acts (sacrificing, etc.) are liable even in an atypical manner.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה פירוש הביטוי 'אחד העובד' במשנה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the Mishnah means one who worships in its usual manner, and then lists specific acts (sacrificing, etc.) even if done not in their usual manner.
sub.desc: רבי ירמיה מבאר שהמשנה התכוונה: אחד העובד כדרכה, ואחד המזבח, המקטר, המנסך והמשתחווה – אפילו שלא כדרכה.

items.text: שאלה ותשובה: מדוע לא נמנה זורק?
items.text_en: Why not list 'throwing'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not list 'throwing' as a separate act. Abaye answers that throwing is included in libation, as Scripture says 'I will not pour their libations of blood'.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מדוע לא נמנה 'זורק' במשנה? אביי עונה: זורק הוא כמו מנסך, שנאמר 'בל אסיך נסכיהם מדם'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why 'one who throws a stone' is not listed, and Abaye answers that throwing is included in libation, as the verse says 'I will not pour their libations of blood'.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע לא נמנתה זריקה במשנה כעבודה?

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that 'throwing' is included in 'libation' (מנסך), as Scripture says 'I will not pour their libations of blood'.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע לא נמנתה זריקה במשנה כעבודה?

items.text: ברייתא: מקורות לחיוב מיתה על עבודות זרה
items.text_en: Derivation of the list from Scripture
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of these laws. A baraisa derives from verses that the death penalty applies to sacrificing, burning incense, and libation to idolatry, and also to prostration. It excludes acts like hugging and kissing, limiting capital punishment to 'inner' forms of worship (like sacrifice). The section explains the hermeneutical principles: sacrifice was singled out to teach that only acts similar to it (inner worship) incur death.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא הדורשת פסוקים: 'זובח לאלהים יחרם' – בזובח לעבודה זרה הכתוב מדבר. מכאן למדים על זביחה, קטור וניסוך. השתחוויה נלמדת מפסוק 'וילך ויעבוד אלהים אחרים וישתחו להם'. אזהרה נלמדת מ'כי לא תשתחווה לאל אחר'. עבודות חיצוניות כמו מגפף ומנשק אינן נכללות בחיוב מיתה, כי זביחה יצאה להקיש: מה זביחה מיוחדת שהיא עבודת פנים וחייבים עליה מיתה, אף כל שהיא עבודת פנים – חייבים מיתה. השתחוויה יצאה לדון בעצמה, זביחה יצאה לדון על הכלל כולו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters (the list of capital offenses for idolatry) derived?
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מניין למדים את החיובים הללו?

sub.desc_en: A baraisa is cited: if the verse said only 'one who sacrifices shall be destroyed', it might refer to sacrificing sacred animals outside the Temple; the addition of 'to other gods' specifies idolatry, and the phrase 'only to the Lord alone' includes burning incense and libation.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא הדורשת את הפסוק 'זובח לאלהים יחרם' – בזובח לעבודה זרה הכתוב מדבר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since sacrifice was singled out to be judged by 'inner' forms of worship, from where do we include prostration? It answers by citing the verse 'and he went and served other gods and bowed to them' with the adjacent verse about execution.
sub.desc: הברייתא שואלת: מניין לרבות השתחוויה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have heard the punishment (for prostration), from where is the warning (prohibition)? It answers by citing the verse 'for you shall not bow to another god'.
sub.desc: הברייתא מוסיפה: עונש שמענו, אזהרה מניין? תלמוד לומר 'כי לא תשתחווה לאל אחר'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: one might think to include hugging, kissing, and shoeing (as capital offenses); the verse says 'one who sacrifices' to exclude them.
sub.desc: הברייתא שואלת: יכול ארבה מגפף ומנשק ומנעיל?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: sacrifice was included in the general category (of idolatrous acts) and was singled out to teach that only acts similar to it — 'inner' forms of worship — incur the death penalty; prostration was singled out to be judged by itself, and sacrifice was singled out to teach about the entire category.

items.text: דיון: מדוע לא נאמר שהפסוק מדבר בזובח קדשים בחוץ?
items.text_en: Clarification: Why not refer to offering outside?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraisa's assumption that one might think the verse refers to offering sacrifices outside the Temple, noting that such an act incurs karet, not death. It explains that the verse teaches that if warned, the punishment is death by court; if not warned, it is karet.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע לא נאמר שהפסוק 'זובח לאלהים יחרם' מדבר בזובח קדשים בחוץ, שחייב כרת? התשובה: סלקא דעתך לומר שאם התרו בו – מיתה, ואם לא התרו בו – כרת, ולכן המשנה באה להשמיע שזה לא נכון.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita's initial assumption that the verse might refer to sacrificing sacred animals outside the Temple is problematic, since that is punishable by כרת (excision), not death; the baraita teaches that the verse actually refers to idolatry.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע לא נאמר שהפסוק מדבר בזובח קדשים בחוץ, שחייב כרת?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the verse teaches that if warned, the punishment is death by court; if not warned, it is karet.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: סלקא דעתך לומר שאם התרו בו – מיתה, ואם לא התרו בו – כרת, ולכן המשנה באה להשמיע שזה לא נכון.

items.text: קושיית רבא בר רב חנן: השתחוויה ללמד על הכלל
items.text_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan challenges Abaye, suggesting that prostration should teach about the entire category. The Gemara responds that the verse for sacrifice is needed for its own case, to teach that one is liable even when intending one form of worship while performing another (e.g., slaughtering for the purpose of libation). It cites a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and others on this point.
items.desc: רבא בר רב חנן מקשה על אביי: יש לומר שהשתחוויה יצאה ללמד על הכלל כולו. ומסביר: זביחה באה לגופה, שמחשבים מעבודה לעבודה. כדאיתא: השוחט בהמה לזרוק דמה לעבודה זרה ולהקטיר חלבה לעבודה זרה – רבי יוחנן אמר...

sub.text_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan's challenge to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Chanan challenges Abaye, arguing that prostration (השתחוואה) should teach about the entire category of idolatrous worship, not just itself.
sub.desc: רבא בר רב חנן מקשה על אביי: יש לומר שהשתחוויה יצאה ללמד על הכלל כולו, ולא כפי שאביי סבר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara responds that the verse for sacrifice (זובח) is needed for its own case, to teach liability when one intends one form of worship while performing another (מחשבין מעבודה לעבודה).
sub.desc: אביי משיב: זביחה באה לגופה, ללמד שמחשבים מעבודה לעבודה.

sub.text_en: Citation of a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and others
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and others regarding one who slaughters an animal for idolatry intending to libate its blood and burn its fat, to illustrate the principle of מחשבין מעבודה לעבודה.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא תומכת לדברי אביי, העוסקת בדין השוחט בהמה לזרוק דמה ולהקטיר חלבה לעבודה זרה.

items.text: Opening dispute between R. Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Opening dispute between R. Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: R. Yochanan and Resh Lakish disagree about the status of an animal that bowed to an idol: R. Yochanan forbids it, Resh Lakish permits it.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan forbids an animal that bowed to an idol, while Resh Lakish permits it.

items.text: Gemara questions the need for a verse for each opinion
items.text_en: Gemara questions the need for a verse for each opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Resh Lakish's leniency requires a verse, but R. Yochanan's stringency also needs a verse to impose the death penalty on a person. Rav Papa and Rav Acha bar Rav Ika challenge each side, arguing that the dispute is only about animals, while for a person the verse is needed to establish liability.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Resh Lakish needs a verse for his leniency regarding an animal, while Rabbi Yochanan's stringency is already supported.
Rav Papa objects that Rabbi Yochanan also needs a verse, because his stringency applies only to animals, while for a person the verse is needed to impose the death penalty.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika objects that Resh Lakish also does not need a verse, because his leniency applies only to animals, while for a person the death penalty is already established from the case of bowing to a mountain.

items.text: Analysis of the verse 'Eicha ya'avdu' and its exclusions
items.text_en: Analysis of the verse 'Eicha ya'avdu' and its exclusions
items.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti cites Rava bar Rav Chanan's statement to Abaye: the verse 'Eicha ya'avdu' comes to teach about the general rule of idolatry, and the exclusion of certain acts. The Gemara considers whether it excludes one who exposes himself to Molech or to Mercury, concluding that it teaches that only acts of honor are included, not disgraceful ones.

sub.text: Rav Acha from Difti to Ravina, citing Rava bar Rav Chanan to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Acha from Difti to Ravina, citing Rava bar Rav Chanan to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti asks Ravina: given Rava bar Rav Chanan's statement to Abaye that the verse 'אֵיכָה יַעַבְדוּ' (how they serve) comes to exclude something from the general rule of idolatry, what does it exclude?

The Gemara suggests the verse excludes one who exposes himself to the זובחים (those who sacrifice), but rejects this because the act of prostration (השתחוואה) already teaches that only acts of honor are included, not disgraceful ones.

The Gemara concludes that the verse excludes one who exposes himself to Mercury (מרקוליס), teaching that even though its worship is normally disgraceful, only acts of honor are included in the general rule, not disgraceful ones.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's derivation for sacrificing to Mercury
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's derivation for sacrificing to Mercury
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer derives that one who sacrifices an animal to Mercury is liable from the verse 'v'lo yizb'chu od et zivcheihem lase'irim'. The Gemara explains that if the verse is not needed for the standard mode of worship, it applies to an atypical mode; but for an atypical mode, the verse of bowing already covers it. The resolution is that the case is one of sacrificing to anger the idol.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is Rabbi Eliezer's source for liability of one who sacrifices an animal to Mercury, citing the verse 'וְלֹא יִזְבְּחוּ עוֹד אֶת זִבְחֵיהֶם לַשְּׂעִירִם'.
The Gemara explains: if the verse is not needed for the standard mode of worship (already covered by 'אֵיכָה יַעַבְדוּ'), it applies to an atypical mode.
The Gemara objects: an atypical mode is already derived from the verse about bowing (השתחוואה).
The Gemara resolves: the case is one of sacrificing to anger the idol (להכעיס), which is not covered by the bowing verse.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's oxen and the contradiction about verbal acceptance
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's oxen and the contradiction about verbal acceptance
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna had oxen slaughtered. Rabbah challenges him with a contradiction: a mishnah says only one who 'worships' is liable, not one who merely 'says', yet another mishnah lists 'I will worship' as a liable statement. Rav Hamnuna resolves that the latter refers to one who says 'I accept it upon myself only through worship.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna's oxen were slaughtered, and Rabbah challenges him with a contradiction between two mishnayot.
Rabbah cites the first mishnah that only 'one who worships' is liable, not one who merely speaks, and contrasts it with the second mishnah that lists verbal statements as liable.
Rav Hamnuna resolves the contradiction by explaining that the second mishnah refers to one who says 'I accept it upon myself only through worship.'

items.text: Rav Yosef's Tannaic dispute and retraction
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's Tannaic dispute and retraction
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef initially says the dispute is between Tannaim: R. Meir holds one liable for saying 'come worship me', R. Yehuda exempts. He then retracts, noting that even R. Yehuda requires a verbal statement ('I will worship') for liability. The dispute is actually about a case where one entices himself and others say 'yes': one opinion holds the enticement is effective, the other not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asserts that the dispute is between Tannaim: Rabbi Meir holds one liable for saying 'come worship me', Rabbi Yehuda exempts.

The gemara explains that all agree on actual worship (due to the verse 'לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה לְךָ פֶסֶל'), but they dispute about mere speech: Rabbi Meir holds speech is significant, Rabbi Yehuda holds it is not.
Rav Yosef retracts, noting that even Rabbi Yehuda requires a verbal statement ('I will worship', 'I will go and worship', 'we will go and worship') for liability.
The gemara clarifies that the actual dispute is about a case where one entices himself and others say 'yes': one opinion holds the enticement is effective, the other holds they are merely speaking.

items.text: Distinction between individual and community enticement
items.text_en: Distinction between individual and community enticement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the enticer himself is not liable, and answers that the Mishnah distinguishes between an individual being enticed (who follows without consulting) and a community (who consults and does not follow).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the enticer himself is not liable when he says 'yes' to the enticed person, suggesting he is mocking them.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah distinguishes between an individual being enticed (who follows without consulting) and a community (who consults and does not follow).

items.text: Rav Yosef's proof from verse
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's proof from verse
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites the verse 'lo toveh lo' to prove that if the enticed person does listen, he is liable, implying a distinction between individual and community.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites the verse 'לֹא תֹאבֶה לוֹ וְלֹא תִשְׁמַע אֵלָיו' (do not consent to him and do not listen to him) to prove that if the enticed person does consent and listen, he is liable.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye objects by citing a baraisa that equates individual and community enticement, with differences only in penalty (body vs. money). The Gemara concludes that the distinction is only in that specific matter.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects by citing a baraisa that equates individual and community enticement, with differences only in penalty (body vs. money).
The Gemara resolves that the distinction between individual and community enticement applies only to that specific matter of penalty, but in all other respects they are equivalent.

items.text: Abaye's alternative distinction: self-enticement vs. others' enticement
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative distinction: self-enticement vs. others' enticement
items.desc_en: Abaye reinterprets the Mishnah's distinction as between being enticed by oneself (where one consults) and by others (where one is drawn after them), citing the same verse as proof.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between being enticed by oneself (where one consults) and by others (where one is drawn after them).
Abaye cites the verse 'לֹא תֹאבֶה לוֹ וְלֹא תִשְׁמַע אֵלָיו' (do not consent to him nor listen to him) to prove that if one consents and listens, he is liable, supporting his distinction.

items.text: Rava's distinction: detailed description vs. no description
items.text_en: Rava's distinction: detailed description vs. no description
items.desc_en: Rava distinguishes within enticement by others: if the enticer describes the idol's benefits (eating, drinking, etc.), the enticed is liable; if not, he is exempt. He proves this from the verse about 'close gods' teaching about 'distant gods'.

sub.desc_en: Rava distinguishes within enticement by others: if the enticer describes the idol's benefits (eating, drinking, etc.), the enticed is liable; if not, he is exempt.
Rava proves his distinction from the verse about 'close gods' teaching about 'distant gods', implying a description of their benefits.
The Gemara concludes that the verse indeed implies a description of the idol's benefits, confirming Rava's distinction.

items.text: Rav Ashi and Ravina's alternative explanations
items.text_en: Rav Ashi and Ravina's alternative explanations
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains the Mishnah's case as involving an apostate Israelite, while Ravina says the Mishnah lists both cases (individual and community) without distinction.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah's latter case involves an apostate Israelite, not a distinction between individual and community enticement.
Ravina asserts that the Mishnah lists both cases (individual and community) without any distinction, using the style 'not only this but also that'.

items.text: Debate on worship out of love or fear
items.text_en: Debate on worship out of love or fear
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava debate whether one who worships an idol out of love or fear is liable. Abaye says liable because he performed an act of worship; Rava says exempt unless he accepted it as a god. They bring proofs from a Mishnah, a baraisa about bowing to Haman, and a discussion about a mistaken Kohen Mashiach.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute: Abaye says one who worships an idol out of love or fear is liable (חייב), Rava says he is exempt (פטור).
Abaye argues liability because he performed an act of worship; Rava counters that liability requires accepting the idol as a god (אלוה).
A mnemonic phrase 'a slave will bow to the Mashiach' is inserted to mark the following proofs.
Abaye cites the Mishnah that says 'one who worships an idol' without qualification, implying even out of love or fear is included.
Rava rejects the proof, explaining that the Mishnah is resolved as Rabbi Yirmeya previously reconciled it (referring to a different distinction).

sub.text: Abaye's second proof from baraisa about bowing to Haman
sub.text_en: Abaye's second proof from baraisa about bowing to Haman
sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraisa that permits bowing to a human but not to one worshipped like Haman, proving that worship out of fear (like Haman) is forbidden and thus liable.
Rava distinguishes: the baraisa refers to Haman himself who was an idol (עבודה זרה), not to one who worships out of fear like Haman's worshippers.

items.text: Abaye's final proof from Kohen Mashiach
items.text_en: Abaye's final proof from Kohen Mashiach
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraisa about a Kohen Mashiach who errs in idolatry, where Rabbi and Sages debate the type of error. The Gemara analyzes the case: if he thought a synagogue was an idol and bowed, his heart is to Heaven; rather, he saw an idol and bowed. If he accepted it as a god, it is intentional.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraisa about a Kohen Mashiach who errs in idolatry, where Rabbi and Sages debate the type of error.
The baraisa adds that both agree the Kohen Mashiach brings a female goat like an individual, and does not bring a suspensive guilt-offering.
The Gemara asks: what is a case of 'error in action' for idolatry? If he thought a synagogue was an idol and bowed, his heart is to Heaven, so it is not an error.
Rather, he saw an idol (אנדרטא) and bowed; if he accepted it as a god, it is intentional, so the error must be that he bowed without accepting it as a god.

items.text: Rava's distinction: 'saying it is permitted' vs. 'partial awareness'
items.text_en: Rava's distinction: 'saying it is permitted' vs. 'partial awareness'
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's earlier position that one who acts out of love or fear is exempt, arguing that if the person did not accept the idol as a god, it is nothing. Rava responds that the case is one who says 'it is permitted'. The Gemara objects that 'saying it is permitted' is itself a case of 'concealment of the matter' (העלם דבר). Rava clarifies: 'saying it is permitted' refers to complete permission (לבטל מקצת), while 'concealment of the matter' involves partial fulfillment and partial nullification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's position: if the person did not accept the idol as a god, it is nothing, so the case must be one acting out of love or fear.
Rava responds that the case is one who says 'it is permitted' (מוּתָּר), not love or fear.
The Gemara objects that 'saying it is permitted' is itself a case of 'concealment of the matter' (העלם דבר), which should not exempt.
Rava clarifies: 'saying it is permitted' refers to complete permission (לבטל מקצת), while 'concealment of the matter' involves partial fulfillment and partial nullification.

items.text: Rabbi Zakkai's baraita and Rabbi Yochanan's dismissal
items.text_en: Rabbi Zakkai's baraita and Rabbi Yochanan's dismissal
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zakkai taught before Rabbi Yochanan: If one performed slaughter, incense-offering, libation, and bowing in a single lapse of awareness, he is liable only once. Rabbi Yochanan told him to go out and teach it outside (i.e., it is incorrect).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zakkai taught before Rabbi Yochanan a baraita: If one performed slaughter, incense-offering, libation, and bowing in a single lapse of awareness, he is liable only once.
Rabbi Yochanan told Rabbi Zakkai to go out and teach it outside, dismissing the baraita as incorrect.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's explanation: the dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Natan
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's explanation: the dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Natan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba explains that Rabbi Zakkai's statement reflects a dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Natan regarding the verse about burning (הבערה) on Shabbat: Rabbi Yosei holds that burning was singled out for a negative commandment (לאזהרה), not to divide liability, while Rabbi Natan holds it was singled out to divide liability. The same logic applies to bowing (השתחוואה) in idolatry: according to Rabbi Yosei, bowing is also for a negative commandment; according to Rabbi Natan, it is to divide liability.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba introduces that Rabbi Zakkai's statement reflects a dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Natan, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei holds that burning (הבערה) on Shabbat was singled out for a negative commandment (לאזהרה).
The baraita records Rabbi Natan's opposing view that burning was singled out to divide liability (לחלק).
Rabbi Abba applies the same logic to bowing (השתחוואה) in idolatry: according to Rabbi Yosei, bowing is also for a negative commandment; according to Rabbi Natan, it is to divide liability.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection: Rabbi Yosei's position on Shabbat derives from 'מאחת מהנה'
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection: Rabbi Yosei's position on Shabbat derives from 'מאחת מהנה'
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects: Rabbi Yosei's ruling about burning on Shabbat is not because it was singled out for a negative commandment, but because he derives the division of labors from the verse 'מאחת מהנה' (one of them). Rabbi Yonatan explains the derivation: the words 'אחת', 'מאחת', 'הנה', 'מהנה' teach various combinations of intent and action. However, in the case of idolatry, where no such derivation exists for dividing labors, everyone agrees that bowing is singled out to divide liability.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects that Rabbi Yosei's position on Shabbat may derive from the verse 'מאחת מהנה' (one of them) rather than from the principle that burning was singled out for a negative commandment.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yosei derives from the verse 'ועשה מאחת מהנה' (and does one of them) that sometimes one is liable for all together and sometimes for each individually.
Rabbi Yonatan explains Rabbi Yosei's reasoning: the words 'אחת', 'מאחת', 'הנה', 'מהנה' teach various combinations of intent and action regarding Shabbat labors.
The Gemara concludes that in the case of idolatry, where no such derivation exists for dividing labors, everyone agrees that bowing was singled out to divide liability.

items.text: Applying the derivation to idolatry: the verse 'מאחת מהנה' for idolatry
items.text_en: Applying the derivation to idolatry: the verse 'מאחת מהנה' for idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Could the division of labors for idolatry also be derived from 'מאחת מהנה'? It explains: 'אחת' refers to slaughter, 'מאחת' to a single sign (siman), 'הנה' to the primary acts (avot) of idolatry (slaughter, incense, libation, bowing), 'מהנה' to derivative acts (toladot) like breaking a stick before it. The combinations of intent and action are then applied to idolatry: intentional idolatry with unwitting acts, and unwitting idolatry with intentional acts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the division of labors for idolatry can also be derived from the verse 'מאחת מהנה', and begins to explain the derivation: 'אחת' refers to slaughter, 'מאחת' to a single siman (organ).

The Gemara continues the derivation: 'הנה' refers to the primary acts (avot) of idolatry—slaughter, incense, libation, and bowing—and 'מהנה' refers to derivative acts (toladot) like breaking a stick before it.
The Gemara applies the combinations of intent and action to idolatry: 'אחת שהיא הנה' means intentional idolatry with unwitting acts, and 'הנה שהיא אחת' means unwitting idolatry with intentional acts.

items.text: Clarifying the case of unwitting idolatry and Rava's question
items.text_en: Clarifying the case of unwitting idolatry and Rava's question
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the case of unwitting idolatry? If one thought a house was a synagogue and bowed to it, his heart is towards Heaven (so it is not idolatry). Rather, it is when one saw a statue (אנדרטא) and bowed to it. If he accepted it as a god, it is intentional; if not, it is nothing. So it must be out of love or fear. This works for Abaye (who holds liable), but for Rava (who holds exempt), what can be said? Rather, it is a case of saying 'it is permitted'. This resolves Rava's question to Rav Nachman about a case where both the idolatry and the acts are unwitting: the answer is that he is liable only once.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the case of unwitting idolatry? If one thought a house was a synagogue and bowed to it, his heart is towards Heaven (so it is not idolatry).
Rather, it is when one saw a statue (אנדרטא) and bowed to it. If he accepted it as a god, it is intentional; if not, it is nothing.
So it must be out of love or fear. This works for Abaye (who holds liable), but for Rava (who holds exempt), what can be said?
Rather, it is a case of saying 'it is permitted'. This resolves Rava's question to Rav Nachman about a case where both the idolatry and the acts are unwitting.
The answer is that he is liable only once, and this resolves the question.

items.text: Objection: the verses apply to an anointed priest, not to idolatry
items.text_en: Objection: the verses apply to an anointed priest, not to idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Can these verses (about different offerings) be applied to idolatry? For a Meshiach (anointed priest) the offering is a bull, for a Nasi a goat, for an individual a lamb or a she-goat. But for idolatry we learned that all are equal with a she-goat as an individual. The discussion concludes with no further resolution, and when Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda came, he said... (the text is cut off).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verses about different offerings for different leaders cannot apply to idolatry, since for idolatry all are equal with a she-goat.
The discussion concludes with no further resolution.
The text notes that when Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda arrived, he said something (the text is cut off).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Shabbat is more stringent than other commandments in that one who performs two prohibited acts in one lapse of awareness is liable for each, while other commandments are more stringent in that one who acts unintentionally without intent is liable, unlike Shabbat.
