sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Shabbat is more stringent than other commandments in that one who performs two prohibited acts in one lapse of awareness is liable for each, while other commandments are more stringent in that one who acts unintentionally without intent is liable, unlike Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara's question and initial challenge
items.text_en: Gemara's question and initial challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's comparison: if the example for Shabbat is two different acts (reaping and grinding), the parallel for other commandments would be eating two different forbidden fats (chelev and blood), which would also yield two liabilities. The Gemara then suggests that the comparison must be between two identical acts (reaping and reaping vs. chelev and chelev), where both yield only one liability, but this undermines the Mishnah's point.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's comparison: if the example for Shabbat is two different acts (reaping and grinding), the parallel for other commandments would be eating two different forbidden fats (chelev and blood), which would also yield two liabilities, undermining the Mishnah's claim.
The Gemara suggests the comparison must be between two identical acts (reaping and reaping vs. chelev and chelev), where both yield only one liability, but this undermines the Mishnah's point.
The Gemara concludes that this is the meaning of the Mishnah's phrase 'go teach it outside' — the comparison is flawed and the Mishnah is self-contradictory.

items.text: Attempted resolution with idolatry
items.text_en: Attempted resolution with idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah's 'other commandments' refers specifically to idolatry, where performing multiple acts (sacrificing, burning incense, pouring libations) in one lapse yields only one liability, as per Rabbi Ami's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects that perhaps the Mishnah's comparison is between two different prohibited acts on Shabbat and idolatry, where according to Rabbi Ami, one who performs multiple idolatrous acts in one lapse is liable only once.
The Gemara proposes that the Mishnah's case involves performing multiple acts (reaping and grinding) in one lapse, and the phrase 'unlike other commandments' comes to include idolatry.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Ami's ruling that one who sacrifices, burns incense, and pours libations in a single lapse of awareness for idolatry is liable only once, supporting the proposed resolution.

items.text: Rejection of idolatry resolution due to the second clause
items.text_en: Rejection of idolatry resolution due to the second clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the idolatry resolution because the Mishnah's second clause (about shogeg b'lo mitkavein) cannot apply to idolatry: if one bows to a house thinking it's a synagogue, his heart is to Heaven; if he bows to an idol without accepting it as a god, it's nothing; if he accepts it, it's intentional. The only possible case is acting out of love or fear, which is disputed by Abaye and Rava, or thinking it's permitted, which is not comparable to Shabbat where one is completely exempt. The Gemara notes that even Rava's question about exemption for both acts was only about one or two liabilities, not complete exemption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the idolatry resolution because the Mishnah's second clause (shogeg b'lo mitkavein) cannot apply to idolatry.

The Gemara asks how a case of shogeg b'lo mitkavein could apply to idolatry, and analyzes possible scenarios: bowing to a house thinking it's a synagogue (heart to Heaven), or bowing to an idol without accepting it as a god (nothing), or accepting it (intentional).
The Gemara considers the case of acting out of love or fear, but objects that this is disputed by Abaye (who holds liable) and Rava (who holds exempt), so it cannot be the Mishnah's uniform case.
The Gemara suggests the case is one who thinks idolatry is permitted, which is not comparable to Shabbat where one is completely exempt.

The Gemara notes that even Rava's question to Rav Nachman was only about whether one is liable for one or two, not about complete exemption, so no one holds that one is completely exempt in such a case.

items.text: Alternative resolution: first clause for idolatry, second for other commandments
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: first clause for idolatry, second for other commandments
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the first clause of the Mishnah refers to idolatry and the second to other commandments. The case of shogeg b'lo mitkavein for other commandments is when one thinks he is swallowing saliva but swallows forbidden fat, where he is liable, unlike Shabbat where one who intends to lift a detached object but cuts an attached one is exempt, following Rav Nachman citing Shmuel's principle of melechet machshevet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the previous difficulty, suggesting an alternative resolution: the first clause of the Mishnah deals with idolatry and the second with other commandments.

The Gemara explains that the case of 'shogeg b'lo mitkavein' for other commandments is when one thinks he is swallowing saliva but swallows forbidden fat, where he is liable, unlike Shabbat where one who intends to lift a detached object but cuts an attached one is exempt.

The Gemara supports this with Rav Nachman's citation of Shmuel's principle that one who is occupied with forbidden fats or illicit relations is liable because he derives benefit, but one occupied with Shabbat labor is exempt because the Torah prohibited only intentional (melechet machshevet) labor.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's principle
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan would not accept the previous resolution because he holds that a Mishnah cannot be interpreted with its first clause based on one reason and its second clause on another; he would rather interpret the entire Mishnah consistently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Yochanan acts according to his own principle, refusing to interpret a Mishnah's first clause with one reason and its second clause with another.

Rabbi Yochanan declares that whoever can explain the Mishnah of the barrel (חָבִית) consistently according to one Tanna, he will carry that person's garments to the bathhouse, illustrating his commitment to uniform interpretation.

items.text: Transition to the main discussion
items.text_en: Transition to the main discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara signals a shift to the main body of the discussion with the term 'Gufa', indicating that the preceding analysis was introductory.

sub.desc_en: The gemara signals a shift to a new topic with the term 'גּוּפָא' (the body of the matter).

items.text: Rabbi Ami's ruling and Abaye's explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami's ruling and Abaye's explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami rules that one who sacrifices, offers incense, and pours libations in a single lapse is liable only once. Abaye explains the scriptural basis: the verse 'you shall not worship them' treats all these acts as one form of worship. The Gemara then notes that Abaye elsewhere holds a different view, so here he is merely explaining Rabbi Ami's reasoning.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami rules that one who sacrifices, offers incense, and pours libations in a single lapse of awareness is liable only once.
Abaye explains Rabbi Ami's reasoning: the verse 'לֹא תָעׇבְדֵם' (you shall not worship them) treats all these acts as one form of worship.
The Gemara objects that Abaye elsewhere holds a different view, as he asks why three bowings are needed for idolatry.
The Gemara resolves that Abaye was merely explaining Rabbi Ami's reasoning, not stating his own view.

items.text: Abaye's three prostrations principle
items.text_en: Abaye's three prostrations principle
items.desc_en: Abaye states that three distinct prostrations to idolatry are needed to establish liability: one for its standard manner, one for a non-standard manner, and one to teach that each act is separate. The Gemara derives the standard manner from the verse 'how these nations worship'. It then refines the categories: one for standard, one for non-standard, and one for division.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that three distinct prostrations to idolatry are needed: one for its standard manner, one for a non-standard manner, and one to teach that each act is separate.
The Gemara derives the standard manner of worship from the verse 'how these nations worship'.
The Gemara refines the categories: one for standard manner, one for non-standard manner, and one for division.

items.text: Liability for verbal acceptance as a god
items.text_en: Liability for verbal acceptance as a god
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman citing Rav rules that one who says to an idol 'You are my god' is liable to bring a sin-offering. The Gemara clarifies this is according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds that speech alone can constitute an act. It distinguishes this from blasphemy, and notes that the verse 'they bowed to him and sacrificed to him' links prostration to sacrifice, implying liability.

sub.desc_en: The mishna lists one who accepts an idol as a god or says 'You are my god' as liable.
Rav Nachman citing Rav rules that saying 'You are my god' renders one liable.
The Gemara asks what liability Rav means, noting that if it is the death penalty, the mishna already states that.
The Gemara answers that Rav means liability to bring a sin-offering.
The Gemara objects that even according to the Rabbis, who require an action for liability, speech alone would not suffice, citing a baraita and Reish Lakish's analysis.
The Gemara resolves that Rav's ruling is according to Rabbi Akiva, who does not require an action.
The Gemara objects that this is obvious, as it is similar to the case of a blasphemer.
The Gemara explains that one might think Rabbi Akiva only obligates an offering for blasphemy where karet is explicit, but here it is not; Rav teaches that it is still liable.
The Gemara provides a verse linking prostration, sacrifice, and speech to show that verbal acceptance is equated with active worship.

items.text: The vav in 'he'elucha' and the dispute with Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
items.text_en: The vav in 'he'elucha' and the dispute with Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says that without the vav in 'he'elucha' (they brought you up), Israel's enemies would have been destroyed. This is presented as a Tannaitic dispute: Acheirim agree, but Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai argues that one who associates God's name with another is uprooted from the world, citing 'to the Lord alone'. He interprets the verse as referring to those who invited many gods.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that without the vav in 'he'elucha' (they brought you up), Israel's enemies would have been destroyed.
Acheirim agree with Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation.

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai objects that one who associates God's name with another is uprooted from the world, citing 'to the Lord alone', and interprets the verse as referring to those who invited many gods.

items.text: Lashes for idolatrous acts and the principle of a general prohibition
items.text_en: Lashes for idolatrous acts and the principle of a general prohibition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar (via Rav Dimi) rules that one is lashed for all idolatrous acts except vowing in its name and fulfilling that vow. The Gemara explains that these two lack a physical act, and the prohibition is a general one (לאו שבכללות), for which lashes are not given. It supports this with a baraita listing various prohibitions derived from 'do not eat upon the blood', including eating before the animal dies, comforting mourners of executed criminals, and the rebellious son.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists idolatrous acts (hugging, kissing, honoring, sprinkling) that are prohibited.
Rav Dimi reports in the name of Rabbi Elazar that one is lashed for all these acts except vowing in the idol's name and fulfilling that vow.
The Gemara asks why vowing and fulfilling are exempt from lashes.
The Gemara explains that vowing lacks a physical act (לאו שאין בו מעשה) and the prohibition is a general one (לאו שבכללות), for which lashes are not given.

A baraita is cited, listing multiple prohibitions derived from 'לֹא תֹאכְלוּ עַל הַדָּם' (do not eat upon the blood), including eating before the animal dies, comforting mourners of executed criminals, and the rebellious son, and Rabbi Avin bar Chiyya (or bar Kahana) concludes that one is not lashed for any of them because they are general prohibitions (לאו שבכללות).

items.text: Ravin's version and the dispute with Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Ravin's version and the dispute with Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Ravin reports Rabbi Elazar's opposite ruling: one is not lashed for any of these acts except vowing and fulfilling. The Gemara explains that the first version considered vowing a general prohibition, while this version considers it an act-less prohibition, which Rabbi Yehuda holds is punishable by lashes. A baraita supports Rabbi Yehuda's view that a negative command followed by a positive command can still incur lashes.

sub.desc_en: Ravin reports Rabbi Elazar's ruling that one is not lashed for any of these acts except vowing in the idol's name and fulfilling the vow.
The Gemara asks why the other acts are exempt from lashes, and answers that they are general prohibitions (לאו שבכללות).
The Gemara explains that vowing and fulfilling are prohibitions without an action (לאו שאין בו מעשה), which are punishable by lashes according to Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara notes that this ruling aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a prohibition without an action incurs lashes.
A baraita is cited, deriving from the verse 'לֹא תוֹתִירוּ' that a negative command followed by a positive command can still incur lashes, supporting Rabbi Yehuda's position.

items.text: Dispute on lashes for mentioning idolatry's name
items.text_en: Dispute on lashes for mentioning idolatry's name
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yaakov argue whether one who mentions the name of idolatry is lashed. Rabbi Yaakov says it is a negative commandment without action, so no lashes; Rabbi Yehuda holds that lashes are given.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who mentions the name of idolatry is not lashed, according to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Yaakov explains that the prohibition is a negative commandment without action (לאו שאין בו מעשה), for which one is not lashed.
The Gemara infers from Rabbi Yaakov's statement that Rabbi Yehuda holds that one is lashed for mentioning idolatry's name.

items.text: Source for prohibition of vowing or fulfilling in idol's name
items.text_en: Source for prohibition of vowing or fulfilling in idol's name
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that one who vows or fulfills in the name of idolatry violates a negative commandment. A baraita is cited: 'וְשֵׁם אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים לֹא תַזְכִּירוּ' prohibits mentioning, and 'לֹא יִשָּׁמַע עַל פִּיךָ' prohibits vowing, fulfilling, or causing others to do so.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that one who vows or fulfills in the name of idolatry violates a negative commandment.

A baraita is cited, interpreting the verses 'וְשֵׁם אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים לֹא תַזְכִּירוּ' and 'לֹא יִשָּׁמַע עַל פִּיךָ' to prohibit vowing, fulfilling, or causing others to do so in the name of idolatry.

items.text: Alternate interpretation: warning for the enticer and the seducer
items.text_en: Alternate interpretation: warning for the enticer and the seducer
items.desc_en: Another interpretation of 'לֹא יִשָּׁמַע עַל פִּיךָ' is a warning for the mesit (enticer) and the madiach (seducer). The Gemara notes that the mesit's warning is explicit elsewhere, so this applies to the madiach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative interpretation: the verse 'לֹא יִשָּׁמַע עַל פִּיךָ' serves as a warning for the mesit (enticer) and the madiach (seducer).
The Gemara clarifies that the mesit's warning is explicit elsewhere, so the verse must apply to the madiach.

items.text: Support for Avuh deShmuel's ruling on partnership with a gentile
items.text_en: Support for Avuh deShmuel's ruling on partnership with a gentile
items.desc_en: The baraita's phrase 'וְלֹא יִגְרוֹם לַאֲחֵרִים' supports Avuh deShmuel's statement that one may not enter a partnership with a gentile, lest he be liable for an oath and swear by the gentile's idol, violating 'לֹא יִשָּׁמַע עַל פִּיךָ'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita's phrase 'וְלֹא יִגְרוֹם לַאֲחֵרִים' as support for Avuh deShmuel's ruling that one may not enter a partnership with a gentile, lest he be liable for an oath and swear by the gentile's idol, violating 'לֹא יִשָּׁמַע עַל פִּיךָ'.

items.text: Permissibility of mentioning idol names written in Torah
items.text_en: Permissibility of mentioning idol names written in Torah
items.desc_en: Ulla lodged in a place called Kalnevo; Rava questioned him for mentioning the name of an idol. Ulla cited Rabbi Yochanan: any idol mentioned in the Torah may be named. Rav Mesharshiya challenges with a case of a zav, but Ravina notes that 'Gad' is also written in the Torah.

sub.desc_en: Ulla lodged in Kalnevo; Rava questioned him for mentioning the idol's name, citing the prohibition of 'וְשֵׁם אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים לֹא תַזְכִּירוּ'.
Ulla answered that Rabbi Yochanan ruled: any idol mentioned in the Torah may be named, and 'נבו' is written in the verse 'כָּרַע בֵּל קֹרֵס נְבוֹ'.

Rav Mesharshiya challenged: if an idol name is not written in the Torah, is it forbidden to mention it? He cited a baraita about a zav that uses the term 'גד' (Gad) as a measure, implying it is a common word.
Ravina resolved: 'גד' is also written in the Torah, as the verse 'הָעֹרְכִים לַגַּד שֻׁלְחָן' shows, so the objection is refuted.

items.text: Permissibility of mockery of idolatry
items.text_en: Permissibility of mockery of idolatry
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that all mockery is forbidden except mockery of idolatry, citing verses that mock Bel and Nebo. The Gemara adds a play on words: 'כְּבוֹדוֹ' is read as 'כְּבֵידוֹ' (his liver), implying the idol's burden is heavy.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that all mockery is forbidden except mockery of idolatry, citing verses mocking Bel and Nebo.
The Gemara adds a wordplay on the verse, reading 'כְּבוֹדוֹ' (his glory) as 'כְּבֵידוֹ' (his liver), implying the idol's burden is heavy.

items.text: Aggadic descriptions of idol worship practices
items.text_en: Aggadic descriptions of idol worship practices
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains that each idolater makes a likeness of his idol and keeps it in his pocket, embracing and kissing it when remembered. Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami describes how priests would starve calves and place idols near their mangers to entice people to sacrifice themselves. Rava reinterprets the verse to mean that one who sacrifices his son to idolatry says the idol desires a great gift and should come and kiss it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains the verse 'וְעַתָּה יוֹסִפוּ לַחֲטֹא' (And now they continue to sin) to mean that each idolater makes a likeness of his idol, keeps it in his pocket, and when he remembers it, he takes it out, embraces and kisses it.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak of the school of Rabbi Ami explains the verse 'זֹבְחֵי אָדָם עֲגָלִים יִשָּׁקוּן' (Those who sacrifice men kiss calves) as describing how priests would starve calves and place idols near their mangers to entice wealthy people to sacrifice themselves to the idol.

Rava reinterprets the verse 'זֹבְחֵי אָדָם עֲגָלִים יִשָּׁקוּן' (Those who sacrifice men kiss calves) to mean that one who sacrifices his son to idolatry says the idol desires a great gift and should come and kiss it.

items.text: Identification of foreign idols and their forms
items.text_en: Identification of foreign idols and their forms
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav identifies various idols: Sukkot Benot (a hen), Nergal (a rooster), Ashima (a bald ram), Nibchaz and Tartak (a dog and a donkey), Adrammelech and Anammelech (a mule and a horse). The Gemara adds that Hezekiah's father sought to do similarly but was stopped by his mother with a salamander.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav identifies the idols Sukkot Benot as a hen, Nergal as a rooster, Ashima as a bald ram, and Nibchaz and Tartak as a dog and a donkey.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav (continued)
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav (continued)
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav identifies Adrammelech as a mule and Anammelech as a horse, explaining their names as referring to carrying loads and responding in battle.
The Gemara adds that Hezekiah's father sought to do similarly but was prevented by his mother with a salamander.

items.text: Israel's knowledge of idolatry's emptiness and its purpose
items.text_en: Israel's knowledge of idolatry's emptiness and its purpose
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that Israel knew idolatry had no substance; they worshipped it only to permit forbidden relations publicly. Rav Mesharshiya objects with a verse comparing idolatry to longing for a son, and the Gemara answers that this was after they had become deeply attached.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that Israel knew idolatry had no substance and only worshipped it to permit forbidden relations publicly.
Rav Mesharshiya objects with a verse comparing idolatry to longing for a son, implying genuine attachment.
The Gemara answers that this longing was after they had become deeply attached to idolatry.

items.text: Story of Elijah and the starving child
items.text_en: Story of Elijah and the starving child
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story of Elijah the prophet finding a starving child in Jerusalem. Elijah teaches the child to recite the Shema daily. The child agrees to learn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a story of Elijah the prophet finding a starving child in Jerusalem.
Elijah asks the child about his family and learns that he is the sole survivor.
Elijah asks the child if he will learn something that will sustain him, and the child agrees.
Elijah teaches the child to recite the Shema daily, and the child responds affirmatively.

items.text: Story of the idolater and Baal Peor
items.text_en: Story of the idolater and Baal Peor
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a story of a person who, not having been taught by his parents, takes out his idol, hugs and kisses it until his stomach bursts, fulfilling the verse about corpses upon idols. This illustrates the extreme devotion to Baal Peor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a story of a person who, not having been taught by his parents, takes out his idol, hugs and kisses it until his stomach bursts, fulfilling the verse about corpses upon idols, illustrating the extreme devotion to Baal Peor.

items.text: The cry against the evil inclination
items.text_en: The cry against the evil inclination
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse about crying out to God and explains that they cried 'Woe, woe' for the evil inclination that destroyed the Temple, killed the righteous, and exiled Israel, yet still dances among them. They reject both it and its reward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a verse about crying out to God and attributes the explanation to Rav Yehuda or Rav Yonatan.

They explain that the people cried 'Woe, woe' for the evil inclination that destroyed the Temple, killed the righteous, and exiled Israel, yet still dances among them, and they reject both it and its reward.
The Gemara notes that this happened after they had become deeply attached to the evil inclination.

items.text: The capture of the evil inclination
items.text_en: The capture of the evil inclination
items.desc_en: They fasted for three days, received a note from heaven saying 'Emet' (truth), and a lion-like fire emerged from the Holy of Holies. The prophet identified it as the evil inclination for idolatry. When they seized it, a hair fell and its roar was heard for 400 parasangs.

sub.desc_en: The people fasted for three days and received a note from heaven inscribed with 'Emet' (truth).
Rabbi Chanina deduces from this that the seal of the Holy One, Blessed be He, is truth.

A lion-like fire emerged from the Holy of Holies; the prophet identified it as the evil inclination for idolatry, and when seized, its roar was heard for 400 parasangs, prompting concern about heavenly mercy.

items.text: Containing the evil inclination and its aftermath
items.text_en: Containing the evil inclination and its aftermath
items.desc_en: The prophet advised sealing it in a lead pot with lead cover to muffle its roar. They prayed for the evil inclination of transgression and it was handed over. They imprisoned it for three days, then found no fresh egg for a sick person, so they blinded it, which stopped people from being enticed to relatives.

sub.desc_en: The prophet instructs to seal the evil inclination in a lead pot with a lead cover to muffle its roar, citing a verse.
The sages propose to pray for the evil inclination of transgression, and it is handed over to them.
They imprison the evil inclination for three days, find no fresh egg for a sick person, and blind it, which stops people from being enticed to relatives.

items.text: Story of the gentile woman and Baal Peor
items.text_en: Story of the gentile woman and Baal Peor
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav tells of a gentile woman who vowed to serve every idol if healed. When she reached Peor, the priests said its worship involves eating leeks, drinking beer, and defecating before it. She preferred to return to illness rather than serve that way. The Gemara contrasts this with Israel's attachment to God.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav tells the story of a gentile woman who vowed to serve every idol if healed, and fulfilled her vow.
The Gemara contrasts the gentile woman's rejection of Peor with Israel's clinging to God, citing verses about attachment.
A baraita interprets the verses about Baal Peor and attachment to God with concrete metaphors.

items.text: Story of Savta ben Allas and Baal Peor
items.text_en: Story of Savta ben Allas and Baal Peor
items.desc_en: The rabbis taught about Savta ben Allas who rented his donkey to a gentile woman. After she entered Peor, he also entered, defecated before it, and wiped his nose. The priests praised him as never having been served so well.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts the story of Savta ben Allas, who rented his donkey to a gentile woman, then entered the shrine of Peor, defecated before it, and wiped his nose, receiving praise from the priests for his service.

items.text: Laws of worship for Peor and Merkulis
items.text_en: Laws of worship for Peor and Merkulis
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who bares himself to Baal Peor is liable even if intending to degrade, and one who throws a stone at Merkulis is liable even if intending to stone it. Rav Menasheh threw a clod at a suspected idol, and the academy ruled that throwing a stone at Merkulis is its worship even if intending to stone it. They also ruled that removing the stone is also liable.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the laws of worship for Baal Peor (baring oneself) and Merkulis (throwing a stone), both liable even if done with intent to degrade.
Rav Menasheh, encountering a suspected idol, threw a clod at it, and when told it was Merkulis, he cited the Mishnah's rule that throwing a stone at Merkulis is its worship.
The academy ruled that throwing a stone at Merkulis is liable even if intending to stone it, and that removing the stone is also liable because each stone leaves a gap for another.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on Molech
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on Molech
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who gives his seed to Molech is not liable until he both gives to Molech and passes through fire. The Gemara questions why the Mishnah separates idolatry and Molech. Rabbi Avin says it follows the view that Molech is not idolatry. Abaye equates Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon and Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonos, who say Molech is any ruler they appoint. Rava says the dispute is about temporary Molech.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the liability for giving seed to Molech requires both handing over to Molech and passing through fire.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah separates idolatry and Molech as distinct categories.
Rabbi Avin explains that the Mishnah follows the view that Molech is not idolatry, citing a baraita where Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon distinguishes between Molech and other idolatry.
Abaye equates Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon and Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonos, citing the latter's statement that Molech is any ruler they appoint, even a pebble or stick.
Rava resolves the dispute by saying the difference between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon is about a temporary Molech (מולך עראי).

items.text: Rabbi Yannai's condition for liability
items.text_en: Rabbi Yannai's condition for liability
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai states that one is not liable for Molech unless he gives his offspring to the priests, as derived from the verse. A baraita supports this by expounding the verse to require both giving and passing through fire, and specifically to Molech.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai states that one is not liable for Molech unless he gives his offspring to the priests, citing the verse 'וּמִזַּרְעֲךָ לֹא תִתֵּן לְהַעֲבִיר לַמֹּלֶךְ'.
A baraita supports Rabbi Yannai by expounding the verse to require both giving and passing through fire, and specifically to Molech.

items.text: Exemption for passing all offspring
items.text_en: Exemption for passing all offspring
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava rules that if one passes all his offspring, he is exempt, as the verse says 'from your seed' and not all your seed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava rules that one who passes all his offspring is exempt, because the verse says 'from your seed' and not 'all your seed'.

items.text: Rav Ashi's inquiries and resolution regarding offspring
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's inquiries and resolution regarding offspring
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises questions about liability for a blind or sleeping child, and for a grandson. A baraita resolves one question by including a son's son and daughter's son from the verse 'in giving of his seed'. The Gemara notes a shift in verses and a second derivation for invalid seed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi raises dilemmas about liability for passing a blind child, a sleeping child, or a grandson through fire to Molekh.
The Gemara resolves one dilemma by citing a baraita that derives liability for a son's son or daughter's son from the verse 'in giving of his seed'.
The Gemara notes that the tanna began with one verse and ended with another, questioning the shift.
The Gemara explains that the second verse is for a different exposition: to include offspring of flawed lineage, such as a mamzer.

items.text: The manner of passing through fire
items.text_en: The manner of passing through fire
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that one must pass the child through fire in a specific manner. Abaye and Rava describe the method, and a baraita supports Rava's view, adding that passing by foot exempts.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that one is not liable unless he passes the child in the typical manner of passing.
The Gemara asks what constitutes the typical manner of passing.
Abaye describes the manner as a latticework of bricks with fire on both sides.
Rava describes the manner as like the leaps of children on Purim.
A baraita supports Rava's view, stating that one is not liable unless he passes the child in the typical manner, and passing by foot exempts.

items.text: Liability for offspring and other idolatry
items.text_en: Liability for offspring and other idolatry
items.desc_en: The baraita specifies that liability is only for one's own children, not parents or siblings, and one who passes himself is exempt except according to Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon. It also rules that one is liable for both Molech and other idolatry, though Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon disagrees.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that liability for Molech applies only to one's own offspring, not parents or siblings, and one who passes himself is exempt except according to Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon.
The baraita states that one is liable for both Molech and other idolatry, while Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon holds liability only for Molech.

items.text: Ulla's explanation and the Rabbis' counter
items.text_en: Ulla's explanation and the Rabbis' counter
items.desc_en: Ulla explains Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon's reasoning from the verse 'in you' meaning oneself. The Gemara questions why the Rabbis do not derive from 'in you', citing a case where it is used for priority of one's own lost object, and answers that there it is from the word 'efes'.

sub.desc_en: Ulla explains that Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon derives from the verse 'לֹא יִמָּצֵא בְךָ' (it shall not be found in you) that the prohibition applies to oneself, thus one who passes himself through fire is liable.

The Gemara questions why the Rabbis do not derive from the word 'בְּךָ' (in you), citing a Mishnah where one's own lost object takes priority over one's father's, which is derived from the word 'בְּךָ'.
Rav Yehuda explains that the priority of one's own lost object is derived from the word 'אֶפֶס' (only) in the verse, not from 'בְּךָ'.
The Gemara resolves that the derivation there is from 'אֶפֶס' (only), not from 'בְּךָ', so the Rabbis do not derive from 'בְּךָ' in the context of Molech.

items.text: Three karet punishments for idolatry
items.text_en: Three karet punishments for idolatry
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina asks why there are three karet punishments for idolatry, and explains they are for its normal manner, abnormal manner, and Molech. The Gemara then discusses the views that Molech is a specific idol or a blasphemer, and concludes with a dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael about the meaning of the three terms for excision.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina asks why there are three karet (excision) punishments for idolatry, and answers that they correspond to its normal manner, abnormal manner, and Molech.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis for the view that Molech is an idol
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis for the view that Molech is an idol
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to the view that Molech is a specific idol, the extra karet for Molech applies to one who passes his child through fire in an abnormal manner.

sub.text: Gemara's question for the view that Molech is a blasphemer
sub.text_en: Gemara's question for the view that Molech is a blasphemer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what purpose the karet for Molech serves according to the view that Molech is a blasphemer.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Akiva's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Akiva interprets the double language 'הִכָּרֵת תִּכָּרֵת' (being cut off) as referring to this world and the World to Come.

Rabbi Yishmael objects that the verse already uses 'וְנִכְרְתָה' (and he shall be cut off), and explains that 'וְנִכְרְתָה' refers to this world, 'הִכָּרֵת' to the World to Come, and 'תִּכָּרֵת' is merely the Torah speaking in human language.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines ba'al ov as a ventriloquist who speaks from his armpits, and yid'oni as one who speaks through his mouth. Both are liable for stoning, and consulting them is a prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines ba'al ov (בעל אוב) as a ventriloquist speaking from the armpits and yid'oni (ידעוני) as one speaking through the mouth, ruling both liable to stoning and consulting them a prohibition.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's omission
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's omission
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah here lists both ba'al ov and yid'oni, while in tractate Karetot only ba'al ov is mentioned and yid'oni is omitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah here lists both ba'al ov and yid'oni, while in tractate Karetot only ba'al ov is mentioned and yid'oni is omitted.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says both are included because they are mentioned in one negative commandment. Reish Lakish says yid'oni is omitted in Karetot because it involves no action. The Gemara explains their reasoning: Rabbi Yochanan holds that a difference in punishment does not constitute a true distinction, while Reish Lakish holds that it does.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers that both ov and yid'oni are included in the list of capital offenses because they are mentioned in a single negative commandment.
Reish Lakish answers that yid'oni is omitted from the list of karet offenses because it involves no action.
The Gemara asks Rabbi Yochanan why the mishnah specifically mentions בעל אוב (ov) rather than yid'oni.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the mishnah mentions בעל אוב because the verse opens with it.
The Gemara asks why Reish Lakish does not accept Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning.
Rav Pappa answers that Reish Lakish holds that ov and yid'oni are distinguished by their different modes of execution.
Rabbi Yochanan holds that a difference in the negative commandment (לאו) is considered a true distinction, but a difference in the mode of execution (מיתה) is not considered a true distinction.

items.text: Why Rabbi Yochanan rejects Reish Lakish's view
items.text_en: Why Rabbi Yochanan rejects Reish Lakish's view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Mishnah in Karetot follows Rabbi Akiva, who does not require a significant action (ma'aseh rabbah) for liability, only a minimal action (ma'aseh zuta). Reish Lakish counters that even Rabbi Akiva requires some action, and the Gemara provides examples: the blashemer's lip movement and the necromancer's arm movement are considered actions.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers that the Mishnah in Karetot follows Rabbi Akiva, who does not require a significant action (מעשה רבה) for liability.
Reish Lakish objects that even Rabbi Akiva requires a minimal action (מעשה זוטא) for liability.
The Gemara provides the example of the blashemer (מגדף), whose lip movement (עקימת שפתיו) is considered a minimal action.
The Gemara provides the example of the necromancer (בעל אוב), whose arm movement (הקשת זרועותיו) is considered a minimal action.

items.text: Challenge from the Rabbis' view and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from the Rabbis' view and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Reish Lakish's position from a baraita that requires an action for liability, listing bowing as an example. Reish Lakish says that baraita follows Rabbi Akiva, while Rabbi Yochanan says even the Rabbis consider bowing an action. The Gemara then questions how Reish Lakish can consider arm movement an action if bowing is not, and concludes that Reish Lakish's statement applies only to Rabbi Akiva, not to the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Reish Lakish's position by citing a baraita that requires an action for liability, listing bowing as an example, implying that even the Rabbis consider bowing an action.
Reish Lakish responds that the baraita listing bowing follows Rabbi Akiva, who does not require an action for liability.
Rabbi Yochanan counters that even according to the Rabbis, bowing (bending one's stature) is considered an action.
The Gemara objects: according to Reish Lakish, if bending one's stature is not an action for the Rabbis, how can arm movement (of the בעל אוב) be considered an action?
The Gemara resolves that Reish Lakish's statement about arm movement being an action applies only to Rabbi Akiva, not to the Rabbis.

items.text: Ulla and Rava's alternative explanations
items.text_en: Ulla and Rava's alternative explanations
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if so, the blashemer and necromancer should be excluded from the list. Ulla explains that the necromancer is liable for burning incense to a demon. Rava counters that this is idolatry, and instead says it is for burning incense to a snake charmer (chabar). Abaye objects that this is the offense of sorcery, and the Gemara concludes that the Torah indeed punishes sorcery with stoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the previous explanation is correct, the blashemer and necromancer should have been excluded from the list of those liable for karet.
Ulla explains that the necromancer is liable for burning incense to a demon.
Rava objects that burning incense to a demon is idolatry, not a distinct offense.
Rava instead explains that the necromancer is liable for burning incense to a snake charmer (חבר).
Abaye objects that burning incense to a snake charmer is the offense of sorcery (חובר חבר).
The Gemara concludes that indeed, the Torah punishes sorcery with stoning, so the necromancer is liable.

items.text: Baraita on sorcery and final discussion
items.text_en: Baraita on sorcery and final discussion
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a sorcerer (chover chaver) is liable for any type of sorcery, even with snakes and scorpions. Abaye rules that one who charms them to prevent harm is still forbidden. The Gemara then asks why Rabbi Yochanan considers bowing an action but not lip movement, and Rava answers that the blashemer is different because his offense is in the heart.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the prohibition of חובר חבר (sorcerer) applies to any type of sorcery, even charming snakes and scorpions.
Abaye rules that one who charms a hornet or scorpion to prevent harm is still forbidden.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yochanan considers bowing an action but not lip movement.
Rava answers that the blashemer is different because his offense is in the heart.

items.text: Gemara's question about zomemim witnesses and the nature of action
items.text_en: Gemara's question about zomemim witnesses and the nature of action
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira challenges the Mishnah's exclusion of zomemim witnesses from capital punishment, arguing that their false testimony involves an action (speech). Rava initially distinguishes them because they are subject to 'kol' (voice), but Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish debate whether 'kol' constitutes an action. Rava then revises his answer, saying zomemim are distinguished because they are subject to 're'iyah' (sight).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira challenges the Mishnah's exclusion of zomemim witnesses from capital punishment, arguing that their false testimony involves an action (speech).
Rava initially distinguishes zomemim witnesses because they are subject to 'קול' (voice), which is not a physical action.

sub.text: Gemara's objection with a debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection with a debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that according to Rabbi Yochanan, voice (קול) is considered an action, citing a dispute where Rabbi Yochanan holds one liable for directing an animal by voice, while Resh Lakish exempts.
Rava revises his answer, saying zomemim witnesses are distinguished because they are subject to 'ראייה' (sight), which is not an action.

items.text: Definitions of ov and yid'oni
items.text_en: Definitions of ov and yid'oni
items.desc_en: The Tannaim define 'ba'al ov' as one who speaks from between his joints, and 'yid'oni' as one who places a known bone in his mouth and speaks. The Gemara attempts to derive from verses that the speech of the ov is natural, but concludes it is from between the joints.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines 'ba'al ov' as one who speaks from between his joints and 'yid'oni' as one who places a known bone in his mouth and speaks spontaneously.
The Gemara challenges the baraita by citing the verse 'וְהָיָה כְּאוֹב מֵאֶרֶץ קוֹלֵךְ' and asking whether it implies the ov speaks naturally.
The Gemara rejects the challenge, explaining that the verse describes the ov speaking from between his joints, not naturally.

items.text: Distinction between raising the dead and consulting a skull
items.text_en: Distinction between raising the dead and consulting a skull
items.desc_en: The Tannaim distinguish between one who raises the dead through a known medium (zekhuro) and one who consults a skull. The former does not arise in his usual manner and not on Shabbat, while the latter does. The Gemara clarifies that 'arises' means 'answers'. The story of Turnusrufus and Rabbi Akiva illustrates that Shabbat is distinct from other days, as proven by the Sambatyon river, the ov, and the father's grave.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the distinction between raising the dead via a known medium (זכורו) and consulting a skull, noting that the former does not arise in its usual manner nor on Shabbat, while the latter does.
The Gemara questions the baraita's use of 'arises' (עולה) for the skull, since the skull is placed before the questioner and does not physically ascend.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by emending the baraita to read 'answers' (עונה) instead of 'arises' (עולה), meaning the skull answers in its usual manner and on Shabbat.

sub.text: Story of Turnusrufus and Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Story of Turnusrufus and Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: Turnusrufus asks Rabbi Akiva how Shabbat differs from other days, and Rabbi Akiva responds by analogy that just as one person is distinguished from another by the Master's will, so too Shabbat is distinguished by God's will.

Rabbi Akiva provides three proofs that Shabbat is distinct: the Sambatyon river, the ov (necromancer), and his father's grave which does not emit smoke on Shabbat, leading Turnusrufus to concede he was shamed.

items.text: The prohibition of consulting the dead and Rabbi Akiva's lament
items.text_en: The prohibition of consulting the dead and Rabbi Akiva's lament
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies 'sho'el ov' with 'doresh el hametim'. A baraita defines 'doresh el hametim' as one who starves himself and sleeps in a cemetery to attract an impure spirit. Rabbi Akiva weeps upon this verse, reasoning that if starving oneself can attract impurity, how much more could it attract purity, but sins prevent it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the prohibition of consulting an ov (אוב) with the verse 'doresh el hametim' (one who inquires of the dead).
A baraita defines 'doresh el hametim' as one who starves himself and sleeps in a cemetery to attract an impure spirit (רוח טומאה).
Rabbi Akiva weeps upon this verse, reasoning that if starving oneself can attract impurity, how much more could it attract purity, but sins prevent it.

items.text: Rabbis creating beings through mystical means
items.text_en: Rabbis creating beings through mystical means
items.desc_en: Rava states that if the righteous wished, they could create a world. He himself created a man and sent him to Rabbi Zeira, who spoke to it but it did not respond, leading Rabbi Zeira to declare it a creation of the rabbis and return it to dust. Similarly, Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Oshaya would study Sefer Yetzirah every Shabbat eve and create a calf to eat.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that if the righteous wished, they could create a world, citing the verse about sins separating from God.
Rava creates a man and sends him to Rabbi Zeira, who speaks to it but receives no response, concluding it is a creation of the rabbis and returning it to dust.

sub.text: Narrative of Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Oshaya
sub.text_en: Narrative of Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Oshaya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Oshaya would study Sefer Yetzirah every Shabbat eve and create a calf to eat.

items.text: Definitions of me'onan and menachesh
items.text_en: Definitions of me'onan and menachesh
items.desc_en: The Tannaim define 'me'onan' as one who passes seven types of male animals over the eye (Rabbi Shimon), one who deceives the eyes (Sages), or one who calculates times and says 'today is good to go out' etc. (Rabbi Akiva). 'Menachesh' is defined as one who interprets omens such as bread falling, a staff falling, a son calling, a raven calling, etc.

sub.desc_en: The Tannaim define 'me'onan' with three opinions: Rabbi Shimon says one who passes seven types of male animals over the eye; the Sages say one who deceives the eyes; Rabbi Akiva says one who calculates times and declares auspicious or inauspicious days.
Rabbi Akiva elaborates that 'me'onan' includes those who determine auspicious times for travel or transactions.

The Tannaim define 'menachesh' as one who interprets various omens, such as bread falling, a staff falling, a son calling, a raven calling, a deer crossing the path, a snake on the right, or a fox on the left.

items.text: Opening baraita on nichush
items.text_en: Opening baraita on nichush
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that interprets the verse 'You shall not practice divination nor soothsaying' as referring to those who divine by means of a weasel, birds, or fish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that interprets the prohibition of nichush (divination) as including those who divine by a weasel, birds, or fish.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on Shabbat desecration
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on Shabbat desecration
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that one who desecrates Shabbat with an act that incurs karet for intentional violation and a sin-offering for unintentional violation is liable. The Gemara infers that there are acts of Shabbat desecration that do not incur these penalties, and identifies them as violating the Shabbat boundaries (techumin) according to Rabbi Akiva, and kindling (hav'arah) according to Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that one who desecrates Shabbat with an act that incurs karet for intentional violation and a sin-offering for unintentional violation is liable.
The Gemara infers that there are acts of Shabbat desecration that do not incur these penalties.
The Gemara identifies these acts as violating the Shabbat boundaries (techumin) according to Rabbi Akiva, and kindling (hav'arah) according to Rabbi Yosei.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on cursing a parent
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on cursing a parent
items.desc_en: The mishnah teaches that one who curses a parent is not liable unless they curse using the Tetragrammaton; if they curse with a substitute name, Rabbi Meir deems them liable and the Sages exempt. The Gemara identifies the Sages as Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yosei, who derives from the verse 'when he blasphemes the Name he shall be put to death' that one is not liable for cursing a parent unless they curse with the Tetragrammaton.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that one who curses a parent is not liable unless they curse with the Tetragrammaton; if they curse with a substitute name, Rabbi Meir deems them liable and the Sages exempt.
The Gemara asks who the Sages are, and answers that it is Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yosei.

A baraita is cited where Rabbi Menachem bar Rabbi Yosei derives from the verse 'when he blasphemes the Name he shall be put to death' that one is not liable for cursing a parent unless they curse with the Tetragrammaton.

items.text: Derivation of inclusion and liability for cursing one parent
items.text_en: Derivation of inclusion and liability for cursing one parent
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verse 'A man who curses his father and his mother' to include a daughter, a tumtum, and an androgynos. It further derives that one is liable for cursing either parent individually, based on the verse 'his father and his mother he has cursed, his blood is upon him' – Rabbi Yoshiyah says this teaches that cursing either father or mother is punishable. Rabbi Yonatan argues that the plain meaning implies both together, but also each individually, unless the verse specifies 'together'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by expounding the repetition 'איש איש' (a man a man) to include a daughter, a טומטום (tumtum), and an אנדרוגינוס (androgynos) in the liability for cursing parents.

Rabbi Yoshiyah derives from the verse 'אביו ואמו קלל דמיו בו' (his father and his mother he has cursed, his blood is upon him) that one is liable for cursing either father alone or mother alone, not only both together.
Rabbi Yonatan argues that the plain meaning of the verse implies both together, but also each individually, unless the verse explicitly specifies 'together' (יחדו).

items.text: Derivation of stoning as the punishment
items.text_en: Derivation of stoning as the punishment
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the punishment for cursing a parent is stoning, using a verbal analogy between 'his blood is upon him' here and 'their blood is upon them' in the context of the necromancer, where stoning is specified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives that the punishment for cursing a parent is stoning, using a verbal analogy between 'דָמָיו בּוֹ' (his blood is upon him) here and 'דְּמֵיהֶם בָּם' (their blood is upon them) in the context of the necromancer, where stoning is specified.

items.text: Derivation of the warning (azharah) for cursing a parent
items.text_en: Derivation of the warning (azharah) for cursing a parent
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the prohibition against cursing a parent. It suggests that if the parent is a judge, the verse 'You shall not curse a judge' applies; if a prince, 'You shall not curse a prince among your people' applies. For a parent who is neither, a binyan av (building from two cases) is constructed from the judge and prince, but this is challenged because their greatness causes the prohibition. The Gemara then introduces the verse 'You shall not curse the deaf' to include all Israelites, but this too is challenged. After a back-and-forth, the Gemara concludes that the verse 'You shall not curse a judge' is superfluous for its own context and is therefore applied to the parent. The discussion then addresses the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva regarding whether 'Elohim' in that verse refers to a judge (profane) or to God (sacred), and how the derivation works for each opinion. The Gemara concludes with a question about the logic of deriving the profane from the sacred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have heard the punishment for cursing a parent, but from where do we derive the warning (אזהרה) not to do so?

The Gemara answers: the verse 'אֱלֹהִים לֹא תְקַלֵּל' (You shall not curse a judge) applies if the parent is a judge, and 'וְנָשִׂיא בְעַמְּךָ לֹא תָאֹר' (You shall not curse a prince) applies if the parent is a prince.
The Gemara asks: if the parent is neither a judge nor a prince, from where do we derive the warning?

The Gemara answers: you can construct a בנין אב (building from two cases) from the judge and the prince, deriving a common feature that they are among your people and you are warned against cursing them, and so too your parent.
The Gemara objects: what about the common feature? Their greatness (being a judge or prince) is what causes the prohibition, which does not apply to a parent.
The Gemara answers: the verse 'לֹא תְקַלֵּל חֵרֵשׁ' (You shall not curse the deaf) includes even the lowly among your people.
The Gemara objects: what about the deaf? His deafness (being vulnerable) is what causes the prohibition, which does not apply to a parent.

The Gemara answers: the prince and judge prove that the prohibition is not solely due to vulnerability, and the deaf proves it is not solely due to greatness; the common feature is that they are among your people, so too your parent.
The Gemara objects: what about the common feature? They are all exceptional (the judge and prince are great, the deaf is vulnerable), which does not apply to a parent.
The Gemara resolves: if so, the verse 'אֱלֹהִים' (You shall not curse a judge) is superfluous for its own context and is therefore applied to the parent.
The Gemara asks: this works for the one who says 'אֱלֹהִים' is profane (referring to a judge), but for the one who says it is sacred (referring to God), what can be said?
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yishmael says 'אֱלֹהִים' is profane, Rabbi Akiva says it is sacred, and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov derives the warning for one who curses God from this verse.
The Gemara answers: for Rabbi Yishmael, the sacred (cursing God) is derived from the profane (cursing a parent); for Rabbi Akiva, the profane is derived from the sacred.
The Gemara questions: for Rabbi Akiva, who says 'אֱלֹהִים' is sacred, perhaps the verse only warns about cursing God, not about cursing a parent (profane)?
The Gemara resolves: if so, the verse should have written 'לֹא תָקֵל' (You shall not curse) without the word 'אֱלֹהִים', indicating that the word 'אֱלֹהִים' is superfluous and applies to the parent.

items.text: Gemara's opening question
items.text_en: Gemara's opening question
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'Do not curse' implies, suggesting it teaches two things.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'Do not curse' implies, suggesting it teaches two things.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who has intercourse with a betrothed young woman is liable only if she is a young virgin betrothed and in her father's house; if two men have intercourse with her, the first is executed by stoning and the second by strangulation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the conditions for liability for intercourse with a betrothed young woman and the punishments for two men who have intercourse with her.

items.text: Baraita and dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.text_en: Baraita and dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds the terms of the Mishnah, and Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav identifies this as the view of Rabbi Meir, while the Sages include even a minor in the term 'na'arah hame'urasah'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita expounds the Mishnah's terms: 'na'arah' excludes a bogeret, 'betulah' excludes a non-virgin, 'me'urasah' excludes a married woman, and 'in her father's house' excludes one who was handed over to the husband's agents.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav identifies the baraita as the view of Rabbi Meir, while the Sages include even a minor in the term 'na'arah hame'urasah'.

items.text: Rav Acha's challenge and Ravina's response
items.text_en: Rav Acha's challenge and Ravina's response
items.desc_en: Rav Acha from Difti challenges Ravina, suggesting the Mishnah might be the Sages' view and only excludes a bogeret. Ravina responds that the Mishnah's phrasing 'eino chayav ad shetehei na'arah' implies it excludes a minor as well.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha miDifti challenges Ravina, suggesting that the Mishnah might reflect the Sages' view and only excludes a bogeret (adult maiden), not a minor.

Ravina responds that the Mishnah's phrasing 'אינו חייב עד שתהא נערה' (he is not liable until she is a na'arah) implies it excludes a minor as well, because otherwise it should have said 'אינו חייב אלא על נערה'.

items.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Adda's question and Rav's silence
items.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Adda's question and Rav's silence
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Adda asks Rav whether Rabbi Meir completely exempts a minor betrothed or only from stoning. Rav answers that he is exempt from stoning, but is challenged by the verse 'umetu gam shneihem' requiring both to be equal, and Rav remains silent.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Adda asks Rav whether Rabbi Meir's exclusion of a minor betrothed is a complete exemption or only from stoning.
Rav answers that Rabbi Meir excludes the minor only from stoning, not completely.
The Gemara objects by citing the verse 'וּמֵתוּ גַּם שְׁנֵיהֶם' (and both of them shall die), which implies both parties must be equal in liability.
Rav remains silent, unable to respond to the objection.

items.text: Shmuel's explanation and the Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Shmuel's explanation and the Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Shmuel explains why Rav was silent, suggesting he could have cited the verse 'umet ha'ish asher shachav imah levado'. This is then presented as a dispute between Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel asks why Rav was silent in response to the objection from the verse 'וּמֵתוּ גַּם שְׁנֵיהֶם'.
Shmuel suggests that Rav could have answered by citing the verse 'וּמֵת הָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר שָׁכַב עִמָּהּ לְבַדּוֹ' (the man alone dies), which implies the man and woman need not be equal.

The gemara presents this as a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Yoshiya requires both parties to be equal (adult), while Rabbi Yonatan cites the verse 'וּמֵת הָאִישׁ... לְבַדּוֹ' to exempt the minor woman from the death penalty.

items.text: Rava's interpretation and the case of ten men
items.text_en: Rava's interpretation and the case of ten men
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the verse 'umetu gam shneihem' excludes cases of 'ma'aseh chidudim', and the other opinion holds that such acts are insignificant. A baraita then discusses a case where ten men have intercourse with her and she remains a virgin, with Rabbi ruling that the first is stoned and the rest strangled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the other opinion (Rabbi Yonatan) interprets the verse 'וּמֵתוּ גַּם שְׁנֵיהֶם' (and both of them shall die).
Rava answers that the verse excludes cases of מַעֲשֵׂה חִידּוּדִים (acts of rubbing without full penetration).
The Gemara asks how the other opinion (Rabbi Yoshiya) treats such acts.
The Gemara explains that the other opinion holds that such acts are insignificant and do not constitute intercourse.
The Gemara asks how the other opinion (Rabbi Yoshiya) interprets the word 'לְבַדּוֹ' (alone).
A baraita is cited: if ten men have intercourse with her and she remains a virgin, all are stoned (according to the first opinion).
Rabbi rules that the first man is stoned and the rest are executed by strangulation.

items.text: Rabbi's view on the daughter of a priest and the dispute between Rav Bibi and Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Rabbi's view on the daughter of a priest and the dispute between Rav Bibi and Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi's interpretation of the verse regarding a priest's daughter, and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua explains that Rabbi follows Rabbi Yishmael's view that a betrothed woman is executed by burning, not a married one. Rav Bibi bar Abaye then corrects this, stating that Rabbi follows Rabbi Meir's view that a woman married to a disqualified person is executed by strangulation.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi's interpretation of the verse regarding a priest's daughter who profanes herself through harlotry, linking it to the verse 'and the man who lay with her shall die alone'.
The gemara asks what Rabbi means by his statement.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua explains that Rabbi follows Rabbi Yishmael's view that a betrothed woman is executed by burning, not a married one, and that the verse speaks of the initial act of harlotry.
The gemara asks what the word 'וכן' (and similarly) in the baraita means.

The gemara explains that 'וכן' means just as there (in the verse about the betrothed maiden) the verse speaks of the initial act of intercourse, so too here (regarding the priest's daughter) the verse speaks of the initial act.
Rav Bibi bar Abaye objects, stating that the master (Rav Yosef) did not say this explanation.

sub.text: Rav Bibi bar Abaye's alternative answer
sub.text_en: Rav Bibi bar Abaye's alternative answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Bibi bar Abaye states that Rabbi actually follows Rabbi Meir's view that a woman married to a disqualified person is executed by strangulation.

Rav Bibi bar Abaye resolves the baraita: if the initial profanation of the priest's daughter is through harlotry (while betrothed to a fit person), she is executed by burning; otherwise (if married to a disqualified person), by strangulation, and the gemara then asks again what 'וכן' means.

items.text: Mishnah: The *Mesit* and the procedure of ambush
items.text_en: Mishnah: The *Mesit* and the procedure of ambush
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines the *mesit* as a layperson who entices another layperson, and describes the unique method of hiding witnesses to catch him. It details the dialogue and the conditions under which he is executed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a mnemonic note, indicating the following is a sign.
The Mishnah defines the *mesit* (inciter) as an ordinary person who entices another ordinary person, describing his speech about an idol's supposed powers.
The Mishnah states a general principle: for all other capital offenses, the court does not hide witnesses, except for this case of the *mesit*.
The Mishnah explains that if the *mesit* spoke to two people, they are his witnesses and bring him to court; if to one, that person says he has friends who are interested.
The Mishnah describes the procedure for hiding witnesses behind a fence when the *mesit* is cunning, including the dialogue and the consequence if he persists.

items.text: Mishnah: List of incriminating statements
items.text_en: Mishnah: List of incriminating statements
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the specific phrases that constitute enticement to idolatry, including various forms of worship.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the specific phrases that constitute enticement to idolatry, including various forms of worship.

items.text: Gemara's initial inference from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's initial inference from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's wording that a prophet who entices is executed by strangulation, and that the *mesit* of a group is executed by strangulation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's wording that a prophet who entices is executed by strangulation, and that the mesit of a group is executed by strangulation.

items.text: Debate over the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Debate over the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which Tanna authored the Mishnah, suggesting it follows Rabbi Shimon, but then notes a contradiction with the later clause about the *maddiach*. Ravina resolves that the entire Mishnah follows the Rabbis and teaches 'not only this but also that'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna authored the Mishnah, suggesting it follows Rabbi Shimon based on a baraita about a prophet who leads astray.
The Gemara objects that the later clause about the *maddiach* (one who leads a city astray) follows the Rabbis, creating a contradiction with the first clause attributed to Rabbi Shimon.
Ravina resolves that the entire Mishnah follows the Rabbis, teaching 'not only this but also that' (לא זו אף זו) — the first clause about the *mesit* is included even though it is not the main point.

items.text: Rav Papa's alternative explanation and the story of ben Satada
items.text_en: Rav Papa's alternative explanation and the story of ben Satada
items.desc_en: Rav Papa explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'the *mesit* is a layperson' refers specifically to the law of ambush. A *baraita* details the ambush procedure, and the Gemara recounts the execution of ben Satada, clarifying his parentage.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'the mesit is a layperson' refers specifically to the law of ambush (הכמנה).
A baraita is cited stating that for all other capital offenders, ambush is not used, except for the mesit.
The baraita details the ambush procedure: lighting a candle in the inner room, placing witnesses in the outer room, and the mesit's entrapment.
The baraita recounts that they did so to ben Satada in Lod, and they hanged him on the eve of Passover.

The Gemara clarifies ben Satada's parentage: Rav Chisda explains that his mother was Satada (a sotah), and the popular saying in Pumbedita identifies her as 'straying from her husband' (סטת דא מבעלה).

items.text: Mishnah: The *Maddiach* and the *Mekhashef*
items.text_en: Mishnah: The *Maddiach* and the *Mekhashef*
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines the *maddiach* as one who says 'let us go and worship idolatry', and distinguishes between a sorcerer who performs an act (liable) and one who merely tricks the eyes (exempt). Rabbi Akiva cites Rabbi Yehoshua's example of cucumber gatherers.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines the *maddiach* as one who says 'let us go and worship idolatry'.
The Mishnah distinguishes between a sorcerer who performs an act (liable) and one who merely tricks the eyes (exempt).
Rabbi Akiva cites Rabbi Yehoshua's example of two cucumber gatherers, one liable and one exempt.
The Mishnah concludes: the performer of an act is liable, the eye-trickster is exempt.

items.text: Gemara on the *Mekhashef* and his execution
items.text_en: Gemara on the *Mekhashef* and his execution
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says the *maddiach* refers to the enticers of an apostate city. A *baraita* teaches that both men and women are liable for sorcery, but the Torah mentions 'sorceress' because women are more common. Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva debate the mode of execution for a sorcerer, using different scriptural analogies.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav explains that the term 'המדיח' (the enticer) in the Mishnah refers to the enticers of an apostate city (עיר הנדחת).
A baraita teaches that the verse 'מְכַשֵּׁפָה' (sorceress) applies to both men and women, but the Torah uses the feminine form because women are more commonly involved in sorcery.
The Gemara asks: what is the mode of execution for a sorcerer?
Rabbi Yose HaGelili argues that the sorcerer is executed by the sword (סייף), deriving a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the phrase 'לֹא תְחַיֶּה' used in the context of the Canaanite nations.
Rabbi Akiva argues that the sorcerer is executed by stoning (סקילה), deriving a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the phrase 'לֹא יִחְיֶה' used in the context of bestiality.
Rabbi Yose HaGelili objects that his own analogy uses the identical phrase 'לֹא תְחַיֶּה' (identical wording), whereas Rabbi Akiva's analogy uses a different phrase 'לֹא יִחְיֶה' (different wording).

Rabbi Akiva rejects the objection, arguing that his analogy compares Israel (the sorcerer) to Israel (the case of bestiality), where the Torah prescribes multiple death penalties, whereas Rabbi Yose's analogy compares Israel to gentiles, for whom the Torah only prescribes one death penalty.

items.text: Ben Azzai's argument for stoning the sorcerer
items.text_en: Ben Azzai's argument for stoning the sorcerer
items.desc_en: Ben Azzai argues that the sorcerer is executed by stoning, based on a verbal analogy linking the verse about sorcery to the verse about bestiality, which is punished by stoning.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the topic of a single death penalty for the sorcerer.
Ben Azzai argues that the sorcerer is executed by stoning, based on a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) linking the verse about sorcery to the verse about bestiality, which is punished by stoning.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's alternative derivation and the Gemara's question
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's alternative derivation and the Gemara's question
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda objects to Ben Azzai's method, deriving stoning for sorcery from the explicit mention of ov and yid'oni (types of sorcerers) which are stoned. The Gemara questions why these two cases are not considered two verses that come as one, which normally do not teach a general principle.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda objects to Ben Azzai's method, arguing that the juxtaposition is unnecessary; instead, the explicit cases of אוֹב וְיִדְּעוֹנִי (types of sorcerers) teach that sorcery is punished by stoning through a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy).

The Gemara questions Rabbi Yehuda's position: since אוֹב and יִדְּעוֹנִי are two verses that come as one (שני כתובים הבאים כאחד), they should not teach a general principle, undermining his derivation.

items.text: Rabbi Zecharya's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Zecharya's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zecharya resolves the difficulty by stating that Rabbi Yehuda holds that two verses that come as one do teach a general principle.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zecharya resolves the difficulty by stating that Rabbi Yehuda holds that two verses that come as one (שני כתובים הבאים כאחד) do teach a general principle.

items.text: Etymology of sorcery and the power of Rabbi Chanina
items.text_en: Etymology of sorcery and the power of Rabbi Chanina
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that sorcerers are called 'mekhashefim' because they weaken the heavenly retinue. Rabbi Chanina adds that the verse 'There is none else besides Him' applies even to sorcery. A story illustrates Rabbi Chanina's immunity to sorcery due to his merit, despite the general principle that sorcery can affect the heavenly realm.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks why sorcerers are called 'mekhashefim' and answers that they weaken (מכחישין) the heavenly retinue (פמליא של מעלה).
Rabbi Chanina cites the verse 'אין עוד מלבדו' (There is none else besides Him) to assert that even sorcery is subject to God's exclusive power.

A story illustrates Rabbi Chanina's immunity to sorcery: a woman tried to take dust from under his foot for sorcery, but he told her that if she succeeds, she may proceed, because 'אין עוד מלבדו' is written.

The gemara raises a contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan said sorcery weakens the heavenly retinue, yet Rabbi Chanina was immune; it resolves that Rabbi Chanina is exceptional because his merit (זכות) is great.

items.text: Distinguishing sorcery from demonic acts and the laws of sorcery
items.text_en: Distinguishing sorcery from demonic acts and the laws of sorcery
items.desc_en: Rabbi Aiyvu bar Nagarei distinguishes between demonic acts and sorcery based on the verses. Abaye further distinguishes by whether the act respects a vessel. Abaye then outlines the halakhot of sorcery, comparing them to Shabbat laws: some are punishable by stoning, some are forbidden but not punishable, and some are permitted ab initio, like the creation of a calf by Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Oshaya.

sub.text: Rabbi Aiyvu bar Nagarei citing Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Aiyvu bar Nagarei citing Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Aiyvu bar Nagarei in the name of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba distinguishes between demonic acts (מעשה שדים) and sorcery (מעשה כשפים) based on the verses 'בלטיהם' and 'בלהטיהם', citing the parallel to 'להט החרב המתהפכת'.
Abaye adds a practical distinction: an act that respects a vessel (קפיד אמנא) is demonic, while one that does not is sorcery.
Abaye introduces a general principle: the laws of sorcery parallel those of Shabbat, with three categories — liable to stoning, exempt but forbidden, and permitted לכתחילה (ab initio).

The gemara specifies the categories: performing a sorcery act is liable to stoning, deceiving the eyes is exempt but forbidden, and permitted לכתחילה (ab initio) is illustrated by Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Oshaya who studied the laws of creation each Shabbat eve and created a third-born calf and ate it.

items.text: Limits of demonic power and optical illusions
items.text_en: Limits of demonic power and optical illusions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer and Rav Papa debate whether demons can create creatures smaller than a barley grain. A story with Rav and Rabbi Chiyya demonstrates that an apparent transformation of a camel was merely an optical illusion (achizat einayim), as the camel's blood and flesh were not present afterward.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi testifies that he saw the father of Karna (a demon) spit out rolled loaves from his nostrils, demonstrating demonic power.
Rabbi Eliezer deduces from the verse that a demon cannot create a creature smaller than a barley grain.
Rav Papa objects that a demon cannot create even a camel-sized creature, but can only gather existing matter.

sub.text: Story of Rav and Rabbi Chiyya
sub.text_en: Story of Rav and Rabbi Chiyya
sub.desc_en: Rav tells Rabbi Chiyya about an Arab who appeared to cut and revive a camel, and Rabbi Chiyya explains it was merely an optical illusion (אחיזת עיניים) since no blood or flesh was present.

items.text: Stories of sorcery and its detection
items.text_en: Stories of sorcery and its detection
items.desc_en: Two stories illustrate sorcery: Ze'iri in Alexandria buys a donkey that turns into a plank of wood when brought to water, and Yannai encounters a hostess who turns water into scorpions and then into wine, exposing her sorcery.

sub.desc_en: Ze'iri goes to Alexandria, buys a donkey that turns into a plank of wood when brought to water, and is told that only because he is Ze'iri do they return his money, as everyone checks such purchases with water.

Yannai stays at an inn, detects sorcery when the hostess's lips move while serving water, spills it to reveal scorpions, then turns the tables by making her drink wine that becomes a donkey, and she rides it through the market.

items.text: The single frog of the plague
items.text_en: The single frog of the plague
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and a Tannaic dispute discuss the plague of frogs: Rabbi Akiva says one frog multiplied to fill Egypt, while Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says one frog summoned the others.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar interprets the singular 'frog' in the verse to mean one frog that spawned and filled all Egypt.
Rabbi Akiva agrees with Rabbi Elazar's position that one frog multiplied to fill Egypt.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya rebukes Rabbi Akiva for engaging in aggadah and tells him to focus on halachic topics of negaim and ohalot.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya offers his own interpretation: one frog whistled and summoned the others.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Akiva's source
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Akiva's source
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Akiva could have learned the law from Rabbi Yehoshua when he was a student of Rabbi Eliezer, citing a baraita about Rabbi Eliezer's illness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Akiva could have learned the law from Rabbi Yehoshua, given that he was a student of Rabbi Eliezer, citing a baraita about Rabbi Eliezer's illness.

items.text: The incident with Hurkanus
items.text_en: The incident with Hurkanus
items.desc_en: The baraita describes how Rabbi Eliezer's son Hurkanus entered to remove his tefillin on Shabbat eve, and Rabbi Eliezer rebuked him for prioritizing a lesser prohibition over a capital one.

sub.desc_en: The baraita sets the scene: it was Shabbat eve, and Rabbi Eliezer's son Hurkanus entered to remove his tefillin.
Rabbi Eliezer rebukes his son for prioritizing the lesser prohibition of removing tefillin on Shabbat (a שבות) over the capital prohibition of violating Shabbat itself (a סקילה).

items.text: The sages visit and Rabbi Eliezer's rebuke
items.text_en: The sages visit and Rabbi Eliezer's rebuke
