items.desc_en: The sages enter and sit four cubits away. Rabbi Eliezer asks why they came, and they say to learn Torah. He rebukes them for not coming earlier, and Rabbi Akiva asks about his own fate, receiving a harsh answer.

sub.desc_en: The sages see that Rabbi Eliezer's mind is settled, enter, and sit four cubits away from him.
Rabbi Eliezer asks the sages why they came.
The sages answer that they came to learn Torah.
Rabbi Eliezer rebukes them for not coming earlier.
The sages excuse themselves, saying they had no time.
Rabbi Eliezer declares that he suspects they will die a natural death (not a righteous one).
Rabbi Akiva asks Rabbi Eliezer what his own fate will be.
Rabbi Eliezer answers that Rabbi Akiva's fate will be harsher than that of the others.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's lament and his teaching of Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's lament and his teaching of Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer laments his vast Torah knowledge, comparing his arms to scrolls, and recounts how he taught Rabbi Akiva the laws of planting cucumbers, demonstrating miraculous results.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer places his arms on his heart and laments that his Torah knowledge, like scrolls, was vast and fully transmitted, yet his students absorbed only a tiny fraction.
Rabbi Eliezer adds that he taught hundreds of laws about a bright skin-blemish (בהרת עז) and about planting cucumbers, but only Rabbi Akiva ever asked about them.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer's story about Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's story about Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer recounts how he taught Rabbi Akiva the laws of planting cucumbers, and with a single teaching the field filled with cucumbers, and with another they all gathered to one place.

items.text: Questions on purity and Rabbi Eliezer's death
items.text_en: Questions on purity and Rabbi Eliezer's death
items.desc_en: The sages ask about the purity of various objects, and Rabbi Eliezer declares them impure but purifiable. He then answers about a shoe on an amum, declares it pure, and dies. Rabbi Yehoshua declares the vow (of excommunication) released.

sub.desc_en: The sages ask Rabbi Eliezer about the purity status of a ball, a shoe-last, an amulet, a pearl bag, and a small scale.
Rabbi Eliezer declares these objects טמאין (impure) but says their purification is possible in their current state.
The sages ask about the purity of a shoe placed on the shoe-last (אִמּוּם).

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer's final answer and death
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's final answer and death
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer declares the shoe pure, and then his soul departs in purity.
Rabbi Yehoshua stands and declares that the vow of excommunication against Rabbi Eliezer is released.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's mourning and eulogy
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's mourning and eulogy
items.desc_en: After Shabbat, Rabbi Akiva meets Rabbi Eliezer's funeral procession, beats himself until blood flows, and eulogizes him as 'my father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its horsemen.'

sub.desc_en: After Shabbat, Rabbi Akiva encounters Rabbi Eliezer's funeral procession and beats himself until blood flows.
Rabbi Akiva eulogizes Rabbi Eliezer as 'my father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its horsemen,' lamenting that he has no one to present his wealth of Torah to.

items.text: Resolution of the Gemara's question
items.text_en: Resolution of the Gemara's question
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Akiva learned the law from Rabbi Eliezer but did not understand it, then learned it again from Rabbi Yehoshua who explained it to him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that Rabbi Akiva learned the law from Rabbi Eliezer but did not understand it, and then learned it again from Rabbi Yehoshua who explained it to him.

items.text: Defense of Rabbi Eliezer's actions
items.text_en: Defense of Rabbi Eliezer's actions
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Eliezer could perform a miraculous act, and answers that it was for the purpose of teaching, which is permitted as one may learn to understand and instruct.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Eliezer could perform a miraculous act, given the Mishnah's rule that one who performs a forbidden act on Shabbat is liable.
The Gemara answers that learning is different, citing the principle that one may learn to understand and instruct, even if the act itself is forbidden.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah defines when a son becomes a ben sorer u'moreh: from the onset of two pubic hairs until the lower beard (pubic hair) surrounds, but not the upper beard. It derives from the verse that it applies to a son, not a daughter, and not an adult man; a minor is exempt because he has not yet entered the age of mitzvot.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines the age range for a ben sorer u'moreh (rebellious son) and derives from the verse that it applies only to a son, not a daughter or adult, and a minor is exempt.

items.text: Gemara's first question and challenge
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state that a minor is exempt, since the verse already says 'son' and not 'man', implying a minor. It then challenges: since the ben sorer u'moreh is executed for his future end, perhaps even a minor should be liable?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to state that a minor is exempt, since the verse already says 'son' and not 'man', implying a minor, and challenges that the verse should not need to exempt him.
The Gemara challenges that since the ben sorer u'moreh is executed for his future end, perhaps even a minor should be liable.
The Gemara notes that the verse 'son' and not 'man' implies a minor, further complicating the exemption.

items.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav's answer
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav explains that the verse 'When a man has a son' implies a son close to the strength of a man, i.e., near adulthood, excluding a minor.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav explains that the verse 'כי יהיה לאיש בן' (When a man has a son) implies a son close to the strength of a man, i.e., near adulthood, excluding a minor.

items.text: Discussion of the lower beard
items.text_en: Discussion of the lower beard
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on the Mishnah's phrase 'until the lower beard surrounds'. Rabbi Chiya teaches it means until the pubic hair forms a crown. Rav Dimi adds that it refers to the hair around the pubic area, not the testicles.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's phrase 'until the lower beard surrounds' as the starting point for discussion.
Rabbi Chiya teaches that 'until the lower beard surrounds' means until the pubic hair forms a crown (עֲטָרָה).
Rav Dimi adds that the reference is to the hair surrounding the pubic area (גִּיד), not the testicles (בֵּיצִים).

items.text: Rav Chisda's teaching and its derivation
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's teaching and its derivation
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda teaches that if a minor fathers a son, that son cannot become a ben sorer u'moreh, derived from the verse 'for a man a son' – a son of a man, not a son of a son. The Gemara questions whether this verse is needed for Rav's teaching, and concludes that the extra wording implies both teachings.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda teaches that if a minor fathers a son, that son cannot become a ben sorer u'moreh, derived from the verse 'for a man a son' – a son of a man, not a son of a son.
The Gemara objects that this verse is already needed for Rav Yehuda's teaching that 'a man's son' means a son close to his manhood.
The Gemara answers that the extra wording 'for a man a son' (לְאִישׁ בֵּן) instead of 'a son to a man' (בֵּן לְאִישׁ) implies both teachings.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the entire verse comes only for Rav Chisda's teaching, not for Rav's.
The Gemara resolves that if the verse were only for Rav Chisda, it would have said 'a man's son' (בֶּן אִישׁ); the extra wording 'for a man a son' (לְאִישׁ בֵּן) implies both teachings.

items.text: Rabbah's disagreement
items.text_en: Rabbah's disagreement
items.desc_en: Rabbah disagrees with Rav Chisda's premise, arguing that a minor cannot father children at all. He derives this from the verse about a man with no redeemer, which must refer to a convert who died without heirs, implying that a minor cannot have children.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces Rabbah's disagreement with Rav Chisda, asserting that a minor cannot father children, and cites the verse 'וְאִם אֵין לָאִישׁ גֹּאֵל' (if the man has no redeemer) to challenge the premise that every Israelite has a redeemer.

Rabbah resolves the difficulty by explaining that the verse refers specifically to the case of a convert's stolen property (גזל הגר), where the convert died without heirs, implying that a minor cannot have children to inherit.

items.text: Opening Gemara: Distinction between 'ish' and 'katan' regarding redemption
items.text_en: Opening Gemara: Distinction between 'ish' and 'katan' regarding redemption
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Torah's use of 'ish' (man) implies that one must investigate whether a murderer has redeemers, but for a minor (katan) it is assumed he has none.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Torah's use of 'איש' (man) requires investigating whether a murderer has redeemers, while for a minor (קטן) it is assumed he has none.

items.text: Abaye's objection and Rava's answer: A nine-year-old is considered 'ish' for intercourse
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and Rava's answer: A nine-year-old is considered 'ish' for intercourse
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that a nine-year-old and one day, who is fit for intercourse, is also called 'ish' by the Torah. Rava responds that such a child can have intercourse but cannot father children, comparing him to unripe produce.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects by citing a baraita that includes a nine-year-old and one day in the category of 'איש' (man) for intercourse, challenging the exclusion of minors.
Rava answers that a nine-year-old can have intercourse but cannot father children, comparing him to unripe produce that has not reached a third of its growth.

items.text: Beit Chizkiya's derivation and the meaning of 'mezid'
items.text_en: Beit Chizkiya's derivation and the meaning of 'mezid'
items.desc_en: Beit Chizkiya teaches that the verse 'When a man (ish) acts wantonly' implies that only an adult can both act wantonly and produce seed, excluding a minor. Rav Mordechai asks Rav Ashi about the meaning of 'mezid', and they connect it to cooking (boiling).

sub.text: Baraita of the school of Hezekiah
sub.text_en: Baraita of the school of Hezekiah
sub.desc_en: The school of Hezekiah teaches that 'איש' implies one who deliberately sins and produces seed, excluding a minor; Rav Mordechai asks Rav Ashi how 'יזד' is known to mean cooking, citing the verse about Jacob cooking a stew.

sub.text: Rav Mordechai's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Mordechai's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Mordechai asks Rav Ashi how we know that the word 'mezid' refers to cooking.
Rav Ashi answers by citing the verse 'And Jacob cooked a stew' to show that 'mezid' means cooking.

items.text: Challenge from Beit Rabbi Yishmael: 'Ben' excludes the father
items.text_en: Challenge from Beit Rabbi Yishmael: 'Ben' excludes the father
items.desc_en: Beit Rabbi Yishmael taught that the word 'ben' (son) in the context of the rebellious son excludes the father. The Gemara analyzes the scenario: if the father conceived after reaching majority and gave birth before growing a beard, there is insufficient time (only three months for the rebellious son). Therefore, it must be that the father conceived while a minor, proving that a minor can father children.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous conclusion by citing the teaching of Beit Rabbi Yishmael that the word 'בן' (son) excludes the father, implying a minor cannot father a child.

The Gemara analyzes the scenario: if the father conceived after reaching majority and gave birth before growing a beard, there is insufficient time (only three months for the rebellious son); therefore, it must be that the father conceived while a minor, proving that a minor can father children.

items.text: Rejection: The father conceived after majority and gave birth after beard
items.text_en: Rejection: The father conceived after majority and gave birth after beard
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, suggesting that the father conceived after reaching majority and gave birth after growing a beard. The difficulty with Rabbi Kruspadai's three-month limit is resolved by a statement from the West: 'ben' excludes one who is fit to be called 'father' (i.e., an adult).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the father conceived after two pubic hairs and gave birth after the beard fully grew; the baraita means 'בן' excludes one who is fit to be called a father.

items.text: Rabbi Kruspadai's statement on the duration of the rebellious son
items.text_en: Rabbi Kruspadai's statement on the duration of the rebellious son
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Kruspadai in the name of Rabbi Shabtai: the entire period of the rebellious son is only three months. The Mishnah states it is from bringing two hairs until the beard surrounds; the Gemara explains that either condition alone suffices.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Kruspadai quoting Rabbi Shabtai states that the entire period of a rebellious son is only three months, and the Mishnah's criteria of two pubic hairs and full beard are interpreted flexibly.
The Gemara questions this by citing the Mishnah which states the period is from bringing two hairs until the beard surrounds.
The Gemara resolves that either condition alone suffices: if the beard surrounds even before three months, or if three months pass even without the beard surrounding.

items.text: Inference: A seven-month pregnancy is not recognizable at one-third of its term
items.text_en: Inference: A seven-month pregnancy is not recognizable at one-third of its term
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov from Nehar Pekod, citing Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua, infers from Rabbi Kruspadai's statement that a woman who gives birth at seven months does not have her pregnancy recognizable at one-third of her days (i.e., at two months and ten days). Otherwise, the three-month period would be unnecessary.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov from Nehar Pekod citing Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov from Nehar Pekod citing Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov from Nehar Pekod, sitting before Ravina, infers from Rabbi Kruspadai's statement that a woman who gives birth at seven months does not have her pregnancy recognizable at one-third of her days.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov from Nehar Pekod's reasoning
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov from Nehar Pekod's reasoning
sub.desc_en: He argues that if the pregnancy were recognizable at one-third of the term, then the three-month period for the wayward son would be unnecessary, as two months and ten days would suffice.

items.text: Ravina's response: Follow the majority
items.text_en: Ravina's response: Follow the majority
items.desc_en: Ravina responds that even if the pregnancy is recognizable at one-third, one should follow the majority (of pregnancies that last nine months), so the three-month period is still needed.

sub.desc_en: Ravina answers that the pregnancy is indeed recognizable at one-third, but one follows the majority (רוב) in such cases.

items.text: Objection: Do we follow the majority in capital cases?
items.text_en: Objection: Do we follow the majority in capital cases?
items.desc_en: Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua objects that in capital cases we do not follow the majority, citing the verse 'and the congregation shall judge and the congregation shall save'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua objects: in capital cases, do we follow the majority? The Torah says 'ושפטו העדה והצילו העדה' (the congregation shall judge and rescue), not rely on majority.

items.text: Ravina's counter: We do follow the majority in capital cases
items.text_en: Ravina's counter: We do follow the majority in capital cases
items.desc_en: Ravina responds that we do follow the majority in capital cases, citing a Mishnah where two witnesses give different dates and their testimony is upheld because most people err in the month's intercalation.

sub.desc_en: Ravina rejects the objection, citing a Mishnah where witnesses disagree on the date but their testimony is upheld because most people err in calculating the month's intercalation, showing that majority is followed even in capital cases.

Ravina cites a Mishnah where two witnesses give different dates and their testimony is upheld because most people err in the month's intercalation, proving that we do follow the majority in capital cases.

items.text: Support from Rabbi Yirmeya: A three-year-old girl's status
items.text_en: Support from Rabbi Yirmeya: A three-year-old girl's status
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya from Difti brings a Mishnah as support: a three-year-old and one day old girl can be betrothed through intercourse, and if a yavam has intercourse with her, he acquires her, and she is subject to the laws of a married woman, including capital punishment for adulterers, while she is exempt.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya from Difti's supporting evidence
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya from Difti's supporting evidence
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya from Difti adds supporting evidence from a Mishnah about a three-year-old girl who can be betrothed through intercourse, and if a yavam (levir) has intercourse with her, he acquires her, and she is liable for capital punishment for adultery, while she is exempt.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution about the mishnah's case
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution about the mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mishnah holds a man liable for intercourse with a minor, suggesting she might be an איילונית (barren woman) and thus not betrothed. It rejects this by invoking the principle of following the majority (רובא), since most women are not איילונית. It then reinterprets the mishnah's 'liable' as referring to a sacrifice, and explains the other clauses as dealing with a father's case or where she accepted him.

items.text: Baraita on a woman who seduces her minor son, and the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Baraita on a woman who seduces her minor son, and the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: a woman who seduces her minor son and he has intercourse with her – Beit Shammai disqualifies her from the priesthood, Beit Hillel permits her. Rav Chisda quoting Ze'iri explains that all agree that intercourse with a boy of nine years and one day is significant, and with a boy under eight is not; the dispute is only about a boy of eight, where Beit Shammai learns from the early generations (דורות הראשונים) that an eight-year-old can father a child, and Beit Hillel does not.

items.text: First proof from the early generations: David's lineage and Ahithophel's age
items.text_en: First proof from the early generations: David's lineage and Ahithophel's age
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the early generations that an eight-year-old can father a child. It calculates the ages of David, Solomon, Absalom, and Ahithophel from biblical verses, concluding that Ahithophel fathered a child at age eight. The calculation involves subtracting years and accounting for leap years.

items.text: Rejection of the first proof: alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rejection of the first proof: alternative explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, suggesting that both Ahithophel and his wife might have been older: he fathered at nine, and she gave birth at six because women are stronger. It notes that she already had a child previously, supporting this possibility.

items.text: Second proof from Terah's genealogy: Sarah's birth at age eight
items.text_en: Second proof from Terah's genealogy: Sarah's birth at age eight
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another proof from the genealogy of Terah. It calculates that Abraham was two years older than Haran, and Sarah (Yiscah) was Haran's daughter. Since Abraham was ten years older than Sarah, and two years older than Haran, it follows that Haran fathered Sarah at age eight.

items.text: Rejection of the second proof: the verses list by wisdom, not age
items.text_en: Rejection of the second proof: the verses list by wisdom, not age
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects this proof, suggesting that Abraham might have been the youngest brother, and the verses list them by wisdom, not age. It supports this with the example of Noah's sons, where Shem is listed first but is actually younger than Japheth, as shown by calculations from the flood and Shem's age.

items.text: Third proof from Bezalel's genealogy: fathering at age eight
items.text_en: Third proof from Bezalel's genealogy: fathering at age eight
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana reports an alternative tradition from Rav Zevid: the proof comes from Bezalel's genealogy. Calculations show that Bezalel was 13 when building the Tabernacle, and his father Hur was born when Caleb was 40. Subtracting years and leap years, it is found that each generation fathered at age eight.

items.text: Transition to the next topic: a son, not a daughter
items.text_en: Transition to the next topic: a son, not a daughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new discussion, stating that the law of the wayward and rebellious son (בן סורר ומורה) applies to a son, not a daughter. Rabbi Shimon comments that it would be fitting for a daughter to be subject to this law, but the verse specifies 'son'.

items.text: Opening statement: the law applies only to a son, not a daughter
items.text_en: Opening statement: the law applies only to a son, not a daughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the verse's use of 'ben' (son) excludes a daughter from the law of the rebellious son, even though daughters are also commonly found in sin. This is a decree of the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the verse's use of 'ben' (son) excludes a daughter from the law of the rebellious son, even though daughters are also commonly found in sin; this is a decree of the verse.

items.text: Mishnah: Minimum amounts and exclusions
items.text_en: Mishnah: Minimum amounts and exclusions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a son becomes liable when he eats a tartemar of meat and drinks half a log of Italian wine. Rabbi Yosei says a maneh of meat and a log of wine. It then lists cases where eating does not make him liable, such as eating at a mitzvah meal, eating non-kosher meat, or not eating meat or drinking wine. The prooftext is 'zolel v'sovei'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the minimum amounts of meat and wine that make a son liable as a בן סורר ומורה (rebellious son), with a dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yosei.
The Mishnah lists exclusions where eating does not make the son liable, such as eating at a mitzvah meal or eating non-kosher meat.
The Mishnah concludes that the son is not liable unless he eats meat and drinks wine, citing the verse 'zolel v'sovei' and a supporting verse from Proverbs.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's deduction about tartemar
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's deduction about tartemar
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira admits he does not know what a tartemar is, but deduces from Rabbi Yosei's doubling of wine that he also doubles the meat, making a tartemar half a maneh.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira questions the meaning of 'tarteimar' and deduces from Rabbi Yosei's doubling of wine that it is half a maneh.

items.text: Rav Huna's conditions: cheap meat and wine, and the definition of 'chai'
items.text_en: Rav Huna's conditions: cheap meat and wine, and the definition of 'chai'
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that the son is only liable if he buys cheap meat and wine, as per the verse 'zolel v'sovei'. He also says he must eat raw meat and drink undiluted wine. The Gemara objects from Rabba and Rav Yosef, who say raw meat and undiluted wine do not make him liable. Ravina resolves that 'chai' means partially cooked meat and partially diluted wine.

sub.text: Rav Huna (via Rav Hanan bar Molada)
sub.text_en: Rav Huna (via Rav Hanan bar Molada)
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that the son is only liable if he buys cheap meat and cheap wine, as derived from the verse 'zolel v'sovei' (glutton and drunkard).

sub.text: Rav Huna (via Rav Hanan bar Molada)
sub.text_en: Rav Huna (via Rav Hanan bar Molada)
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna further states that the son must eat raw meat and drink undiluted wine to be liable.
The Gemara objects: Rabba and Rav Yosef both say that eating raw meat and drinking undiluted wine does not make him a rebellious son.
Ravina resolves that 'chai' (raw) here means partially diluted wine and partially cooked meat, like the meat thieves eat.

items.text: Rabba and Rav Yosef: salted meat and wine from the vat
items.text_en: Rabba and Rav Yosef: salted meat and wine from the vat
items.desc_en: Rabba and Rav Yosef rule that eating salted meat and drinking wine from the vat does not make one a rebellious son. The Gemara brings a parallel from the laws of Tisha b'Av, where such items are permitted. It then discusses the definitions of 'salted meat' (as long as it is like peace-offerings) and 'wine from the vat' (as long as it is fermenting, up to three days). The Gemara distinguishes between the two contexts: there it is about joy, here it is about being drawn after it.

sub.desc_en: Rabba and Rav Yosef rule that eating salted meat and drinking wine from the vat does not make one a rebellious son.
The Gemara cites a parallel baraita from the laws of Tisha b'Av, where salted meat and wine from the vat are permitted.
The Gemara asks for the definitional limits of 'salted meat' and 'wine from the vat'.

sub.text: Rabbi Chanina bar Kahana and Gemara's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Kahana and Gemara's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Kahana defines salted meat as long as it is like peace-offerings, and the Gemara defines wine from the vat as fermenting up to three days, but distinguishes the contexts: there (Tisha b'Av) it is about joy, here (rebellious son) it is about being drawn after it, so wine is excluded up to forty days.

items.text: Aggadic teachings on wine
items.text_en: Aggadic teachings on wine
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan says wine was created only to comfort mourners and reward the wicked. Rabbi Yitzchak and Rava expound on the verse 'Al te're yayin ki yit'adam', interpreting it as wine that reddens faces in this world and whitens them in the next, or that its end is blood. Rav Kahana and Rava note that 'tirosh' can be read as 'rosh' (head) or 'rash' (poor), and 'yeshameach' as 'mesame'ach' (gladdens) or 'meshamem' (devastates).

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan states that wine was created only to comfort mourners and reward the wicked, citing the verse 'תנו שכר לאובד ויין למרי נפש'.
Rabbi Yitzchak interprets the verse 'אל תרא יין כי יתאדם' as wine that reddens the faces of the wicked in this world and whitens them in the world to come.
Rava offers an alternative interpretation: 'אל תרא יין כי יתאדם' means do not look at wine whose end is blood.

Rav Kahana notes the word 'תירוש' can be read as 'תירש' (you will inherit) or 'תירש' (you will become poor), implying that if one merits, wine makes him a head (ראש), and if not, it makes him poor (רש).
Rava notes the word 'ישמח' can be read as 'ישמח' (gladdens) or 'ישמם' (devastates), concluding that wine and spices make one wise.

items.text: More aggadic teachings: the dangers of wine and the thirteen vavs
items.text_en: More aggadic teachings: the dangers of wine and the thirteen vavs
items.desc_en: Rav Amram quotes Rabbi Chanina on the verse 'Le'mi oy...' which can be expounded from beginning to end or end to beginning. The Gemara then cites a drasha by Oveir Galila'ah, listing thirteen 'vav's in the story of Noah's drunkenness, showing the chain of events caused by wine.

sub.text: Rav Amram bar Rabbi Shimon bar Abba quoting Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rav Amram bar Rabbi Shimon bar Abba quoting Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rav Amram quotes Rabbi Chanina on the verse 'לְמִי אוֹי' (Who has woe?), and Rav Dimi reports that in the West they say this verse can be expounded from beginning to end or end to beginning.
Oveir Galila'ah lists thirteen 'ו' (vav) conjunctions in the story of Noah's drunkenness, showing the chain of calamities caused by wine.

items.text: What did Cham do to Noah? And the tree of knowledge
items.text_en: What did Cham do to Noah? And the tree of knowledge
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate whether Cham castrated Noah or sodomized him. The Gemara supports both views with scriptural parallels. It then recounts that God criticized Noah for not learning from Adam, who was also brought low by wine, citing the opinion that the Tree of Knowledge was a grapevine.

sub.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate whether Cham castrated Noah or sodomized him.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of the castration view
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the castration view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the one who says Cham castrated Noah derives it from the fact that Noah cursed Canaan, the fourth son, corresponding to the fourth son who would be harmed by castration.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of the sodomy view
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the sodomy view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the one who says Cham sodomized Noah derives it from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between the word 'וַיַּרְא' (saw) here and in the story of Shechem and Dinah.
The Gemara objects: according to the sodomy view, why specifically curse the fourth son? Why not curse Cham directly?
The Gemara resolves that both acts occurred: Cham both castrated and sodomized Noah.

sub.text: Rav Chisda citing Rav Ukva (or Mar Ukva citing Rabbi Zakkai)
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda citing Rav Ukva (or Mar Ukva citing Rabbi Zakkai)
sub.desc_en: God criticizes Noah for not learning from Adam, who was brought low by wine, implying the Tree of Knowledge was a grapevine.
A baraita supports the view that the Tree of Knowledge was a grapevine, as Rabbi Meir explicitly states.

items.text: Opening dispute on the Tree of Knowledge
items.text_en: Opening dispute on the Tree of Knowledge
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute about which fruit was the Tree of Knowledge: Rabbi Yehuda says wheat, Rabbi Nechemya says a fig, and the first opinion says wine, because nothing brings wailing to a person except wine.

sub.desc_en: The first opinion states that the Tree of Knowledge was a vine, because nothing brings wailing to a person except wine.
Rabbi Yehuda says the tree was wheat, because a child cannot call father and mother until tasting grain.
Rabbi Nechemya says the tree was a fig, because they were repaired with the very thing they sinned with, as it is written: 'And they sewed fig leaves.'

items.text: Aggadic exposition of Proverbs 31: Lemuel and his mother
items.text_en: Aggadic exposition of Proverbs 31: Lemuel and his mother
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai explains that Lemuel is Solomon, and his mother rebuked him about wine. She recounts her dedication to bear him and warns him against kings who drink wine and forget God.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai explains that Lemuel is Solomon, and his mother rebuked him by the pillar, interpreting the first phrase as a warning about his father's piety.

sub.text: Mother's speech (via Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai)
sub.text_en: Mother's speech (via Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai)
sub.desc_en: The mother recounts her unique dedication: while other wives of the king ceased seeing him after pregnancy, she pressed in to bear a son who would be energetic and refined.

sub.text: Mother's speech (via Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai)
sub.text_en: Mother's speech (via Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai)
sub.desc_en: The mother contrasts her vow with other women: they vowed a son fit for kingship, but she vowed a son sharp in Torah and fit for prophecy.

sub.text: Mother's rebuke (via Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai) and alternative interpretation
sub.text_en: Mother's rebuke (via Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai) and alternative interpretation
sub.desc_en: The mother warns Solomon against kings who drink wine and forget God, and some say the verse refers to one to whom all the world's secrets are revealed—should he drink and become drunk?

items.text: Solomon's admission to his mother
items.text_en: Solomon's admission to his mother
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak proves that Solomon later admitted his mother was right, citing the verse 'For I am more brutish than any man' – referring to Noah and Adam.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak proves that Solomon later admitted his mother was right, citing the verse 'For I am more brutish than any man' – referring to Noah and Adam.

items.text: Eating at a mitzvah gathering
items.text_en: Eating at a mitzvah gathering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu says the son is not liable unless he eats in a group of worthless people. The Gemara clarifies that even in such a group, if engaged in a mitzvah, he is not drawn after his desire.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the son ate at a mitzvah gathering, he is not liable.
Rabbi Avahu adds that the son is not liable unless he eats in a group composed entirely of worthless people.
The Gemara questions: from the Mishnah, the exemption is only for a mitzvah gathering; otherwise, even if not all are worthless, the son would be liable — contradicting Rabbi Avahu's requirement.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Avahu teaches that even in a group of worthless people, since they are engaged in a mitzvah, the son is not drawn after his desire.

items.text: Eating at the intercalation of the month
items.text_en: Eating at the intercalation of the month
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether meat and wine are served at the intercalation feast, citing a baraita that only bread, legumes, and vegetables are eaten. It resolves that even if he brought meat and wine, since it is a mitzvah, he is not drawn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the mishnah's mention of eating at the intercalation implies that meat and wine are served at that feast.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that states one may only eat bread, grain, and legumes at the intercalation feast, not meat and wine.
The Gemara resolves that even if he brought meat and wine contrary to the baraita, since he is engaged in a mitzvah, he is not drawn after the food.
A baraita is cited detailing the rules of the intercalation feast: at least ten participants, only bread and legumes, and held at night.
The Gemara objects by citing another baraita that contradicts the first, stating the feast is held by day, not by night.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by citing Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba's advice to his sons: enter early and leave early so people hear about you, implying the feast begins at night and ends by day.

items.text: Eating second tithe in Jerusalem and forbidden foods
items.text_en: Eating second tithe in Jerusalem and forbidden foods
items.desc_en: Eating second tithe in Jerusalem is not considered gluttony since it is normal. Rava says eating poultry does not make one a wayward son. The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's list of forbidden foods is to complete the list, not to exclude kosher meat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that eating second tithe in Jerusalem does not make one a wayward son because it is normal consumption.
Rava rules that eating poultry does not make one a wayward son.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's list implies that eating kosher meat does make one a wayward son, contradicting Rava.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's list is merely to complete the enumeration, not to exclude kosher meat.

items.text: Eating a mitzvah or transgression food
items.text_en: Eating a mitzvah or transgression food
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists examples: comforting mourners (mitzvah) and a public fast (transgression). The reason is the verse 'he does not listen to our voice' – meaning the voice of the parents, not the voice of God.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists examples of eating for a mitzvah (comforting mourners) and for a transgression (a public fast).

The Gemara explains the reason: the verse 'איננו שומע בקולנו' (he does not listen to our voice) means the voice of the parents, not the voice of God, so eating for God's command or prohibition does not make him a rebellious son.

items.text: Eating any food without meat, drinking any drink without wine
items.text_en: Eating any food without meat, drinking any drink without wine
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's phrase 'ate any food but not meat' includes dried fig cake; 'drank any drink but not wine' includes honey and milk, as taught in a baraita about entering the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'ate any food but not meat' includes dried fig cake, and 'drank any drink but not wine' includes honey and milk.
A baraita is cited to support the inclusion: one who ate dried fig cake or drank honey and milk and entered the Temple is liable.

items.text: Opening baraita on the requirement of meat and wine
items.text_en: Opening baraita on the requirement of meat and wine
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a son becomes a wayward and rebellious son only if he eats meat and drinks wine. A baraita elaborates that eating any other food or drinking any other beverage does not qualify, citing the verse 'zolel ve'soveh' (glutton and drunkard). Rabbi Zeira adds a homiletical remark about sleeping in the study hall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a baraita stating that a wayward and rebellious son (בן סורר ומורה) is only liable if he eats meat and drinks wine, citing the verse 'zolel ve'soveh' (glutton and drunkard).

The baraita provides additional support from Proverbs, linking gluttony and drunkenness to poverty, and Rabbi Zeira adds a homiletical remark that sleeping in the study hall causes one's Torah to become torn.

items.text: Mishnah: Conditions of theft and domain
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conditions of theft and domain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a son becomes a wayward and rebellious son only if he steals from his father and eats in another's domain. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda adds that he must steal from both his father and his mother.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the conditions for a son becoming a wayward and rebellious son: he must steal from his father and eat in another's domain, and Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda adds that he must steal from both his father and his mother.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's cases
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the rationale behind each case: stealing from his father and eating in his father's domain involves fear (ba'it) but not availability; stealing from others and eating in others' domain involves availability but not fear; the required case is stealing from his father and eating in others' domain, which combines availability and lack of fear.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that stealing from his father and eating in his father's domain involves fear (בעת) but not availability.

The Gemara explains that stealing from others and eating in others' domain involves availability but not fear, and the combination of stealing from others and eating in his father's domain lacks both.
The Gemara concludes that the required case is stealing from his father and eating in others' domain, which combines availability and lack of fear.

items.text: Discussion of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's opinion
items.text_en: Discussion of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a son can steal from his mother, since a husband acquires his wife's property. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina answers that it refers to a meal prepared for both parents. A challenge is raised from Rav Huna's statement that the son must buy cheap meat and wine, so the Gemara emends to 'from the money of a meal prepared for his father and mother.' An alternative answer is given that another gave the mother property on condition that her husband have no rights to it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a son can steal from his mother, since a husband acquires his wife's property.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina answers that it refers to a meal prepared for both parents.
A challenge is raised from Rav Huna's statement that the son must buy cheap meat and wine.
The Gemara emends the answer to 'from the money of a meal prepared for his father and mother.'
An alternative answer is given that another gave the mother property on condition that her husband have no rights to it.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on parental willingness and similarity
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on parental willingness and similarity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that both parents must be willing for the son to be liable. Rabbi Yehuda adds that if the mother is not 'suitable' for the father, the son is not liable. The Gemara clarifies that 'suitable' means equal in voice, appearance, and height, as derived from the verse 'einenu shome'a be'koleinu' (he does not listen to our voice).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the son is not liable as a בן סורר ומורה unless both parents are willing.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that if the mother is not 'suitable' for the father, the son is not liable.
The Gemara asks what 'not suitable' means, suggesting it might refer to a woman forbidden to the father under penalty of כרת or court-imposed death.
The Gemara rejects this interpretation, noting that the father and mother are still the biological parents regardless of any prohibition.
The Gemara explains that 'suitable' means equal to the father in appearance and stature.
A baraita supports this, stating that Rabbi Yehuda requires the mother to be equal to the father in voice, appearance, and height.
The Gemara derives this from the verse 'איננו שומע בקולנו' (he does not listen to our voice), implying that since voice must be equal, appearance and height must also be equal.

items.text: Debate on whether a wayward son ever existed
items.text_en: Debate on whether a wayward son ever existed
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that a wayward and rebellious son never existed and never will, and the Torah wrote it for study and reward. It attributes this view to Rabbi Yehuda (based on his stringent conditions) or to Rabbi Shimon. Similar statements are made about the condemned city (עיר הנדחת) attributed to Rabbi Eliezer, and the leprous house (בית המנוגע) attributed to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Yonatan claims to have seen the grave of a wayward son and the mound of a condemned city.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion aligns with the baraita that a wayward son never existed and never will, and was written only for study and reward.
The Gemara suggests the baraita aligns with Rabbi Yehuda, who imposes stringent conditions for the wayward son.
The Gemara alternatively attributes the baraita to Rabbi Shimon, who argues that eating a small amount of meat and wine does not warrant stoning.
Rabbi Yonatan claims to have seen the grave of a wayward son, contradicting the claim that such a son never existed.

sub.text: Gemara's question about the condemned city
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about the condemned city
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion aligns with the baraita that a condemned city never existed and never will.

sub.text: Gemara's answer for the condemned city
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer for the condemned city
sub.desc_en: The Gemara attributes the baraita to Rabbi Eliezer, who rules that a city with even one mezuzah cannot become a condemned city.

sub.text: Rabbi Yonatan's testimony about the condemned city
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yonatan's testimony about the condemned city
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan claims to have seen the mound of a condemned city, contradicting the claim that such a city never existed.

sub.text: Gemara's question about the leprous house
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about the leprous house
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion aligns with the baraita that a leprous house never existed and never will.

sub.text: Gemara's answer for the leprous house
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer for the leprous house
sub.desc_en: The Gemara attributes the baraita to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, who requires the plague to appear on two stones in a corner for the house to be impure.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon derives his requirement from the juxtaposition of 'קיר' (wall) and 'קירות' (walls), indicating a corner.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok's testimony
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok's testimony
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Tzadok testifies that there was a place in the territory of Gaza called 'the sealed ruin,' suggesting a leprous house existed.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ish Kfar Akko's testimony
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ish Kfar Akko's testimony
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ish Kfar Akko testifies that he saw a marked place in the Galilee where leprous stones were deposited, suggesting a leprous house existed.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on parental physical disabilities and warning procedure
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on parental physical disabilities and warning procedure
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists physical disabilities (amputee, lame, mute, blind, deaf) that disqualify parents from bringing the charge, based on verses. It then describes the procedure: warning before three judges, flogging, and if he repeats, judgment by 23 judges, with the original three present. The Gemara begins to question whether the verse must be read literally.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists physical disabilities (amputee, lame, mute, blind, deaf) that disqualify parents from bringing the charge, each derived from a verse.
The Mishnah describes the procedure: warning before three judges, flogging, and if he repeats, judgment by 23 judges, with the original three present.
The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's derivation implies that the verse must be read literally, and begins to answer that this case is different.

items.text: Warning before three and lashes for the rebellious son
items.text_en: Warning before three and lashes for the rebellious son
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse requires warning before three, since two would suffice. Abaye explains that the verse means warning before two and flogging before three. The source for lashes is derived via Rabbi Avahu's gezerah shavah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse requires warning before three, since two would suffice.
Abaye explains that the verse means warning before two and flogging before three.
The source for lashes is derived via Rabbi Avahu's גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the verse about flogging.

items.text: The extra word 'zeh' teaches two things
items.text_en: The extra word 'zeh' teaches two things
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the mishnah's phrase 'he relapsed and was judged by twenty-three' is derived from the word 'zeh' in the verse, which excludes the blind and also teaches the requirement for a court of twenty-three.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the word 'zeh' in the verse is needed to exclude the blind, rather than teaching the requirement for twenty-three judges.
The Gemara answers that the extra word 'zeh' teaches both exclusions: the blind and the requirement for twenty-three judges.

items.text: Mishnah: Change of status after flight
items.text_en: Mishnah: Change of status after flight
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that if the son fled before his verdict was finalized and then grew pubic hair, he is exempt; but if he fled after the verdict, he remains liable even if he later matures.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that if the son fled before his verdict was finalized and then grew pubic hair, he is exempt; but if he fled after the verdict, he remains liable even if he later matures.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's principle and attempted support from the mishnah
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's principle and attempted support from the mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that a Noahide who blasphemed and then converted is exempt because his law and death penalty changed. The Gemara attempts to support this from the mishnah's first case, but rejects it, explaining that the exemption is because he is no longer liable to execution at all.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that a Noahide who blasphemed and then converted is exempt because his law and death penalty changed.
The Gemara attempts to support Rabbi Chanina from the mishnah's case of a minor who fled and then grew pubic hair, suggesting the exemption is due to the change in status.
The Gemara rejects the support, explaining that the mishnah's exemption is because the minor is no longer liable to execution at all, not because of a change in law.

items.text: Challenge from the mishnah's second case
items.text_en: Challenge from the mishnah's second case
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Chanina from the mishnah's second case, where after the verdict the son is liable even if he matures. But the Gemara retorts that after the verdict he is already considered a dead man, so the case is irrelevant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Chanina by citing the mishnah's second case, where after the verdict the son is liable even if he matures.
The Gemara retorts that after the verdict he is already considered a dead man, so the case is irrelevant to Rabbi Chanina's principle.

items.text: Baraita on a Noahide who converts and the principle of changed law and death
items.text_en: Baraita on a Noahide who converts and the principle of changed law and death
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a Noahide who struck his fellow or committed adultery and then converted is exempt, but if he did so as an Israelite and then converted he is liable. The Gemara explains that exemption requires both law and death to change, and analyzes the cases of murder and adultery according to different opinions on which death penalty is more severe, concluding with Rabbi Shimon's view that all Noahide deaths are strangulation.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: a Noahide who struck his fellow or committed adultery and then converted is exempt, but if he did so as an Israelite and then converted he is liable, challenging the principle that a change in status changes liability.
The Gemara answers that exemption requires both the trial procedure and the death penalty to change; here only the trial procedure changed, not the death penalty.
The Gemara objects: for a murderer the death penalty remains the sword, but for adultery it changes from sword to strangulation, so both law and death changed.
The Gemara answers that the case involves a betrothed young woman, where both as a Noahide and as a Jew the penalty is stoning, so the death penalty did not change.
The Gemara objects that the baraita says 'did so in Israel' parallel to 'wife of his fellow', implying a fully married woman, not a betrothed young woman.
The Gemara resolves that the lenient punishment (strangulation) is included in the severe one (sword), so the convert remains liable.
The Gemara objects that this works for the Rabbis who say sword is more severe, but for Rabbi Shimon who says strangulation is more severe, what can be said?
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Shimon holds like the tanna of the school of Menasheh, who says all Noahide deaths are strangulation, so the penalty does not become more severe.

The Gemara resolves that for a married woman the penalty remains strangulation, and for a murderer the lenient penalty (strangulation) is included in the severe one (sword), so the convert remains liable.

items.text: Attempted support from a case of a betrothed young woman who matured
items.text_en: Attempted support from a case of a betrothed young woman who matured
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to support Rabbi Chanina from a case where a betrothed young woman sinned and then matured, which would normally change her penalty from stoning to strangulation. Rabbi Yochanan corrects the Tanna to say she is judged by stoning, showing that a change of status does not change the penalty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to support Rabbi Chanina by citing a case where a betrothed young woman sinned and then reached majority, arguing that her penalty changes from stoning to strangulation because her status changed.
Rabbi Yochanan tells the Tanna to emend the baraita and teach that she is judged by stoning, rejecting the attempted support.

items.text: Mishnah: The rebellious son is judged for his eventual fate
items.text_en: Mishnah: The rebellious son is judged for his eventual fate
items.desc_en: The mishnah teaches that the rebellious son is judged based on his eventual destiny, and lists various phenomena (wine, sleep, dispersion, gathering, quiet) that are beneficial or harmful to the wicked and the righteous.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating that the rebellious son is judged based on his eventual fate, and that it is better for him to die innocent than guilty.
The mishnah lists wine and sleep as beneficial for the wicked and harmful for the righteous.
The mishnah concludes by listing dispersion, gathering, and quiet as phenomena that benefit or harm the wicked and righteous respectively.

items.text: Baraita on the wayward son and general principles
items.text_en: Baraita on the wayward son and general principles
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili explains that the Torah's law of the wayward son anticipates his eventual criminal path. The baraita then lists contrasting effects of death, sleep, wine, peace, and dispersion on the righteous and the wicked.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili questions why the Torah would execute a son for eating and drinking, explaining that the Torah anticipates his eventual criminal path of robbery and murder.
The baraita lists contrasting effects of death, sleep, wine, peace, and dispersion on the righteous and the wicked, showing that the wicked benefit from death while the righteous suffer.

items.text: Mishnah: The burglar is judged based on his end
items.text_en: Mishnah: The burglar is judged based on his end
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a burglar (ba bamachteret) is judged based on his presumed intent to kill. If he breaks a barrel, he is liable if he has blood (i.e., the owner can kill him), but exempt if he has no blood (i.e., the owner cannot kill him).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a burglar (ba bamachteret) is judged based on his end; if he breaks a barrel, he is liable if the owner has blood (i.e., the owner may kill him), but exempt if the owner has no blood.

items.text: Rava's reasoning for the burglar's liability
items.text_en: Rava's reasoning for the burglar's liability
items.desc_en: Rava explains the logic: a person will not stand by while his property is taken, so the burglar assumes the owner will confront him, and the burglar intends to kill. The Torah says: if someone comes to kill you, rise early and kill him.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains the logic behind the law of the burglar (הבא במחתרת): a person will not stand by while his property is taken, so the burglar assumes the owner will confront him and intends to kill, and the Torah says: if someone comes to kill you, rise early and kill him.

items.text: Rav's ruling on taking vessels and the dispute with Rava
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on taking vessels and the dispute with Rava
items.desc_en: Rav rules that a burglar who takes vessels and leaves is exempt, because he acquired them through blood (i.e., the owner's potential killing). Rava limits this to breaking, not taking. The Gemara questions this from a case where the burglar had blood but they were lost, and resolves that the acquisition is not complete.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that a burglar who enters through a breach, takes vessels, and leaves is exempt because he acquired them through the owner's blood (i.e., the potential killing).
Rava limits Rav's ruling to a case where the burglar broke the vessels, but not when he merely took them.
The Gemara challenges Rava from a case where the burglar had blood but the vessels were lost, implying they are in his domain, so here too they should be in his domain.
The Gemara resolves that the Torah placed the vessels in the burglar's domain only for liability for accidents, but for acquisition they remain in the owner's domain, like a borrower.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the Mishnah that only breaking is mentioned, implying taking is not exempt. It answers that the same applies even to taking, and the Mishnah teaches that even breaking obligates payment when he has blood. A further objection about intentional damage is raised and left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the Mishnah that only breaking is mentioned, implying that taking is not exempt when the burglar has no blood money.
The Gemara answers that the same law applies even to taking, and the Mishnah teaches that even breaking obligates payment when he has blood money.
The Gemara objects that the ruling is obvious, and raises an unresolved difficulty about the principle that a person is always forewarned (אדם מועד לעולם).

items.text: Rav Beivai bar Abaye's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye objects from a case of stealing a purse on Shabbat, where the thief is liable if the theft precedes the Shabbat violation, but exempt if they occur simultaneously. The Gemara concludes that the case is like throwing it into a river.

sub.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye objects from a baraita about a thief who steals a purse on Shabbat, where liability depends on whether the theft precedes the Shabbat violation.
The baraita adds that if the thief drags the purse out, the prohibitions of theft and Shabbat desecration arise simultaneously, making him exempt from the death penalty.
The Gemara concludes that the case of the burglar is analogous to throwing the purse into a river, where the acquisition and the damage are simultaneous, so the burglar is exempt.

items.text: Rava's practical ruling
items.text_en: Rava's practical ruling
items.desc_en: Rava's rams were stolen by a burglar; they were returned, but Rava did not accept them, citing Rav's ruling that the burglar acquires them through blood.

sub.desc_en: Rava's rams were stolen by a burglar; they were returned, but Rava refused to accept them, citing Rav's ruling that the burglar acquires them through blood.

items.text: Two baraitot on 'if the sun rose' and their resolution
items.text_en: Two baraitot on 'if the sun rose' and their resolution
items.desc_en: Two baraitot interpret the verse 'if the sun rose upon him' – one says if it is clear as the sun that he has no peace with you, kill him; the other says if it is clear as the sun that he has peace with you, do not kill him. The Gemara notes the apparent contradiction and begins to resolve it.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita interprets the verse 'if the sun rose upon him' to mean that if it is as clear as the sun that the burglar has no peace with you, you may kill him; otherwise, do not.
The second baraita interprets the same verse oppositely: if it is as clear as the sun that the burglar has peace with you, do not kill him; otherwise, kill him.
The Gemara notes the apparent contradiction between the two baraitot.
The Gemara begins to resolve the contradiction, stating that it is not difficult.

items.text: Distinction between father and son in the burglar's case
items.text_en: Distinction between father and son in the burglar's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between two scenarios: one where the father is the burglar and the son is the homeowner, and one where the son is the burglar and the father is the homeowner, based on the verse 'דמים לו'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between two scenarios: one where the father is the burglar and the son is the homeowner, and one where the son is the burglar and the father is the homeowner, based on the verse 'דמים לו'.

items.text: Rav's personal ruling on a burglar
items.text_en: Rav's personal ruling on a burglar
items.desc_en: Rav declares that he would kill any burglar who comes against him, except for Rav Chanina bar Shela, because he knows that Rav Chanina would have mercy on him like a father on a son.

sub.desc_en: Rav declares that he would kill any burglar who comes through a tunnel, except for Rabbi Chanina bar Sheila, because he knows that Rabbi Chanina has compassion on him like a father's compassion on his son.
Rav excepts Rav Chanina bar Shela from his ruling.
The gemara asks for the reason for the exception.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of a possible reason
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of a possible reason
sub.desc_en: The gemara rejects the possibility that the exception is because Rav Chanina is righteous, since he is still a burglar.
Rav explains that he knows Rav Chanina would have mercy on him like a father on a son.

items.text: The law applies on Shabbat and the case of a collapsed wall
items.text_en: The law applies on Shabbat and the case of a collapsed wall
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that the law of 'דמים לו' applies both on weekdays and Shabbat. The Gemara questions why 'דמים לו' is needed on Shabbat, since if it doesn't apply on weekdays, certainly not on Shabbat. Rav Sheishes answers that it is needed to permit clearing a pile of rubble on Shabbat to save the burglar.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that the law of 'דמים לו' (the burglar's blood is forfeit) applies both on weekdays and Shabbat.
The Gemara questions why the baraisa needs to state that 'דמים לו' applies on Shabbat, since if the burglar is not killed on a weekday, certainly not on Shabbat.
Rav Sheishes answers that the statement is needed to permit clearing a pile of rubble on Shabbat to save the burglar.

items.text: The verse 'והוכה' and 'ומת' – anyone may kill and any death
items.text_en: The verse 'והוכה' and 'ומת' – anyone may kill and any death
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that 'והוכה' means by any person, and 'ומת' means by any death. The Gemara questions the need for 'ומת', deriving it from the law of a murderer via a gezerah shavah. It is rejected because the two verses are two scriptures that come as one and do not teach a general principle.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that 'והוכה' means by any person and 'ומת' means by any death.
The Gemara questions why the phrase 'ומת' is needed, since the law of a murderer already teaches that any death is permissible.
The Gemara answers that the law of a murderer is derived from a baraita on 'מות יומת', which teaches that any death is valid.
The Gemara objects that the case of a murderer is different because the verse explicitly says 'מות יומת'.
The Gemara rejects the derivation because the verses of murderer and blood redeemer are two scriptures that come as one and do not teach a general principle.

items.text: Two baraisos on the scope of 'מחתרת'
items.text_en: Two baraisos on the scope of 'מחתרת'
items.desc_en: Two baraisos teach that the law applies not only to a burglar who tunnels but also to one who enters via the roof, courtyard, or enclosure. The first baraisa says the verse 'מחתרת' is because most burglars tunnel; the second says the tunneling itself is his warning.

sub.desc_en: The first baraisa teaches that the law of the burglar applies even if he enters via the roof, courtyard, or enclosure, and explains that the verse specifies 'מחתרת' (tunneling) because most burglars tunnel.
The second baraisa similarly extends the law to non-tunneling entries, but explains that the tunneling itself serves as the burglar's warning (התראה).

items.text: A minor pursuer and the requirement of warning
items.text_en: A minor pursuer and the requirement of warning
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a minor who is a pursuer may be killed to save the pursued, as a pursuer does not require warning. The Gemara challenges this from the case of a woman in labor, but distinguishes it as a heavenly pursuit. It then brings a baraisa that seems to require warning, but Rav Huna explains it refers to a case where the pursuer is across a river and cannot be saved otherwise, or he aligns himself with the tanna who says the tunneling itself is the warning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a minor who is a pursuer may be killed to save the pursued, because a pursuer does not require warning, whether adult or minor.
Rav Chisda objects from the case of a woman in labor: once the baby's head emerges, one may not touch it, even though it is a pursuer.
The Gemara distinguishes the case of childbirth as a heavenly pursuit, not a human one.
The Gemara cites a baraisa about a pursuer who is warned, which seems to require warning, potentially supporting Rav Huna's view.
The Gemara rejects the support, identifying the baraisa as Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's view that a colleague (חָבֵר) does not need warning.
The Gemara brings another baraisa that explicitly requires warning for a pursuer, contradicting Rav Huna.
The Gemara resolves that the baraisa refers to a case where the pursuer is across a river, so the rescuer cannot save the pursued directly and must bring the case to court, which requires warning.
Alternatively, Rav Huna aligns himself with the tanna who says that the tunneling itself is the warning, so no separate warning is needed.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those pursued whom one may save by killing the pursuer: one pursuing another to kill him, a male (for sodomy), or a betrothed young woman (for rape). It excludes one pursuing an animal, a Shabbat desecrator, or an idolater.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those pursued whom one may save by killing the pursuer, and those excluded.

items.text: Derivation for saving a pursued person
items.text_en: Derivation for saving a pursued person
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita deriving the obligation to save a pursued person from 'Do not stand by the blood of your neighbor.' It questions whether this verse is needed for that or for saving a drowning person, and concludes it applies to both. Then it seeks the source for killing the pursuer, deriving it via a kal vachomer from a betrothed young woman.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'Do not stand by the blood of your neighbor' as the source for the obligation to save a pursued person by killing the pursuer.
The Gemara objects that this verse is needed for the obligation to save a drowning person, not for killing the pursuer.
The Gemara concedes that the verse indeed applies to both cases.
The Gemara asks: if the verse is for saving a drowning person, what is the source for killing the pursuer?
The Gemara derives the permission to kill the pursuer via a kal vachomer (a fortiori) from the case of a betrothed young woman.

items.text: Rejection of kal vachomer and alternative derivation via hekesh
items.text_en: Rejection of kal vachomer and alternative derivation via hekesh
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that one cannot derive a punishment from a kal vachomer. The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught that it is a hekesh (analogy) from the verse about a man rising against his neighbor to murder, comparing a murderer to a betrothed young woman, thus allowing saving the pursued by killing the pursuer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that one cannot derive a punishment (saving the pursued by killing the pursuer) from a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument.

The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught that the derivation is not a kal vachomer but a hekesh (analogy) from the verse about a man rising against his neighbor, comparing a murderer to a betrothed young woman, thus allowing saving the pursued by killing the pursuer.

items.text: Source for saving a betrothed young woman
items.text_en: Source for saving a betrothed young woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for saving a betrothed young woman herself. The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught from the verse 'And there is no savior for her' that if there is a savior, he may save her by any means.

sub.text: Baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: from where do we derive the law for the betrothed young woman herself? It cites the school of Rabbi Yishmael, who derives from 'וְאֵין מוֹשִׁיעַ לָהּ' (and there is no savior for her) that if there is a savior, he may save her by any means.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches from the verse 'וְאֵין מוֹשִׁיעַ לָהּ' (and there is no savior for her) that if there is a savior, he may save her by any means.

items.text: Source for saving a drowning person and additional obligation
items.text_en: Source for saving a drowning person and additional obligation
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the baraita about saving a drowning person, questioning why it needs a separate verse. It answers that the verse 'And you shall return it to him' teaches the obligation to save his body (as lost property). Without this, one might think only saving his life is required, but not hiring workers to save him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse 'לֹא תַעֲמֹד עַל דַּם רֵעֶךָ' is needed for saving a drowning person, since it already derives from the obligation to return lost property.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'וַהֲשֵׁבֹתוֹ לוֹ' (And you shall return it to him) teaches the obligation to save his body as lost property.
The Gemara objects that from the lost-property verse one might think only saving his life is required, but not hiring workers to save him.
The Gemara resolves that the verse 'לֹא תַעֲמֹד עַל דַּם רֵעֶךָ' teaches the additional obligation to hire workers to save him.

items.text: Baraita expanding the list of those saved
items.text_en: Baraita expanding the list of those saved
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one saves by killing the pursuer for one pursuing to kill, for sodomy with a male, for a betrothed young woman, and for those liable for court-imposed death or karet. Exceptions include a widow for a High Priest, a divorced or halutzah for a common priest, if the transgression was already committed, or if she has a savior. Rabbi Yehuda adds if she says 'Leave him' so he won't kill her.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists those pursued for whom one saves by killing the pursuer: one pursuing to kill, for sodomy with a male, for a betrothed young woman, and for those liable for court-imposed death or karet; and lists exceptions: a widow for a High Priest, a divorced or halutzah for a common priest.
The baraita adds further exceptions: if the transgression was already committed, if she has a savior, and Rabbi Yehuda adds if she says 'Leave him' so he won't kill her.

items.text: Derivation of the expanded list from a verse
items.text_en: Derivation of the expanded list from a verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the categories from the verse 'And to the young woman you shall do nothing; there is no sin of death for the young woman.' It interprets 'young man' as a male, 'young woman' as a betrothed young woman, 'sin' as those liable for karet, and 'death' as those liable for court-imposed death. It then explains why all these terms are necessary: each teaches a case that might otherwise be excluded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the expanded list and interprets the verse 'וְלַנַּעֲרָה לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה דָבָר' to derive the categories: 'נַעַר' (male), 'נַעֲרָה' (betrothed young woman), 'חֵטְא' (those liable for karet), 'מָוֶת' (those liable for court-imposed death).
The Gemara asks why all these terms are necessary and explains that 'נַעַר' alone might have excluded a female, since it is not her natural way to pursue.
The Gemara continues the explanation: 'נַעֲרָה' alone might have excluded a male, since the male does not suffer degradation; therefore both terms are needed.

items.text: Gemara's deductive proof: the need for both
items.text_en: Gemara's deductive proof: the need for both
items.desc_en: The Gemara shows why both

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Torah wrote 'חֵטְא (sin)' to include other forbidden relations, since one might have thought only the two cases (betrothed young woman and married woman) are saved at the cost of the attacker's life due to their unique degradation.

The Gemara notes that had the Torah written only 'חֵטְא (sin)', one might have thought the law applies even to those forbidden by a mere prohibition, so the Torah wrote 'מָוֶת (death)' to limit it to capital offenses.

The Gemara explains that had the Torah written only 'מָוֶת (death)', one might have thought only those liable to court-imposed death are included, but not those liable to כרת (karet), so the Torah wrote 'חֵטְא (sin)' to include them.

items.text: Resolution of superfluous
items.text_en: Resolution of superfluous
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that two exclusions are needed (for acts like serving idolatry or desecrating Shabbat that might have been derived via verbal analogy), but for Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon, who already exclude certain cases, one of the exclusions is a mere literary effect.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse needed the words 'נַעַר' and 'נַעֲרָה' if the phrase 'חֵטְא מָוֶת' already includes all relevant cases.
The Gemara answers that the words are not needed for inclusion but for exclusion: one excludes an idol worshipper, the other excludes bestiality and Shabbat desecration.
The Gemara asks according to Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, who already holds that an idol worshipper is saved at the cost of his life, why are two exclusions needed?
The Gemara answers that one exclusion is for bestiality and the other for Shabbat desecration.
The Gemara explains that one might have thought to derive Shabbat from idol worship via a verbal analogy on 'חִילּוּל', so a separate exclusion is needed.
The Gemara asks according to Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon, who already derives Shabbat from idol worship via verbal analogy, what is the purpose of the two exclusions?
The Gemara answers that one exclusion is for bestiality, and the other is merely a literary effect because the Torah wrote 'נַעַר' and therefore also wrote 'נַעֲרָה'.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis about the maiden who says leave me
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis about the maiden who says leave me
items.desc_en: Rava frames the dispute: the Rabbis hold the Torah cares about the blemish itself, and here the maiden is blemishing herself, so one who rescues her by force is exempt; Rabbi Yehuda holds the Torah only cares because she is forfeiting her life, and if she does not forfeit it, the rescuer is liable.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that a maiden who says 'leave him' to prevent her death is included in the law.
The Gemara asks: on what principle do Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis disagree?
Rava explains the dispute: the maiden is concerned about her blemish and allows him to kill her rather than be blemished.
Rava states the Rabbis' view: the Torah cares about the blemish itself, and here she is blemishing herself, so the rescuer is exempt.
Rava states Rabbi Yehuda's view: the Torah only cares because she is forfeiting her life, and if she does not forfeit it, the rescuer is liable.

items.text: Rav Papa's question about a widow to a High Priest
items.text_en: Rav Papa's question about a widow to a High Priest
items.desc_en: Rav Papa asks whether a widow marrying a High Priest is also considered blemished, so that the rescuer of a betrothed maiden who is a widow to a High Priest would be exempt. Abaye answers that the Torah only cares about a major blemish, not this minor one.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: does a widow betrothed to a High Priest also suffer a defect (פגם)?
Abaye answers that the Torah is concerned about a major defect (פגם רבה) but not a minor defect (פגם זוטא).

items.text: Contradiction between the mishnah and the baraisa about fines for a betrothed maiden
items.text_en: Contradiction between the mishnah and the baraisa about fines for a betrothed maiden
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the baraisa lists sisters as liable to a fine, but the mishnah says a betrothed maiden is exempt. After an initial resolution that the exemption applies only from the time of העראה onward, the Gemara questions that resolution for one who holds that העראה is the beginning of intercourse. A second resolution by Rav Chisda and a third by Rava conclude that the case is one where the man originally raped her unnaturally and then naturally, or where the maiden tells the rescuer to leave him, which is the position of Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraisa listing sisters as liable to a fine and raises a contradiction with the mishnah that exempts a betrothed maiden.
The rabbis propose that from the time of העראה (the beginning of intercourse) the man is exempt from execution, but he does not pay the fine until the act is complete.
The Gemara objects that this resolution works only for one who holds that העראה is merely kissing, but not for one who holds it is the actual insertion of the corona.
Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by positing a case where the man first raped her unnaturally (anal intercourse) and then naturally (vaginal intercourse).
Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining that the case is where the maiden tells the rescuer to leave him alone, which aligns with the position of Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Rav Pappa's position on the case of a pursuer
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's position on the case of a pursuer
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that the dispute about killing a pursuer applies only when the woman is already engaged in sexual relations (מפותה), and all agree in other cases.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that the dispute about killing a pursuer applies only when the woman is a מפותה (seduced woman), and all agree in other cases.

items.text: Abaye's explanation and Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul's baraita
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation and Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul's baraita
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the dispute is when one can save the pursued by maiming the pursuer (באחד מאיבריו), citing Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul who rules that if one could save by maiming and did not, the pursuer is killed.
