sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the dispute concerns a case where one can save the pursued by maiming the pursuer (באחד מאיבריו), and attributes this view to Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul
sub.desc_en: The gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul rules that a pursuer who could have been stopped by maiming but was not is killed.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul's source from the verse about fighting men, and Rabbi Elazar's interpretation. It then questions how one could be liable for payment if he could have saved by maiming, and considers the possibility that the case involves death to one and payment to another.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of Rabbi Yonatan ben Shaul's ruling that a pursuer who could be stopped by maiming is killed.
The Gemara cites the verse about fighting men and Rabbi Elazar's interpretation that the verse speaks of a mortal struggle, yet the Torah exempts from payment if no death occurs.
The Gemara explains that if one can save by maiming, he is not permitted to kill, so the case of payment fits when he could have maimed but killed instead.
The Gemara objects: if even when one can save by maiming he is permitted to kill, how can there ever be a case of payment?
The Gemara resolves that the case is different because death is to one person and payment to another.

items.text: Rava's laws of a pursuer breaking vessels
items.text_en: Rava's laws of a pursuer breaking vessels
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a pursuer who breaks vessels while chasing is exempt from payment, as he is liable for death. The pursued who breaks the pursuer's vessels is exempt, but if he breaks others' vessels he is liable. A third party trying to save the pursued is exempt from paying for any vessels broken.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a pursuer who breaks vessels while chasing is exempt from payment, because he is already liable for death.
Rava rules that the pursued who breaks the pursuer's vessels is exempt, but if he breaks others' vessels he is liable, because he saves himself with another's property.
Rava rules that a third party trying to save the pursued is exempt from paying for any vessels broken, as a rabbinic enactment to encourage rescue.

items.text: Pursuer after an animal and the principle of 'oneshin min hadin'
items.text_en: Pursuer after an animal and the principle of 'oneshin min hadin'
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a pursuer after an animal, and then cites Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai who says an idolater may be killed based on a kal vachomer, and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon who extends this to Shabbat desecration via a gezerah shavah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of a pursuer after an animal.

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai rules that an idolater may be killed based on a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument, and the Gemara notes that he holds the principle of 'oneshin min hadin' (punishment derived from logical inference).

sub.text: Baraita of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon extends the same logic to Shabbat desecration, deriving it from idolatry via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'חילול' (desecration).

items.text: The ruling from the attic of Beit Nitzah in Lod
items.text_en: The ruling from the attic of Beit Nitzah in Lod
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak reports that the sages voted and concluded that for all transgressions one should transgress rather than be killed, except for idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and murder.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan reports that the sages voted and concluded that for all transgressions one should transgress rather than be killed, except for idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and murder.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Yishmael and resolution with Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Yishmael and resolution with Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Rabbi Yishmael taught one may commit idolatry in private to save one's life, but the sages in Lod follow Rabbi Eliezer who derives from 'bechol nafshecha' and 'bechol me'odecha' that one must give up life and money for God.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Rabbi Yishmael taught one may commit idolatry in private to save one's life, citing the verse 'וחי בהם' (and live by them).

The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yishmael's leniency applies only in private, but in public (פרהסיא) one must give up life, as derived from the verse 'ולא תחללו את שם קדשי' (do not profane My holy name).

The Gemara explains that the sages in Lod follow Rabbi Eliezer, who derives from the verse 'בכל נפשך ובכל מאדך' (with all your soul and all your might) that one must give up both life and money for God, thus requiring martyrdom even in private for idolatry.

items.text: Derivation for forbidden sexual relations and murder from Rabbi
items.text_en: Derivation for forbidden sexual relations and murder from Rabbi
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that forbidden sexual relations and murder are derived from Rabbi's teaching, which compares a murderer to a betrothed young woman: just as she may be killed to prevent the sin, so too a murderer; and just as a murderer must be killed rather than transgress, so too she. The source for murder itself is a logical argument from the case of one ordered to kill under threat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that forbidden sexual relations and murder are derived from Rabbi's teaching, citing a baraita where Rabbi asks what we learn from the murderer.
Rabbi explains that the verse makes a reciprocal analogy: just as a betrothed young woman may be killed to prevent the sin, so too a murderer may be killed to prevent the murder.
Rabbi completes the analogy: just as a murderer must be killed rather than transgress, so too a betrothed young woman must be killed rather than commit the sin.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the rule for murder itself?

The Gemara answers that it is a logical argument (סברא), citing the case of a man who came before Rabbah and was told by his master to kill someone or be killed; Rabbah ruled that one must let himself be killed rather than kill, because one's own blood is not redder than the other's.

items.text: Distinction between times of persecution and public vs. private
items.text_en: Distinction between times of persecution and public vs. private
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that the leniency of transgressing rather than being killed applies only when not in a time of religious persecution (שעת השמד); during persecution, even a light commandment requires martyrdom. Another version adds that even without persecution, in public (פרהסיא) one must be killed rather than transgress even a light commandment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that the leniency of transgressing rather than being killed applies only outside a time of religious persecution (שעת השמד), but during persecution one must be killed even for a light commandment.
Ravin transmits an alternative version of Rabbi Yochanan's statement: even outside persecution, in public (פרהסיא) one must be killed rather than transgress even a light commandment.
The Gemara asks what constitutes a 'light commandment' in this context.

sub.text: Rava bar Rav Yitzchak citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rava bar Rav Yitzchak citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Yitzchak begins to cite Rav's answer to the question about the light commandment, but the text cuts off at the section boundary.

items.text: Opening statement: even for changing a shoelace
items.text_en: Opening statement: even for changing a shoelace
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that even for a minor transgression like changing a shoelace, one must give up one's life in a public setting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that even for a minor transgression like changing a shoelace, one must give up one's life in a public setting.

items.text: Definition of public setting and the query about a gentile
items.text_en: Definition of public setting and the query about a gentile
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yochanan defines public as ten people. Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether nine Israelites and one gentile count. Rav Yannai answers via a verbal analogy that all ten must be Israelites.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: How many people constitute a public setting (פרהסיא)?

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers: Public setting is no fewer than ten people.
The Gemara notes it is obvious that all ten must be Israelites, citing the verse 'וְנִקְדַּשְׁתִּי בְּתוֹךְ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל' (I will be sanctified among the children of Israel).
Rabbi Yirmeya asks: What is the law if there are nine Israelites and one gentile — does that count as a public setting?
Rav Yannai answers via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'תּוֹךְ' (among): just as in the case of Korach's assembly there were ten Israelites, so too here all ten must be Israelites.

items.text: Challenge from Esther and resolution via personal benefit
items.text_en: Challenge from Esther and resolution via personal benefit
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Esther acted publicly. Abaye answers that Esther was like natural ground (forced). Rava says the case of personal benefit is different, citing the example of giving wine to idolaters for their own enjoyment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Esther's public marriage to Achashverosh was a public act of idolatry, contradicting the rule that one must die rather than transgress publicly.
Abaye answers that Esther was like natural ground (קרקע עולם), meaning she was forced and passive, not acting voluntarily, so the rule of public transgression does not apply.
Rava answers that the case of personal benefit (הנאת עצמן) is different, citing the example of giving wine to idolaters for their own enjoyment, which is permitted even publicly.

items.text: Rava's principle: intent to cause transgression vs. murder
items.text_en: Rava's principle: intent to cause transgression vs. murder
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if a gentile demands a Jew kill an animal on Shabbat to feed it to beasts, the Jew should comply rather than be killed; but if the demand is to throw it into a river (no benefit), the Jew should be killed rather than comply, because the gentile intends to cause transgression.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces Rava's principle that when a gentile demands a Jew violate Shabbat, the Jew's obligation depends on whether the gentile's intent is to cause transgression or to benefit from the act.

items.text: Query: Is a Noahide commanded on sanctification of God's name?
items.text_en: Query: Is a Noahide commanded on sanctification of God's name?
items.desc_en: They asked Rabbi Ammi whether a Noahide is commanded on sanctification of God's name. Abaye cites the seven Noahide laws, implying no eighth. Rava responds that those seven include all their subcategories.

sub.desc_en: The questioners ask Rabbi Ammi whether a Noahide (בן נח) is commanded on the sanctification of God's name (קידוש השם).
Abaye cites the tradition that Noahides were commanded only seven laws, arguing that if sanctification were included there would be eight, implying it is not commanded.
Rava responds that the seven enumerated laws include all their subcategories, so sanctification could be a subcategory of one of the seven, not a separate eighth command.

items.text: Resolution from Naaman's story
items.text_en: Resolution from Naaman's story
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava cites a proof from the house of Rav: the verse about Naaman bowing in the house of Rimmon and Elisha's response 'Go in peace' shows that a Noahide may bow to an idol under duress, indicating they are not commanded on sanctification of God's name.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the resolution is regarding whether a Noahide is commanded on sanctification of God's name.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava citing the House of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava citing the House of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava cites a proof from the House of Rav: the verse about Naaman bowing in the house of Rimmon and Elisha's response 'Go in peace' shows that a Noahide may bow to an idol under duress, indicating they are not commanded on sanctification of God's name.

items.text: Distinction between private and public contexts
items.text_en: Distinction between private and public contexts
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between a private and a public setting for the leniency of whispering to an engaged woman to save her life; in private it is permitted, in public it is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a private setting (צנעה) where whispering is permitted and a public setting (פרהסיא) where it is forbidden.

items.text: Story of a man who became ill from lust
items.text_en: Story of a man who became ill from lust
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports a case of a man who became gravely ill from lust for a woman. The doctors said the only cure was for her to be available to him, but the Sages ruled that he should die rather than any forbidden intimacy, including less severe acts.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports a case of a man who became ill from lust, and the Sages ruled that he should die rather than engage in any forbidden intimacy with the woman.

items.text: Dispute about the woman's marital status
items.text_en: Dispute about the woman's marital status
items.desc_en: R. Yaakov bar Idi and R. Shmuel bar Nachmani disagree about whether the woman was married or unmarried. They explain that for the married version the severity is obvious, but for the unmarried version the Gemara questions why such extreme measures were taken.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani over whether the woman in the story was married (אשת איש) or unmarried (פנויה).
The Gemara notes that according to the view that she was married, the severity is understandable, but asks: according to the view that she was unmarried, why was such extreme prohibition necessary?

items.text: Two answers for the unmarried case
items.text_en: Two answers for the unmarried case
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that the reason is to prevent family blemish (פגם משפחה) and Rav Acha bar Rav Ika adds that it is to prevent promiscuity among Jewish women. The Gemara then explains that marrying her would not calm his desire, citing R. Yitzchak that after the destruction, forbidden relations have a greater appeal.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that the prohibition is due to family blemish (פגם משפחה).
Rav Acha bar Rav Ika answers that the prohibition is to prevent Jewish women from becoming promiscuous in forbidden relations.
The Gemara asks why the man cannot simply marry the woman to calm his desire.
The Gemara answers that marriage would not calm his desire, citing Rabbi Yitzchak.

Rabbi Yitzchak explains that since the Temple's destruction, the taste of forbidden relations is given to transgressors, citing the verse 'Stolen waters are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant.'

items.text: Conclusion of the perek and opening of the new one
items.text_en: Conclusion of the perek and opening of the new one
items.desc_en: The Gemara marks the end of the chapter on the wayward son and begins the Mishnah listing those executed by burning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter on the wayward and rebellious son and begins the Mishnah listing those executed by burning.

items.text: Mishnah: Those liable for burning
items.text_en: Mishnah: Those liable for burning
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those executed by burning: one who has relations with a woman and her daughter, and a priest's daughter who committed adultery. It then expands the category of 'woman and her daughter' to include various other relatives.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing those executed by burning: one who has relations with a woman and her daughter, and a priest's daughter who committed adultery.

The Mishnah expands the category of 'woman and her daughter' to include the daughter's daughter, son's daughter, wife's daughter, wife's daughter's daughter, wife's son's daughter, mother-in-law, mother-in-law's mother, and father-in-law's mother.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's language
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's language
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'one who has relations with a woman and her daughter' implying two are forbidden, namely the mother-in-law and mother-in-law's mother. It then notes that the Mishnah's extension includes both exegetically derived and explicit cases. The Gemara resolves this with the views of Abaye (who says the dispute is about interpreting the plain meaning) and Rava (who says the dispute is about after death). Rava would amend the Mishnah text.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not say 'one who has relations with a woman who married her daughter' but rather 'one who has relations with a woman and her daughter,' implying both are forbidden, and identifies them as the mother-in-law and the mother-in-law's mother.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'there is included in a woman and her daughter,' implying that both are explicitly written, while the others are derived exegetically.
The Gemara resolves that according to Abaye, who says the dispute is about interpreting the plain meaning, the Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva.

The Gemara resolves that according to Rava, who says the dispute is about the mother-in-law after death, Rava would amend the Mishnah text to read 'one who has relations with a woman who married her daughter.'

items.text: Reconciling the list according to Abaye and Rava
items.text_en: Reconciling the list according to Abaye and Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Abaye, because the Mishnah needed to list 'mother of his father-in-law', it also listed the other close relatives. According to Rava, because it needed to list 'mother of his father-in-law' and 'mother of his mother-in-law', it incidentally listed 'mother-in-law' as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's list of relatives included in the category of 'woman and her daughter'.
According to Abaye, because the Mishnah needed to list 'mother of his father-in-law', it also listed 'mother-in-law' and 'mother of his mother-in-law'.
According to Rava, because the Mishnah needed to list 'mother of his father-in-law' and 'mother of his mother-in-law', it incidentally listed 'mother-in-law' as well.

items.text: Derivation from biblical gezerah shavah on 'zimmah'
items.text_en: Derivation from biblical gezerah shavah on 'zimmah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the inclusion of a woman's daughter, granddaughter, and granddaughter through a son from the аналоги of zimmah. It also derives that males (e.g., stepfather) are treated like females, and lower generations (grandchildren) are like upper generations (mother-in-law).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (the additional relatives listed in the mishna) derived? It cites a baraita that begins with the explicit verse 'איש אשר יקח את אשה ואת אמה' (a man who takes a woman and her mother) and notes that only the woman and her mother are explicitly stated, raising the question of the source for the daughter, granddaughter, and great-granddaughter.

The baraita answers by invoking a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'זִמָּה' (lewdness): just as in the prohibition in Leviticus 18:17 the daughter, granddaughter, and great-granddaughter are included, so too in the punishment verse (Leviticus 20:14) they are included.

The baraita continues: From where is it derived to treat males (e.g., the father-in-law's mother) like females (the mother-in-law's mother)? It applies the same גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on 'זִמָּה' to extend the punishment to male relatives.

The baraita further derives: From where is it to treat lower generations (grandchildren) like upper generations (mother-in-law)? The same גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on 'זִמָּה' teaches that the punishment applies both upward and downward in the family line.

items.text: Clarification of 'males like females' and 'father-in-law's mother'
items.text_en: Clarification of 'males like females' and 'father-in-law's mother'
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that 'males like females' refers to comparing the mother of the father-in-law to the mother of the mother-in-law, not the son's daughter to the daughter's daughter. It then asks whether the mother of the father-in-law is actually derived later or earlier.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of 'males like females' in the baraita, asking whether it refers to comparing a son's daughter to a daughter's daughter, and notes that both are already derived together.

The Gemara clarifies that 'males like females' refers to comparing the mother of the father-in-law to the mother of the mother-in-law, and then questions whether the mother of the father-in-law is actually derived later or earlier in the baraita.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's initial derivation
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's initial derivation
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the verse uses "zimmah" to equate the male's relatives (sher haba mimmenu) with the female's relatives (sher haba mimmenah). Rava cites Rav Yitzchak bar Avudimi who adds a gezerah shavah from "hennah" to "hennah."

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the verse uses 'זִמָּה' (zimmah) to equate the male's relatives (שאר הבא ממנו) with the female's relatives (שאר הבא ממנה), but the gemara objects that the male's own relatives do not have 'זִמָּה' written.

sub.text: Rava citing Rav Yitzchak bar Avudimi
sub.text_en: Rava citing Rav Yitzchak bar Avudimi
sub.desc_en: Rava cites Rav Yitzchak bar Avudimi who adds a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'הֵנָּה' to 'הֵנָּה' and from 'זִמָּה' to 'זִמָּה' to resolve the objection.

items.text: Question on 'below like above'
items.text_en: Question on 'below like above'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of 'below like above' in the baraita. It rejects the interpretation that it refers to a daughter's daughter or son's daughter, as they are already included. It suggests it refers to the mother-in-law's mother, but then it should be 'above like below,' and the baraita is corrected to read 'above like below.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of 'below like above' in the baraita and rejects the interpretation that it refers to a daughter's daughter or son's daughter, as they are already included.
The Gemara suggests it refers to the mother-in-law's mother, but then it should be 'above like below,' and the baraita is corrected to read 'above like below.'

items.text: Objection to the gezerah shavah
items.text_en: Objection to the gezerah shavah
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the gezerah shavah from 'zimmah' applies, then the female's relatives (e.g., mother-in-law) are not explicitly written with 'zimmah,' yet the derivation would apply to them as well, which seems problematic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the gezerah shavah from 'zimmah' applies, then the female's relatives (e.g., mother-in-law) are not explicitly written with 'zimmah,' yet the derivation would apply to them as well, which seems problematic.

items.text: Abaye's resolution: three generations
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: three generations
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the baraita means to equate three generations above with three generations below, using the gezerah shavah from 'zimmah.' Just as below there are three generations (e.g., daughter, granddaughter), so too above there are three generations (e.g., mother, grandmother). This applies both to punishment and to the prohibition (azharah).

sub.desc_en: Abaye introduces the gezerah shavah (verbal analogy) from 'zimmah' to equate three generations above with three generations below.
Abaye concludes that just as the punishment applies equally to three generations below and above, so too the prohibition (אזהרה) applies equally above and below.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative: 'below' in prohibition
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative: 'below' in prohibition
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi says the baraita is as originally taught, and 'below' refers to the level of prohibition. The Gemara asks if this means the mother's mother is forbidden for the man, just as the woman's mother's mother is forbidden for her. Abaye answers that the verse says 'her mother she is,' so one is liable for his mother but not for his mother's mother.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asserts that the baraita is as originally taught, and 'below' refers to the level of prohibition.
The Gemara asks whether, just as the woman's mother's mother is forbidden for her, so too the man's mother's mother should be forbidden for him.
Abaye answers that the verse says 'her mother she is,' so one is liable for his mother but not for his mother's mother.

items.text: Rava's analysis: 'Dan minah u-minah' vs. 'Dan minah v'okei b'atreh'
items.text_en: Rava's analysis: 'Dan minah u-minah' vs. 'Dan minah v'okei b'atreh'
items.desc_en: Rava analyzes whether the derivation works according to two hermeneutical principles: 'Dan minah u-minah' (derive both the prohibition and the punishment from the analogy) and 'Dan minah v'okei b'atreh' (derive the prohibition but keep the punishment in its place). He shows that both approaches face difficulties regarding the punishment (burning vs. stoning) for the mother's mother, and the Gemara discusses the objections according to the views that burning is more severe or stoning is more severe.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that according to both hermeneutical principles, the derivation of the mother's mother being forbidden and punished by burning does not come.

The Gemara elaborates the view of 'Dan minah u-minah': just as the mother of her mother is forbidden and punished by burning, so too the mother of his mother would be forbidden and punished by burning.

sub.text: Gemara's objection for those who say burning is more severe
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection for those who say burning is more severe
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects according to the view that burning is more severe: the analogy can be refuted because the mother of his wife is punished by burning, but his mother is punished by stoning.
The Gemara raises a further objection: if his mother is punished by stoning, could it be that the mother of his mother, a more distant relative, is punished by the more severe burning?

The Gemara raises a third objection: just as with her relatives you did not distinguish between her mother and the mother of her mother, so too with his relatives you should not distinguish between his mother and the mother of his mother.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution for those who say stoning is more severe
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution for those who say stoning is more severe
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to the view that stoning is more severe, the first two objections are not relevant, but the third objection still prevents the derivation.

sub.text: Gemara's elaboration for 'Dan minah v'okei b'atreh'
sub.text_en: Gemara's elaboration for 'Dan minah v'okei b'atreh'
sub.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates the view of 'Dan minah v'okei b'atreh': the prohibition is derived (mother of his mother is forbidden), but the punishment is kept in its place — stoning, as found for his mother.

sub.text: Gemara's objection for those who say burning is more severe
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection for those who say burning is more severe
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to the view that burning is more severe, the derivation can still be refuted.

items.text: Initial comparison between the man and the woman
items.text_en: Initial comparison between the man and the woman
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by comparing the case of a man who has relations with his daughter-in-law to a woman who has relations with her father-in-law, questioning whether the same punishment applies. It notes that the mother of the woman is punished by burning, while the mother of the man is punished by stoning, and argues that just as the woman's punishment does not distinguish between her daughter and her mother, so too the man's punishment should not distinguish between his daughter and his mother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the punishment for a man with his daughter-in-law can be derived from the woman's case, noting the difference in severity between burning for the woman's mother and stoning for the man's mother.

The Gemara argues that just as the woman's punishment does not distinguish between her daughter and her mother's mother, so too the man's punishment should not distinguish between his daughter and his mother's mother.
The Gemara notes that according to the view that stoning is more severe, this difficulty prevents deriving the halakha.
The Gemara asks whether, if a parallel is drawn, just as the man's daughter-in-law is forbidden, so too the woman's daughter-in-law should be forbidden.

items.text: Abaye's derivation from the verse
items.text_en: Abaye's derivation from the verse
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a verse to show that the man is punished for his daughter-in-law because she is his son's wife, not because she is his daughter's mother. This resolves the comparison.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites the verse 'אֵשֶׁת בִּנְךָ הִיא' (she is your son's wife) to show that the man is liable for his daughter-in-law because she is his son's wife, not because she is his wife's daughter, thereby resolving the attempted comparison.

items.text: Rava's analysis using the principles of 'דון מינה ומינה' and 'דון מינה ואוקי באתרה'
items.text_en: Rava's analysis using the principles of 'דון מינה ומינה' and 'דון מינה ואוקי באתרה'
items.desc_en: Rava explains that regardless of whether one uses the principle of 'דון מינה ומינה' (derive from it and apply it) or 'דון מינה ואוקי באתרה' (derive from it and leave it in its place), the comparison fails. He then analyzes the arguments for each principle, considering the severity of stoning versus burning, and concludes that the comparison is invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that the comparison fails under both hermeneutical principles: 'דון מינה ומינה' (derive from it and apply it) and 'דון מינה ואוקי באתרה' (derive from it and leave it in its place).

Rava explains that under the principle of 'דון מינה ומינה', one would derive both the prohibition and the punishment: just as a man's daughter-in-law is forbidden and punished by stoning, so too a woman's daughter-in-law would be forbidden and punished by stoning.

sub.text: Objection from the severity of stoning
sub.text_en: Objection from the severity of stoning
sub.desc_en: An objection is raised: for one who holds stoning is more severe, the comparison can be refuted because the man's mother is punished by stoning, while the woman's mother is punished by burning.

A second objection is raised: the woman's daughter is punished by burning while her daughter-in-law would be punished by stoning, but the man himself shows that his daughter is punished by burning and his daughter-in-law by stoning, so the inconsistency is not unique.

Rava resolves: just as the man's punishment does not distinguish between his mother and his daughter-in-law, so too the woman's punishment should not distinguish between her mother and her daughter-in-law; and for one who holds burning is more severe, this refutation is not applied.

sub.text: Rava's analysis under 'דון מינה ואוקי באתרה'
sub.text_en: Rava's analysis under 'דון מינה ואוקי באתרה'
sub.desc_en: Rava explains that under the principle of 'דון מינה ואוקי באתרה', one derives the prohibition but leaves the punishment in its place: the woman's daughter-in-law is forbidden, but her punishment is burning, as found with her mother.

sub.text: Objection from the severity of stoning
sub.text_en: Objection from the severity of stoning
sub.desc_en: An objection is raised: for one who holds stoning is more severe, the comparison can be refuted because the man's mother is punished by stoning, while the woman's mother is punished by burning.

Rava resolves with a second objection: just as the man's punishment distinguishes between his daughter and his daughter-in-law, so too the woman's punishment should distinguish between her daughter and her daughter-in-law; and for one who holds burning is more severe, this refutation is not applied.

items.text: Source for punishment of one's daughter from an anusot
items.text_en: Source for punishment of one's daughter from an anusot
items.desc_en: Abaye proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if one is punished for his granddaughter, certainly he should be punished for his daughter. The Gemara objects that punishment cannot be derived through logical inference, but Abaye responds that it is merely revealing the intent of the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where is the punishment for one's daughter from an anusot (a raped woman) derived?
Abaye proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if one is punished for his granddaughter, certainly he should be punished for his daughter.
The Gemara objects: punishment cannot be derived through logical inference (עונשין מן הדין).
The Gemara resolves that Abaye's argument is merely revealing the intent of the verse (גלויי מילתא בעלמא), not deriving a new punishment.

items.text: Rava's derivation via 'הנה' and 'זמה'
items.text_en: Rava's derivation via 'הנה' and 'זמה'
items.desc_en: Rava cites Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi who derives the punishment through a verbal analogy using the words 'הנה' and 'זמה'. Additionally, the father of Rabbi Avin teaches that the verse 'ובת איש כהן' was necessary to teach the punishment for one's daughter from an anusot.

sub.text: Rava citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi
sub.text_en: Rava citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi
sub.desc_en: Rava reports Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi's verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) linking the words 'הנה' and 'זמה' to derive the punishment for one's daughter from an anusot.
The father of Rabbi Avin teaches that the verse 'ובת איש כהן' was necessary to teach the punishment for one's daughter from an anusot, since it was not derived elsewhere.

items.text: Comparison to the daughter of a kohen
items.text_en: Comparison to the daughter of a kohen
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the punishment for one's daughter from an anusot is the same as for a daughter of a kohen, where the woman is burned but her partner is not. Abaye cites a verse to exclude this case, and Rava explains the difference: in the case of a kohen's daughter, the partner is judged as a regular Israelite, but here, the partner would be judged as a bachelor, which is not a valid category.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: just as in the case of a kohen's daughter, she is burned but her partner is not, perhaps the same applies to one's daughter from an anusot (a raped woman), where she is burned but her partner is not.
Abaye cites a verse: 'אֶת אָבִיהָ הִיא מְחַלֶּלֶת' (she profanes her father) — implying that only one who profanes her father is burned, excluding this case where her father profanes her.

Rava explains the difference: in the case of a kohen's daughter, the partner is removed from the law of a kohen's daughter and placed under the law of an Israelite daughter, but here, there is no valid category of 'bachelor' to place him under.

items.text: Source for the warning (אזהרה) regarding one's daughter from an anusot
items.text_en: Source for the warning (אזהרה) regarding one's daughter from an anusot
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the prohibition (אזהרה) against having relations with one's daughter from an anusot. For Abaye and Rava, the warning is derived from the same source as the punishment. For the father of Rabbi Avin, Rabbi Ila'a cites the verse 'אל תחלל את בתך להזנותה'. Rabbi Yaakov challenges this, suggesting the verse is needed for another teaching, but the Gemara resolves that the verse implies two lessons. Abaye and Rava interpret the verse differently, and Rabbi Mani and Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva offer additional interpretations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the warning (אזהרה) against having relations with one's daughter from an anusot.
The Gemara notes that for Abaye and Rava, the warning is derived from the same source as the punishment.

sub.text: Gemara's question (for the father of Rabbi Avin)
sub.text_en: Gemara's question (for the father of Rabbi Avin)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the source is for the father of Rabbi Avin, who holds a different position.
Rabbi Ila'a cites the verse 'אַל תְּחַלֵּל אֶת בִּתְּךָ לְהַזְנוֹתָהּ' (Do not profane your daughter by making her a harlot) as the source.
Rabbi Yaakov challenges that the verse is needed for another teaching about a priest marrying his daughter to a Levite or Israelite.
The Gemara resolves that the verse uses the fuller form 'תְּחַלֵּל' to imply two lessons, thus both teachings are derived.
The Gemara asks how Abaye and Rava interpret the verse 'אַל תְּחַלֵּל'.
Rabbi Mani explains that the verse refers to one who marries his daughter to an old man.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Eliezer says the verse refers to one who marries his daughter to an old man, and Rabbi Akiva says it refers to one who delays his daughter's marriage past maturity.

sub.text: Rav Kahana's statement in the name of Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana's statement in the name of Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana says in the name of Rabbi Akiva that the only poor person in Israel is a cunning wicked person, and one who delays his daughter's marriage past maturity.
The Gemara questions whether one who delays his daughter's marriage is not already included in the category of a cunning wicked person.
Abaye begins to answer the question, but the text cuts off at the section boundary.

items.text: Opening statements on improper marriages and returning lost objects
items.text_en: Opening statements on improper marriages and returning lost objects
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the 'wicked cunning poor man' is one who delays his daughter's marriage past puberty. Rav Yehuda cites Rav that marrying a daughter to an old man, marrying a son to a minor, or returning a lost object to a gentile incurs a severe biblical curse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the 'wicked cunning poor man' is one who delays his daughter's marriage past puberty.
Rav Kahana cites Rabbi Akiva's warning to be cautious of one who advises you according to his own interest.
Rav Yehuda cites Rav that marrying a daughter to an old man, marrying a son to a minor, or returning a lost object to a gentile incurs a severe biblical curse.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding marrying children close to maturity
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding marrying children close to maturity
items.desc_en: A baraisa is cited praising one who marries off his children 'close to their maturity' (סמוך לפרקן), which seems to contradict Rav's statement. The Gemara resolves that 'close to their maturity' is different from marrying a minor or an old man.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that praises one who marries off his children close to their maturity, contradicting Rav's condemnation.
The Gemara resolves that marrying off children close to their maturity is different and praiseworthy, unlike delaying past puberty.

items.text: Baraisa on loving neighbors and marrying a sister's daughter
items.text_en: Baraisa on loving neighbors and marrying a sister's daughter
items.desc_en: A baraisa lists praiseworthy acts: loving neighbors, drawing close relatives, marrying a sister's daughter, and lending to a poor person in need, with a promise that God will answer.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists praiseworthy acts including loving neighbors, marrying a sister's daughter, and lending to the poor in need, with a biblical blessing.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva on 'אותו ואתהן'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva on 'אותו ואתהן'
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the phrase 'אותו ואתהן' regarding the punishment for a man who marries a woman and her daughter or her mother. Rabbi Yishmael interprets it as him and one of them, while Rabbi Akiva says him and both. Abaye and Rava debate the practical difference: Abaye says it's a matter of scriptural interpretation, while Rava says it concerns the punishment for the mother-in-law after the wife's death.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited presenting the dispute: Rabbi Yishmael interprets 'אותו ואתהן' as 'him and one of them', while Rabbi Akiva says 'him and both of them'.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two interpretations.
Abaye answers that the difference lies in how they interpret the meaning of the phrase.

Abaye elaborates: Rabbi Yishmael reads 'ואתהן' as 'and one of them' based on Greek usage, deriving the mother-in-law from a separate exposition; Rabbi Akiva reads it as 'and both of them', with the mother-in-law explicitly written in the verse.

Rava offers a different practical difference: the case of the mother-in-law after the wife's death — Rabbi Yishmael holds she is executed by burning, while Rabbi Akiva holds she is only subject to a prohibition.

items.text: Mishnah: Those executed and laws of murder
items.text_en: Mishnah: Those executed and laws of murder
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those executed: a murderer and the inhabitants of an apostate city. It details cases of murder: if one strikes another with a stone or iron, or forces him into water or fire where he cannot escape, he is liable. If the victim could have escaped, he is exempt. Setting a dog or snake on him exempts, but if he incites a snake to bite, Rabbi Yehuda holds him liable while the Sages exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing those executed: a murderer and the inhabitants of an apostate city.
The Mishnah details that a murderer who strikes another with a stone or iron, or forces him into water or fire where he cannot escape, is liable.
The Mishnah states that if the victim could have escaped, the perpetrator is exempt, and setting a dog or snake on him also exempts.
The Mishnah records a dispute: if he incites a snake to bite, Rabbi Yehuda holds him liable while the Sages exempt.

items.text: Gemara: Why no 'hand' measurement for iron
items.text_en: Gemara: Why no 'hand' measurement for iron
items.desc_en: Shmuel explains that the Torah did not require a 'hand' measurement for iron because iron kills in any amount. A baraisa supports this, adding that this applies only when the iron is sharp.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel asks why the Torah did not require a 'hand' measurement (a minimum size) for iron as a murder weapon.
Shmuel answers that iron kills in any amount, so no minimum size is needed.
A baraita supports Shmuel: Rabbi states that since iron kills in any amount, the Torah gave no measure for it.
The gemara qualifies that this rule applies only when the iron is sharp (i.e., its blade is honed).

items.text: Gemara: Analysis of 'forcing' (כבישה) and the case of צמצום
items.text_en: Gemara: Analysis of 'forcing' (כבישה) and the case of צמצום
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's first clause teaches liability even without pushing, and the latter clause teaches exemption even if he pushed. Shmuel derives the law of 'forcing' (מצמצם) from the verse 'או באיבה'. A story is told of a man who trapped another's snake in the sun, causing its death; Ravina holds him liable via a kal vachomer from murder, while Rav Acha bar Rav exempts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's first clause teaches liability even without pushing, and the latter clause teaches exemption even if he pushed.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the law of 'forcing' (כבישה)?
Shmuel answers that the verse 'או באיבה' (or with enmity) includes the case of one who forces (מצמצם) the victim into the water.
A story is told of a man who trapped another's snake in the sun, causing its death; Ravina holds him liable and Rav Acha bar Rav exempts.

Ravina holds him liable via a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from murder: if murder, where an unintentional act is not treated like intentional, still holds the 'forcer' liable, then all the more so here.

items.text: Argument from damages to murder liability
items.text_en: Argument from damages to murder liability
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer: if one is liable for damages even when acting unintentionally or under duress, then surely one should be liable for murder when constricting (מצמצם). Rav Acha bar Rav Poter rejects this, citing a verse that limits liability for constriction to murder cases only.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if one is liable for damages even when acting unintentionally (שוגג) or under duress (אונס), then surely one should be liable for murder when constricting (מצמצם) the victim.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Poter's rejection
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Poter's rejection
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Poter rejects the kal vachomer, citing the verse 'מוֹת יוּמַת הַמַּכֶּה רֹצֵחַ הוּא' (the striker shall be put to death, he is a murderer) to limit liability for constriction (מצמצם) to murder cases only, not to damages.

items.text: Rava's cases of indirect killing
items.text_en: Rava's cases of indirect killing
items.desc_en: Rava presents several cases: tying someone up and they die of starvation (exempt), tying in sun/rain (liable if death is immediate, exempt if eventual), tying before a lion (exempt) or before mosquitoes (liable). Rav Ashi argues even mosquitoes exempt because they come and go.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that one who ties another and the victim dies of starvation is exempt from capital liability.
Rava rules that tying someone in the sun or cold where death is immediate is liable, but if death is only eventual (when the sun or cold returns) it is exempt.
Rava rules that tying someone before a lion is exempt (the lion acts independently), but before mosquitoes is liable (the tying is the direct cause).
Rav Ashi argues that even the case of mosquitoes is exempt because mosquitoes come and go, so the tying is not the direct cause of death.

items.text: Dispute about covering with a barrel or beam
items.text_en: Dispute about covering with a barrel or beam
items.desc_en: A dispute between Rava and Rabbi Zeira: if one covered someone with a barrel or collapsed a beam on them, one says liable, the other says exempt.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Rava and Rabbi Zeira regarding liability for covering someone with a barrel or collapsing a beam on them.

items.text: Attempt to identify the exempt opinion
items.text_en: Attempt to identify the exempt opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to determine which Amora holds exempt: it suggests Rava based on his starvation case, but counters with Rabbi Zeira's case of locking someone in a plaster house without lighting a lamp (exempt), implying he holds exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rava is the one who holds exempt, citing his ruling that one who starves a bound victim is exempt.
The Gemara counters that Rabbi Zeira is the one who holds exempt, based on his case of locking someone in a plaster house without lighting a lamp, implying exemption.

items.text: Distinction regarding heat
items.text_en: Distinction regarding heat
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes Rabbi Zeira's case: without a lamp, the heat (הבלא) does not begin, so it is not comparable to the barrel/beam case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing Rabbi Zeira's case: without a lamp (שרגא), the heat (הבלא) does not begin, so it is not comparable to the barrel/beam case.

items.text: Continuation of the previous discussion about heat in a pit
items.text_en: Continuation of the previous discussion about heat in a pit
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that here, even without a lamp, the heat begins immediately, contrasting with the earlier case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that in the current case, even without a lamp, the heat begins immediately, distinguishing it from the earlier case.

items.text: Siman for the following statements
items.text_en: Siman for the following statements
items.desc_en: A mnemonic sign (סִימָן) is given for the series of halakhot that follow: סוּלָּם (ladder), תְּרִיס (shield), סַמָּנִין (medicines), בַּכּוֹתֶל (against a wall).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a mnemonic sign (סִימָן) listing the topics: ladder, shield, medicines, and against a wall.

items.text: Rava's three cases of exemption due to potential rescue
items.text_en: Rava's three cases of exemption due to potential rescue
items.desc_en: Rava presents three cases: one who pushed another into a pit with a ladder inside, one who shot an arrow while the victim held a shield, and one who shot an arrow while the victim had medicines. In all cases, the perpetrator is exempt because at the time of the act, the victim could have saved himself.

sub.desc_en: Rava presents the first case: one who pushed another into a pit that had a ladder inside is exempt, because at the time of the push the victim could have climbed out.
Rava presents the second case: one who shot an arrow while the victim held a shield is exempt, because at the time of the shot the arrow would have been intercepted by the shield.
Rava presents the third case: one who shot an arrow while the victim had medicines is exempt, because at the time of the shot the victim could have healed himself.

items.text: Rav Ashi's ruling and Rav Acha's question about medicines in the market
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's ruling and Rav Acha's question about medicines in the market
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi rules that even if medicines are available in the market, the killer is exempt. Rav Acha bar Rava asks what if medicines were readily available to the victim, and Rav Ashi responds that he would leave the court acquitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi rules that even if medicines are available in the market, the shooter is exempt because the victim could have obtained them.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi: if medicines happened to be available to the victim, what is the law?
Rav Ashi answers that the shooter is acquitted and leaves the court exonerated.

items.text: Rava's case of throwing a stone against a wall that rebounds
items.text_en: Rava's case of throwing a stone against a wall that rebounds
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if one throws a stone against a wall and it rebounds and kills, he is liable. A baraita is cited about those playing ball who kill: if intentional, they are executed; if unintentional, they are exiled. The Gemara explains that the novel point is the intentional case, lest one think it is a case of uncertain warning (הַתְרָאַת סָפֵק).

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if one throws a stone against a wall and it rebounds and kills, he is liable.
A baraita is cited about those playing ball who kill: if intentional, they are executed; if unintentional, they are exiled.
The Gemara questions why the baraita needed to state the obvious case of unintentional killing leading to exile.
The Gemara explains that the novel point is the intentional case, lest one think it is a case of uncertain warning (הַתְרָאַת סָפֵק).

items.text: Rav Tachlifa's baraita about ball players within four cubits
items.text_en: Rav Tachlifa's baraita about ball players within four cubits
items.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arva taught before Rabbi Avahu: ball players who kill within four cubits are exempt, beyond four cubits are liable. Ravina asks Rav Ashi for clarification, and Rav Ashi explains that ball players generally want the ball to go far, so beyond four cubits it is considered their direct force.

sub.desc_en: Rav Tachlifa bar Ma'arva taught before Rabbi Avahu a baraita about ball players: if they kill within four cubits they are exempt, beyond four cubits they are liable.

Ravina asks Rav Ashi for clarification: if the ball player wants the ball to go far, even a short distance should be considered his direct force; if he does not want it, even a long distance should not be considered his direct force.
Rav Ashi answers that ball players generally want the ball to go as far as possible, so beyond four cubits it is considered their direct force (כוחו).

items.text: Challenge from the laws of purification water and response
items.text_en: Challenge from the laws of purification water and response
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle of direct force (כֹּחוֹ) from a mishna about sanctification water that falls on the hand or side and then into a cistern, which is invalid. It answers that the case is where the water drips (שׁוֹתֵת). Another challenge from a needle on a potsherd is answered by Rav Chinana bar Yehuda in the name of Rav that the text says 'found' (מָצָא), implying a different scenario.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle of direct force (כֹּחוֹ) by citing a mishna where sanctification water that falls on the hand or side and then into a cistern is invalid.
The Gemara answers that the case involves water that drips (שׁוֹתֵת), not direct force.
The Gemara raises another challenge from a case of a needle on a potsherd where the sprinkling is uncertain and invalid.

sub.text: Rav Chinana bar Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chinana bar Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Yehuda resolves the challenge by noting that the mishna uses the term 'found' (מָצָא), implying a different scenario where the water dripped onto the needle after being found on the potsherd.

items.text: Rav Pappa's rulings on indirect force
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's rulings on indirect force
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that if one ties up another and pours a bucket of water on him, it is considered his direct force (גִּירֵי דִידֵיהּ) and he is liable, but only with initial force (כֹּחַ רִאשׁוֹן); secondary force is merely indirect causation (גְּרָמָא). He also rules that throwing a stone upward that goes sideways and kills is liable. Mar bar Rav Ashi questions this, asking why it is considered his force if it goes sideways.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that if one ties up another and pours a bucket of water on him, it is considered his direct force (גִּירֵי דִידֵיהּ) and he is liable.
Rav Pappa qualifies that this liability applies only with initial force (כֹּחַ רִאשׁוֹן); secondary force is merely indirect causation (גְּרָמָא).
Rav Pappa rules that throwing a stone upward that goes sideways and kills renders the thrower liable.
Mar bar Rav Ashi questions Rav Pappa, asking why the stone's sideways motion is considered his force.
Mar bar Rav Ashi objects that if it were truly his force, the stone should go upward, not sideways.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution on the previous Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution on the previous Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the logic of the Mishnah's ruling about a blow that is not sufficient to kill, and resolves that the force is weak (koach kachush).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the blow is not his force, why does the Mishnah rule that the blow goes down (to the grave)?
The Gemara resolves: it is a weak force (כוח כחוש) that is insufficient to kill on its own.

items.text: Baraita on ten assailants and Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation
items.text_en: Baraita on ten assailants and Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if ten people strike a person with ten sticks and he dies, they are all exempt, but Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira holds the last one liable. Rabbi Yochanan explains both derive their views from the same verse, 'And if a man strikes any soul of a man'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute: ten assailants are all exempt, but Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira holds the last one liable for hastening death.

Rabbi Yochanan explains that both sides derive their positions from the same verse, interpreting 'כל נפש' (any soul) differently: the Rabbis require a complete soul, while Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira requires any soul.

items.text: Rava's ruling on killing a treifa and a goses
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on killing a treifa and a goses
items.desc_en: Rava states that all agree one who kills a treifa is exempt, and one who kills a goses bidei shamayim (dying by natural causes) is liable. The dispute is only about a goses bidei adam (dying by human hand), comparing it either to a treifa or to a goses bidei shamayim.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that all agree one who kills a טריפה (animal with a fatal defect) is exempt, and one who kills a גוסס בידי שמים (dying by natural causes) is liable, while the dispute is only about a גוסס בידי אדם (dying by human hand).

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the first opinion
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the first opinion
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the opinion comparing a גוסס בידי אדם to a טריפה reasons that unlike a גוסס בידי שמים, a human act has been performed on him.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the second opinion
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the second opinion
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the opinion comparing a גוסס בידי אדם to a גוסס בידי שמים reasons that unlike a טריפה, the simanim (trachea and esophagus) are not severed.

items.text: Tanna's teaching before Rav Sheishet and its clarification
items.text_en: Tanna's teaching before Rav Sheishet and its clarification
items.desc_en: A tanna taught before Rav Sheishet that one who strikes his friend without enough force to kill, and another comes and kills him, the latter is liable. The Gemara clarifies that the case is actually where the first blow had enough force to kill, and the ruling aligns with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.

sub.desc_en: A tanna teaches before Rav Sheishet that one who strikes his friend without enough force to kill, and another comes and kills him, the latter is liable.
The Gemara objects that if the first blow lacked lethal force, the ruling is obvious.
The Gemara clarifies that the case is actually where the first blow had enough force to kill, and the ruling aligns with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.

items.text: Rava's series of rulings on treifa and related cases
items.text_en: Rava's series of rulings on treifa and related cases
items.desc_en: Rava rules on various cases involving a treifa: one who kills a treifa is exempt; a treifa who kills before a court is liable, but not before a non-court; one who sodomizes a treifa is liable; witnesses who testified about a treifa and were disqualified are not killed; a treifa ox that kills is liable, but an ox of a treifa person that kills is exempt. Rav Ashi disagrees on some points.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that one who kills a טריפה (animal with a fatal condition) is exempt, and a טריפה that kills before a court is liable but not before a non-court.
Rava explains the reasoning: before a court, the verse 'וּבִעַרְתָּ הָרָע מִקִּרְבֶּךָ' applies; outside court, the testimony cannot be disqualified, so it is invalid.
Rava rules that one who sodomizes a טריפה is liable, and a טריפה that sodomizes before a court is liable but not outside court, with the same reasoning.
The Gemara questions why Rava repeated the same ruling about a טריפה that kills and a טריפה that sodomizes, suggesting the second case might be redundant.

The Gemara explains that the case of one who sodomizes a טריפה was necessary to teach that it is not like using a dead body (which would be exempt), but rather the liability is due to the pleasure derived.

Rava rules that witnesses who testified about a טריפה and were disqualified are not killed, but witnesses of a טריפה who were disqualified are killed; Rav Ashi disagrees, saying even the latter are not killed because they cannot be subject to further disqualification.

Rava rules that a טריפה ox that kills is liable, but an ox of a טריפה person that kills is exempt, based on the verse 'הַשּׁוֹר יִסָּקֵל וְגַם בְּעָלָיו יוּמָת' — only where the owner could be killed does the ox get stoned.
Rav Ashi objects, arguing that even a טריפה ox that kills is exempt, since if the owners were exempt (being טריפה), the ox is also exempt.

items.text: Dispute about snake venom and liability
items.text_en: Dispute about snake venom and liability
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding a case where one incited a dog or snake to kill: according to Rabbi Yehuda, the snake's venom is between its teeth, so the inciter is killed by sword and the snake is exempt; according to the Sages, the snake vomits its venom, so the snake is stoned and the inciter is exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains that according to Rabbi Yehuda, the snake's venom is between its teeth, so the inciter is killed by sword and the snake is exempt.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains that according to the Sages, the snake vomits its venom, so the snake is stoned and the inciter is exempt.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on one who strikes and the victim later dies
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on one who strikes and the victim later dies
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one strikes his friend, the victim is assessed for death, then improves, then worsens and dies, the assailant is liable; Rabbi Nechemya exempts because 'there are legs to the matter' (the improvement shows the death was from another cause). The Gemara begins to cite a baraita on this.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: one who strikes his friend, the victim is assessed for death, then improves, then worsens and dies, the assailant is liable; Rabbi Nechemya exempts because 'there are legs to the matter' (the improvement shows the death was from another cause).
The Gemara cites a baraita that Rabbi Nechemya derived his position from the verse 'If he rises and walks outside' (Exodus 21:19), indicating that improvement shows the death was not from the blow.

items.text: Gemara's interpretation of the verse
items.text_en: Gemara's interpretation of the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse "and the striker shall be acquitted" as referring to a case where the victim was assessed for death but then improved, and later worsened and died – in such a case the striker is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'and the striker shall be acquitted' as referring to a case where the victim was assessed for death, improved, then worsened and died, exempting the striker.

items.text: The Rabbis' interpretation of the verse
items.text_en: The Rabbis' interpretation of the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis derive from the same verse, and answers that it teaches that the striker is imprisoned.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis derive from the phrase 'and the striker shall be acquitted', and answers that it teaches that the striker is imprisoned pending investigation.
The Gemara answers that the verse teaches that the striker is imprisoned.

items.text: Source for imprisonment: Rabbi Nechemiah vs. Rabbis
items.text_en: Source for imprisonment: Rabbi Nechemiah vs. Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the source for imprisonment according to Rabbi Nechemiah, who learns it from the wood-gatherer, while the Rabbis reject this because the wood-gatherer was clearly liable for death, unlike this case. Rabbi Nechemiah then learns from the blasphemer, but the Rabbis respond that the blasphemer was a hora'at sha'ah (temporary ruling). A baraisa elaborates on what Moses knew and did not know in each case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where does Rabbi Nechemiah derive the law of imprisonment?
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Nechemiah learns imprisonment from the wood-gatherer (מקושש).

The Rabbis object: Why not learn from the wood-gatherer? They explain that the wood-gatherer was clearly liable for death, but Moses did not know which death penalty to apply, unlike this case where we do not know if the assailant is liable at all.
Rabbi Nechemiah learns instead from the blasphemer (מגדף), where Moses did not know if he was liable for death, yet they imprisoned him.
The Rabbis reject this: the blasphemer case was a temporary ruling (הוראת שעה), not a general precedent.
A baraita elaborates: Moses knew the wood-gatherer was liable for death but did not know which death, while regarding the blasphemer he did not even know if he was liable for death at all.

items.text: The need for two assessments
items.text_en: The need for two assessments
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Nechemiah, two assessments are written in the verse: one for a case where the victim was assessed for death and lived, and another where he was assessed for death and improved. The Rabbis, however, need two assessments for a case where he was assessed for death and lived, and a case where he was assessed for life and died. Rabbi Nechemiah holds that the latter case does not require a verse, since he left the court acquitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to Rabbi Nechemiah, the two assessments in the verse are understood, but for the Rabbis, why are two assessments needed?
The Gemara answers: one assessment is for a case where he was assessed for death and lived, and another for a case where he was assessed for life and died.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Nechemiah's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Nechemiah's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Nechemiah does not need a verse for the case of assessed for life and died, since the assailant left the court acquitted.

items.text: Baraisa: Dispute between Rabbi Nechemiah and the Sages
items.text_en: Baraisa: Dispute between Rabbi Nechemiah and the Sages
items.desc_en: A baraisa presents the dispute: if the victim was assessed for death and improved, a second assessment for monetary compensation is made; if he later worsened and died, Rabbi Nechemiah says to follow the intermediate assessment, while the Sages say there is no assessment after assessment.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita states: one who strikes another and the victim was assessed for death but lived is acquitted.
If the victim was assessed for death but improved, a second assessment for monetary compensation is made.
Rabbi Nechemya rules: if the victim later worsened and died, we follow the intermediate assessment (אומד האמצעי).
The Sages disagree, stating that there is no reassessment after an initial assessment.

items.text: Another baraisa and its ruling
items.text_en: Another baraisa and its ruling
items.desc_en: Another baraisa states that if the victim was assessed for death, a second assessment for life is made; but if assessed for life, no assessment for death is made. If he improved and then died, the striker pays damages and pain to the heirs from the time of the blow. The Gemara notes that this unattributed ruling follows Rabbi Nechemiah.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that if the victim was assessed for death, a second assessment for life is made; if assessed for life, no assessment for death is made; if he improved and then died, the striker pays damages and pain to the heirs.
The Gemara clarifies that payment begins from the time of the blow, and notes that this unattributed ruling follows Rabbi Nechemiah.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of unintended killing
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of unintended killing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where one is exempt from execution: intending to kill an animal but killing a person, intending to kill a gentile but killing a Jew, intending to kill a non-viable fetus but killing a viable child, and intending to strike a non-lethal blow to the loins but the blow went to the heart and was lethal.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three cases of unintended killing where the killer is exempt from execution: intending to kill an animal but killing a person, intending to kill a gentile but killing a Jew, and intending to kill a non-viable fetus but killing a viable child.
The Mishnah adds a fourth case: intending to strike a non-lethal blow to the loins, but the blow went to the heart and was lethal, and the killer is exempt.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Cases of unintended killing
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Cases of unintended killing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where the blow was intended for one body part or person but struck another, ruling that if the blow was sufficient to kill the intended target but not the actual one, the assailant is exempt; if sufficient for the actual target, he is liable. Rabbi Shimon exempts even when intending to kill one person and killing another.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a case where a blow sufficient to kill on the heart lands on the lower back and is insufficient there, exempting the assailant.
The Mishnah adds cases of intending to strike a large person but hitting a small one, or vice versa, where the blow is insufficient for the intended target, exempting the assailant.
The Mishnah states that if the blow was sufficient for the actual target, the assailant is liable.
Rabbi Shimon rules that even if one intended to kill this person and killed that person, he is exempt.

items.text: Gemara's question: To which part of the Mishnah does Rabbi Shimon refer?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: To which part of the Mishnah does Rabbi Shimon refer?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Shimon's statement applies to the latter cases (where the assailant is liable) or the former (where he is exempt). It concludes that Rabbi Shimon refers to the first part, where the Mishnah implies liability for intending to kill one person and killing another, but Rabbi Shimon exempts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks to which part of the Mishnah Rabbi Shimon's statement refers, and rejects the possibility that it refers to the latter part (the cases where the Mishnah says the assailant is liable).
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Shimon refers to the first part of the Mishnah, where the Mishnah implies liability for intending to kill one person and killing another, but Rabbi Shimon exempts.

items.text: Clarifying the dispute: Cases of uncertainty
items.text_en: Clarifying the dispute: Cases of uncertainty
items.desc_en: The Gemara explores scenarios where the assailant intended to hit one of two people but is unsure which, or mistook one for the other. It cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon requires explicit intent: 'I intend to kill so-and-so.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if Reuven and Shimon are standing and the assailant says 'I intend to hit Reuven, not Shimon,' that is exactly the dispute — so why is it obvious?
The Gemara raises two additional scenarios: if the assailant said 'I intend to one of them' but is unsure which, or if he thought the victim was Reuven but it turned out to be Shimon.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon explicitly requires the assailant to say 'I intend to so-and-so,' resolving the uncertainty scenarios.

items.text: The rationale of Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis
items.text_en: The rationale of Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon derives his position from the verse 'and he lies in wait for him' (Deut. 19:11), requiring specific intent. The Rabbis, citing the school of Rabbi Yannai, exclude a case where one throws a stone into a crowd. The Gemara analyzes the scenario of a mixed crowd of Jews and Gentiles, concluding that a fixed Gentile is considered half-and-half, leading to exemption due to doubt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Shimon's rationale for his position.

sub.text: Gemara's answer citing Rabbi Shimon's verse
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer citing Rabbi Shimon's verse
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon derives his position from the verse 'וְאָרַב לוֹ' (and he lies in wait for him), requiring specific intent toward that individual.

sub.text: Rabbis' position citing the school of Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Rabbis' position citing the school of Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: The Rabbis, citing the school of Rabbi Yannai, exclude the case of one who throws a stone into a crowd (where specific intent is impossible).
The Gemara asks what scenario is being described.
If the crowd has nine Gentiles and one Jew, the majority is Gentiles, or if half-and-half, the principle of ספק נפשות להקל (doubt in capital cases is lenient) applies, making the case obvious.
The case is where there are nine Jews and one fixed Gentile (גוי קבוע), which is treated as half-and-half, leading to exemption due to doubt.

items.text: Biblical derivation for the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon's interpretation
items.text_en: Biblical derivation for the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon's interpretation
items.desc_en: The Rabbis derive liability for unintended killing from the verse 'And if men strive and hurt a pregnant woman' (Ex. 21:22), interpreted by Rabbi Elazar as referring to a mortal struggle. Rabbi Shimon interprets 'life for life' (Ex. 21:23) as monetary compensation, citing Rabbi's teaching that it means payment, not actual capital punishment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Rabbis, who hold one liable for intending to kill one person and killing another, derive this from the verse 'And if men strive and hurt a pregnant woman' (Ex. 21:22).
Rabbi Elazar explains that the verse speaks of a mortal struggle, as it concludes 'if there be a fatality, then you shall give life for life' (Ex. 21:23).
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Shimon does with the verse 'life for life' (Ex. 21:23).
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Shimon interprets 'life for life' as monetary compensation, consistent with Rabbi's teaching that it means payment.
The baraita cites Rabbi's argument that 'life for life' means monetary payment, not literal capital punishment, based on a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) using the word 'giving' (נתינה).

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's statement that a murderer who is mixed with others is exempt, and Rabbi Yehuda says they are confined to a cell.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces a comparison: just as in the earlier case of the ox (described above) there is monetary liability, so too here there is monetary liability.

items.text: Rava's analysis of the baraita from the school of Hezekiah
items.text_en: Rava's analysis of the baraita from the school of Hezekiah
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the baraita from the school of Hezekiah derives from Rabbi's opinion and from the Rabbis, comparing killing a person to killing an animal. The Gemara then questions the meaning of 'not intending' and concludes that the person is neither liable for death nor for monetary payment.

sub.desc_en: Rava introduces the baraita from the school of Hezekiah, which derives from Rabbi's opinion and the Rabbis, comparing killing a person to killing an animal to establish liability for monetary payment.

The Gemara questions the meaning of 'not intending' in the baraita, clarifying that it cannot mean no intention at all (which would be accidental), but rather intending for one person but hitting another.
The Gemara objects: if the killer is liable for death (בן קטלא), why would the baraita need to exempt him from monetary payment?
The Gemara concludes that the killer is neither liable for death nor for monetary payment.

items.text: Mishnah: Mixed capital offenders
items.text_en: Mishnah: Mixed capital offenders
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases of a murderer mixed with others, and capital offenders of different death penalties mixed together. Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis dispute which death penalty is applied when those liable for stoning and burning are mixed, and similarly for decapitation and strangulation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a murderer mixed with others, where all are exempt, and Rabbi Yehuda says they are gathered into a cell.

The Mishnah states that when capital offenders of different death penalties are mixed, they are judged by the lighter penalty, and then presents the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages regarding stoning vs. burning.
Rabbi Shimon argues that burning is more severe because it was given to the daughter of a priest who committed adultery.
The Sages counter that stoning is more severe because it was given to the blasphemer and idolater.
The Mishnah concludes with the case of those liable for decapitation mixed with those liable for strangulation, where Rabbi Shimon says decapitation and the Sages say strangulation.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rabbi Abahu's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rabbi Abahu's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions who 'others' refers to, and Rabbi Abahu in the name of Shmuel explains that the case involves a murderer whose trial was not completed mixed with those whose trials were completed. The Rabbis hold that all are exempt because a trial cannot be completed in absentia, while Rabbi Yehuda holds they are confined to a cell.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who 'others' refers to, questioning whether it could mean kosher people and why Rabbi Yehuda would then confine them.

sub.text: Rabbi Abahu in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abahu in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu in the name of Shmuel explains that the case involves a murderer whose trial was not completed mixed with other murderers whose trials were completed.
The Rabbis hold that all are exempt because a trial cannot be completed in absentia.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that since they are murderers, they are not entirely exempt, and they are confined to a cell.

items.text: Resh Lakish's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish argues that the dispute is about an ox whose trial was not completed mixed with oxen whose trials were completed, not about a person. The Rabbis exempt all because an ox's death follows its owner's status, while Rabbi Yehuda says they are confined to a cell.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish says: in the case of a person, everyone agrees they are exempt; the dispute here is about an ox whose trial was not completed mixed with other oxen whose trials were completed.

sub.text: Reason of the Rabbis regarding an ox
sub.text_en: Reason of the Rabbis regarding an ox
sub.desc_en: The Rabbis reason: just as the death penalty for the owner (when the ox is condemned) requires the ox's trial in its presence, so too the ox's own trial cannot be completed in its absence; therefore all are exempt.

sub.text: Reason of Rabbi Yehuda regarding an ox
sub.text_en: Reason of Rabbi Yehuda regarding an ox
