sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda holds: they are confined to a cell (presumably because of the dangerous nature of the oxen).

items.text: Rava's statement begins
items.text_en: Rava's statement begins
items.desc_en: Rava begins to speak, likely continuing the analysis, but the text cuts off here.

sub.desc_en: Rava begins a statement which will continue beyond this segment.

items.text: Rava's reinterpretation of the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Rava's reinterpretation of the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah refers to two people standing with an arrow passing between them, killing someone, and both are exempt. Rabbi Yosei adds that even if Abba Chalfta were between them, they would still be exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement about Rabbi Yosei's exemption even if Abba Chalfta were between them.

Rava reinterprets the Mishnah: two people standing with an arrow passing between them killing someone are both exempt, and Rabbi Yosei adds that even if Abba Chalfta were between them they would still be exempt.

items.text: Mishnah: Ox sentenced to stoning mixed with others
items.text_en: Mishnah: Ox sentenced to stoning mixed with others
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if an ox whose trial was completed gets mixed with other oxen, all are stoned. Rabbi Yehuda says they are confined to a pen.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that if an ox whose trial was completed gets mixed with other oxen, all are stoned.
Rabbi Yehuda offers a dissenting opinion that the mixed oxen are confined to a pen rather than stoned.

items.text: Baraita: Cow that killed and gave birth
items.text_en: Baraita: Cow that killed and gave birth
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a cow that killed and then gave birth: if it gave birth before sentencing, the offspring is permitted; if after sentencing, it is forbidden. If mixed with others, they are confined to a pen. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon says they are brought to court and stoned.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the rule for a cow that killed and then gave birth: if before sentencing the offspring is permitted, if after sentencing it is forbidden.
The baraita continues: if the cow mixed with others, they are confined to a pen.
Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon disputes and says they are brought to court and stoned.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution on the baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution on the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita: if the cow was pregnant when it gored, the offspring should be forbidden even before sentencing, as per Rava's principle. It resolves by emending the baraita to say 'if it became pregnant and gave birth before sentencing, the offspring is permitted; if after sentencing, it is forbidden.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita: if the cow was pregnant when it gored, the offspring should be forbidden even before sentencing, as per Rava's principle that the offspring is forbidden because it participated in the goring.
The Gemara resolves by emending the baraita to say 'if it became pregnant and gave birth before sentencing, the offspring is permitted; if after sentencing, it is forbidden.'

items.text: Conditional application of the resolution
items.text_en: Conditional application of the resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this resolution works only for the opinion that a mixture of permitted and forbidden factors is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the resolution applies only to the opinion that a mixture of permitted and forbidden factors (זה וזה גורם) is forbidden.

items.text: Resolution of the fetus's status based on timing of birth
items.text_en: Resolution of the fetus's status based on timing of birth
items.desc_en: Ravina resolves the earlier difficulty: if the woman gave birth before her trial was concluded, the fetus is permitted; if after, it is forbidden, because the fetus is considered a limb of its mother.

sub.desc_en: Ravina resolves the difficulty by distinguishing based on timing: if the woman gave birth before her trial concluded, the fetus is permitted; if after, it is forbidden, because the fetus is considered a limb of its mother (עובר ירך אמו).

items.text: Inference about warning for a severe matter
items.text_en: Inference about warning for a severe matter
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the previous discussion that warning for a severe matter is considered warning for a light matter as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the preceding discussion that warning (התראה) for a severe matter constitutes valid warning for a light matter as well.

items.text: Dispute about the requirement of specifying the mode of death in warning
items.text_en: Dispute about the requirement of specifying the mode of death in warning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the case involves a general warning. The Tanna Kamma requires warning that one is liable to court-imposed death, while Rabbi Yehuda requires specifying the exact mode of execution. The Tanna Kamma derives this from the wood-gatherer, but Rabbi Yehuda considers that a temporary ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya opens by asking what case we are dealing with, and answers that it is a case of a general warning (התרו בו סתם).

The gemara cites a baraita that states the Tanna Kamma's position: for all capital offenses, the court must warn the defendant that he is liable to court-imposed death (מיתת בית דין), without specifying the mode.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda's position in the baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's position in the baraita
sub.desc_en: The baraita records Rabbi Yehuda's dissenting opinion: the warning must specify the exact mode of execution (באי זה מיתה הוא נהרג).

The gemara explains the dispute: the Tanna Kamma derives the requirement of a general warning from the wood-gatherer (מקושש), while Rabbi Yehuda rejects that derivation because the wood-gatherer's case was a temporary ruling (הוראת שעה).

items.text: Initial version of the baraita about those liable to stoning and burning
items.text_en: Initial version of the baraita about those liable to stoning and burning
items.desc_en: Rav Yechezkel taught his son Rami a baraita: those liable to stoning among those liable to burning are judged by stoning, according to Rabbi Shimon, because burning is more severe.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yechezkel teaches his son Rami a baraita: those liable to stoning among those liable to burning are judged by stoning, according to Rabbi Shimon, because burning is more severe.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's objection to the baraita's wording
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's objection to the baraita's wording
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda objects to his father's version: why mention severity? The majority of those liable are stoning victims, so they should be stoned regardless. He asks for the correct version.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda's objection to Rav Yechezkel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda's objection to Rav Yechezkel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda objects to his father's version of the baraita, questioning why severity is mentioned when the majority of those liable are stoning victims.
Rav Yehuda argues that since most capital offenders are stoned, the ruling should follow the majority without needing to compare severity.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda's request for the correct version
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda's request for the correct version
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda asks his father for the correct version of the baraita.

items.text: Corrected version and the Sages' counter-argument
items.text_en: Corrected version and the Sages' counter-argument
items.desc_en: The corrected baraita states: those liable to stoning among those liable to burning are judged by stoning because burning is more severe. The Sages respond: according to you, Rabbi Shimon, stoning is more severe. The Gemara explains that the Sages are arguing within Rabbi Shimon's own reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The corrected baraita states: those liable to stoning among those liable to burning are judged by stoning because burning is more severe.
The Sages respond: according to you, Rabbi Shimon, stoning is more severe.
The Gemara explains that the Sages are arguing within Rabbi Shimon's own reasoning, telling him: according to your view that burning is more severe, no, stoning is more severe.

items.text: Shmuel's address to Rav Yehuda
items.text_en: Shmuel's address to Rav Yehuda
items.desc_en: Shmuel addresses Rav Yehuda as 'Shinana' (sharp one), beginning a new statement that likely continues the discussion.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel addresses Rav Yehuda as 'Shinana' (sharp one), beginning a new statement.

items.text: Opening baraita on honoring a father
items.text_en: Opening baraita on honoring a father
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one should not directly tell a father he violated Torah, but hint at it. The Gemara notes the subtlety is lost, so one should merely cite the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita teaching that one should not directly tell a father he violated Torah, but instead hint by citing the verse.

items.text: Mishnah: Two death penalties
items.text_en: Mishnah: Two death penalties
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one liable for two court-imposed death penalties is judged by the stricter one; if one committed a single transgression carrying two death penalties, he is judged by the stricter one. Rabbi Yosei says he is judged by the first liability that came upon him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: one liable for two court-imposed death penalties is judged by the stricter one.
The Mishnah adds the case of a single transgression carrying two death penalties, also judged by the stricter one.
Rabbi Yosei dissents: the defendant is judged by the first liability that came upon him.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rava's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rava's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah is necessary, as it seems obvious. Rava explains the case: one committed a light transgression, had his verdict sealed for it, then committed a severe transgression; we might think he is already considered dead, so the Mishnah teaches he is judged by the stricter one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah is necessary, as it seems obvious, and suggests perhaps it teaches a novel case of one who committed two transgressions.

Rava explains the case: one committed a light transgression, had his verdict sealed for it, then committed a severe transgression; we might think he is already considered dead, so the Mishnah teaches he is judged by the stricter one.

items.text: Scriptural source for the principle
items.text_en: Scriptural source for the principle
items.desc_en: Abaye's father asks Rabbah bar Natan for the source that one liable for two death penalties is judged by the stricter one. He cites Ezekiel's verse about a son who commits murder, adultery, and idolatry, implying he is judged by the strictest penalty, stoning.

sub.text: Abaye's father's question to Rabbah bar Natan
sub.text_en: Abaye's father's question to Rabbah bar Natan
sub.desc_en: Abaye's father asks Rabbah bar Natan for the scriptural source of the principle that one liable for two death penalties is judged by the stricter one.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Natan's answer citing Ezekiel
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Natan's answer citing Ezekiel
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Natan cites Ezekiel's verse about a son who commits murder (by sword), adultery (by strangulation), and idolatry (by stoning), and the verse concludes 'he shall be put to death, his blood is upon him' — implying stoning, the strictest penalty.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that all three sins could be punishable by stoning (rebellious son, betrothed maiden, idolatry). The Gemara counters that then Ezekiel would merely be repeating Torah; if so, he should have repeated it exactly as Moses did.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that all three sins in Ezekiel's verse could be interpreted as punishable by stoning: the rebellious son, the betrothed maiden, and idolatry.

The Gemara resolves that if all three sins were stoning, Ezekiel would merely be repeating the Torah; but if so, he should have repeated it exactly as Moses did, implying the verse teaches a different principle.

items.text: Aggadic interpretation and Rabban Gamliel's tears
items.text_en: Aggadic interpretation and Rabban Gamliel's tears
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Chanina interprets Ezekiel's verses allegorically: not eating on mountains means not relying on ancestral merit; not lifting eyes to idols means not walking arrogantly; not defiling a neighbor's wife means not encroaching on a friend's livelihood; not approaching a menstruant means not benefiting from charity. Rabban Gamliel weeps, thinking only one who does all these lives, but Rabbi Akiva shows from a verse that even one who does one of them lives.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Chanina interprets Ezekiel's verses allegorically: not eating on mountains means not relying on ancestral merit; not lifting eyes to idols means not walking arrogantly; not defiling a neighbor's wife means not encroaching on a friend's livelihood; not approaching a menstruant means not benefiting from charity.
Rabban Gamliel weeps upon reaching this verse, questioning whether only one who does all these things lives, but not one who does only one of them.
Rabbi Akiva resolves the difficulty by citing a parallel verse where 'in all these' means 'in any one of these', showing that even one such deed suffices for life.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's opinion clarified
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's opinion clarified
items.desc_en: A baraita explains Rabbi Yosei's view: if one first sinned with his mother-in-law and she later became a married woman, he is judged for the mother-in-law; if she was first a married woman and later became his mother-in-law, he is judged for the married woman. Rav Adda bar Ahava questions this, arguing that the additional prohibition of adultery should apply, citing Rabbi Avahu that Rabbi Yosei concedes in cases of an added prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The baraita explains Rabbi Yosei's position: if one first sinned with his mother-in-law (חמותו) and she later became a married woman (אשת איש), he is judged for the mother-in-law; if she was first a married woman and later became his mother-in-law, he is judged for the married woman.
Rav Adda bar Ahava questions Rava: in the case where the mother-in-law later became a married woman, why is he judged only for the mother-in-law?

Rav Adda bar Ahava argues that the additional prohibition of adultery (איסור אשת איש) should also apply, citing Rabbi Avahu's principle that Rabbi Yosei concedes in cases of an added prohibition (איסור מוסיף).

items.text: Opening anecdote: Ada's question
items.text_en: Opening anecdote: Ada's question
items.desc_en: A brief story: someone says to Ada, 'Did you kill him with two killings?' This serves as a lead-in to the Mishnah about a repeat offender.

sub.desc_en: A person asks Ada whether he killed the man with two killings, introducing the topic of repeat offenders.

items.text: Mishnah: Repeat offender placed in the kippah
items.text_en: Mishnah: Repeat offender placed in the kippah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a person is lashed and repeats the offense, the court places him in a confined cell (kippah) and feeds him barley until his stomach bursts.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who was flogged and repeated the offense is confined to a cell (כיפה) and force-fed barley until his stomach bursts.

items.text: Gemara's question and Resh Lakish's explanation
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Resh Lakish's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why is he placed in the kippah just for repeating? Rabbi Yirmeya quoting Resh Lakish explains that we are dealing with lashes for kareit offenses, where the person is actually liable for death, but his death was not carried out. Since he is being lenient with himself (by repeating), we hasten his death. Rabbi Yaakov then clarifies that this applies only to one type of kareit, but if he committed multiple different kareit offenses, he is just tasting prohibitions and is not being lenient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a person who merely repeated an offense is placed in the kippah (narrow cell).

Rabbi Yirmeya quoting Resh Lakish explains that the case involves lashes for kareit (extirpation) offenses, where the person is actually liable for death but his execution was not carried out; since he is being lenient with himself by repeating, we hasten his death.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov to Rabbi Yirmeya bar Tachlifa
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov to Rabbi Yirmeya bar Tachlifa
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov clarifies that this applies only to one type of kareit offense, but if he committed multiple different kareit offenses, he is merely tasting prohibitions and is not being lenient.

items.text: Does the Mishnah require three times?
items.text_en: Does the Mishnah require three times?
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'lashed and repeated' even if he did not do it a third time. This might contradict Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who holds that a presumption (chazakah) is only established after three times. Ravina answers that even according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, the offenses themselves establish the presumption, not the lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah, which says 'repeated' even without a third time, contradicts Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's rule that a presumption (חזקה) requires three occurrences.
Ravina answers that even according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, the offenses themselves (עבירות) establish the presumption, not the lashes.

items.text: Supporting baraita and dispute about what establishes the presumption
items.text_en: Supporting baraita and dispute about what establishes the presumption
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: for a transgression with lashes, the first and second times he is lashed, the third time he is placed in the kippah. Abba Shaul says the third time he is still lashed, and only the fourth time is he placed in the kippah. The Gemara initially thinks the dispute is about whether lashes establish a presumption, but then concludes that everyone agrees with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and the dispute is whether offenses establish the presumption or lashes establish it.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: for a transgression with lashes, the first and second times he is lashed, the third time he is placed in the kippah; Abba Shaul says the third time he is still lashed, and only the fourth time is he placed in the kippah.
The Gemara asks: is it not that everyone agrees lashes establish the presumption, and the dispute is between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel?
The Gemara rejects this: everyone agrees with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and the dispute is whether transgressions establish the presumption or lashes establish it.

items.text: Another baraita: warning without lashes
items.text_en: Another baraita: warning without lashes
items.desc_en: Another baraita discusses a case where he is warned and remains silent or nods his head: the first and second times he is warned, the third time he is placed in the kippah. Abba Shaul says the third time he is still warned, and only the fourth time is he placed in the kippah. Since there are no lashes here, the dispute must be about whether the kippah requires prior warning. Ravina explains that they dispute whether the kippah requires warning.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: if one is warned and remains silent or nods, the first and second times he is warned, the third time he is placed in the kippah; Abba Shaul says the third time he is still warned, and only the fourth time is he placed in the kippah.
The Gemara notes that in this baraita there are no lashes, and asks: over what do they disagree?
Ravina answers that they disagree about whether placement in the kippah requires prior warning.

items.text: Description of the kippah and a related verse
items.text_en: Description of the kippah and a related verse
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that the kippah is a cell as high as a person's full height. Resh Lakish cites a verse: 'Evil will kill the wicked.' Then Resh Lakish expounds on a verse about fish caught in a 'bad net' (metzodah ra'ah), explaining that it refers to a hook (chakkah).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the kippah is, and Rav Yehuda answers that it is a cell as high as a person's full height.
The Gemara asks where this is hinted at in Scripture, and Resh Lakish cites the verse 'Evil will kill the wicked.'

items.text: Mishnah: Murderer without witnesses
items.text_en: Mishnah: Murderer without witnesses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if someone kills a person without (valid) witnesses, they place him in the kippah and feed him bread of adversity and water of affliction.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who kills a person without witnesses is confined to the cell and fed bread of distress and water of affliction.

items.text: Gemara: How do we know he killed?
items.text_en: Gemara: How do we know he killed?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know he killed. Rav says: through 'unique testimony' (eidut meyuchedet). Shmuel says: without warning. Rav Chisda citing Avimi says: when the witnesses contradicted each other in the bedikot (cross-examination) but not in the chakirot (interrogations), as in the case of Ben Zakkai who examined about fig stalks.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that the person actually killed, given the lack of valid witnesses.
Rav answers that it is through 'unique testimony' (עדות מיוחדת), where each witness testifies separately about the same event.
Shmuel answers that it is when the witnesses did not give the killer a formal warning (התראה) before the act.

Rav Chisda citing Avimi answers that it is a case where the witnesses contradicted each other in the bedikot (cross-examination) but not in the chakirot (interrogations), as in the precedent of Ben Zakkai who examined witnesses about fig stalks.

items.text: Difference between the two Mishnahs regarding food
items.text_en: Difference between the two Mishnahs regarding food
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why in the first Mishnah it says 'feed him barley until his stomach bursts' and here it says 'bread of adversity and water of affliction'. Rav Sheshet answers: first they give him bread and water to shrink his intestines, then they feed him barley until his stomach bursts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah here says 'bread of distress and water of affliction' while the earlier Mishnah says 'feed him barley until his stomach bursts'.
Rav Sheshet answers that both procedures are followed: first they give him bread and water to shrink his intestines, then they feed him barley until his stomach bursts.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases where zealots may kill
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases where zealots may kill
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where zealots may strike the offender: one who steals a sacred vessel (kasvah), one who curses using a sorcerer (kosem), and one who has relations with a gentile woman. A priest who serves while impure is taken out by young priests and his head is split with logs. A non-priest who serves in the Temple: Rabbi Akiva says by strangulation, the Sages say by Heaven.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where zealots may strike the offender: one who steals a sacred vessel, one who curses using sorcery, one who marries a non-Jewish woman; a priest who serves in impurity is dealt with by young priests; a non-priest who serves is subject to strangulation (Rabbi Akiva) or divine punishment (Sages).

items.text: Gemara: Explanation of kasvah and kosem
items.text_en: Gemara: Explanation of kasvah and kosem
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that kasvah is a service vessel, citing a verse. The Gemara asks for a scriptural hint, and cites a verse about not coming to see the holy things being swallowed. For the one who curses with a kosem, Rav Yosef teaches: 'let a kosem strike his kosem' (i.e., his sorcerer). Others say: 'let a kosem strike him, his owner, and his buyer.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'kasvah' means in the Mishnah.
Rav Yehuda explains that 'kasvah' is a service vessel in the Temple.
The Gemara cites a verse (Numbers 4:7) that uses the word 'kesot' (related to 'kasvah') in the context of libation vessels.
The Gemara asks for a scriptural hint that the thief of a service vessel is executed by zealots.
The Gemara cites a verse (Numbers 4:20) about being 'swallowed' when seeing the holy things, hinting at the penalty for stealing a sacred vessel.
The Gemara turns to the second case in the Mishnah: one who curses using a sorcerer (kosem).
Rav Yosef teaches: 'let a kosem (sorcerer) strike his kosem (his sorcerer),' meaning the zealot strikes the sorcerer who cursed.

sub.text: Alternative version from Rabbah bar Mari
sub.text_en: Alternative version from Rabbah bar Mari
sub.desc_en: An alternative version (attributed to Rabbah bar Mari) says: 'let a kosem strike him, his owner, and his buyer,' expanding the penalty to include those involved in the sorcery.

items.text: Question about the one who has relations with a gentile woman
items.text_en: Question about the one who has relations with a gentile woman
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Rav a question about the case of one who has relations with a gentile woman, which is the final case in the Mishnah. The daf ends with this question.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana asks Rav a question (the content is cut off, but the move is the inquiry itself).

items.text: Rav's dream and the interpretation of the verse
items.text_en: Rav's dream and the interpretation of the verse
items.desc_en: Rav forgot his learning, and was reminded through a dream of a verse from Malachi. The verse is interpreted as referring to idolatry, male homosexuality, a harlot, and one who has relations with a non-Jewish woman. The continuation of the verse is applied to a Torah scholar or a priest who commits such an act.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: if zealots did not strike him, what is the law? It then reports that Rav forgot his learning.
Rav Kahana was taught a verse from Malachi in a dream, which he then recited to Rav, restoring Rav's memory.

Rav interprets each phrase of the verse: 'בגדה יהודה' refers to idolatry, 'תועבה' to male homosexuality, 'חלל יהודה קודש ה׳' to a harlot, and 'בעל בת אל נכר' to one who has relations with a non-Jewish woman.
The gemara applies the continuation of the verse: if the offender is a Torah scholar, he will have no one to answer in the study hall; if a priest, he will have no son to offer sacrifice.

items.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avuya: One who has relations with a non-Jewess is like one who marries idolatry
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avuya: One who has relations with a non-Jewess is like one who marries idolatry
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avuya states that one who has relations with a non-Jewish woman is as if he marries idolatry, based on the verse 'and married the daughter of a strange god'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avuya states that one who has relations with a non-Jewish woman is like one who marries idolatry, citing the verse 'וּבָעַל בַּת אֵל נֵכָר' (and married the daughter of a strange god).

items.text: The skull of Jehoiakim and the inscription 'this and another'
items.text_en: The skull of Jehoiakim and the inscription 'this and another'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avuya relates that on the skull of Jehoiakim was written 'this and another'. The grandfather of Rabbi Perida found the skull, buried it multiple times, but it was repeatedly exhumed. He then wrapped it in silk and placed it in a chest, but his wife burned it, fulfilling the inscription.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Avuya states that an inscription reading 'this and another' was written on the skull of King Jehoiakim.

sub.text: Story of grandfather of Rabbi Perida
sub.text_en: Story of grandfather of Rabbi Perida
sub.desc_en: The grandfather of Rabbi Perida found the skull discarded at the gates of Jerusalem, recognized it as Jehoiakim's, and buried it twice only to have it repeatedly exhumed.
Regarding the king's honor, the grandfather wrapped the skull in silk and placed it in a chest, but his wife burned it after neighbors convinced her it was a sorcerer's tool.
Upon returning, the grandfather concluded that the incineration of the skull fulfilled the inscription 'this and another'.

items.text: The decree of the Hasmonean court and the dispute about the prohibitions
items.text_en: The decree of the Hasmonean court and the dispute about the prohibitions
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that the Hasmonean court decreed that one who has relations with a non-Jewess is liable for violating the prohibitions of Niddah, a Canaanite slave-woman, a non-Jewess, and a married woman. Ravin reports a different version: Niddah, a Canaanite slave-woman, a non-Jewess, and a harlot, but not for marital status, as non-Jews do not nullify their wives.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that the Hasmonean court decreed that one who has relations with a non-Jewess is liable for violating the prohibitions of Niddah, a Canaanite slave-woman, a non-Jewess, and a married woman.
Ravin reports a different version: the prohibitions are Niddah, a Canaanite slave-woman, a non-Jewess, and a harlot, but not for marital status, as non-Jews do not nullify their wives.

items.text: The rule for one who seeks advice: we do not instruct him
items.text_en: The rule for one who seeks advice: we do not instruct him
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbi Yochanan state that if one comes to seek advice about whether to kill a zealot's target, we do not instruct him. Furthermore, if Zimri separated and Pinchas killed him, Pinchas is executed; but if Zimri turned and killed Pinchas, he is not executed because Pinchas is a pursuer.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that if one comes to seek advice about killing a zealot's target, we do not instruct him.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: It is also stated that Rabbah bar bar Chanah said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: one who comes to seek advice is not instructed.
The gemara adds that if Zimri separated and Pinchas killed him, Pinchas is executed; but if Zimri turned and killed Pinchas, he is not executed because Pinchas is a pursuer.

items.text: The story of Zimri and Cozbi
items.text_en: The story of Zimri and Cozbi
items.desc_en: The tribe of Shimon approached Zimri, who then gathered 24,000 men and went to Cozbi. He brought her before Moses, challenging him about the permissibility of his own marriage to a Midianite woman. The halakha was forgotten, and the people wept, leading to the verse about Pinchas.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that the tribe of Shimon approached Zimri, who gathered 24,000 men and went to Cozbi, claiming he was greater than Moses.
Zimri brought Cozbi before Moses and challenged him: if this woman is forbidden, how was your own marriage to a Midianite woman permitted?
The halakha was forgotten from Moses, and the people wept, leading to the verse about Pinchas.

items.text: What Pinchas saw: three opinions
items.text_en: What Pinchas saw: three opinions
items.desc_en: Rav says Pinchas saw the act and remembered the halakha that zealots may strike one who has relations with a non-Jewess. Samuel says he saw that there is no wisdom against God when there is a desecration of His name. Rabbi Yitzchak says Rabbi Eliezer said he saw an angel destroying the people.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Pinchas saw that prompted him to act.
Rav says Pinchas saw the act and remembered the halakha that zealots may strike one who has relations with a non-Jewess, and Moshe told him to carry out the punishment himself.
Samuel says Pinchas saw that there is no wisdom against God when there is a desecration of His name, so one does not honor the rabbi in such a case.
Rabbi Yitzchak says in the name of Rabbi Eliezer that Pinchas saw an angel destroying the people.

items.text: Pinchas takes a spear: a lesson about entering the study hall with weapons
items.text_en: Pinchas takes a spear: a lesson about entering the study hall with weapons
items.desc_en: From the verse 'And he rose from the midst of the congregation and took a spear in his hand', we learn that one may not enter the study hall with weapons. Pinchas removed the blade and placed it in his cloak.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about Pinchas taking a spear and derives that one may not enter the study hall with weapons, and describes how Pinchas removed the blade and placed it in his cloak.

items.text: Opening narrative: Zimri's confrontation with Pinchas
items.text_en: Opening narrative: Zimri's confrontation with Pinchas
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Zimri leaned on his staff and, upon reaching the tribe of Shimon, questioned the superiority of Levi over Shimon. The people told him to leave it alone, and he entered to do his business. The Perushim (Pharisees) permitted the matter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Zimri leaned on his staff, questioned the superiority of Levi over Shimon, and the Perushim permitted the matter.

items.text: Six miracles performed for Pinchas
items.text_en: Six miracles performed for Pinchas
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan lists six miracles that occurred for Pinchas during his act of zealotry: Zimri should have separated but didn't, he should have spoken but didn't, Pinchas aimed at the male's and female's reproductive organs, the spear did not slip, an angel raised the lintel, and an angel destroyed the people.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan lists six miracles performed for Pinchas during the incident with Zimri.

items.text: Pinchas's prayer and the angels' response
items.text_en: Pinchas's prayer and the angels' response
items.desc_en: Pinchas brought the sinners before God, questioning why 24,000 should die for them. Rabbi Elazar explains that the verse says 'vayefalel' (he judged) rather than 'vayitpallel' (he prayed), indicating that Pinchas argued with his Creator. The ministering angels sought to push him away, but God told them to leave him alone, as he is a zealot son of a zealot.

sub.desc_en: Pinchas brings the sinners before God and argues that 24,000 Israelites should not die for them, citing the verse 'וַיַּעֲמֹד פִּינְחָס וַיְפַלֵּל'.

Rabbi Elazar explains that the verse uses 'וַיְפַלֵּל' (he judged) rather than 'וַיִּתְפַּלֵּל' (he prayed), indicating Pinchas argued with his Creator; the ministering angels sought to push him away, but God told them to leave him alone, calling him a zealot son of a zealot.

items.text: Tribes disparage Pinchas; God honors him
items.text_en: Tribes disparage Pinchas; God honors him
items.desc_en: The tribes began to disparage Pinchas, calling him 'ben Puti' (son of one who fattened calves for idolatry) and accusing him of killing a tribal prince. The verse then traces his lineage to Aaron the priest. God told Moses to greet Pinchas with peace, and that this atonement would be effective forever.

sub.desc_en: The tribes disparage Pinchas, calling him 'ben Puti' (son of one who fattened calves for idolatry) and accusing him of killing a tribal prince, but the verse traces his lineage to Aaron the priest.
God tells Moses to greet Pinchas with peace, declaring that this atonement will be effective forever.

items.text: Zimri's many acts and Pinchas's patience
items.text_en: Zimri's many acts and Pinchas's patience
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman citing Rav explains the verse 'Zarzir motnayim o tayish' as referring to Zimri's 424 acts of intercourse that day, and Pinchas waited until his strength waned. A baraita teaches that he did so 60 times until he became like a 'muzeret egg', and her seat was a beit se'ah. Rav Yosef taught that her grave was an amah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman citing Rav interprets the verse 'Zarzir motnayim o tayish' as referring to Zimri's 424 acts of intercourse that day, and Pinchas waited until his strength waned.
A baraita teaches that Zimri performed 60 acts until he became like a 'muzeret egg', and her seat was like a garden bed full of water.
Rav Kahana adds that her seat was a beit se'ah (a large area).
Rav Yosef taught that her grave was an amah (a cubit) in size.

items.text: The true name of Cozbi and its meaning
items.text_en: The true name of Cozbi and its meaning
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet states that her name was not Cozbi but Shvilnai bat Tzur, and she was called Cozbi because she lied to her father or because she said 'a cup is in me for this people'. The Gemara cites a folk saying about her being among the reeds and her mother's gaffe.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet states that Cozbi's true name was Shvilnai bat Tzur, not Cozbi.
The Gemara explains that she was called Cozbi either because she lied to her father or because she said 'a cup is in me for this people'.
The Gemara cites a folk saying about Shvilnai being among the reeds and her mother's gaffe, supporting the name's origin.

items.text: Five names of Zimri
items.text_en: Five names of Zimri
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan lists five names for Zimri: Zimri (because he became like a muzeret egg), ben Salu (because he made his family's sins repulsive), Shaul (because he lent himself to transgression), ben haKena'anit (because he acted like a Canaanite), and his real name was Shelumiel ben Tzuri Shaddai.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan lists five names of Zimri and explains the meaning of each.

items.text: Legal discussion: Priest who served while impure
items.text_en: Legal discussion: Priest who served while impure
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Huna asks Rav Sheshet whether a priest who served in the Temple while impure is liable to death by heaven. Rav Sheshet responds that the Mishnah teaches that young priests take him out and split his skull, implying he is not liable to heaven. The Gemara then addresses objections from other cases (one who stole the kasvah, one who cursed the kosem, one who had relations with a gentile) and concludes with a baraita listing Temple services performed outside that are exempt from liability.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Huna asked Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Huna asked Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Huna asks Rav Sheshet whether a priest who served in a state of טומאה (ritual impurity) is liable to death at the hands of Heaven.

Rav Sheshet answers by citing a baraita that young priests take such a priest out and split his skull, implying he is not liable to death at the hands of Heaven, otherwise they would leave him to that punishment.
The Gemara objects: if Heaven exempts him, how can we kill him?
The Gemara further objects with a mishnah that a repeat offender is confined, yet Heaven exempts him, so how can we kill him?
Rabbi Yirmeya in the name of Resh Lakish resolves that we are dealing with lashes for כרת (extirpation), where the person is already liable to death.
The Gemara objects with the case of one who steals a sacred vessel, which is punished by human court.
Rav Yehuda resolves that the case involves a service vessel, which is punishable by death from Heaven as per the verse.
The Gemara objects with the case of one who curses a sorcerer.
Rav Yosef resolves that the case involves one who strikes a sorcerer, which appears like blessing the Name, so it is punishable by human court.
The Gemara objects with the case of one who engages in relations with an Aramean woman.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Kahana was taught in a dream, and Rav recalled his learning, indicating that such a case is punishable by zealots.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita listing various Temple services performed outside the Temple, which are exempt from punishment.
The baraita concludes that they are not liable, implying that the priest who served in impurity is also exempt from human punishment.

items.text: Clarifying the death penalty for a non-priest who burns incense
items.text_en: Clarifying the death penalty for a non-priest who burns incense
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier statement that a non-priest who burns incense is liable does not necessarily mean the death penalty; it could refer to a mere prohibition (אזהרה). The Gemara then questions this, noting that a non-priest who serves is explicitly subject to death, and resolves that the two statements refer to different cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the liability for a non-priest who burns incense (מקטר) implies the death penalty or merely a prohibition (אזהרה).
The Gemara answers that the liability is merely a prohibition (אזהרה), and resolves the apparent contradiction with the verse 'וְהַזָּר הַקָּרֵב יוּמָת' by distinguishing between different cases.

items.text: The prohibition for a non-priest who pours and mixes
items.text_en: The prohibition for a non-priest who pours and mixes
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that a non-priest who pours oil or mixes the meal offering is also not liable for death, but only for a prohibition. It cites a baraita that derives this prohibition from the verse 'קְדֹשִׁים יִהְיוּ וְלֹא יְחַלְּלוּ', but concludes that this is only a rabbinic support (אסמכתא בעלמא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the earlier statement implies that pouring and mixing (יוצק ובולל) are not even prohibited.
A baraita is cited that derives a prohibition for pouring and mixing from the verse 'קְדֹשִׁים יִהְיוּ וְלֹא יְחַלְּלוּ', but the Gemara clarifies this is only a rabbinic support (אסמכתא).
The Gemara concludes that this derivation is only a rabbinic support (אסמכתא בעלמא), not a Torah-level prohibition.

items.text: Objection from a baraita listing those liable for death
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita listing those liable for death
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that explicitly lists a טמא ששימש (an impure priest who served) among those liable for death, contradicting the previous assumption that such a case is only a prohibition. The Gemara concludes that this is a refutation (תיוּבְתָּא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita listing those liable to death, including a טמא ששימש (impure priest who served), which contradicts the earlier position.
The Gemara declares that this baraita constitutes a conclusive refutation (תיוּבְתָּא) of the previous position.

items.text: The full list of those liable for death and those only prohibited
items.text_en: The full list of those liable for death and those only prohibited
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the baraita in full, listing those who are liable for death (including a non-priest who serves, an impure priest who serves, etc.) and those who are only prohibited (an uncircumcised priest, an onen, a sitting priest). It also records a dispute between Rabbi and the Sages regarding a blemished priest and one who intentionally commits me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists those liable for death at the hand of Heaven, including one who eats untithed produce, an impure priest who eats pure תרומה (priestly portion), a non-priest who eats תרומה, a non-priest who serves, an impure priest who serves, a טבול יום (one who immersed that day) who serves, a priest lacking vestments, lacking atonement, unwashed hands and feet, intoxicated, or with overgrown hair.
The baraita states that an uncircumcised priest, an אונן (acute mourner), and a sitting priest are not liable for death but only for violating a prohibition.
רבי (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) rules that a blemished priest who serves is liable for death.
The חכמים (Sages) disagree and rule that a blemished priest is only liable for violating a prohibition.
רבי (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) rules that one who intentionally commits מעילה (misuse of consecrated property) is liable for death.
The חכמים (Sages) disagree and rule that one who intentionally commits מעילה is only liable for violating a prohibition.

items.text: Source for the death penalty for eating tevel
items.text_en: Source for the death penalty for eating tevel
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the death penalty for one who eats tevel (untithed produce). Shmuel cites Rabbi Eliezer, deriving it from a gezerah shavah of 'חילול' from terumah. The Gemara considers an alternative derivation from notar (which would yield karet), but concludes that the derivation from terumah is preferable, with Ravina adding that 'חילול דרבים' is better learned from 'חילול דרבים'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that one who eats tevel (untithed produce) is liable to receive death at the hand of Heaven?

Shmuel in the name of רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer) answers: The verse 'וְלֹא יְחַלְּלוּ אֶת קָדְשֵׁי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵת אֲשֶׁר יָרִימוּ לַה (They shall not desecrate the sacred items of the children of Israel, which they will set apart unto the Lord)' speaks about items destined to be separated, i.e., tevel.
The Gemara explains that the tanna derives the punishment via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'חילול' from תרומה (terumah): just as there the punishment is death, so too here.
The Gemara objects: Why not derive the punishment from נותר (notar) via the same verbal analogy, which would yield כרת (karet) instead of death?

The Gemara answers: It is more reasonable to derive from תרומה (terumah) because of multiple common elements: both are outside the land, permitted, in plural, produce, and not subject to פיגול (piggul) and נותר (notar).
The Gemara counters: On the contrary, deriving from נותר (notar) is more fitting because both involve unfit food and have no remedy through immersion in a מקוה (ritual bath).
The Gemara resolves: The common elements with תרומה (terumah) are more numerous, so that derivation is preferred.
רבינא (Ravina) adds an alternative reasoning: deriving 'חילול' in the plural from 'חילול' in the plural is preferable.

items.text: Source for the death penalty for a tamei priest eating pure terumah
items.text_en: Source for the death penalty for a tamei priest eating pure terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the death penalty for a tamei priest who eats pure terumah. Shmuel derives it from the verse 'וְשָׁמְרוּ אֶת מִשְׁמַרְתִּי וְלֹא יִשְׂאוּ עָלָיו חֵטְא'. It then notes that this applies only to pure terumah, not to impure terumah, as Shmuel said in the name of Rabbi Eliezer, citing the verse 'וּמֵתוּ בוֹ כִּי יְחַלְּלֻהוּ'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a tamei priest who eats pure terumah is liable to death at the hands of Heaven.
Shmuel derives the death penalty from the verse 'וְשָׁמְרוּ אֶת מִשְׁמַרְתִּי וְלֹא יִשְׂאוּ עָלָיו חֵטְא' (they shall keep My charge and not bear sin for it).
The Gemara notes that this applies only to pure terumah, not to impure terumah.

Shmuel in the name of Rabbi Eliezer cites the verse 'וּמֵתוּ בוֹ כִּי יְחַלְּלֻהוּ' (they shall die in it because they profane it) to prove that a tamei priest who eats impure terumah is not liable to death.

items.text: Continuation of the Mishnah: the already-redeemed animal
items.text_en: Continuation of the Mishnah: the already-redeemed animal
items.desc_en: The segment concludes the Mishnah's list of those liable for death, adding the case of an animal that has already been redeemed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes its list of those liable for death by excluding an animal that has already been redeemed.

items.text: The zar who eats terumah: death penalty or not?
items.text_en: The zar who eats terumah: death penalty or not?
items.desc_en: Rav states that a non-priest who eats terumah is lashed, but Rav Kahana and Rav Asi challenge him, citing a verse that implies death. The Gemara resolves that the verse is interrupted, and a baraita listing those liable for death includes a zar eating terumah, but Rav is a Tanna and disputes it.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that a non-priest (זר) who eats תרומה (priestly portion) is lashed, not executed.

sub.text: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's challenge
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's challenge
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi challenge Rav, suggesting the penalty should be death based on the verse 'וְכׇל זָר לֹא יֹאכַל קֹדֶשׁ' (and any non-priest shall not eat sacred food).
The Gemara answers that the verse is interrupted by 'אֲנִי ה׳ מְקַדְּשָׁם' (I am the Lord who sanctifies them), separating the death penalty from the context of eating תרומה.
A baraita is cited listing those liable for death, including a non-priest who eats תרומה, contradicting Rav's position.
The Gemara resolves that Rav, as a Tanna (תנא), has the authority to dispute the baraita, so his position stands.

items.text: The zar who serves: death penalty
items.text_en: The zar who serves: death penalty
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse that a non-priest who approaches the sanctuary is put to death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'וְהַזָּר הַקָּרֵב יוּמָת' (the non-priest who approaches shall be put to death) to establish that a zar (non-priest) who performs service is liable to the death penalty.

items.text: The tamei who serves: death penalty derived from terumah
items.text_en: The tamei who serves: death penalty derived from terumah
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin asks for the source that an impure priest who serves is liable for death. The Gemara derives it from a verbal analogy (חילול) between the verse about priests not profaning the sanctuary and terumah, where the penalty is death. An objection is raised to derive it from notar (which carries karet), but the Gemara prefers the analogy from terumah because it shares more common elements, especially the public nature of the profanation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin asks Rav Yosef for the source that an impure priest who serves is liable for death, citing the verse 'וְיִנָּזְרוּ מִקׇּדְשֵׁי בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְלֹא יְחַלְּלוּ'.
The Gemara derives the death penalty for an impure priest who serves via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'חילול' from terumah, where the penalty is death.
An objection is raised: why not derive the penalty from notar (leftover sacrificial meat), which carries karet, via the same verbal analogy?
The Gemara rejects the objection, arguing that deriving from terumah is more fitting because it shares more common elements: both involve the body, impurity, a mikveh, and a public context.
A counter-objection argues that notar is a better source because it shares elements of holiness, being inside the Temple, and the categories of piggul and notar.
The Gemara resolves the debate: deriving from a public profanation (terumah) is preferable to deriving from a private one (notar).

items.text: The tevul yom who serves: death penalty
items.text_en: The tevul yom who serves: death penalty
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that an immersed person who has not yet completed his purification (tevul yom) who serves is liable. Rabbi Simai derives it from the verse 'קְדֹשִׁים יִהְיוּ... וְלֹא יְחַלְּלוּ', applying it to tevul yom since the case of tamei is already covered. The penalty is derived via the same verbal analogy (חילול) from terumah, yielding death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a tevul yom (immersed person awaiting sunset) who serves in the Temple is liable.
A baraita is cited in which Rabbi Simai derives a hint for tevul yom from the verse 'קְדֹשִׁים יִהְיוּ... וְלֹא יְחַלְּלוּ' (they shall be holy... and not profane).
The Gemara explains that since the case of a tamei (impure) person serving is already derived from 'וְיִנָּזְרוּ', the verse is applied to tevul yom who serves.
The penalty is derived via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'חילול' from תרומה (terumah): just as there the penalty is death, so too here it is death.

items.text: The mechusar begadim who serves: death penalty
items.text_en: The mechusar begadim who serves: death penalty
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, derives from the verse 'וְחָגַרְתָּ אֹתָם אַבְנֵט' that when the priests wear their garments, their priesthood is upon them; without them, they are like non-priests, and a non-priest who serves is liable for death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that a priest lacking garments who serves is liable for death?

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu citing Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, derives from the verse 'וְחָגַרְתָּ אֹתָם אַבְנֵט' that when the priests wear their garments, their priesthood is upon them; without them, they are like non-priests, and a non-priest who serves is liable for death.

items.text: The mechusar kapparah who serves: death penalty
items.text_en: The mechusar kapparah who serves: death penalty
items.desc_en: Rav Huna derives from the verse 'וְכִפֶּר עָלֶיהָ הַכֹּהֵן וְטָהֵרָה' that a person lacking atonement is still considered impure, and an impure person who serves is liable for death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that a mechusar kapparah (one lacking atonement) who serves is liable for death?

Rav Huna cites the verse 'וְכִפֶּר עָלֶיהָ הַכֹּהֵן וְטָהֵרָה' (and the priest shall make atonement for her, and she shall be clean), inferring that before atonement she is still impure, and the master said that an impure person who serves is liable for death.

items.text: Other disqualifications: unwashed hands, drunk, and unkempt hair
items.text_en: Other disqualifications: unwashed hands, drunk, and unkempt hair
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses for those who serve without washing hands and feet (death penalty), those who are drunk (death penalty), and those with unkempt hair (death penalty, derived via an analogy to drunkards).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that a priest who serves without washing hands and feet is liable to death, and cites the verse 'בְּבֹאָם אֶל אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד יִרְחֲצוּ מַיִם וְלֹא יָמוּתוּ' (when they enter the Tent of Meeting they shall wash with water, so that they not die).
The Gemara cites the verse 'יַיִן וְשֵׁכָר אַל תֵּשְׁתְּ' (wine and strong drink do not drink) as the source that a drunken priest who serves is liable to death.

The Gemara derives that a priest with unkempt hair is liable to death via an analogy (היקש) to drunken priests, based on the juxtaposition of the verses 'רֹאשָׁם לֹא יְגַלֵּחוּ' (they shall not shave their heads) and 'וְיַיִן לֹא יִשְׁתּוּ' (and wine they shall not drink).

items.text: Disqualifications that are only prohibitions: uncircumcised, mourner, sitting
items.text_en: Disqualifications that are only prohibitions: uncircumcised, mourner, sitting
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that an uncircumcised priest, a mourner (onen), and one who sits while serving are only subject to a prohibition (azharah), not death. It begins to derive the source for the uncircumcised from Ezekiel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that an uncircumcised priest, a mourner (onen), and one who sits while serving are only subject to a prohibition (azharah), not death.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive the source for the uncircumcised priest?
Rav Chisda answers that this matter was not learned from the Torah of Moses until Ezekiel ben Buzi came and taught it from the verse 'כל בן נכר ערל לב' (every foreigner uncircumcised of heart).

items.text: Derivation of death penalty for an onen
items.text_en: Derivation of death penalty for an onen
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that an onen (one who has not yet buried his close relative) who serves in the Temple is liable to death. This is learned from the verse 'and from the sanctuary he shall not go out, nor profane the sanctuary of his God' — implying that another who does not go out (i.e., serves while an onen) has profaned it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where is the death penalty for an onen (one who has not yet buried his close relative) derived?

The Gemara answers: it is derived from the verse 'and from the sanctuary he shall not go out, nor profane the sanctuary of his God' — implying that another who does not go out (i.e., serves while an onen) has profaned it.

items.text: Rejection of a gezeirah shava from terumah for an onen
items.text_en: Rejection of a gezeirah shava from terumah for an onen
items.desc_en: Rav Adda proposes to Rava that the death penalty for an onen could be learned via a gezeirah shava (verbal analogy) from terumah, where 'profanation' leads to death. The Gemara rejects this because the word 'profanation' in the onen verse is derived from a general principle, and a matter derived from a general principle cannot be used for a gezeirah shava.

sub.desc_en: Rav Adda proposes to Rava that the death penalty for an onen (mourner before burial) who serves in the Temple could be derived via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from תרומה (priestly portion), where 'profanation' (חילול) leads to death.

The Gemara rejects the proposal because the word 'profanation' in the onen verse is derived from a general principle (כלל), and a matter derived from a general principle cannot be used for a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy).

items.text: Derivation of prohibition for a seated priest
items.text_en: Derivation of prohibition for a seated priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives that a priest who serves while seated is liable. Rava in the name of Rav Nachman states that the verse 'to stand to serve' teaches that God chose the priests for standing, not sitting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the prohibition for a seated priest is derived from.

sub.text: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rava in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rava quoting Rav Nachman cites the verse 'לעמוד לשרת' (to stand to serve), teaching that the priesthood was chosen for standing, not sitting.

items.text: Debate on the penalty for a blemished priest
items.text_en: Debate on the penalty for a blemished priest
items.desc_en: Rabbi holds that a blemished priest who serves is liable to death, while the Sages hold it is only a prohibition. Rabbi derives this via a gezeirah shava from terumah. The Gemara considers learning from notar (remnant) instead, but concludes that the correct analogy is from a tamei (impure) priest who served, using multiple shared characteristics. The Sages derive their view from the word 'bo' (in him), excluding a blemished priest from the death penalty.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the dispute: Rabbi holds a blemished priest who serves is liable to death (מיתה), while the Sages hold it is only a prohibition (אזהרה).

The Gemara explains Rabbi's reasoning: he derives a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'חילול' (profanation) used in the context of תרומה (priestly portion), where the penalty is death, applying it to a blemished priest.
The Gemara objects: why not derive the penalty from נותר (remnant of a sacrifice), which carries כרת (excision), instead of from תרומה?

The Gemara initially argues that learning from תרומה is more logical because both involve a physical defect (פסול הגוף), but counters that learning from נותר is also logical because both involve קודש (sanctity), פנים (inside the Temple), פיגול (improper intent), and נותר (remnant).

The Gemara resolves: Rabbi actually derives the death penalty from a טמא (impure) priest who served, using multiple shared characteristics (פסול הגוף, קודש, פנים, פיגול, נותר) to establish the analogy.
The Sages derive their view from the word 'בו' (in him) in the verse, excluding a blemished priest from the death penalty.

items.text: Debate on the penalty for intentional me'ilah
items.text_en: Debate on the penalty for intentional me'ilah
items.desc_en: Rabbi holds that one who intentionally commits me'ilah (misuse of sacred property) is liable to death, while the Sages hold it is only a prohibition. Rabbi Avahu states that Rabbi derives this via a gezeirah shava of 'chet' (sin) from terumah. The Sages derive their view from the word 'bo' (in him), excluding me'ilah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the dispute: Rabbi holds that intentional me'ilah is punishable by death, while the Sages hold it is only a prohibition.
Rabbi Avahu explains that Rabbi derives the death penalty for me'ilah via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'חטא' (sin) from תרומה (priestly portion).
The Sages counter that the verse uses the word 'בו' (in him), which excludes me'ilah from the death penalty.

items.text: Debate on the mode of execution for a non-priest who serves
items.text_en: Debate on the mode of execution for a non-priest who serves
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Yishmael says a non-priest who serves is executed by Heaven (death at the hands of Heaven), learning from the verse about the Levites. Rabbi Akiva says stoning, learning from the verse about a prophet who incites idolatry. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says strangulation. The Gemara explains the logic behind each position: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva differ on whether to derive 'yumat' from 'yumat' or 'yumat' from 'yamut', and on whether to derive a commoner from a commoner or from a prophet. Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri differ based on a Tannaitic dispute about the execution of a prophet who incites. The Gemara concludes that there are two Tannaim who support Rabbi Akiva: the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon (who says strangulation) in support of Rabbi Akiva, while the baraita follows the Sages (who say stoning) in support of Rabbi Akiva.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Yishmael's position: a non-priest who serves is executed by Heaven (בידי שמים), derived from a verbal analogy between the verses 'יומת' and 'ימות'.
The baraita continues with Rabbi Akiva's position (stoning, derived from the prophet who incites) and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's position (strangulation, derived from the same verse).

The Gemara asks what underlies the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva, and explains: Rabbi Akiva derives 'יומת' from 'יומת' (the same conjugation), while Rabbi Yishmael derives a commoner from a commoner, not from a prophet; Rabbi Akiva counters that a prophet who incites is no better than a commoner.

The Gemara asks what underlies the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, and explains it depends on a Tannaitic dispute about the execution of a prophet who incites: the Sages say stoning, Rabbi Shimon says strangulation, and the Mishnah records Rabbi Akiva as saying strangulation.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: there are two Tannaim who support Rabbi Akiva — the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon (strangulation) in support of Rabbi Akiva, while the baraita follows the Sages (stoning) in support of Rabbi Akiva.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those executed by strangulation: one who strikes his father or mother, a kidnapper of a Jew, a rebellious elder, a false prophet, one who prophesies in the name of idolatry, an adulterer, and false witnesses against a priest's daughter or her paramour.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those executed by strangulation: one who strikes his father or mother, a kidnapper of a Jew, a rebellious elder, a false prophet, one who prophesies in the name of idolatry, an adulterer, and false witnesses against a priest's daughter or her paramour.

items.text: Gemara's initial derivation for striking a parent
items.text_en: Gemara's initial derivation for striking a parent
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the death penalty for striking a parent, citing the verse "And one who strikes his father or mother shall be put to death" and the principle that any unspecified death in the Torah is strangulation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that one who strikes his father or mother is executed by strangulation? It answers: because the verse says 'one who strikes his father or mother shall be put to death', and any death stated in the Torah without specification is only strangulation.
The Gemara cites the verse and the principle that any unspecified death penalty in the Torah is strangulation.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the nature of the blow
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the nature of the blow
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that perhaps the verse requires killing the parent, but then asks how one could be killed by sword while the parent by strangulation. It then notes a dispute about whether strangulation is lenient or severe, and resolves by citing verses that distinguish a fatal blow from a non-fatal one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that perhaps the verse requires killing the parent, but then asks how one could be killed by sword while the parent by strangulation.
The Gemara notes a dispute about whether strangulation is lenient or severe, and questions the objection for those who hold strangulation is severe.
The Gemara resolves by citing verses that distinguish a fatal blow from a non-fatal one, showing that 'striking' alone does not imply death.

items.text: Need for both verses
items.text_en: Need for both verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both verses "one who strikes a man" and "anyone who strikes a soul" are necessary: one to exclude a minor, the other to include even an eight-month-old fetus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both verses 'one who strikes a man' and 'one who strikes a soul' were necessary, to include a minor and exclude a fetus or an eight-month-old.

items.text: Requirement of a wound
items.text_en: Requirement of a wound
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one is liable even without causing a wound, citing the Mishnah that requires a wound. It then derives from the analogy of striking a person and striking an animal that a wound is necessary, as with an animal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one is liable for striking a parent even without causing a wound, and cites the Mishnah that requires a wound.
The Gemara derives from the analogy of striking a person and striking an animal that a wound is necessary, as with an animal.

items.text: Rav Yirmeya's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yirmeya's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya challenges the analogy, arguing that if one weakens an animal with stones he is liable, so the analogy must be applied differently. The Gemara then cites the teaching of the school of Chizkiya, and for those who reject it, the analogy teaches that one who strikes for medical purposes is exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya objects to the analogy from animal to human, arguing that if one weakens an animal with stones he is liable, so the analogy must be applied to human striking as well.

sub.text: Gemara's answer citing the school of Chizkiya
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer citing the school of Chizkiya
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the analogy is needed for the teaching of the school of Chizkiya.

sub.text: Gemara's question for those who reject the school of Chizkiya
sub.text_en: Gemara's question for those who reject the school of Chizkiya
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for those who do not accept the teaching of the school of Chizkiya, what purpose does the analogy serve?
The Gemara resolves that the analogy teaches that one who strikes a person for medical purposes is exempt, just as one who strikes an animal for medical purposes is exempt.

items.text: Whether a son may perform medical procedures on his father
items.text_en: Whether a son may perform medical procedures on his father
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether a son may let blood from his father. Rav Mattana and Rav Dimi bar Chinana offer different proofs. The Gemara then notes that Rav did not allow his son to remove a splinter, and Mar bar Ravina did not allow his son to open a vein, fearing an accidental transgression.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question whether a son may perform bloodletting on his father.
Rav Mattana answers that the verse 'וְאָהַבְתָּ לְרֵעֲךָ כָּמוֹךָ' (love your neighbor as yourself) permits it, as one would heal himself.

Rav Dimi bar Chinana answers by citing the analogy of 'מַכֵּה אָדָם וּמַכֵּה בְהֵמָה' (one who strikes a person and one who strikes an animal): just as striking an animal for healing is exempt, so too striking a person for healing is exempt.
The Gemara notes that Rav did not allow his son to remove a splinter from him, fearing an accidental wound.
The Gemara notes that Mar bar Ravina did not allow his son to open a vein for him, fearing an accidental transgression.

The Gemara resolves the concern: a stranger would only be liable for a negative commandment (לאו), but a son would be liable for strangulation (חנק), so the stricter stringency for a son is justified.

items.text: Objection from a needle for a thorn and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a needle for a thorn and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if one fears accidental transgression, then taking a needle to remove a thorn should also be forbidden due to fear of stoning. It answers that there it is destructive, and this is only exempt according to Rabbi Shimon who holds that one who causes a wound destructively is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if a son fears accidental transgression when bloodletting his father, then taking a needle to remove a thorn should also be forbidden due to fear of accidental stoning.
The Gemara answers that removing a thorn is destructive, not constructive, so the concern about accidental transgression does not apply.
The Gemara objects that this answer works only for the view that one who causes a wound destructively is exempt, but what about the view that he is liable?
The Gemara resolves that the view that one who causes a wound destructively is liable is that of Rabbi Shimon, and the Mishnah's ruling follows the other sages.

items.text: Question about a son as agent for his father
items.text_en: Question about a son as agent for his father
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a son may be appointed as an agent to strike or curse his father, given Rabbi Shimon's principle that unnecessary labor is exempt. Rav Sheshet answers that just as a stranger is not permitted, a son is also not permitted, because the honor of Heaven takes precedence over the honor of the father.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Shimon's principle
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Shimon's principle
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Shimon's principle that any unnecessary labor (מלאכה שאינה צריכה לגופה) is exempt from liability.
The Gemara asks Rav Sheshet whether a son may be appointed as an agent to strike or curse his father, given the exemption for unnecessary labor.

Rav Sheshet answers that just as a stranger is not permitted to strike or curse the father, a son is also not permitted, because the honor of Heaven (כבוד שמים) takes precedence over the honor of the father.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that argues: if it is a commandment not to strike someone whom it is a commandment to strike (i.e., a court executioner), then certainly it is a commandment not to strike someone whom it is not a commandment to strike. The Gemara initially assumes this refers to a son versus a stranger, but then resolves that both cases are in a place of commandment, and the distinction is between a place of commandment and not a place of commandment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if it is a commandment not to strike someone whom it is a commandment to strike, then certainly it is a commandment not to strike someone whom it is not a commandment to strike.
The Gemara initially assumes that both clauses of the baraita refer to a place of commandment, and the distinction is between a son and another person.
The Gemara rejects that interpretation, stating that there is no difference between a son and another; rather, the distinction is between a place of commandment and a place not of commandment.
The Gemara explains the baraita accordingly: in a place of commandment, there is a commandment not to exceed the lashes; in a place not of commandment, there is a commandment not to strike at all.

items.text: Proof from a mishna about one going to be executed
items.text_en: Proof from a mishna about one going to be executed
items.desc_en: A mishna states that if a son strikes or curses his father who is being led to execution, the son is liable, but a stranger is exempt. Rav Chisda explains this is when they are delaying the execution. Rav Sheshet sets the case where they are not delaying, and then the stranger is exempt because he is a dead man. The Gemara questions this based on Rav Sheshet's own ruling that one is liable for embarrassing a sleeping person who then dies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita as a proof: if a son strikes or curses his father being led to execution, the son is liable, but a stranger is exempt; Rav Chisda explains this is when they are imploring him to go out but he refuses.
Rav Sheshet interprets the baraita as referring to a case where they are not imploring him to go out.
The Gemara objects: if so, even a stranger should be liable? The Gemara answers: a stranger is exempt because the condemned man is considered a dead man.

items.text: Resolution: the blow was worth less than a perutah
items.text_en: Resolution: the blow was worth less than a perutah
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the case involves a blow worth less than a perutah. Rabbi Ami in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that for such a blow one is lashed. Therefore, 'exempt' in the mishna means exempt from monetary payment, implying the son is liable for monetary payment. The Gemara concludes that the son is liable for his judgment (i.e., lashes), and the stranger is exempt from monetary payment but liable for lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: Rav Sheshet ruled that one who shames a sleeping person who then dies is liable, yet the baraita exempts a stranger who strikes a condemned man.
The Gemara answers that the case involves a blow worth less than a perutah (פרוטה), so no monetary liability applies.
The Gemara objects: Rabbi Ami in the name of Rabbi Yochanan ruled that one who strikes a blow worth less than a perutah (פרוטה) is lashed, so why is the stranger exempt?
The Gemara answers that 'exempt' (פטור) in the baraita means exempt from monetary payment, not from lashes.
The Gemara infers that the son would be liable for monetary payment, and questions this.
The Gemara resolves that the son is liable for his judgment (i.e., lashes), not monetary payment, and the same applies to the stranger.

items.text: Alternative explanation: the stranger is exempt due to the verse
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: the stranger is exempt due to the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another explanation: the stranger is exempt from lashes because the verse 'and a prince among your people you shall not curse' applies only to one who does the deeds of your people. This is derived for striking from cursing. The son, however, is liable because the father has repented. Rav Mari adds that 'among your people' refers to one who is established among your people, excluding the condemned man. The Gemara questions whether the son is also excluded, but the discussion ends unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the stranger is exempt from lashes because the verse 'וְנָשִׂיא בְעַמְּךָ לֹא תָאֹר' (and a prince among your people you shall not curse) applies only to one who does the deeds of your people.
The Gemara asks: this works for cursing, but from where do we derive the same for striking? It answers that we derive striking from cursing through a juxtaposition.
The Gemara objects: if so, the son should also be exempt when the father does not act as a Jew. It answers, as Rav Pinchas says, that the case is where the father repented.

The Gemara objects: if the father repented, the stranger should also be liable. Rav Mari answers that 'בְּעַמְּךָ' (among your people) refers to one who is established among your people, excluding the condemned man.
The Gemara questions: if so, the son should also be exempt since the father's execution is imminent, but the discussion ends unresolved.

items.text: The son as agent for a mesit
items.text_en: The son as agent for a mesit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what was the outcome of the case regarding a son who acts as an agent for his father. Rabba bar Rav Huna and the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael state that a son is never made an agent to strike or curse his father, except in the case of a mesit (an enticer to idolatry), as the Torah says 'you shall not pity nor conceal him.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what was the outcome of the case regarding a son who acts as an agent for his father after the father's death.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Huna and Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna and Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna and the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael state that a son is never made an agent to strike or curse his father, except in the case of a mesit (an enticer to idolatry), as the Torah says 'you shall not pity nor conceal him.'

items.text: Mishnah: Striking vs. cursing parents
items.text_en: Mishnah: Striking vs. cursing parents
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who strikes his father or mother is not liable unless he causes a wound. This is a stringency for the one who curses, as one who curses after death is liable, while one who strikes after death is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who strikes his father or mother is not liable unless he causes a wound; this is a stringency for the one who curses, as cursing after death is liable, while striking after death is exempt.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation that cursing after death is liable
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation that cursing after death is liable
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita that derives from the verse 'his father and his mother he cursed' that it applies after death. It refutes a possible kal vachomer from striking, and concludes with the verse itself teaching liability after death.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the verse 'אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ קִלֵּל' (his father and his mother he cursed) applies to cursing after death.

The baraita raises a possible objection: since striking and cursing are both punishable, one might think that just as striking is only liable when the parent is alive, so too cursing is only liable when alive.

The baraita presents an a fortiori argument: if striking, which treats a sinner like a righteous person, is not liable after death, then cursing, which also treats a sinner like a righteous person, should certainly not be liable after death.
The baraita resolves the objection by citing the verse 'אָבִיו וְאִמּוֹ קִלֵּל' (his father and his mother he cursed) to teach that one is liable for cursing even after death.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yonatan and Rabbi Yoshiya on the verse
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yonatan and Rabbi Yoshiya on the verse
