items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the derivation according to Rabbi Yonatan, for whom the phrase 'his father and his mother' is extra, but for Rabbi Yoshiya it is needed to teach that cursing either parent alone is liable. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yonatan derives the inclusion of a daughter, tumtum, and androgynos from another verse, while Rabbi Yoshiya holds that the Torah speaks in human language.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: this works for רבי יונתן (Rabbi Yonatan), for whom the phrase 'אביו ואמו' is extra, but according to רבי יאשיה (Rabbi Yoshiya) what can be said?

A baraita is cited: 'איש איש' comes to include a daughter, a טומטום (one whose sexual organs are indeterminate), and an אנדרוגינוס (hermaphrodite), and 'אביו ואמו קלל' teaches that cursing either parent alone is liable — these are the words of רבי יאשיה.
רבי יונתן says the verse's phrasing implies both together and each one separately, unless the Torah specifies 'together'.
The Gemara asks: from where does רבי יאשיה derive liability for cursing a parent after death? — from the verse 'ומקלל אביו ואמו מות יומת'.
The Gemara asks: but רבי יונתן needs that verse to include a daughter, a טומטום, and an אנדרוגינוס.
The Gemara rejects deriving it from 'איש איש' because רבי יונתן holds דיברה תורה כלשון בני אדם (the Torah speaks in the language of people).
The Gemara asks why the mishna does not also teach a stringency of the striker over the curser, namely that striking a sinner is treated like striking a fellow Jew, which is not so for cursing.
The Gemara answers: the tanna holds that we liken striking to cursing (מקשינן הכאה לקללה), so no such stringency exists.

items.text: Comparison of striking and cursing regarding a Cuthean
items.text_en: Comparison of striking and cursing regarding a Cuthean
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether striking and cursing are compared (היקש) regarding a Cuthean. It presents two baraitot that differ on whether one is commanded about striking a Cuthean but not cursing, or neither. The Gemara initially suggests the dispute is about the comparison, but then considers it is about whether Cutheans are true converts. It concludes that the dispute is indeed about the comparison.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute between the two baraitot about a כותי (Samaritan) mirrors the earlier tannaitic dispute, and cites the first baraita that one is commanded about striking him but not cursing him.
A second baraita is cited stating that one is commanded neither about cursing a כותי nor about striking him.
The Gemara assumes everyone agrees כותים (Samaritans) are true converts, and suggests the baraitot dispute whether striking is likened to cursing (מקשינן הכאה לקללה).
The Gemara rejects the parallel: everyone agrees striking is not likened to cursing, and the baraitot instead dispute whether כותים are true converts or converts under duress (גירי אריות).
The Gemara objects that if the second baraita held כותים are not true converts, it would not teach that his ox is treated like a Jew's.
The Gemara concludes that the baraitot indeed dispute whether striking is likened to cursing (בהקישא פליגי).

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of kidnapping
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of kidnapping
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who kidnaps a person from Israel is not liable until he brings him into his domain. Rabbi Yehuda requires also use (עימור). It discusses cases of kidnapping one's son, and a half-slave half-free person.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the laws of kidnapping: one is not liable until he brings the victim into his domain; Rabbi Yehuda requires use; Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka holds one liable for kidnapping his son; the Sages exempt; and for a half-slave half-free person, Rabbi Yehuda holds liable and the Sages exempt.
Rabbi Yehuda adds the requirement of use (עימור) of the victim, citing the verse 'והתעמר בו ומכרו'.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka holds that one who kidnaps his own son is liable.
The Sages exempt one who kidnaps his own son.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that one who kidnaps a half-slave half-free person is liable.
The Sages exempt one who kidnaps a half-slave half-free person.

items.text: Gemara: The requirement of עימור and its definition
items.text_en: Gemara: The requirement of עימור and its definition
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda is about whether use less than a perutah is considered use. Rabbi Yirmeya raises questions about selling a sleeping person or a pregnant woman, and the Gemara suggests that there is use in those cases. The questions remain unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Tanna Kamma does not require עימור (use) of the stolen person.
Rabbi Acha bar Rava answers that the dispute is about use of less than a perutah (שווה פרוטה) in value.
Rabbi Yirmeya raises two cases: selling a sleeping person and selling a pregnant woman, asking whether there is a way of עימור (use) in such cases.
The Gemara objects that perhaps there is no עימור (use) at all in these cases.
The Gemara explains that the cases involve potential use (sleeping person can be leaned on, woman can be placed against the wind), and leaves the question unresolved (תיקו).
The Gemara concludes that the questions remain unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Baraitot on who is liable for kidnapping
items.text_en: Baraitot on who is liable for kidnapping
items.desc_en: Two baraitot derive from verses that a woman who kidnaps is liable, and that one who kidnaps a man, woman, convert, freed slave, or minor is liable. Exemptions include not selling, selling while still in his domain, and kidnapping slaves.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita derives from the verse that a woman who kidnaps is also liable.
The baraita extends liability to a woman who kidnaps a woman, using the general phrase 'the thief shall die'.

The second baraita lists all categories of victims (man, woman, convert, freed slave, minor) for whom the kidnapper is liable, and specifies exemptions for not selling, selling while still in his domain, and kidnapping slaves.

items.text: Tanna's statement before Rav Sheshet
items.text_en: Tanna's statement before Rav Sheshet
items.desc_en: A tanna recites a baraita before Rav Sheshet stating that Rabbi Shimon exempts a father who steals his son from the death penalty, and Rav Sheshet instructs him to teach that the father is exempt.

sub.desc_en: A tanna recites a baraita before Rav Sheshet stating that Rabbi Shimon exempts a father who steals his son from the death penalty, and Rav Sheshet instructs him to teach that the father is exempt.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the difficulty, suggesting that the baraita might follow Rabbi Shimon while the Mishnah follows the Rabbis. It then cites Rabbi Yochanan's principle that unattributed sources correspond to specific Tannaim, implying that the baraita (Sifrei) is indeed Rabbi Shimon's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the difficulty, suggesting that the baraita might follow Rabbi Shimon while the Mishnah follows the Rabbis.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion by citing Rabbi Yochanan's principle that unattributed sources correspond to specific Tannaim, implying the baraita (Sifrei) is Rabbi Shimon's view.

items.text: Reason for the Rabbis' exemption
items.text_en: Reason for the Rabbis' exemption
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the Rabbis derive the exemption from the verse 'כי ימצא' (when found), excluding a child who is already found (i.e., with his father). Rav Pappa challenges this by comparing it to the case of adultery, but Abaye clarifies that his derivation is from 'ונמצא בידו' (and found in his hand).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reason of the Rabbis (who exempt one who steals his own son).
Abaye answers that the verse 'כי ימצא' (when found) excludes a child who is already found (i.e., with his father).
Rav Pappa objects by comparing to the case of adultery, where the same phrase 'כי ימצא' would absurdly exempt a woman who is already found (i.e., a known prostitute).
Abaye clarifies that his derivation is not from 'כי ימצא' alone but from the phrase 'ונמצא בידו' (and found in his hand), which applies specifically to theft.

items.text: Rava's ruling on teachers
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on teachers
items.desc_en: Rava concludes that teachers of children and those who teach Mishnah to children are considered as if the children are found in their hands, and are therefore exempt from the death penalty for kidnapping.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that teachers of children and those who teach rabbinic students are considered 'found in their hand' and are exempt from the death penalty for kidnapping.

items.text: Derivation regarding a half-slave half-free person
items.text_en: Derivation regarding a half-slave half-free person
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's case of one who steals a half-slave half-free person. It explains Rabbi Yehuda's view that such a person is exempt from the death penalty, derived from multiple exclusions in the verse, while the Rabbis interpret the verses differently to exclude slaves and half-slaves.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's case of one who steals a half-slave half-free person and references Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that slaves have no shame.

The Gemara asks for Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning and explains that he derives from the verse 'איש ואחיו' (a man and his brother) that only one with brotherhood is included, excluding a slave who lacks brotherhood.
The Rabbis counter that a slave is considered a brother in matters of commandments, so the exclusion does not apply.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Yehuda interprets the verses in the context of the half-slave half-free person.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that 'מאחיו' excludes slaves, 'בני ישראל' excludes the half-slave, and 'מבני ישראל' also excludes the half-slave, creating a double exclusion that comes to include.
The Rabbis reject the exclusion from 'מאחיו' because a slave is a brother in commandments, and they use 'בני ישראל' and 'מבני ישראל' to exclude a full slave and a half-slave respectively.

items.text: Source of the prohibition against kidnapping
items.text_en: Source of the prohibition against kidnapping
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yochanan debate the source of the negative commandment for kidnapping: one derives it from 'לא תגנוב' and the other from 'לא ימכרו ממכרת עבד'. Two baraitot are cited, each using the hermeneutic principle of context to determine whether the verse refers to kidnapping or theft of property.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where is the negative commandment (אזהרה) for kidnapping derived?
Rabbi Yoshiya answers: from the verse 'לֹא תִגְנֹב' (You shall not steal).
Rabbi Yochanan answers: from the verse 'לֹא יִמָּכְרוּ מִמְכֶּרֶת עֶבֶד' (They shall not be sold as a slave is sold).
The Gemara resolves that the two rabbis do not disagree; one counts the negative commandment of theft, the other counts the negative commandment of sale.
A baraita is taught: the verse 'לֹא תִגְנֹב' speaks of kidnapping, derived by context (דבר הלמד מעניינו).
Another baraita is taught: the verse 'לֹא תִגְנֹבוּ' speaks of theft of property, also derived by context.

items.text: Dispute about conspiring witnesses in a kidnapping case
items.text_en: Dispute about conspiring witnesses in a kidnapping case
items.desc_en: Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan argue whether witnesses who testified about the theft and sale of a person and were later found to be conspirators are executed. Chizkiya, following Rabbi Akiva, says they are not executed because testimony about a half-matter is invalid, while Rabbi Yochanan, following the Rabbis, says they are executed. Chizkiya concedes in the case of a rebellious son.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a dispute: Chizkiya says witnesses who testified about the theft and sale of a person and were later found to be conspirators (עדים זוממים) are not executed, while Rabbi Yochanan says they are executed.

The gemara explains that Chizkiya follows Rabbi Akiva's principle that testimony must be about a complete matter (דבר) and not a half-matter (חצי דבר), while Rabbi Yochanan follows the Rabbis who hold that testimony is valid even for a half-matter.

Chizkiya concedes that in the case of a rebellious son (בן סורר ומורה), the later witnesses who testified about his rebellious acts and were found to be conspirators are executed, because the earlier witnesses can be said to have testified about the entire matter.

items.text: Chizkiya's reasoning for witnesses of sale not being killed
items.text_en: Chizkiya's reasoning for witnesses of sale not being killed
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Chizkiya, witnesses of the sale are not killed because they can claim they came only to have the thief lashed, not to cause his death. The other witnesses (of the theft) are doing a complete 'thing' (causing death).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Chizkiya, witnesses of the sale are not killed because they can claim they came only to have the thief lashed, not to cause his death, while the other witnesses (of the theft) are doing a complete 'thing' (causing death).

items.text: Rav Pappa's challenge and the dispute between Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's challenge and the dispute between Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges: if so, witnesses of sale should also be killed, since witnesses of theft can claim they came only to have him lashed. But Chizkiya holds that witnesses of theft are not lashed? The Gemara notes the dispute: Chizkiya says witnesses of theft in a capital case who are zomemin are lashed, Rabbi Yochanan says they are not lashed. It concludes that Chizkiya holds they are lashed, so his statement that they are not killed is consistent.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa challenges: if so, witnesses of sale should also be killed, since witnesses of theft can claim they came only to have him lashed; and if you say Chizkiya holds they are not lashed...
The Gemara cites the dispute between Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan regarding whether witnesses of theft in a capital case who are zomemin are lashed, and concludes that Chizkiya holds they are lashed.

The Gemara explains that according to Rabbi Yochanan, since the witnesses are killed, the prohibition is a לאו שניתן לאזהרת מיתת בית דין (a prohibition that comes as a warning for a court-imposed death penalty), and one is not lashed for such a prohibition.

items.text: Rav Pappa's resolution: the dispute is about witnesses of theft
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's resolution: the dispute is about witnesses of theft
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that everyone agrees witnesses of sale are killed. The dispute is only about witnesses of theft: Chizkiya says they are not killed because theft and sale are separate acts, while Rabbi Yochanan says they are killed because theft is the beginning of the sale.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the dispute by stating that all agree witnesses of sale are killed, and the disagreement is only about witnesses of theft: Chizkiya holds they are not killed because theft and sale are separate acts, while Rabbi Yochanan holds they are killed because theft is the beginning of the sale.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan concedes in the case of a rebellious son
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan concedes in the case of a rebellious son
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan concedes that the first witnesses of a rebellious son (ben sorer u'moreh) who are zomemin are not killed, because they can claim they came only to have him lashed.

sub.text: Stam's summary of Rabbi Yochanan's concession
sub.text_en: Stam's summary of Rabbi Yochanan's concession
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan concedes that the first witnesses of a rebellious son (בן סורר ומורה) who are zomemin are not killed, because they can claim they came only to have him lashed.

items.text: Abaye's clarification: everyone agrees in some cases, disputes in others
items.text_en: Abaye's clarification: everyone agrees in some cases, disputes in others
items.desc_en: Abaye states: everyone agrees regarding the rebellious son in the case of first witnesses (not killed) and last witnesses (killed). The dispute is when two say 'he stole in our presence' and two say 'he ate in our presence'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye opens by stating that everyone agrees in some cases regarding the rebellious son (בן סורר ומורה) and disputes in others.
Abaye clarifies that everyone agrees regarding the first witnesses of the rebellious son: they are not killed because they can claim they came to have him lashed.
Abaye clarifies that everyone agrees regarding the last witnesses: they are killed because the first witnesses can claim they came for lashes, while the last witnesses fully incriminated him.
Abaye resolves that the dispute is when two witnesses say 'he stole in our presence' and two say 'he ate in our presence'.

items.text: Rav Asi's statement and its analysis
items.text_en: Rav Asi's statement and its analysis
items.desc_en: Rav Asi says witnesses of sale who are zomemin are not killed because they can claim 'I sold my slave'. Rav Yosef says this follows Rabbi Akiva who says 'a matter' not half a matter. Abaye challenges that even according to the Rabbis they would not be killed because of the 'since' argument. The Gemara concludes that Rav Asi's statement is needed even if the witnesses of theft later came, and even if they only hinted, teaching that hinting is nothing.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi states that witnesses of a sale who are zomemin (scheming witnesses) are not killed because the accused can claim 'I sold my slave'.
Rav Yosef questions whose opinion Rav Asi's ruling follows, suggesting it aligns with Rabbi Akiva who holds that a 'matter' (דבר) requires a complete matter, not half a matter.

Abaye objects that even according to the Rabbis (who disagree with Rabbi Akiva), the witnesses would not be killed because Rav Asi's reasoning is based on the 'since' (מתוך) argument, not on the principle of 'half a matter'.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Asi's statement is needed even according to the Rabbis, in a case where the witnesses of theft did not come initially but came later.
The Gemara adds that Rav Asi's statement is also needed to teach that even if the witnesses only hinted (רמזי) at the sale, their hinting is nothing (לאו כלום הוא), contrary to what one might think.

items.text: Mishnah: The rebellious elder (zaken mamre)
items.text_en: Mishnah: The rebellious elder (zaken mamre)
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for a rebellious elder: three courts in the Temple, the process of appeal, and that if he returns to his city and teaches as before he is exempt, but if he rules for action he is liable. A student who rules for action is exempt, making his stringency his leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by defining the rebellious elder (זקן ממרא) and citing the verse that establishes his authority to challenge the court.
The Mishnah describes the three courts in the Temple: at the entrance of the Temple Mount, at the entrance of the Temple courtyard, and in the Chamber of Hewn Stone.
The Mishnah explains the procedure: the elder first goes to the court at the Temple Mount entrance and presents his teaching; if they have a tradition, they tell him.
If the first court does not have a tradition, the elder proceeds to the court at the Temple courtyard entrance, where the same process repeats.
If still unresolved, all parties go to the Great Court in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, from which Torah goes forth to all Israel, citing the verse.
The Mishnah rules that if the elder returns to his city and teaches as before, he is exempt; but if he rules for action, he is liable, citing the verse.
The Mishnah concludes that a student who rules for action is exempt, so his stringency becomes his leniency.

items.text: Gemara begins: the verse for the rebellious elder
items.text_en: Gemara begins: the verse for the rebellious elder
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins with a baraita citing the verse 'כִּי יִפָּלֵא מִמְּךָ דָבָר' as the source for the rebellious elder.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing a baraita that introduces the verse 'כִּי יִפָּלֵא מִמְּךָ דָבָר' as the scriptural source for the rebellious elder (זקן ממרא).

items.text: Baraita: Exegesis of the verses on the rebellious elder
items.text_en: Baraita: Exegesis of the verses on the rebellious elder
items.desc_en: A baraita interprets the key words of the verse 'כי יפלא ממך דבר למשפט' to identify the court, the advisor, and the types of cases that require the high court. It also expounds 'בין דם לדם', 'בין דין לדין', 'בין נגע לנגע', and other terms to specify the scope of the law.

sub.desc_en: The baraita identifies the subject of the verse as the מופלא (expert) of the court, interprets 'ממך' as the advisor (יועץ), 'דבר' as הלכה (halacha), and 'למשפט' as the law (דין).

sub.text: Baraita's detailed exegesis of 'בין דם לדם' etc.
sub.text_en: Baraita's detailed exegesis of 'בין דם לדם' etc.
sub.desc_en: The baraita expounds the phrases 'בין דם לדם', 'בין דין לדין', and 'בין נגע לנגע' to specify the categories of cases: blood types (menstrual, childbirth, zav), legal cases (capital, monetary, lashes), and plagues (human, houses, garments).

The baraita interprets 'דברי' as vows of consecration (חרמים, ערכין, הקדשות), 'ריבות' as the sotah ordeal, the heifer ritual, and purification of the leper, and 'בשעריך' as the agricultural gifts of gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and the corner of the field.

The baraita interprets 'וקמת' as arising from the court, 'ועלית' as teaching that the Temple Mount is higher than the land of Israel and the land of Israel higher than all other lands, and 'אל המקום' as teaching that the place (the Temple) is the determining factor.
The gemara questions the source for the claim that the land of Israel is higher than all other lands, since the verse only mentions ascending to the Temple.
The gemara answers by citing a verse from Jeremiah that uses the language of 'העלה' (brought up) for the return from exile, implying that the land of Israel is elevated above all other lands.

items.text: Gemara's question: Source for Eretz Yisrael's height
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Source for Eretz Yisrael's height
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's claim that the Temple is higher than Eretz Yisrael and that Eretz Yisrael is higher than all other lands. It finds a scriptural source for the latter from a verse in Jeremiah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the source for the claim that Eretz Yisrael is higher than all other lands, since the verse 'ועליתה' only supports the Temple's height over Eretz Yisrael.
The Gemara answers by citing a verse from Jeremiah that uses the language of 'העלה' (bringing up) from all lands, implying Eretz Yisrael is elevated above them.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute: What makes a zaken mamre liable
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute: What makes a zaken mamre liable
items.desc_en: A baraita presents three Tannaitic opinions on the types of rulings that render a rebellious elder liable: Rabbi Meir says only on a matter whose intentional violation is karet and unintentional a chatat; Rabbi Yehuda says on a matter whose essence is from Torah but its interpretation from Scribes; Rabbi Shimon says even on a single detail of the Scribes.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that the rebellious elder is liable only for a matter whose intentional violation carries כרת (karet) and whose unintentional violation requires a חטאת (sin-offering) — Rabbi Meir's view; Rabbi Yehuda says for a matter whose essence is from the Torah but whose interpretation is from the Scribes; Rabbi Shimon says even for a single detail of the Scribes' details.
Rabbi Yehuda states that liability applies to a matter whose essence is from Torah but its interpretation from Scribes.
Rabbi Shimon adds that even a single detail of the Scribes renders the elder liable.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural sources for each Tanna
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural sources for each Tanna
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the scriptural basis for each opinion: Rabbi Meir uses a gezerah shavah from 'דבר' to the sin-offering; Rabbi Yehuda derives from 'על פי התורה אשר יורוך' requiring both Torah and instruction; Rabbi Shimon derives from 'אשר יגידו לך מן המקום ההוא' including even the slightest matter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural basis of Rabbi Meir's position.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir derives his position via a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) from the word 'דבר' in the sin-offering passage.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda derives his position from the verse requiring both 'תורה' (Torah) and 'יורוך' (instruction).
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon derives his position from the verse 'אשר יגידו לך מן המקום ההוא', which includes even the slightest matter.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Chinana's request and Rava's explanation
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana's request and Rava's explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana asks Rava to explain the Mishnah according to Rabbi Meir. Rava instructs Rav Pappa to explain it. Rav Pappa then expounds the verse 'כי יפלא' to refer to the expert of the court, and 'ממך' to the advisor who knows intercalation. He illustrates with a dispute about the tenth day of the month, citing Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana asks Rava to explain the Mishnah according to Rabbi Meir, and Rava delegates the task to Rav Pappa.
Rav Pappa begins his explanation: the verse 'כי יפלא' refers to the expert of the court, and 'ממך' to the advisor who knows intercalation, citing a baraita about the month of Adar.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's illustration of intercalation error
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's illustration of intercalation error
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa illustrates that an error in intercalation could permit חמץ (leaven) on פסח (Passover).
Rav Pappa explains that 'דבר' refers to a halachic dispute about the tenth day, citing the positions of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish.
Rabbi Yochanan holds that the tenth day requires שמירה (guarding) like the ninth day.
Reish Lakish holds that the tenth day does not require שמירה (guarding), like the eleventh day.

items.text: Conclusion: 'משפט' refers to judgment
items.text_en: Conclusion: 'משפט' refers to judgment
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the exegesis by stating that 'משפט' refers to the judgment itself, completing the interpretation of the verse.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa concludes that 'משפט' refers to the law (דין).

items.text: Introduction to the hermeneutic principle
items.text_en: Introduction to the hermeneutic principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the method of deriving laws by comparing similar phrases (gezerah shavah) using 'hennah' and 'zimmah' to connect the case of one's daughter from rape to other laws.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the topic of deriving the law of one's daughter from rape.

sub.text: Rava citing Rav Yitzchak bar Avudimi
sub.text_en: Rava citing Rav Yitzchak bar Avudimi
sub.desc_en: Rava reports that Rav Yitzchak bar Avudimi taught the hermeneutic principle: the word 'הנה' (hennah) and 'זמה' (zimmah) are each used in a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) to connect the case of one's daughter from rape to other laws.

items.text: Dispute about blood types: menstrual blood
items.text_en: Dispute about blood types: menstrual blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'between blood and blood' refers to menstrual blood, birth blood, and zav blood. For menstrual blood, the dispute is between Akavya ben Mahalalel and the Sages regarding green blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the three types of blood distinguished by the verse: menstrual blood, birth blood, and zav blood.
The Gemara cites the dispute between Akavya ben Mahalalel and the Sages regarding green menstrual blood: Akavya declares it טמא (ritually impure) while the Sages declare it טהור (ritually pure).

items.text: Dispute about birth blood: Rav and Levi
items.text_en: Dispute about birth blood: Rav and Levi
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute between Rav and Levi regarding birth blood: Rav holds it is a single source that the Torah alternately deems impure and pure, while Levi holds there are two distinct sources.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute about birth blood (דם לידה) as a disagreement between Rav and Levi.
Rav holds that birth blood comes from a single source (מעין אחד) which the Torah alternately deems impure and pure.
Levi holds that there are two distinct sources (שני מעיינות) for birth blood: when the impure source closes, the pure one opens, and vice versa.

items.text: Dispute about zav blood: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Dispute about zav blood: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding a woman who experiences pain for three days within the eleven days of zivah: Rabbi Eliezer considers her a yoledet b'zov if she rests a full day, while Rabbi Yehoshua requires a night and a day like Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Eliezer's position: a woman who experiences pain for three days within the eleven days of zivah and then rests a full day (מעת לעת) before giving birth is considered a יולדת בזוב (one who gives birth while in a state of זיבה).
Rabbi Yehoshua counters that the required rest is a night and a day (לילה ויום) like Shabbat, and specifies that the rest must be from the pain (צער) and not merely from the blood.

items.text: Disputes about court systems: monetary, capital, and lashes
items.text_en: Disputes about court systems: monetary, capital, and lashes
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains 'between judgment and judgment' as referring to monetary, capital, and lashes cases. For monetary cases, the dispute is between Shmuel and Rabbi Avahu about two judges; for capital cases, between Rabbi and the Sages about monetary compensation; for lashes, between Rabbi Yishmael and the Sages about the number of judges.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by explaining that the phrase 'between judgment and judgment' refers to three categories: monetary cases, capital cases, and lashes.

The Gemara cites the dispute between Shmuel and Rabbi Avahu regarding monetary cases: Shmuel holds that two judges' verdict is valid but they are called a 'brazen court', while Rabbi Avahu holds it is invalid.

The Gemara cites the dispute between Rabbi and the Sages regarding capital cases: Rabbi interprets 'and you shall give a life for a life' as monetary compensation, using a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'נתינה' (giving).

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael and the Sages' dispute
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael and the Sages' dispute
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and the Sages regarding lashes: the Sages require three judges, while Rabbi Yishmael requires twenty-three.

items.text: Disputes about plagues: human, houses, and garments
items.text_en: Disputes about plagues: human, houses, and garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains 'between plague and plague' as referring to plagues of humans, houses, and garments. For human plagues, the dispute is between Rabbi Yehoshua and the Sages about the order of bright spot and white hair; for houses, between Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon and the Sages about the size and location; for garments, the dispute begins with Rabbi Yonatan ben Avtulmos.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the section by explaining that the phrase 'between plague and plague' refers to plagues of humans, houses, and garments.

The Gemara cites a baraita about human plagues, where the dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua and the Sages concerns the order of bright spot and white hair, and Rava explains that 'כֵּהָה' means the person is pure.

The Gemara cites a baraita about house plagues, where Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon requires the plague to appear as two gris on two stones in two walls at a corner, and the Gemara explains his reasoning from the verses 'קִיר' and 'קִירֹת'.
The Gemara begins to cite a baraita about garment plagues, where the dispute is between Rabbi Yonatan ben Avtulmos and the Sages, but the baraita is cut off at the end of the daf.

items.text: Opening analogy: פריחה בבגדים
items.text_en: Opening analogy: פריחה בבגדים
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by explaining the Mishnah's term 'דברים' (things) with an analogy from leprosy: just as a person with a bald patch who becomes entirely bald is pure, so too a garment that becomes entirely affected is pure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's term 'דברים' (things) is analogous to the case of a garment that becomes entirely affected by leprosy and is thereby pure.

The Gemara answers by drawing a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the terms 'קרחת' and 'גבחת' used for both a person and a garment, concluding that just as a person whose baldness spreads entirely is pure, so too a garment entirely affected is pure.

items.text: דברים – ערכין, חרמים, הקדשות
items.text_en: דברים – ערכין, חרמים, הקדשות
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the 'דברים' (things) as valuations (ערכין), dedications (חרמים), and consecrations (הקדשות), each with a dispute: valuations between Rabbi Meir and the Sages, dedications between Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and the Sages, and consecrations between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the 'דברים' (things) as valuations (ערכין), dedications (חרמים), and consecrations (הקדשות).
The Gemara cites the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding one who makes a valuation of an infant less than a month old.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's opinion that unspecified dedications (חרמים) go to the Temple treasury, based on the verse 'כל חרם קדש קדשים הוא לה׳'.
The Sages argue that unspecified dedications go to the priest, and explain the verse as applying to consecrated items.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion that even a small pipe of consecrated property requires ten people to redeem it.

items.text: ריבוֹת – השקאת סוטה, עריפת עגלה, טהרת מצורע
items.text_en: ריבוֹת – השקאת סוטה, עריפת עגלה, טהרת מצורע
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains 'ריבוֹת' (multitudes) as the water ordeal for a suspected adulteress (סוטה), the heifer neck-breaking (עגלה ערופה), and the purification of a leper (מצורע), each with disputes: sotah between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, heifer between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva, and leper between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies 'ריבוֹת' (multitudes) as referring to the water ordeal for a suspected adulteress (סוטה), the heifer neck-breaking (עגלה ערופה), and the purification of a leper (מצורע).

The Gemara cites a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding the number of witnesses required for the sotah ordeal: Rabbi Eliezer requires two witnesses for the warning but one for the drinking, while Rabbi Yehoshua requires two for both.

The Gemara cites a dispute about the measurement point for the heifer neck-breaking: Rabbi Eliezer says from the navel, Rabbi Akiva says from the nose, and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says from the neck where the wound is made.

The Gemara cites a dispute about a leper lacking a right thumb, toe, or ear: the Sages say he has no purification, Rabbi Eliezer says to apply the blood to the spot, and Rabbi Shimon says to apply it to the left side and he may go out.

items.text: בשעריך – לקט, שכחה, פאה
items.text_en: בשעריך – לקט, שכחה, פאה
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains 'בשעריך' (in your gates) as gleanings (לקט), forgotten sheaves (שכחה), and the corner of the field (פאה), with disputes: Beit Shammai on the number of stalks, and Rabbi Yishmael on the timing of separating pe'ah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies 'בשעריך' (in your gates) as referring to the gifts to the poor: gleanings (לקט), forgotten sheaves (שכחה), and the corner of the field (פאה), citing the Mishnah's definitions of the quantities that constitute each gift.
Beit Shammai rules that for all these gifts, three stalks or sheaves go to the poor and four remain for the householder.
The Sages teach the order of separating pe'ah: ideally from the standing grain, but if not, from the sheaves, and if not, from the heap before it is smoothed, after which one must tithe and give it.
In the name of Rabbi Yishmael, the Sages add that one may even separate pe'ah from the dough (עיסה).

items.text: Dispute on the rebellious elder's execution
items.text_en: Dispute on the rebellious elder's execution
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rabbi Elazar dispute the conditions for executing a rebellious elder (זקן ממרא). Rav Kahana says he is not executed unless he says 'so it appears to me' and they say 'from tradition'. Rabbi Elazar says even if he says 'from tradition' and they say 'so it appears to us', he is executed to prevent disputes, citing the case of Akavya ben Mahalalel who was not executed because he did not rule for practice.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana states that if both the elder and the court claim tradition, the elder is not executed.

Rav Kahana elaborates that the elder is executed only when he says 'so it appears to me' and the court says 'from tradition', citing the case of Akavya ben Mahalalel who was not executed because he did not rule for practice.

Rabbi Elazar objects that even if the elder claims tradition and the court says 'so it appears to us', he is executed to prevent disputes, and explains that Akavya was spared only because he did not rule for practice.

items.text: Supporting evidence from the Mishnah and Rabbi Yoshiya
items.text_en: Supporting evidence from the Mishnah and Rabbi Yoshiya
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to support Rav Kahana's view from the Mishnah's phrasing, but deflects it. Then it cites Rabbi Yoshiya reporting from Zeira about a husband who forgave his warning (קינוי) being valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's phrasing 'I taught thus and my colleagues taught thus' implies a case where one says 'from tradition' and the other says 'it appears to us'.
The Gemara deflects the question, explaining that the Mishnah actually refers to a case where one says 'it appears to me' and the other says 'from tradition'.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Yoshiya reporting from Zeira of Jerusalem that a husband who forgave his warning (קינוי) — his warning is void.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Pardon for the rebellious son and elder
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Pardon for the rebellious son and elder
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the parents of a rebellious son (ben sorer u'moreh) or the court of a rebellious elder (zaken mamre) wish to pardon them, they may. However, when the author went to the southern sages, they agreed on two cases but not on the elder, to prevent disputes. The text ends with 'teyuvta' (a refutation).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the parents of a rebellious son (בן סורר ומורה) may pardon him.
The Mishnah adds that the court of a rebellious elder (זקן ממרא) may also pardon him.
The Mishnah reports that the southern sages agreed on the first two cases but not on the elder, to prevent disputes, ending with 'תיוּבְתָּא' (a refutation).

items.text: Baraita: The hierarchy of courts and the process of inquiry
items.text_en: Baraita: The hierarchy of courts and the process of inquiry
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yose describes the original court system: the Great Sanhedrin in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, two smaller courts at the Temple Mount and the Courtyard, and local courts. When a question arises, it is asked locally, then escalated. If unresolved, the inquirer presents his reasoning before the Great Sanhedrin, which decides by majority. The baraita concludes with a description of the qualifications for judges and a praise of humility.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yose describes the original court hierarchy: the Great Sanhedrin in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, two smaller courts at the Temple Mount and the Courtyard, and local courts in all towns.

The baraita details the escalation process: a question is first asked in the local court, then to the court nearest the town, then to the court at the Temple Mount, and finally to the court at the Courtyard.

sub.text: Baraita: Presentation before the Great Sanhedrin
sub.text_en: Baraita: Presentation before the Great Sanhedrin
sub.desc_en: The inquirer presents his reasoning and that of his colleagues; if unresolved, all come to the Chamber of Hewn Stone, where the Sanhedrin sits from the morning daily offering until the afternoon daily offering.
On Shabbat and festivals the Sanhedrin sits in the חיל (the rampart); if they have no tradition, they vote, and the majority decides whether to declare impure or pure.
The baraita explains that when the disciples of Shammai and Hillel multiplied without having served their masters sufficiently, disputes increased and the Torah became like two Torahs.

sub.text: Baraita: Qualifications and promotion of judges
sub.text_en: Baraita: Qualifications and promotion of judges
sub.desc_en: The baraita describes the criteria for appointing a judge: wisdom, humility, and public approval, and the promotion from city court to the Temple Mount, then to the Courtyard, then to the Chamber of Hewn Stone.

The baraita concludes with a message from the Sanhedrin defining a person of the World to Come as humble, lowly, constantly engaged in Torah, and not claiming credit, and the rabbis applied this to Rav Ulla bar Abba.

items.text: Gemara: Liability of the rebellious elder
items.text_en: Gemara: Liability of the rebellious elder
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the conditions for a rebellious elder's liability: he must either act on his own ruling or instruct others who act. A difficulty arises: if he acts himself, he was already liable before his ruling? The Gemara resolves that initially he needed a warning, but now he does not. For a mesit (enticer), the difference is that initially his reasoning was accepted, but now it is not.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a rebellious elder is not liable unless he either acts on his own ruling or instructs others who act on it.
The Gemara questions the case where the elder acts himself: if he already violated the law before his ruling, why is he now liable for a new capital offense?

sub.text: First answer (distinction between forbidden fat/blood and capital cases)
sub.text_en: First answer (distinction between forbidden fat/blood and capital cases)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the baraita refers to a case where the elder ruled about forbidden fat or blood, where initially he was not liable for death, but after his ruling he becomes liable.
The Gemara resolves that initially the elder needed a warning (התראה) to be liable, but after his rebellious ruling he no longer needs a warning.
The Gemara extends the logic to a mesit (enticer to idolatry), explaining that initially his reasoning was accepted, but after his enticement it is no longer accepted.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Severity of scribal laws and the case of tefillin
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Severity of scribal laws and the case of tefillin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that violating scribal laws is more severe than Torah laws: one who says 'there are no tefillin' is exempt, but one who says 'five compartments' is liable. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Oshaya explain that liability applies only to a matter whose essence is from the Torah but interpretation from scribes, with room for addition that detracts. The Gemara questions why lulav and tzitzit are not similar, and answers based on whether binding is required.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who says 'there are no tefillin' is exempt, but one who says 'five compartments' is liable.

Rabbi Elazar says that Rabbi Oshaya explains liability applies only to a matter whose essence is from the Torah but interpretation from scribes, with room for addition that detracts, and only tefillin fits, according to Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara questions why the case of lulav is not similar to tefillin.
The Gemara answers that regarding lulav, if binding is not required, adding does not detract; if binding is required, the mitzva is already compromised.
The Gemara questions why the case of tzitzit is not similar to tefillin.
The Gemara begins to answer that regarding tzitzit, if the upper knot is not Torah-mandated, adding does not detract.

items.text: Gemara's continuation of the previous discussion on tefillin
items.text_en: Gemara's continuation of the previous discussion on tefillin
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the logic about a 'deficient and standing' object applies to tefillin as well, and resolves it with Rabbi Zeira's ruling about an outer compartment that does not see the air.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the logic of 'deficient and standing' applies to tefillin, based on the principle that the upper knot is Torah law.
The Gemara resolves the question by citing Rabbi Zeira's ruling that an outer compartment that does not see the air is invalid, thereby addressing the tefillin case.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on the rebellious elder's execution
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on the rebellious elder's execution
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a rebellious elder is not executed in his local court or in Yavneh, but is brought to the Great Court in Jerusalem and executed on a festival. Rabbi Yehuda argues for immediate execution with announcements. The Gemara cites a baraita with the same dispute and Rabbi Yehuda's scriptural reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a condemned person is not executed in his local court but is brought up to the Great Court in Jerusalem, and his execution is delayed until a festival, according to Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that the judgment of this person should not be delayed; rather, he is executed immediately, and messengers are sent to announce his conviction.
A baraita repeats Rabbi Akiva's position, citing the verse 'וְכׇל הָעָם יִשְׁמְעוּ וְיִרָאוּ' (and all the people shall hear and fear) to support the delay until the festival.

Rabbi Yehuda objects to Rabbi Akiva's interpretation, arguing that the verse says 'יִשְׁמְעוּ וְיִירָאוּ' (they shall hear and fear), not 'יִרְאוּ וְיִירָאוּ' (they shall see and fear), so there is no reason to delay the judgment.
Rabbi Yehuda concludes that the condemned person is executed immediately, and messengers are sent to announce his conviction.

items.text: Baraita on four who require proclamation
items.text_en: Baraita on four who require proclamation
items.desc_en: A baraita lists four types of offenders who require a public proclamation: the enticer, the rebellious son, the rebellious elder, and conspiring witnesses. It explains the scriptural basis for each.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists four types of offenders who require a public announcement: the enticer, the rebellious son, the rebellious elder, and conspiring witnesses.

The Gemara explains that for the first three, the verse uses 'וְכׇל הָעָם' (and all the people) or 'כׇל יִשְׂרָאֵל' (all Israel), but for conspiring witnesses, the verse uses 'וְהַנִּשְׁאָרִים' (and the rest), because not everyone is fit for testimony.
The baraita explains that for conspiring witnesses, the verse uses 'וְהַנִּשְׁאָרִים' (and the rest) because not everyone is fit to testify, so the proclamation is limited to those who are qualified.

items.text: Mishnah on the false prophet and other capital cases
items.text_en: Mishnah on the false prophet and other capital cases
items.desc_en: The Mishnah distinguishes between a false prophet who prophesies what he did not hear or what was not said to him (executed by human court) and one who suppresses his prophecy, disregards a prophet's words, or violates his own prophecy (executed by Heaven). It also lists other capital cases: one who prophesies in the name of idolatry, one who has relations with a married woman, and conspiring witnesses of a priest's daughter.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a false prophet who prophesies what he did not hear or what was not said to him is executed by human hands.

The Mishnah continues that one who suppresses his prophecy, disregards a prophet's words, or violates his own prophecy is executed by Heaven, as it says 'אָנֹכִי אֶדְרֹשׁ מֵעִמּוֹ' (I will require it of him).
The Mishnah adds that one who prophesies in the name of idolatry, even if he correctly rules on impurity and purity, is executed by human hands.
The Mishnah states that one who has relations with a married woman, once she has entered the husband's domain for marriage even if not yet intimate, is executed by strangulation.
The Mishnah concludes that conspiring witnesses against a priest's daughter and her paramour are an exception: they are not executed by the same death as the accused, but by a different one.

items.text: Gemara: Scriptural sources for the three categories
items.text_en: Gemara: Scriptural sources for the three categories
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing three executed by humans and three by Heaven. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav derives the sources from verses: the false prophet who prophesies what he did not hear, what was not said to him, or in the name of idolatry are executed by strangulation. The other three are executed by Heaven, derived from the verse 'I will demand it from him.'

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists three categories of false prophets executed by human court and three executed by Heaven.
The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the baraita's categories.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav derives the three human-executed categories from Deuteronomy 18:20, concluding that their death is by strangulation.
The Gemara derives the three Heaven-executed categories from Deuteronomy 18:19, interpreting the verse to refer to suppressing prophecy, disregarding a prophet, and violating one's own prophecy.

items.text: Examples of prophesying what was not heard: Tzidkiyahu ben Kena'anah
items.text_en: Examples of prophesying what was not heard: Tzidkiyahu ben Kena'anah
items.desc_en: The Gemara gives the example of Tzidkiyahu ben Kena'anah, who was misled by the spirit of Navot. Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Yochanan explain the spirit. The Gemara notes that Tzidkiyahu should have known Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that no two prophets prophesy in the same style, which Yehoshafat knew.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the example of Tzidkiyahu ben Kena'anah, who prophesied falsely because the spirit of Navot misled him, citing the biblical account.
Rav Yehuda explains that 'go forth' means the spirit was expelled from God's proximity, and Rabbi Yochanan identifies the spirit as that of Navot the Yizre'eli.
The Gemara notes that Tzidkiyahu should have discerned the false prophecy based on Rabbi Yitzchak's principle that no two prophets prophesy in the same style.
The Gemara illustrates the principle by contrasting the different styles of Obadiah and Jeremiah, and concludes that the false prophets' identical style proves their prophecy is false.
The Gemara resolves that Yehoshafat was present and informed them of Rabbi Yitzchak's tradition, so Tzidkiyahu should have known.

items.text: Example of prophesying what was not said to him: Chananyah ben Azzur
items.text_en: Example of prophesying what was not said to him: Chananyah ben Azzur
items.desc_en: The Gemara gives the example of Chananyah ben Azzur, who derived a kal vachomer from Yirmeyahu's prophecy about Elam and applied it to Babylonia. Rav Pappa questions Abaye whether this was not said to him at all, and Abaye explains that since a kal vachomer can be derived, it is considered as if it was said to him, but not to him specifically.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the example of Chananyah ben Azzur, who derived a kal vachomer from Yirmeyahu's prophecy about Elam and falsely prophesied the breaking of Babylonia's yoke.
Rav Pappa questions Abaye whether this prophecy was not said to any other prophet at all, making the classification problematic.
Abaye explains that since a kal vachomer can be legitimately derived, it is considered as if the prophecy was said to Yirmeyahu, but not to Chananyah specifically.

items.text: Examples of prophesying in the name of idolatry and suppressing prophecy
items.text_en: Examples of prophesying in the name of idolatry and suppressing prophecy
items.desc_en: The Gemara gives examples: prophesying in the name of idolatry is like the prophets of Baal; suppressing prophecy is like Yonah ben Amitai. The text cuts off at the example of disregarding a prophet's words.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides examples for each category: prophesying in the name of idolatry is exemplified by the prophets of Baal, and suppressing prophecy by Yonah ben Amitai, but the text cuts off before completing the example of disregarding a prophet's words.

items.text: Examples of prophets who violated their own prophecy
items.text_en: Examples of prophets who violated their own prophecy
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides examples of prophets who were punished for violating their own prophetic word: the companion of Micha and the prophet Iddo.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the case of Micha's companion, a prophet who was punished for disobeying a divine command.
The Gemara cites the case of the prophet Iddo, who violated his own prophecy and was killed by a lion.

items.text: The one who suppresses his prophecy is lashed
items.text_en: The one who suppresses his prophecy is lashed
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who suppresses his prophecy is lashed. Rav Chisda questions how this is possible without witnesses and warning. Abaye explains that fellow prophets know through divine revelation, and addresses the case of Jonah where the prophecy was retracted.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna recites a baraita before Rav Chisda stating that one who suppresses his prophecy is lashed.
Rav Chisda objects that without witnesses and warning, how can the prophet be liable for lashes.
Abaye answers that fellow prophets serve as witnesses, knowing through divine revelation.
The gemara asks how the fellow prophets know the prophecy.
Abaye cites the verse that God reveals His secret to all prophets, so they know each other's prophecies.
The gemara objects that perhaps the prophecy was retracted, so the fellow prophets would not know the final status.
The gemara rejects the objection, stating that if a prophecy were retracted, all prophets would be informed.
The gemara objects citing Jonah, whose prophecy was retracted without informing him.
The gemara resolves that Jonah's prophecy was ambiguous from the start—'Nineveh will be overturned'—and he did not know if it meant for good or for evil.

items.text: How one knows to obey a prophet without a sign
items.text_en: How one knows to obey a prophet without a sign
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how one knows to obey a prophet who gives no sign, and answers that a prophet who is already established (מוחזק) is trusted. Examples of Micha, Abraham at Mount Moriah, and Elijah at Mount Carmel are given.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how one knows that one is punished for violating a prophet's words when no sign is given.
The Gemara answers that the prophet gives a sign.
The Gemara objects with the case of Micha, where no sign was given yet the man was punished.
The Gemara resolves that for an already established prophet (מוחזק) the rule is different.

items.text: After what event was Abraham tested?
items.text_en: After what event was Abraham tested?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what event preceded the binding of Isaac. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra explains it was after Satan's accusation that Abraham did not offer a sacrifice from the feast for Isaac.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what event preceded the binding of Isaac, citing the verse 'וַיְהִי אַחַר הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה' (And it came to pass after these things).

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra explains that the test followed Satan's accusation that Abraham did not offer a sacrifice from the feast for Isaac, leading God to command the binding of Isaac.

items.text: The dialogue between God and Abraham, and Satan's attempts
items.text_en: The dialogue between God and Abraham, and Satan's attempts
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba explains that 'na' is a request. The Gemara details God's gradual command to Abraham, and Satan's attempts to dissuade him, culminating in Satan's false claim that Isaac is not for the offering.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba explains that 'na' (נא) is a term of request, and provides a parable of a king asking his warrior to stand in a battle to prove the earlier battles were genuine, applied to God's request to Abraham.
The Gemara describes how God gradually revealed the command to Abraham, specifying 'your son', 'your only one', 'whom you love', and finally 'Isaac', to avoid overwhelming him.
Satan confronts Abraham on the way, quoting verses to dissuade him, but Abraham responds that he walks in his integrity.

sub.text: Satan's false claim and Abraham's response
sub.text_en: Satan's false claim and Abraham's response
sub.desc_en: Satan claims he heard from behind the curtain that the lamb is for the burnt offering, not Isaac, but Abraham rejects this, stating that a liar is not believed even when telling the truth.

items.text: Alternative explanation: after Ishmael's boast
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: after Ishmael's boast
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi says the test came after Ishmael boasted to Isaac about his circumcision at age thirteen, leading Isaac to offer himself entirely.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi explains that the binding of Isaac occurred after Ishmael boasted to Isaac about his circumcision at age thirteen, prompting Isaac to offer himself entirely.

items.text: The punishment for a prophet who incites idolatry
items.text_en: The punishment for a prophet who incites idolatry
items.desc_en: The Tannaim debate whether a prophet who incites idolatry is executed by stoning or strangulation. The Gemara derives the punishment through verbal analogy (הדחה הדחה) from the enticer (מסית) or from the prophet himself, and discusses the case of the inciters of an apostate city.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma rules that a prophet who incites idolatry is executed by stoning, while Rabbi Shimon says by strangulation.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning of the Rabbis regarding the prophet who incites.
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis derive the punishment via a verbal analogy (הדחה הדחה) from the enticer (מסית), who is stoned.
Rabbi Shimon argues that since the Torah mentions death without specification, it defaults to strangulation.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning of the Rabbis regarding the inciters of an apostate city.
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis derive the stoning for the inciters of an apostate city via a verbal analogy from either the enticer or the prophet who incites.
Rabbi Shimon derives the punishment for the inciters of an apostate city via a verbal analogy from the prophet who incites.

An objection is raised: why not derive from the enticer (מסית) instead? The Gemara counters that one derives a case of many enticers from many enticers, not from a single enticer, and that one derives a layperson from a layperson, not from a prophet.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon considers the prophet who incites as no different from a layperson, since once he incites, he is no better than any ordinary enticer.

items.text: Rav Chisda's statement
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda begins a statement that is cut off, likely continuing the discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda begins a statement that is cut off, likely continuing the discussion.

items.text: Initial clarification of the dispute
items.text_en: Initial clarification of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the earlier dispute (between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages) applies only to uprooting the entire body of idolatry, while for other mitzvot all agree the penalty is strangulation; for partial nullification of other mitzvot all agree one is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages applies only to uprooting the entire body of idolatry, while for other mitzvot all agree the penalty is strangulation, and for partial nullification of other mitzvot all agree one is exempt.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's objection
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna challenges the previous explanation by citing a verse that distinguishes between a positive and negative commandment, arguing that if the dispute is about idolatry, there is no positive commandment in idolatry to uproot. Rav Chisda resolves this by referring to the commandment to destroy idolatry.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna objects by citing a baraita that interprets the verse 'לָלֶכֶת בָּהּ' as referring to a positive commandment and a negative commandment, and questions how a positive commandment could apply to idolatry; Rav Chisda resolves that the positive commandment is 'וְנִתַּצְתֶּם' (you shall demolish).
Rav Chisda resolves the objection by interpreting the positive commandment as the commandment to destroy idolatry (ונתצתם).

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's alternative position
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's alternative position
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna asserts that the dispute applies to uprooting the entire body of both idolatry and other mitzvot, and to partial nullification of idolatry, but for partial nullification of other mitzvot all agree one is exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna offers his own explanation: the dispute applies to uprooting the entire body of idolatry and other mitzvot, and to partial nullification of idolatry, but for partial nullification of other mitzvot all agree one is exempt.

items.text: Baraita on the false prophet
items.text_en: Baraita on the false prophet
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one who prophesies to uproot a Torah law is liable; to partially nullify, Rabbi Shimon exempts; but for idolatry, even saying 'worship it today and nullify it tomorrow' all agree one is liable.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one who prophesies to uproot something from the Torah is liable; for partial nullification, Rabbi Shimon exempts; but for idolatry, even saying 'worship it today and nullify it tomorrow' makes all liable.

items.text: Reconciliation of the baraita with each position
items.text_en: Reconciliation of the baraita with each position
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava each reconcile the baraita according to their respective masters: Abaye follows Rav Chisda, Rava follows Rav Hamnuna. Each explains that the baraita's rulings align with their view, with the dispute only about partial nullification of other mitzvot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Abaye holds like Rav Chisda and Rava holds like Rav Hamnuna, and each explains the baraita accordingly.

Abaye explains the baraita according to Rav Chisda: abolishing a Torah matter is universally strangulation; partial nullification of other mitzvot is exempt for all; idol worship even temporarily is liable, with the death penalty differing per sage.

Rava explains the baraita according to Rav Hamnuna: abolishing any Torah matter (including idol worship) is liable; partial nullification of other mitzvot is exempt; idol worship even temporarily is liable, with the death penalty differing per sage.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's rule and Rabbi Yose HaGlili's support
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's rule and Rabbi Yose HaGlili's support
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one may listen to a prophet who says to violate Torah except for idolatry, even if he performs a miracle. Rabbi Yose HaGlili explains that the Torah gave special power to idolatry because it is so seductive. Rabbi Akiva adds that God would not perform a miracle for a false prophet.

sub.text: רבי אבהו (Rabbi Avahu) quoting רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan)
sub.text_en: רבי אבהו (Rabbi Avahu) quoting רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan)
sub.desc_en: רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) rules that one may heed a prophet who says to violate Torah except for idolatry, even if he performs a miracle.
רבי יוסי הגלילי (Rabbi Yose HaGlili) explains that the Torah gave special power to idolatry because it is so seductive, so even a miracle should not be heeded.

רבי עקיבא (Rabbi Akiva) adds that God would not perform a miracle for a false prophet; rather, the case is like חנניה בן עזור (Hananiah ben Azzur), who started as a true prophet and later became false.

items.text: Source for zomemei bat kohen
items.text_en: Source for zomemei bat kohen
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that false witnesses against a priest's daughter are executed by strangulation, not burning. Rabbi Yose derives from the verse 'as he conspired to do to his brother' that the punishment is like that of the accused, and since the priest's daughter is burned but her paramour is strangled, the witnesses are strangled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source that false witnesses against a priest's daughter are executed by strangulation rather than burning.

Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika cites a baraita where Rabbi Yose derives from the verse 'as he conspired to do to his brother' that the punishment of false witnesses matches that of the accused, and in all cases the witnesses and the paramour receive the same penalty.
The baraita notes that the priest's daughter is burned but her paramour is strangled, creating uncertainty whether the witnesses are likened to him or to her.
The baraita resolves the uncertainty by citing the verse 'to his brother' — the witnesses are likened to the paramour (brother), not to the priest's daughter (sister), so they are strangled.
The Gemara marks the conclusion of the chapter with the formula 'we return to you, These Are the Strangled Ones'.

items.text: Mishnah: Those with no share in the World to Come
items.text_en: Mishnah: Those with no share in the World to Come
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all Israel have a share in the World to Come, except for one who denies resurrection from the Torah, one who denies Torah from Heaven, and an Epicurean. Rabbi Akiva adds one who reads external books or whispers a healing verse; Abba Shaul adds one who pronounces the Tetragrammaton. Three kings and four commoners are also excluded, with a dispute about Menashe.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that all Israel have a share in the World to Come, except for three categories: one who denies resurrection from the Torah, one who denies Torah from Heaven, and an Epicurean.
רבי עקיבא (Rabbi Akiva) adds that one who reads external books or whispers a healing verse also has no share in the World to Come.
אבא שאול (Abba Shaul) adds that one who pronounces the ineffable name of God as it is written also has no share in the World to Come.
The Mishnah lists three kings (Jeroboam, Ahab, Manasseh) and four commoners who have no share in the World to Come.
רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) argues that Manasseh has a share in the World to Come, citing the verse that God restored him to his kingdom after his prayer.
The Sages respond to רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) that God restored Manasseh to his kingdom but not to life in the World to Come.
The Mishnah concludes by listing the four commoners: Balaam, Doeg, Ahithophel, and Gehazi.

items.text: Gemara: Measure for measure
items.text_en: Gemara: Measure for measure
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the one who denies resurrection has no share: because he denied it, he is punished measure for measure. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani cites a verse from Elisha to prove that all God's measures are measure for measure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the one who denies resurrection is punished so severely.
The Tanna answers that because he denied resurrection, he is punished measure for measure, as all God's measures are measure for measure.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan cites a verse from Elisha (II Kings 7:1-2) to prove that all God's measures are measure for measure.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding Elisha's curse
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding Elisha's curse
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the death of the officer was caused by Elisha's curse rather than by his disbelief in resurrection, and resolves that the verse specifies 'in the gate' to indicate it was about the gate (i.e., disbelief in the resurrection).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the officer's death was caused by Elisha's curse rather than by disbelief in resurrection, citing Rav Yehuda's principle that a sage's curse is effective even if undeserved.
The Gemara resolves that the verse specifies 'in the gate' to indicate the death was about the gate (i.e., disbelief in resurrection), not the curse.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's proof from terumah to Aaron
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's proof from terumah to Aaron
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan proves resurrection from the verse commanding terumah to be given to Aaron, implying Aaron will live again to receive it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives resurrection from the Torah: the verse commands giving תרומה (priestly portion) to Aaron, implying Aaron will live again to receive it.
The gemara objects that Aaron did not enter the Land of Israel to receive terumah.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves that the verse teaches Aaron will live again to receive terumah, proving resurrection from the Torah.

items.text: Derivation from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Derivation from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael interprets 'to Aaron' as meaning 'like Aaron' – just as Aaron was a scholar, so his sons must be scholars, implying a halakhic principle about terumah.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the word 'to Aaron' implies 'like Aaron' — just as Aaron was a חבר (scholar), so his sons must be scholars to receive תרומה.

items.text: Discussion on giving terumah to an ignorant priest
items.text_en: Discussion on giving terumah to an ignorant priest
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, Rabbi Acha bar Adda, Rabbi Yochanan, and the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov discuss the prohibition and danger of giving terumah to an ignorant priest, citing verses and analogies.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan asks for the scriptural source that one may not give תרומה (priestly portion) to an ignorant priest (עם הארץ), and cites a verse about strengthening Torah study.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Adda said Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Adda said Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Adda in the name of Rav Yehuda compares giving תרומה to an ignorant priest to giving it before a lion, since there is uncertainty whether the priest will eat it in a state of טהרה (ritual purity) or טומאה (impurity).
Rabbi Yochanan adds that giving תרומה to an ignorant priest causes the priest's death, citing the verse that those who profane the sacred offerings die.

sub.text: School of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: School of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov teaches that giving תרומה to an ignorant priest also causes him to incur guilt, as per the verse about causing others to bear guilt by eating sacred food.

items.text: Rabbi Simai's proof from the covenant with the patriarchs
items.text_en: Rabbi Simai's proof from the covenant with the patriarchs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Simai proves resurrection from the verse where God says 'I established My covenant with them' (the patriarchs), not 'with you', implying they will live to receive the land.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Simai derives resurrection from the verse 'I established My covenant with them to give them the land of Canaan' — using 'them' (לָהֶם) rather than 'you' (לָכֶם), implying the patriarchs will live to receive it.

items.text: Sadducees question Rabban Gamliel
items.text_en: Sadducees question Rabban Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Sadducees ask Rabban Gamliel for proof of resurrection. He brings proofs from Torah, Prophets, and Writings, but they reject each until he cites the verse 'which the Lord swore to give to them' (the patriarchs), which they accept.

sub.desc_en: The Sadducees ask Rabban Gamliel for a proof of resurrection from the Torah, and he offers proofs from Torah, Prophets, and Writings, but they reject each one.

sub.text: Rabban Gamliel's first proof from Torah
sub.text_en: Rabban Gamliel's first proof from Torah
sub.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel cites the verse 'הנך שוכב עם אבותיך וקם' (you will lie with your fathers and arise), but the Sadducees reject it, arguing the verse continues 'וקם העם הזה וזנה' (this people will arise and stray).

sub.text: Rabban Gamliel's second proof from Prophets
sub.text_en: Rabban Gamliel's second proof from Prophets
sub.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel cites the verse 'יחיו מתיך נבלתי יקומון' (your dead will live), but the Sadducees reject it, suggesting it refers to the dead Ezekiel revived.

sub.text: Rabban Gamliel's third proof from Writings
sub.text_en: Rabban Gamliel's third proof from Writings
sub.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel cites the verse 'דובב שפתי ישנים' (lips of sleepers murmur), but the Sadducees reject it, explaining it refers to the lips of the righteous moving in the grave when their teachings are cited, as per Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotsadak.

sub.text: Rabban Gamliel's final proof from Torah
sub.text_en: Rabban Gamliel's final proof from Torah
sub.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel finally cites the verse 'אשר נשבע ה' לאבותיכם לתת להם' (which the Lord swore to your ancestors to give to them), noting it says 'להם' (to them) not 'לכם' (to you), proving the patriarchs will receive the land in the resurrection, and the Sadducees accept this proof.

items.text: Alternative proof from 'And you who cling to the Lord'
items.text_en: Alternative proof from 'And you who cling to the Lord'
items.desc_en: Some say Rabban Gamliel cited the verse 'And you who cling to the Lord your God are all alive today', interpreting that even on a day when all die, they remain alive, implying resurrection.

sub.desc_en: An alternative tradition says Rabban Gamliel cited the verse 'you who cling to the Lord your God are all alive today,' interpreting 'today' as even on a day when all die, and applying it to the World to Come.

items.text: Romans question Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
items.text_en: Romans question Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
items.desc_en: Romans ask Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya for proof of resurrection and divine foreknowledge. He cites the verse 'Behold, you lie with your fathers and rise', and they accept at least the proof of foreknowledge.

sub.desc_en: The Romans ask Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya for a biblical source for resurrection and divine foreknowledge.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya answers that both are derived from the verse 'הִנְּךָ שֹׁכֵב עִם אֲבֹתֶיךָ וְקָם הָעָם הַזֶּה וְזָנָה' (Behold, you lie with your fathers and this people will rise and stray).
The Romans object that the verse might refer to the people rising to sin, not to resurrection.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya concedes that at least the proof of divine foreknowledge is accepted from the verse.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai supports that both resurrection and foreknowledge are derived from the same verse.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei refutes the Samaritans
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei refutes the Samaritans
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei proves resurrection from the verse 'that soul shall be cut off, its iniquity is upon it', arguing that 'cut off' refers to this world and 'its iniquity is upon it' to the next world. Rav Pappa questions why not use this verse, but the Samaritans claim the Torah speaks in human language.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei reports that he refuted the Samaritans by citing the verse 'הכרת תכרת הנפש ההיא עונה בה' (that soul shall be cut off, its iniquity is upon it), arguing that 'הכרת תכרת' refers to this world and 'עונה בה' to the next world, proving resurrection.

Rav Pappa asks Abaye why Rabbi Eliezer did not use both parts of the verse to prove resurrection, and the Samaritans respond that the Torah speaks in human language, so the repetition is not significant.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on 'hikaret tikaret'
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on 'hikaret tikaret'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael debate the meaning of 'hikaret tikaret': Rabbi Akiva sees it as referring to two worlds, while Rabbi Yishmael says the Torah speaks in human language. Both agree that 'its iniquity is upon it' excludes one who repented.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva interprets 'הִכָּרֵת תִּכָּרֵת' as referring to two worlds: 'הִכָּרֵת' in this world and 'תִּכָּרֵת' in the World to Come.
Rabbi Yishmael objects that the verse 'וְנִכְרְתָה' would imply three worlds, which is impossible.
Rabbi Yishmael explains that 'וְנִכְרְתָה' refers to this world, 'הִכָּרֵת' to the World to Come, and 'הִכָּרֵת תִּכָּרֵת' is merely the Torah speaking in human language.
Both Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael agree that 'עֲוֹנָהּ בָּהּ' excludes one who repented, as taught in a baraita.

items.text: Queen Cleopatra asks Rabbi Meir about the dead rising clothed
items.text_en: Queen Cleopatra asks Rabbi Meir about the dead rising clothed
items.desc_en: Queen Cleopatra asks Rabbi Meir whether the dead will rise naked or clothed. He answers with a kal vachomer from wheat, which is buried naked but emerges with many garments.

sub.text: Queen Cleopatra's question to Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Queen Cleopatra's question to Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Queen Cleopatra asks Rabbi Meir whether the resurrected dead will rise naked or clothed, citing the verse 'they will sprout like grass.'
Rabbi Meir answers with a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if wheat, buried naked, emerges with many garments, then the righteous, buried clothed, will certainly rise clothed.

items.text: Caesar questions Rabban Gamliel about dust coming to life
items.text_en: Caesar questions Rabban Gamliel about dust coming to life
items.desc_en: Caesar asks Rabban Gamliel how dust can come back to life, challenging the concept of resurrection.

sub.desc_en: Caesar asks Rabban Gamliel how the dead can live again if they have turned to dust, questioning whether dust can live.

items.text: The daughter's parable and the kal vachomer from glass vessels
items.text_en: The daughter's parable and the kal vachomer from glass vessels
