items.desc_en: The daughter of a heretic uses a parable about two potters to argue that if God can create from water, He can certainly create from dust, implying resurrection. The school of Rabbi Yishmael adds a kal vachomer from glass vessels: if human-made glass can be repaired, human bodies made by God can certainly be resurrected.

sub.desc_en: The heretic's daughter uses a parable about two potters to argue that if God can create from water, He can certainly create from dust, implying resurrection.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael adds a kal vachomer from glass vessels: if human-made glass can be repaired, human bodies made by God can certainly be resurrected.

items.text: Rabbi Ammi's parable of the palace and the snail
items.text_en: Rabbi Ammi's parable of the palace and the snail
items.desc_en: A heretic asks Rabbi Ammi how the dead can live if they are dust. Rabbi Ammi responds with a parable: a king's servants built a palace without water and earth, and when it fell, the king argued they could rebuild it where water and earth exist. He then gives examples of a mouse that becomes all flesh and a mountain that fills with snails after rain, showing that God can resurrect the dead.

sub.desc_en: A heretic challenges Rabbi Ammi: if the dead become dust, how can dust live again?
Rabbi Ammi responds with a parable of a king who commands building a palace without water and earth, then argues that rebuilding where those exist is even easier.
Rabbi Ammi provides two natural proofs: a mouse that becomes all flesh and a mountain that fills with snails after rain, showing God can resurrect the dead.

items.text: Geviha ben Pesisa's retort to the heretic
items.text_en: Geviha ben Pesisa's retort to the heretic
items.desc_en: A heretic mocks the idea of resurrection, arguing that if the living die, how can the dead live? Geviha ben Pesisa retorts that if those who never lived can be born, then those who lived can certainly be resurrected. The heretic threatens him, but Geviha offers to heal him for a fee.

sub.desc_en: The heretic mocks Geviha ben Pesisa, arguing that if the living die, how can the dead live?
Geviha retorts that if those who never lived can be born, then those who lived can certainly be resurrected.
The heretic threatens Geviha, saying he will kick him and straighten his hump.
Geviha offers to heal the heretic's hump for a fee, turning the threat into a business opportunity.

items.text: First dispute: The Canaanites' claim to the land
items.text_en: First dispute: The Canaanites' claim to the land
items.desc_en: The children of Africa claim the land of Israel because Canaan is their ancestor. Geviha ben Pesisa argues that Canaan was cursed to be a slave, and a slave's property belongs to his master (Israel). The Africans fail to respond and flee, leaving their fields.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the dispute: the Children of Africa claim the land of Canaan before Alexander of Macedon, citing the verse 'אֶרֶץ כְּנַעַן לִגְבֻלֹתֶיהָ' (the land of Canaan according to its borders) and arguing that Canaan is their ancestor.

sub.text: Geviha ben Pesisa to the Sages
sub.text_en: Geviha ben Pesisa to the Sages
sub.desc_en: Geviha ben Pesisa asks the Sages for permission to argue the case, proposing a strategy: if he loses, they can say 'you defeated our simplest member'; if he wins, they can say 'the Torah of Moses defeated you'.

Geviha ben Pesisa argues from the Torah that Canaan was cursed to be a slave (עֶבֶד עֲבָדִים), and a slave's property belongs to his master (Israel); moreover, the Africans have not served Israel for many years.
Alexander demands a response; the Africans ask for three days, fail to find an answer, and flee, abandoning their fields (which were sown and planted) during a שְׁבִיעִית (sabbatical year).

items.text: Second dispute: The Egyptians' claim for gold and silver
items.text_en: Second dispute: The Egyptians' claim for gold and silver
items.desc_en: The Egyptians demand the return of gold and silver taken by the Israelites. Geviha ben Pesisa counters by demanding wages for 430 years of slavery for 600,000 Israelites. The Egyptians fail to respond and flee.

sub.desc_en: The Egyptians come to court before Alexander of Macedon, citing the verse 'וַה׳ נָתַן אֶת חֵן הָעָם' to demand the return of gold and silver borrowed by the Israelites.
Geviha ben Pesisa asks the sages for permission to argue the case, with the condition that if he loses they say a commoner defeated them, and if he wins they say the Torah of Moses defeated them.

Geviha ben Pesisa counters the Egyptian claim by citing the verse 'וּמוֹשַׁב בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל... שְׁלֹשִׁים שָׁנָה וְאַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה' and demanding wages for 430 years of slavery for 600,000 Israelites.
Alexander gives the Egyptians three days to respond; they search for an answer, find none, and flee, abandoning their fields and vineyards during the seventh year.

items.text: Third dispute: The Ishmaelites' claim to the land
items.text_en: Third dispute: The Ishmaelites' claim to the land
items.desc_en: The children of Ishmael and Keturah claim the land of Israel as their inheritance. Geviha ben Pesisa argues that Abraham gave all his possessions to Isaac and sent away the sons of the concubines with gifts, implying they have no claim. Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba explains the gifts included the name of impurity.

sub.desc_en: The children of Ishmael and Keturah come to argue before Alexander of Macedon that the land of Canaan belongs to them equally, citing the genealogical verses of Ishmael and Isaac.

sub.text: Geviha ben Pesisa to the Sages
sub.text_en: Geviha ben Pesisa to the Sages
sub.desc_en: Geviha ben Pesisa asks the Sages for permission to argue the case, proposing that if he loses they can say a layman was defeated, but if he wins they can say the Torah of Moses prevailed.

sub.text: Geviha ben Pesisa to the Ishmaelites
sub.text_en: Geviha ben Pesisa to the Ishmaelites
sub.desc_en: Geviha ben Pesisa asks the Ishmaelites for their proof, then counters from the Torah that Abraham gave all his possessions to Isaac and sent away the sons of the concubines with gifts, implying they have no claim.
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba explains that the 'gifts' Abraham gave to the sons of the concubines were the name of impurity (sorcery or demonic power), not land.

items.text: Antoninus and Rabbi: The body and soul debate
items.text_en: Antoninus and Rabbi: The body and soul debate
items.desc_en: Antoninus asks Rabbi how body and soul can be judged together, as each blames the other for sin. Rabbi responds with a parable of a king who had a beautiful orchard with... (the text is cut off).

sub.desc_en: Antoninus asks Rabbi how body and soul can be judged together, since each blames the other for sin: the body claims the soul sinned because without it the body is inert, and the soul claims the body sinned because without it the soul flies free.
Rabbi responds with a parable of a king who had a beautiful orchard, beginning to illustrate how body and soul are jointly accountable.

items.text: Parable of the lame and blind guards
items.text_en: Parable of the lame and blind guards
items.desc_en: A parable about a lame and blind guard who together steal fruit, illustrating that God judges the soul and body as a single unit. The owner mounts the lame on the blind and judges them together, just as God brings the soul and body together for judgment.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a parable of a lame and blind guard who together steal fruit from an orchard.
The owner mounts the lame on the blind and judges them together, illustrating joint responsibility.
The gemara applies the parable: God brings soul and body together for judgment, citing the verse 'יִקְרָא אֶל הַשָּׁמַיִם מֵעָל וְאֶל הָאָרֶץ לָדִין עַמּוֹ'.

items.text: Antoninus asks about the sun's path
items.text_en: Antoninus asks about the sun's path
items.desc_en: Antoninus asks Rabbi why the sun rises in the east and sets in the west. Rabbi answers that it sets in the west to greet its Creator, as per the verse. Antoninus objects that it could greet halfway and then proceed, and the Gemara explains the reason is for workers and travelers.

sub.desc_en: Antoninus asks Rabbi why the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, clarifying that his real question is why it sets in the west.
Rabbi answers that the sun sets in the west to greet its Creator, citing the verse 'and the host of heaven bows to You'.
Antoninus objects that the sun could greet its Creator halfway across the sky and then continue on its way.
The Gemara explains that the sun sets in the west for the sake of workers and travelers, so they know when to stop work or journey.

items.text: When is the soul given?
items.text_en: When is the soul given?
items.desc_en: Antoninus asks whether the soul is given at the moment of conception or at formation. Rabbi initially says at formation, but Antoninus argues that meat without salt would rot in three days, so it must be at conception. Rabbi concedes and cites a supporting verse.

sub.desc_en: Antoninus asks Rabbi whether the soul is given at the moment of conception (פקידה) or at the moment of formation (יצירה).
Rabbi answers that the soul is given at the time of formation (יצירה).
Antoninus objects that a piece of meat without salt would rot in three days, so the soul must be given at conception (פקידה) to preserve the embryo.
Rabbi concedes that Antoninus taught him this, and cites a supporting verse (איוב י:יב) that the soul guards the body from the time of conception (פקידה).

items.text: When does the evil inclination rule?
items.text_en: When does the evil inclination rule?
items.desc_en: Antoninus asks whether the evil inclination rules from formation or from birth. Rabbi says from formation, but Antoninus argues that if so, the fetus would kick its mother and leave; it must be from birth. Rabbi agrees and cites a supporting verse.

sub.desc_en: Antoninus asks Rabbi whether the evil inclination (יצר הרע) rules from the time of formation (יצירה) or from the time of birth (יציאה).
Rabbi initially answers that the evil inclination rules from the time of formation.
Antoninus objects that if the evil inclination ruled from formation, the fetus would kick its mother's innards and leave the womb.
Antoninus concludes that the evil inclination must rule from the time of birth, not formation.
Rabbi acknowledges that Antoninus taught him this, and cites a supporting verse: 'לַפֶּתַח חַטָּאת רֹבֵץ' (sin crouches at the door).

items.text: Resolving contradictions about the future
items.text_en: Resolving contradictions about the future
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish, Ulla, Rav Chisda, and Rava each resolve apparent contradictions between verses about the state of the disabled, death, the moon's light, and God's actions. The resolutions distinguish between different eras (e.g., days of the Messiah vs. the World to Come) or groups (Israel vs. nations).

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish raises a contradiction between a verse describing the disabled in the future and a verse describing their healing.
Reish Lakish resolves that the disabled will stand with their defect and then be healed.
Ulla raises a contradiction between a verse promising the swallowing of death and a verse implying death will still occur.
Ulla resolves that the swallowing of death applies to Israel, while death for the nations continues, as they serve Israel.
Rav Chisda raises a contradiction between a verse describing the moon's shame and another describing its light becoming like the sun.
Rav Chisda resolves that the shame applies to the days of the Messiah, while the increased light applies to the World to Come.
The gemara objects that according to Shmuel, who says the only difference between this world and the days of the Messiah is subjugation to the nations, the distinction between eras is problematic.
The gemara resolves that the shame applies to the camp of the righteous, while the increased light applies to the camp of the Divine Presence.

items.text: Proof of resurrection from the Torah
items.text_en: Proof of resurrection from the Torah
items.desc_en: Rava resolves a contradiction between verses about God killing and reviving, showing that death and revival happen to the same person. The Tanna Kamma then derives from this that resurrection is from the Torah, refuting those who deny it.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises a contradiction between two verses: one says 'I kill and I revive' and the other says 'I have wounded and I will heal.'
God resolves the contradiction: the same person whom I kill I revive, and after that, the one I wounded I heal.
The Sages taught in a baraita: one might think that death and life apply to different people, but the verse 'I have wounded and I will heal' teaches that both happen to the same person.
The baraita concludes that from here there is a refutation to those who say resurrection of the dead is not derived from the Torah.

items.text: Additional proofs for resurrection
items.text_en: Additional proofs for resurrection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and Rabbi Yochanan each bring a verse with a future tense verb to prove resurrection from the Torah. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that one who praises God in this world will do so in the World to Come. Rabbi Yochanan adds that all prophets will sing together.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir cites a verse with a future tense verb ('יָשִׁיר') to prove resurrection from the Torah.
The Gemara objects that the same future tense verb ('יִבְנֶה') is used for Solomon building a high place for idolatry, which cannot imply resurrection.
The Gemara resolves that the verse treats Solomon's future act as if he had already built it, not as a proof for resurrection.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi cites a verse with a future tense verb ('יְהַלְלוּךָ') to prove resurrection from the Torah.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that one who praises God in this world will do so in the World to Come, citing the same verse.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan, transmitted by Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, cites a verse with a future tense verb ('יְרַנֵּנוּ') to prove resurrection from the Torah.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan adds that all prophets will sing together in the future, citing the same verse.

items.text: Withholding Torah from a student
items.text_en: Withholding Torah from a student
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda and Rav Chana bar Bizna teach that one who withholds a halacha from a student is like robbing him of his ancestral inheritance, and even fetuses curse him. The verse 'One who withholds grain' is cited.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that one who withholds a halacha from a student is like robbing him of his ancestral inheritance, citing the verse 'תּוֹרָה צִוָּה לָנוּ מֹשֶׁה מוֹרָשָׁה קְהִלַּת יַעֲקֹב' (the Torah that Moses commanded us is an inheritance of the congregation of Jacob).

sub.text: Rav Chana bar Bizna citing Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.text_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna citing Rabbi Shimon Chasida
sub.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Bizna in the name of Rabbi Shimon Chasida adds that one who withholds a halacha from a student is cursed even by fetuses in the womb, citing the verse 'מֹנֵעַ בָּר' (one who withholds grain).

items.text: Punishment for one who does not teach Torah
items.text_en: Punishment for one who does not teach Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'יִקְּבֻהוּ לְאוֹם' as a curse on those who do not teach Torah to others, with Ulla bar Yishmael explaining the punishment as being pierced like a sieve, citing a verse about a hole in a door.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'יִקְּבֻהוּ לְאוֹם' as a curse on those who do not teach Torah, defining each key term.
Ulla bar Yishmael explains that the punishment is being pierced like a sieve, and Abaye clarifies the metaphor.

items.text: Reward for teaching Torah
items.text_en: Reward for teaching Torah
items.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rav Sheshet states that one who teaches Torah is blessed like Joseph, and Rav Sheshet adds that such a person will teach Torah in the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what reward one receives for teaching Torah to another.

sub.text: Rava in the name of Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rava in the name of Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rav Sheshet answers that one who teaches Torah is blessed like Joseph, citing the verse 'וּבְרָכָה לְרֹאשׁ מַשְׁבִּיר' (a blessing on the head of the provider) and identifying 'מַשְׁבִּיר' (provider) with Joseph.
Rav Sheshet adds that one who teaches Torah in this world merits to teach it in the World to Come, citing the verse 'וּמַרְוֶה גַּם הוּא יוֹרֶה' (one who saturates will also teach).

items.text: Proofs for resurrection from the Torah
items.text_en: Proofs for resurrection from the Torah
items.desc_en: Rava, Ravina, and Rav Ashi each bring a verse to prove resurrection of the dead from the Torah, citing verses about Reuben, Daniel, and the resurrection of many.

sub.desc_en: Rava derives resurrection from the verse 'יְחִי רְאוּבֵן וְאַל יָמֹת', interpreting it as life in this world and the next.
Ravina cites a verse from Daniel about many awakening from the dust to eternal life or shame.
Rav Ashi cites a verse from Daniel about resting and standing for one's lot at the end of days.

items.text: Reward for a gentle leader
items.text_en: Reward for a gentle leader
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that a leader who guides the community gently will lead them in the World to Come, citing a verse about God leading with mercy.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that a leader who guides the community gently merits to lead them in the World to Come.

items.text: Greatness of knowledge and the Temple
items.text_en: Greatness of knowledge and the Temple
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar declares that knowledge (דעה) is great because it is placed between two letters of God's name, and similarly the Temple is great. Rav Adda Karḥina’a objects that revenge is also between two letters, but the Gemara resolves that both are true, one for good and one for punishment. Rabbi Elazar then says that a person with knowledge is as if the Temple is built in his days.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar declares that knowledge (דעה) is great because it is placed between two letters of God's name, citing the verse 'כי אל דעות ה׳'.
Rabbi Elazar declares that the Temple is great because it is placed between two letters of God's name, citing the verse 'פעלת ה׳ מקדש ה׳ כוננו ידיך'.
Rav Adda Karḥina’a objects that revenge (נקמה) is also placed between two letters of God's name, citing the verse 'אל נקמות ה׳ אל נקמות הופיע'.
The Gemara resolves that both are true, citing Ulla's teaching that the two appearances of 'הופיע' in the verse refer one to the attribute of good and one to the attribute of punishment.
Rabbi Elazar concludes that a person with knowledge (דעה) is as if the Temple is built in his days, because both are placed between two letters of God's name.

items.text: Sayings of Rabbi Elazar on knowledge and related topics
items.text_en: Sayings of Rabbi Elazar on knowledge and related topics
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar delivers a series of sayings: a person with knowledge becomes wealthy; one without knowledge should not be pitied; feeding such a person brings suffering; one without knowledge will be exiled; a house without Torah at night is consumed by fire; one who does not benefit Torah scholars sees no blessing; one who does not leave bread on the table sees no blessing (with a resolution about leaving whole bread); changing one's speech is like idolatry; looking at nakedness weakens one's bow; and one should always be humble, supported by a mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that a person with knowledge (דֵּעָה) will ultimately become wealthy, citing a verse.
Rabbi Elazar says that one without knowledge (דֵּעָה) is forbidden to be pitied, citing a verse.
Rabbi Elazar says that feeding someone without knowledge (דֵּעָה) brings suffering upon the giver, citing a verse.
Rabbi Elazar says that one without knowledge (דֵּעָה) will ultimately be exiled, citing a verse.
Rabbi Elazar says that a house where Torah is not heard at night will be consumed by fire, citing a verse.
Rabbi Elazar says that one who does not benefit Torah scholars from his property will never see a sign of blessing, citing a verse.
Rabbi Elazar says that one who does not leave bread on his table will never see a sign of blessing, citing a verse.
The Gemara objects: Rabbi Elazar himself said that leaving crumbs on the table is like idolatry, citing a verse.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: leaving bread is praiseworthy when there is a whole loaf alongside, but forbidden when there is no whole loaf.
Rabbi Elazar says that one who changes his speech is like an idolater, citing a verse.
Rabbi Elazar says that one who looks at nakedness has his bow weakened, citing a verse.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar's tenth saying and Rabbi Zeira's support
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's tenth saying and Rabbi Zeira's support
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says one should always be humble and submissive; Rabbi Zeira supports this from a mishnah about a dark house and leprosy signs.

items.text: Proof of resurrection from the womb and the grave
items.text_en: Proof of resurrection from the womb and the grave
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tavi in the name of Rabbi Yoshiya compares the womb and the grave: as the womb takes in and brings out, so does the grave. A kal vachomer argument shows that if birth involves noise, resurrection will involve even greater noise, refuting those who deny resurrection. The Tanna debe Eliyahu adds that the righteous will not return to dust.

sub.text: Rabbi Tavi in the name of Rabbi Yoshiya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Tavi in the name of Rabbi Yoshiya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tavi in the name of Rabbi Yoshiya asks about the verse comparing Sheol and the womb, and answers that just as the womb takes in and brings out, so does the grave.

The gemara presents a kal vachomer argument: if the womb, which receives silently, brings forth with great noise, then the grave, which receives with noise, will certainly bring forth with great noise, refuting those who deny resurrection from the Torah.
The Tanna debe Eliyahu adds that the righteous whom the Holy One will resurrect will not return to dust, as a verse compares them to the holy and eternal.

items.text: The righteous in the future world
items.text_en: The righteous in the future world
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers what the righteous will do during the years when God renews the world, suggesting they will have wings like eagles and fly over water, with no pain, as per verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the righteous will do during the years when God renews the world.
The Gemara answers that God will give them wings like eagles to fly over water without pain, citing verses.

items.text: Rejecting proof from Ezekiel's revival
items.text_en: Rejecting proof from Ezekiel's revival
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests learning from the dead Ezekiel revived, but rejects it because the opinion holds it was only a parable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether we can learn from the dead that Ezekiel revived as a proof for the righteous having wings.
The Gemara rejects the proof because the opinion holds that Ezekiel's revival was only a parable, not a literal event.

items.text: Debate on the nature of Ezekiel's dead
items.text_en: Debate on the nature of Ezekiel's dead
items.desc_en: A baraita records disputes: Rabbi Eliezer says they stood, sang, and died; Rabbi Yehoshua says they sang a different song; Rabbi Yehuda says it was a true parable. Rabbi Nehemya questions the phrase 'true parable', and Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGlili says they married and had children, with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira claiming descent from them.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that the dead revived by Ezekiel stood, sang a song, and died again.
Rabbi Yehoshua gives a different version of the song they sang.
Rabbi Yehuda states that the event was a true parable.
Rabbi Nehemya objects to the phrase 'true parable', arguing that if it is true it is not a parable, and if a parable it is not true, and concludes it was a true parable.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGlili
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGlili
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGlili says the revived dead went to the Land of Israel, married, and had children.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira stands and testifies that he is a descendant of those people, showing tefillin (תפילין) handed down from them.

items.text: Identifications of the dead Ezekiel revived
items.text_en: Identifications of the dead Ezekiel revived
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who the dead were, and various Amoraim offer identifications: Rav says they were the tribe of Ephraim who miscalculated the redemption; Shmuel says they were those who denied resurrection; Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba says they were people without moisture of mitzvot; Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha says they were those who defiled the Temple; Rabbi Yochanan says they were the dead in the valley of Dura, explaining the context of Nebuchadnezzar's persecution.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the identity of the dead whom Ezekiel revived.
Rav identifies them as the tribe of Ephraim who miscalculated the redemption and were killed.
Shmuel identifies them as those who denied the resurrection of the dead.
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba identifies them as people lacking the moisture of mitzvot (commandments).
Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha identifies them as those who defiled the Temple with abominations.
Rabbi Yochanan identifies them as the dead in the valley of Dura, explaining the context of Nebuchadnezzar's persecution.

items.text: The revival and Nebuchadnezzar's reaction
items.text_en: The revival and Nebuchadnezzar's reaction
items.desc_en: The rabbis taught that when Nebuchadnezzar cast Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah into the furnace, God told Ezekiel to revive the dead in the valley of Dura. The revived dead slapped the wicked king, who then praised God.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts that when Nebuchadnezzar cast Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah into the furnace, God commanded Ezekiel to revive the dead in the valley of Dura; the revived dead slapped the wicked king, who then praised God.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's comment on Nebuchadnezzar
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's comment on Nebuchadnezzar
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak says that molten gold should have been poured into the wicked king's mouth, because had an angel not struck him, he would have disparaged all of David's songs in Psalms.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak declares that molten gold should have been poured into Nebuchadnezzar's mouth, because had an angel not struck him, he would have disparaged all of David's songs in Psalms.

items.text: Six miracles of that day
items.text_en: Six miracles of that day
items.desc_en: The rabbis taught that six miracles occurred that day: the furnace floated, was breached, the secret was melted, the idol's face was turned, four kingdoms were burned, and Ezekiel revived the dead. The Gemara notes that all are from tradition except the four kingdoms, which is from a verse listing Nebuchadnezzar's officials.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists six miracles that occurred on that day: the furnace floated, was breached, the secret was melted, the idol's face was turned, four kingdoms were burned, and Ezekiel revived the dead in the Dura valley.
The Gemara notes that all six miracles are known from tradition (גמרא), except the burning of the four kingdoms, which is derived from a verse listing Nebuchadnezzar's officials.

items.text: Lesson on maintaining dignity in danger
items.text_en: Lesson on maintaining dignity in danger
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov teaches that even in danger one should not change from his rabbinic dignity, as shown by the verse describing the men in their cloaks. Rabbi Yochanan begins a statement that is cut off.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov teaches that even in danger one should not change from his rabbinic dignity, citing the verse about the men in their cloaks.
Rabbi Yochanan begins a statement that is cut off at the end of the daf.

items.text: Opening statement: The greatness of the righteous
items.text_en: Opening statement: The greatness of the righteous
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the righteous are greater than the ministering angels, citing the verse where Nebuchadnezzar sees four men walking in the fire, with the fourth resembling a divine being.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the righteous are greater than the ministering angels, citing the verse where Nebuchadnezzar sees four men walking in the fire, with the fourth resembling a divine being.

items.text: Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai's teaching
items.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai's teaching
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai describes how when Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah emerged from the furnace, the nations of the world taunted Israel, and the three responded with a verse acknowledging God's righteousness and their shame.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai recounts that when Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah emerged from the furnace, the nations taunted Israel, and Israel responded with a verse acknowledging God's righteousness and their own shame.

items.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
items.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quotes Rabbi Yonatan interpreting the verse about ascending a palm tree: Israel is the palm, but only one cluster (sansin) of Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah was achieved.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan interprets the verse 'I said I will climb the palm tree' as referring to Israel, but only one cluster (Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah) was achieved.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation of Zechariah's vision
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation of Zechariah's vision
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets the vision of a man on a red horse: God sought to turn the world to night and blood, but upon seeing Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah (the myrtles in the deep), His mind was calmed. Rabbi Pappa adds that a white horse is good for dreams.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan opens by citing the verse from Zechariah and interprets the vision: God sought to turn the world to night and blood.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that when God saw Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah (the myrtles in the deep), His anger was calmed and the red horses became white.
Rabbi Pappa derives from this that seeing a white horse in a dream is auspicious.

items.text: Debate on the fate of Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah
items.text_en: Debate on the fate of Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks where Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah went after the furnace. Rav says they died from the evil eye, Shmuel says they drowned in spittle, and Rabbi Yochanan says they went to Eretz Yisrael and had children. This is then presented as a Tannaitic dispute with Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yehoshua, and the Sages, who cite a verse about men of wonder.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah went after being saved from the furnace.
Rav answers that they died from the evil eye (עַיִן הָרָע).
Shmuel answers that they drowned in spittle (רוֹק).
Rabbi Yochanan answers that they went to Eretz Yisrael, married, and had children.
The Gemara presents a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says they died from the evil eye.
Rabbi Yehoshua says they drowned in spittle.
The Sages say they went to Eretz Yisrael, married, and had children, citing a verse about 'men of wonder' (אַנְשֵׁי מוֹפֵת).

items.text: Debate on Daniel's whereabouts
items.text_en: Debate on Daniel's whereabouts
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks where Daniel went. Rav says to supply the great river in Tiberias, Shmuel says to bring seed for the seeder, and Rabbi Yochanan says to bring pigs from Alexandria of Egypt. The Gemara objects based on a baraita about pigs from Alexandria, and resolves that he brought small ones without their mothers' knowledge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where Daniel went, presenting three opinions: Rav says to supply fish to Tiberias, Shmuel says to bring seeds for asparagus, and Rabbi Yochanan says to bring pigs from Alexandria, but the Gemara objects with a baraita about pigs being castrated, and resolves that he brought small pigs without their knowledge.
Rav says Daniel went to supply the great river in Tiberias.
Shmuel says Daniel went to bring seed for the seeder.
Rabbi Yochanan says Daniel went to bring pigs from Alexandria of Egypt.
The Gemara objects based on a baraita from Todros the doctor that no pig leaves Alexandria without having its womb cut to prevent reproduction.
The Gemara resolves that Daniel brought small pigs without their mothers' knowledge, circumventing the restriction.

items.text: The three-way counsel regarding Daniel's absence
items.text_en: The three-way counsel regarding Daniel's absence
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that three parties were involved in Daniel's absence from the furnace: God wanted Daniel gone so they wouldn't say he was saved by his merit; Daniel wanted to leave to avoid the verse about burning idols; Nebuchadnezzar wanted Daniel gone so they wouldn't say he burned his God. The Gemara proves that Nebuchadnezzar bowed to Daniel.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces that three parties—God, Daniel, and Nebuchadnezzar—were involved in the counsel regarding Daniel's absence from the furnace, with God wanting Daniel gone so they wouldn't say he was saved by his merit.
Daniel wanted to leave to avoid the fulfillment of the verse 'You shall burn the idols of their gods with fire'.
Nebuchadnezzar wanted Daniel gone so they wouldn't say he burned his God, and the Gemara proves from a verse that Nebuchadnezzar bowed to Daniel.

items.text: The fate of Ahab and Zedekiah
items.text_en: The fate of Ahab and Zedekiah
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the false prophets Ahab and Zedekiah, who were roasted by the king of Babylon. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai teaches that they were made like roasted grain (kaluyot).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses about Ahab and Zedekiah, and Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai explains that the word 'קָלָם' (roasted) indicates they were made like roasted grains.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai teaches that the verse 'קָלָם' (roasted them) indicates they were made like roasted grain (קליות).

items.text: The sin and punishment of Ahab and Zedekiah
items.text_en: The sin and punishment of Ahab and Zedekiah
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Ahab and Zedekiah committed adultery with Nebuchadnezzar's daughter, each claiming a prophecy. She reported to her father, who tested them by throwing them into the fire along with Joshua the High Priest. The wicked were burned, but Joshua was only singed because he was alone among the wicked, who had permission to burn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse condemning Ahab and Zedekiah for adultery.
The Gemara asks what exactly they did.
The Gemara recounts that Ahab and Zedekiah went to Nebuchadnezzar's daughter, each claiming a prophecy, and she reported to her father, who noted that their God hates lewdness.
The Gemara continues: Nebuchadnezzar summoned them, they claimed prophecy, and he decided to test them by fire like Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.
Ahab and Zedekiah requested Joshua the High Priest join them, hoping his merit would protect them.
They were thrown into the fire: the wicked were burned, but Joshua was only singed, as per the verses.
The Gemara explains that Joshua was singed because he was alone among the wicked, who had permission to burn, as per the proverb: dry twigs burn the moist one.

items.text: Why Joshua was punished
items.text_en: Why Joshua was punished
items.desc_en: Rabbi Pappa explains that Joshua was punished because his sons married women unfit for the priesthood and he did not protest, as indicated by the verse about his filthy garments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Joshua was punished, and Rav Papa answers that his sons married women unfit for the priesthood and he did not protest, citing the verse about Joshua wearing filthy garments.
Rabbi Pappa answers that Joshua was punished because his sons married women unfit for the priesthood and he did not protest.

items.text: Bar Kappara's teaching on Boaz's gift
items.text_en: Bar Kappara's teaching on Boaz's gift
items.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum reports that Bar Kappara taught in Tzippori about the verse 'six barley' given by Boaz, questioning whether it was literal barley or something else.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum reports that Bar Kappara in Tzippori asked about the verse 'six barley', questioning whether Boaz would give such a small gift, leaving the interpretation incomplete.

items.text: The six se'ah and the hint of six sons
items.text_en: The six se'ah and the hint of six sons
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a woman could take six se'ah, explaining that it was a hint that six sons would come from her, blessed with six blessings: David, Messiah, Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a woman could take six se'ah, implying it is an unusual amount.
The Gemara explains that the six se'ah were a hint that six sons blessed with six blessings would come from her: David, Messiah, Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah.

items.text: David's qualities and Doeg's evil speech
items.text_en: David's qualities and Doeg's evil speech
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about David and explains that Doeg spoke it in evil speech, interpreting each phrase as a Torah-related quality. It then notes that Jonathan said his son was like David in all but the phrase 'God is with him,' which caused Saul's jealousy, and identifies Doeg as the speaker.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about David, listing his qualities as described by the young man.
Rav Yehuda said Rav explains that Doeg spoke the entire verse in לשון הרע (evil speech), interpreting each phrase as a Torah-related quality.
The Gemara notes that Jonathan said his son was like David in all qualities except 'God is with him,' which caused Saul's jealousy, citing verses about Saul and David.
The Gemara identifies Doeg as the speaker by linking the term 'one of the young men' to the verse about Doeg the Edomite.

items.text: The Messiah's qualities and Bar Koziba
items.text_en: The Messiah's qualities and Bar Koziba
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses about the Messiah, with Rabbi Alexandri explaining that he is laden with mitzvot and suffering like millstones, and Rava explaining that he smells and judges. It then recounts that Bar Koziba claimed to be the Messiah, but when the rabbis saw he could not smell and judge, they killed him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses about the Messiah, including the spirit of wisdom and understanding resting upon him and his ability to smell with the fear of God.
Rabbi Alexandri explains that the verse teaches that the Messiah is laden with מצות (commandments) and suffering like millstones.
Rava states that the Messiah smells and judges, citing the verse that he does not judge by sight but judges the poor with righteousness.
The Gemara recounts that Bar Koziba ruled for two and a half years and claimed to the rabbis that he was the Messiah.
The rabbis object that the Messiah is described as smelling and judging, so they propose to test whether Bar Koziba can do so.
When they saw that Bar Koziba could not smell and judge, they killed him, resolving the test negatively.

items.text: Daniel and his companions' virtues
items.text_en: Daniel and his companions' virtues
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse describing Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, and explains that they had no blemish, even a minor one, and that they restrained themselves from laughter, conversation, and sleep, and stood when needing to relieve themselves out of fear of the king.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse describing Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah as having no blemish, good appearance, and wisdom.
The Gemara asks what the phrase 'who had no blemish' means in this context.
Rabbi Chama bar Chananya explains that they had no blemish, not even a minor one like a wart.
The Gemara asks what the phrase 'who had strength to stand in the king's palace' means.

sub.text: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina's answer
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina explains that they restrained themselves from laughter, conversation, and sleep, and stood when needing to relieve themselves out of fear of the king.

items.text: Tribal origins of Daniel and his companions
items.text_en: Tribal origins of Daniel and his companions
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates whether all four were from the tribe of Judah or only Daniel, with Rabbi Eliezer saying all were from Judah and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani saying Daniel was from Judah and the others from other tribes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse listing Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah as being from the tribe of Judah.
Rabbi Eliezer states that all four were from the tribe of Judah.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani argues that only Daniel was from Judah, while the others were from other tribes.

items.text: The meaning of 'sarisim' and its implications
items.text_en: The meaning of 'sarisim' and its implications
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates whether 'sarisim' means literal eunuchs or that idolatry was castrated in their days. It reconciles the verse 'no injury' with both views, and discusses the verse about eunuchs in Isaiah, concluding that both conditions applied to them.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the verse and asks what "סָרִיסִים" (eunuchs) means here.
Rav holds that "סָרִיסִים" means literal eunuchs.
Rabbi Chanina holds that it means idolatry was castrated (defeated) in their days.
The gemara notes that according to Rabbi Chanina, the verse "וַחֲבָל לָא אִיתַי בְּהוֹן" (no injury was found in them) fits perfectly, referring to idolatry's defeat.

The gemara objects: according to Rav, what does "וַחֲבָל לָא אִיתַי בְּהוֹן" (no injury) refer to? It answers that it means no injury from fire, as another verse already says no smell of fire clung to them, implying both no harm and no smoke smell.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis for Rabbi Chanina (second verse)
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis for Rabbi Chanina (second verse)
sub.desc_en: The gemara points out that for Rabbi Chanina, the verse in Isaiah that addresses eunuchs (סָרִיסִים) who keep Shabbat makes sense, referring to these righteous men.

The gemara objects: according to Rav, would Scripture speak disparagingly of righteous people (as literal eunuchs)? The gemara resolves: both conditions applied to them — they were literal eunuchs and idolatry was defeated in their days.

The gemara notes that for Rav, the verse "יָד וָשֵׁם טוֹב מִבָּנִים וּמִבָּנוֹת" (a hand and a name better than sons and daughters) fits perfectly, as literal eunuchs could not have biological children.

sub.text: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Chanina (Isaiah verse)
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection to Rabbi Chanina (Isaiah verse)
sub.desc_en: The gemara objects: according to Rabbi Chanina, what does "טוֹב מִבָּנִים וּמִבָּנוֹת" (better than sons and daughters) mean? Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers: it means better than the sons they already had who died.

sub.text: Rabbi Tanchum in the name of Bar Kappara
sub.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum in the name of Bar Kappara
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum, citing Bar Kappara, explains that "שֵׁם עוֹלָם" (eternal name) refers to the Book of Daniel, which is named after him.

items.text: Why Nehemiah's book is not named after him
items.text_en: Why Nehemiah's book is not named after him
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the book of Nehemiah is not named after him: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba says because he took credit for himself, and Rav Yosef says because he spoke disparagingly of earlier leaders. It then proves Daniel was greater than Nehemiah, identifying the men with him as Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the book of Nehemiah is not named after him, given that all the words of Ezra were actually spoken by Nehemiah.

Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba answers that Nehemiah's book is not named after him because he took credit for himself, as he said 'זׇכְרָה לִּי אֱלֹהַי לְטוֹבָה' (Remember me, my God, for good), and the Gemara deflects a potential objection from David's similar request.
Rav Yosef offers an alternative reason: Nehemiah's book is not named after him because he spoke disparagingly of earlier leaders, and even spoke ill of Daniel who was greater than him.
The Gemara proves that Daniel was greater than Nehemiah by citing the verse where Daniel alone saw the vision while the men with him did not.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya / Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya / Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya (or alternatively Rabbi Chiya bar Abba) identifies the men who were with Daniel as Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.

items.text: The vision of the prophets and the mazal
items.text_en: The vision of the prophets and the mazal
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the prophets who sought to see the divine chariot were greater than Hezekiah in prophecy, but Hezekiah saw what they did not. Ravina deduces that even if a person does not see a frightening vision, their mazal sees it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the prophets were greater than Hezekiah because they were prophets, but Hezekiah was greater because he saw what they did not.
The Gemara asks: since they did not see, why did they seek the vision?
The Gemara answers that even though they did not see, their mazal (constellation) saw.
Ravina deduces that one who is frightened, even if he does not see, his mazal sees.

items.text: Remedy for fright
items.text_en: Remedy for fright
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides remedies for one who is frightened: moving four cubits from one's place, reciting the Shema, or saying a specific phrase if in a filthy place.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the remedy is for one who is frightened.
One remedy is to move four cubits from one's place.
Another remedy is to recite the Shema.
If one is in a filthy place, the remedy is to say a specific phrase about a fat goat from the butcher's house.

items.text: Why the mem in למרבה is closed: Hezekiah as Messiah
items.text_en: Why the mem in למרבה is closed: Hezekiah as Messiah
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara explains that the closed mem in למרבה indicates that God wanted to make Hezekiah the Messiah and Sennacherib Gog and Magog, but the Attribute of Justice objected because David sang many songs while Hezekiah did not. The earth then sang a song on Hezekiah's behalf, and the Prince of the World asked for his will to be fulfilled. A bat kol responded with a cryptic verse, and Rava or Rabbi Yitzchak explained that this refers to successive betrayals.

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara asks why the mem in למרבה is closed, unlike all other medial mems.

Bar Kappara explains that God wanted to make Hezekiah the Messiah and Sennacherib Gog and Magog, but the Attribute of Justice objected because David sang many songs while Hezekiah did not, so the mem was closed.
The earth sang a song on Hezekiah's behalf, citing the verse 'מכנף הארץ זמירות שמענו צבי לצדיק'.

sub.text: Prince of the World and Bat Kol
sub.text_en: Prince of the World and Bat Kol
sub.desc_en: The Prince of the World asked for Hezekiah's will to be fulfilled, a bat kol responded with a cryptic verse, and Rava or Rabbi Yitzchak explained that this refers to successive betrayals until the end.

items.text: The angel Dumah and the spirits
items.text_en: The angel Dumah and the spirits
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan identifies the angel in charge of spirits as Dumah. All the spirits gathered and asked him about the night, and he responded with a verse from Isaiah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan identifies the angel in charge of the spirits as Dumah.
All the spirits gather before Dumah and ask him about the night, quoting the verse from Isaiah.
Dumah responds with the continuation of the verse, indicating that morning comes and then night, and urging them to return.

items.text: The disgrace of Hezekiah and his generation, and of Moses and Israel
items.text_en: The disgrace of Hezekiah and his generation, and of Moses and Israel
items.desc_en: A Tanna in the name of Rabbi Pappias states that it was a disgrace for Hezekiah and his army that they did not sing until the earth sang. Similarly, it was a disgrace for Moses and the 600,000 that they did not say 'Baruch' until Jethro did.

sub.text: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Pappias
sub.text_en: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Pappias
sub.desc_en: A Tanna in the name of Rabbi Pappias states that it was a disgrace for Hezekiah and his army that they did not sing until the earth sang, and similarly for Moses and the 600,000 that they did not say 'Baruch' until Jethro did.

items.text: The meaning of ויחד יתרו
items.text_en: The meaning of ויחד יתרו
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate the meaning of ויחד: Rav says he passed a sharp sword over his flesh (circumcision), Shmuel says his flesh became prickly. Rav then cites a folk saying about not disparaging a convert before an Aramean.

sub.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate the meaning of ויחד: Rav says he passed a sharp sword over his flesh (circumcision), Shmuel says his flesh became prickly.
Rav cites a folk saying about not disparaging a convert before an Aramean, supporting his interpretation that Jethro underwent circumcision.

items.text: The eight names of Hezekiah and Sennacherib
items.text_en: The eight names of Hezekiah and Sennacherib
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that God sent 'razon' against Sennacherib's fat ones, meaning that Hezekiah, who has eight names, would take revenge on Sennacherib, who also has eight names. The names are listed and explained.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that God sent 'razon' against Sennacherib's fat ones, meaning Hezekiah, who has eight names, would take revenge on Sennacherib, who also has eight names.
The Gemara lists Hezekiah's eight names from the verse 'Pele Yoetz El Gibor Avi Ad Sar Shalom' and explains the name 'Hezekiah' as 'God strengthened him' or 'he strengthened Israel.'
The Gemara lists Sennacherib's eight names (Tiglath-Pileser, Pul, etc.) and explains the name 'Sennacherib' as 'his conversation is strife' or 'he spoke and blasphemed things upward.'

items.text: Why Sennacherib was called great and honorable
items.text_en: Why Sennacherib was called great and honorable
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Sennacherib was called 'great and honorable' because he did not disparage the land of Israel, saying he would take them to a land like theirs. Rav and Shmuel debate whether he was clever or foolish. The Gemara then discusses where he exiled the ten tribes and contrasts with Israel who disparaged the land.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Sennacherib was called 'great and honorable' because he did not disparage the land of Israel, saying he would take them to a land like theirs.
The Gemara reports a debate between Rav and Shmuel whether Sennacherib was clever or foolish, and explains each position.
The Gemara discusses where Sennacherib exiled the ten tribes and contrasts with Israel who disparaged the land.

items.text: The meaning of 'under His glory'
items.text_en: The meaning of 'under His glory'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar debate whether 'under His glory' means not His actual glory (like Rabbi Yochanan calling his garments 'my honors') or His actual glory, like the burning of Aaron's sons where the soul burned but the body remained.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse 'תַּחַת כְּבֹדוֹ יֵקַד' to mean 'under His glory' but not His actual glory, comparing it to his own practice of calling his garments 'my honors'.
Rabbi Elazar argues that 'under His glory' means His actual glory, analogous to the burning of Aaron's sons where the soul burned but the body remained intact.

items.text: Contrast between Pharaoh and Sennacherib's punishment
items.text_en: Contrast between Pharaoh and Sennacherib's punishment
items.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts Pharaoh, who denied God directly, and was punished directly by God, with Sennacherib, who blasphemed through messengers, and was punished through an angel.

items.text: Sennacherib's arrogant plan
items.text_en: Sennacherib's arrogant plan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa notes a contradiction in verses about Sennacherib's 'height' and 'lodging,' explaining that the wicked king planned to first destroy the earthly dwelling (the Temple) and then the heavenly one.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa notes a contradiction between the verses 'מְרוֹם קִצּוֹ' (height of his branch) and 'מְלוֹן קִצּוֹ' (lodging of his branch), and explains that Sennacherib planned to first destroy the earthly dwelling (the Temple) and then the heavenly one.

items.text: The prophet's message and its Aramaic translation
items.text_en: The prophet's message and its Aramaic translation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains the verse where Sennacherib claims God sent him, citing the prophet's rebuke of Israel for rejecting the gentle waters of Shiloah. Rav Yosef then provides the Aramaic translation of that verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asks about the meaning of the verse where Sennacherib claims God sent him to destroy Jerusalem.
He explains that Sennacherib heard the prophet's rebuke of Israel for rejecting the gentle waters of Shiloah and rejoicing in Rezin and Pekah ben Remaliah.
Rav Yosef provides the Aramaic translation of the verse, clarifying that the people rejected the gentle kingdom of the House of David and rejoiced in Rezin and Pekah ben Remaliah.

items.text: Pekach ben Remalyahu and Hezekiah contrasted
items.text_en: Pekach ben Remalyahu and Hezekiah contrasted
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets a verse: 'The curse of God in the house of the wicked' refers to Pekach ben Remalyahu, who ate extravagantly, while 'the dwelling of the righteous He blesses' refers to Hezekiah, who ate modestly.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse: 'The curse of God in the house of the wicked' refers to Pekach ben Remalyahu, who ate extravagantly, while 'the dwelling of the righteous He blesses' refers to Hezekiah, who ate modestly.

items.text: Why Sennacherib was punished and the merit of Torah study
items.text_en: Why Sennacherib was punished and the merit of Torah study
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Sennacherib was punished, explaining that the prophet's message was only for the ten tribes, but Sennacherib applied it to all of Jerusalem. Rabbi Elazar bar Berechya then interprets a verse about those who lighten or burden the yoke of Torah, and the potential for a miracle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about Sennacherib's invasion and questions why he was punished, since he acted as God's agent.
The Gemara explains that the prophet's message was only for the ten tribes, but Sennacherib applied it to all of Jerusalem, exceeding his mandate.
Rabbi Elazar bar Berechya interprets a verse to mean that a people weary with Torah study is not handed over to one who oppresses them.
The Gemara interprets the verse about the first and later times as referring to those who lightened or burdened the yoke of Torah, and the potential for a miracle if they repent.

items.text: The oath and God's plan for Sennacherib
items.text_en: The oath and God's plan for Sennacherib
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what event preceded Sennacherib's invasion. Ravina explains that God swore to bring Sennacherib to Hezekiah, but Hezekiah refused, so God swore to bring him anyway, making him a 'feeding trough' for Hezekiah and his party.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what event preceded Sennacherib's invasion, noting the verse 'After these things and this truth, Sennacherib came' and questioning the connection.
Ravina explains that after God swore to bring Sennacherib to Hezekiah, Hezekiah refused, saying he wanted neither Sennacherib nor his terror.
Rabbi Yochanan concludes that God swore to bring Sennacherib and his party to serve as a 'feeding trough' (אֵבוּס) for Hezekiah and his party.

items.text: Hezekiah's Torah devotion and the resulting abundance
items.text_en: Hezekiah's Torah devotion and the resulting abundance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha explains that Sennacherib's yoke was broken due to Hezekiah's oil (light) in synagogues. Hezekiah's decree of Torah study led to universal scholarship, and the verse describes the resulting agricultural abundance despite the siege.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha explains that the yoke of Sennacherib was broken because of Hezekiah's oil (שמן) that burned in synagogues and study halls.

The gemara describes Hezekiah's drastic decree: he planted a sword at the study hall entrance, compelling Torah study, resulting in universal scholarship from Dan to Beersheba and from Gevat to Antipatras.
The gemara cites verses (Isaiah 7:21, 7:23) to show that despite the siege, the land would produce abundant crops, indicating divine blessing for that generation's Torah devotion.

items.text: The distribution of spoils and the purification of property
items.text_en: The distribution of spoils and the purification of property
items.desc_en: The prophet instructs Israel to gather spoils like a locust, each for himself. When they question the mixture with the ten tribes' property, the prophet compares it to pits that purify, and Rav Papa cites a precedent that Ammon and Moab were purified through Sihon.

sub.desc_en: The prophet instructs Israel to gather spoils like a locust, each for himself.
Israel questions how to handle spoils mixed with the ten tribes' property.
The prophet compares the purification to pits that purify, stating that property fallen into gentile hands is immediately purified.
Rav Papa cites a precedent that Ammon and Moab were purified through Sihon, supporting the prophet's ruling.

items.text: Sennacherib's ten journeys and the prophet's reassurance
items.text_en: Sennacherib's ten journeys and the prophet's reassurance
items.desc_en: Rav Huna lists ten journeys Sennacherib made in one day, citing verses. The Gemara then explains that the prophet tells Israel not to fear Sennacherib but to fear Nebuchadnezzar, who is likened to a lion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that Sennacherib made ten journeys in one day, citing the verses that list the locations he passed through.
The Gemara questions whether the list actually contains more than ten locations, implying a discrepancy.

The Gemara explains that the phrase 'צַהֲלִי קוֹלֵךְ בַּת גַּלִּים' is not part of Sennacherib's itinerary but a prophet's reassurance to Israel not to fear Sennacherib but to fear Nebuchadnezzar, who is likened to a lion.

items.text: Interpretation of 'ari' and 'layish' in the verse about Sennacherib
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'ari' and 'layish' in the verse about Sennacherib
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the apparent contradiction between two verses that refer to the Assyrian king as both 'ari' (lion) and 'layish' (lion). Rabbi Yochanan resolves this by listing six names for a lion, explaining that the two terms are not contradictory but simply different names for the same animal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a verse from Jeremiah and notes an apparent contradiction: one verse calls the Assyrian king 'ארי' (lion) while another calls him 'ליש' (lion).
Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by listing six names for a lion, showing that 'ארי' and 'ליש' are not contradictory but synonyms.
The Gemara objects that if there are six names, then the two verses would still be redundant, and notes that two of the names are actually from a different context.

items.text: Sennacherib's march to Jerusalem and the miracle of the angel's strike
items.text_en: Sennacherib's march to Jerusalem and the miracle of the angel's strike
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse 'still today he stands at Nob' as referring to the day when the sin of Nob was left unpunished. Sennacherib's astrologers advised him to attack immediately, and he miraculously traveled a ten-day journey in one day. Upon seeing Jerusalem, he mocked its small size, but that night an angel struck his camp, killing 185,000 soldiers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of the verse 'עוֹד הַיּוֹם בְּנֹב לַעֲמֹד' (still today he stands at Nob).
Rav Huna explains that the verse refers to the day when the sin of Nob (the city of priests) was left unpunished.
Sennacherib's astrologers advised him that if he attacked immediately he could conquer Jerusalem, but not otherwise.
Sennacherib miraculously traveled a ten-day journey in one day.
Upon reaching Jerusalem, Sennacherib mocked its small size and gestured contemptuously toward the Temple Mount.
Sennacherib's officers proposed to attack immediately, but he delayed; that night an angel struck his camp, killing 185,000 soldiers.
Rav Pappa concludes with the folk saying: 'בָּת דִּינָא – בְּטַל דִּינָא' (the house of judgment — the dew of judgment), referring to the angel's strike.

items.text: David's sin of Nob and his choice of punishment
items.text_en: David's sin of Nob and his choice of punishment
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets 'Ishbi ben Nob' as a man who came regarding the matter of Nob. God rebukes David for causing the death of the priests of Nob, the exile of Doeg, and the deaths of Saul and his sons. David is given a choice: either his seed will be destroyed or he will be delivered into enemy hands. David chooses the latter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'Ishbi ben Nob' means, and Rav Yehuda citing Rav answers that it refers to a man who came regarding the matter of Nob.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav explains that 'Ishbi ben Nob' means a man who came regarding the matter of Nob.
God rebukes David for causing the death of the priests of Nob, the exile of Doeg, and the deaths of Saul and his sons.
God gives David a choice: either his seed will be destroyed or he will be delivered into enemy hands.
David chooses to be delivered into enemy hands rather than have his seed destroyed.

items.text: David's capture by Ishbi ben Nob and Abishai's rescue
items.text_en: David's capture by Ishbi ben Nob and Abishai's rescue
items.desc_en: The narrative describes how Satan led David into Philistine territory, where Ishbi ben Nob captured him and placed him under a press. A miracle occurred as the ground expanded beneath David. Abishai, sensing David's distress through signs, sought permission from the beit midrash to ride a donkey in a time of danger, then miraculously traveled to David's location, killing Orpah along the way.

sub.desc_en: The narrative opens with David going out to hunt, Satan appearing as a deer, and David being led to Philistine territory where Ishbi ben Nob captures him and places him under a press, but a miracle expands the ground beneath him.
The scene shifts to Abishai, who perceives David's distress through signs and receives permission from the beit midrash to ride a donkey in a time of danger.
Abishai rides his donkey, the earth miraculously contracts for him, and he encounters and kills Orpah, the mother of the Philistine giants, on the way.

items.text: Abishai's prayer and the killing of Ishbi ben Nob
items.text_en: Abishai's prayer and the killing of Ishbi ben Nob
items.desc_en: Ishbi ben Nob throws David into the air and impales him on a spear. Abishai, through the power of God's name, suspends David between heaven and earth. Abishai rebukes David for his earlier prayer, then prays for David's rescue. They flee, and when Ishbi pursues, they invoke his mother's name to weaken him, ultimately killing him.

sub.desc_en: Ishbi ben Nob sees David, throws him into the air, and impales him on a spear.
Abishai considers falling on David to kill him, but then invokes God's name to suspend David between heaven and earth.
Abishai uses God's name to suspend David between heaven and earth, preventing his fall.
The gemara asks why Abishai did not simply tell David to invoke God's name himself, and answers that a prisoner cannot release himself.
Abishai rebukes David for his earlier prayer, telling him to reverse it and not to worry about his grandson's fate.
David asks Abishai to help, and Abishai prays and brings David down; Rav Yehuda says Rav explains that Abishai helped through prayer.
Ishbi pursues them, but they invoke his mother's name to weaken him and kill him; afterward, David's men swear he will no longer go to battle.

items.text: Three for whom the earth contracted
items.text_en: Three for whom the earth contracted
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the earth contracted for three individuals: Eliezer, servant of Abraham; Jacob our father; and Abishai ben Tzeruiah. The Gemara briefly explains the proof for each.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists three individuals for whom the earth contracted: Eliezer, Jacob, and Abishai.
The Gemara notes that Abishai's case is the one already discussed in the narrative.
The Gemara proves Eliezer's case from the verse 'I came today to the well', implying he traveled the same day.
The Gemara begins to cite the proof for Jacob, but the text is cut off here.

items.text: Jacob's journey and the miracle of the sun
items.text_en: Jacob's journey and the miracle of the sun
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when Jacob reached Haran, he realized he had passed the place where his fathers prayed without praying himself. He decided to return, and the earth contracted for him. After he prayed, God caused the sun to set so he would stay overnight, and then caused it to rise again for him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Jacob, upon reaching Haran, realized he had passed the place where his fathers prayed, and the earth contracted for him when he decided to return.
The Gemara offers an alternative interpretation that 'פגיעה' (encounter) refers to prayer, citing a verse.
The Gemara concludes that after Jacob prayed, God caused the sun to set so he would stay overnight, and Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the sun set and rose only for Jacob.

items.text: The survival of David's seed through Evyatar
items.text_en: The survival of David's seed through Evyatar
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how David's lineage survived Athaliah's massacre, noting that Evyatar remained. Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav that had Evyatar not survived, no remnant of David's seed would have remained.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that David's lineage was wiped out, citing the verse about Athaliah destroying all royal seed.
The Gemara objects that Yoash survived, and notes that Evyatar also survived, citing the verse about his escape.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav resolves that had Evyatar not survived, no remnant of David's seed would have remained.

items.text: The size and composition of Sennacherib's army
items.text_en: The size and composition of Sennacherib's army
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav that Sennacherib came with 45,000 princes, 80,000 warriors, 60,000 swordsmen, and others. A baraita describes the camp's length as 400 parasangs and the width of the horses' necks as 40 parasangs, totaling 260 myriad minus one. Abaye questions whether the missing one is a myriad, thousand, hundred, or one.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav describes the vast size and composition of Sennacherib's army, including princes, warriors, swordsmen, and horsemen, and notes that similarly large armies came against Abraham and will come with Gog and Magog.
A baraita provides additional details: the camp's length was 400 parasangs, the width of the horses' necks 40 parasangs, and the total count 260 myriad minus one.
Abaye questions whether the 'missing one' in the count refers to a myriad, a thousand, a hundred, or a single unit.
The gemara leaves the question unresolved with תֵּיקוּ (let it stand).

items.text: The three divisions of the Assyrian army
items.text_en: The three divisions of the Assyrian army
items.desc_en: A baraita describes how the first division passed through Judah by wading, the middle by standing upright, and the last raised dust and had to bring water from elsewhere to drink.

sub.desc_en: A baraita describes the three divisions of the Assyrian army: the first waded through Judah, the middle stood upright, and the last raised dust and brought water from elsewhere to drink.

items.text: The discrepancy in casualty numbers and its resolution
items.text_en: The discrepancy in casualty numbers and its resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: one verse says 185,000 were killed, while another implies more. Rabbi Avahu explains that those were the generals. Rav Ashi and Ravina support this with verses referring to the fat ones and the mighty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: one verse states that the angel killed 185,000 in the Assyrian camp, while another implies a much larger army.
Rabbi Avahu resolves the contradiction by explaining that the 185,000 were only the generals, not the entire army.
Rav Ashi supports Rabbi Avahu by citing a verse that refers to 'the fat ones' (the mighty) being destroyed.
Ravina further supports the resolution by citing a verse that describes the destruction of 'every mighty warrior, commander, and officer' in the camp.

items.text: How Sennacherib's army was killed
items.text_en: How Sennacherib's army was killed
items.desc_en: Various opinions are given: Rabbi Eliezer says by hand, Rabbi Yehoshua says by finger, Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGlili says Gabriel used a sickle, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says Gabriel was sent to ripen fruits, some say by a snort, Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba says by clapping hands, and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha says by revealing ears to hear the song of the Chayot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: With what were they (Sennacherib's army) struck?
Rabbi Eliezer says they were struck by the hand of God, citing the verse 'וַיַּרְא יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת הַיָּד הַגְּדֹלָה' (the great hand).
Rabbi Yehoshua says they were struck by the finger of God, citing the verse 'אֶצְבַּע אֱלֹהִים הִיא' (the finger of God).

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGlili
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGlili
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei HaGlili says God told Gabriel to use his sickle (מגל) that had been ready since the six days of creation, citing the verse 'מִפְּנֵי חֶרֶב נְטוּשָׁה' (from the drawn sword).

Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai says it was the season for ripening fruits, and God told Gabriel to attend to them while going to ripen fruits, citing the verse 'מִדֵּי עָבְרוֹ יִקַּח אֶתְכֶם' (as he passes he will take you).
Some say they were killed by a snort from God's nose, citing the verse 'וְגַם נָשַׁף בָּהֶם וַיִּבָשׁוּ' (He blew upon them and they withered).

Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba says God clapped His hands against them and they died, citing the verse 'וְגַם אֲנִי אַכֶּה כַפִּי אֶל כַּפִּי וַהֲנִחֹתִי חֲמָתִי' (I will strike my hands together and satisfy my fury).

Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha says God revealed their ears so they heard the song of the Chayot (heavenly creatures) and died, citing the verse 'מֵרוֹמְמֻתֶךָ נָפְצוּ גּוֹיִם' (from Your exaltation the nations scattered).

items.text: How many survived from Sennacherib's army
items.text_en: How many survived from Sennacherib's army
items.desc_en: Rav says ten survived, Shmuel says nine, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says fourteen, and Rabbi Yochanan says five: Sennacherib, his two sons, Nebuchadnezzar, and Nevuzaradan. Proofs are brought from verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how many survived from Sennacherib's army, and Rav answers ten, citing the verse 'וּשְׁאָר עֵץ יַעְרוֹ מִסְפָּר יִהְיוּ וְנַעַר יִכְתְּבֵם' (the rest of the trees of his forest shall be few, and a child can write them).

Shmuel says nine survived, citing the verse 'וְנִשְׁאַר בּוֹ עוֹלֵלֹת כְּנֹקֶף זַיִת שְׁנַיִם שְׁלֹשָׁה גַּרְגְּרִים בְּרֹאשׁ אָמִיר אַרְבָּעָה חֲמִשָּׁה בִּסְעִפֶיהָ' (and there shall be left in it gleanings like the shaking of an olive tree, two or three berries at the top of the highest branch, four or five on its branches).
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says fourteen survived, interpreting the same verse as listing two, three, four, and five, totaling fourteen.
Rabbi Yochanan says five survived: Sennacherib, his two sons, Nebuchadnezzar, and Nevuzaradan, providing proofs from verses for each.

items.text: God's appearance to Sennacherib and the advice to flee
items.text_en: God's appearance to Sennacherib and the advice to flee
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu says a verse describes God shaving Sennacherib. God appeared to him as an old man and asked what he would say to the kings whose sons he killed. Sennacherib was terrified and asked what to do. God advised him to go.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu introduces a verse that describes God shaving Sennacherib with a hired razor.
The Holy One appeared to Sennacherib as an old man and asked what he would say to the kings whose sons he killed.
Sennacherib, terrified, acknowledges that even that man (himself) sits in fear.
Sennacherib asks what to do, and God advises him to go (flee).

items.text: Sennacherib's encounter with the angels and the barber
items.text_en: Sennacherib's encounter with the angels and the barber
items.desc_en: Sennacherib, after being told to change his appearance, goes to get a barber. He encounters ministering angels who make him grind stones, and when he returns with fire, it catches his beard, leading to the proverb about the Aramaean.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks how Sennacherib was to change his appearance, and he is told to get a barber; he goes to a house and finds ministering angels grinding stones.
The angels demand he grind a measure of stones for a barber; he does so, but fire catches his beard, and Rav Pappa cites the proverb about the Aramaean.

items.text: Sennacherib's idolatry and his sons' murder
items.text_en: Sennacherib's idolatry and his sons' murder
items.desc_en: Sennacherib finds a plank from Noah's ark, declares it the great god, and vows to sacrifice his sons if he succeeds. His sons hear and kill him, fulfilling the verse about Adrammelech and Sharezer.

sub.desc_en: Sennacherib finds a plank from Noah's ark and vows to sacrifice his sons if he succeeds.
Sennacherib's sons hear his vow and kill him, fulfilling the verse about Adrammelech and Sharezer.

items.text: The angel who fought for Abraham
items.text_en: The angel who fought for Abraham
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates the identity of the angel who helped Abraham at night. Rabbi Yochanan says his name was 'Night', while Rabbi Yitzchak Napacha says he performed a night-like action. Resh Lakish comments on the superiority of the smith's opinion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about Abraham dividing his forces at night.
Rabbi Yochanan identifies the angel who helped Abraham as named 'לַיְלָה' (Night), citing the verse 'וְהַלַּיְלָה אָמַר הֹרָה גָבֶר'.
Rabbi Yitzchak Napacha argues that the angel performed a night-like action (מעשה לילה), citing the verse about stars fighting from heaven against Sisera.
Resh Lakish comments that the opinion of the smith (Rabbi Yitzchak Napacha) is superior to the statement of the smith (Rabbi Yochanan).

items.text: Abraham's weakness at Dan and the wicked's strength
items.text_en: Abraham's weakness at Dan and the wicked's strength
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that when Abraham reached Dan, his strength waned because he foresaw his descendants worshipping idols there. Similarly, the wicked (Jeroboam's calves) only gained strength at Dan.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that when Abraham reached Dan, his strength waned because he foresaw his descendants worshipping idols there.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that the wicked (Jeroboam's calves) only gained strength at Dan, as the verse says 'מִדָּן נִשְׁמַע נַחְרַת סוּסָיו' (from Dan is heard the snorting of his horses).

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's warning about the elder who forgot his learning
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's warning about the elder who forgot his learning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira quotes Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's warning to be careful with an elder who forgot his learning due to duress, with veins like Rabbi Yehuda, and with the children of the ignorant, from whom Torah emerges.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira introduces a warning from Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira about being careful with an elder who forgot his learning due to duress.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's citation of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's citation of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira continues the warning, cautioning about the veins like Rabbi Yehuda and about the children of the ignorant, from whom Torah emerges.
Rabbi Zeira concludes that this matter is made known to them.

items.text: Jeremiah's complaint and God's response through a parable
items.text_en: Jeremiah's complaint and God's response through a parable
items.desc_en: Jeremiah questions why the wicked prosper. God responds with a parable: if Jeremiah tires running after a footman, how can he compete with horses? Similarly, if God rewards the wicked for four steps, how much more will He reward the patriarchs who ran like horses.

sub.desc_en: Jeremiah questions God's justice, asking why the wicked prosper and the treacherous flourish.
God responds with a rhetorical question: if Jeremiah tires running after footmen, how can he compete with horses?
A parable illustrates the principle: a man who claims he can run three parasangs before horses in marshland tires after three miles on dry land before a footman, showing the greater challenge.
God applies the parable: if He rewards the wicked for four steps run for His honor, how much more will He reward the patriarchs who ran like horses.

items.text: The four steps of Merodach-baladan's messenger
items.text_en: The four steps of Merodach-baladan's messenger
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the four steps taken by the messenger of Merodach-baladan, who ran after Hezekiah's recovery. Gabriel stopped him, and Rabbi Yochanan says that without Gabriel, there would be no remedy for Israel's enemies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the four steps refer to, and introduces the story of Merodach-baladan sending letters and a gift to Hezekiah after his recovery.
The Gemara explains that the sun's shadow was reversed ten degrees as a sign of Hezekiah's recovery, and Merodach-baladan wrote a letter praising God, Jerusalem, and Hezekiah.
