The Gemara recounts that Nebuchadnezzar was Baladan's scribe, objected to the order of the letter, and ran after the messenger to correct it.

The Gemara concludes that Nebuchadnezzar ran four steps after the messenger, but Gabriel stopped him; Rabbi Yochanan states that without Gabriel's intervention, there would be no remedy for Israel's enemies.

items.text: The meaning of 'Baladan son of Baladan' and the honor of father and master
items.text_en: The meaning of 'Baladan son of Baladan' and the honor of father and master
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Baladan was a king who became like a dog, so his son wrote both names. This illustrates the verse 'A son honors his father', while 'a servant his master' is shown by Nebuzaradan's obedience to Nebuchadnezzar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the meaning of the double name 'Baladan son of Baladan'.

The Gemara answers that Baladan was a king whose face changed to become like a dog, so his son wrote both his own name and his father's name, illustrating the verse 'A son honors his father and a servant his master'.
The Gemara cites a verse to show that 'A son honors his father' applies to Baladan's son, and 'a servant his master' applies to Nebuzaradan's obedience to Nebuchadnezzar.

items.text: Did Nebuchadnezzar actually go up to Jerusalem?
items.text_en: Did Nebuchadnezzar actually go up to Jerusalem?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Nebuchadnezzar himself went up to Jerusalem, citing a verse that he was brought to the king of Babylon in Riblah (Antioch). Rav Hisda and Rav Yitzchak bar Avudimi offer two explanations: either an image of Nebuchadnezzar was engraved on his chariot, or he had such awe of him that it seemed as if he stood before him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Nebuchadnezzar himself went up to Jerusalem, citing a verse that he was brought to the king of Babylon in Riblah.
Rabbi Abahu identifies Riblah as Antioch, implying Nebuchadnezzar was brought there, not Jerusalem.
Rav Chisda explains that an image of Nebuchadnezzar was engraved on his chariot, so he was considered present.
Rav Yitzchak bar Avudimi explains that Nebuchadnezzar had such awe of him that it seemed as if he stood before him.

items.text: Nebuzaradan's iron axes and the opening of the Temple gate
items.text_en: Nebuzaradan's iron axes and the opening of the Temple gate
items.desc_en: Rava recounts that Nebuchadnezzar sent Nebuzaradan 300 iron axes, but the gate of Jerusalem swallowed them all. When Nebuzaradan hesitated to return, a heavenly voice told him to leap, as the time had come for the Temple to be destroyed. He struck the gate with one remaining axe and it opened.

sub.desc_en: Rava recounts that Nebuchadnezzar sent Nebuzaradan 300 iron axes, but the gate of Jerusalem swallowed them all.
A heavenly voice tells Nebuzaradan to leap, as the time for the Temple's destruction has come, and he strikes the gate with one remaining axe, opening it.

items.text: The Temple set on fire and the heavenly voice
items.text_en: The Temple set on fire and the heavenly voice
items.desc_en: Nebuzaradan reached the Temple, set it on fire, and it ascended. A heavenly voice told him he had killed a slain people and burned a burned Temple, citing a verse about grinding flour, not wheat.

sub.desc_en: Nebuzaradan reaches the Temple, sets it on fire, and the Temple ascends.

A heavenly voice tells Nebuzaradan that he has killed a slain people and burned a burned Temple, citing the verse 'קחי רחים וטחני קמח' (take millstones and grind flour) to emphasize that the grinding was already done.

items.text: The blood of Zechariah and Nebuzaradan's conversion
items.text_en: The blood of Zechariah and Nebuzaradan's conversion
items.desc_en: Nebuzaradan saw the blood of Zechariah boiling and, after being told it was the blood of a priest and prophet killed by Israel, he tried to appease it by killing many people. Only when he offered to kill all of them did the blood rest. He then repented, converted, and sent a will to his household.

sub.desc_en: Nebuzaradan sees the blood of Zechariah boiling and asks what it is.
The sages claim it is spilled blood of sacrifices, but a test shows it does not congeal.
Nebuzaradan threatens to torture them if they do not reveal the truth.
The sages reveal that it is the blood of Zechariah, a priest and prophet whom Israel killed.
Nebuzaradan tries to appease the blood by killing rabbis, schoolchildren, and young priests, but it does not rest.
Nebuzaradan offers to kill all of Israel, and the blood finally rests.
Nebuzaradan repents, converts, and sends a will to his household.

items.text: Descendants of wicked nations who converted
items.text_en: Descendants of wicked nations who converted
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that Naaman was a ger toshav, Nebuzaradan a ger tzedek, and descendants of Sisera and Sennacherib taught Torah in Jerusalem. The Gemara discusses the descendants of Haman and the wicked Nebuchadnezzar, and the angels' objection to God bringing them under the wings of the Shekhinah.

sub.desc_en: The Sages taught a baraita listing descendants of wicked nations who converted: Naaman as a ger toshav, Nebuzaradan as a ger tzedek, and descendants of Sisera and Sennacherib who taught Torah in Jerusalem.
The Gemara asks who these descendants are.
The Gemara answers that they are Shmaya and Avtalyon.
The Gemara adds that descendants of Haman taught Torah in Bnei Brak, and that the Holy One sought to bring descendants of that wicked one (Nebuchadnezzar) under the wings of the Shekhinah.
The ministering angels objected to God, asking how He could bring under the wings of the Shekhinah one who destroyed His house and burned His Temple.
The Gemara cites the verse 'We healed Babylon but she was not healed' as the response to the angels' objection.

sub.text: Ulla and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani
sub.text_en: Ulla and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani
sub.desc_en: Ulla identifies the subject as Nebuchadnezzar, while Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani identifies it as the rivers of Babylon, with the Targum interpreting them as the dried-up canals of the Babylonians.

items.text: Ammon and Moab's correspondence with Nebuchadnezzar
items.text_en: Ammon and Moab's correspondence with Nebuchadnezzar
items.desc_en: Ulla explains that Ammon and Moab were wicked neighbors of Jerusalem who sent messages to Nebuchadnezzar encouraging him to attack, citing verses that God was far away and that the righteous would not intervene. They eventually convinced him to come, even offering the graves of Jerusalem's kings as better than his palaces.

sub.desc_en: Ulla introduces that Ammon and Moab were wicked neighbors of Jerusalem who, upon hearing prophecies of destruction, sent a message to Nebuchadnezzar urging him to come.
Nebuchadnezzar expresses fear that the Jews might treat him as they did the earlier attackers (Sennacherib).
They reassure him that God (the 'man') is far away, citing the verse 'כי אין האיש בביתו' and interpreting 'איש' as God.
Nebuchadnezzar objects that God is near and can come quickly.
They insist that God has gone on a distant journey, but Nebuchadnezzar counters that the righteous could pray and bring Him back.
They argue that the righteous (symbolized by 'כסף') have been taken away, citing the verse 'צרור הכסף לקח בידו'.
Nebuchadnezzar objects that the wicked (Israel) might repent and bring God back.
They respond that God has already set a fixed time (כֶּסֶא) for judgment, implying no repentance will help.
Nebuchadnezzar objects that it is winter and he cannot travel due to snow and rain.
They invite him to come via the mountain pass (אַשִּׁינָּא דְּטוּרָא), citing the verse 'שלחו כר מושל ארץ'.
Nebuchadnezzar objects that he has no place to stay if he comes.
They resolve his concern by claiming that the graves of Jerusalem's kings are better than his palaces, citing the verse about the bones of the kings being scattered.

items.text: When will the son of the fallen one come?
items.text_en: When will the son of the fallen one come?
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rabbi Yitzchak when 'Bar Naflei' (the son of the fallen one) will come, and Rabbi Yitzchak clarifies that this refers to the Messiah, citing a verse about the fallen sukkah of David.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asks Rabbi Yitzchak when 'Bar Naflei' (the son of the fallen one) will come.
Rabbi Yitzchak asks who 'Bar Naflei' refers to.
Rav Nachman explains that 'Bar Naflei' refers to the Messiah.
Rabbi Yitzchak objects to calling the Messiah 'Bar Naflei'.
Rav Nachman affirms and cites the verse 'בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא אָקִים' (On that day I will raise up) to support the identification.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on the generation of the Messiah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on the generation of the Messiah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan describes the generation when the son of David comes: scholars diminish, the rest suffer, and troubles multiply.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan describes the generation when the son of David comes: scholars diminish, the rest suffer, and troubles multiply.

items.text: Baraita on the seven-year cycle before the Messiah
items.text_en: Baraita on the seven-year cycle before the Messiah
items.desc_en: A baraita details the sequence of events in the seven years leading to the Messiah's arrival, including famine, plenty, and war.

sub.desc_en: A baraita details the seven-year cycle leading to the Messiah's arrival, with alternating famine, war, and eventual redemption.

items.text: Rav Yosef and Abaye question the baraita
items.text_en: Rav Yosef and Abaye question the baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects that many such cycles have passed without the Messiah coming. Abaye adds that the signs of sounds in the sixth year and war in the seventh have not occurred in order.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects that many such cycles have passed without the Messiah coming.
Abaye responds that the required signs (sounds in the sixth year, wars in the seventh) have not occurred in order.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda on the generation's moral decay
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda on the generation's moral decay
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda describes the generation of the Messiah: the study hall becomes licentious, the Galilee destroyed, and wisdom of scribes putrid.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda describes the generation of the Messiah: the study house becomes licentious, the Galilee destroyed, and the face of the generation like a dog.

items.text: Interpretation of 'truth is lacking'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'truth is lacking'
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'truth is lacking' as truth becoming scattered, and 'turning from evil is foolish' as one who turns from evil is considered foolish by people.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of the verse 'and truth is lacking'.
Be Rav explains that truth has become scattered in groups and departed.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the phrase 'and he who departs from evil is considered mad'.
Be Rabbi Sheila explains that anyone who departs from evil is considered mad by the people.
Be Rabbi Sheila explains that anyone who turns from evil is considered foolish by people.

items.text: Rava's story about truthfulness
items.text_en: Rava's story about truthfulness
items.desc_en: Rava recounts a story about a place called Kushta where people never lied, and how his wife's white lie led to the death of his two sons, teaching the severity of falsehood.

sub.desc_en: Rava recounts a story about a place called 'Truth' where people never lied and no one died prematurely, and he married a woman from there.

sub.text: Rava's story about the place Kushta
sub.text_en: Rava's story about the place Kushta
sub.desc_en: Rava describes how he once visited a place called Kushta where people never lied and no one died prematurely, and he married a woman from there who bore him two sons.
Rava recounts how his wife's white lie to a neighbor led to the death of his two sons, and the people of the place asked him to leave so as not to cause further deaths.

items.text: Rabbi Nehorai on the generation's inversion
items.text_en: Rabbi Nehorai on the generation's inversion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Nehorai describes the generation: youths shame elders, elders stand before youths, and the son is not ashamed before his father.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nehorai describes the generation of the Messiah: youths shame elders, elders stand before youths, and the face of the generation is like a dog.

items.text: Rabbi Nechemya and Rabbi Yitzchak on the kingdom's heresy
items.text_en: Rabbi Nechemya and Rabbi Yitzchak on the kingdom's heresy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Nechemya says the generation will see increased insolence and the entire kingdom turning to heresy. Rabbi Yitzchak supports this, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nechemya describes the generation: insolence increases, wine is expensive, and the entire kingdom turns to heresy.
Rabbi Yitzchak supports Rabbi Nechemya, saying the son of David will not come until the entire kingdom turns to heresy.
Rava cites a verse 'all of it turned white, it is pure' as a scriptural support for the turning to heresy.

items.text: Conditions for the Messiah's arrival
items.text_en: Conditions for the Messiah's arrival
items.desc_en: A baraita lists conditions: informers increase, students diminish, the purse is empty, and people despair of redemption.

sub.desc_en: A baraita lists four conditions for the Messiah's arrival: many informers, few students, empty pockets, and despair of redemption.
The baraita adds a second condition: students of Torah diminish.
The baraita adds a third condition: the purse is empty of coins.
The baraita adds a fourth condition: people despair of redemption, citing the verse 'ואפס עצור ועזוב' as proof.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira on the Messiah coming unexpectedly
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira on the Messiah coming unexpectedly
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks the sages not to push away the Messiah, as he comes when one is distracted, like a found object or a scorpion.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks the rabbis not to push away the calculation of the end, citing a mishnah that three things come unexpectedly: Messiah, a found object, and a scorpion.

items.text: Rav Katina and Abaye on the world's six thousand years
items.text_en: Rav Katina and Abaye on the world's six thousand years
items.desc_en: Rav Katina says the world exists for six thousand years and one thousand are desolate. Abaye says two thousand are desolate. A baraita supports Rav Katina with the Sabbatical cycle.

sub.desc_en: Rav Katina states that the world exists for six thousand years and one thousand are desolate, citing the verse 'ונשגב ה' לבדו ביום ההוא' (the Lord alone will be exalted on that day).

Abaye counters that two thousand years are desolate, citing the verse 'יחיינו מיומים ביום השלישי יקימנו ונחיה לפניו' (He will revive us after two days, on the third day He will raise us up and we shall live before Him).

A baraita supports Rav Katina by comparing the world's millennia to the Sabbatical cycle: as the seventh year is a sabbatical, so the seventh millennium is a cosmic sabbatical, citing verses 'ונשגב ה לבדו' and 'כי אלף שנים בעיניך כיום אתמול' (for a thousand years in Your eyes are like yesterday).

items.text: Tanna debei Eliyahu on the six millennia
items.text_en: Tanna debei Eliyahu on the six millennia
items.desc_en: Tanna debei Eliyahu states the world lasts six thousand years: two thousand chaos, two thousand Torah, two thousand the days of the Messiah.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna debei Eliyahu divides world history into three two-thousand-year periods: chaos, Torah, and the days of the Messiah.

items.text: Elijah's prophecy to Rav Yehuda about the end
items.text_en: Elijah's prophecy to Rav Yehuda about the end
items.desc_en: Elijah tells Rav Yehuda that the world will last at least 85 jubilees, and the son of David will come in the last jubilee. Rav Yehuda asks whether at its beginning or end, and whether it will be completed or not, but Elijah does not know. Rav Ashi clarifies that Elijah said not to look for him until then, but after that one may.

sub.desc_en: Elijah tells Rav Yehuda that the world will last at least 85 jubilees, and the son of David will come in the last jubilee.
Rav Yehuda asks whether the son of David will come at the beginning or end of the last jubilee, and Elijah responds that he does not know.
Rav Yehuda asks whether the jubilee will be completed or not, and Elijah again says he does not know.
Rav Ashi clarifies that Elijah told Rav Yehuda not to look for the son of David until that time, but after that one may.

items.text: A scroll from Rome with a timeline
items.text_en: A scroll from Rome with a timeline
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Tachlifa sends a report to Rav Yosef about a scroll found in Rome, written in Ashurit and the holy tongue, which states that after 4291 years from creation the world will be orphaned, with wars of tanninim, Gog and Magog, and the rest of the messianic era, and that God will renew the world after 7000 years. Rav Acha bar Rava says it was said after 5000 years.

sub.text: Rav Chanan bar Tachlifa's report to Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Tachlifa's report to Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Tachlifa sends a report to Rav Yosef about finding a scroll in Rome, written in Ashurit and the holy tongue.

The scroll states that after 4291 years from creation the world will be orphaned, with wars of tanninim, Gog and Magog, and the rest of the messianic era, and that God will renew the world after 7000 years.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava's alternative tradition
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava's alternative tradition
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava says that the renewal of the world was said to occur after 5000 years, not 7000.

items.text: Rabbi Natan's verse and rejection of other calculations
items.text_en: Rabbi Natan's verse and rejection of other calculations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Natan cites a verse that pierces to the depths about the appointed time. The Gemara rejects the interpretations of the Rabbis, Rabbi Simlai, and Rabbi Akiva, and instead gives a historical calculation: first kingdom 70 years, second 52, and the kingdom of ben Koziva 2.5 years.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Natan cites a verse (Habakkuk 2:3) that pierces to the depths about the appointed time for redemption.

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of the Rabbis' interpretation
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of the Rabbis' interpretation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the interpretation of the Rabbis who expounded the verse 'עַד עִדָּן עִדָּנִין וּפְלַג עִדָּן' (until a time, times, and half a time).

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of Rabbi Simlai's interpretation
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of Rabbi Simlai's interpretation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the interpretation of Rabbi Simlai who expounded the verse 'הֶאֱכַלְתָּם לֶחֶם דִּמְעָה וַתַּשְׁקֵמוֹ בִּדְמָעוֹת שְׁלִישׁ' (You fed them bread of tears and gave them tears to drink in full measure).

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of Rabbi Akiva's interpretation
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of Rabbi Akiva's interpretation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the interpretation of Rabbi Akiva who expounded the verse 'עוֹד אַחַת מְעַט הִיא וַאֲנִי מַרְעִישׁ אֶת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֶת הָאָרֶץ' (Yet one little while and I will shake the heavens and the earth).
The Gemara provides a historical calculation: the first kingdom (Babylonian exile) lasted 70 years, the second kingdom (Persian rule) 52 years, and the kingdom of ben Koziva (Bar Kokhba) 2.5 years.

items.text: The curse on calculators of the end and the need to wait
items.text_en: The curse on calculators of the end and the need to wait
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan curses those who calculate the end, saying that if the end comes and he does not come, they think he will never come. Instead, one must wait, as the verse says. The Gemara asks what delays the redemption, answering that the attribute of justice delays it, and we wait for reward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of the verse 'וְיָפֵחַ לַקֵּץ וְלֹא יְכַזֵּב' (it breathes toward the end and does not lie).

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan curses those who calculate the end, saying that if the end comes and he does not come, they think he will never come, and instead one must wait as the verse says.
The Gemara raises a concern: perhaps we wait but God does not wait for us.
The Gemara answers with a verse that God also waits, citing 'וְלָכֵן יְחַכֶּה ה׳ לַחֲנַנְכֶם' (therefore the Lord waits to be gracious to you).
The Gemara asks: since both we and God wait, what delays the redemption?
The Gemara answers that the attribute of justice (מִדַּת הַדִּין) delays the redemption.
The Gemara asks: since the attribute of justice delays, why should we wait?
The Gemara answers that we wait to receive reward, citing the verse 'אַשְׁרֵי כׇּל חוֹכֵי לוֹ' (fortunate are all who wait for Him).

items.text: The number of righteous who receive the Divine Presence
items.text_en: The number of righteous who receive the Divine Presence
items.desc_en: Abaye says the world never has fewer than 36 righteous who receive the Divine Presence each generation, based on a gematria. Rava objects that the Divine Presence spans 18,000 parasangs. The Gemara resolves that those who see through a bright specularia are few, while those who see through a non-bright one are many. Another objection from Chizkiya is resolved by distinguishing between those who enter with permission and those who enter without.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that the world never has fewer than 36 righteous who receive the Divine Presence each generation, based on a gematria of the word 'לוֹ' (36).
Rava objects that the Divine Presence spans 18,000 parasangs, implying far more than 36 righteous can be present.
The Gemara resolves that those who see through a bright specularia (the 36) are few, while those who see through a non-bright one are many.
Chizkiya objects that the righteous are few, citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai who said he and his son are among them, implying only a handful.
The Gemara resolves that the few are those who enter without permission, while the many (including the 36) enter with permission.

items.text: Debate between Rav and Shmuel, and between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on repentance and redemption
items.text_en: Debate between Rav and Shmuel, and between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on repentance and redemption
items.desc_en: Rav says all ends have passed and the matter depends only on repentance and good deeds. Shmuel says it is enough for the mourner to stand in his mourning. A baraita records Rabbi Eliezer saying Israel is redeemed only if they repent, while Rabbi Yehoshua says even if they do not, God will appoint a harsh king to force repentance. Another baraita has Rabbi Eliezer citing a verse for repentance, Rabbi Yehoshua citing a verse for unconditional redemption, and they exchange further verses.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that all the appointed ends have passed, and redemption depends only on repentance and good deeds.
Shmuel counters with a metaphor: it is enough for the mourner to stand in his mourning, implying that the time itself suffices without repentance.

A baraita records Rabbi Eliezer's position that Israel is redeemed only if they repent, and Rabbi Yehoshua's objection that even without repentance, God will appoint a harsh king to force them back to good.

A second baraita presents Rabbi Eliezer citing a verse for repentance, and Rabbi Yehoshua citing a verse for unconditional redemption, explaining that the verse 'חִנָּם נִמְכַּרְתֶּם' teaches redemption without repentance.
Rabbi Eliezer objects by citing the verse 'שׁוּבוּ אֵלַי וְאָשׁוּבָה אֲלֵיכֶם' (Return to Me and I will return to you), implying repentance is necessary.

Rabbi Yehoshua counters by citing the verse 'כִּי אָנֹכִי בָּעַלְתִּי בָכֶם... וְהֵבֵאתִי אֶתְכֶם צִיּוֹן' (I will take you one from a city and two from a family and bring you to Zion), showing redemption without repentance.
Rabbi Eliezer objects further by citing the verse 'בְּשׁוּבָה וָנַחַת תִּוָּשֵׁעוּן' (In returning and rest you shall be saved), emphasizing repentance.

Rabbi Yehoshua counters by citing the verse 'כֹּה אָמַר ה׳ גֹּאֵל יִשְׂרָאֵל... לִבְזֹה נֶפֶשׁ לִמְתָעֵב גּוֹי לְעֶבֶד מֹשְׁלִים' (Thus says the Lord, the Redeemer of Israel... to one despised, abhorred by the nation, a servant of rulers), implying redemption despite Israel's lowly state.

items.text: Debate on the revealed end-time
items.text_en: Debate on the revealed end-time
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua dispute whether a clear end-time is revealed in Scripture. Rabbi Eliezer cites a verse about Israel's return, but Rabbi Yehoshua counters with a verse about a fixed period, silencing Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by quoting a verse about kings rising and bowing, setting up the debate on the revealed end-time.
Rabbi Eliezer cites a verse about Israel's return as evidence for a revealed end-time.
Rabbi Yehoshua counters with a verse about a fixed period of 'a time, times, and half a time,' silencing Rabbi Eliezer.
The Gemara reports that Rabbi Eliezer was silenced, indicating Rabbi Yehoshua's position prevailed.

items.text: Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Eliezer on additional signs
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Eliezer on additional signs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba identifies a clear end-time from a verse about Israel's fruitfulness, while Rabbi Eliezer adds another sign from a verse about a time when human and animal wages cease.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba states that there is no clearer end-time than the verse about Israel's fruitfulness.
Rabbi Eliezer adds another sign from a verse about the cessation of wages for man and beast.

items.text: Interpretation of the verse about no peace
items.text_en: Interpretation of the verse about no peace
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel interpret the verse 'no peace for the goer and comer from the oppressor'. Rav says it refers to Torah scholars who lack peace due to oppressors, while Shmuel says it means until all measures are equal.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks for the interpretation of the verse about no peace for the goer and comer from the oppressor.
Rav interprets the verse as referring to Torah scholars who lack peace due to oppressors.
Shmuel interprets the verse as meaning until all measures are equal.

items.text: Four conditions for the coming of the Son of David
items.text_en: Four conditions for the coming of the Son of David
items.desc_en: Four Amoraim each state a condition for the Messiah's arrival: Rabbi Chanina says until a small fish is unavailable for a sick person; Rabbi Chama bar Chanina says until the insolent kingdom ends; Ze'iri says until the arrogant are gone; Rabbi Simlai says until all judges and officers are gone.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that the Son of David will not come until a small fish is unavailable for a sick person, citing a verse.
Rabbi Chama bar Chanina states that the Son of David will not come until the insolent kingdom ends, citing a verse.
Ze'iri in the name of Rabbi Chanina states that the Son of David will not come until the arrogant are gone, citing a verse.

sub.text: Rabbi Simlai citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Simlai citing Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Simlai in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon states that the Son of David will not come until all judges and officers are gone, citing a verse.

items.text: Ulla and Rav Pappa on redemption through righteousness
items.text_en: Ulla and Rav Pappa on redemption through righteousness
items.desc_en: Ulla states that Jerusalem is redeemed only through charity. Rav Pappa adds that if the arrogant cease, the magi cease; if judges cease, the gzirot cease, citing verses.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that Jerusalem is redeemed only through charity, citing the verse 'צִיּוֹן בְּמִשְׁפָּט תִּפָּדֶה וְשָׁבֶיהָ בִּצְדָקָה'.
Rav Pappa adds that if the arrogant cease, the magi cease; if judges cease, the gzirot cease, citing verses 'וְאֶצְרֹף כַּבֹּר סִיגָיִךְ' and 'הֵסִיר ה׳ מִשְׁפָּטַיִךְ פִּנָּה אֹיְבֵךְ'.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on signs of the generation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on signs of the generation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan gives three signs: if the generation diminishes, wait for him; if many troubles come like a river, wait for him; and the Messiah comes in a generation that is entirely righteous or entirely guilty.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that if you see a generation diminishing, wait for the Messiah, citing a verse.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that if you see a generation overwhelmed by troubles like a river, wait for the Messiah, citing a verse.
Rabbi Yochanan concludes that the Messiah comes only in a generation that is entirely righteous or entirely guilty, citing verses for both possibilities.

items.text: Rabbi Alexandri on the paradox of the time
items.text_en: Rabbi Alexandri on the paradox of the time
items.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri reports that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi resolves two contradictions: between 'in its time' and 'I will hasten it' (merit hastens), and between coming with clouds and riding a donkey (merit brings clouds, otherwise a donkey).

sub.text: Rabbi Alexandri citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Alexandri citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri reports that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi resolves the contradiction between the verses 'בעתה' (in its time) and 'אחישנה' (I will hasten it): if the generation merits, the redemption is hastened; if not, it comes in its appointed time.

sub.text: Rabbi Alexandri citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Alexandri citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri further reports that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi resolves another contradiction: between the messiah coming 'עם ענני שמיא' (with the clouds of heaven) and 'עני ורוכב על חמור' (poor and riding a donkey); merit brings the clouds, otherwise a donkey.

items.text: King Shapur's question to Shmuel
items.text_en: King Shapur's question to Shmuel
items.desc_en: King Shapur asks Shmuel if the Messiah comes on a donkey, offering a horse instead. Shmuel responds by asking if he has a multi-colored horse.

sub.desc_en: King Shapur asks Shmuel if the Messiah comes on a donkey, offering to send him a horse instead.
Shmuel responds by asking if King Shapur has a multi-colored horse, implying the Messiah's donkey is unique.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's encounter with Elijah and the Messiah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's encounter with Elijah and the Messiah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi finds Elijah at the cave of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, asks about the world to come, then asks when the Messiah will come. Elijah directs him to ask the Messiah himself, who is at the gate of Rome among the sick. The Messiah answers 'today', but Elijah explains it means 'today if you listen to His voice'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi finds Elijah at the entrance of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's cave and asks about the world to come; Elijah responds conditionally, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reports hearing two voices and a third.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asks Elijah when the Messiah will come; Elijah directs him to ask the Messiah himself, who is at the gate of Rome among the sick, and describes his distinguishing behavior.

Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi goes to the Messiah, who answers 'today'; Elijah explains that the Messiah meant 'today, if you listen to His voice' (Psalm 95:7), and assures Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi of his share in the world to come.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma's sign for the Messiah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma's sign for the Messiah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma's students ask when the Messiah will come. He initially refuses to give a sign, but then says when a certain gate falls, is rebuilt, falls again, and before it can be rebuilt the Messiah comes. They ask for a sign, and he turns the waters of the Pamias cave into blood.

sub.desc_en: The students ask Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma when the Messiah will come, and he initially expresses fear that they will ask for a sign, but they reassure him they will not.

Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma gives a sign: when a certain gate falls, is rebuilt, falls again, and before it can be rebuilt the Messiah comes, but then the students ask for a sign and he rebukes them for contradicting their earlier promise.
Despite the rebuke, the students persist in asking for a sign, and Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma turns the waters of the Pamias cave into blood as a miraculous sign.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's final instruction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's final instruction
items.desc_en: At his death, Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma instructs his students to deepen his coffin.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma's final instruction
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma's final instruction
sub.desc_en: At his death, Rabbi Yosei ben Kisma instructs his students to deepen his coffin.

items.text: Opening metaphor about Babylonian date palms and Persian horses
items.text_en: Opening metaphor about Babylonian date palms and Persian horses
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a vivid metaphor describing the abundance of date palms in Babylonia and the prevalence of Persian horses tied to them, as well as the many chests in Eretz Yisrael used for feeding Median horses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a metaphor describing Babylonian date palms tied to Persian horses and chests in Eretz Yisrael used for feeding Median horses.

items.text: Rav's statement on the timing of the Messiah's arrival
items.text_en: Rav's statement on the timing of the Messiah's arrival
items.desc_en: Rav states that the son of David will not come until the wicked kingdom spreads over Israel for nine months, citing the verse 'Therefore He will give them up until the time she who is in labor gives birth.'

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the son of David will not come until the wicked kingdom spreads over Israel for nine months, citing the verse from Micah.

items.text: Amoraic reactions: desire to see or avoid the Messiah
items.text_en: Amoraic reactions: desire to see or avoid the Messiah
items.desc_en: Ulla and Rabbah express a wish that the Messiah come but that they not see him, while Rav Yosef hopes to see him and sit in the shade of his donkey's saddle.

sub.desc_en: Ulla expresses a wish that the Messiah come but that he not see him.
Rabbah similarly expresses a wish that the Messiah come but that he not see him.
Rav Yosef expresses a wish to see the Messiah and sit in the shade of his donkey's saddle.

items.text: Abaye's question and the danger of sin
items.text_en: Abaye's question and the danger of sin
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah why he does not want to see the Messiah, suggesting it might be due to the birth pangs of the Messiah. Rabbah responds that sin may cause one to be unworthy, citing a contradiction in verses about Jacob's fear despite God's promise.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah why he does not want to see the Messiah, suggesting it might be due to the birth pangs of the Messiah, and cites a baraita that one can be saved from those pangs through Torah and acts of kindness, which Rabbah already possesses.
Rabbah answers that sin may cause one to be unworthy, citing Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi's resolution of a contradiction in verses about Jacob's fear despite God's promise of protection.
The gemara elaborates that Jacob feared sin might cause him to be unworthy, citing a baraita that Israel was worthy of a miracle in the second entry like the first, but sin prevented it.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish on the suffering of the Messianic era
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish on the suffering of the Messianic era
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan also wishes not to see the Messiah. Resh Lakish questions this, and Rabbi Yochanan explains it is due to the verse about a man fleeing a lion, meeting a bear, and being bitten by a snake, which is a metaphor for successive calamities. Rav Pappa adds a folk saying about an ox falling and a horse being placed in its stall.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that he wishes the Messiah would come but that he not see him.
Resh Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan for the reason behind his wish.
Resh Lakish suggests that Rabbi Yochanan's reason might be the verse about a man fleeing a lion, meeting a bear, and being bitten by a snake.
Resh Lakish provides an allegorical interpretation of the verse, comparing the lion to a Roman officer, the bear to a tax collector, and the snake to finding one's children starving.
Resh Lakish rejects the previous explanation and instead attributes Rabbi Yochanan's wish to a different verse describing the anguish of the Messianic era.
Rava bar Yitzchak in the name of Rav explains that 'every man' refers to the Holy One, blessed be He, who possesses all strength.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that 'all faces turn pale' refers to the heavenly and earthly retinues, as God wonders how He can destroy one group for the sake of the other.
Rav Pappa adds a folk saying about an ox falling and a horse being placed in its stall, illustrating the cascading calamities.

items.text: Rav Giddel and Rav Yosef on Israel eating the years of the Messiah
items.text_en: Rav Giddel and Rav Yosef on Israel eating the years of the Messiah
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel says in the name of Rav that Israel will eat the years of the Messiah. Rav Yosef finds this obvious, except to refute Rabbi Hillel who said there is no Messiah for Israel since they already consumed him in the days of Hezekiah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel states in the name of Rav that Israel will eat the years of the Messiah.
Rav Yosef objects that the statement is obvious, asking rhetorically who else would eat the years of the Messiah.
Rav Yosef explains that the statement is needed to refute Rabbi Hillel, who claimed there is no Messiah for Israel since they already consumed him in the days of Hezekiah.

items.text: Various opinions on the purpose of creation and the name of the Messiah
items.text_en: Various opinions on the purpose of creation and the name of the Messiah
items.desc_en: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan debate whether the world was created for David, Moses, or the Messiah. Then, various schools offer names for the Messiah: Shiloh, Yinon, Chaninah, Menachem ben Chizkiyah, and the leprous one of the house of Rabbi. Rav Nachman and Rav identify possible living or dead candidates. Rav Yehuda says God will establish another David, and Rav Pappa questions this with a verse.

sub.desc_en: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan each state that the world was created for David, Moses, or the Messiah respectively.

sub.text: Bei Rabbi Sheila, Bei Rabbi Yannai, Bei Rabbi Chanina, Yesh Omrim, Rabbanan
sub.text_en: Bei Rabbi Sheila, Bei Rabbi Yannai, Bei Rabbi Chanina, Yesh Omrim, Rabbanan
sub.desc_en: Various schools offer names for the Messiah: Shiloh, Yinon, Chaninah, Menachem ben Chizkiyah, and the leprous one of the house of Rabbi, each citing a verse.
Rav Nachman and Rav identify possible living or dead candidates for the Messiah: Rav Nachman himself, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, or Daniel.
Rav Yehuda says God will establish another David, and Rav Pappa questions this with a verse, to which Abaye responds that it is like a Caesar and a subordinate Caesar.

items.text: Rabbi Simlai's parable of the rooster and the bat
items.text_en: Rabbi Simlai's parable of the rooster and the bat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Simlai interprets the verse 'Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord' with a parable: a rooster and a bat await light, but the rooster says the light is for him, while the bat has no need for it, illustrating that the wicked do not benefit from the day of the Lord.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Simlai interprets the verse 'Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord' with a parable: a rooster and a bat await light, but the rooster says the light is for him, while the bat has no need for it, illustrating that the wicked do not benefit from the day of the Lord.

items.text: Opening story: heretic asks Rabbi Abbahu when the Messiah will come
items.text_en: Opening story: heretic asks Rabbi Abbahu when the Messiah will come
items.desc_en: A heretic asks Rabbi Abbahu when the Messiah will come. Rabbi Abbahu responds cryptically, quoting Isaiah 60:2, implying that the Messiah will come when darkness covers the nations. The heretic perceives this as a curse.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts a heretic asking Rabbi Abbahu when the Messiah will come, and Rabbi Abbahu responds with a verse from Isaiah about darkness covering the nations.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute on the duration of the messianic era
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on the duration of the messianic era
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says the messianic era lasts 40 years, Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says 70 years, Rabbi (Judah the Prince) says three generations, and Rabbi Hillel says Israel has no Messiah because they already consumed him in the days of Hezekiah. Rav Yosef strongly criticizes Rabbi Hillel's view, arguing that Hezekiah was in the First Temple period, while Zechariah prophesied about the Messiah in the Second Temple period.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that the messianic era lasts 40 years, citing a verse.
Rabbi (Judah the Prince) says three generations, and Rabbi Hillel says Israel has no Messiah because they already consumed him in Hezekiah's days.
Rav Yosef strongly criticizes Rabbi Hillel, arguing that Hezekiah was in the First Temple period while Zechariah prophesied about the Messiah in the Second Temple period.

items.text: Further tannaitic disputes on the length of the messianic era
items.text_en: Further tannaitic disputes on the length of the messianic era
items.desc_en: Another baraita presents additional opinions: Rabbi Eliezer again says 40 years, deriving it from the wilderness period; Rabbi Dosa says 400 years, corresponding to the Egyptian bondage; Rabbi (Judah the Prince) says 365 years, like the days of the solar year, based on Isaiah 63:4.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that the messianic era lasts 40 years, derived from the wilderness period.
Rabbi Dosa argues for 400 years, corresponding to the Egyptian bondage.
Rabbi (Judah the Prince) says 365 years, like the solar year, based on Isaiah 63:4.

items.text: Interpretation of 'day of vengeance in My heart'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'day of vengeance in My heart'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of the phrase 'day of vengeance in My heart' from Isaiah 63:4. Rabbi Yochanan says God revealed it to His heart but not to His limbs. Resh Lakish says God revealed it to His heart but not to the ministering angels.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks about the meaning of the phrase 'day of vengeance in My heart' from the verse.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that God revealed the day of vengeance to His heart but not to His limbs.
Reish Lakish explains that God revealed it to His heart but not to the ministering angels.

items.text: Amoraic opinions on the duration of the messianic era
items.text_en: Amoraic opinions on the duration of the messianic era
items.desc_en: Avimi bar Rabbi Abbahu says the messianic era will last 7,000 years. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says it will last from the creation of the world until now. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says it will last from the days of Noah until now.

sub.desc_en: Avimi bar Rabbi Abbahu teaches that the messianic era for Israel will last 7,000 years, citing the verse 'וּמְשׂוֹשׂ חָתָן עַל כַּלָּה' (as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride).

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel states that the messianic era will last from the creation of the world until now, citing the verse 'כִּימֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם עַל הָאָרֶץ' (as the days of heaven upon the earth).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says the messianic era will last from the days of Noah until now, citing the verse 'כִּי מֵי נֹחַ זֹאת לִי' (for the waters of Noah this is to me).

items.text: Prophecy pertains only to the messianic era, not the World to Come
items.text_en: Prophecy pertains only to the messianic era, not the World to Come
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that all the prophets prophesied only about the messianic era, but regarding the World to Come, 'no eye has seen God but You'. This disagrees with Shmuel, who said the only difference between this world and the messianic era is the subjugation to the kingdoms.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that all prophets prophesied only about the days of the Messiah, but for the World to Come, 'no eye has seen God besides You.'
The gemara notes that this statement disagrees with Shmuel, who said there is no difference between this world and the days of the Messiah except for subjugation to the kingdoms.

items.text: Prophecy is for penitents, not for complete righteous
items.text_en: Prophecy is for penitents, not for complete righteous
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says the prophets prophesied only about penitents, but for the completely righteous, 'no eye has seen'. This disagrees with Rabbi Abbahu in the name of Rav, who says that penitents stand in a place where the completely righteous cannot stand. Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'far' and 'near' in Isaiah 57:19 differently.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that all prophets prophesied only for penitents, but for the completely righteous, 'no eye has seen'.
The gemara notes that this disagrees with Rabbi Abbahu in the name of Rav, who says penitents stand in a place where the completely righteous cannot stand.

sub.text: Rabbi Abbahu in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abbahu in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abbahu cites Isaiah 57:19, interpreting 'far' as one who was originally far (a penitent) and 'near' as one who was originally near and remains near (a righteous person).

Rabbi Yochanan offers a different interpretation: 'far' means one who is far from transgression (a righteous person), and 'near' means one who was near to transgression but has distanced himself (a penitent).

items.text: Prophecy is for those who support Torah scholars
items.text_en: Prophecy is for those who support Torah scholars
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says the prophets prophesied only about one who marries his daughter to a Torah scholar, or does business for a Torah scholar, or benefits a Torah scholar from his property. But for Torah scholars themselves, 'no eye has seen'. The Gemara then explains 'no eye has seen' as referring to the wine preserved in its grapes since the six days of creation (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi) or to Eden (Resh Lakish).

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that all prophets prophesied only about one who marries his daughter to a Torah scholar, does business for a Torah scholar, or benefits a Torah scholar from his property, but for Torah scholars themselves, 'no eye has seen'.
The Gemara asks: What is the meaning of 'no eye has seen'?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi answers: This refers to the wine preserved in its grapes since the six days of creation.
Resh Lakish answers: This refers to Eden, which no eye has ever seen.
The Gemara clarifies that Eden and the Garden are distinct, citing the verse 'a river flows from Eden to water the Garden'.

items.text: Interpretations of 'כי דבר ה' בזה' – one who despises the word of God
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'כי דבר ה' בזה' – one who despises the word of God
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a series of tannaitic interpretations of the verse 'כי דבר ה' בזה ומצותו הפר הכרת תכרת'. These include: one who says the Torah is not from Heaven; an epikoros; one who reveals faces in the Torah (interprets it improperly); one who violates the covenant of circumcision; one who desecrates sacred things, despises the festivals, etc. (Rabbi Elazar HaModai). Further interpretations: one who says the whole Torah is from Heaven except one verse (baraita); one who learns Torah but does not teach (Rabbi Meir); one who does not attend to the Mishna (Rabbi Natan); one who can engage in Torah but does not (Rabbi Nehorai); one who worships idolatry (Rabbi Yishmael); one who learns Torah but does not review it (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha); one who learns Torah and forgets it (Rabbi Yehoshua). The section ends with the beginning of Rabbi Akiva's statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the first tannaitic interpretation of the verse 'כי דבר ה' בזה' as referring to one who denies the divine origin of the Torah.
The baraita offers a second interpretation: the verse refers to an epikoros (a heretic who scoffs at the Torah).

The baraita continues: the verse applies to one who improperly interprets the Torah, violates the covenant of circumcision, and desecrates sacred things; Rabbi Elazar HaModai adds that such a person has no share in the World to Come.
Another baraita teaches that even one who accepts the entire Torah except for a single verse or a single exegetical deduction is considered to have despised the word of God.
Rabbi Meir states that one who learns Torah but does not teach it is guilty of despising the word of God.
Rabbi Natan says that one who does not attend to the Mishna is considered to have despised the word of God.
Rabbi Nehorai says that one who is able to engage in Torah study but does not do so is guilty of despising the word of God.
Rabbi Yishmael interprets the verse as referring to an idolater, citing the school of Rabbi Yishmael that despising the word of God includes despising the first two commandments.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says that one who learns Torah but does not review it is like one who sows but does not reap.
Rabbi Yehoshua says that one who learns Torah and forgets it is like a woman who gives birth and buries her child.
The section ends with the beginning of Rabbi Akiva's statement, which continues in the next section.

items.text: The purpose of human toil: Torah study
items.text_en: The purpose of human toil: Torah study
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avudimi and Rabbi Elazar discuss the verse 'For man is born to toil,' concluding that man was created for the toil of Torah, not idle conversation. Rava adds that all bodies are vessels, and fortunate is one who merits to be a vessel of Torah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avudimi interprets the verse 'A toiling soul toils for itself' to mean that one who toils in Torah study has his Torah toil for him elsewhere.
Rabbi Elazar deduces from verses that man was created for the toil of Torah, not idle conversation.
Rava concludes that all bodies are vessels, and fortunate is one who merits to be a vessel of Torah.

items.text: The adulterer of the heart: studying Torah in fragments
items.text_en: The adulterer of the heart: studying Torah in fragments
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish interprets the verse 'An adulterous woman lacks a heart' as referring to one who studies Torah in fragments, citing a verse about keeping words together in one's belly.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish interprets the verse 'נֹאֵף אִשָּׁה חֲסַר לֵב' (an adulterous woman lacks a heart) as referring to one who studies Torah in fragments, citing the verse 'כִּי נָעִים כִּי תִשְׁמְרֵם בְּבִטְנֶךָ יִכֹּנוּ יַחְדָּו עַל שְׂפָתֶיךָ' (for it is pleasant if you keep them in your belly, they will be established together on your lips).

items.text: Menasseh ben Hezekiah and the sin of mocking Torah
items.text_en: Menasseh ben Hezekiah and the sin of mocking Torah
items.desc_en: The Sages identify Menasseh ben Hezekiah as one who 'acts with a high hand' by sitting and expounding heretical homilies. He questioned why Moses wrote seemingly trivial verses, and a heavenly voice rebuked him. The Gemara then explains the verse about drawing iniquity with cords of falsehood, with Rabbi Assi comparing the evil inclination to a spider's thread that becomes thick as a cart rope.

sub.desc_en: The Sages identify Menasseh ben Hezekiah as one who acts with a high hand by sitting and expounding heretical homilies.
Menasseh questions why Moses wrote seemingly trivial verses like 'the sister of Lotan was Timna' and 'Reuben went and found mandrakes in the field'.
A heavenly voice rebukes Menasseh, citing the verse 'You sit and speak against your brother, you slander your own mother's son'.
The Gemara cites the verse 'Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of falsehood and sin as with a cart rope' as applying to Menasseh.
Rabbi Assi explains that the evil inclination (יצר הרע) initially resembles a spider's thread but eventually becomes thick as a cart rope.

items.text: The story of Timna and the mandrakes of Reuben
items.text_en: The story of Timna and the mandrakes of Reuben
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the story of Timna, who sought to convert but was rejected by the patriarchs, becoming a concubine to Eliphaz and giving birth to Amalek. It then discusses Reuben's finding of mandrakes, with various rabbis identifying them as jasmine, violets, or other plants, and notes that the righteous do not steal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the biblical figure Timna, explaining that she was a princess, as indicated by the title 'אלוף' (chieftain) for her and her brother Lotan.

The Gemara recounts that Timna sought to convert but was rejected by the patriarchs, so she became a concubine to Eliphaz, giving birth to Amalek who afflicted Israel, implying the patriarchs should not have distanced her.
Rava bar Yitzchak citing Rav derives from Reuben's finding of mandrakes that the righteous do not steal.
The Gemara asks what the 'דודאים' (mandrakes) are.
Rav identifies the mandrakes as יברוחי (jasmine).
Levi identifies the mandrakes as סיגלי (violets).
Rabbi Yonatan identifies the mandrakes as סביסקי (a type of plant).

items.text: The rewards of Torah study and teaching
items.text_en: The rewards of Torah study and teaching
items.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri says that one who studies Torah for its own sake makes peace in the heavenly and earthly families. Rav, Rabbi Yochanan, and Levi add that it is as if they built palaces, protect the world, and hasten redemption. Reish Lakish, Rabbi Elazar, and Rava teach that teaching Torah to another is considered as if one created them, the words of Torah, or oneself. Rabbi Abahu extends this to causing another to perform a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Alexandri states that one who studies Torah for its own sake makes peace in the heavenly and earthly families, citing a verse.
Rav adds that such a person is considered as if they built palaces above and below, citing a verse.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that such a person also protects the entire world, citing a verse.
Levi adds that such a person hastens the redemption, citing a verse.
Reish Lakish teaches that one who teaches Torah to another is considered as if they created them, citing a verse.
Rabbi Elazar says it is as if they created the words of Torah, citing a verse.
Rava says it is as if they created themselves, using a homiletic reading of a verse.
Rabbi Abahu extends the principle to one who causes another to perform a mitzvah, citing a verse about Moses and Aaron.

items.text: Defining the epikoros and the one who reveals faces in the Torah
items.text_en: Defining the epikoros and the one who reveals faces in the Torah
items.desc_en: Rav and Rabbi Chanina define an epikoros as one who insults a Torah scholar, while Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi say it is one who insults another in front of a scholar. The Gemara distinguishes between an epikoros and one who 'reveals faces in the Torah' (denies the divine origin of Torah). Various examples are given, including Menasseh ben Hezekiah, those who say 'what benefit are the rabbis to us,' and a student who attributes a teaching to himself rather than his teacher.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by presenting two definitions of an epikoros: Rav and Rabbi Chanina say it is one who insults a Torah scholar, while Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi say it is one who insults another in front of a Torah scholar.

The Gemara analyzes the first version of the dispute: according to the opinion that insulting another in front of a scholar is an epikoros, insulting the scholar himself is 'revealing faces in the Torah' (denying Torah's divine origin), and asks what constitutes 'revealing faces' according to the opinion that insulting the scholar himself is an epikoros, answering with the example of Menasseh ben Hezekiah.
The Gemara presents an alternative version of the dispute, where the definitions are applied to 'revealing faces in the Torah' rather than to 'epikoros'.

The Gemara analyzes the alternative version: according to the opinion that insulting a scholar is 'revealing faces', insulting another in front of a scholar is an epikoros, and asks what constitutes an epikoros according to the other opinion, with Rav Yosef answering that it refers to those who say 'what benefit are the rabbis to us'.

Abaye objects that those who say 'what benefit are the rabbis' are also 'revealing faces in the Torah', citing verses that show Torah and rabbis are essential for the world's existence, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports this with another verse.

The Gemara resolves the question by defining an epikoros as a student who attributes a teaching to himself rather than to his teacher, and Rava adds that it also refers to those from the house of Benjamin the physician who say 'what benefit are the rabbis to us at all'.

items.text: Rava's analogy of permitting ravens and forbidding doves
items.text_en: Rava's analogy of permitting ravens and forbidding doves
items.desc_en: Rava uses the analogy of permitting ravens and forbidding doves to describe his rulings on kosher status. When he saw a reason to permit a treifa from the house of Benjamin, he said 'See, I am permitting a raven for you'; when he saw a reason to forbid, he said 'See, I am forbidding a dove for you'.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens with a general statement: they did not permit a raven for us nor forbid a dove for us.
Rava illustrates the principle: when he permitted a treifa from the house of Benjamin, he said 'see, I am permitting a raven for you'; when he forbade, he said 'see, I am forbidding a dove for you'.

items.text: Rav Pappa's statement about saying 'these rabbis'
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's statement about saying 'these rabbis'
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa says that one who says 'these rabbis' (in a derogatory manner) is considered a heretic. He himself once mistakenly said 'like these rabbis' and had to fast as penance.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa defines a heretic as one who says 'these rabbis' derogatorily, and recounts that he himself once mistakenly said 'like these rabbis' and fasted as penance.

items.text: Levi bar Shmuel and Rav Huna bar Chiyya on the Megillat Esther
items.text_en: Levi bar Shmuel and Rav Huna bar Chiyya on the Megillat Esther
items.desc_en: Levi bar Shmuel and Rav Huna bar Chiyya were preparing covers for scrolls in Rav Yehuda's house. When they reached the Megillat Esther, they said it does not need a cover. Rav Yehuda told them that this too appears like disrespect.

sub.desc_en: Levi bar Shmuel and Rav Huna bar Chiyya were preparing covers for scrolls in Rav Yehuda's house, and when they reached the Megillat Esther they said it does not need a cover, but Rav Yehuda told them that this too appears like disrespect.

items.text: Rav Nachman: One who calls his rabbi by name
items.text_en: Rav Nachman: One who calls his rabbi by name
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman says that one who calls his rabbi by his name is a heretic, citing Rabbi Yochanan's statement that Geichazi was punished because he called Elisha by his name, as the verse says 'And Geichazi said, My lord the king, this is the woman and this is her son whom Elisha revived'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that one who calls his rabbi by his name is a heretic.
Rav Nachman supports his statement by citing Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that Geichazi was punished for calling Elisha by his name, as proven from the verse.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's teaching about the future stream and the story of the student who mocked Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's teaching about the future stream and the story of the student who mocked Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya, sitting before Rabbi Zeira, taught that the Holy One will bring forth a stream from the Holy of Holies with all kinds of delicacies. An old man said 'Yishar' (may it be straight), and Rabbi Yochanan also said 'Yishar'. Rabbi Yirmeya asked Rabbi Zeira if this appears like disrespect. Rabbi Zeira responded that the old man was actually supporting him, and then related a story about Rabbi Yochanan teaching that God will bring precious stones thirty by thirty cubits and place them at the gates of Jerusalem. A student mocked him, but later saw angels sawing such stones and repented. Rabbi Yochanan punished him with a glance, turning him into a pile of bones.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya, sitting before Rabbi Zeira, teaches that the Holy One will bring forth a stream from the Holy of Holies bearing all kinds of delicacies, citing a verse.

sub.text: Old man's response and Rabbi Yochanan's agreement
sub.text_en: Old man's response and Rabbi Yochanan's agreement
sub.desc_en: An old man responds 'Yishar' (may it be straight) to Rabbi Yirmeya's teaching, and Rabbi Yochanan is also reported to have said 'Yishar'.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether the old man's response appears like disrespect (אפקירותא).
Rabbi Zeira reassures Rabbi Yirmeya that the old man was actually supporting him, and then introduces a related story about Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's teaching about precious stones
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's teaching about precious stones
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira relates that Rabbi Yochanan taught that God will bring precious stones thirty by thirty cubits and place them at the gates of Jerusalem, citing a verse.
A student mocks Rabbi Yochanan, arguing that if we cannot even find small precious stones now, how can we find such huge ones?
Later, the student's ship is carried out to sea, and he sees angels sawing precious stones of that size, confirming Rabbi Yochanan's teaching.

The student returns, admits his error, and asks Rabbi Yochanan to continue teaching; Rabbi Yochanan rebukes him for mocking the words of the sages and punishes him with a glance, turning him into a pile of bones.

items.text: Objection from the verse 'Vaolech etchem komemiyut' and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the verse 'Vaolech etchem komemiyut' and resolution
items.desc_en: An objection is raised from a baraita where Rabbi Meir says the future height of people will be 200 cubits, like two heights of Adam, and Rabbi Yehuda says 100 cubits, corresponding to the Temple and its walls. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan was speaking about the windows of the Temple (not the people's height).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that interprets the verse 'וָאוֹלֵךְ אֶתְכֶם קוֹמְמִיּוּת' (I led you upright) as referring to the future height of people, with Rabbi Meir saying 200 cubits and Rabbi Yehuda saying 100 cubits, contradicting Rabbi Yochanan's statement about the height of the Temple windows.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that Rabbi Yochanan's statement about the height of 100 cubits referred specifically to the windows of the Temple (דְּבֵי זִיקָא), not to the height of people.

items.text: Interpretations of 've'alehu literufah'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 've'alehu literufah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the meaning of 'and its leaf for healing' (Ezekiel 47:12). Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avudimi and Rav Chisda disagree: one says it opens the mouth of the mute, the other says it opens the mouth of the barren. Chizkiya says it opens the mouth of the mute, bar Kappara says it opens the mouth of the barren, Rabbi Yochanan says it is actual healing, and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says it is for the facial complexion of those who speak.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of 'and its leaf for healing' (Ezekiel 47:12), and presents a dispute between Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avudimi and Rav Chisda: one says it opens the mouth of the mute (upper mouth), the other says it opens the mouth of the barren (lower mouth).

The Gemara cites a parallel tradition: Chizkiya says it opens the mouth of the mute, bar Kappara says it opens the mouth of the barren, Rabbi Yochanan says it is actual healing, and Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says it is for the facial complexion of those who speak.

items.text: Reward for those who study Torah with self-sacrifice
items.text_en: Reward for those who study Torah with self-sacrifice
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Simon teaches that one who darkens his face over words of Torah in this world, God will brighten his countenance in the World to Come. Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai teaches that one who starves himself over words of Torah in this world, God will satisfy him in the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda bar Rabbi Simon teaches that one who darkens his face over words of Torah in this world, God will brighten his countenance in the World to Come, citing a verse.
Rabbi Tanchum bar Rabbi Chanilai adds that one who starves himself over words of Torah in this world, God will satisfy him in the World to Come, citing a verse.

items.text: Rav Dimi's teaching about God giving each righteous person his full load, and Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Rav Dimi's teaching about God giving each righteous person his full load, and Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi says that in the future God will give each righteous person his full load, citing the verse 'Blessed be the Lord, day by day He bears our burden'. Abaye objects, asking how this is possible given the verse 'Who measured the waters in the hollow of His hand and meted out heaven with the span'. Rav Dimi responds by citing a tradition from the West in the name of Rava bar Mari that God will give each righteous person 310 worlds, based on the gematria of 'yesh' (310).

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi teaches that in the future God will give each righteous person his full load, citing the verse 'Blessed be the Lord, day by day He bears our burden'.
Abaye objects, asking how God can give each righteous person his full load when the verse says God measured the heavens with a span, implying limited capacity.

sub.text: Rav Dimi's response citing a tradition from the West
sub.text_en: Rav Dimi's response citing a tradition from the West
sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi responds by citing a tradition from the West in the name of Rava bar Mari that God will give each righteous person 310 worlds, based on the gematria of 'yesh' (310).

items.text: Rabbi Meir's principle of measure for measure and Rabbi Yehoshua's question
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's principle of measure for measure and Rabbi Yehoshua's question
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that Rabbi Meir says with the measure a person measures, they are measured, citing the verse 'In measure, when it is sent forth, you contend with it'. Rabbi Yehoshua questions this, arguing that if a person gives a poor person his full load in this world, can God give him his full load in the World to Come, given the verse 'Who meted out heaven with the span'? He then asks which measure is greater: the measure of goodness or the measure of punishment.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces Rabbi Meir's principle that a person is measured with the same measure they use, citing the verse 'בסאסאה בשלחה תריבנה' (In measure, when it is sent forth, you contend with it).

Rabbi Yehoshua questions Rabbi Meir's principle, arguing that if a person gives a poor person his full load in this world, God cannot give him his full load in the World to Come given the verse 'שמים בזרת תכן' (Who meted out heaven with the span), and then asks which measure is greater: the measure of goodness or the measure of punishment.

items.text: Principle of measure for measure
items.text_en: Principle of measure for measure
items.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that God's attribute of goodness is greater than His attribute of punishment, citing verses about the manna and the flood. It then explains that just as God gives strength to the wicked to endure punishment, so He gives strength to the righteous to receive their reward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that God's attribute of goodness is greater than His attribute of punishment, citing verses about the manna and the flood.
The Gemara questions how the wicked can endure eternal punishment, given that even a finger in fire is immediately burned.
The Gemara answers that God gives strength to the wicked to endure punishment, and similarly gives strength to the righteous to receive their reward.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's statement on external books
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's statement on external books
items.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: Rabbi Akiva says one who reads external books has no portion in the World to Come. The Gemara clarifies that these are books of heretics. Rav Yosef adds that even the book of Ben Sira is forbidden to read.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: Rabbi Akiva says one who reads external books has no portion in the World to Come.
A Tanna clarifies that the external books are books of heretics.
Rav Yosef adds that even the book of Ben Sira is forbidden to read.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef for the reason why the book of Ben Sira is forbidden.
Abaye objects that if the reason is a verse about not wasting skin, the Torah itself says not to destroy a fruit tree, and the verse merely teaches derekh eretz.
Abaye objects that if the reason is a verse about the burden of daughters, the rabbis themselves said similar things.
Abaye objects that if the reason is a verse about not bringing worry into the heart, King Solomon and the rabbis said similar things.
Abaye objects that if the reason is a verse about limiting guests, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said the same.
Abaye objects that if the reason is a verse about a stingy person, it is merely practical advice.
Rav Yosef resolves that the good sayings in Ben Sira may be expounded, but the book as a whole is forbidden.

items.text: Abaye's first objection: the verse about not wasting wood
items.text_en: Abaye's first objection: the verse about not wasting wood
items.desc_en: Abaye questions Rav Yosef's ruling, suggesting that the reason might be a verse in Ben Sira about not wasting wood. He argues that this is either already in the Torah or teaches proper conduct, so it cannot be a reason to forbid the book.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef why the book of Ben Sira is forbidden, suggesting it might be because of a verse about not wasting wood, and argues that this either is already in the Torah or teaches proper conduct, so it cannot be a reason to forbid the book.

items.text: Abaye's second objection: the verse about daughters
items.text_en: Abaye's second objection: the verse about daughters
items.desc_en: Abaye suggests another possible reason: a verse in Ben Sira about the troubles of having a daughter. But he notes that the Sages themselves said similar things, so this too cannot be a reason to forbid the book.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the verse in Ben Sira about the troubles of having a daughter cannot be the reason to forbid the book, because the Sages themselves said similar things.

items.text: Abaye's third objection: the verse about worry
items.text_en: Abaye's third objection: the verse about worry
items.desc_en: Abaye suggests another possible reason: a verse about not letting worry enter the heart. But he notes that King Solomon already said something similar, and the Sages debated its interpretation, so this too cannot be a reason to forbid the book.

sub.desc_en: Abaye proposes that the book of Ben Sira is forbidden because it contains the verse 'Do not bring worry into your heart, for worry has killed mighty men.'

Abaye notes that King Solomon already said a similar idea in Proverbs, and the Sages (Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi) debated its interpretation, so this verse cannot be a unique reason to forbid the book.

items.text: Abaye's fourth objection: the verse about not bringing everyone into your house
items.text_en: Abaye's fourth objection: the verse about not bringing everyone into your house
items.desc_en: Abaye suggests another possible reason: a verse about not bringing many people into your house. But he notes that Rabbi himself said something similar, so this too cannot be a reason to forbid the book.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the verse 'מְנַע רַבִּים מִתּוֹךְ בֵּיתֶךָ' (keep many out of your house) might be the reason to forbid Ben Sira, but he questions this.

Abaye rejects this, noting that Rabbi himself taught the same principle from the verse 'אִישׁ רֵעִים לְהִתְרוֹעֵעַ' (a man of many friends comes to ruin), so this cannot be a unique reason to forbid the book.

items.text: Abaye's fifth objection: the verse about the stingy man
items.text_en: Abaye's fifth objection: the verse about the stingy man
items.desc_en: Abaye suggests another possible reason: a verse about a stingy man who does not share his bread. But this is just common sense, so it cannot be a reason to forbid the book.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the verse about the stingy man is merely common sense, so it cannot be a reason to forbid the book of Ben Sira.

items.text: Rav Yosef's conclusion: only worthy teachings are expounded
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's conclusion: only worthy teachings are expounded
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef concludes that the worthy teachings in Ben Sira, such as those about good and bad wives, may be expounded. He then cites several such teachings from Ben Sira, including advice about women, worry, and the poor.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef rules that the worthy teachings in Ben Sira may be expounded, and cites Ben Sira's sayings about good and bad wives.
Rav Yosef continues citing Ben Sira's advice about avoiding temptation, guarding secrets, and not worrying about tomorrow.
Rav Yosef cites Ben Sira's saying that the poor have bad days and nights, with a poetic description of their lowly dwelling and high vineyard.

items.text: Siman (mnemonic)
items.text_en: Siman (mnemonic)
items.desc_en: A mnemonic is provided listing the names of the rabbis who will offer interpretations of the verse 'All the days of the poor are evil'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a mnemonic listing the names of the rabbis who will interpret the verse 'All the days of the poor are evil'.

items.text: Interpretations of 'All the days of the poor are evil'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'All the days of the poor are evil'
items.desc_en: Various rabbis offer interpretations of the verse: Rabbi Zeira says it refers to Talmud scholars, Rava says the opposite, Rabbi Chanina says it refers to one with a bad wife, Rabbi Yannai says it refers to a fastidious person, Rabbi Yochanan says it refers to a merciful person, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says it refers to... (the text breaks off).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav interprets the verse 'All the days of the poor are evil' as referring to Talmud scholars, and 'a good heart is a constant feast' as referring to Mishnah scholars.
Rava reverses the interpretation, citing Rav Mesharshiya that Mishnah scholars are the 'movers of stones' and Talmud scholars are the 'splitters of wood'.
Rabbi Chanina interprets the verse as referring to a man with a bad wife, and the second half to a man with a good wife.
Rabbi Yannai interprets the verse as referring to a fastidious person, and the second half to one with a good disposition.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse as referring to a merciful person, and the second half to a cruel person.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi begins his interpretation of the verse, but the text breaks off before completing it.

items.text: Interpretation of verses about good and bad days
items.text_en: Interpretation of verses about good and bad days
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets verses from Proverbs about a bad heart and a good heart, and cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi on the days of the poor being bad. It questions whether Shabbat and holidays are included, and answers with Shmuel's statement that a change in routine is the beginning of intestinal illness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'וְטוֹב לֵב מִשְׁתֶּה תָמִיד' as referring to one with a broad mind.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that all the days of a poor person are bad.
The Gemara questions whether Shabbat and holidays are included in the bad days.
Shmuel explains that a change in routine is the beginning of intestinal illness, implying that even on Shabbat and holidays, the poor person's routine change causes discomfort.

items.text: Prohibition of using Torah verses as a song or at a banquet
items.text_en: Prohibition of using Torah verses as a song or at a banquet
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that one who recites a verse from Song of Songs as a song, or recites a verse at a banquet out of its proper time, brings evil to the world. The Torah complains to God, who suggests that people should engage in Torah study instead. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar testifies that one who recites a verse at its proper time brings good to the world.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach that reciting a Song of Songs verse as a song or a verse at a banquet out of its proper time brings evil to the world, as the Torah complains to God.
God asks the Torah what people should occupy themselves with while eating and drinking.

The Torah responds that people should engage in Torah, Prophets, Writings, Mishnah, halachot, aggadot, or Talmud according to their level, specifically studying the laws of each festival in its season.

sub.text: Testimony of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Testimony of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar testifies in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Chananya that one who recites a verse at its proper time brings good to the world, citing the verse 'And a word in its time, how good it is'.

items.text: Whispering over a wound and spitting
items.text_en: Whispering over a wound and spitting
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses one who whispers over a wound. Rabbi Yochanan adds that one must spit, because God's name is not mentioned over spittle. Rav and Rabbi Chanina debate which verses are included in the prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited, introducing the topic of one who whispers over a wound.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that one must spit on the wound, because God's name is not mentioned over spittle.
Rav and Rabbi Chanina debate which verses are included in the prohibition of whispering over a wound.

items.text: Permitted actions on Shabbat for healing and incantations
