items.text_en: Permitted actions on Shabbat for healing and incantations
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that one may anoint and massage the intestines on Shabbat, whisper incantations for snakes and scorpions, and pass a vessel over the eye. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel limits this to a vessel that may be moved. One may not consult demons on Shabbat, and Rabbi Yosei forbids it even on weekdays. Rav Huna rules like Rabbi Yosei, and explains the danger with a story about Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists permitted healing actions on Shabbat: anointing and massaging the intestines, whispering incantations for snakes and scorpions, and passing a vessel over the eye.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel qualifies the rule about passing a vessel over the eye: it is permitted only with a vessel that may be moved on Shabbat (כלי הניטל), but forbidden with one that may not be moved (כלי שאינו ניטל).
The baraita states that one may not consult demons on Shabbat.
Rabbi Yosei forbids consulting demons even on weekdays.
Rav Huna rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yosei.
The gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei's prohibition is only due to danger, not because consulting demons is inherently forbidden.

sub.text: Story about Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef
sub.desc_en: The gemara supports the danger claim with a story: Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef was swallowed by a cedar tree and was saved only by a miracle when the tree split and expelled him.

items.text: Method of anointing and massaging on Shabbat
items.text_en: Method of anointing and massaging on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that one may anoint and massage on Shabbat, provided it is not done in the usual weekday manner. Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yochanan debate the proper order: anoint then massage, or both simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach a baraita that one may anoint and massage the intestines on Shabbat, provided it is not done in the usual weekday manner.
The Gemara asks: How should one perform this action (anoint and massage) on Shabbat?
Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina answers: One anoints first and then massages.
Rabbi Yochanan answers: One anoints and massages simultaneously.

items.text: Divination with oil and eggs, and a story about healing
items.text_en: Divination with oil and eggs, and a story about healing
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that one may consult oil and eggs for divination, but they are unreliable. Whispering is done over oil in a vessel, not on the hand. A story is told about Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta who was healed by a woman after a failed oil divination.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that one may consult oil and eggs for divination, though they are unreliable, and prescribes whispering over oil in a vessel but not on the hand.

sub.text: Story (Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta)
sub.text_en: Story (Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta)
sub.desc_en: A story is told about Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta who, after a failed oil divination, was healed by a woman who recognized the problem.

items.text: Interpretation of the verse about God as healer
items.text_en: Interpretation of the verse about God as healer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba asks Rabba bar Mari about the verse that says God will not place the diseases of Egypt on Israel but is their healer. Rabba bar Mari explains that Rabbi Yochanan interpreted the verse: if you listen, I will not place; if not, I will place, but still I am your healer.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba asks Rabba bar Mari why the verse promises healing if God says He will not place the diseases.

sub.text: Rabba bar Mari's answer in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Mari's answer in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Mari explains that Rabbi Yochanan interpreted the verse as conditional: if you listen, I will not place the diseases; if not, I will place them, but still I am your healer.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's illness and Rabbi Akiva's joy at suffering
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's illness and Rabbi Akiva's joy at suffering
items.desc_en: When Rabbi Eliezer fell ill, his students visited and wept, but Rabbi Akiva laughed. He explained that he was happy because Rabbi Eliezer's suffering indicated he had not yet received his full reward in this world. Rabbi Eliezer asked if he had lacked any Torah, and Rabbi Akiva cited the verse that no one is so righteous as to never sin.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports that when Rabbi Eliezer fell ill, his students wept but Rabbi Akiva laughed.
The students ask Rabbi Akiva why he laughs while they weep over the suffering of their Torah teacher.
Rabbi Akiva explains that he rejoices because Rabbi Eliezer's suffering shows he has not yet received his full reward in this world.
Rabbi Eliezer asks Rabbi Akiva if he has lacked any Torah knowledge.
Rabbi Akiva cites the verse that no one is so righteous as to never sin, implying that suffering atones for minor sins.

items.text: Four elders visit Rabbi Eliezer and praise him
items.text_en: Four elders visit Rabbi Eliezer and praise him
items.desc_en: When Rabbi Eliezer fell ill, four elders visited: Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, and Rabbi Akiva. Each praised him, comparing him to rain, the sun, and parents. Rabbi Akiva declared that suffering is precious, and Rabbi Eliezer asked to hear his reasoning. Rabbi Akiva derived from the verse about Menashe that even a righteous person suffers for his sins.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the story of four elders visiting the ill Rabbi Eliezer.
Rabbi Tarfon praises Rabbi Eliezer, comparing him to rain that benefits only this world, while Rabbi Eliezer benefits both worlds.
Rabbi Yehoshua praises Rabbi Eliezer, comparing him to the sun that benefits only this world, while Rabbi Eliezer benefits both worlds.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya praises Rabbi Eliezer, comparing him to parents who benefit only this world, while Rabbi Eliezer benefits both worlds.
Rabbi Akiva declares that suffering is precious, prompting Rabbi Eliezer to ask for his reasoning.
Rabbi Akiva answers Rabbi Eliezer's question by deriving from the verse about Menashe that even a righteous person suffers for his sins.

items.text: Suffering is precious: the lesson from Menashe
items.text_en: Suffering is precious: the lesson from Menashe
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the proverbs of Solomon were copied by Hezekiah's men, noting that Hezekiah taught Torah to the whole world but failed to teach his own son Menashe. It answers that only suffering brought Menashe to repentance, as shown by the verses describing his distress and prayer, concluding that suffering is beloved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Hezekiah's men copied Solomon's proverbs, given that Hezekiah taught Torah to the whole world but failed to teach his own son Menashe.
The Gemara answers that only suffering (יסורין) brought Menashe to repentance, citing verses about his distress and prayer, concluding that suffering is beloved.

items.text: Three who came with a pretext: Cain, Esau, and Menashe
items.text_en: Three who came with a pretext: Cain, Esau, and Menashe
items.desc_en: The Sages teach that three individuals came with a pretext (בעלילה): Cain, who claimed his sin was too great to forgive; Esau, who complained about a single blessing; and Menashe, who initially called upon many gods but later turned to the God of his fathers.

sub.desc_en: The Sages teach that three individuals came with a pretext (בעלילה): Cain, Esau, and Menashe.
Cain's pretext is cited from the verse 'גָּדוֹל עֲוֹנִי מִנְּשׂוֹא' (my sin is too great to bear), arguing that his sin is greater than the sixty myriads who will sin and be forgiven.
Esau's pretext is cited from the verse 'הַבְרָכָה אַחַת הִיא לָךְ אָבִי' (is there only one blessing for you, my father?), complaining about a single blessing.
Menashe's pretext is that initially he called upon many gods, but ultimately he called upon the God of his fathers.

items.text: Abba Shaul's addition: one who pronounces the Name
items.text_en: Abba Shaul's addition: one who pronounces the Name
items.desc_en: Abba Shaul adds to the list of those who have no share in the World to Come: one who pronounces the Tetragrammaton as it is written. A Tanna adds that this applies in the provinces (outside the Temple) and in a secular language.

sub.desc_en: Abba Shaul adds to the list of those who have no share in the World to Come: one who pronounces the Tetragrammaton as it is written.
A Tanna adds that this prohibition applies in the provinces (outside the Temple) and when using a secular language.

items.text: Etymologies of Jeroboam and his father Nebat
items.text_en: Etymologies of Jeroboam and his father Nebat
items.desc_en: The Sages explain the name Jeroboam (ירבעם) through multiple interpretations: he stirred up strife among the people and between Israel and their Father in Heaven. His father Nebat is identified with Michah and Sheva ben Bichri, with explanations for each name.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the first etymology of Jeroboam: he made the people numerous (ריבה עם).
A second interpretation: Jeroboam stirred up strife (מריבה) among the people.
A third interpretation: Jeroboam stirred up strife between Israel and their Father in Heaven.
The baraita explains Nebat's name: he had a prophetic vision (ניבט) but did not see its fulfillment.
A Tanna identifies Nebat with Michah and Sheva ben Bichri, asserting they are the same person.
The Tanna repeats the etymology of Nebat: he prophesied but did not see fulfillment.
The Tanna explains Michah's name: he was crushed (נתמכמך) in the building (of the golden calf).
The Tanna concludes that his real name is Sheva ben Bichri.

items.text: Three who prophesied but did not see: Nebat, Ahitophel, and Pharaoh's astrologers
items.text_en: Three who prophesied but did not see: Nebat, Ahitophel, and Pharaoh's astrologers
items.desc_en: The Sages list three who prophesied but did not see the fulfillment: Nebat, Ahitophel, and Pharaoh's astrologers. Nebat saw fire emerging from his membrum and thought he would rule, but it was Jeroboam. Ahitophel saw leprosy on his membrum and thought he would rule, but it was Solomon. Pharaoh's astrologers saw that Israel's savior would be punished through water and decreed drowning, but they erred—it was the waters of Meribah.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing three who prophesied but did not see the fulfillment: Nebat, Ahitophel, and Pharaoh's astrologers.
The baraita explains that Nebat saw fire emerging from his membrum and thought he would rule, but it was Jeroboam who came from him.
The baraita explains that Ahitophel saw leprosy on his membrum and thought he would rule, but it was Solomon who came from his daughter Bathsheba.

sub.text: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina — explanation of Pharaoh's astrologers
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina — explanation of Pharaoh's astrologers
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Rabbi Chanina explains that Pharaoh's astrologers saw that Israel's savior would be punished through water and decreed drowning, but they erred—it was the waters of Meribah.

items.text: Jeroboam's exclusion from the World to Come
items.text_en: Jeroboam's exclusion from the World to Come
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves that Jeroboam has no share in the World to Come from the verse 'to cut off and to destroy from the face of the earth'—'to cut off' refers to this world, 'to destroy' to the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we know that Jeroboam has no share in the World to Come?
The Gemara answers by citing the verse 'to cut off and to destroy from the face of the earth' and interprets 'to cut off' as this world and 'to destroy' as the World to Come.

items.text: Why Jeroboam merited kingship and why he was punished
items.text_en: Why Jeroboam merited kingship and why he was punished
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Jeroboam merited kingship because he rebuked Solomon, but was punished because he did so publicly. Rav Nachman adds that Jeroboam removed his tefillin in Solomon's presence, and his arrogance led him to sin. The Gemara details Jeroboam's fear that the people would return to Rehoboam, leading him to set up golden calves, and recounts his consultation with a righteous and a wicked man.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks why Jeroboam merited kingship and answers that it was because he rebuked Solomon.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that Jeroboam was punished because he rebuked Solomon publicly, citing the verse about closing the breach for Pharaoh's daughter.
Rav Nachman explains that Jeroboam's disrespect was removing his tefillin in Solomon's presence.
Rav Nachman states that Jeroboam's arrogance drove him from the world, citing his fear that the people would return to Rehoboam.
The Gemara explains Jeroboam's reasoning: only kings of Judah may sit in the Temple courtyard, so he feared being seen as a rebel and set up golden calves in Bethel and Dan.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda's explanation of the consultation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's explanation of the consultation
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda explains that Jeroboam seated a wicked man next to a righteous man, and the wicked man convinced the righteous that Jeroboam only wanted to test them, not to actually worship idols.

items.text: Why Ahijah signed for Jeroboam
items.text_en: Why Ahijah signed for Jeroboam
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Ahijah the Shilonite signed the prophecy for Jeroboam, given that Jehu was a great righteous person. Abaye and Rava offer explanations: Abaye says a covenant is established with the lips (the words spoken), while Rava says Ahijah saw the seal of Ahijah and erred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Ahijah the Shilonite signed the prophecy for Jeroboam, given that Jehu was a great righteous person yet later sinned.
Abaye explains that a covenant is established with the lips (the words spoken), citing the verse where Ahab served Baal a little and Jehu would serve him much.
Rava explains that Ahijah saw the seal of Ahijah (the prophet) and erred, mistaking Jeroboam for someone worthy.

items.text: The depth of their sin
items.text_en: The depth of their sin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse 'They have made deep the slaughter of the idols' to mean that God said they deepened from what was His, contrasting God's command that one who does not ascend for the festival violates a positive commandment with their statement that one who ascends should be killed by the sword.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse to mean that God said they deepened from what was His, contrasting God's command that one who does not ascend for the festival violates a positive commandment with their statement that one who ascends should be killed by the sword.

items.text: Times and places designated for punishment
items.text_en: Times and places designated for punishment
items.desc_en: A series of teachings in the name of Rabbi Yosei identify various times and places as designated for punishment: the time when Jeroboam went out from Jerusalem, the time of their visitation, the day of visitation, and the place Shechem, where multiple sins occurred.

sub.text: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: The Tanna cites the verse about Jeroboam leaving Jerusalem and declares that this time was designated for punishment.

sub.text: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: The Tanna cites additional verses about 'the time of their visitation' and 'the day of visitation,' each designated for punishment, and one verse designated for good.

sub.text: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.text_en: Tanna in the name of Rabbi Yosei
sub.desc_en: The Tanna cites the verse about Rehoboam going to Shechem and declares that Shechem was a place designated for punishment, listing sins that occurred there.

items.text: Interpretations of the encounter between Ahijah and Jeroboam
items.text_en: Interpretations of the encounter between Ahijah and Jeroboam
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa explains that Jeroboam went out from the 'pitka' of Jerusalem. Rav Nachman interprets the 'new cloak' as meaning his Torah was without blemish, and another interpretation says they innovated things never heard. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains 'both of them alone in the field' as all Torah scholars being like grass before them, or all reasons of Torah being revealed to them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa explains that Jeroboam went out from the 'pitka' (the small opening) of Jerusalem.
The gemara asks what is meant by the 'new cloak' (שַׂלְמָה חֲדָשָׁה) in the verse.
Rav Nachman interprets the 'new cloak' as meaning that Jeroboam's Torah was without any blemish, just as a new garment has no defect.
Another interpretation states that the 'new cloak' refers to Jeroboam and his followers innovating halachic teachings that had never been heard before.
The gemara asks what is meant by the phrase 'both of them alone in the field'.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that all Torah scholars appeared before Ahijah and Jeroboam like grass of the field, i.e., insignificant in comparison.
An alternative explanation states that all reasons of the Torah were revealed to them as clearly as an open field.

items.text: The bat kol and the sin of benefiting without a blessing
items.text_en: The bat kol and the sin of benefiting without a blessing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa says a bat kol told them that those who killed Goliath and gave them Gath should not send gifts to his sons. He then teaches that one who benefits from this world without a blessing is like one who robs God and the Congregation of Israel, and is a companion to Jeroboam who corrupted Israel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa explains that a bat kol (heavenly voice) rebuked those who sent gifts to the sons of the one who killed Goliath and gave them Gath.

Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa teaches that one who benefits from this world without a blessing (ברכה) is like one who robs God and the Congregation of Israel, citing verses that identify God as 'father' and the Congregation of Israel as 'mother'.
The gemara clarifies that the 'companion to a destroyer' in the verse refers to Jeroboam ben Nevat, who corrupted Israel before their Father in Heaven.

items.text: The severity of Jeroboam's sin and the golden calf
items.text_en: The severity of Jeroboam's sin and the golden calf
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanin compares Jeroboam's sin to two sticks striking each other. The school of Rabbi Yannai says that the abundance of silver and gold caused Israel to make a golden calf, like a lion that only attacks from a basket of meat. Rabbi Oshaya says until Jeroboam, Israel nursed from one calf, but afterward from two or three. Rabbi Yitzchak says every punishment contains a fraction of the first calf. Rabbi Chanina says this verse was collected after 24 generations.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanin compares Jeroboam's sin to two sticks striking each other, illustrating mutual reinforcement of evil.
The school of Rabbi Yannai explains that the abundance of silver and gold caused Israel to make the golden calf, using a parable of a lion attacking from a meat basket.
Rabbi Oshaya states that until Jeroboam, Israel nursed from one calf, but afterward from two or three calves.
Rabbi Yitzchak teaches that every punishment contains one twenty-fourth of the first calf's sin, citing the verse 'ובפקוד פקדתי' (and I will remember their sin).
Rabbi Chanina concludes that this verse was collected after 24 generations, citing the verse 'קרובו פקודות העיר' (draw near, visitations of the city).

items.text: Jeroboam's refusal to repent
items.text_en: Jeroboam's refusal to repent
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba explains that after God seized Jeroboam by his garment and offered him to walk in the Garden of Eden with God and the son of Jesse, Jeroboam refused because the son of Jesse would be first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'after' in the verse refers to.

Rabbi Abba explains that after God seized Jeroboam by his garment and offered him to walk in the Garden of Eden with God and the son of Jesse, Jeroboam refused because the son of Jesse would be first.
Jeroboam asks who will lead, and is told the son of Jesse (David) will be first.
Jeroboam refuses the offer because he would not be first.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's practice regarding the three kings
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's practice regarding the three kings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu was accustomed to expound on the three kings (who have no share in the World to Come), but became weak and accepted upon himself not to expound.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rabbi Avahu was accustomed to expound on the three kings (who have no share in the World to Come), but became weak and accepted upon himself not to expound.

items.text: Rav Ashi's dream encounter with King Manasseh
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's dream encounter with King Manasseh
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi prepares to lecture on the three kings, but Manasseh appears to him in a dream, rebuking him for calling him a 'friend'. Manasseh tests Rav Ashi on the law of 'hamotzi', then explains why he worshipped idolatry: if Rav Ashi had been in his place, he would have done the same. Rav Ashi then changes his lecture topic to 'rabbvota' (the great ones).

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi sets up a lecture on the three kings and announces he will open with 'friends'.
Manasseh appears to Rav Ashi in a dream and rebukes him for calling the wicked kings 'friends'.
Manasseh tests Rav Ashi on the law of where to begin cutting the bread for the blessing 'המוציא' (Who brings forth bread from the earth).
Manasseh teaches Rav Ashi that the blessing is recited over the place where the bread is most baked (the crust).
Rav Ashi asks Manasseh why he worshipped idolatry despite his wisdom.
Manasseh explains that if Rav Ashi had been in his place, he too would have succumbed to idolatry.
The next day, Rav Ashi changes his lecture topic to 'the great ones' (rabbvota) instead of the three kings.

items.text: Etymology of Ahab's name
items.text_en: Etymology of Ahab's name
items.desc_en: Ahab's name is interpreted as 'brother to Heaven' (אח לשמים) and 'father to idolatry' (אב לעבודה זרה), based on verses about brotherhood and fatherly mercy.

sub.desc_en: The gemara interprets Ahab's name as 'brother to Heaven' and 'father to idolatry'.
The gemara cites verses to support each part of the etymology: 'a brother is born for adversity' and 'as a father has mercy on children'.

items.text: Ahab's sins and exclusion from the World to Come
items.text_en: Ahab's sins and exclusion from the World to Come
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Ahab's 'light' sins were as severe as Jeroboam's 'heavy' ones, and that Ahab placed idolatry on every furrow in Israel. The Gemara proves Ahab has no share in the World to Come from the verse 'I will cut off from Ahab...' interpreting 'atzur' as this world and 'azuv' as the next.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Ahab's 'light' sins were as severe as Jeroboam's 'heavy' ones, and that the verse attributes them to Jeroboam because he initiated the corruption.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that Ahab placed idolatry on every furrow in the land of Israel.
The Gemara proves that Ahab has no share in the World to Come from the verse 'I will cut off from Ahab...' interpreting 'atzur' as this world and 'azuv' as the next.

items.text: Why Omri and Ahab merited kingship
items.text_en: Why Omri and Ahab merited kingship
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that Omri merited kingship for adding a city (Samaria). Ahab merited 22 years of kingship for honoring the Torah, which was given with 22 letters. The Gemara identifies 'every desirable thing of your eyes' as a Torah scroll, rejecting the possibility of idolatry because the elders and people advised against it, and because there were righteous people in Israel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks why Omri merited kingship and answers that it was because he added a city (Samaria) in the land of Israel.

Rabbi Yochanan asks why Ahab merited 22 years of kingship and answers that it was because he honored the Torah, which was given with 22 letters, as shown by his refusal to hand over a Torah scroll to Ben Hadad.
The Gemara asks what 'every desirable thing of your eyes' refers to, suggesting it is a Torah scroll.
The Gemara objects that it might be idolatry, but rejects this because the elders and people advised against it, though it notes that the elders of Absalom were also corrupt.
The Gemara resolves that the phrase 'and all the people' indicates there were righteous people in Israel, so the 'desirable thing' must be a Torah scroll, not idolatry.

items.text: Was Ahab balanced? Rav Nachman vs. Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Was Ahab balanced? Rav Nachman vs. Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman says Ahab was 'shakul' (balanced), citing the verse where God asks who will entice Ahab. Rav Yosef objects, noting Ahab was sold to evil and his wife weighed gold for idolatry daily. Rav Yosef concludes Ahab was generous with his money, and because he benefited Torah scholars, half his sins were atoned.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman asserts that Ahab was 'shakul' (balanced in merits and sins), citing the verse where God asks who will entice Ahab to fall at Ramot Gilead.
Rav Yosef objects, citing the verse that Ahab 'sold himself to do evil' and the tradition that Jezebel weighed gold for idolatry daily, arguing Ahab cannot be called balanced.
Rav Yosef resolves that Ahab was generous with his money, and because he benefited Torah scholars from his wealth, half his sins were atoned.

items.text: The spirit of Naboth and the meaning of 'go out'
items.text_en: The spirit of Naboth and the meaning of 'go out'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan identifies the 'spirit' that stood before God as the spirit of Naboth the Jezreelite. Ravina explains 'go out' means 'go out from My partition', as liars cannot stand before God. Rav Papa notes the folk saying: one who tears down his neighbor's house destroys his own.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the identity of the 'spirit' that stood before God.
Rabbi Yochanan identifies the spirit as the spirit of Naboth the Jezreelite.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the word 'צֵא' (go out) in the verse.
Ravina explains that 'צֵא' means 'go out from My partition', citing the verse that liars cannot stand before God.
Rav Papa notes the folk saying that one who tears down his neighbor's house destroys his own.

items.text: Ahab's inscription and Ahaziah's concealment
items.text_en: Ahab's inscription and Ahaziah's concealment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says Ahab wrote on the gates of Samaria 'Ahab denied the God of Israel', therefore he has no portion in the God of Israel. Rabbi Levi explains that Ahaziah was captured while hiding in Samaria because he would scrape off the Divine Name and write idolatry underneath.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Ahab wrote on the gates of Samaria that he denied the God of Israel, therefore he has no portion in the God of Israel.
Rabbi Levi explains that Ahaziah was captured while hiding in Samaria because he would scrape off the Divine Name and write idolatry underneath.

items.text: Manasseh's exclusion and the dispute over his repentance
items.text_en: Manasseh's exclusion and the dispute over his repentance
items.desc_en: Manasseh's name is interpreted as 'he forgot God' or 'he caused Israel to forget'. The Gemara proves he has no share in the World to Come by comparing him to Ahab. Rabbi Yehuda argues Manasseh does have a share because he prayed and was answered. Rabbi Yochanan says both derive from the same verse: one holds that Manasseh repented but the generation did not, and the other holds otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the name Manasseh as 'he forgot God' or 'he caused Israel to forget their Father in Heaven'.
The Gemara proves Manasseh has no share in the World to Come by comparing him to Ahab through the verse that says he did as Ahab did.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that Manasseh does have a share in the World to Come, citing the verse that he prayed and God was entreated by him.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves the dispute by explaining that both derive from the same verse: one holds that Manasseh repented but the generation did not, and the other holds otherwise.

items.text: Manasseh's repentance and its duration
items.text_en: Manasseh's repentance and its duration
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Manasseh was excluded from the World to Come because he did not repent, but Rabbi Yochanan argues that saying he has no portion weakens the hands of penitents. A baraita taught before Rabbi Yochanan states that Manasseh repented for 33 years, derived from the length of his reign compared to Ahab's.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that Manasseh was excluded from the World to Come because he did not repent.
Rabbi Yochanan objects that saying Manasseh has no portion in the World to Come weakens the hands of penitents.
A baraita taught before Rabbi Yochanan provides evidence that Manasseh repented for 33 years, derived from the length of his reign compared to Ahab's.

items.text: God's acceptance of Manasseh's repentance
items.text_en: God's acceptance of Manasseh's repentance
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai explains the verse 'and He heard him and granted his request' (וַיֵּחָתֶר לוֹ) as meaning God made a kind of opening in the firmament to accept his repentance, despite the attribute of justice.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai explains that the unusual word 'וַיֵּחָתֶר' (and He made a breach) teaches that God created a hidden opening in the firmament to accept Manasseh's repentance, circumventing the attribute of justice.

items.text: God's consideration of Jehoiakim and Zedekiah's generations
items.text_en: God's consideration of Jehoiakim and Zedekiah's generations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai questions why the verse mentions 'the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim' and 'the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah' separately. The Gemara explains that God sought to destroy the world because of Jehoiakim but was appeased by his generation, and similarly for Zedekiah's generation, but was appeased by Zedekiah himself, though he was wicked for not rebuking others.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai asks why the verse mentions 'the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim' and 'the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah' separately, implying that there were no kings before them.
The Gemara explains that God sought to destroy the world because of Jehoiakim, but was appeased by his generation.
The Gemara explains that God sought to destroy the world because of Zedekiah's generation, but was appeased by Zedekiah himself, though he was wicked for failing to rebuke others.

items.text: God's anger with Ahaz and laughter with Amaziah
items.text_en: God's anger with Ahaz and laughter with Amaziah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai explains a verse about a wise man and a fool: God was angry with Ahaz and gave him over to the kings of Damascus, leading him to worship their gods. God laughed with Amaziah and gave him victory over Edom, but he then worshipped their gods. Rav Pappa comments on the popular saying about a master who cannot distinguish good from bad.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai asks about the verse 'A wise man judges a fool, and he rages and laughs, and there is no rest', and explains that God was angry with Ahaz and gave him over to the kings of Damascus, leading him to worship their gods.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan continues: God laughed with Amaziah and gave him victory over Edom, but he then worshipped their gods, as the verse states.
Rav Pappa comments on the popular saying about a master who cannot distinguish good from bad.

items.text: The place where halakhot are decided
items.text_en: The place where halakhot are decided
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai interprets 'the gate of the middle' (שַׁעַר הַתָּוֶךְ) as the place where halakhot are cut (decided). Rav Pappa comments on the popular saying about a place where the master hangs his weapons.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai interprets 'the gate of the middle' (שַׁעַר הַתָּוֶךְ) as the place where halakhot are cut (decided).
Rav Pappa supports the interpretation with a popular saying: in a place where the master hangs his weapons, a poor shepherd hangs his own sling.

items.text: Allegorical interpretation of the lazy man's field
items.text_en: Allegorical interpretation of the lazy man's field
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda quoting Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba interprets the verse about the field of a lazy man as referring to Ahaz, the vineyard of a senseless man as Manasseh, the thorns as Amon, the nettles as Jehoiakim, and the broken stone wall as Zedekiah, in whose days the Temple was destroyed.

sub.text: Rav Chisda quoting Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda quoting Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba interprets the verse about the lazy man's field allegorically, identifying each element with a wicked king of Judah.

items.text: Four groups that do not receive the Divine Presence
items.text_en: Four groups that do not receive the Divine Presence
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda quoting Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba lists four groups that do not receive the Divine Presence: scoffers, liars, flatterers, and slanderers, each supported by a biblical verse.

sub.text: Rav Chisda quoting Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda quoting Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba lists four groups that do not receive the Divine Presence: scoffers, liars, flatterers, and slanderers, each supported by a biblical verse.

items.text: Interpretation of the blessing 'No evil shall befall you'
items.text_en: Interpretation of the blessing 'No evil shall befall you'
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda quoting Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba interprets the verse 'No evil shall befall you' as protection from the evil inclination, and 'no plague shall come near your tent' as protection from a wife being a doubtful menstruant. An alternative interpretation: protection from bad dreams and thoughts, and from a son or student who embarrasses in public, like Jesus the Nazarene. The Gemara notes that up to this point the father blessed, then the mother blessed, and then heaven blessed.

sub.text: Rav Chisda quoting Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda quoting Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba interprets the verse 'No evil shall befall you' as protection from the evil inclination, and 'no plague shall come near your tent' as protection from finding one's wife a doubtful menstruant upon returning from a journey.

An alternative interpretation: 'No evil shall befall you' means protection from bad dreams and evil thoughts, and 'no plague shall come near your tent' means protection from a son or student who embarrasses in public, like Jesus the Nazarene.
The Gemara notes that up to this point the father blessed, and from here onward the mother blessed, citing the verses about angels guarding on all paths and treading on lion and viper.
The Gemara concludes that up to this point the mother blessed, and from here onward heaven blessed.

items.text: Opening verse
items.text_en: Opening verse
items.desc_en: The daf opens with a verse from Psalms describing God's protection of those who love Him.

sub.desc_en: The daf opens with a verse from Psalms describing God's protection of those who love Him.

items.text: Resh Lakish on the wicked and the debate about writing the verse
items.text_en: Resh Lakish on the wicked and the debate about writing the verse
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish explains a verse about the wicked, and then a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar arises about why a certain verse was not written at all, attributing it to the honor of David or Nechemya.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish asks the meaning of a verse about the wicked, explaining that when a person becomes wicked below, he becomes impoverished above.
The Gemara asks why the verse was not written at all.
One opinion (Rabbi Yochanan or Rabbi Elazar) says the verse was not written because of the honor of David.
The other opinion says the verse was not written because of the honor of Nechemya ben Chachalyah.

items.text: Tannaitic teachings on Menashe, Ahab, Yerovam, and Avshalom
items.text_en: Tannaitic teachings on Menashe, Ahab, Yerovam, and Avshalom
items.desc_en: A baraisa lists the number of Torah portions each wicked king studied, and another baraisa states that Avshalom has no share in the World to Come, and that certain kings are neither judged nor resurrected.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa lists the number of Torah portions studied by Menashe (55), Ahab (85), and Yerovam (103).
Rabbi Meir teaches that Avshalom has no share in the World to Come, interpreting the verse 'they struck him and killed him' as referring to this world and the next.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar citing Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar citing Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reports in the name of Rabbi Meir that Ahaz, Ahaziah, and all kings of Israel who did evil are neither resurrected nor judged.

items.text: Menashe's sins: killing Yeshayahu and making idols
items.text_en: Menashe's sins: killing Yeshayahu and making idols
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the verse about Menashe's bloodshed, with interpretations that he killed Yeshayahu or made a massive idol. Rabbi Yochanan explains that Menashe initially made one face for the idol and later four, to provoke the Shechinah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse describing Menashe's extensive bloodshed and idolatry.
The Gemara reports that in Babylonia they interpret the verse as referring to Menashe killing the prophet Yeshayahu.
In Eretz Yisrael they interpret the verse as referring to Menashe making a massive idol requiring a thousand men to carry, killing them daily.
The Gemara asks which interpretation aligns with Rabba bar bar Chana's statement that one righteous soul is equivalent to the entire world.
The Gemara concludes that Rabba bar bar Chana's statement aligns with the interpretation that Menashe killed Yeshayahu.
The Gemara notes the inconsistency between the singular 'פֶּסֶל' (idol) and the plural 'פְּסִילִים' (idols) in the verses about Menashe.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that Menashe initially made one face for the idol and later four faces, to provoke the Shechinah (Divine Presence) to see and become angry.

items.text: Placement of idols by Ahaz, Menashe, and Amon
items.text_en: Placement of idols by Ahaz, Menashe, and Amon
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes where each wicked king placed his idol: Ahaz on the roof, Menashe in the Temple, and Amon in the Holy of Holies. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani explains the verse about the short bed and narrow covering, and Rabbi Yonatan weeps over it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Ahaz placed his idol on the roof, citing a verse, and that Menashe placed his idol in the Temple, citing another verse.
The Gemara states that Amon brought his idol into the Holy of Holies, citing a verse about a short bed and narrow covering.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the verse 'for the bed is too short to stretch out on'.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan explains that the bed is too short for two friends to rule over it together.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the verse 'and the covering is narrow'.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani reports that Rabbi Yonatan would weep upon reaching this verse, lamenting that the One who gathers the waters of the sea should have a narrow covering made for Him.

items.text: Specific sins of Ahaz, Menashe, and Amon
items.text_en: Specific sins of Ahaz, Menashe, and Amon
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists the sins: Ahaz abolished the service and sealed the Torah; Menashe erased the Divine Name and destroyed the altar; Amon burned the Torah and committed incest with his mother. A dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar arises about Amon's primary sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists the specific sins of Ahaz, Menashe, and Amon: Ahaz abolished the service and sealed the Torah; Menashe erased the Divine Name and destroyed the altar; Amon burned the Torah and committed incest with his mother.
The Gemara cites the verse 'כִּי הוּא אָמוֹן הִרְבָּה אַשְׁמָה' to support that Amon committed incest with his mother.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar's dispute
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar's dispute
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar dispute whether Amon's primary sin was burning the Torah or committing incest with his mother.
Amon's mother rebukes him, and he responds that he acts only to anger his Creator.

items.text: Yehoyakim's arrogance and the reason he was not counted
items.text_en: Yehoyakim's arrogance and the reason he was not counted
items.desc_en: Yehoyakim boasts about using gold from Parvayim, but is rebuked. Rava asks why Yehoyakim was not counted among the wicked kings, and Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar dispute whether he engraved an idol's name or God's name on his flesh.

sub.desc_en: Yehoyakim boasts that earlier kings did not know how to anger God, claiming they need only light from the gold of Parvayim, and the people rebuke him with verses showing the gold belongs to God.
Rava asks Rabba bar Mari why Yehoyakim was not counted among the wicked kings, citing the verse that mentions 'that which was found upon him'.
One opinion (Rabbi Yochanan) says Yehoyakim engraved the name of an idol on his flesh.
The other opinion (Rabbi Elazar) says Yehoyakim engraved the name of Heaven (God) on his flesh.

items.text: Why Michah was not counted and the merit of hospitality
items.text_en: Why Michah was not counted and the merit of hospitality
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Michah was not counted because his bread was available to travelers. The Gemara describes the smoke from Michah's idol mixing with the smoke of the Mishkan, and the angels wanting to push him away, but God spares him due to his hospitality. The sin of the people of Giv'ah is mentioned.

sub.text: Rava's question to Rabba bar Mari
sub.text_en: Rava's question to Rabba bar Mari
sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabba bar Mari why Michah was not counted among the kings, and Rabba bar Mari answers that it is because his bread was available to travelers.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation and supporting baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation and supporting baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan identifies the verse as referring to Michah's idol, and Rabbi Natan's baraita describes the smoke from Michah's idol mixing with the smoke of the Mishkan.
The Gemara concludes that the ministering angels wanted to push Michah away, but God spared him due to his hospitality, and the people of Giv'ah were punished for not showing similar hospitality.

items.text: The power of hospitality (legimah)
items.text_en: The power of hospitality (legimah)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yose ben Kisma teaches that hospitality (legimah) is great, as it distanced two families from Israel. Rabbi Yochanan himself adds that it distances relatives, brings close the distant, and causes the Shechinah to rest on prophets of Baal.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yose ben Kisma
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Yose ben Kisma
sub.desc_en: רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) in the name of רבי יוסי בן קסמא (Rabbi Yose ben Kisma) teaches that hospitality (לגימה) is great, as it distanced two families from Israel, citing the verse 'על דבר אשר לא קדמו אתכם בלחם ובמים' (because they did not meet you with bread and water).

רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) himself adds that hospitality distances relatives, brings close the distant, averts eyes from the wicked, causes the Divine Presence to rest on prophets of Baal, and makes an unwitting transgression count as intentional.
The Gemara begins to elaborate on the statement that hospitality distances the near, but the text is cut off.

items.text: The Gemara's explanation of 'bringing close the distant' from Jethro
items.text_en: The Gemara's explanation of 'bringing close the distant' from Jethro
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the phrase 'bringing close the distant' refers to Jethro. Rabbi Yochanan states that because Jethro invited Moses to eat bread, his descendants merited to sit in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, as proven by scriptural verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the phrase 'bringing close the distant' as referring to Jethro.
Rabbi Yochanan states that because Jethro invited Moses to eat bread, his descendants merited to sit in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, supported by scriptural verses.

items.text: Further examples of God's attribute of mercy and the consequence of sin
items.text_en: Further examples of God's attribute of mercy and the consequence of sin
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues with examples: 'closing eyes from the wicked' from Micah, 'resting the Shechinah on prophets of Baal' from the colleague of Iddo the prophet, and 'its inadvertent sin is considered intentional' as taught by Rav Yehuda citing Rav, who explains that had Jonathan lent David two loaves of bread, many tragedies would have been avoided.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces two examples of God's attribute of mercy: closing eyes from the wicked (from Micah) and resting the Shechinah on prophets of Baal (from the colleague of Iddo the prophet).
Rav Yehuda citing Rav teaches that had Jonathan lent David two loaves of bread, many tragedies would have been avoided, illustrating that inadvertent sin is considered intentional.

items.text: Why Ahaz was not listed among those without a share
items.text_en: Why Ahaz was not listed among those without a share
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Ahaz was not counted among those who have no share in the World to Come. Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba answers because he was sandwiched between two righteous kings, Jotham and Hezekiah. Rav Yosef offers another reason: because he had shame from Isaiah, as explained by the verse and the interpretation of the word 'כובס'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Ahaz was not listed among those who have no share in the World to Come.
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba answers that Ahaz was not listed because he was sandwiched between two righteous kings, Jotham and Hezekiah.
Rav Yosef offers another reason: Ahaz had shame from Isaiah, as indicated by the verse where Isaiah is told to go to the path of the field of the fuller (כובס).
The Gemara digresses to interpret the word 'כובס' (fuller): some say it means Isaiah covered his face and passed by, others say a fuller's basket was placed on his head and he passed by.

items.text: Why Amon was not listed and the principle of a son not acquitting a father
items.text_en: Why Amon was not listed and the principle of a son not acquitting a father
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Amon was not listed, answering it was due to the honor of Josiah. It then questions why Manasseh was not similarly spared for Hezekiah's honor, and explains that a son can acquit a father but a father cannot acquit a son, citing a verse. The Gemara then applies this reasoning to Ahaz as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Amon was not listed among the kings who have no share in the World to Come.
The Gemara answers that Amon was omitted out of respect for his righteous son Josiah.
The Gemara objects that Manasseh should also have been omitted out of respect for his righteous father Hezekiah, yet he was listed.

The Gemara resolves that a son can acquit a father (Josiah for Amon), but a father cannot acquit a son (Hezekiah cannot save Manasseh), citing the verse 'וְאֵין מִיָּדִי מַצִּיל' and the examples of Abraham not saving Ishmael and Isaac not saving Esau.
The Gemara now applies the same reasoning to Ahaz, concluding that he too was not listed out of respect for his son Hezekiah.

items.text: Why Jehoiakim was not listed and the story of his skull
items.text_en: Why Jehoiakim was not listed and the story of his skull
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Jehoiakim was not listed. Rabbi Chiya bar Avuya explains that it was written on his skull 'this and another'. The Gemara relates a story about the grandfather of Rabbi Pereda who found Jehoiakim's skull, tried to bury it but it was rejected, and eventually his wife burned it in an oven, fulfilling the verse 'this and another'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Jehoiakim was not included in the list of those who have no share in the World to Come.
Rabbi Chiya bar Avuya explains that it was written on Jehoiakim's skull 'this and another', indicating his punishment was already fulfilled.

sub.text: Story about the grandfather of Rabbi Pereda
sub.text_en: Story about the grandfather of Rabbi Pereda
sub.desc_en: The grandfather of Rabbi Pereda found a skull with the inscription 'this and another' and repeatedly tried to bury it, but it was rejected by the earth.
The grandfather realizes it is Jehoiakim's skull, as the verse says he will be buried like a donkey, and wraps it in silk and places it on a chest.
His wife, thinking it is a skull of a former wife, burns it in an oven.
The Gemara concludes that this fulfills the verse 'this and another', meaning Jehoiakim's punishment was complete.

items.text: The sin of Hezekiah showing his treasures to the Babylonians
items.text_en: The sin of Hezekiah showing his treasures to the Babylonians
items.desc_en: A Tosefta states that because Hezekiah said 'I have done what is good in Your eyes' and asked for a sign, gentiles ate at his table, which caused exile for his children. This supports Hezekiah's own statement that hosting a gentile causes exile. The Gemara then discusses the verse about Hezekiah showing his treasures, with Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan offering different interpretations of 'בית נכתה'.

sub.desc_en: A Tosefta by Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states that because Hezekiah said 'I have done what is good in Your eyes' and asked for a sign, gentiles ate at his table, which caused exile for his children.
The Tosefta supports Hezekiah's own statement that hosting a gentile causes exile for one's children, citing the verse about his descendants being taken as eunuchs in Babylon.
The Gemara cites the verse about Hezekiah showing his treasures to the Babylonians, introducing the term 'בית נכתה' for interpretation.
Rav interprets 'בית נכתה' as referring to his wife who poured drinks for them.
Shmuel interprets 'בית נכתה' as his treasury house which he showed them.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'בית נכתה' as weapons eating weapons (armor) which he showed them.

items.text: Aggadic interpretations of the book of Lamentations
items.text_en: Aggadic interpretations of the book of Lamentations
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a series of aggadic interpretations of verses from Lamentations. Rava citing Rabbi Yochanan explains that Israel was punished with 'איכה' because they violated 36 kareit punishments. Rabbi Yochanan adds that they were punished with the aleph-bet because they violated the Torah given with the aleph-bet. Further interpretations explain 'ישבה בדד', 'העיר רבתי עם', 'היתה כאלמנה', and 'רבתי בגוים'.

sub.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains that Israel was punished with the word 'איכה' because they violated the 36 kareit punishments in the Torah.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that they were punished with the aleph-bet because they violated the Torah given with the aleph-bet.
Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'ישבה בדד' as God's contrast between Israel's former secure dwelling and their current solitary exile.
Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'העיר רבתי עם' as referring to the practice of marrying young to old and old to young to produce many children.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav interprets 'היתה כאלמנה' as like a widow but not a real widow, comparing it to a woman whose husband went overseas but intends to return.
Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'רבתי בגוים שרתי במדינות' as meaning that wherever Israel goes, they become masters over their captors.

items.text: A story of two captives on Mount Carmel
items.text_en: A story of two captives on Mount Carmel
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new narrative: a story about two people who were captured on Mount Carmel, with their captor walking behind them.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens a story about two people captured on Mount Carmel, with their captor walking behind them.

items.text: The story of the camel and the gentiles
items.text_en: The story of the camel and the gentiles
items.desc_en: A gentile asks two Jews how they know a camel is blind in one eye, carries two wineskins (one wine, one oil), and is led by a Jew and a gentile. They explain their deductions, and the gentile confirms their wisdom, honors them, and blesses God for giving wisdom to Abraham's descendants.

sub.desc_en: One Jew observes to his companion that the approaching camel is blind in one eye, carries two wineskins (one wine, one oil), and is led by a Jew and a gentile.
The gentile, Shabbai, scolds them as a stiff-necked people and asks how they know these things.

The Jews explain their deductions: the camel eats only grass on one side (blind eye), the wine drips and sinks while oil floats, and a gentile relieves himself on the road while a Jew goes to the side.
The gentile pursues them, confirms their words, honors them with a feast and a blessing to God for giving wisdom to Abraham's descendants, and sends them home in peace.

items.text: Two cries for the two Temples
items.text_en: Two cries for the two Temples
items.desc_en: Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan interprets the double crying in 'Bakoh tivkeh' as one for the First Temple and one for the Second Temple. The night refers to the night of Tisha B'Av, when the Israelites wept in vain, and God established that night as a time of weeping for generations.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'Bakoh tivkeh' (weeping you will weep) uses a double expression of crying.

sub.text: Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains that the two cries refer to the First Temple and the Second Temple.
The Gemara explains that 'night' refers to the incident of the spies, as it is written 'and the people wept that night.'

sub.text: Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that that day was the night of Tisha B'Av.
God tells Israel: You wept a vain weeping, and I will establish for you weeping for generations.

items.text: Additional interpretations of 'balailah'
items.text_en: Additional interpretations of 'balailah'
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers three alternative interpretations of 'balailah': one who cries at night is heard, the stars and constellations cry with him, and the listener cries with him. A story is told of a woman who cried at night, and Rabban Gamliel cried with her until his eyelashes fell out.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the first alternative interpretation of 'balailah': one who cries at night is heard.
The Gemara offers the second alternative: the stars and constellations cry with one who cries at night.
The Gemara gives the third alternative: the listener cries with the one who cries at night.
A story is told of a woman who cried at night for her son, and Rabban Gamliel cried with her until his eyelashes fell out, leading his students to remove her from the neighborhood.

items.text: Interpretations of 'dim'atah al lecheyah' and 'hayu tzareha lerosh'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'dim'atah al lecheyah' and 'hayu tzareha lerosh'
items.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'dim'atah al lecheyah' as a woman crying for the husband of her youth. He then interprets 'hayu tzareha lerosh' as anyone who causes distress to Israel becomes a leader, and anyone who oppresses Israel does not tire.

sub.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'dim'atah al lecheyah' as a woman weeping for the husband of her youth, citing a supporting verse.
Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'hayu tzareha lerosh' as anyone who causes distress to Israel becomes a leader, citing a supporting verse.
Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan adds that anyone who oppresses Israel does not tire.

items.text: Comparison of Jerusalem's sin to Sodom's
items.text_en: Comparison of Jerusalem's sin to Sodom's
items.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan derives from 'lo aleichem kol overei derech' that one may complain from the Torah. Rav Amram in the name of Rav says the verse makes Israel like those who transgress the law, as Jerusalem's punishment was worse than Sodom's. Rava explains that Jerusalem had an extra measure of sin: while Sodom did not support the poor, Jerusalem's compassionate women boiled their children.

sub.text: Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verse 'לֹא אֲלֵיכֶם כׇּל עֹבְרֵי דֶרֶךְ' that one may complain from the Torah.

sub.text: Rav Amram in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Amram in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Amram in the name of Rav interprets the verse as making Israel like those who transgress the law, citing that Jerusalem's punishment was worse than Sodom's.
The gemara questions how Jerusalem could be punished more severely than Sodom, implying favoritism.

sub.text: Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers that Jerusalem had an extra measure of sin: while Sodom did not support the poor, Jerusalem's compassionate women boiled their children.

items.text: Interpretations of 'silah kol abirai' and 'patzu alayich pihem'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'silah kol abirai' and 'patzu alayich pihem'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains 'silah kol abirai' as like a coin that is invalidated. Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains that in 'patzu alayich pihem', the letter peh precedes ayin because the spies said with their mouths what they did not see with their eyes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse 'סִלָּה כׇל אַבִּירַי' (He has removed all my mighty ones) as analogous to a person telling his friend that a coin has been invalidated.

sub.text: Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains that in the phrase 'פָּצוּ עָלַיִךְ פִּיהֶם' (they opened their mouth against you), the letter peh (פ) precedes ayin (ע) because the spies spoke with their mouths what they did not see with their eyes.

items.text: Interpretation of 'ochlei ami' and the attempt to add another to the list
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'ochlei ami' and the attempt to add another to the list
items.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says one who eats from Israel's bread tastes the taste of bread. Rav and Shmuel debate whether 'Hashem lo kara'u' refers to judges or teachers. Rav Ashi says the Men of the Great Assembly counted them. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says they sought to add one more, but a divine image and fire did not deter them. A bat kol declared that one who prioritized God's house over his own would stand before kings, but they did not heed. Another bat kol rebuked them.

sub.desc_en: Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that one who eats from Israel's bread tastes the taste of bread, while one who does not eat from it does not taste bread.
The gemara introduces the phrase 'ה׳ לֹא קָרָאוּ' (they did not call upon the Lord) as the basis for a dispute.
Rav interprets 'ה׳ לֹא קָרָאוּ' as referring to the judges who did not call upon God.
Shmuel interprets the phrase as referring to teachers of young children who did not call upon God.
The gemara asks who counted these judges or teachers.
Rav Ashi answers that the Men of the Great Assembly counted them.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav reports that they sought to add one more to the list, but a divine image and fire did not deter them.
A bat kol declares that one who prioritized God's house over his own would stand before kings, but they did not heed.
The gemara notes that they still did not heed the bat kol's message.
A second bat kol rebukes them with a verse implying that their rejection is final.

items.text: Dorshei Reshumot: All come to the World to Come
items.text_en: Dorshei Reshumot: All come to the World to Come
items.desc_en: The Dorshei Reshumot say that all the wicked kings of Israel (Ahab, Menashe, Jeroboam, Ahitophel) will come to the World to Come, as derived from a verse in Psalms.

sub.desc_en: The Dorshei Reshumot assert that all the wicked kings of Israel (Ahab, Menashe, Jeroboam, Ahitophel) will come to the World to Come, deriving this from a verse in Psalms.

items.text: Interpretation of Psalms regarding Doeg and Gihazi
items.text_en: Interpretation of Psalms regarding Doeg and Gihazi
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets verses from Psalms, linking 'Moab is my washpot' to Gihazi, who was punished for matters of washing, and 'over Edom I cast my shoe' to Doeg the Edomite. It then recounts a dialogue between the ministering angels and God about David.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'Moab is my washpot' as referring to Gihazi, who was punished for washing matters, and 'over Edom I cast my shoe' as referring to Doeg the Edomite, then recounts a dialogue between the ministering angels and God about David.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel on the dialogue between prophet and Israel
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel on the dialogue between prophet and Israel
items.desc_en: Rav explains that the verse 'Why is this people of Jerusalem turned away with a perpetual backsliding' refers to Israel's response to the prophet's call for repentance. Shmuel offers a different interpretation, where ten men sit before the prophet and argue that they cannot return to God because they have been sold as slaves or divorced.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'Why is this people of Jerusalem turned away with a perpetual backsliding' as the basis for the discussion.
Rav explains that the verse describes Israel's perpetual refusal to repent, as they retort to the prophet that their sinful ancestors are gone and the prophets themselves are not eternal.

Shmuel interprets the verse as ten men sitting before the prophet, arguing that they cannot return to God because they are like a sold slave or a divorced wife, and God responds that their sins caused their separation.

items.text: Resh Lakish on David and Nebuchadnezzar as servants
items.text_en: Resh Lakish on David and Nebuchadnezzar as servants
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish explains why Scripture calls both David and Nebuchadnezzar 'My servant'—it was known that Israel would later claim they are like slaves sold to Nebuchadnezzar, so God preemptively called him His servant to show that the slave's property belongs to the master.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish explains that God preemptively called Nebuchadnezzar 'My servant' because He knew Israel would later claim they are slaves to Nebuchadnezzar, establishing that a slave's property belongs to the master.

items.text: Rav Nachman on God's anger and redemption
items.text_en: Rav Nachman on God's anger and redemption
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman comments on the verse where God says He will reign over Israel with a strong hand, expressing that if such anger is necessary for redemption, then let God be angry and redeem them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman comments on the verse about God's anger, saying that if such anger is necessary for redemption, then let God be angry and redeem them.

items.text: Rabba bar bar Chana on the evil inclination
items.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana on the evil inclination
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana explains that the prophet told Israel to repent, but they said they cannot because the evil inclination rules over them. The prophet then told them to discipline their inclination, and they responded that God will teach them.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana introduces the verse and states that the prophet called Israel to repent.
Israel responds that they cannot repent because the evil inclination (יצר הרע) rules over them.
The prophet instructs Israel to discipline their evil inclination.
Israel responds that God will teach them, concluding the exchange.

items.text: The four commoners: Balaam, Doeg, Ahitophel, and Gihazi
items.text_en: The four commoners: Balaam, Doeg, Ahitophel, and Gihazi
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists four commoners (הדיווטות) who have no share in the World to Come: Balaam, Doeg, Ahitophel, and Gihazi. It then explains the names 'Balaam' and 'Ben Beor' through wordplay, and a Tanna identifies Beor as Cushan Rishathaim and Laban the Aramean. Rabbi Yochanan notes that Balaam's father was his son in prophecy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara lists four commoners (הדיווטות) who have no share in the World to Come: Balaam, Doeg, Ahitophel, and Gihazi, and explains the names 'Balaam' and 'Ben Beor' through wordplay.
A Tanna identifies Beor as Cushan Rishathaim and Laban the Aramean, explaining the names through wordplay and deeds.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves the textual variation between 'Ben Beor' and 'Beno Beor' by stating that Balaam's father was his son in prophecy.

items.text: Balaam's exclusion from the World to Come and the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Balaam's exclusion from the World to Come and the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah that Balaam does not come to the World to Come implies that other wicked gentiles do, and identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Yehoshua. It then cites a dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says that 'the wicked return to the grave' refers to Jewish sinners and 'all nations who forget God' to gentile sinners, while Rabbi Yehoshua argues that the verse means all nations who forget God are the wicked who return to the grave. Balaam himself gave a sign: if he dies the death of the upright, his end will be like theirs; otherwise, he goes to his people.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's statement that Balaam does not come to the World to Come implies that other wicked gentiles do, and inquires which Tanna authored this Mishnah.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehoshua, and introduces a supporting baraita.
The baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer's position that the verse 'יָשׁוּבוּ רְשָׁעִים לִשְׁאוֹלָה' refers to Jewish sinners and 'כׇּל גּוֹיִם שְׁכֵחֵי אֱלֹהִים' to gentile sinners.
Rabbi Yehoshua objects that the verse does not say 'בְּכׇל גּוֹיִם' but rather 'כׇּל גּוֹיִם שְׁכֵחֵי אֱלֹהִים', arguing that the entire verse refers to the same group.
Rabbi Yehoshua resolves that the wicked who return to the grave are precisely 'all nations who forget God', meaning all gentile sinners, not a separate category.
The Gemara notes that Balaam himself gave a sign: if he dies the death of the upright, his end will be like theirs; otherwise, he goes to his people.

items.text: The elders of Moab and Midian, and the audacity of Balaam
items.text_en: The elders of Moab and Midian, and the audacity of Balaam
items.desc_en: A Tanna relates a parable about two dogs that unite against a wolf, explaining why Moab and Midian, who were never at peace, joined together against Israel. Rav Nachman comments on Balaam's audacity, noting that initially God said 'do not go with them' but later said 'rise and go with them'. Rav Sheshet adds that audacity is effective even towards heaven, citing David's complaint about the sons of Zeruiah.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna introduces a parable about two dogs that were hostile to each other but united against a wolf, explaining why Moab and Midian, perpetual enemies, joined forces against Israel.
Rav Pappa cites a folk proverb about a weasel and a cat celebrating a wedding from the fat of a bad-luck animal, reinforcing the parable's lesson.
The Gemara asks where the elders of Midian went, and explains that when Balaam said 'stay here tonight,' they concluded that a father does not hate his son, so they left.
Rav Nachman states that audacity (חוצפה) is effective even towards heaven, citing that initially God said 'do not go with them' but later said 'rise and go with them' regarding Balaam.
Rav Sheshet adds that audacity is like a kingdom without a crown, citing David's complaint about the sons of Zeruiah being too harsh for him.

items.text: Balaam's physical deformities and sorcery
items.text_en: Balaam's physical deformities and sorcery
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Balaam was lame in one foot, based on the verse 'and he went limping', while Samson was lame in both feet. Balaam was also blind in one eye, as it says 'shut of eye'. The Gemara then debates whether Balaam was a sorcerer through his membrum or engaged in bestiality, citing verses to support each view.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Balaam was lame in one foot and blind in one eye, citing verses for each.
The Gemara introduces a debate: was Balaam a sorcerer through his membrum, based on a verbal analogy with Haman?
Mar Zutra asserts that Balaam was a sorcerer through his membrum, as per the verbal analogy.
Mar brei d'Ravina argues that Balaam engaged in bestiality with his donkey, citing a verbal analogy from the verse 'between her legs'.

items.text: Balaam's knowledge of the Divine anger
items.text_en: Balaam's knowledge of the Divine anger
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Balaam could know the mind of the Most High if he did not even understand his donkey's mind. It explains that his knowledge was limited to knowing the exact moment of God's anger, and recounts the donkey's rebuke.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Balaam could know the mind of the Most High if he did not even understand his donkey's mind.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the donkey's mind
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the donkey's mind
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the donkey's mind: Balaam was asked why he did not ride a horse, and he replied that he had set it out in a meadow.
The donkey rebukes Balaam, citing the verses to show she has been his faithful mount and even performed acts of intimacy at night.
The Gemara answers that Balaam's knowledge was limited to knowing the exact moment of God's anger.

items.text: God's restraint during Balaam's time
items.text_en: God's restraint during Balaam's time
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that God did not express anger during Balaam's days, which was a kindness to Israel, as otherwise they would have been destroyed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that God's restraint from anger during Balaam's days was a kindness to Israel, preventing their destruction.

items.text: The duration and sign of God's anger
items.text_en: The duration and sign of God's anger
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the duration of God's anger, which is a mere moment, and identifies the time of day when it occurs—during the first three hours when the rooster's comb turns white.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the topic by citing Balaam's statement to Balak and the verse about God's momentary anger.
The Gemara provides an alternative explanation, identifying the moment of anger as the first three hours when the rooster's comb turns white without red streaks.

items.text: A heretic and the proper time for cursing
items.text_en: A heretic and the proper time for cursing
items.desc_en: A story about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and a heretic illustrates that one should not curse even a heretic at the moment of God's anger, as it is not proper conduct. A baraita from Rabbi Meir describes the exact moment of anger: when kings bow to the sun.

sub.desc_en: A story is told about a heretic who tormented Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi; the rabbi prepared to curse him at the moment of divine anger but fell asleep, concluding that such conduct is improper.

sub.text: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: A baraita from Rabbi Meir specifies the exact moment of God's anger: when kings bow to the sun at sunrise.

items.text: Love and hate override protocol
items.text_en: Love and hate override protocol
items.desc_en: A baraita from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teaches that love (Abraham) and hate (Balaam) cause one to bypass the usual protocol of having servants prepare the donkey.

sub.text: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.text_en: Baraita in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teaches that love (Abraham) and hate (Balaam) override the protocol of having servants prepare the donkey, as both personally saddled their donkeys.

items.text: Reward for Balak and the principle of non-jealousy
items.text_en: Reward for Balak and the principle of non-jealousy
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says one should engage in Torah even for ulterior motives, as Balak's 42 sacrifices merited Ruth. Rabbi Yosei bar Huna identifies Ruth as Balak's descendant. Rava questions a verse about Solomon, and the Gemara explains it as a euphemism. Rabbi Yosei bar Choni states that one is not jealous of one's son or student.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that one should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even for ulterior motives (שלא לשמה), because from such engagement one comes to do it for its own sake (לשמה); as a reward for Balak's 42 sacrifices, Ruth descended from him.
Rabbi Yosei bar Huna specifies that Ruth was the daughter of Eglon, who was the grandson of Balak king of Moab, thus tracing the reward lineage.

sub.text: Rava's question to Rabba bar Mari
sub.text_en: Rava's question to Rabba bar Mari
sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabba bar Mari about a verse where it says 'God will make Solomon's name better than yours and his throne greater than yours' — is it proper to say such a thing to a king?

Rabba bar Mari answers that the speaker was speaking in a comparative manner (מעין), and supports this with a parallel from the verse about Yael, where she is compared to the matriarchs, showing that such comparative language is proper.
Rabbi Yosei bar Choni states that a person is jealous of everyone except his son and his student — his son from the example of Solomon, and his student from the verses about Elisha and Elijah.

items.text: Balaam's blessings as hidden curses
items.text_en: Balaam's blessings as hidden curses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yonatan debate whether an angel or a hook restrained Balaam. Rabbi Yochanan explains that Balaam's blessings were actually curses, which Rabbi Abba bar Kahana says were all reversed except for synagogues and study halls.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the verse and presents a dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yonatan over whether an angel or a hook restrained Balaam.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that Balaam's blessings were actually hidden curses, listing each blessing and its intended curse.
Rabbi Abba bar Kahana resolves that all the curses reverted except for synagogues and study halls, citing a verse that only one curse was turned to blessing.

items.text: The value of rebuke over blessing
items.text_en: The value of rebuke over blessing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quotes Rabbi Yonatan that the curse of Achiyah HaShiloni was more beneficial than Balaam's blessings, comparing Israel to a reed that bends but does not break.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani quoting Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan introduces the principle that the curse of Achiyah HaShiloni was more beneficial than Balaam's blessings, comparing Israel to a reed that bends but does not break.

items.text: Parable of the reed and the cedar
items.text_en: Parable of the reed and the cedar
items.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts the blessing of Israel as a reed (flexible and enduring) with Balaam's curse as a cedar (easily uprooted). The reed's roots are many and it withstands all winds, while the cedar's roots are few and it is overturned by the south wind.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a parable: Israel is blessed as a reed, which is flexible, has many roots, and withstands all winds, returning to its place when they cease.

The Gemara contrasts Balaam's curse likening Israel to a cedar, which has few roots, does not regenerate, and is easily uprooted by the south wind, and notes that the reed merited to be used for writing Torah scrolls.

items.text: Balaam's address to the Kenite and the three advisors
items.text_en: Balaam's address to the Kenite and the three advisors
items.desc_en: Balaam asks Jethro (the Kenite) why he was not part of the evil counsel against Israel. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Simai states that three were in that counsel: Balaam (who advised and was killed), Job (who was silent and suffered), and Jethro (who fled and merited descendants sitting in the Chamber of Hewn Stone).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse where Balaam sees the Kenite and asks Jethro why he was not part of the evil counsel, yet now sits among the enduring ones of the world.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Simai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Simai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Simai states that three were in that counsel: Balaam (who advised and was killed), Job (who was silent and suffered), and Jethro (who fled and merited descendants sitting in the Chamber of Hewn Stone), supported by verses.

items.text: Interpretation of 'Oiy mi yichyeh misumo El'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'Oiy mi yichyeh misumo El'
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets the verse as 'woe to one who revives himself with the name of God' (i.e., using God's name for sorcery). Rabbi Yochanan interprets it as woe to the nation that is found when God redeems His children, comparing it to one who throws his garment between a lion and lioness when they mate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse: 'And he took up his parable and said: Alas, who shall live when God establishes him?'
