Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish interprets: 'Woe to one who keeps himself alive by the name of El' (i.e., by sorcery or blasphemy).
Rabbi Yochanan interprets: 'Woe to the nation that is found when the Holy One redeems His children' — like one who throws his cloak between a lion and lioness when they are mating.

items.text: Interpretation of 'Vetzim miyad Kitim'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'Vetzim miyad Kitim'
items.desc_en: Rav explains that 'Kitim' refers to Libon Aspir (a place), and the verse means that until Assyria they killed, and from there on they subjugated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'And ships from the coast of Kittim' and Rav identifies 'Kittim' as 'Libon Aspir' (a place name).
Rav explains the verse: 'They will afflict Assyria and afflict Eber' — until Assyria they kill outright, from then on they subjugate.

items.text: Balaam's self-curse in his advice
items.text_en: Balaam's self-curse in his advice
items.desc_en: The verse says 'asher ya'aseh ha'am hazeh le'amekha' (what this people will do to your people) instead of 'le'am zeh' (to this people). Rabbi Abba bar Kahana explains that Balaam cursed himself and attributed the curse to others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse where Balaam says 'I am going to my people; come, I will advise you what this people will do to your people.'
The Gemara questions the phrasing: it should have said 'your people to this people' rather than 'this people to your people.'
Rabbi Abba bar Kahana explains: Balaam cursed himself but attributed the curse to others, like one who curses himself and blames others.

items.text: Balaam's advice to Balak and the incident of Baal Peor
items.text_en: Balaam's advice to Balak and the incident of Baal Peor
items.desc_en: Balaam advises Balak to set up booths with prostitutes to entice Israel to sin with Baal Peor. The plan is executed: old women outside sell linen garments cheaply, young women inside seduce the men, eventually leading them to worship Peor and deny the Torah of Moses.

sub.desc_en: Balaam advises Balak that Israel's God hates licentiousness and that they desire linen garments, so he suggests setting up booths with prostitutes to entice them.
Balak executes the plan, setting up booths from Mount Snow to Beth Yeshimot, with old women outside selling linen and young women inside offering lower prices repeatedly.
The young woman invites the Israelite man inside, offers him Ammonite wine (not yet forbidden), and he becomes inflamed with desire after drinking.
The woman demands that the man worship Peor by defecating before it, and when he protests being Jewish, she insists that only this act is required, ultimately leading him to deny the Torah of Moses.

items.text: Etymologies of Shittim, Refidim, and the word 'vayeshev'
items.text_en: Etymologies of Shittim, Refidim, and the word 'vayeshev'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua debate the meaning of Shittim (place name vs. foolishness) and Refidim (place name vs. weakening from Torah). Rabbi Yochanan states that wherever 'vayeshev' is used, it implies trouble, citing verses about Israel in Shittim, Jacob, and Solomon.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that Shittim is simply the place name.
Rabbi Yehoshua interprets Shittim as referring to the people engaging in foolishness (שטות).
Rabbi Eliezer explains the verse 'וַתִּקְרֶאןָ לָעָם לְזִבְחֵי אֱלֹהֵיהֶן' as meaning that nakedness (ערוּמּוֹת) confronted them.
Rabbi Yehoshua interprets the same verse as meaning that they all became owners of calluses (from sexual immorality).
The Gemara asks about the meaning of the name 'Refidim'.
Rabbi Eliezer states that Refidim is simply the place name.
Rabbi Yehoshua interprets Refidim as meaning that they weakened themselves (ריפו) from words of Torah, citing a supporting verse.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that wherever the word 'וַיֵּשֶׁב' (and he dwelt) appears, it implies trouble, citing verses about Israel in Shittim, Jacob, Israel in Goshen, and Solomon.

items.text: Balaam's death and his transformation from prophet to sorcerer
items.text_en: Balaam's death and his transformation from prophet to sorcerer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Balaam was among the Midianite kings. Rabbi Yochanan says he went to collect his reward for the 24,000 Israelites who died. Mar Zutra bar Toviya quotes a proverb: the camel went to seek horns, and its ears were cut off. The verse calls Balaam a 'kosem' (sorcerer); Rabbi Yochanan explains he was initially a prophet but later became a sorcerer. Rav Pappa quotes a proverb: from being a minister and ruler, he became a carpenter's apprentice.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Balaam was among the Midianite kings who were killed.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that Balaam went to collect his reward for the 24,000 Israelites who died through his advice.

sub.text: Mar Zutra bar Toviya citing Rav
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra bar Toviya citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Toviya cites a proverb: the camel went to seek horns, and its ears were cut off.
The Gemara questions why the verse calls Balaam a 'kosem' (sorcerer) when he was a prophet.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that Balaam was initially a prophet but later became a sorcerer.
Rav Pappa cites a proverb: from being a minister and ruler, he became a carpenter's apprentice.

items.text: Opening statement: The four deaths of Balaam
items.text_en: Opening statement: The four deaths of Balaam
items.desc_en: Rav interprets a verse to mean that Balaam was executed by all four court-ordered deaths: stoning, burning, decapitation, and strangulation.

sub.desc_en: Rav interprets the verse to mean that Balaam was executed by all four court-ordered deaths.

items.text: Balaam's age at death and the value of studying him
items.text_en: Balaam's age at death and the value of studying him
items.desc_en: A heretic asks Rabbi Chanina about Balaam's age; Rabbi Chanina deduces he was 33 or 34. The heretic confirms from Balaam's diary that he was 33 when Pinchas killed him. Mar bar Ravina then instructs his son to expound on Balaam the wicked as much as possible.

sub.desc_en: A heretic asks Rabbi Chanina how old Balaam was at his death.
Rabbi Chanina deduces from the verse 'אנשי דמים ומרמה לא יחצו ימיהם' that Balaam died at 33 or 34.
The heretic confirms from Balaam's diary that Balaam was 33 when Pinchas killed him.
Mar bar Ravina instructs his son to expound on Balaam the wicked as much as possible, unlike other topics.

items.text: Doeg's name and God's initial concern
items.text_en: Doeg's name and God's initial concern
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains the dual spelling of Doeg's name: initially God was concerned (דּוֹאֵג) that he would become evil, and after he did, God lamented (דּוֹיֵיג).

sub.desc_en: The gemara notes the dual spelling of Doeg's name in Scripture.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that initially God was concerned (דּוֹאֵג) that Doeg would become evil, and after he did, God lamented (דּוֹיֵיג).

items.text: Mnemonic for the following sections
items.text_en: Mnemonic for the following sections
items.desc_en: A mnemonic lists key words: Gibbor, Rasha, Tzaddik, Chayil, Sofer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a mnemonic listing key words for the following sections: Gibbor, Rasha, Tzaddik, Chayil, Sofer.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's five expositions on Doeg
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's five expositions on Doeg
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak delivers five derashot on verses about Doeg: God questions Doeg's pride in Torah despite his evil; Doeg only studied Torah superficially; the righteous initially fear Doeg's fate but later rejoice; David asks for Doeg's death but God says he will be expelled; David prevents Doeg from entering the World to Come and from having Torah scholars as descendants.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak opens with a verse asking why Doeg boasts in evil, and God questions Doeg's pride in Torah despite his wickedness.
Rabbi Yitzchak cites a verse where God rebukes Doeg for reciting laws while being a murderer and slanderer, and Rabbi Ami comments that Doeg's Torah was only superficial.
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the righteous initially fear Doeg's fate but later rejoice.
Rabbi Yitzchak recounts David's request for Doeg's death and God's response that Doeg will be expelled from his wealth.
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that David prevented Doeg from entering the World to Come and from having Torah scholars as descendants.
Rabbi Yitzchak interprets a verse about a scribe and weigher as referring to Doeg's mastery of all Torah letters and three hundred settled halakhot.

items.text: Doeg and Ahithophel's unresolved questions and the decline of generations
items.text_en: Doeg and Ahithophel's unresolved questions and the decline of generations
items.desc_en: Rabbi says Doeg and Ahithophel asked 400 questions about a flying tower and none were resolved. Rava questions the boast, noting that in Rav Yehuda's time they only studied Nezikin, while we study many tractates. Rav Yehuda could bring rain by removing his shoes, but we cry out and are ignored—God desires the heart.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi reports that Doeg and Ahithophel asked 400 questions about the flying tower and none were resolved.
Rava questions the boast, noting that in Rav Yehuda's time they only studied Nezikin, while we study many tractates like Uktzin.
The Gemara adds that when Rav Yehuda reached certain Mishnayot, he saw the debates of Rav and Shmuel, while we teach thirteen sessions on Uktzin.
The Gemara concludes that Rav Yehuda could bring rain by removing his shoes, but we cry out and are ignored—God desires the heart.

items.text: Doeg and Ahithophel's understanding of halakha
items.text_en: Doeg and Ahithophel's understanding of halakha
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya claims Doeg and Ahithophel did not understand halakha. Mar Zutra objects, citing their mastery of 300 laws. The resolution is that they could not arrive at the final halakha, as 'the secret of God is with those who fear Him.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya asserts that Doeg and Ahithophel did not understand halakha (שמעתא).
Mar Zutra objects, citing the verse that describes Doeg and Ahithophel as counting 300 laws, arguing they must have understood halakha.
The gemara resolves that they knew the laws but could not determine the final halakha (הלכה), as 'the secret of God is with those who fear Him.'

items.text: Doeg's punishment: forgetfulness or leprosy
items.text_en: Doeg's punishment: forgetfulness or leprosy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami says Doeg forgot his Torah study before death. Rav Ashi says he was afflicted with leprosy, citing a verse and the translation of 'tzamitat' as 'complete leprosy,' which requires hair unshorn and garments torn.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami states that Doeg died having forgotten his Torah study, citing the verse 'הוּא יָמוּת בְּאֵין מוּסָר וּבְרֹב אִוַּלְתּוֹ יִשְׁגֶּה' (he dies for lack of discipline, and in his great folly he goes astray).

Rav Ashi argues that Doeg was afflicted with leprosy, citing the verse 'הִצְמַתָּה כָּל זוֹנֶה מִמֶּךָּ' and linking the term 'צמיתות' (complete destruction) to the halachic state of a confirmed leper (מוחלט), which requires hair unshorn and garments torn.

items.text: Mnemonic for the following sections
items.text_en: Mnemonic for the following sections
items.desc_en: A mnemonic lists key words: Shlosha, Ra'u, Chatzu, Kar'u.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a mnemonic of key words (שְׁלֹשָׁה, רָאוּ, וְחָצוּ, וְקָרְאוּ) to organize the following sections about Doeg and Ahitophel.

items.text: Three angels, lifespan, and David's relationship with Ahithophel
items.text_en: Three angels, lifespan, and David's relationship with Ahithophel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says three angels of destruction attended Doeg: one made him forget his learning, one burned his soul, one scattered his ashes in synagogues. Doeg and Ahithophel never saw each other. They did not live out their full years—Doeg died at 34, Ahithophel at 33. David initially called Ahithophel his teacher, then his friend, then his student.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that three angels of destruction attended Doeg: one made him forget his learning, one burned his soul, one scattered his ashes in synagogues and study halls.
Rabbi Yochanan notes that Doeg and Ahithophel never saw each other because Doeg lived in Saul's time and Ahithophel in David's time.
Rabbi Yochanan states that Doeg and Ahithophel did not live out their full years, citing a baraita that Doeg died at 34 and Ahithophel at 33.
Rabbi Yochanan describes how David initially called Ahithophel his teacher, then his friend, and finally his student, citing verses for each stage.

items.text: Opening verse
items.text_en: Opening verse
items.desc_en: The daf opens with a verse from Psalms (41:10) about one who eats bread with another and then acts deceitfully, setting the stage for the discussion of David's sin.

sub.desc_en: The daf opens with a verse from Psalms (41:10) about one who eats bread with another and then acts deceitfully, setting the stage for the discussion of David's sin.

items.text: David brings himself to trial and is tested
items.text_en: David brings himself to trial and is tested
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav teaches that one should never bring oneself to trial, as David did and failed. David asked why he is not called 'God of David' like the patriarchs, and God said they were tested but he was not. David asked to be tested, and God warned him it would be with a matter of adultery. The narrative describes David's encounter with Bathsheba.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda (Rav Yehuda) in the name of רב (Rav) teaches that one should never bring oneself to an ordeal, as David did and failed; David asks why he is not called 'God of David' like the patriarchs.
God answers that the patriarchs were tested but David was not.
David asks God to examine and test him, citing Psalms 26:2.
God agrees to test David, informing him that the test will involve a matter of adultery.
The Gemara cites the verse from II Samuel 11:2 as the immediate narrative following God's warning.
Rav Yehuda (Rav Yehuda) explains that David changed his sleeping pattern to quell lust, but a halakha escaped him: a small limb, if satiated, becomes hungry, and if starved, becomes satisfied.
The Gemara describes the scene: Bathsheba was shampooing behind a beehive, Satan appeared as a bird, David shot an arrow that severed the beehive, exposing Bathsheba.

items.text: David's sin with Bathsheba and his remorse
items.text_en: David's sin with Bathsheba and his remorse
items.desc_en: The verse describes David taking Bathsheba, and David reflects on his sin, saying that if anyone had spoken ill of him, he would have been silenced, but now his mouth is stopped.

sub.desc_en: The verse recounts David sending for Bathsheba and lying with her after her purification.
David reflects that if a muzzle had fallen on his mouth, he would not have spoken the challenge that led to his sin.

items.text: Rava's homilies on David's sin and its consequences
items.text_en: Rava's homilies on David's sin and its consequences
items.desc_en: Rava delivers several homilies: David asks forgiveness so that people won't say a bird (Bathsheba) drove him from the mountain; David admits his sin was only before God, not to give license to servants; Bathsheba was destined for David but came with pain; David's blood would not flow if his flesh were torn; and the Sages taunt him about the death penalty for adultery, to which David responds that the adulterer has a share in the World to Come, but the one who embarrasses another in public does not.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens a homily on a psalm: David asks God to forgive his sin so that people won't say a bird (Bathsheba) drove him from the mountain.
Rava explains that David admitted his sin was only before God, to prevent servants from claiming they overcame their master's inclination.
Rava and the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael teach that Bathsheba was destined for David from creation but came to him with pain (like an unripe fruit).
Rava explains that David's blood would not flow if his flesh were torn, indicating his innocence regarding the sin.
David responds to the Sages who taunt him about the death penalty for adultery: the adulterer has a share in the World to Come, but the one who embarrasses another in public does not.

items.text: David's piety and near-idolatry
items.text_en: David's piety and near-idolatry
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says that even during his illness, David observed eighteen 'onot' (times of intimacy), and that David sought to worship idolatry, but Hushai the Archite rebuked him, leading David to prefer idolatry over public desecration of God's name.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that even during his illness, David observed eighteen 'onot' (times of intimacy), citing a verse.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav adds that David sought to worship idolatry, citing a verse where 'ראש' (head) is interpreted as idolatry.
Hushai the Archite confronts David, questioning how a king like him could worship idolatry.
David responds that it is better to worship idolatry than to cause a public desecration of God's name by having his son kill him.

items.text: The connection between יפת תואר and the rebellious son
items.text_en: The connection between יפת תואר and the rebellious son
items.desc_en: A discussion about why David married a יפת תואר (captive woman), and the Gemara notes that the verse about the rebellious son is adjacent, implying that one who marries a יפת תואר will have a rebellious son.

sub.desc_en: Hushai asks David why he married יפת תואר (a beautiful captive woman), and David replies that the Torah permitted it.

Hushai objects that David did not interpret the סמוכין (adjacent verses), for the passage about יפת תואר is followed by the passage about the בן סורר ומורה (wayward and rebellious son), implying that one who marries a יפת תואר will have such a son.

items.text: David's plea for forgiveness and God's response
items.text_en: David's plea for forgiveness and God's response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Dostai compares David to a merchant; David asks God to forgive his sins, but God says it is impossible because even the letter 'yod' that was taken from Sarah's name cried out for years until Joshua was given it, and Solomon will say that one who touches fire will be burned. David accepts suffering.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Dostai compares David to a merchant; David asks God to forgive his sins, and God grants forgiveness for each request until David asks that his sin not be recorded.
God objects that it is impossible, citing the precedent of the letter 'yod' taken from Sarah's name that cried out for years until Joshua received it.

sub.text: David's plea and God's final answer
sub.text_en: David's plea and God's final answer
sub.desc_en: David asks for complete forgiveness; God says Solomon will teach that one who touches fire is burned, and advises David to accept suffering, which David does.

items.text: David's punishment: leprosy, withdrawal of Shekhinah, and Sanhedrin
items.text_en: David's punishment: leprosy, withdrawal of Shekhinah, and Sanhedrin
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says David was afflicted with leprosy for six months, the Shekhinah departed from him, and the Sanhedrin separated from him, all derived from verses.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav concludes that David was afflicted with leprosy for six months, the Shechinah departed from him, and the Sanhedrin separated from him, citing verses for each and deriving the six months from the verse about David's forty-year reign.

items.text: David's leprosy and forgiveness
items.text_en: David's leprosy and forgiveness
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves that David was afflicted with leprosy from the discrepancy in his reign lengths. David prays for forgiveness, and God forgives him but only reveals it during Solomon's building of the Temple, when the gates open after Solomon mentions David's merits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the discrepancy in David's reign lengths that he was afflicted with leprosy.
David asks God for forgiveness, and God grants it.
God tells David that the forgiveness will be revealed only during Solomon's lifetime.
Solomon attempts to bring the Ark into the Holy of Holies, but the gates stick together despite his entreaties.
When Solomon mentions David's merits, the gates open, revealing God's forgiveness of David's sin.

items.text: Gehazi's rejection by Elisha
items.text_en: Gehazi's rejection by Elisha
items.desc_en: Elisha goes to Damascus to bring Gehazi back in repentance, but Gehazi refuses, citing the principle that one who sins and causes others to sin is not given the opportunity to repent. Various explanations are given for Gehazi's sins, and the Gemara concludes with a teaching that the left hand should push away while the right hand draws near, unlike Elisha who pushed Gehazi away with both hands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the story of Gehazi, citing the verse that Elisha went to Damascus, and Rabbi Yochanan explains that Elisha went to bring Gehazi back in repentance, but Gehazi did not return.
Elisha tells Gehazi to repent, but Gehazi refuses, citing the received tradition that one who sins and causes others to sin is not given the opportunity to repent.
The Gemara asks: What did Gehazi do (to cause others to sin)?
Some say Gehazi suspended a magnetic stone for the sin of Jeroboam, and others say he engraved the Divine Name in its mouth, causing it to proclaim the first two commandments.
Others say Gehazi drove away the disciples from Elisha, as implied by the verse that the place was too narrow for them.

The baraita teaches that the left hand should push away and the right hand draw near, unlike Elisha who pushed Gehazi away with both hands, and unlike Yehoshua ben Perachyah who pushed Jesus the Nazarene away with both hands.

items.text: The story of Naaman and Gehazi's leprosy
items.text_en: The story of Naaman and Gehazi's leprosy
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Naaman was cured of leprosy by Elisha, and Gehazi secretly took gifts from him. Elisha curses Gehazi with Naaman's leprosy, and Rabbi Yochanan identifies the four leprous men at the gate as Gehazi and his three sons.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens the story of Gehazi by citing the biblical verses about Naaman's gift and Gehazi's deception, and raises a difficulty: did Gehazi take all those items or only silver and garments?

Rabbi Yitzchak explains that Elisha was teaching about eight creeping things, and Naaman was a leprous general who was healed by Elisha through immersion in the Jordan, then Gehazi secretly took gifts from him.

sub.text: Gemara's conclusion with Rabbi Yochanan's identification
sub.text_en: Gemara's conclusion with Rabbi Yochanan's identification
sub.desc_en: Elisha sees leprosy spreading on Gehazi's head and curses him with Naaman's leprosy, and Rabbi Yochanan identifies the four leprous men at the gate as Gehazi and his three sons.

items.text: Joshua ben Perachiah and Jesus
items.text_en: Joshua ben Perachiah and Jesus
items.desc_en: The Gemara tells how Joshua ben Perachiah and Jesus fled to Alexandria. Upon returning, Joshua praised their host's inn, but Jesus misinterpreted his comment about the hostess's eyes. Joshua excommunicated him, and despite multiple attempts at reconciliation, Jesus refused to repent, leading to his idolatry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the story of Joshua ben Perachiah and Jesus, recounting their flight to Alexandria and the message from Shimon ben Shetach urging return.
Upon returning, Joshua praises the inn, but Jesus misinterprets his comment about the hostess's eyes, leading Joshua to excommunicate him with four hundred shofars.
Despite multiple attempts at reconciliation, Jesus refuses to repent, leading to his idolatry and the Gemara's statement that he practiced sorcery and led Israel astray.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's teaching
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's teaching
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teaches that regarding the evil inclination, a child, and a woman, the left hand should push away while the right hand draws near.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teaches in a baraita that regarding the evil inclination (יצר), a child, and a woman, the left hand should push away while the right hand draws near.

items.text: Elisha's three illnesses and the origin of old age and sickness
items.text_en: Elisha's three illnesses and the origin of old age and sickness
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists three illnesses Elisha suffered: one for sending bears against children, one for pushing Gehazi away, and the one from which he died. It then recounts how Abraham prayed for old age, Jacob for sickness, and Elisha for recovery from illness.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists three illnesses Elisha suffered: one for sending bears against children, one for pushing Gehazi away, and the one from which he died.
The Gemara recounts how Abraham prayed for old age, Jacob for sickness, and Elisha for recovery from illness, establishing the origin of these conditions.

items.text: Mishnah: The fate of the generations of the Flood, Dispersion, and Sodom
items.text_en: Mishnah: The fate of the generations of the Flood, Dispersion, and Sodom
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the generation of the Flood has no share in the World to Come and does not stand in judgment. The generation of the Dispersion has no share in the World to Come. The people of Sodom have no share in the World to Come but do stand in judgment. Rabbi Nechemya argues that none of them stand in judgment.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the generation of the Flood has no share in the World to Come and does not stand in judgment; the generation of the Dispersion has no share; the people of Sodom have no share but do stand in judgment.
Rabbi Nechemya argues that none of these groups stand in judgment, citing the verse 'עַל כֵּן לֹא יָקֻמוּ' (therefore they shall not rise).

items.text: Mishnah: Groups with no share in the World to Come
items.text_en: Mishnah: Groups with no share in the World to Come
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the Generation of the Flood, the people of Sodom, the spies, the Generation of the Wilderness, and Korah's assembly as having no portion in the World to Come, with scriptural proofs. Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer debate the fate of the Generation of the Wilderness and Korah's assembly.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the Generation of the Flood and the people of Sodom as having no share in the World to Come, with scriptural proofs.
The Mishnah states that the spies have no portion in the World to Come, citing a verse to prove their death in this world and the plague for the next.
Rabbi Akiva rules that the Generation of the Wilderness has no share in the World to Come and does not stand in judgment, citing a verse.
Rabbi Eliezer objects, arguing that the Generation of the Wilderness will be gathered as God's pious ones, implying they have a share.
Rabbi Akiva rules that Korah's assembly will not ascend, citing verses about their death in this world and destruction in the next.
Rabbi Eliezer objects, citing a verse that God brings down to the grave and raises up, implying Korah's assembly will eventually rise.

items.text: Gemara: The Generation of the Flood's fate
items.text_en: Gemara: The Generation of the Flood's fate
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Akiva says the Generation of the Flood has no share in the World to Come, while Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says they are neither alive nor judged. Rabbi Menachem bar Yosef adds that even when souls return to bodies, their souls are pained in Gehinnom.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Akiva's position that the Generation of the Flood has no share in the World to Come, citing verses.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira states that the Generation of the Flood are neither alive nor judged, interpreting the verse 'לֹא יָדוֹן רוּחִי' to mean their souls will not return to their bodies.

Rabbi Menachem bar Yosef adds that even when God returns souls to dead bodies, the souls of the Generation of the Flood will be pained in Gehinnom, citing the verse 'תַּהֲרוּ חֲשַׁשׁ תֵּלְדוּ קַשׁ רוּחֲכֶם אֵשׁ תֹּאכַלְכֶם'.

items.text: The sin and punishment of the Generation of the Flood
items.text_en: The sin and punishment of the Generation of the Flood
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Generation of the Flood became arrogant due to God's goodness, leading them to deny Him. God punishes them with water, measure for measure. Rabbi Yosei adds that they sinned through the eye (lust) and were punished with water, which resembles the eye.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the Generation of the Flood became arrogant only because of the goodness God showered upon them, citing verses describing their prosperity and sudden downfall.
The baraita explains that their prosperity led them to deny God, claiming they did not need His rain, so God punished them measure for measure with the very water He had given them.
Rabbi Yosei adds that they sinned through the eye (lust) and were punished with water, which resembles the eye, citing the verse about the fountains of the deep and the windows of heaven.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan: Great sin and great punishment
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan: Great sin and great punishment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the Generation of the Flood sinned greatly and were punished greatly, citing verses. He also notes that three remnants of the flood remain. Rabbi Abba bar Kahana adds that all animals interbred except the tushlami.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the Generation of the Flood sinned greatly and were punished greatly, citing verses.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that three remnants of the flood remain: the cave of Gader, the hot springs of Tiberias, and the great spring of Beiram.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the corruption of all flesh included bestiality across all species.
Rabbi Abba bar Kahana adds that all animals interbred except the tushlami (a specific hybrid).

items.text: The power of theft and Noah's decree
items.text_en: The power of theft and Noah's decree
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan emphasizes the severity of theft, as the Generation of the Flood was only punished after committing robbery. Rabbi Elazar describes the personified theft standing before God. A baraita adds that even Noah was initially decreed upon but found grace.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan declares that the power of theft (חמס) is so great that the Generation of the Flood was only punished after they committed robbery, citing the verse 'כי מלאה הארץ חמס'.
Rabbi Elazar personifies the theft (חמס) as standing before God like a staff, reciting the verse 'לא מהם ולא מהמונם'.
A baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael adds that even Noah was initially decreed upon, but he found grace (חן) in God's eyes, citing the verse 'נחמתי כי עשיתם ונח מצא חן בעיני ה׳'.

items.text: Interpretation of 'Vayinachem'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'Vayinachem'
items.desc_en: The Gemara debates the meaning of 'Vayinachem Hashem' regarding the creation of man. One view says God did well to provide graves in the earth; another says He did not do well, interpreting 'vayinachem' as regret.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi interprets 'וַיִּנָּחֶם' (and God was comforted) to mean that God did well by providing graves in the earth for man, citing a parallel verse where 'וַיְנַחֵם' means comfort.
An alternative view interprets 'וַיִּנָּחֶם' as regret, meaning God did not do well by providing graves, citing a verse where 'וַיִּנָּחֶם' means regret over evil.

items.text: Noah's righteousness in his generations
items.text_en: Noah's righteousness in his generations
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish debate whether 'in his generations' implies Noah was righteous only relative to his wicked generation or even more so in a righteous generation. Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Oshaya offer parables to illustrate their views.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets 'in his generations' to mean Noah was righteous only relative to his own wicked generation, not to others.
Reish Lakish argues that 'in his generations' implies Noah was righteous even more so in a righteous generation.
Rabbi Chanina illustrates Rabbi Yochanan's view with a parable of a wine jug in a vinegar cellar, whose fragrance is noticeable only in its place.
Rabbi Oshaya illustrates Reish Lakish's view with a parable of a flask of oil in a garbage dump, whose fragrance is noticeable there and all the more so in a spice shop.

items.text: Why animals were destroyed and Noah's warning
items.text_en: Why animals were destroyed and Noah's warning
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why animals were destroyed if only humans sinned. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha explains with a parable: the world was created for man, so when man sinned, animals were no longer needed. Rabbi Yosei of Caesarea describes Noah's warning to the generation, and the Gemara notes that they cleared paths for vineyards but were obstinate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why animals were destroyed if only humans sinned.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha answers with a parable: the world was created for man, so when man sinned, animals were no longer needed.
The Gemara notes that only land animals were destroyed, not fish in the sea.
Rabbi Yosei of Caesarea describes Noah's warning to the generation: repent or be destroyed by the flood and cursed for all generations.
The Gemara notes that the generation cleared paths for vineyards but were obstinate, and Noah told them he had one way to remove them.

items.text: Noah's rebuke and the generation's response
items.text_en: Noah's rebuke and the generation's response
items.desc_en: Rava explains that Noah rebuked his generation with harsh words, but they mocked him and boasted that they could escape any flood. They claimed to have protections against fire, water from the earth, and water from the heavens. Noah responded that the flood would come from between their feet, and a baraita explains that the waters were as hot as semen. Rav Chisda adds that they sinned with heat and were punished with heat.

sub.desc_en: Rava introduces the verse and explains that Noah rebuked the generation with harsh words, and they mocked him with boasts of various protections against flood.
Noah answers that the flood will come from between their feet, citing the verse.
A baraita supports that the flood waters were as hot as semen, citing the same verse.
Rav Chisda concludes that they sinned with heat and were punished with heat.

items.text: The seven days before the flood
items.text_en: The seven days before the flood
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the seven days before the flood were for. Rav says they were the days of mourning for Methuselah, teaching that the eulogy of the righteous delays punishment. Another explanation is that God changed the order of creation, or that He set a long time then a short time, or that He gave them a taste of the World to Come so they would know what they lost.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the seven days before the flood were for.
Rav says these were the days of mourning for Methuselah, teaching that the eulogy of the righteous delays punishment.
Another explanation says God changed the order of creation for seven days, so the sun rose in the west and set in the east.
Another explanation says God set a long time then a short time for them.
Another explanation says God gave them a taste of the World to Come so they would know what they lost.

items.text: Selecting clean animals for the ark
items.text_en: Selecting clean animals for the ark
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Noah took seven pairs of clean animals, as animals do not have marriage. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says they were from those that had not been used for forbidden intercourse. Rav Chisda explains that Noah passed them before the ark; those the ark accepted were pure, and those it rejected were impure. Rabbi Abahu says they came of their own accord.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Noah could take seven pairs of each clean animal, since animals do not have marriage (אישות).

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani answers that the seven pairs were taken from animals that had not been used for forbidden intercourse.
The Gemara asks how Noah could know which animals had not been used for forbidden intercourse.
Rav Chisda explains that Noah passed the animals before the ark; those the ark accepted were pure, and those it rejected were impure.
Rabbi Abahu says that the animals came of their own accord.

items.text: Details of the ark's construction
items.text_en: Details of the ark's construction
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the materials and structure of the ark. 'Gopher' wood is identified as either 'mavliga' or 'gulmeish'. Rabbi Yochanan says God told Noah to set precious stones in the ark to provide light. The ark was finished to a cubit at the top, and had three levels: lower for waste, middle for animals, upper for humans.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'gopher' wood is, and cites two opinions: Rav Adda in the name of Bei Rabbi Sheila identifies it as 'mavliga', and an alternative tradition says 'gulmeish'.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that God told Noah to set precious stones in the ark to provide light like the noonday sun.
The Gemara notes that the ark was finished to a cubit at the top, indicating its shape.
A Tanna teaches that the three levels of the ark were designated: lower for waste, middle for animals, upper for humans.

items.text: The raven's complaint and the prohibition of marital relations
items.text_en: The raven's complaint and the prohibition of marital relations
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish says the raven gave a convincing retort to Noah, arguing that Noah's master (God) hates him (the raven) and Noah himself hates him, since he sends a raven from the impure species while leaving the pure ones. The raven also feared for his mate. Noah responded that the raven is wicked, as what is permitted to him (his wife) is forbidden, so the forbidden is even more so. Rabbi Yochanan derives from verses that marital relations were forbidden in the ark. A baraita lists three who engaged in relations in the ark and were punished: the dog, the raven, and Ham.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish reports the raven's victorious retort to Noah, arguing that both God and Noah hate him, and questioning Noah's motive for sending him.
Noah rebukes the raven as wicked, arguing that if what is permitted to him (his wife) is forbidden, then what is forbidden to him is certainly forbidden.
Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verses about entering and leaving the ark that marital relations were forbidden during the flood.
A baraita lists three who engaged in relations in the ark and were punished: the dog, the raven, and Ham.

items.text: The dove and the olive leaf
items.text_en: The dove and the olive leaf
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya learns that pure birds dwell with the righteous. Rabbi Elazar explains the dove's prayer: it preferred bitter sustenance from God over sweet sustenance from humans. The word 'taraf' is shown to mean sustenance, as in 'hatrifeni lechem chuki'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya deduces from the dove's mission that pure birds dwell with the righteous.
Rabbi Elazar interprets the dove's olive leaf as a prayer preferring bitter sustenance from God over sweet sustenance from humans.
The Gemara asks how the word 'taraf' in the verse is proven to mean sustenance.
The Gemara answers by citing the verse 'hatrifeni lechem chuki' (Proverbs 30:8) where 'taraf' clearly means sustenance.

items.text: The animals' exit and the hardships in the ark
items.text_en: The animals' exit and the hardships in the ark
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan notes that the verse says 'according to their families' they left, not 'they themselves'. Rav Chana bar Bizna relates that Eliezer asked Shem the Great where they were during the flood. Shem described the great difficulty: they fed each creature at its proper time, but the chameleon was a problem until a worm fell from a pomegranate. The lion was fed by fire, and the phoenix was found sleeping and refused to disturb Noah, earning a blessing of long life.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan notes that the verse says 'according to their families' they left, not 'they themselves', implying a distinction.

sub.text: Eliezer's question to Shem the Great
sub.text_en: Eliezer's question to Shem the Great
sub.desc_en: Eliezer asks Shem the Great where they were during the flood, given the verse about leaving by families.
Shem describes the great difficulty in the ark: they fed each creature at its proper time, but the chameleon was a problem until a worm fell from a pomegranate.
Rav explains that the lion was fed by fire, citing that fire sustains no less than six and no more than twelve months.
The phoenix was found sleeping in the ark and refused to disturb Noah, earning a blessing of long life.

items.text: Abraham's help in war and Nachum Ish Gam Zu
items.text_en: Abraham's help in war and Nachum Ish Gam Zu
items.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Levi relates that Shem the Great asked Eliezer how they fared when kings attacked. Eliezer said God seated Abraham at His right hand, and they threw dust that became swords and stubble that became arrows. The daf then transitions to Nachum Ish Gam Zu, who always said 'gam zu l'tovah'. When Israel wanted to send a gift to the emperor, they sent it with him.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chana bar Levi reports that Shem the Great asked Eliezer how they fared when the kings of east and west attacked.
Eliezer answers that God seated Abraham at His right hand, and they threw dust that became swords and stubble that became arrows, citing verses.

sub.text: Transition to Nachum Ish Gam Zu
sub.text_en: Transition to Nachum Ish Gam Zu
sub.desc_en: The daf transitions to Nachum Ish Gam Zu, who always said 'גם זו לטובה' (this too is for good), and when Israel wanted to send a gift to the emperor, they sent it with him.

items.text: The story of Nachum Ish Gam Zu and the dust of Avraham
items.text_en: The story of Nachum Ish Gam Zu and the dust of Avraham
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts how Nachum Ish Gam Zu was sent to deliver a chest of gold to the emperor, but innkeepers replaced it with dust. When the emperor discovered the dust, he ordered Nachum's execution, but Eliyahu appeared and explained that the dust was from Avraham Avinu, which turned into swords and arrows. The dust was used to conquer a city, and Nachum was rewarded with gold, while the innkeepers were punished.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who should be sent with the gift to the emperor and answers that Nachum Ish Gam Zu should be sent because he is experienced with miracles.
The story recounts how Nachum stopped at an inn, the innkeepers asked what he carried, and at night they replaced his gold with dust.

When the emperor found dust instead of gold and ordered Nachum's execution, Eliyahu appeared disguised as a courtier and suggested the dust might be from Avraham Avinu, which turns into weapons; they tested it and found it true.
The dust was used to conquer a city, Nachum was rewarded with gold, and when the innkeepers tried to imitate him, they were executed.

items.text: The sin of the generation of the Dispersion
items.text_en: The sin of the generation of the Dispersion
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the sin of the generation of the Dispersion (Dor Haflagah). One opinion states they built a tower to strike the heavens and make its waters flow. Another opinion, from Rabbi Yirmeya bar Elazar, says they were divided into three groups: one wanted to dwell in heaven, one wanted to wage war, and one wanted to worship idols. Each group received a different punishment.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the generation of the Dispersion has no share in the World to Come.
The Gemara asks: What did they do (to deserve this)?
The school of Rabbi Shila answers: They planned to build a tower and strike the heavens with axes to make its waters flow.
The Western sages mock this: If so, they should have built on one mountain (not a tower).
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Elazar states they were divided into three groups with different intentions.
Each group received a distinct punishment: dispersion, transformation into demons, or confusion of language.

items.text: Rabbi Natan's opinion on the generation of the Dispersion
items.text_en: Rabbi Natan's opinion on the generation of the Dispersion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Natan argues that all three groups intended for idolatry, as the verse says 'let us make a name' and elsewhere 'name' refers to idolatry.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Natan who says all three groups intended idolatry, proven by a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'שם' (name).

items.text: Additional statements about the tower and Bavel
items.text_en: Additional statements about the tower and Bavel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says a third of the tower was burned, a third swallowed, and a third remains. Rav says the air of the tower causes forgetfulness. Rav Yosef says Bavel and Borsif are a bad sign for Torah, and Rabbi Asi explains Borsif means 'a pit that swallows'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan reports that one third of the tower was burned, one third swallowed, and one third remains standing.
Rav says the air of the tower causes forgetfulness.
Rav Yosef says Bavel and Borsif are a bad sign for Torah.
Rabbi Asi explains that Borsif means a pit that drains (water).

items.text: The people of Sodom: their evil and punishment
items.text_en: The people of Sodom: their evil and punishment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the people of Sodom have no share in the World to Come. The Gemara expounds on the verse 'And the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners against the Lord exceedingly', with different interpretations of 'wicked' and 'sinners' referring to their bodies and property. A baraisa adds that 'exceedingly' refers to bloodshed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the people of Sodom have no share in the World to Come.
A baraisa expounds the verse 'וְאַנְשֵׁי סְדֹם רָעִים וְחַטָּאִים' (wicked and sinners) to mean 'wicked' in this world and 'sinners' for the World to Come.

Rav Yehuda interprets 'wicked' as referring to their bodies and 'sinners' to their property, citing verses for each, and explains 'לַה׳' (to the Lord) as blasphemy and 'מְאֹד' (exceedingly) as intentional sin.
A baraisa reverses the interpretation: 'wicked' refers to their property and 'sinners' to their bodies, and adds that 'מְאֹד' (exceedingly) refers to bloodshed, citing a verse about Menashe.

items.text: The arrogance of Sodom and their decree against travelers
items.text_en: The arrogance of Sodom and their decree against travelers
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the people of Sodom became arrogant due to the great bounty God gave them, as described in Job. They decided to cause travelers to forget the way to their land, citing verses that support their wicked plan.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that the people of Sodom became arrogant only because of the great bounty God gave them, and it cites verses from Job describing their land's wealth.
The people of Sodom reason that since their land is so rich, travelers only come to take from their wealth, so they decide to eliminate travelers.
They decree to cause travelers to forget the way to their land, citing a verse from Job that supports their plan.

items.text: Rava's exposition on Sodom's crimes
items.text_en: Rava's exposition on Sodom's crimes
items.desc_en: Rava expounds on verses describing Sodom's wickedness: they would place a wealthy person near a leaning wall and push it on him to steal his money, and they would deposit expensive perfume with a rich man and later sniff it out like dogs to find and steal it. Additional verses describe their cruelty to the poor and orphans.

sub.desc_en: Rava expounds on a verse to describe how the people of Sodom would place a wealthy man near a leaning wall and push it on him to steal his money.
Rava expounds on another verse to describe how they would deposit expensive perfume with a rich man and later sniff it out like dogs to find and steal it.
The gemara cites additional verses describing the cruelty of the people of Sodom toward the poor and orphans.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei of Tzippori and the thieves; the law of grazing cattle
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei of Tzippori and the thieves; the law of grazing cattle
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei of Tzippori was troubled by thieves who dug 300 tunnels in one night. When accused of guiding thieves, he defended himself. At his death, the gutters of Tzippori flowed with blood. The Gemara then describes a Sodomite law: one who owned one ox would graze it one day, and one who owned none would graze it two days. An orphan who killed the oxen he was given was confronted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei of Tzippori taught about Sodomite theft methods, and that night 300 tunnels were dug in Tzippori.
Homeowners came and harassed Rabbi Yosei, accusing him of giving thieves a method.
Rabbi Yosei defended himself, saying he did not know thieves would come.
When Rabbi Yosei died, the gutters of Tzippori miraculously flowed with blood.
The Gemara describes a Sodomite law: one who owns an ox grazes it one day, one who owns none grazes it two days.
An orphan son of a widow was given oxen to herd, but he killed them, and the narrative cuts off as he begins to speak.

items.text: Sodom's corrupt justice system
items.text_en: Sodom's corrupt justice system
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes the perverse laws of Sodom, where judges would rule based on a person's wealth, and the story of Eliezer, Abraham's servant, who outwits them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes Sodom's perverse law that a man with one ox gives one hide, while a man with no ox gives two, justified by the judge's claim that the end of the judgment matches its beginning.
The Gemara gives another example: a ferry toll of one zuz for those who cross the bridge and two for those who do not, and a story of a brick-taker who claims each brick as his own.
The Gemara lists the four corrupt judges of Sodom and describes their rulings: for injuring a pregnant woman, cutting a donkey's ear, or wounding a fellow, the victim must pay the perpetrator.
The Gemara tells of a ferry toll of four zuzim for bridge-crossers and eight for water-crossers, and the story of a launderer who was beaten and then charged for the bloodletting and the toll.
Eliezer, Abraham's servant, outwits the Sodomite judge by throwing a clod at him, then demanding the judge pay the original plaintiff for the bloodletting, while keeping his own zuzim.

items.text: More Sodomite practices and Eliezer's cunning
items.text_en: More Sodomite practices and Eliezer's cunning
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues with more examples of Sodom's wickedness: their bed for guests, their charity scam, and their wedding custom. Eliezer again outsmarts them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes the Sodomite bed for guests, where they would cut a tall guest or stretch a short one, and Eliezer avoids it by claiming a vow.
The Gemara recounts the Sodomite charity scam: each gives a dinar with his name, but no bread is provided, so when the poor man dies, each takes back his coin.
The Gemara describes the Sodomite wedding custom where each guest must send his cloak, and Eliezer outsmarts them by claiming each neighbor invited him, causing them to flee and leave him the feast.

items.text: The fate of the charitable girl and the verse's interpretation
items.text_en: The fate of the charitable girl and the verse's interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara tells the story of a girl who gave bread to a poor person in a pitcher, leading to her death by bees. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav interprets the verse 'Za'akat Sedom' as referring to this incident of strife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara tells the story of a girl who secretly gave bread to a poor person in a pitcher, and when discovered, she was smeared with honey and placed on the city wall.
The girl was stung to death by bees, fulfilling the punishment.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav interprets the verse 'Za'akat Sedom' as referring to this incident of strife (ריב).

items.text: The spies and Korach's assembly have no share in the World to Come
items.text_en: The spies and Korach's assembly have no share in the World to Come
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the spies and Korach's assembly have no share in the World to Come, citing verses. Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer debate the fate of Korach's assembly.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the spies have no share in the World to Come, citing a verse to prove their punishment in both worlds.
The Mishnah states that Korach's assembly has no share in the World to Come, citing a verse to prove their punishment in both worlds.
Rabbi Akiva is cited as the authority for the ruling that Korach's assembly has no share in the World to Come.
Rabbi Eliezer objects, citing a verse that God brings down to the grave and raises up, implying that Korach's assembly may eventually be redeemed.

items.text: A baraisa on Korach's assembly
items.text_en: A baraisa on Korach's assembly
items.desc_en: A baraisa repeats the Mishnah's ruling, with Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira offering different interpretations of their fate.

sub.desc_en: The baraisa opens by stating that Korach's assembly has no share in the World to Come, citing verses, and attributes this view to Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira offers an alternative interpretation, comparing Korach's assembly to a lost object that is sought, citing a verse from Psalms.

items.text: Exegesis of the names of Korach and his associates
items.text_en: Exegesis of the names of Korach and his associates
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish and Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak offer homiletical interpretations of the names Korach, Datan, Aviram, On, and Pelet, and why Jacob is not listed among them.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish interprets the name Korach and his lineage homiletically, each element pointing to his sin and punishment.
The Gemara asks why the verse does not also list Jacob as an ancestor of Korach, given that Jacob's name could be interpreted negatively.
Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak answers that Jacob prayed to be excluded from the assembly of Korach and the spies, as recorded in his blessing.
The Gemara provides homiletical interpretations for the names Datan, Aviram, On, Pelet, and the tribal name Reuben, explaining their negative connotations.

items.text: On ben Pelet's wife saves him
items.text_en: On ben Pelet's wife saves him
items.desc_en: Rav relates how On ben Pelet's wife saved him from Korach's rebellion by getting him drunk and guarding the entrance to their tent.

sub.desc_en: Rav relates that On ben Pelet's wife saved him from Korach's rebellion by getting him drunk and guarding the tent entrance.

items.text: Korach's wife incites him
items.text_en: Korach's wife incites him
items.desc_en: Korach's wife criticizes Moses for nepotism and power, claiming he takes all honors for himself. She also mocks the commandment of tekhelet, arguing that if it were so important, Moses would have made all garments tekhelet. This leads to the verse about wise and foolish women.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that Korach's wife shaved his hair and everyone who saw him turned back, and then they were swallowed.
Korach's wife incites him by accusing Moses of nepotism and power-grabbing, claiming Moses took all honors for himself and his family.
Korach responds that Moses also acts similarly, and his wife retorts that since all authority is Moses's, he can say 'let my soul die with the Philistines.'
She further mocks the commandment of tekhelet (תְּכֵלֶת), arguing that if it were so important, Moses would have made all garments tekhelet.
The gemara concludes that this explains the verse about wise and foolish women: the wise woman is On ben Pelet's wife, and the foolish woman is Korach's wife.

items.text: Description of the 250 men
items.text_en: Description of the 250 men
items.desc_en: The verse describes the 250 men who joined Korach as distinguished leaders, knowledgeable in intercalation and setting months, and famous throughout the world.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse describing the 250 men who joined Korach as distinguished leaders, knowledgeable in intercalation and setting months, and famous throughout the world.

items.text: What Moses heard that made him fall
items.text_en: What Moses heard that made him fall
items.desc_en: Two opinions explain what Moses heard: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani says he was suspected of adultery, and Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak says each man was jealous of Moses regarding his wife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what report Moses heard that caused him to fall on his face.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan answers that Moses heard he was suspected of adultery with another man's wife, citing the verse 'וַיְקַנְאוּ לְמֹשֶׁה בַּמַּחֲנֶה' (they were jealous of Moses in the camp).

Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak answers that each man was jealous of Moses regarding his own wife, citing the verse 'וּמֹשֶׁה יִקַּח אֶת הָאֹהֶל וְנָטָה לוֹ מִחוּץ לַמַּחֲנֶה' (and Moses took the tent and pitched it outside the camp).

items.text: Lessons from Moses going to Datan and Aviram
items.text_en: Lessons from Moses going to Datan and Aviram
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish learns that one should not persist in a dispute, citing Rav's statement that doing so violates a negative commandment. Rav Ashi adds that such a person is liable to leprosy, based on a verbal analogy.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish cites the verse of Moses going to Datan and Aviram to derive that one should not persist in a dispute.
Rav states that anyone who persists in a dispute violates a negative commandment, as derived from the verse about Korach.
Rav Ashi adds that one who persists in a dispute is liable to leprosy, based on a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the word 'hand' in the verses about Moses and the leprous hand.

items.text: Punishments for opposing authority
items.text_en: Punishments for opposing authority
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei says one who opposes the Davidic dynasty deserves to be bitten by a snake. Rav Chisda says opposing one's teacher is like opposing the Shekhinah, and Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa says complaining against one's teacher is like complaining against God. Rabbi Abahu adds that even harboring thoughts against one's teacher is like doing so against the Shekhinah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states that one who opposes the Davidic dynasty deserves to be bitten by a snake, citing a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between the word 'זֹחֶלֶת' (crawling) in Adoniyahu's sacrifice and 'זֹחֲלֵי עָפָר' (crawlers of the dust) in the verse about snake venom.

Rav Chisda teaches that one who opposes his teacher is considered as opposing the Shekhinah (Divine Presence), citing the verse where the Israelites' quarrel with Moses is described as quarreling with God.
Rabbi Chama bar Chanina adds that one who engages in a dispute with his teacher is like one who disputes with the Shekhinah, citing the same verse about the waters of Meribah.

Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa states that one who complains against his teacher is as if complaining against the Shekhinah, citing the verse where the Israelites' complaints against Moses are redirected to God.
Rabbi Abahu adds that even harboring thoughts against one's teacher is like harboring thoughts against the Shekhinah, citing the verse where the people spoke against God and Moses.

items.text: Korach's wealth and hidden treasures
items.text_en: Korach's wealth and hidden treasures
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish identifies Korach as the subject of the verse about wealth kept for harm. Rabbi Elazar explains that wealth keeps a person standing. Rabbi Levi describes the immense keys to Korach's treasuries. Rabbi Chama bar Chanina says Joseph hid three treasures in Egypt, one of which was revealed to Korach.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish identifies the verse about wealth kept for harm as referring to Korach's wealth.
Rabbi Elazar explains that the phrase 'all the substance at their feet' refers to a person's money that keeps him standing.
Rabbi Levi describes the enormous weight of the keys to Korach's treasuries, carried by three hundred white mules.
Rabbi Chama bar Chanina says Joseph hid three treasures in Egypt, one of which was revealed to Korach.

items.text: Korach's fate: swallowed or burned?
items.text_en: Korach's fate: swallowed or burned?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says Korach was neither swallowed nor burned, citing verses that exclude him. However, a baraita teaches that Korach was both swallowed and burned, citing other verses that include him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Korach was neither among the swallowed nor among the burned, citing verses that exclude him from both fates.
A baraita contradicts Rabbi Yochanan, teaching that Korach was both among the swallowed and among the burned, citing verses that include him.

items.text: Aggadic expansions: sun and moon, Gehinnom, and Korach's sons
items.text_en: Aggadic expansions: sun and moon, Gehinnom, and Korach's sons
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the sun and moon refused to shine until God shot arrows at them, because they had not protested against Moses. Rava also interprets Moses' prayer for a new creation as opening the mouth of Gehinnom. Finally, a tradition states that Korach's sons repented and sit in a special place in Gehinnom reciting songs, and Rabba bar bar Chana recounts a story of hearing them declare Moses and his Torah true.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks about the verse describing the sun and moon standing in their heavenly dwelling due to God's arrows.
Rava explains that the sun and moon ascended to the heavenly Zevul and refused to shine until God shot arrows at them, rebuking them for not protesting earlier.
Rava asks about the verse where Moses prays for a new creation and the earth opening its mouth.
Rava explains that Moses asked God to open the mouth of Gehinnom if it already existed, or create it anew, but the creation was merely opening its entrance.
A baraita states that Korach's sons repented and were given a special place in Gehinnom where they sit and recite songs.
Rabba bar bar Chana recounts a story where a guide showed him the fissures of Korach's rebellion, and he heard voices declaring Moses and his Torah true, and themselves liars.

items.text: Opening statement on the generation of the wilderness
items.text_en: Opening statement on the generation of the wilderness
items.desc_en: A statement is made that every thirty days the generation of the wilderness is turned over in Gehenna like meat in a pot, and they say 'Moses and his Torah are true, and they are liars.'

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that every thirty days the generation of the wilderness is turned over in Gehenna like meat in a pot, and they admit that Moses and his Torah are true while they are liars.

items.text: Dispute on the generation of the wilderness
items.text_en: Dispute on the generation of the wilderness
items.desc_en: A baraita states that the generation of the wilderness has no share in the World to Come, according to Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Eliezer argues they do come, citing a verse. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha interprets the verse as referring to future generations. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya also says they come, and Rabbi Yochanan comments that Rabbi Akiva abandoned his piety.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the generation of the wilderness has no share in the World to Come, citing verses, as the opinion of Rabbi Akiva.
Rabbi Eliezer argues that they do come to the World to Come, citing a verse, and explains that God's oath was made in anger and later retracted.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha interprets the verse as referring to future generations, identifying the righteous of every generation and those who sacrificed themselves for Torah.
Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya asserts they come to the World to Come, citing a verse, and Rabbi Yochanan comments that Rabbi Akiva abandoned his piety by contradicting his own earlier lenient position.

items.text: Mishnah on the Ten Tribes
items.text_en: Mishnah on the Ten Tribes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Ten Tribes will not return, according to Rabbi Akiva, while Rabbi Eliezer argues they will return, comparing them to a day that darkens and then lights up.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Ten Tribes will not return, with Rabbi Akiva citing a verse analogy to the day that does not return, and Rabbi Eliezer arguing that just as the day darkens and then brightens, so too will they return.
Rabbi Eliezer argues that the Ten Tribes will return, interpreting 'כַּיּוֹם הַזֶּה' as a day that darkens and then lights up, so too their darkness will be followed by light.

items.text: Gemara on the Ten Tribes
items.text_en: Gemara on the Ten Tribes
items.desc_en: A baraita repeats the dispute: Rabbi Akiva says the Ten Tribes have no share in the World to Come, while Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says they return if their deeds are not like 'this day.' Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) says they do come, and Rabbi Yochanan again comments that Rabbi Akiva abandoned his piety.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the Ten Tribes have no share in the World to Come according to Rabbi Akiva, while Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Shimon that if their deeds are like today they do not return, but if not they return.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says they come to the World to Come, citing a verse, and Rabbi Yochanan comments that Rabbi Akiva abandoned his piety by contradicting his own earlier position.
Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) rules that the Ten Tribes do come to the World to Come, citing a verse about the great shofar and God's promise not to bear a grudge forever.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Akiva abandoned his piety (חסידות), citing a verse about God's mercy.

items.text: Dispute on the children of the wicked of Israel
items.text_en: Dispute on the children of the wicked of Israel
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Akiva's 'piety': a baraita states that minor children of the wicked of Israel do not come to the World to Come, according to Rabban Gamliel. Rabbi Akiva argues they do come, citing verses. For minor children of the wicked of the nations, all agree they do not come.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Akiva's piety consists of, prompting the following baraita.
A baraita states that minor children of the wicked of Israel do not come to the World to Come, citing a verse, according to Rabban Gamliel.
Rabbi Akiva argues that they do come, citing verses and reinterpreting the prooftext about root and branch.
An alternative interpretation identifies 'root' as the soul and 'branch' as the body.
The Gemara concludes that for minor children of the wicked of the nations, all agree they do not come, and Rabban Gamliel derives this from a verse.

items.text: When does a minor enter the World to Come?
items.text_en: When does a minor enter the World to Come?
items.desc_en: Amoraim dispute the age at which a minor enters the World to Come: from birth (Rabbi Chiyya or Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi), from when they speak, from conception (Ravina), from circumcision (Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak), or from when they say 'Amen' (Rabbi Meir).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks at what point a minor enters the World to Come.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
sub.desc_en: One of them says from birth, citing 'יָבֹאוּ וְיַגִּידוּ צִדְקָתוֹ לְעַם נוֹלָד'; the other says from when the child speaks, citing 'זֶרַע יַעַבְדֶנּוּ יְסֻפַּר לַה׳ לַדּוֹר'.
Ravina says from conception, citing 'זֶרַע יַעַבְדֶנּוּ'.
Rabbi Nachman bar Yitzchak says from circumcision, citing 'עָנִי אֲנִי וְגֹוֵעַ מִנֹּעַר נָשָׂאתִי אֵמֶיךָ אָפוּנָה'.
A Tanna teaches in the name of Rabbi Meir that the minor enters from the time he says 'Amen', reinterpreting 'שֹׁמֵר אֱמֻנִים' as 'שֶׁאוֹמֵר אָמֵן'.

items.text: Meaning of 'Amen'
items.text_en: Meaning of 'Amen'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'Amen' means, and Rabbi Chanina answers that it is an acronym for 'El Melech Ne'eman' (God, faithful King).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the word 'Amen' means.
Rabbi Chanina answers that 'Amen' is an acronym for 'אל מלך נאמן' (God, faithful King).

items.text: Interpretation of 'without a statute' and the remnant
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'without a statute' and the remnant
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets 'without a statute' as referring to one who leaves even one statute unfulfilled, while Rabbi Yochanan corrects him, saying it refers to one who learned only one statute. Similarly, Resh Lakish interprets 'a third' as a third of the Name, but Rabbi Yochanan says it means even a third of Noah.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets the verse 'לִבְלִי חֹק' (without a statute) as referring to one who leaves even one statute unfulfilled.
Rabbi Yochanan objects to Resh Lakish's interpretation, correcting that the verse refers to one who learned only one statute, not one who left one unfulfilled.
Resh Lakish interprets 'the third' in the verse as a third of the Divine Name.
Rabbi Yochanan objects again, correcting that the verse refers even to a third of Noah, not a third of the Name.

items.text: Interpretation of 'one from a city and two from a family'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'one from a city and two from a family'
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets the verse literally, but Rabbi Yochanan corrects him, saying that one righteous person can acquit an entire city, and two can acquit an entire family. Rav Kahana repeats Resh Lakish's view before Rav, and Rav corrects him similarly.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish interprets the verse 'one from a city and two from a family' literally, as referring to the actual number of survivors.
Rabbi Yochanan objects, saying that the verse means one righteous person acquits the entire city, and two acquit the entire family.
Rav Kahana repeats Resh Lakish's literal interpretation while sitting before Rav.
Rav corrects Rav Kahana with the same interpretation as Rabbi Yochanan, that one righteous person acquits the city and two acquit the family.

items.text: Rav's rebuke of Rav Kahana
items.text_en: Rav's rebuke of Rav Kahana
items.desc_en: Rav sees Rav Kahana washing his head and sitting before him, and quotes a verse implying he will not be found in the land of the living. Rav Kahana protests, and Rav explains that the verse refers to one who 'keeps himself alive' (i.e., is arrogant) over Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes Rav seeing Rav Kahana washing his head and sitting before him.
Rav quotes the verse 'and you will not be found in the land of the living' to rebuke Rav Kahana.
Rav Kahana protests that Rav is cursing him.
Rav explains that he is citing a verse meaning Torah will not be found in one who keeps himself alive (is arrogant) over it.

items.text: Baraita on the Exodus and the future redemption
items.text_en: Baraita on the Exodus and the future redemption
items.desc_en: A baraita taught by Rav Simai compares the Exodus to the entry into the Land, stating that only two out of sixty myriads entered the Land, and similarly only two out of sixty myriads left Egypt. Rava applies this to the days of the Messiah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Simai's baraita compares the Exodus to the entry into the Land, teaching that only two out of sixty myriads entered the Land and likewise only two out of sixty myriads left Egypt.
Rava applies the baraita's pattern to the days of the Messiah, citing a verse that compares the future redemption to the Exodus.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yosei in Alexandria and God's rebuke of Moses
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yosei in Alexandria and God's rebuke of Moses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yosei recounts meeting an elder in Alexandria who showed him the harm done to the Israelites by the Egyptians. The Gemara then relates that God rebuked Moses for questioning His ways, contrasting the faith of the Patriarchs with Moses' complaint.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Yosei recounts meeting an elder in Alexandria who showed him the harm done to the Israelites by the Egyptians, and states that Moses was punished for this.

sub.text: The Holy One, Blessed be He
sub.text_en: The Holy One, Blessed be He
sub.desc_en: God rebukes Moses for questioning His ways, contrasting the faith of the Patriarchs who did not complain despite hardships, and tells Moses he will see the war against Pharaoh but not the future war against thirty-one kings.

items.text: What Moses saw and the attribute of patience
items.text_en: What Moses saw and the attribute of patience
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Moses saw that made him bow. Rabbi Chanina ben Gamla says he saw 'Erech Apayim' (slow to anger), and the Rabbis say he saw 'Emet' (truth). A baraita supports that he saw 'Erech Apayim', and when he questioned why it was for the righteous, God said it is also for the wicked. Later, when Israel sinned, God reminded Moses of his earlier statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Moses saw that caused him to bow and prostrate himself.
Rabbi Chanina ben Gamla says Moses saw the attribute of ארך אפים (slow to anger).
The Rabbis say Moses saw the attribute of אמת (truth).
A baraita is cited in support of the opinion that Moses saw ארך אפים (slow to anger).

The baraita recounts that when Moses ascended on high, he found God writing ארך אפים (slow to anger), and when Moses questioned why it was only for the righteous, God said it is also for the wicked, and that Moses would later see why he needed this attribute.
The Gemara concludes that when Israel later sinned, God reminded Moses that he had previously said ארך אפים (slow to anger) is only for the righteous, but now he needed it for the wicked.

items.text: Moses' plea and the attribute of patience
items.text_en: Moses' plea and the attribute of patience
items.desc_en: Moses argues before God that He should be patient with sinners, citing His own words. This introduces the theme of divine patience.

sub.desc_en: Moses argues before God that He should be patient with sinners, citing His own words.

items.text: Rabbi Chaggai's inference from a verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Chaggai's inference from a verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chaggai hears a child reciting a verse and infers that God is patient (ארך אפים).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chaggai ascends the stairs of the house of Rabbah bar Sheila, hears a child reciting a verse about God's faithfulness and the adjacent verse about Moses' prayer, and infers that God is patient (ארך אפים).

items.text: God as a crown for the righteous and the interpretation of verses
items.text_en: God as a crown for the righteous and the interpretation of verses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina teaches that God will be a crown for each righteous person. The Gemara then interprets a series of verses describing various righteous acts.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina teaches that God will be a crown for each righteous person, citing a verse.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the verse's phrase 'for a crown of beauty and a diadem of glory'.
The Gemara answers that the crown is for those who do God's will and await His salvation, but not for everyone—only for those who make themselves like remnants.

The Gemara interprets a series of verses describing righteous acts: one who conquers his evil inclination, judges truthfully, overcomes his inclination, engages in Torah study, and frequents synagogues and study halls.

items.text: The Attribute of Justice questions the distinction
items.text_en: The Attribute of Justice questions the distinction
items.desc_en: The Attribute of Justice (מדת הדין) asks why some are saved and others not. God responds that even the righteous among the wicked are punished due to their association with sin, referencing Gehinnom.

sub.desc_en: The Attribute of Justice (מדת הדין) asks God why some are saved and others not.
God responds that even the righteous among the wicked are punished due to their association with sin, referencing Gehinnom.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of the apostate city (עיר הנדחת)
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of the apostate city (עיר הנדחת)
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that inhabitants of an apostate city have no share in the World to Come. It details the conditions for the city to be judged as such, including the requirement that the instigators be from that city and tribe, and that the majority be led astray. It also discusses the execution method (sword) and the fate of property, including the distinction between righteous and wicked people's assets, and the prohibition against rebuilding the city.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that inhabitants of an apostate city (עיר הנדחת) have no share in the World to Come, and lists the conditions for the city to be judged as such, including that the instigators must be from that city and tribe, the majority must be led astray, and the instigators must be men.
The Mishnah contrasts the severity for individuals (stoning, property saved) versus the many (sword, property lost).
The Mishnah cites the verse about striking the city with the sword and notes that a passing caravan saves the city.
The Mishnah derives from the verse that property of righteous people inside the city is lost, but outside is saved, while property of the wicked is always lost.
The Mishnah discusses the requirement to gather the spoil into the city square, and if there is no square, one is made, or if it is outside, it is brought inside.
The Mishnah derives from the verse that consecrated property is redeemed, terumah (תרומה) is left to rot, and second tithe and sacred writings are hidden.
Rabbi Shimon explains that performing judgment on the apostate city is considered as if one offers a whole burnt offering before God.

sub.text: Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva debate whether the city can be made into gardens and orchards, and the Mishnah concludes that when the wicked are gone, God's wrath departs.

items.text: Gemara: Exegesis of the verses regarding the instigators
items.text_en: Gemara: Exegesis of the verses regarding the instigators
