items.desc_en: The Gemara (Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael) expounds on the words of the verse: 'they went out' excludes agents, 'men' excludes women and minors, 'sons of Belial' means those who threw off the yoke of Heaven, 'from your midst' excludes the border, 'inhabitants of their city' excludes another city, and 'saying' requires witnesses and warning for each individual.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael expounds that 'they went out' excludes agents, and 'men' excludes women and minors.

The Tanna debei Rabbi Yishmael continues expounding that 'sons of Belial' means those who threw off the yoke of Heaven, 'from your midst' excludes the border, 'inhabitants of their city' excludes another city, and 'saying' requires witnesses and warning for each individual.

items.text: Dispute: Can a single city be divided between two tribes?
items.text_en: Dispute: Can a single city be divided between two tribes?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish argue whether a single city can be divided between two tribes. Rabbi Yochanan brings a proof from the Mishnah that the instigators must be from the same tribe, implying division is possible. Reish Lakish deflects by suggesting the city was inherited or given as a gift. Rabbi Yochanan then brings another proof from the division of Levitical cities, but Reish Lakish counters that the distribution was uneven (four from one tribe, five from another). The Gemara objects that if so, the verse should have specified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan holds that a single city can be divided between two tribes, while Reish Lakish holds it cannot.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish from the Mishnah: the requirement that the instigators be from the same tribe implies that a city can be divided between two tribes.
Reish Lakish deflects by suggesting the city was inherited by or given as a gift to a single tribe, not divided.
Rabbi Yochanan brings a proof from the division of Levitical cities: the verse implies that nine cities were split between two tribes, suggesting a single city can be divided.
Reish Lakish counters that the distribution was uneven: four cities from one tribe and five from the other, not a division of a single city.
The Gemara objects that if the distribution were uneven, the verse should have specified the exact numbers explicitly.

items.text: The question of those led astray on their own
items.text_en: The question of those led astray on their own
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if people were led astray on their own (not by others), are they considered part of the 'ir hanidachat? A proof is brought from a baraita about women and minors who led others astray, but it is rejected because they follow their own desires, not those of the women and minors.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if people were led astray on their own (not by others), are they considered part of the 'ir hanidachat?
The Gemara attempts to prove the matter from a baraita about women and minors who led others astray, arguing that they should be like those led astray on their own.
The Gemara rejects the proof, distinguishing that those led astray by women and minors follow the women and minors, not their own desires.

items.text: The procedure for judging the city
items.text_en: The procedure for judging the city
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses how to carry out the judgment of the city until the majority is led astray. Rav Yehuda suggests judging and imprisoning repeatedly, but Ulla objects that this would delay justice. Ulla proposes judging and stoning repeatedly. Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Ulla, while Reish Lakish suggests increasing the number of courts. A difficulty is raised from a baraita that one does not bring the entire city to the gates, and the resolution is that they increase courts, investigate, and then bring the case to the Great Sanhedrin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to carry out the judgment of the city until the majority is led astray, and Rav Yehuda proposes judging and imprisoning repeatedly.
Ulla objects that Rav Yehuda's method delays justice, and instead proposes judging and stoning repeatedly.
Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Ulla's method, while Reish Lakish suggests increasing the number of courts.
The Gemara raises a difficulty from a baraita that one does not bring the entire city to the gates for judgment.
The Gemara resolves that they increase courts, investigate, and then bring the case to the Great Sanhedrin for final judgment and execution.

items.text: The status of temporary residents
items.text_en: The status of temporary residents
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses the status of a caravan that passes through and is led astray: if they stayed 30 days, they are killed by the sword and their property is lost; if less, they are stoned and their property is saved. This is contradicted by another baraita that says one becomes a resident after 12 months. Rava resolves the contradiction: the 30-day rule applies to being considered a 'resident' for the city's laws, while the 12-month rule applies to being considered a 'son of the city' for other purposes. A supporting baraita about a vow of benefit is cited.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that a caravan that stayed 30 days in an idolatrous city is killed by the sword and its property lost; less than 30 days, stoning and property saved.
The gemara raises a contradiction: another baraita states that one becomes a resident of the city only after 12 months.

Rava resolves the contradiction: the 30-day rule applies to being considered a 'resident' (יושבי מתא) for the city's laws, while the 12-month rule applies to being considered a 'son of the city' (בני מתא) for other purposes.

A supporting baraita about a vow of benefit confirms the distinction: one who stays 12 months is considered a 'son of the city' (בני העיר), while one who stays 30 days is considered a 'resident' (יושבי העיר).

items.text: Property of the righteous and wicked
items.text_en: Property of the righteous and wicked
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verse: 'the property of the righteous outside the city is excluded, the property of the righteous inside is included, the property of the wicked outside is included.' Rabbi Shimon explains that the righteous inside lose their property because their wealth caused them to live there. Rav Chisda adds that the property of the wicked outside is only included if it was gathered into the city.

sub.desc_en: The baraita expounds the verse to exclude property of righteous outside the city, include property of righteous inside, exclude heavenly property, and include property of wicked outside.
Rabbi Shimon explains that the righteous inside lose their property because their wealth caused them to live in the city.
Mar reiterates the baraita's inclusion of property of the wicked outside the city.
Rav Chisda qualifies that the property of the wicked outside is only included if it was gathered into the city.

items.text: Deposits belonging to other cities
items.text_en: Deposits belonging to other cities
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that deposits belonging to residents of other cities that are in the apostate city are permitted. The Gemara clarifies the case: it is when the deposit is from another city and the owner accepted responsibility for it. Without that, it would be obvious that it is permitted; with responsibility, one might think it is considered his own, so the ruling teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that deposits belonging to residents of the apostate city are permitted.
The Gemara asks to clarify the circumstances of Rav Chisda's ruling.
The Gemara objects that if the deposit is from another city and located within the apostate city, it is obviously permitted since it is not considered the city's spoils.
The Gemara objects further that if the deposit belongs to residents of the apostate city but is located elsewhere, and the owners gathered into the city, why would it be permitted?
The Gemara objects that if the owners did not gather into the city, Rav Chisda already stated this ruling once before.

The Gemara resolves that the case is where the deposit is from another city but the bailee accepted responsibility for it, and the ruling teaches that despite the responsibility, it is not considered his own property.

items.text: Partially owned animals and dough
items.text_en: Partially owned animals and dough
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that an animal half-owned by the apostate city and half by another city is forbidden, but dough in the same situation is permitted. The reason is that an animal is considered undivided, while dough is considered divided.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that an animal half-owned by the apostate city is forbidden, but dough in the same situation is permitted, because an animal is considered undivided while dough is considered divided.

items.text: Questions about slaughter and hair
items.text_en: Questions about slaughter and hair
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks whether slaughter of an animal of the apostate city is effective to purify it from neveilah. Rav Yosef asks about the hair of righteous women. Rava answers that the hair of wicked women is forbidden because it requires plucking, gathering, and burning, unlike other items. Rava then asks about a gentile's sidelock: if attached, it is like the body; if hanging, is it like property of the righteous inside or like clothing? All questions remain unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks whether slaughter of the animal of an apostate city is effective to purify it from neveilah (carcass impurity), and the question remains unresolved (teiku).

Rav Yosef asks about the status of hair of righteous women in the apostate city, and Rava answers that hair of wicked women is forbidden because it requires plucking, gathering, and burning, unlike other items.
Rava asks about a gentile's sidelock: if attached, it is like the body; if hanging, is it like property of the righteous inside or like clothing? The question remains unresolved (teiku).

items.text: The requirement of a plaza
items.text_en: The requirement of a plaza
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if the city has no plaza, it cannot become an apostate city according to Rabbi Yishmael. Rabbi Akiva says they make a plaza. The dispute is over the meaning of 'its plaza': one holds it means from the beginning, the other holds it means even now.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabbi Yishmael's position: a city without a plaza cannot become an apostate city.
Rabbi Akiva counters that if the city has no plaza, they make one for it.
The Gemara resolves the dispute: one sage interprets 'its plaza' as meaning from the beginning, the other as meaning even now.

items.text: Opening Tosefta on consecrated items in an apostate city
items.text_en: Opening Tosefta on consecrated items in an apostate city
items.desc_en: The Tosefta lists the fate of different types of consecrated property in an apostate city: most holy sacrifices die, Temple funds are redeemed, terumot rot, and second tithe and sacred writings are hidden. Rabbi Shimon adds exceptions for firstborn and tithe animals, and for consecrated money.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta lists the fate of consecrated items in an apostate city: most holy sacrifices die, Temple funds are redeemed, terumot rot, and second tithe and sacred writings are hidden.
Rabbi Shimon adds exceptions for firstborn and tithe animals, and for consecrated money.

items.text: Gemara's question on why most holy sacrifices die
items.text_en: Gemara's question on why most holy sacrifices die
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why most holy sacrifices must die rather than be left to become blemished and sold. Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish offer different reasons: Rabbi Yochanan cites 'the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination', while Reish Lakish holds that these are the owner's property, referring to sacrifices for which the owner is liable.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks why most holy sacrifices must die rather than be left to become blemished, sold, and the proceeds donated.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the verse 'the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination' applies here.
Reish Lakish answers that the sacrifices are considered the owner's property, and the case involves sacrifices for which the owner bears responsibility, according to Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Reconciliation of the Tosefta with Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
items.text_en: Reconciliation of the Tosefta with Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the latter part of the Tosefta follows Rabbi Shimon, but the first part does not. It suggests that the first part deals with lesser holy sacrifices according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who considers them the owner's property, while most holy sacrifices would be redeemed. The Gemara then questions why the Tanna didn't make this distinction explicit, and answers that the case of a sin-offering whose owners died is an exception.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects that if the latter part is Rabbi Shimon, the first part must be someone else, and suggests it deals with קדשים קלים (lesser holy sacrifices) according to Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, but for most holy sacrifices they would be redeemed.

The gemara rejects this, arguing that the Tosefta should have distinguished within its own clause, but because there is a חטאת (sin-offering) whose owners died, which goes to death, the Tanna did not make the distinction.
The Gemara objects that the Tanna should have made this distinction explicit in the first part itself, rather than leaving it implicit.
The Gemara resolves that the Tanna could not make a blanket distinction because of the exceptional case of a sin-offering whose owners died, which must die and cannot be redeemed.

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why each sage does not adopt the other's view: Rabbi Yochanan relies on the verse 'the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination', while Reish Lakish argues that this applies only when the sacrifice is intact, but here it has changed status.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks why Reish Lakish does not accept Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning.
Reish Lakish explains that the verse applies only when the sacrifices are intact, but here, since they have changed (by becoming blemished), the rule changes.

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi Shimon's exclusion of firstborn and tithe
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi Shimon's exclusion of firstborn and tithe
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Shimon's exclusion of firstborn and tithe animals from the spoils. If they are unblemished, they are sacred; if blemished, they are the owner's property. Ravina explains that the exclusion applies to blemished animals that are eaten as ordinary meat, but firstborn and tithe are not eaten in that category.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what case Rabbi Shimon is discussing: if the animals are unblemished, they are sacred (שלל שמים), but if blemished, they are the owner's spoils (שללה).

Ravina answers that the case is blemished animals that are eaten as ordinary meat (בהמתה), but firstborn and tithe are excluded because they are eaten under their own sacred category, making them שלל שמים.

items.text: Shmuel's alternative interpretation
items.text_en: Shmuel's alternative interpretation
items.desc_en: Shmuel offers a different explanation: everything that can be offered when unblemished and redeemed when blemished is included in 'her spoils', but firstborn and tithe, which cannot be redeemed when blemished, are excluded by 'her cattle'.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel's statement disagrees with Ravina's explanation, ruling that anything that can be offered when unblemished and redeemed when blemished is excluded from 'her animal', while firstborn and tithe animals are excluded from 'her animal' entirely.
Shmuel states that everything that can be offered when unblemished and redeemed when blemished is included in 'her spoils'.
The gemara asks what Shmuel means by this statement.

The gemara explains that Shmuel interprets the verse: anything that can be offered when unblemished and redeemed when blemished is excluded by 'her spoils', but firstborn and tithe, which cannot be redeemed when blemished, are excluded by 'her cattle'.

items.text: Discussion on terumot: burning vs. giving to a priest
items.text_en: Discussion on terumot: burning vs. giving to a priest
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda initially says that terumah in the hands of an Israelite rots, but in the hands of a priest it is burned. Rav Yosef objects based on the parallel with second tithe, which is hidden even though it is like terumah in a priest's hands. The Gemara revises: terumah in a priest's hands rots, but in an Israelite's hands it is given to a priest in another city.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda distinguishes between terumah in an Israelite's hands, which rots, and in a priest's hands, which is burned.
Rav Yosef objects by citing the baraita that second tithe, which is analogous to terumah in a priest's hands, is hidden rather than burned.

sub.text: Revised version of Rav Chisda's statement
sub.text_en: Revised version of Rav Chisda's statement
sub.desc_en: The Gemara revises Rav Chisda's statement: terumah in a priest's hands rots, but in an Israelite's hands it is given to a priest in another city.

items.text: Discussion on second tithe: hidden vs. redeemed
items.text_en: Discussion on second tithe: hidden vs. redeemed
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages about second tithe in Jerusalem, and questions why the Tosefta says second tithe is hidden. It considers whether this applies in Jerusalem (which cannot be an apostate city) or elsewhere, and concludes that it deals with a case where the tithe became impure. Rabbi Elazar notes that impure second tithe can be redeemed even in Jerusalem, but the Gemara ultimately says the case is about purchased second tithe.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah from another tractate: Rabbi Meir exempts dough of second tithe from חלה (priestly portion), while the Sages obligate it.

Rav Chisda explains the dispute: in Jerusalem, Rabbi Meir considers second tithe ממון גבוה (sacred property), while the Sages consider it ממון הדיוט (ordinary property); outside Jerusalem, all agree it is exempt.

Rav Yosef objects from the Tosefta that second tithe is hidden (יגנזו), questioning whether this applies in Jerusalem (which cannot be an apostate city) or elsewhere (where walls would have absorbed it).
The Gemara initially considers that the Tosefta refers to the provinces, but then resolves that it deals with a case where the tithe became impure, even in another city.
The Gemara objects: why not redeem it? It cites Rabbi Elazar's proof that impure second tithe may be redeemed even in Jerusalem, based on the verse 'לא תוכל שאתו' (you cannot bear it).
The Gemara resolves that the case involves purchased second tithe (לקוח), which cannot be redeemed in Jerusalem.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer about the Mishnah's ruling on sacred books
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about the Mishnah's ruling on sacred books
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says sacred books are to be hidden (יגנזו) in the case of an apostate city, suggesting it could be redeemed if impure. It resolves that the case is when the city is pure but its partitions fell, citing Rava's distinction between the Torah law of eating and the rabbinic law of absorbing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah rules that sacred books are hidden (יגנזו) in an apostate city, since if impure they could be redeemed, and if pure they should be permitted; it notes that according to Rabbi Yehuda they would be buried, but then asks why the case is specifically an apostate city.

The Gemara resolves that the case is when the city is pure but its partitions (מחיצות) have fallen, citing Rava's distinction between the Torah law of eating and the rabbinic law of absorbing impurity.

items.text: Mishnah's ruling not according to Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Mishnah's ruling not according to Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling that sacred books are hidden contradicts Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that any city with even one mezuzah cannot become an apostate city, based on the verse 'You shall not do so to the Lord your God.'

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that the Mishnah's ruling that sacred books are hidden (יגנזו) does not follow Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that any city with even one mezuzah cannot become an apostate city, citing the verse 'and you shall not do so to the Lord your God'.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Eliezer regarding the verse
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Eliezer regarding the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Eliezer is based on Rabbi Avin's principle about general and specific statements. It concludes that both accept Rabbi Avin's principle, but they disagree on the meaning of 'עוד' (still): one says it means forever, the other says it means it cannot be rebuilt as a city but can be made into gardens and orchards.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Eliezer is based on Rabbi Avin's principle about general and specific statements.
The Gemara initially suggests that one sage accepts Rabbi Avin's principle and the other does not.

The Gemara rejects that explanation and concludes that both accept Rabbi Avin's principle, but they disagree on the meaning of 'עוֹד' (still): one says it means forever, the other says it means it cannot be rebuilt as a city but can be made into gardens and orchards.

items.text: Baraita about trees in an apostate city and the story of Jericho
items.text_en: Baraita about trees in an apostate city and the story of Jericho
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses the status of trees in an apostate city: detached trees are forbidden, attached ones are permitted. It then explains that 'another city' refers to Jericho, citing the curse of Joshua. A further baraita clarifies that Jericho cannot be rebuilt under another name, and another city cannot be named Jericho. The Gemara elaborates on the deaths of Abiram and Segub, showing that the curse was fulfilled gradually.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating the rule for trees in an apostate city: detached trees are forbidden, attached ones are permitted.
The baraita adds that trees from 'another city' are forbidden whether detached or attached.
The Gemara asks what 'another city' refers to.
Rav Chisda answers that 'another city' refers to Jericho, citing Joshua's curse.
A supporting baraita clarifies that Jericho cannot be rebuilt under another name, nor another city named Jericho, citing the story of Hiel.
A baraita comments that Abiram the firstborn was wicked and should have learned from the curse, while Segub the youngest should have learned.
The Gemara asks what the baraita means by 'should have learned' regarding Abiram and Segub.
The Gemara explains that the baraita means the wicked Hiel should have learned from Abiram's death, and the phrase 'Segub his youngest' teaches that he was burying continuously from Abiram to Segub.

items.text: Story of Ahab, Elijah, and the keys of rain and resurrection
items.text_en: Story of Ahab, Elijah, and the keys of rain and resurrection
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Ahab was Elijah's best man. Elijah and Ahab went to visit a mourner, and Elijah confirmed Joshua's curse. Ahab argued that Moses' curse (of drought) was not fulfilled despite idolatry, so Joshua's curse would not hold. Elijah then swore there would be no rain. Later, Elijah prayed for rain and received the key of rain, but when he prayed for resurrection, he was told that three keys (birth, rain, resurrection) are not given to a messenger, so he had to return the key of rain to receive the key of resurrection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Ahab was Elijah's best man; they visited a mourner, and Elijah confirmed that Joshua's curse applied to Jericho.
Ahab objects that Moses' curse of drought was not fulfilled despite widespread idolatry, so Joshua's curse should not hold either.
Elijah immediately swears there will be no rain, prays, receives the key of rain, and departs.

sub.text: Gemara's narrative with Rav Yehuda and Rav
sub.text_en: Gemara's narrative with Rav Yehuda and Rav
sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts Elijah's hiding at the brook Cherith, where ravens brought him food from Ahab's slaughterhouse, and later the brook dried up.

Elijah prays for the key of resurrection but is told that three keys (birth, rain, resurrection) are not given to a messenger; he must return the key of rain to receive the key of resurrection, and God commands him to go to Ahab to give rain.

items.text: Parable of Elijah and the key, and Rabbi Yosei's teaching
items.text_en: Parable of Elijah and the key, and Rabbi Yosei's teaching
items.desc_en: A Galilean taught a parable: Elijah is like a man whose ship was wrecked and lost his key. Rabbi Yosei of Tzippori taught about 'Abba Elijah' (a title for Elijah).

sub.desc_en: A Galilean preacher taught a parable before Rav Chisda: Elijah is like a man whose ship was wrecked and who lost his key.
Rabbi Yosei of Tzippori taught that Elijah is called 'Abba Elijah' (a title of honor).

items.text: Story about Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's strictness
items.text_en: Story about Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's strictness
items.desc_en: A story illustrates Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's strictness: a student who was accustomed to visiting him stayed away for three days after being called 'strict,' and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi then called himself strict.

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi as strict and describes that a student who regularly visited him stayed away for three days.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asks the student why he did not come.
The student answers that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi called him strict, implying offense.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi resolves the tension by pointing out that the student himself is now being strict by staying away.

items.text: Interpretation of the verse about the ban
items.text_en: Interpretation of the verse about the ban
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'And nothing of the banned item shall cleave to your hand' to mean that as long as the wicked are in the world, wrath is in the world. Rav Yosef identifies the wicked as thieves.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'וְלֹא יִדְבַּק בְּיָדְךָ מְאוּמָה מִן הַחֵרֶם' (And nothing of the banned item shall cleave to your hand) to mean that as long as the wicked are in the world, wrath (חרון אף) is in the world.
The Gemara asks: Who are these wicked (רשעים) referred to in the interpretation?
Rav Yosef answers: The wicked are thieves (גנבי).

items.text: Baraita on the arrival and departure of the righteous and wicked
items.text_en: Baraita on the arrival and departure of the righteous and wicked
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that when a wicked person comes into the world, wrath comes; when a wicked person perishes, good comes; when a righteous person departs, evil comes; when a righteous person arrives, good comes, each supported by a biblical verse.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that when a wicked person comes into the world, wrath comes, citing the verse 'בבוא רשע בא גם בוז ועם קלון חרפה' (When a wicked person comes, contempt also comes, and with disgrace, reproach).
The baraita continues: when a wicked person perishes from the world, good comes, citing the verse 'ובאבוד רשעים רנה' (And when the wicked perish, there is rejoicing).

The baraita states: when a righteous person departs from the world, evil comes, citing the verse 'הצדיק אבד ואין איש שם על לב... כי מפני הרעה נאסף הצדיק' (The righteous perishes and no one takes it to heart... for because of the evil the righteous is gathered).

The baraita concludes: when a righteous person comes into the world, good comes, citing the verse 'זה ינחמנו ממעשינו ומעצבון ידינו' (This one will comfort us from our work and from the pain of our hands).
